PREFACE 

It has been almost thirty years since the landmark work, 

"How To Defend A Criminal Case," by Housel and 

Walser, was written. The fact that there is still a great demand for this book, although it has never been kept up to date, and it has been out of print for a considerable time, attests to the importance of the subject and the dearth of published material thereon. The question most frequently asked of me by lawyers during my twenty-odd years in the law book business has been "What do you have on Criminal Procedure for New York?" And my answer has invariably been "Nothing." 29 The purpose of this book is to fill this void in our criminal jurisprudence. Every word of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure, and other relevant statutes, as well as thousands of judicial decisions, have been carefully examined, with the view towards making this work as comprehensive and accurate as possible. The advice of personnel of all branches of our criminal court system has been sought about the actual procedures to be followed therein. 

I am especially indebted to Henry W. Schober, Esq., former Chief of the Appeals Bureau, of the Queens County District Attorney's office, for supplying most of the information for the Practical Suggestions, at the head of many chapters of the instant work. 

My sincere thanks and appreciation go to Edward

Marks, Esq., of the Nassau County Bar, for his editorial assistance and his round the clock labors in the compilation of the index herein. This is a book that the specialist in criminal matters cannot be without and the general practitioner dare not be without. 

New York, 1960

The Publisher

PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

Ordinarily, a person who is arrested by the police, is taken into custody by invitation or physical force and detention. The arrestee is invited by the officer to accompany him to the stationhouse so that an investigation can be made by interrogation. After the officer has completed his investigation, the arrestee is booked. This is a process of fingerprinting the defendant and filling out a police department form, calling for the accused's name, address, other identifying data and the crime with which he is charged. This form is then taken to Police Headquaters to obtain information regarding any prior police record.

After the defendant is booked, he is taken to Police Headquarters where he is usually placed in a lineup, is photographed and inter- 1

§ 

rogated by a representative of the Police Department in the presence of other police officers, and then brought to a court for arraignment and preliminary examination. If the defendant is arrested at a time when court is not in session, he is kept in custody in the local precinct, and then brought to lineup and arraignment the following morning.

An attorney is usually called on the telephone by a friend or relative of the accused, or by the accused himself, and informed of the arrest. The attorney should contact a bail bondsman immediately to obtain bail for the prisoner, if the offense is a bailable one. He should then notify the police officer in charge of the investigation that he is appearing for the defendant and attempt to relieve his client of further police interrogation. If the accused phones the attorney directly, he should be asked merely to state his place of detention, and to say nothing more at this time, lest he be overheard. He should also be warned to sign nothing and to refrain from discussing the case with anyone, even friends or relatives. 

The accused should be told to reveal nothing to the police, except his name and address.

The attorney must attempt to interview his client, without delay, and should request the officer in charge to allow him to do so. If this request is not granted, the attorney should demand that his client be brought to court for immediate arraignment. If this demand is likewise denied, the attorney should seek the release of his client by instituting a habeas corpus proceeding. (See chapter on "Habeas Corpus.")

Sec. 1. Definitions. Code of Crim. Proc. sec. 167 defines an arrest as "the taking of a person into custody that he may be held to answer for a crime." This definition is substantially identical to that contained in the American Law In stitute's Model Code of Criminal Procedure, section 18: 

"Arrest is the taking of a person into custody in order that he may be forthcoming to answer for the commission of an offense." Code Crim. Proc., sec. 171, states: “An arrest is made by an actual restraint of the person of the defendant, or by his submission to the custody of the officer." This section is comparable to the Model Code, section 19 (1): "An arrest is made by an actual restraint of the person to 2

$be arrested, or by his submission to the custody of the person making the arrest." 

All of the above definitions are substantial re-enactments of the common law rules, and all leave much unsaid. "It is said there was no arrest; and some cases are cited to show that submission to process without compulsion, is no arrest nor imprisonment. Yet we understand the law to be well settled, that no manual touching the body, or actual force is necessary to constitute an arrest and imprisonment. It is sufficient if the party be within the power of the officer and submits to the arrest." (Gold and Sill v. Bissell, 1 Wend. 210, 215.) However, although no "manual touching" is necessary, an oral direction alone, by a police officer, directed to a person, ordering that person to be in court on a certain date, in the future, has been held insufficient to constitute an arrest. "While it may be true that such a procedure has about all the binding force of a 'Royal invitation'-in other words, of a command-I do not think that it amounted to an arrest." (People v. Yerman, 138 

Misc. 272, 246 N.Y.S.665.)

It has also been held that a temporary detention of a person, for a purpose other than the holding to answer for a crime, is not an arrest. In People v. Marendi, 213 N.Y. 

600, the Court of Appeals stated: "The defendant was not taken into custody by Officer Mutha 'that he might be held to answer for a crime' but only that he might be searched. *** although there was an arrest in the sense of a detention, the People's evidence unmistakably shows that the defendant was not taken into custody that he might be held to answer for a felony or for any crime." Thus, it was held that there was insufficient evidence to uphold defendant's conviction of the felony of escaping from the lawful custody of an officer while being held upon a charge or arrest. 

A useful list of the requisites of an arrest is given by 

Professor Perkins in "The Law of Arrest," 24 Iowa L. Rev. 

201, 208: "(1) A purpose to take the person into custody, (2) Under a real or pretended authority, (3) Resulting in an actual or constructive seizure or detention of his person, 3

$ 

cas (4) So understood by the arrestee." In accordance with the usage of some courts (See, e.g., State v. District Court, 106 

Mont. 347, 78 Pac. 2d 353), the term "arrestee" will be used herein to refer to the subject of the arrest; the term "arrestor" to refer to the person making, or attempting to make, the arrest. The distinction between an arrest and a response to a summons is discussed in the succeeding chapter. The phrase "without warrant" used in the title to this chapter is intended to cover all arrests without warrant, including those made under the special authority of the arrestor, such as in the case of a magistrate orally ordering an arrest under powers given him in Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 182.

Sec. 2. History. One of the earliest authorities to discuss the law of arrest, in England, in detail was Dalton in "The Countrye Justice," the first edition of which was published in 1618. As quoted in Hall, Legal and Social Aspects of Arrest Without a Warrant, 49 Harv. L. Rev. 566, 567-568,

Dalton stated that "every private person" may arrest without warrant "whom he knoeth or seeth to have committed a *** felonie. *** Also when a felony is committed, every man may arrest suspicious persons that be of evill fame. ***But for the arresting of such suspicious persons, note, that there must be some felony committed indeed. 

Sherife, Bailifes, Constables, and other the Kings Officers may arrest and imprison offenders, in all cases where a private person may, and without any writ or warrant. * * *

The Justice of the Peace may arrest and imprison offenders in all cases where a private person may." 

In keeping with the relatively minor status of police officers at that time, little attention was directed, or extra authority given, them. Hale, writing in his famous treatise, "Pleas of the Crown", at pages 84-85, later stated: "*** these officers may without any other warrant but from themselves arrest felons, and they that are probably suspected of felonies." Hale, therefore, apparently recognized a greater authority to be vested in police officers, and com-

§parable officials, than that vested in private persons, and he stated that officers are "more eminently trusted they are by law punishable if they neglect their duty and therefore*** they should have the greatest protection and encouragement in the due execution of their office." 

Hale also stated, however, that with respect to both private persons and officers, there had, in fact, to be a felony actually committed to justify an arrest without a warrant. 

Blackstone stated: "Upon probable suspicion also a private person may arrest a felon, *** [Officers may arrest] in case of felony actually committed, *** he may upon probable suspicion arrest the felon." (4 Bl. Comm. 292-3.) It should be noted that professional police forces came into being no earlier than 1753, when the "Bow Street Runners" were organized, and the establishment of the first modern police force, like those now in existence, occurred in 1829. 

Thus there was little reason, prior to that time, to give much thought to the need for police officers to have greater powers concerning arrests than those given private persons.

At common law, the rules concerning arrests without warrants were, in many respects, similar to the rules now embodied in the Code of Criminal Procedure. Then, private persons could not arrest for misdemeanors without warrant, unless they were also breaches of the peace, and there was a division of authority concerning an officer's authority to arrest for such an offense; if a breach of the peace were involved, both could arrest to end or prevent the crime. This right extended to the arrest of the perpetrator of the crime for a period shortly after the crime had been committed. A private person could then arrest for the commission of a felony if the crime, in fact, had been committed, and if the arrestor had a reasonable belief that the arrestee had committed the felony. An officer, on the other hand, could arrest for a felony, even if it were not in fact committed, if he had a reasonable belief that the crime had been committed and that the arrestee was the guilty party.

§ 

 Sec. 3. When Arrest Without Warrant Allowable. Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 177, states: "A peace officer may, without a warrant, arrest a person, 1. For a crime, committed or attempted in his presence; 

2. When the person arrested has committed a felony, although not in his presence; 

3. When a felony has in fact been committed, and he has reasonable cause for believing the person to be arrested to have committed it; 

4. When he has reasonable cause for believing that a felony has been committed, and that the person arrested has committed it, though it should afterward appear that no felony has been committed, or, if committed, that the person arrested did not commit it."

Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 183 states: "A private person may arrest another, 1. For a crime committed or attempted in his presence; 

2. When the person arrested has committed a felony, though not in his presence."

Thus the authority of a peace officer, under Section 177, and of private persons, under Section 183, is greater than at common law insofar as those sections give the right to arrest for any crime committed in the presence of the arrestor. The word "crime" in those sections includes all misdemeanors, including those not breaches of the peace (People v. Averill, 124 Misc. 383, 208 N.Y.S. 774; Squadrito v. Guebock, 1 N.Y. 2d 471, 154 N.Y.S. 2d 37), a right not extended at common law (Breland v. Gray, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 291).

Until subdivision 4 of Section 177 was added, in 1958, peace officers in New York, were subjected to greater restraints than at common law insofar as they were not given authority to arrest without a warrant when they had a reasonable belief that a felony had been committed; without that subdivision, officers, as are private persons under Section 183, were restricted to arrests for crimes that had, in fact, been committed. Now officers in New 

York have been given the same rights as those given of-

§ ficers in the later days of the common law, while private persons are subjected to greater restrictions than were imposed in those days.

Authority is given to peace officers, in Vehicle and Traffic Law, section 70 (5-c), to arrest, without a warrant, for certain violations of the traffic laws, "which in fact have been committed, although not in his presence, when the officer has reasonable cause to believe that the violation was committed by [the arrestee]". The violations, in summary, are operating a vehicle while intoxicated, when coupled with an accident or collision in which the arrestee was involved, and leaving the scene of an accident, or of an injury to certain animals, without reporting it when the arrestee was involved in the operation of a vehicle involved in the accident or injury.

In People v. Belcher, 302 N.Y. 529, defendant was arrested, without a warrant, by an officer who had arrived at the scene of an automobile accident in which the defendant was involved, and who, while there, perceived defendant to have the smell of liquor on his breath and noted defendant's "unsteady and staggering gait." The defendant also admitted to the officer that he had been the driver of one of the cars involved in the accident. The Court of Appeals stated: "No warrant of arrest was sought or requested; and none was necessary in view of defendant's unquestionably lawful arrest ***" The practicalities which require the allowance of such arrests without warrants are obvious. The word "crime" in sections 177 and 180, includes traffic offenses also. As stated by the Court of Appeals in Squadrito v. Greibock, 1 N.Y. 2d 479, 154 N.Y.S. 2d 37, if it were not so construed "a peace officer could never make an arrest for a traffic violation without a warrant, pursuant to Section 177, even if the offense were committed in his presence. Before an officer would be privileged to take the offender into custoday, he would have to find a magistrate, perhaps miles away, and obtain a warrant of arrest, a consequence that would not only hamper prompt and effective enforcement

§ (a) 

but would favor nonresidents over residents of the State without basis or reason." Thus, under Section 177, arrests without warrants may be made when the traffic offense is committed in the officer's presence, and under Code Crim. 

Proc., sec. 180, the officer need not inform the arrestee of the reason for his arrest. 

Sec. 3(a). Arrests by Police. If a felony has in fact been committed, it is not necessary that the reasonable belief of the arresting officer arise out of his personal knowledge based on his investigation of the crime. In Saunders v. 

State, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 138, a claimant sought to sue the State of New York for false imprisonment, false arrest and malicious prosecution. He had been arrested by New York 

City police for a crime committed in Nassau County. Nassau County police officers came to his place of detention with the alleged victim of the crime. The victim, upon seeing the claimant in another room, identified him as the perpetrator of the crime, whereupon the Nassau County policeman took him to that county for trial. He was subsequently indicted and the indictment was dismissed. The court stated: "The arrest was without warrant but a felony had in fact been committed. The claimant having been identified as the perpetrator thereof by the victim, the police officers had reasonable cause to believe that [he] ***had committed the crime. Therefore, a warrant was not necessary. 

However, a third person's complaint will not suffice to justify a police officer's use of force to effect an arrest in all situations. In People v. Field, 15 N.Y.S. 2d 561, defendant was charged with assault upon a police officer. Defendant's wife had gone to a police station to report a charge against the defendant. Two police officers were assigned to investigate the matter and, upon arriving at defendant's house, requested the defendant to allow them to enter in order to discuss the matter with him. Defendant opened the door slightly and one officer wedged his foot therein, whereupon defendant attempted to close the door, the of-

§3(a) ficer forced his way into the house, a fight ensued and after subduing defendant he was taken to the police station and later tried for assault. While dismissing the information filed against defendant, the court stated: "the complaining police officer entered the defendant's home by force and against his will. He had no warrant for his arrest. No felony had been committed pointing to him. No crime was then being perpetrated therein, nor had the defendant at the time of entry committed any crime in his presence. 

The officers, therefore, when they proceeded to defendant's home, had no right to arrest him. Having no authority to arrest, they had no right to forcibly enter. Their entrance was unlawful. In attempting to justify the right of the complainant officers to forcibly enter and then arrest, the prosecution urges that the defendant 'slammed the door on the police officer's foot, thereby assaulting the police officers,' and so warranted the officer in arresting him. It is a novel and startling proposition that a householder may not slam his door in the face of an intruder who unlawfully puts his foot in the open crack of the door, without thereby committing an assault! The threshold of a door is still a barrier to a citizen's castle which may not lawfully, except on invitation, be crossed by a stranger with no present authority to arrest. A complaint from the defendant's wife may explain the officers' presence, but mere complaint did not justify force-where no crime was being committed.

Certain courts have indicated that different standards should be applied to determine the reasonableness of the officer's belief that the arrestee is the guilty party, the standards varying depending upon the type of action in which the question is raised. However at this point it should be noted that, generally, an inference that the belief was reasonable, will be raised by either a holding of the arrestee, by a magistrate, for examination, or by an indictment of the defendant by a Grand Jury. "Is the holding by the magistrate and the indictment by the Grand Jury prima facie evidence that the arresting officer had

§ 3(a) 

reasonable cause to believe that the [arrestee] was guilty of the crime charged. *** It would be so if the action were for malicious prosecution. Does the same presumption arise when the only issue is the existence of 'reasonable cause' for making the arrest? We think this court is committed to the doctrine that the same rule is applicable to both."

As stated above, both officers and private persons may arrest for crimes committed or attempted in their presence. The definition of presence for this purpose has given rise to certain problems. In People v. Esposito, 118 Misc. 

867, 194 N.Y.S. 326, while discussing the lawfulness of an arrest for the crime of illegally possessing a concealed weapon, the court stated: "Was the crime committed in the presence of the officer? The defendant was on the street a few paces from the officer; all that intervened between the officers and the physical object, the body of the offense, was a brief space and a bit of cloth. To this mere propinquity were joined visible indications in some degree sig nificant. [These indications] *** 

*** might reasonably have been considered flight, with its implication of guilt. Personal presence includes corporeal extension within the sphere of sense perception. Presence is not the same as view. To justify arrest without a warrant by an officer for a misdemeanor, the statute requires that the offense be actually committed or attempted in the officer's presence. 

There is no definite statement of the necessary extent of the evidence conveyed to the officer's consciousness. The purpose of the permission is promptness, to secure apprehension and identification. In the emergency the officer proceeds or tarries at his peril. If he does not act, he may incur penalty of dereliction. If in arresting he makes mistake of law or fact as to the commission of the offense, no matter how clearly apparent to him may seem the doing of the forbidden act by the person arrested, the officer is a trespasser and liable accordingly."

The courts very generally hold that an offense is committed within the presence of an officer when his senses 10

§3(a) afford him knowledge that such is the fact. Garshe v. 

United States, 1 F. 2d 620 (8th Cir.) Under the federal as well as the state statutes, to justify a search and seizure, or an arrest without a warrant the officer must have direct knowledge through his hearing, sight or other sense of the commission of the crime. *** The rule as to when a crime is committed in the presence of an officer is well stated in Ex Parte Morill (C.C.) 35 Fed. 261, 267, where 

Judge Deady held that 'A crime is committed in the presence of an officer when the facts and circumstances occurring within his observation, in connection with what under the circumstances, may be considered as common knowledge, give him probable cause to believe or reasonable ground to suspect, that such is the case. It is not necessary, therefore, that the officer should be an eye or an ear witness of every fact and circumstance involved in the charge, or necessary to the commission of the crime.' (Agnello v. United States, 290 Fed. 671, 679.)

In Leach v. State, 235 Pac. 2d 968 (Okla.), the court stated: "The constitution and statutes of Oklahoma is that where the offense is not a felony an officer cannot arrest without a warrant, unless the offense was committed or attempted in his presence, and, where the officer does not know of the act constituting the offense, it is not committed in his presence." Although there appears to be no Court of Appeals decision in New York on this point, it is doubtful that an argument advocating adoption of the Oklahoma rule would be successful, particularly since the Oklahoma courts recognize that their rule is not in accord with the majority view. It appears that the majority rule, synonymous with that enunciated by the court in People v. 

Esposito, supra, gives sufficient protection to the arrestee, without unduly hampering the police. A reasonable basis for the officer's belief is required, and the definition of presence is in accord with the realities of the situation. 

Once an arrest has been made the officer has committed himself, and any mistake on his part gives rise to a remedy 11

§ 3(b) 

on the part of the arrestee. Of course that remedy is not without its limitations.

Sec. 3(b). Private Persons. A private person may arrest only for a felony that has been committed, and may, rightfully, arrest only the guilty party therefor. He cannot, as in the case of an officer, arrest when there has been either a felony committed or reasonable ground for believing so, and when there are reasonable grounds for believing that the arrestee is the guilty party, otherwise, private persons have the same rights as officers, and the same rules would apply. 

In Doherty v. Lester, 4 Misc. 2nd 741, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 219, plaintiff sued a private detective for assault. The detective had shot the plaintiff during a chase, after plaintiff had fled from a group of persons chasing him and two friends, one of whom had previously appropriated a taxicab without authority. The court stated: "A private detective is not a police officer and has no greater right to make an arrest than ordinary citizens. * * * As such, before he or anyone else, not a police officer, can attempt an arrest, for a crime not committed in his presence, a felony must in fact have been committed, and by the person arrested. Code Crim. 

Proc. sec. 183. Thus, if a private person *** assumes the role of a policeman, he does so at his peril, and if he arrests the wrong person, he is answerable." Some language in the 1909 decision in Gearity v. Strasbourger, 133 App. Div. 

701, 118 N.Y.S. 257, indicates that that court might have attempted a distinction in the definition of "presence," applicable in the case of a private person making an arrest, from that presence required in the case of an officer. The 

Appellate Division there stated, in an action brought for false imprisonment, false arrest and malicious prosecution, arising out of an arrest for shoplifting: "If the plaintiff committed the crime of petit larcency, there is no evidence that either of the appellants saw her commit it. 

The arrest therefore was unlawful." However, that statement was only dictum, and it is doubtful that a successful 12

§argument can be made advocating a stricter definition of presence to be applied in the case of private persons. There appears to be no reason for such an approach. 

Sec. 4. Assisting in Arrests. Penal Law, section 1848, states: "A person who after having been lawfully commanded to aid an officer in arresting any person, or in retaking any person who has escaped from legal custody or in executing any legal process, wilfully neglects or refuses to aid such officer is guilty of a misdemeanor." See Burlington v. Yellow Taxi Corp., 250 N.Y. 14, for a discussion of the history of this section. However, the main problem in this area arises out of suits against persons assisting officers, where the officer is later determined to have been acting unlawfully. The difficult case is posed when the officer would, without doubt, be recognized as such by the average person at the time of the request; but where the person whose aid is requested is not connected with the proceeding in any way, acting, when aiding the officer, as the normal person would, and as the normal person must, upon penalty of the law. In Elder v. Morrison, 10 Wend. 

128, the court stated: "If a stranger comes in aid of an officer in doing a lawful act, as executing legal process, but the officer, by reason of some subsequent improper act, becomes a trespasser ab initio, the stranger does not thereby become a trespasser **but when the original act of the officer is unlawful, any stranger who aids him. will be a trespasser, though he acts by the officer's command." 

In Jennings v. Carter, 2 Wend. 446, the court recognized the now generally prevailing rule that a private person, summoned to the aid of an officer, is under only the very slightest duty to ascertain the lawfulness of the officer's conduct and authority, and upon fulfillment of this slight duty, the stranger or private person will not be liable if the officer's acts later are determined to have been unlawful. 

Certainly, that rule is the more equitable one; to impose upon ordinary persons the duty to ascertain correctly the 13

§ 

extent of an officer's authority, or to be guilty of a misdemeanor for underestimating that authority, or to become liable for suit if the estimate was slightly generous, where determination of that question might not be easily made by legal counsel, is to place a person between Scylla and Charybdis. 99 

Sec. 5. Vagrants and Disorderly Persons. Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 890 states: "A peace officer must, when required by any person, bring a vagrant before a magistrate of the same city, village or town, or, in the City of New York, before a City Magistrate, for the purpose of examination." Code Crim. Proc., sec. 887, defines vagrants, and

Section 894 states: "It is the duty of every peace officer of the county, city or village or town, where a person described in the seventh subdivision of section eight hundred and eighty-seven is found [disguised persons on a road, highway, field or lot] to arrest and take him before a magistrate *** to be proceeded against as a vagrant.' 

Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 895, states: "A private citizen of the county may also, without warrant, exercise the powers conferred upon a peace officer by the last section." Despite the seeming limitation of the sections last cited to only one type of a vagrant (that type described in section 887, subdivision 7), the court, in People v. Formiscio, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 

149, stated: "The implication of sections 890, 894 and 895 seems clear that peace officers have the power, on their own initiative, to arrest summarily in all cases of vagrancy." However, in People v. Formiscio, supra, the officer effecting the arrest did so pursuant to the direction of the District Attorney and, therefore, came within the scope of Section 890. The court held "The [District At torney] *** is such a person as may require the arrest of a vagrant by a peace officer, within the meaning of said section." 

Code of Crim. Proc., sections 899 through 913, concern the proceedings to be had in the case of disorderly persons. 

Section 899 describes such persons as those abandoning 14

cos or threatening to abandon dependents without support, fortune tellers, gamblers, madames and "Common showmen and mountebanks who exhibit or perform for profit idle shows, acts or feats, ". The last quoted phrase, at first glance, appears to be one of those enacted in the distant past, but still maintained on the statute books through inadvertence. However such is not the case. In 1949, that section was amended to add the word "common" and to delete, after that word, "jugglers, common, and those who perform puppet shows, wire and rope dancers." In any event, it is doubtful that any serious problems will arise under that section. 

In People v. Phillips, 284 N.Y. 235, the Court of Appeals held that disorderly persons, as defined in Section 899, cannot be arrested summarily unless they commit a breach of the peace (in which event they could be arrested summarily without the section). When there has been no breach of the peace, the Court held, the magistrate could obtain jurisdiction only pursuant to a warrant issued under section 900. In People v. Formiscio, supra, the Court noted that no provision exists, comparable to section 900, applicable to vagrants.

Sec. 6. Use of Force. To Effect Arrest. Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 178, gives, to peace officers making arrests without warrants, authority to break open doors, windows, etc., if "After notice of his office and purpose, he be refused admittance thereto," when such admittance is necessary to effect an arrest. This section is similar to Section 175, which gives similar powers to officers executing warrants of arrest. Arrests without warrants are treated in Part IV, Chapter IV, of Title 3 of the Code; arrests with warrants are treated in Chapter III thereof. Section 174 of Chapter 

III (arrests with warrant) empowers officers to "use all necessary means to effect the arrest" if, after the officer gives notice of his office and purpose, the defendant flees or forcibly resists the arrest. There is no comparable provision in Chapter IV (arrests without warrant). However, 15

§ 

by its terms, Section 174 is not limited to cases of arrests under a warrant. Penal Law, section 246, states, in part, that the "use or attempt or offer to use, force or violence upon or towards the person of another is not unlawful in the following cases: 

1. When necessarily committed by a public officer in the performance of a legal duty; or by any other person assisting him or acting by his direction; 

2. When necessarily committed by any person in arresting one who has committed a felony. * * * " Thus officers, and those assisting them in effecting arrests without warrants, are excepted, by the above quoted sections, from prosecution for assault concerning actions taken while in the course of such conduct. In Lippert v. State, 207 Misc. 

632, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 751, the arrestee had been stopped, by police officers, while driving a car and asked for his driver's license and registration, pursuant to authority given the officers by Vehicle and Traffic Law sections 11 (4) and 20 (1) (f). He refused to accede to the request and, according to the officers, became violent and abusive. He was thereupon subdued, handcuffed, and arrested for disorderly conduct. He later made claim against the State for damages arising out of the alleged assault against him, and sued for false arrest and imprisonment. The court dismissed his claim, noting that his conduct constituted a breach of the peace, and that after the officers had told him that they were effecting the arrest for disorderly conduct, the subsequent "use of force was not 

ance of *** regular duty. Penal Law, sec. 246. There was no assault committed, therefore, unless the force used upon claimant *** under the circumstances herein was more than that necessary to effect claimant's arrest. The troopers could not employ force carelessly or unnecessarily. If they did so employ force and injured claimant, they could be penalized. Whether they did or did not is a question of fact." A similar situation was considered by 16

§ 6(a) the court in Houghtaling v. State, 11 Misc. 2d 1049, 175 

N.Y.S.2d 659.

Thus, even though there is no specific statutory authority empowering officers to use force in effecting arrests without warrants for offenses other than felonies, use of the necessary amount of force to effect the arrest will not be considered unlawful, and, obviously, is necessary for the functioning of the police force. It is, of course, an officer's duty to suppress any offense being committed in his presence. Therefore, under Penal Law, section 246, his use of force in so doing, if reasonable, will not constitute an assault. The officer, in all cases, may use only that amount of force necessary to effect the arrest and subdue the arrestee. If the officer could "with diligence and caution have taken and held [arrestee] ***, to shoot him to prevent his escape was unnecessary, *** firing indiscriminately at a man approximately eight feet away was gross negligence." (Fletcher v. State, 183 N.Y.S. 2d 265.) "a police officer has a right to use as much force as is necessary to make an arrest, and the jury should not measure precisely the limits to which he went, unless they find he exceeded all proper and rational bounds." (People v. Denker, 225 App. Div. 517, 234 N.Y.S. 32.) "A police officer has a right to use whatever means necessary to make an arrest and unless he exceeds proper and rational bounds or acts in a negligent or wanton manner, he is not liable for damages sustained, even by innocent parties." (Wrubel v. 

State, 11 Misc. 2d 878, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 687.) 

Sec. 6(a). To Resist Arrest. One being unlawfully arrested may use force to resist the arrest. Thus, in People v. 

Massey, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 473, defendant, who had been convicted of assault and resisting arrest, on appeal, had his conviction reversed. The court stated: "the record does establish appellant's assault, if any, upon the officer occurred during the course of appellant's resistance to the attempt of that officer, without warrant, to force appellant, against his will, to accompany to the stationhouse for 17

§ (a) 

questioning as a suspect in the commission of a reported crime of stone throwing, a misdemeanor. Under the circumstances the conduct of the police officer constituted an unlawful arrest of the appellant and justified his resistance and the counter assault upon the police officer." 

One of the leading cases in this area is People v. Cherry, 307 N.Y. 308. There, defendant, while on his way home at night, was apprehended by two persons who claimed to be police officers. He attempted to escape from them, was restrained, and then fought against his restraint. The 

Court of Appeals, while reversing his conviction of third degree assault, stated: "The police officers were, as everyone acknowledges, guilty of an illegal arrest and an unlawful assault. * * * Defendant had the privilege, therefore, of resisting and using 'force and violence' against his assailants, even though they were police officers, 'to prevent an offense against his person *** if the force and violence *** [was] not more than sufficient to prevent such offense.' (Penal Law, sec. 246, subd. 3.) The standard by which defendant must be judged is phrased solely in terms of the physical necessities of the situation presented. If force is necessary to prevent an unlawful arrest, then force may be employed, the one limitation on its exercise being that the victim may not pursue his counterattack merely for the sake of revenge or the infliction of needless injury. ***

If defendant had any right to prevent his arrest, he was privileged to take effective steps toward that end and was not confined to words or pushes or other futile gestures." 

Penal Law, sec. 1851, provides that any person who wilfully resists a public officer in discharging, or attempting to discharge, his duty, is guilty of a misdemeanor. 

However that section does not make persons rightfully resisting an arrest, or an illegal search or seizure, misdemeanants (People v. Richter, 265 App. Div. 767, 40 N.Y.S. 

2d 751). Penal Law, sec. 1825, makes resistance, by force or violence, to the performance of duty by an executive officer, a misdemeanor. Police officers are considered executive officers within the meaning of that section (People v. 18

$

Stewart, 182 Misc. 212, 47 N.Y.S. 2d 349). However that section also does not apply to one resisting an unlawful arrest (People v. O'Connor, 257 N.Y. 473; People v. Mc- 

Carthy, 188 Misc. 133, 67 N.Y.S. 2d 560). Unlawful resistance to arrest is a felony (second degree assault) if accompanied by an assault upon the arrestor (Penal Law, sec. 242 (5); otherwise it is a misdemeanor under the sections above cited. (Penal Law, sec. 1842.) 

Sec. 7. Pursuit and Retaking of Arrestee. Code of Crim. 

Proc., sections 186 and 187, concern the retaking of an escaped or rescued arrestee. Section 186 states: "If a person arrested escape or be rescued, the person, from whose custody he escaped or was rescued, may immediately pursue and retake him, at any time, and in any place in the State." Section 187 gives, to the pursuer, the same rights to break into buildings, etc., that are given to arresting officers when effecting an original arrest. 

New York has enacted the Uniform Close Pursuit Act (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 860) which, generally, allows officers of other States to enter this State when in close pursuit of a person with the intent of arresting that person. The crime for which the intended arrestee is sought must also be a crime in this State. The out-of-State arrestor, after effecting the arrest, must take the arrestee before a magistrate in this State "who shall conduct a hearing for the sole purpose of determining if the arrest was in accordance with the provisions of * * * this section, and not of determining the guilt or innocence of the arrested person." If the arrest is determined to have been lawful, the arrestor shall, without unnecessary delay take [the arrestee] *** to the State from which he fled." If the arrest is determined to have been unlawful, the magistrate "shall discharge the person arrested."

The purpose of the last mentioned section, and of the Act in general, is to overcome the territorial limitations imposed upon officers arising out of sovereignty. For example, the Attorney General of New York has given an 19

§

opinion that an officer of a village, when making an arrest outside the territorial limits of the village which appointed him, acts only in the capacity of a private person. The differences in the powers of private persons and officers have been discussed previously. Similar limitations exist in interstate situations. The rules concerning interstate arrests have been stated to be: "A person found without the territorial jurisdiction in which he is charged with a crime may be arrested and legally convicted upon being tried therein. * * * A fugitive from justice is returnable in extradition to the State in which he committed a felony crime and in the absence of proof that he was unlawfully taken there, regularity is presumed." (People v. Adams, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 575.) To this list should be now added the right to arrest when within the provisions of the Close 

Pursuit Act. 

The laws of one State cannot, by themselves, govern actions in other States. Therefore, absent interstate agreements, officers of one State, effecting an arrest in another, would have no powers greater than those of any other person in the other State. He would then be subject to that 

State's rules of arrest, such as the one in force in Tennessee, where a private person has no authority, without a warrant, to arrest a person outside the county in which he resides, unless a close pursuit situation exists (McCaslin v. McCord, 116 Tenn. 690, 94 S.W. 79). Some States have indicated that the right to arrest for a felony, without warrant, only applies to felonies committed within the 

State (Tarrers v. State, 90 Tenn. 485, 16 S.W. 1041; Malcolmson v. Scott, 56 Mich. 459, 23 N.W.166). In those States, officers of neighboring States, without Close Pursuit Act authority, would not have the right to arrest after the defendant crossed the borders of the other state. With adoption of the Act by the other State, such limitations would not be imposed. 

Sec. 8. Time of Arrest. Due to the nature of the right, when anyone is arresting for a misdemeanor or a felony at- 20

§ tempted or committed in his presence, there is no limitation upon the time of day, or day of the week, when the arrest may be made. Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 179, gives to an officer the right to arrest at night, without a warrant, when the officer has reasonable ground to believe that a felony has been committed and that the arrestee is the guilty party. As a private person does not have the right to arrest under those circumstances, there is no comparable section governing the time within which the arrest may be made. Since neither a private person nor an officer has the right to arrest without warrant for a misdemeanor not committed or attempted in his presence, there is no time prescribed within which such an arrest may be made. 

In People v. Bradley, 58 Misc. 507, 111 N.Y.S. 625, defendants were arrested without warrant in the evening, for a misdemeanor. Citing Sections 170 and 177 of the

Code, the Court stated: "The plain intendment of the statute is that for a commission or attempted commission of a felony, and where the officer has reasonable cause for believing the person guilty of a felony, he may arrest without a warrant at any time, but, where the offense committed is of the grade of misdemeanor, the officer may only arrest the offender where it is committed or attempted in his presence; but where not so committed, he must apply for a warrant, which cannot be executed at night or on 

Sunday without the direction of the magistrate indorsed on the warrant. *** all petit offenses are included in the class of misdemeanors *** the defendant is entitled to bail such charge as of right upon ***the [and has] right to be called to answer only during the hours when magistrates are required to be in attendance to either dispose of their case or accept the bail." 

Sec. 9. Procedure After the Arrest. Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 180, states: "When arresting a person without a warrant the officer must inform him of the authority of the officer and the cause of the arrest, except when the person 21

§ 

arrested is in the actual commission of a crime, or is pursued immediately after an escape." The title of that section reads: "Must state his authority and cause of arrest where party is committing felony or is pursued after escape.' 

However, the word "crime" in the body of the section has been held to include misdemeanors and traffic offenses (Squadrito v. Griebsch, 1 N.Y. 2d 471, 154 N.Y.S. 2d 37).

In People v. Gallo, 206 Misc. 935, 135 N.Y.S. 2d 845, defendant's motion for dismissal of a complaint, which charged assault upon a police officer, was granted. Defendant and his brother had been arrested without warrant by the complainant police officer, who had not identified himself. After the officer "restrained" defendant's brother, defendant forcibly tried to free him and, in the course of such conduct, fought with the officer. The court held that due to the lack of identification by the officer, defendant could not be held to have "acted unreasonably or without legal justification under the circumstances." Since the arrest was illegal,, having been made without a warrant, where there had been no crime committed in the officer's presence and no reasonable ground for the officer's belief that a felony had been committed, defendant could take all reasonable steps to resist the officer's action.

If a private person arrests without a warrant he must, "without unnecessary delay, take him before a magistrate, or deliver him to a peace officer." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 185.) Failure to comply with this section is a misdemeanor (Penal Law, sec. 1844), and, though an arrest might be otherwise lawful, the delay, if unnecessary or unreasonable, will give rise to liability, on the part of the arrestor, for, at least, the unlawful period of detention of the arrestee (Tobin v. Bell, 73 App. Div. 41, 70 

N.Y.S. 425). That case indicated that failure to comply with this section made the arrest illegal, ab initio, thus imposing upon the arrester liability for all the actions taken by him. Code Crim. Proc., sec. 165, states: "The defendant must in all cases be taken before the magistrate 22

§ without unnecessary delay, and he may give bail at any hour of the day or night." See the discussion of the effect of this section in the Bradley case, supra. This section is applicable to arrests without warrant for crimes committed in the presence of the officer (People v. Bradell, 4 

Misc. 2d 945, 160 N.Y.S. 2d 167). The consequences ensuing from a violation of this section are similar to those discussed above in cases of unnecessary delay in turning the arrestee over to an officer. Thus, the State has been held liable for damages resulting from the delay, and, in some cases, for false arrest and imprisonment damages for the entire period of the detention. "If there was such unnecessary delay, then the arrest itself became unlawful on the theory that the defendants were trespassers ab initio and so continued down to the time when the plaintiff was lawfully held." (Hendrix v. Manhattan Beach Development 

Co., 181 App. Div. 111, 117, 168 N.Y.S. 316.) “There was unnecessary delay in the arraignment *** and *** by reason thereof the State of New York became a trespasser ab initio, and * the ensuing imprisonment became illegal ab initio and remained so down to the time when there was a legal arraignment." (Bass v. State, 196 Misc. 

177, 92 N.Y.S. 2d 42.) One statutory definition of a reasonable time for which an arrestee can be confined without an arraignment is contained in New York City Crim. Cts. 

Act, sec. 107, which allows, in certain cases, commitment of the defendant for up to 48 hours without defendant's consent. * * 

In People v. Lovello, 1 N.Y. 2d 436, 154 N.Y.S. 2d 8, defendant had been arrested on Saturday evening, and not arraigned until Monday morning, although he could have been arraigned on Sunday morning. Purported confessions were made by defendant during the period of his detention while he was being questioned by officers. In reversing defendant's conviction, the court stated: "The delay in arraignment was illegal. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

165; Penal Law, Consol. Laws c. 40, sec. 1844.) Therefore it was error *** for the court to refuse the requested in- 23

§ 

struction and, similarly, error for the court to submit to the jury as a question of fact whether the delay was 'unnecessary or unreasonable.' * * * These incorrect instructions *** were the more serious since some of the most damaging evidence presented by the prosecution consisted of alleged admissions made by defendant during that period of unlawful delay in arraignment." The above decision does not hold that because a confession is made during an illegal delay it is inadmissible; such factors are indications, to be weighed by the jury, during their determination of the weight to be given to the confession. 

(Stern v. State of New York, 346 U.S. 156, 97 L. Ed. 

1522.) During the period of the illegal delay the defendant is, by definition, being held unlawfully. Therefore, a writ of habeas corpus would lie. However, the illegality of the detention ceases upon defendant's arraignment; thus the use of that writ might not be a valuable aid. The succeeding sections discuss defendant's rights to damages for the unlawful detention. 

Sec. 10. Release. Usually, one unlawfully arrested and in custody, will be most desirous of obtaining his releaseproblems concerning his right to damages for the unlawful detention, and the possible criminal prosecution of the arrestor, will not seem important to most persons at that time. Too, the release of those unlawfully arrested would seem the most effective method of demonstrating to arrestors, and to police departments, the need for careful consideration before an arrest is made or ordered. The early decisions on this point are discussed in People v. 

Park, 92 Misc. 369, 156 N.Y.S. 816. First, it should be noted, as discussed in the preceding section, that the unlawfulness of the confinement ceases upon a proper arraignment, for purposes of determining the period. In the Park case, supra, the court stated: "A judgment of conviction rendered by a court which had jurisdiction of the defendant and of the offense is not affected by the fact that the defendant was wrongfully arrested without a warrant. * * * 24

§ 

The general rule is that it is no defense to a criminal prosecution that the defendant was illegally or forcibly brought within the jurisdiction of the court. My conclusion is that a conviction should not be set aside because the defendant was illegally arrested. The only office of the information and the warrant is to bring the defendant before the magistrate. If the defendant is before the magistrate and after being before the magistrate has a fair trial and is convicted on sufficient evidence every substantial right of the defendant is protected. What happens before the defendant is brought before the magistrate is of no importance as bearing on the justice of his conviction. 

This rule does not deprive the defendant of the benefit of the provisions of the law relating to arrest. If it develops that he is illegally arrested, he has his remedy in an action for false imprisonment. Nor does this rule, apply where there is an examination before the magistrate instead of a trial. *** It is doubtless true that if a defendant is unlawfully arrested, and an attempt is made to adjourn the trial and detain the defendant, the courts will release him*** but when a defendant is brought before a magistrate and charged with crime, and the trial proceeds without delay, the magistrate has jurisdiction of the defendant and his conviction as the result of such trial must stand." 

The distinction, referred to in the above decision, between situations wherein the question is the Magistrate's power to hold a defendant illegally arrested on examination, and that of a court to hold such a defendant for trial, was rejected by the court in Rose v. McKean, 190 Misc. 982, 76 N.Y.S. 2d 391. There, the defendant was illegally arrested, without a warrant, and, after commencement, by a magistrate, of a preliminary hearing on the complaint, defendant applied for an order of prohibition, enjoining the magistrate from further proceeding with the hearings. Defendant there alleged that the magistrate was without jurisdiction over him as a result of the admittedly illegal arrest. The court stated: "I hold that, since 25

§ (a) 

the magistrate had jurisdiction of the subject matter and the petitioner-defendant was physically before him, the manner in which the arrest was made is immaterial in determining the court's jurisdiction to proceed. *** while an unlawful arrest is an invasion of a person's constitutional rights. * * * it has been the policy of the law to protect the citizen from violation * * * by affording an action for damages for unlawful arrest and providing that an unlawful arrest is a crime. * * * To permit [its] 

legality *** to be considered in determining the jurisdiction of a court to hear evidence of the commission of a crime would inject an unnecessary impediment in the administration of criminal justice. Undue delays would result." See also, for a similar result in a similar situation, People v. Bonner, 5 Misc. 2d 355, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 53. * * * Thus, the illegality of the arrest will not warrant the arrestee's release based on an argument that the court has not properly acquired jurisdiction over the arrestee, when there have been some further proceedings which properly brought the arrestee before the court. Of course, while plaintiff is being detained by the arrester, or by the police department, prior to arraignment, a writ of habeas corpus would lie, at least until a proper warrant is obtained by the arrester. There is no Federally-based right that would affect the above rule (Mahon v. Justice, 127 U.S. 700, 32 L. 

Ed. 283).

Sec. 10(a). Civil Remedies. Damages may be obtained by the arrestee for an illegal arrest or imprisonment. When one's rights have been invaded, he has been the victim of a tort, and an action lies. However, the choice of remedy may vary, depending upon the circumstances, and the necessary proof may vary, depending upon the choice of remedy. 

The remedies which may be available are, usually, suits for false arrest, false imprisonment, or malicious prosecution. Extended discussions of these remedies may be found in works dealing with the law of torts. 26

§ 

Sec. 10(b). Criminal Prosecution of Arrestor. The various sections of the Penal Law which proscribe wrongful arrests have been mentioned above. The victim of such an arrest may, by complaint, institute criminal proceedings against the arrester. Similarly, if there has been an illegal assault committed while the arrester was effecting the arrest, criminal charges based on that action may be instituted in a similar manner. 

Sec. 11. Waiver. Some cases have considered the problem of the waiver of the requirements for a lawful arrest. In 

People v. Burns, 19 Misc. 680, 44 N.Y.S. 1106, it was held that defendant's plea of guilty, upon arraignment, precluded later objections based on the unlawfulness of the arrest. See also People v. Warden, 123 App. Div. 289, 107 

N.Y.S. 1103, and People v. Brenner, 3 Hun. 666. However, as stated by the court in People v. Burns, supra: "These cases, involving the question of waiver, seem to imply that unless there is a waiver by the defendant, the court does not acquire jurisdiction of the person. In most, if not all, of these cases in which the question of waiver was considered, however, it does not appear that any question was considered by the court except the question of waiver. The broader question as to whether or not the court acquires jurisdiction when the defendant is brought before a magistrate and charged with a crime was not considered." In the light of the rules on this latter point, extended discussion of the waiver problem appears unwarranted. Of course it would be to the advantage of any unlawfully arrested person to raise all warranted objections whenever possible so that any later suit for false arrest or false imprisonment, or both, is not affected. "A false arrest does not necessarily deprive the court of jurisdiction of the proceeding in which it was made. When there was an appropriate accusation whether by indictment or information, a court may acquire jurisdiction over the person of the defendant by his voluntary appearance." (Albrecht v. 

United States, 273 U.S. 1, 71 L. Ed. 505.) 27
