An information is a statement in writing, sworn to before a magistrate, charging a designated person, with a specific crime. 

It is to be distinguished from the instrument, also known as an information, which the District Attorney draws and files with the Court of Special Sessions in misdemeanor cases. In the latter situation, an information in the Court of Special Sessions performs the same function as an indictment, which alleges the commission of a felony, and is triable in the Supreme, County, or General Sessions Courts.

The information, as considered in this chapter, should be attacked by counsel at the arraignment of the defendant before the magistrate. If a defect appears on the face of the information, which counsel believes cannot be corrected or amended by the District Attorney, he should move to dismiss the information at the commencement of the preliminary examination. 

Ordinarily, motions to dismiss the information are made at the conclusion of the hearing before the magistrate, after the prosecution's witnesses have been heard. The motion is directed not only to the form and recitals of the information, but is predicated 28

INFORMATIONS 

$12 also upon the depositions of the witnesses, with special emphasis on the latter.

If an attack is to be made on the information, after the committing magistrate is divested of jurisdiction, it must be made by habeas corpus. (See chapter so entitled.) 

Sec. 12. Definitions. "The information is the allegation made to a magistrate, that a person has been guilty of some designated crime." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 145, subd. 1.) It performs the function of an indictment and, like an indictment, "shall not allege that a person has previously been convicted of any crime or offense nor shall it set forth any record thereof, unless such previous conviction affects the degree of the crime charged * * * or is an element of such crime or *** [affects] the jurisdiction." (Code of Crim. Proc. sec. 145, subd. 2.)

Once an information is "laid before a magistrate [magistrates are defined, for this purpose, in Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 146], *** he must examine on oath the informant or prosecutor, and any witnesses he may produce, and take their depositions in writing, and cause them to be subscribed by the parties making them." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 149.) Then, "if the magistrate be satisfied, from such depositions, that the crime complained of has been committed, [and that he has jurisdiction over such offense] *** and the person charged with the commission of the crime is a citizen of the state and a resident of the city or town where the information is laid, *** the magistrate may, in his discretion, instead of issuing a warrant *** issue a summons. 

If the magistrate be satisfied from such depositions that the crime complained of has been committed, and that there is reasonable ground to believe that the defendant has committed it, and if the case [is not one where it lies in the magistrate's discretion to issue a summons] *** he must issue a warrant of arrest." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 150.) 29

$

Sec. 13. Purposes. Informations have two purposes, or perhaps to be more accurate, two uses other than notice and prevention of double jeopardy, as mentioned in the discussion of indictments. An information may be the basis for the issuance of a warrant of arrest or a summons, as discussed above. "It is well-settled law that where an information is used, as the basis for the issuance of a warrant of arrest or subpoena, it is insufficient if it rests on information and belief without a statement of the sources of the information and grounds of the belief. * * * The reasons for this rule are said to be that a reasonable guarantee of probable cause is required before interference with a person's liberty, ensuing from the issue of a warrant, is justified *** and that such probable cause is not shown where the information is based solely on information and belief without a statement of the sources thereof and the grounds of belief. *** the information, whether used as the basis for issuance of a warrant or subpoenas, or only as a pleading, has a function in addition to informing defendant of the charge against him and barring subsequent prosecution for the same offense. It exposed this defendant to the necessity of procuring bail in default of which she would be imprisoned. *It is also the formal charge against defendant-the paper which institutes the prosecution against her." (People v. James, 4 N.Y. 2d 482, 484-5.) * * The other functions of informations, other than as the basis for issuance of warrants, is as a pleading and as the jurisdictional foundation of the magistrate's power to require the attendance of witnesses, and to take depositions in order to determine if a warrant should be issued (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 148). 

In People v. Belcher, 302 N.Y. 529, 534, the Court of

Appeals, after discussing the requisites of informations as basis for warrants, stated: "The situation is different, however, where, as here, the trial court acquired jurisdiction of the person of the defendant by a valid arrest, law- 30

INFORMATIONS 

§ 14 fully made without a warrant, the information then serves only the function of a pleading. 

"There is no explicit constitutional or statutory requirement that the information, when so utilized, be sworn to by a person competent to testify to the facts recited. Whether such a requirement is nevertheless to be enforced, by analogy, upon considerations of policy *** or by reference to the English common law governing informations * * * or whether, on the other hand, the requisites of an information as a pleading are to be no more stringent than those for an indictment as a pleading, is an open question in this court *** we find it unnecessary to decide it here."

However, in People v. James, supra, that question was presented. Defendant was charged with the unlicensed sale of liquor and, after reversal of a conviction, and before presentation of evidence in the new trial, defendant moved for dismissal of the information because it was founded on information and belief without a statement of the sources thereof. After making the statement quoted above, the court noted that the same reasons of policy applicable where the information is used as the basis for a warrant, apply when it is used as a pleading. 

Sec. 14. History. The use of information as a method of instituting the prosecution of a crime arose at about the same time as the use of indictments. The King would, through his attorneys in the criminal courts, or through his Attorney-General, commence a criminal proceeding which might be based upon information adduced by his officers, or upon information supplied by a subject. At an early date the abuses made possible by this type of procedure became apparent. Political reasons were often the motivation for the institution of a proceeding. Thereafter, the use of informations was restricted to minor offenses. 

In this country, at least in the Federal courts, "informations were principally, if not exclusively, used for the recovery of fines and forfeitures." (Ex parte Wilson, 114 

U.S. 417.) In recent years, with the increasing criticism of 31

§ 

 the Grand Jury system, (1 Nat. Comm. on Law Observ. 

and Enf., Rep. on Pros. 126), and the abolition of the Grand 

Jury system in England, there is a probability of greater emphasis upon the information as a means of commencing prosecutions. See Dession, From Indictment to Information, 42 Yale L.J. 163. 

Sec. 15. Procedure. The first step in the prosecution of a person for having committed a criminal act is, generally, notification to the proper authorities of the commission of the crime. Cases involving citizen's arrests, and arrests by officers who witness the act, are exceptions to this. This notice is usually effected by a "complaint". These "complaints" may be made to grand jurors, complaint clerks of District Attorney's offices or of courts, police officials. 

They are to be distinguished from the more formal accusation which is the "information", and might be the next step in the proceeding. New York City Crim. Cts. Act, sec. 

116, states that where an information, "oral or written" is presented to a Magistrate, he may issue a summons directing the accused to appear. Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

742 provides the form of information to be used in Special Sessions courts in New York City and obviously refers to a formal, written paper, not an oral statement. It states: “All criminal actions in the Courts of Special Sessions in New York City must be prosecuted by information made by the District Attorney." Once the information is filed in 

Special Sessions, jurisdiction over the proceeding is removed from the committing magistrate (People v. Barr, 223 App. Div. 168, 227 N.Y.S. 614). After the proceeding has been transferred to Special Sessions, it may then be removed to General Sessions if a "certificate of reasonableness" is obtained, pursuant to New York City Crim. Cts. 

Act., sec. 31. 

The first "complaint" mentioned above need not meet the requirements of definiteness that an information or indictment must (People ex rel. Traino v. Slattery, 179 

Misc. 206, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 553). However, once the preliminary 32

INFORMATIONS 

§ 16 proceedings are concluded, an information of the more formal type must be prepared and filed. Thus, sometimes confusion in the discussion of the requirements of informations arises. This is sometimes the result of applying cases, deciding what an information that is to be the basis for a warrant of arrest must contain, to cases concerning informations to be used for other purposes, such as the basis for subpoenaing witnesses. More confusion arises when the "complaint" is also called an information. "The statute, therefore, contemplates an information and one or more depositions. The two, however, may be combined if the affidavit made before the magistrate is complete enough to fulfill the functions of both an information and a deposition, and sets forth facts sufficient to justify the issuance of a warrant without further evidence." (People v. Mezzatesta, 203 Misc. 253, 115 N.Y.S. 

2d 498, 500.) The above statement appears to conflict with that made by the court in People v. Enright, 112 Misc. 568, 184 N.Y.S. 248, 251, where it was said: "An information differs radically from an affidavit. It resembles an indictment and differs from it only in being presented by a competent public official on his oath in office, instead of by a 

Grand Jury on their oath.** Excepting mere formal parts, at the beginning and close, it is precisely like an indictment ***. Indictments and informations are tested by the same rules so far as the substantive description of the offense is concerned." 

Sec. 16. Necessity of Information. "An information is one of the essential steps in the prosecution of a misdemeanor. The information, therefore, being vital to the initiation of the proceedings, is also jurisdictional in the part it plays in the prosecution of any defendant." (People ex rel Goldberg v. Calkins, 11 Misc. 2d 968, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 

824, 826.) If an information is jurisdictional its lack could not, of course, be waived. "Minor defects in informations and indictments which do not prejudice any substantial rights of a defendant are waived unless objection is made 33

§ 

before the defendant is called for judgment.

*** but if an information does not set forth facts sufficient to constitute a crime the defect is jurisdictional and cannot be waived." (People ex rel. Goldberg v. Calkins, supra). Earlier cases had indicated that the lack of an information or an affidavit or deposition or a warrant of arrest could be waived by a defendant proceeding to trial without objection (People v. McIntosh, 41 Hun 639; City of Buffalo v. Murphy, 228 App. Div. 279, 239 N.Y.S. 206). The later rule appears to be more consistent with the general attitude of the courts today and with the recent decisions in the analagous area of indictments.

Sec. 17. Waiver of Defects. Minor defects in informations have generally been held to have been waived by pleas of guilty (People v. Scutt, 160 Misc. 25, 289, N.Y.S. 1042; 

People v. Banner, 5 Misc. 2d 355, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 53). Thus where the information was based upon information and belief without a statement of the grounds therefor, the defect was held waived by defendant's plea of guilty, and his proceeding to trial without objecting to the information (People ex rel. Travis v. Daniels, 182 Misc. 856, 44 

N.Y.S. 2d 700; People v. Sly, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 474). However, the information's failure to allege a crime was held a jurisdictional defect and thus not waived in People v. Patrick, 175 Misc. 997, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 183. But compare People ex rel. Krohn v. Thomas, 133 Misc. 145, 231 N.Y.S. 271, where a plea of guilty and a general appearance was held a waiver of the objection that the information did not allege a crime. 

In People v. Jones, 4 N.Y. 2d 482, a conviction was reversed, and an information dismissed, where defendant submitted to an illegal arrest because of lack of knowledge of its illegality, the court noting that this lack of knowledge prevented her acts from being considered a waiver. 

Sec. 18. Sufficiency of the Information. This has been previously discussed in a general manner in the first section of this chapter. The necessity for sworn allegations, not based 34

INFORMATIONS 

§ 18 on hearsay, unless a statement of the grounds therefor is included, was mentioned above in the discussion of the 

Mezzatesta case, and the Calkins case. Informations must, generally, meet the same standards as indictments (People v. Wilson, 4 N.Y.S. 2d 592). However, they must do even more than a simplified indictment. An information must stand by itself. It is either good or bad according to its contents and it cannot be supplemented or pieced out by affidavits or by a bill of particulars in the Magistrate's Court. An information must state the offense charged and acts constituting it and must set forth the specific acts constituting the alleged offense and may not leave them to conjecture.

The time of the commission of the offense charged should be alleged in the information and, of course, should be a time prior to the date of the information (People v. 

Schweizer, 160 Misc. 23, 289 N.Y.S. 964). However, an erroneous allegation as to time, even an allegation that the act was committed after the date of the information, may be cured by an amendment (People v. Easton, 307 N.Y. 

336). The reason for the allowance of amendments to informations more readily than in the case of indictments was explained by the court in People v. Kraemer, 175 N.Y. 

S. 175 N.Y.S. 2d 508. There, the court distinguished between indictments which depend for their vitality upon actions by Grand Juries, and informations, which are not dependent upon such an independent body, stating that "the court can permit the amendment of an information even though the amendment affects a matter of substance." 

The place of the commission of the offense should be alleged, particularly in order to show jurisdiction in the court in which the proceeding is pending (People v. 

Bevilacqua, 12 Misc. 2d 558, 170 N.Y.S. 2d 423, rev'd on other grounds, 5 N.Y. 2d 867).

The information must be verified, whether used solely as a pleading (People v. Scott, 3 N.Y. 2d 148), or as the basis for the issuance of a warrant (People v. Mosier, 10 

Misc. 2d 934, 82 N.Y.S. 2d 462). The term information in 35

§ 

the above cases was used to refer to both the formal information and the supporting affidavits. It has been held that the verification must be before an officer duly authorized to take oaths; thus, an information charging drunken driving was held invalid where the oath was given before a policeman, not authorized to administer oaths (People v. 

Sledge, 192 Misc. 934, 82 N.Y.S. 2d 462). The examination of the informant or complainant must be before a magistrate, and on oath, before a warrant can be issued (People v. Gade, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 1018). Where the information did not, on its face, reveal that it was given under oath, but where there was testimony by a police clerk, named as a witness thereto, that it was so given, it was held that the information was valid (People v. Goldberg, 8 App. Div. 2d 660, 185 

N.Y.S. 2d 54).

While, as discussed above, there is some language in some cases indicating that an information need not be in writing (People ex rel. Jackson v. Fennelly, 5 App. Div. 

2d 71, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 1018, and cases cited under "Necessity of the Information," above), it has also been held that where more than a minor "offense", for which summary proceedings may be held, is charged a written information is necessary (People v. Scott, supra). One case held this requirement not "jurisdictional", and thus waivable (People ex rel. Wojek v. Henderson, 134 Misc. 228, 235 

N.Y.S. 173). The depositions must be in writing (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 149; People v. Vituskey, 155 App. Div. 

139, 140 N.Y.S. 19). The defendant is entitled to copies of the depositions and statements taken at the preliminary examination upon payment of the stated fees (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 206).

If an information is not, by itself, sufficient, but the magistrate's examination discloses additional information sufficient to warrant the holding of the accused, the defect in the information has been held cured, and therefore it should not be dismissed (People v. Schenk, 142 N.Y.S. 

1081; People v. Ehrlich, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 125; but compare 

People v. Banner, supra). 36

INFORMATIONS 

§ 19 An information must charge the commission of a crime or offense, with the requisite intent if such intent is required by statute, together with allegations of acts sufficient to constitute the crime or offense. See discussion of intent in chapter titled "Indictments." An information. charging violation of the Multiple Dwelling Law was held defective as failing to charge a crime or offense (People v. 

Schildhaus, 10 Misc. 2d 641, 173 N.Y.S. 2d 115). However, an information, charging that defendant did "willfully, wrongly and unlawfully violate the provisions of Section 

43 of the Penal Law *** in that *** [he] acted in a manner which openly outraged public decency", was indicated to be sufficient in People ex rel. Shannon v. Combs, 4 Misc. 2d 

817, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 245. However, in the Combs case, the defendant attempted to raise the issue of the sufficiency of the information after conviction by habeas corpus, and the court held that the proper method of such attack was by appeal. 

Sec. 19. Magistrates' Powers. A magistrate has no power, in the absence of a sufficient information, to issue subpoenas and examine witnesses. In People ex rel. Livingston v. Wyatt, 186 N.Y. 383, a magistrate had issued a subpoena directing the party to appear before him for the purpose of investigating whether an offense which the magistrate "had reason to suppose had been committed," had, in fact, been committed. The court held the magistrate without jurisdiction to issue the subpoena and ordered the witness, imprisoned for contempt for disobedience of it, released upon application for habeas corpus. 

In People ex rel. Travis v. Knott, 204 App. Div. 379, 383, 198 N.Y.S. 142, 145, a magistrate issued a subpoena directing the Comptroller of the State to appear in an investigation to determine if the proceeds of the sale of certain bonds were paid out fraudulently. The court stated: "The 

Grand Jury can investigate to discover whether a crime has been committed, and what person committed it, with- 37

§ 

out any formal presentation to it. It can act on rumor or suspicion. The magistrate can only act on the presentation of a sworn information stating that a person has been guilty of some designated crime. The fact that the informant is a Deputy Assistant District Attorney *** does not make the information an official act, nor dispense with the requirements as to definiteness of allegation." 

In Gaffney v. Kampf, 268 App. Div. 308, 52 N.Y.S. 2d 1, a magistrate issued a subpoena to the Superintendent of the New York State Police, based upon an information alleging that six unknown persons had conspired to, and did, assault the complainant. The arrest warrant issued named the six as John Doe, Richard Roe, etc., and the magistrate stated that he had issued the subpoena to aid the complainant in identifying his assailants. The court held the information insufficient and the subpoena invalid, stating: "The information should be filed, witnesses in support thereof should be examined, and the depositions containing the facts filed in advance of the issuance of the warrant. No case has been called to our attention which supports in the slightest degree the procedure adopted here, namely, to conduct a John Doe fishing expedition to aid the police in apprehending John Doe and his fictitious associates." Where the name of the accused is unknown, the fact should be stated and the reasons for the lack of knowledge given, and a description, to the best of the complainant's ability, included. 

Where an arrest has been lawfully made without a warrant, as where the defendant has been apprehended during the commission of an offense, an information is nonetheless necessary before the magistrate can commit the prisoner after arraignment (People ex rel. Farley v. Crane, 94 App. Div. 397, 88 N.Y.S. 343). The information may be prepared after the defendant has been brought before the magistrate (People v. Ostrosky, 95 Misc. 104, 160 N.Y.S. 493). 38

INFORMATIONS 

§ 21 

Sec. 20. District Attorney's Powers. After a preliminary examination by the magistrate, a district attorney may file an information (Dodge v. Supreme Court, 276 N.Y. 

444). The Dodge case also held that the information must be filed with the clerk of the proper court in order for the court to gain jurisdiction, and that the court could not proceed solely on the basis of the complaint or affidavit made by the complainant. Since 1926, the District Attorney may also file informations upon receipt of a direction to do so and approval by the court, for which the Grand Jury was drawn, of such direction (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

742; People v. Gold Key Club, Inc., 2 Misc. 2d 380, 152 N.Y. 

S. 2d 669). If such direction is not received, the District

Attorney must await receipt of a return by a magistrate, pursuant to Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 221. These returns attest that an examination has been held and that the magistrate has determined that there is sufficient cause to believe that the accused has committed a crime. If the defendant is discharged by the magistrate, the District Attorney may proceed further against him, but only by indictment (People v. Dillon, 197 N.Y. 254). The District

Attorney may not, after a refusal to indict by the Grand Jury, proceed by information against the accused for a misdemeanor included within the offense considered by the Grand Jury (People v. Benson, 208 Misc. 138, 143 N.Y. 

S. 2d 563). 

Sec. 21. Attacks Upon Informations. There are various times, as well as means, to attack informations. It has been stated that "the proper procedure for a person who feels that an information is insufficient, especially when he is represented by counsel, is to appear specially and object to the sufficiency of the information." (People v. Talarico, 72 N.Y.S. 2d 39, 40.) In the Talarico case, the defendant represented by counsel, after pleading guilty to a traffic offense, raised objections to the sufficiency of the allegations in the information. The court held that, as there was jurisdiction over the person of the defendant and over 39

§ 

the subject matter, his guilty plea waived this defect. Once the objection is made and an exception taken to the overruling thereof, further action, such as going to trial, will not be considered a waiver (People v. Strassner, 299 N.Y. 

325). Thus, the first step in an attack upon an information should be a special appearance by counsel and an objection to its sufficiency. If the defendant is brought before the court by means of a warrant of arrest which has been issued pursuant to an information, a motion to set aside the warrant may be made, and the sufficiency of the information tested in that manner (People v. Tighe, 146 App. Div. 

491, 131 N.Y.S.693).

If the information is filed by the District Attorney pursuant to the direction of the Grand Jury, as discussed in the preceding section, a motion to reconsider the court's approval of the Grand Jury's direction may be made (Innes v. Cosgrove, 263 App. Div. 880, 32 N.Y.S. 2d 149, aff'd. 288 

N.Y. 700). The motion must be directed to the same judge who granted the original approval. In the Innes case, the grounds alleged for the reconsideration were, generally, similar to those listed in Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 313. 

Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 321, states that the only pleading on the part of a defendant is a demurrer or plea. "The only plea to an information in a Court of Special Sessions is, guilty or not guilty, or former judgment of conviction or acquittal of the crime charged. *** Defendant may, however, at any time, move to dismiss the information on the ground that it fails to allege the crime charged or any crime." (People v. Lee, 151 Misc. 431, 272 N.Y.S. 817, 819.)

In the Lee case, defendant demurred to the information, but the court treated the demurrer as a motion to dismiss. 

This analogy was also noted by the court in People v. 

Rudnick, 280 N.Y. 5, however from the opposite viewpoint. 

The court there stated: "We think this motion [to dismiss the information on the ground that it failed to allege a crime] was the equivalent of a demurrer to the information." It should be noted that defendants in courts of special sessions and in police courts are allowed the same 40

INFORMATIONS 

§ 21 pleas to informations as are allowed defendants under indictments by Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 332 (Code Crim. 

Proc. Sec. 700). In People v. Perrin, 170 App. Div. 375, 155

N.Y.S. 698, the court indicated that courts of special sessions could set aside informations only upon the same grounds as those provided by Code of Crim. Proc. Sec. 313, for setting aside indictments. It therefore appears that a motion to set aside that indictment be utilized rather than a demurrer, although the Rudnick case can be used to argue that demurrers to indictments are allowable, at least in courts other than special sessions. 

After trial, providing the objection to the information was raised previously and proper exception taken, the sufficiency of an information may be attacked upon appeal or by habeas corpus, if the ground alleged for the insufficiency goes to the jurisdiction of the court, such as the failure of the information to allege facts that constitute a crime, or if it is based on information and belief without a statement of the sources thereof (People v. 

Taylor, 159 Misc. 536, 289 N.Y.S. 668; People v. Knapp, 242 App. Div. 811, 275 N.Y.S. 637). In one case, a motion in arrest of judgment, similar to that referred to in Code of Crim. Proc. Sec. 331, concerning indictments, was allowed in a case initiated by information. The grounds alleged were the failure of the information to allege facts sufficient to constitute a crime and, therefore the lack of jurisdiction of the court (People v. Sullivan, 244 App. Div. 

469, 280 N.Y.S.48).

An order was granted dismissing an information on the ground that it did not state a prima facie case of the commission of a crime, in People v. Malmud, 4 App. Div. 2d 86, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 204. However, in that case an appeal from the order was allowed the prosecution under Code of Crim. 

Proc. Sec. 518, subd. 3. 41

PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

If there is reason to believe that a warrant of arrest or the papers upon which it is predicated are defective, there are two summary remedies available to counsel. A motion to dismiss the warrant may be made at the preliminary examination, or at any time prior thereto, as soon as it is learned that it has been executed and issued. 

Counsel may also resort to a writ of habeas corpus, to test the sufficiency of the warrant, or the depositions underlying the warrant. (See chapter on Habeas Corpus.)

Good strategy might dictate that the above remedies be deferred or waived entirely where it is felt that the District Attorney would be enabled to correct the defects in the warrant or depositions, if his attention is directed thereto by motion or writ. If counsel permits these defects or insufficiencies to go unnoticed, he may gain some advantage for his client at the preliminary examination, or at a later stage of the prosecution. 

Sec. 22. Definitions. "A warrant of arrest is an order in writing in the name of the People, signed by a magistrate commanding the arrest of the defendant, and may be substantially in the following form, the blanks being properly filled: 42

§ (a) "County of ( ). "In the name of the People of the State of New York, to any Peace Officer in the ( ). "Information upon oath, having been this day laid before me that the crime of ( ) has been committed and accusing ( ) thereof, "You are, therefore, commanded forthwith to arrest the above named ( ), and bring him before ( ), at "[Date and subscription]" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

151). The section goes on to state: "The warrant must direct that the defendant be brought before the magistrate issuing the warrant, or, without naming a specific magistrate, before any magistrate of the town", except in certain circumstances discussed below. The Restatement of Torts, section 113, defines a warrant as "a written order directing the arrest of a person or persons issued by a court, body or official, having authority to issue warrants." 

Sec. 22(a). Bench Warrant. There are two other processes, that may be used to bring persons before a court, which should be noted at this point. One of these is a bench warrant, which may be issued "If the defendant has been discharged on bail *** and do not appear to be arraigned, or if the defendant be for any cause absent when his personal attendance is necessary." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 297.) 

That section allows the court to order the clerk to issue such a warrant; Section 300 allows the clerk, upon application of the District Attorney, to issue the warrant after entry of the above mentioned order, and empowers the District Attorney to issue a bench warrant for the arrest of any defendant indicted "at any time after the indictment is found."

The form of the bench warrant is prescribed by section 301, and is generally similar to the form of an arrest warrant, as above quoted. However, the bench warrant will recite the finding of the indictment, if such has been found, and will direct that the arrestee be brought before the 43

§ (b) 

court in which the indictment has been found. Thus the bench warrant is used, primarily, to secure the presence of one who has been indicted, or who has previously been before the court in some manner and has defaulted in appearance. Code of Crim. Proc., sections 302 through 307, govern the proceedings to be had upon such warrants, and Section 304 states that the warrant may be served in the same manner as an arrest warrant, except "that when served in another county, it need not be indorsed by a magistrate of that county." (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

475 through 479 provide for the use of a bench warrant to secure a defendant's presence after judgment of conviction. The procedure is generally similar to that of bench warrants under the sections above cited.) 

Sec. 22 (b). Summons. After a magistrate has received the depositions upon which an arrest may be issued, and in which a charge of crime is contained, he "may, in his discretion, instead of issuing a warrant *** issue a summons." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 150.) The summons, instead of being addressed to a peace officer as is a warrant, is addressed to the accused, and recites that a complaint has been made by the complainant against the accused, and that the accused is "hereby summoned" to appear before the appropriate court "to the end that an investigation may be made of said complaint; and upon your failure to appear you are liable to a fine of not exceeding twenty-five dollars." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

150.) The summons may be signed by the complainant, a person appointed by the magistrate, or a peace officer, and must contain a "brief description of the offense complained of." Upon the return of the summons (except in 

Youth Court cases) the magistrate will investigate the complaint in the same manner as if a warrant of arrest had been issued. Failure to appear in response to a summons is a contempt of court, which may be punished by a fine of up to $25.00. “If a summons shall have been issued *** and the person summoned shall have failed to appear 44

§ (b) *** determines or shall have appeared and the magistrate that there is reasonable ground therefor, a warrant of arrest may be issued." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 150.) "A 'summons', as a criminal process, is comparatively new ***. It is not the process by which an officer is authorized to make an arrest. Its function is to give notice to a person that there is a complaint against him on a definite charge, which it is desired to investigate. It constitutes a somewhat peremptory invitation to come before the magistrate to share or assist in such investigation. In my judgment it is intended to obviate the usual procedure of arrest with or without warrant in certain minor crimes, and in the case of somewhat doubtful complaints made before magistrates, when an investigation rather than a trial is first desired. It is a process in the nature of a subpoena, leading to an investigation, but not to a definite trial and punishment, unless the person summoned elects to proceed to trial without issuance of a formal warrant." (City of 

Buffalo v. Neubeck, 209 App. Div. 386, 204 N.Y.S. 737.) A summons may be utilized, in the place of a warrant, if "The crime charged is one of which a court of special sessions or the Youth Court has exclusive jurisdiction, or is one of the offenses enumerated in Section 56, and the person charged with the commission of the crime is a citizen of the State and a resident of the city or town where the information is laid, or if the charge be against a child accused of an offense of the grade of or *** permitted to be tried as a misdemeanor or an offense for which such child can be found guilty of juvenile delinquency, and in any other case in which the magistrate has power to commit children as provided by law." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 150.) The offenses enumerated in Section 56 are, generally, misdemeanors and offenses ranging from "Racing, running or testing the speed of any animal within one mile of the place where any court is held," through forty-two other offenses to perjury in the second degree as defined in Penal Law, sec. 1634.

Thus the distinctions between the above three types of 45

§ 

legal process are many. Generally the distinctions are based on the desired effect of the process. A warrant of arrest is used, generally, to secure the presence of the accused in court in response to a complaint lodged, and one executing it at that time arrests the person named. A bench warrant, which is executed in the same manner as a warrant of arrest, is used to secure the presence of a person who, usually, has been indicted or otherwise has been previously before the court, but has disobeyed an order concerning his presence at some other time and is thus absent at the time of its issuance. A summons, when served, does not result in an arrest of the person named therein at that time; it is in the nature of a subpoena or other civil process commanding the presence of the person named, before the court, at some future date. There is no seizure or detention of the person, or taking of the person into custody when the summons is served. 

Sec. 23. History. "Between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries, summonses and warrants developed and took the place formerly occupied by the hue and cry ***. Without any statute, warrants were frequently granted in the seventeenth century. Consequently various statutes recognized the granting of warrants, and this was done indisputably in 1848. The power of justices to issue such process had previously been disputed for centuries." (Orfield, Crim. Proc. from Arrest to Appeal, p. 9.) At common law, when an arrest warrant was issued by a Justice of the Peace, it was valid only in the county of that Justice, but could be indorsed by other Justices of the Peace in other counties, whereupon it became valid in those counties also. However, if the warrant were issued by a judge of the King's Bench it could be executed throughout the kingdom. Similarly, at common law, it appeared that the judge's or justice's authority to issue warrants varied, depending upon the crime involved. A Justice of the Peace did not have authority to issue warrants on felony charges 46

§ when he did not have authority to try such a case (Hale, Pleas of the Crown, p. 291-292).

Under the early common law, a "known officer making an arrest in his own bailiwick was not required to show his warrant, even upon demand made by the arrestee. Unless excused, he was, however, required to acquaint the arrestee with the substance of the warrant in order that the reason for the arrest might be known. However if the arrest was made by other than [such an officer] *** he was required to exhibit the warrant if requested to do so.' (Perkins, The Law of Arrest, 25 Iowa L. Rev. 224.) Under the early common law, warrants could be executed only by those to whom they were directed, although sheriffs had the authority to deputize others to execute warrants directed to them. Other officers, to whom warrants were directed for execution, had to execute them in person although, of course, they could request others to assist them. (2 Hawk. Pleas of the Crown c. 13, sec. 29.) Under the common law, warrants could also be directed to private persons, however these private persons were not under a duty to execute the warrants, whereas officers, to whom warrants were directed, were under such a duty. (2 Hale, Pleas of the Crown, p. 110.)

Sec. 24. Procedure in Issuance of a Warrant. Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 148, states: "When an information is laid before a magistrate, of the commission of a crime, he must examine on oath the informant or prosecutor, and any witnesses he may produce, and take their depositions in writing, and cause them to be subscribed by the persons making them." These depositions "must set forth the facts stated by the prosecutor and his witnesses, tending to establish the commission of the crime and the guilt of the defendant." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 149.) In People v. 

Mezzatesta, 203 Misc. 253, 115 N.Y.S. 2d 498, defendant appealed from a judgment of conviction of reckless driving which caused the death of another. On the appeal, he contended that the information, which commenced the pro- 47

§ 

ceedings, and which was the basis for the issuance of the warrant of arrest, was insufficient. He had moved, during the trial, for dismissal of the information. The court stated: "The information constitutes the only written charge upon which the warrant of arrest was issued or upon which the defendant was put on trial. There were no depositions and no witnesses were sworn by the justice to form a basis for issuing the warrant. The Code of Criminal Procedure contemplates a written information upon which the magistrate before whom it is laid may examine witnesses, take depositions, and from which he must be satisfied that a crime was committed and that there are reasonable grounds to believe the defendant committed it before he should issue a warrant of arrest. * * * The statute there fore contemplates an information and one or more depositions. The two, however, may be combined if the affidavit made before the magistrate is complete enough to fulfill the functions of both an information and a deposition and sets forth facts sufficient to justify the issuance of a warrant without further evidence. *** If, however the information is made solely on information and belief, or based solely on hearsay, the defendant is entitled to a dismissal of the proceedings. ***I do not feel that any of the three grounds set forth in the information signed * * * are sufficient to justify the issuance of the warrant; consequently, the justice was without jurisdiction. *** When [the information] * * * *** serves as the basis for the issuance of the warrant of arrest, as it does here, it must be made by someone with knowledge of the facts or be supported by sworn depositions of persons competent to testify to its contents and must contain facts, showing the commission of the crime and the defendant's probable guilt. In the absence of such facts, the magistrate lacks jurisdiction and a conviction cannot be upheld."

In People v. Resciniti, 191 Misc. 719, 81 N.Y.S. 2d 338, in a similar situation, the court stated: "The information in this case consists of an affidavit made by * * * the arresting officer. Its wording and form would indicate an intention 48

§ to comply with the requirements of Sections 145, 148 and 

149 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. No question of jurisdiction is raised *** here because of the lack of a separate deposition and information, but an examination of the authorities would seem to indicate no objection to this method of procedure providing the instrument prepared is complete enough to comply with the requirements of the three sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure above mentioned. The test seems to be whether it sets forth sufficient facts to authorize a warrant without further evidence." Thus the need for an information, then depositions, may be obviated if the information itself meets the requisites imposed by the Code before a warrant can be issued. See chapter on Informations, for discussion of necessary requirements thereof, dependent upon the use thereof; where used only as a pleading, less stringent requisites for sufficiency must be met; if used as the basis for the issuance of a warrant, and thus as the basis for the acquisition by the court, of jurisdiction over the person of the accused, more stringent requirements must be met. 

"Even to justify the issuance of subpoenas to take depositions in support of an information, the latter must set forth facts tending to show the commission of a crime by the defendant. It cannot rest wholely upon information and belief. The statute does not permit simple hearsay to become the basis of such a proceeding. (People ex rel. 

Livingston v. Wyatt, 186 N.Y. 383, 79 N.E. 330)

There, the court held an information made solely upon information and belief insufficient even to confer jurisdiction upon the magistrate to proceed to take depositions in support of it. It seems clear that, if an information is insufficient for that purpose, it is all the more insufficient to sustain the issuance of a warrant for the defendant's arrest." (People v. Taylor, 159 Misc. 36, 289 N.Y.S. 668.)

After the information has been made and filed, and after the examination has been had, and, if necessary, depositions have been taken, and if the magistrate is satisfied, from all the evidence "that the crime complained of has 49

§ 

been committed, and that there is reasonable ground to believe that the defendant has committed it" (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 150, subd. 2), the warrant, in the form above quoted, will be issued. "The warrant must be directed to, and executed by, a peace officer." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 153.) This requirement differs from the common law practice. "Peace officers" are defined in section 154. 

Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 155 and 156, prescribe the type of peace officer to whom the warrant may be directed, the choice depending upon the type of judge who issued the warrant. If a Supreme Court Justice, County Judge, Gen eral Sessions Judge, or Nassau County District Court Judge has issued the warrant, or if the warrant was issued by a City Court Judge, or the Recorder of a city, under special authority vested in him by statute, the warrant "may be directed generally to any peace officer in the state, and may be executed by any of these officers to whom it may be delivered." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 155.) "If it be issued by any other magistrate, it may be directed generally to any peace officer in the county in which it is issued, and may be executed in that county," or it or it may be executed in another county, in which the accused is located, upon endorsement of the warrant by a magistrate of that county. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 156.) That section also provides that if the warrant is directed to a sheriff, or deputy sheriff of a county, it may be executed by a sheriff or deputy sheriff of any county of the state if it contains the proper endorsement thereon. However, in New York

City, the warrant may be executed anywhere therein without the aforesaid endorsement.

The New York State Police may execute warrants throughout the State without any endorsements thereon (Op. Atty. Gen., 1934, p. 93), and the absence of the endorsements mentioned in the above sections has been held to constitute only a procedural irregularity, not a jurisdictional defect, and therefore is not a ground for the arrestee's release (People v. Harmer, 75 Misc. 399, 135 N.Y. 

S. 529). Before the indorsements above mentioned can be 50

§ made, Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 157, requires that there be proof of the handwriting of the magistrate who originally issued the warrant.

The arrest may be made at any time if the crime charged is a felony; if the crime is a misdemeanor, absent a direction of the magistrate on the warrant to the contrary, the arrest may be made only during the daytime, and not on 

Sunday. Under Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 174, the officer "may use all necessary means to effect the arrest" if the arrestee resists the arrest, or flees from the officer. When effecting the arrest, the officer must inform the arrestee "that he acts under authority of the warrant, and he must also show the warrant, if required." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 173.) The usual powers to break open doors, etc., such as are discussed in the preceding chapter, are given to officers executing warrants by Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

175 and 176.

After the arrest, if the arrestee is charged with a felony, the officer must take the arrestee before the magistrate who issued the warrant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 158) unless that magistrate is absent or unable to attend. If such is the case the officer must take the arrestee before an "available magistrate of a town in the county in which the offense was committed who is nearest or most accessible with reference to the place where the arrest is made. 

The officer must, at the same time, deliver to the magistrate the warrant, with his return indorsed and subscribed by him." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 164.) "The defendant must in all cases be taken before the magistrate without unnecessary delay, and he may give bail at any hour of the day or night." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 165.) See preceding chapter for a discussion of the effect of a failure to comply with this section. "If the defendant be taken before a magistrate other than the one who issued the warrant, the depositions on which the warrant was granted must be sent to that magistrate or if they cannot be procured, the prosecutor and his witnesses must be summoned to give their testimony anew." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 51

§ 

166.) Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 162 and 163, give, generally, to the officer who executed the warrant, the right to take the arrestee through other counties on his way to the place where the warrant specifies that the arrestee be produced, and the right to take necessary steps to retain the arrestee in safe custody during that trip. After the production of the arrestee before the magistrate, the arrestee's examination will take place. 

If the defendant has been arrested for a misdemeanor, in a county other than that in which the warrant was issued, he may demand that he be taken before a magistrate in that county, "who must admit the defendant to bail, for his appearance before the magistrate named in the warrant, and take bail from him accordingly." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 159.) When and if the deferred Youth Court provisions go into effect, the above section will not apply to arrestees within the jurisdiction of the Youth Court. 

Arrestees within the jurisdiction of that court will, regardless of the charge against them, be required to be taken without unnecessary delay before a Youth Court Judge, or if such a judge cannot be found, before the nearest magistrate. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 159-a.) If bail is taken by the magistrate, such fact must be certified by the magistrate on the warrant, and the warrant and the bail undertaking must be delivered by the magistrate to the arresting officer. That officer must then discharge the arrestee from arrest, and deliver the warrant and undertaking to the magistrate named in the warrant as the one before whom the defendant is to appear (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 160). 

Sec. 25. Attacks upon Warrants. The Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution states, in part: "The right of the People to be secure in their persons against unreasonable seizures, shall not be violated, and no warrants shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing ** the persons 

*** to be seized." Article I, Section 12, of the 

52

§ New York State Constitution contains identical language. 

Some of the cases, requiring informations, or complaints, which form the basis for the issuance of the warrant, to contain statements based upon personal knowledge of the facts have been discussed above. "The law is well established that the warrant is merely the process by which a defendant is brought before the court, and that the information is the foundation for the jurisdiction of the magistrate." (People v. Kryzan, 183 Misc. 1010, 52 N.Y.S. 

2d 411.) Thus, as in the Krzyzan case, where the allegation made by the accused is that the depositions do not contain facts giving rise to probable cause to believe that a crime was committed, or that the defendant committed it, and therefore there was no authority for the magistrate to issue the warrant, the usual method for the attack will be by a motion to dismiss the information. The use of a writ of habeas corpus to secure the release of an arrestee under a warrant is discussed in the chapter entitled "HABEAS 

CORPUS."

While there is no statutory provision authorizing or regulating such procedure, the courts have recognized that objections to the jurisdiction of the magistrate to issue the warrant, and other objections directed to the validity of the warrant and its supporting papers, may be raised by a motion to set aside or quash the warrant. This motion may be made at the first stage of the proceedings, prior to any habeas corpus proceeding being instituted. 

Thus, in People v. Tighe, 146 App. Div. 491, 131 N.Y.S. 693, the defendant, after his arrest under a warrant, "moved to set aside the warrant and to dismiss the proceeding on the ground that the 'information' was insufficient, and *** that the depositions of the witnesses * * * had not been signed by the witnesses." The motion was denied, an examination was conducted, and the defendant was committed pending the termination of the examination. 

Defendant thereupon obtained a writ of habeas corpus, and, in the cited case, the writ was sustained. The court 53

§ 

noted that there had been no waiver of defendant's right to object to the sufficiency of the warrant as his "objection [by motion to set aside] was made in due time." 

However the value of this remedy, as noted in the preceding chapter, is little. The arrestee may be re-arrested immediately upon his release. Further, if before his motion to set aside the warrant is made, the court has by some other means properly acquired jurisdiction over his person, that jurisdiction will not be affected by the invalidity of the arrest. "If before granting the warrant, the defendants had entered a voluntary appearance, the reference and the affidavits could have been treated as surplusage, and would not have vitiated the information. The fact that the information and affidavits were used as a basis for the application for a warrant did not affect the validity of the information as such. Whether the whole proceeding was later vitiated by the false arrest remains to be considered. 

The invalidity of the warrant is not comparable to the invalidity of an indictment." (Albrecht v. United States, 273 U.S. 1, 71 L. Ed. 505.) The court went on to note that the furnishing of bail bonds by the defendants did not constitute a waiver of their right to object to the arrest, and stated: “An objection to the illegality of the arrest could have been taken thereafter by a motion to quash the warrants." However, the court noted that by the time that motion was made, "There was no occasion to apply for a new warrant, because the defendants were already in court. *** By failing to move to quash the warrant before the defect had been cured, the defendants lost their right to object." The court cited, in a footnote, several cases concerning amendments of warrants, after objections had been taken thereto, and quoted State v. Turner, 170 N.C. 

701, 86 S.E. 1019, where the court said: "Even if one is wrongfully arrested on process that is defective, being in court, he would not be discharged, but the process would be amended then and there, or if the service were defective it could be served again." 54

§ 

Sec. 26. Civil Remedies-False Arrest, etc. A reference to the possible suits that may be commenced by the wrongfully arrested arrestee, against the arrestor, based on the tort actions of false arrest, false imprisonment, and malicious prosecution, is contained in the preceding chapter. 

Most of the principles there discussed are applicable, regardless of whether the wrongful arrest was made under a warrant, or without a warrant. However, where the arrest has been made under a warrant there is one vital distinction. The general rule is: "A ministerial officer is protected in the execution of valid process issued by a court, even if the process is irregular in form. But, in addition thereto, he is privileged to arrest or detain where, though the process actually be invalid, it is 'fair on its face'. (Restatement, Torts, sections 122, 123, 124.) He is not required to embark upon an investigation to determine whether the process or order is valid, so long as there is nothing on its face to indicate that it is not valid. * * * The officer is protected in obeying its command, if the process will pass the following test: 'It must have been issued by a court or officer having authority of law to issue such process, and there must be nothing on the face of the process apprising the officer to whom it is delivered that in the particular case there was no authority for issuing it."" (Schildhaus v. City of New York, 7 Misc. 2d 859, 163 N.Y.S. 

2d 201.) The last cited decision contains a discussion of some New York cases where it was held that the warrants involved were not "fair on their face". Thus, in the usual case, the arrestee's claim for damages, absent the arresting officer's failure to meet the above test, will have to be directed against those initiating the prosecution, not against the officer or his employer-the municipality or state. 55
