The easiest and most direct way to obtain bail, in all instances, is to enlist the services of a professional surety company bondsman. 56

BAIL He is familiar with all the short cuts and refinements of this procedure. He invariably knows where to locate an Assistant District 

Attorney to approve the amount of bail and a judge or justice of the court, to fix the amount of bail and approve the bond. 

In cases of certain misdemeanors and offenses, particularly where the amount of bail is fixed by statute, it is advisable to accompany a bail bondsman to the police station where the defendant has been booked. The commanding officer is empowered to accept bail, summarily, in accordance with the provisions of the statutes. 

In this instance, it is a wise practice to post cash or surety company bail. A private citizen may act as surety for the defendant. 

He must make an affidavit stating that he is possessed of cash or other property, to the extent of twice the amount of bail demanded. If the commanding officer requests it, bank books or other indicia of property ownership must be exhibited. It should be noted that if private citizens, acting as sureties, list real property, as evidence of their net worth, a lien is immediately filed against it, in many counties of the state. Thus, a friend or relative who performs a service to the defendant by acting as his surety, may seriously inconvenience himself by listing his real property as an asset. 

In felonies, and in other misdemeanor cases, bail must be fixed by the court authorized to do so, as described in the instant chapter. Furthermore, in felony cases the defendant must first be fingerprinted, and a fingerprint record furnished to the court, in order to apprise it of the criminal record of the accused, if any exists. After the bail has been so fixed by the court, it may be furnished by a surety company bond, or by private citizens as sureties, who have established their net worth as hereinbefore described.

Where bail has not been set by the court, it may be applied for to a County Judge or a Justice of the Supreme Court, in chambers, even if court is not in session, provided the fingerprint record is furnished, and the consent of the District Attorney, or one of his assistants, is obtained to the amount of bail to be fixed. The Judge or Justice will then fix the amount of bail, and if surety company bail is provided, will approve the bond at the same time. Where other than surety company bail is furnished, it can be fixed only by the court while in session, and with the approval of the District Attorney or his assistant.

If the amount of bail that has been fixed is deemed excessive, a motion may be made to reduce the amount of bail. This motion is 57

§ 

made before the Judge or Justice who fixed bail in the first instance, or, in any event, in the court where the prosecution is then pending. If the application for reduction of bail is denied, or if bail is refused entirely, habeas corpus will lie. (See chapter on Habeas Corpus.)

Sec. 27. General Discussion. Bail is generally defined as the security given by an accused for his appearance at a future judicial proceeding, in order to obtain his release from incarceration. The term "bail" is also used to describe the person who gives the security which enables the accused to be released. The words "surety" or "bailor” are synonyms for bail as employed in this sense. 

Section 551 of the Code of Criminal Procedure incorpo rates both of the above meanings within the statutory definition: "The taking of bail consists in the acceptance, by a competent court or magistrate, of the undertaking of sufficient bail for the appearance of the defendant according to the terms of the undertaking, or that the bail will pay to the people of this state a specified sum." 

The bail system is designed to enable a person charged with the commission of a crime to obtain a provisional release until his guilt or innocence may be adjudged, while at the same time giving the government a means of securing the person's presence at the trial or other proceeding 

(People ex rel. Rothensies v. Searles, 229 App. Div. 603, 

243 N.Y.S. 15). The bail bond or undertaking is a contract between the governmental authority on the one hand, and the offender and his surety on the other. The government enters into this agreement on the premise that the surety would prefer to produce the defendant in subsequent judicial proceedings rather than forfeit the amount of the undertaking.

Upon first analysis, one may feel that the liberated defendant is the only beneficiary of the bail system; however, the public is also benefited by a proper administration of bail procedure. The governmental authority is spared the expense of maintaining an added number of persons in 58

BAIL § our already overcrowded jails. Secondly, the loss of earning power and resulting effects upon the defendant's family are averted until such time as the defendant's guilt is determined. A less tangible but equally important objective is served when adolescent or innocent defendants are relieved of the humiliation and psychological repercussions of being detained in a penitentiary. 

One of the initial duties to be performed by the attorney after learning of the defendant's imprisonment is to secure his client's release. This may be accomplished either by way of bail or by a deposit in lieu of bail, the former being the most frequently utilized procedure. 

Sec. 28. Defendant's Right To Bail. The first consideration is whether the person charged with the commission of a crime has a right to be released on bail. The majority of 

State constitutions guarantee the right to bail in all cases other than in the commission of a capital offense where the proof is evident or the presumption great. There is no similar guarantee of a right to bail in the New York State 

Constitution. Article I, Section 5 of the New York State 

Constitution prohibits the fixing of excessive bail, and the constitutional right of an accused person pursuant to this section can only be violated if the bail is excessive, not because it is denied (People v. Ackerson, 166 Misc. 130, 3 

N.Y.S. 2d 427; People ex rel. Deliz v. Warden, 260 App. 

Div. 155, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 435).

The defendant's right to bail prior to conviction is determined by statute, and Section 553 of the Code of Criminal Procedure guarantees the admission to bail before conviction, as a matter of right, only where the crime committed is a misdemeanor. There is one minor additional category where the accused has a right to bail which is afforded by Section 554 (a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, whereby specified railroad and motor vehicle employees charged with a crime arising from an accident while engaged in the course of their duties have a right to 59

§ 

bail whether or not the crime is a misdemeanor (Op. Atty. 

Gen., 45 St. Dept. 604).

Section 553 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure pro vides that in all other cases, i.e. felonies, admission to bail before conviction is a matter of discretion. This statute is an embodiment of the prior case law (People ex rel. Ackerson v. Warden of City Prison, 167 Misc. 475, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 

412). The discretionary power vested in the court does not permit an unreasonable or capricious denial of bail. As the court stated in People ex rel. Shapiro v. Keeper of City 

Prison, 290 N.Y. 293: "We are by no means holding that this grant by the Legislature to the courts of discretionary power to deny bail in non-capital felony cases, can be exercised arbitrarily. Denial of bail is no light matter, and needs to be buttressed by a real showing of reasons therefor." The court, in a dictum in the Shapiro case, supra, said that "in cases involving crimes punishable by death no court has the power to fix bail." It is noted that this limitation is not present in the statute, and two courts have sustained the court's discretionary power to admit to bail a defendant accused of murder (People ex rel. McManus v. Warden of City Prison, 226 App. Div. 364, 235 N.Y.S. 

112; People v. Perry, 8 Abb. Pr., N.S. 27); but, until the

Court of Appeals speaks out clearly on this point, we must consider ourselves bound by its dictum. 

Sec. 29. Judicial Authority To Whom Application Must Be 

Made. After determining whether the defendant is entitled to bail, either as a matter of right or discretion, the next consideration is the judicial authority from whom the defendant can obtain such bail. The answer to this question in part depends upon the stage of the proceeding when the accused is seeking bail. Section 554 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure states that prior to conviction the defendant may be admitted to bail: (1) for his appearance before the magistrate on the examination of the charge, before being held to answer; (2) to appear at the court to which he has been held to answer, subsequent to examination; (3) after 60

BAIL § indictment, either upon the bench warrant issued for his arrest or upon an order of the court committing him or enlarging the amount of bail, or upon his being surrendered by his bond to answer his indictment in the court in which it is found or to which it may be sent or removed for trial.

The statutory scheme as to the particular tribunal or jurist to whom the bail application is made correlates to the foregoing section of the Code, and is dependent upon when the application is made, i.e. for examination-Section 550, Code of Criminal Procedure; when held to answer -Sec. 557; after indictment, prior to conviction-Sections 

578, 579. Bail after conviction, under Section 555 of the

Code of the Criminal Procedure, is discussed, infra. 

Section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure specifies and limits the judicial authority competent to admit a defendant to bail, dependent upon the offense committed or the offense plus prior criminal record. This section governs every stage of the proceeding set forth above, prior to conviction. This states that a defendant cannot be admitted to bail except by a Justice of the Supreme Court, or by a Judge of the Court of General Sessions or a judge of the County Court where the defendant is charged: (1) with a crime punishable with death; (2) with the infliction of a probably fatal injury upon another and under such circumstances as that, if death ensue, the crime would be murder, (viz.: attempted murder or felonious assault); (3) “With a felony or with any of the misdemeanors or offenses" [below listed] and there is reason to believe that he has either "been convicted within the state of a felony" or attempted felony, or of a crime under the laws of another jurisdiction which if committed in New York State would be a felony; or has two convictions of any one or combination of the listed misdemeanors. 

The misdemeanors listed are: (1) illegally using, carrying or possessing a pistol or other dangerous weapon; (2) making or possessing burglars' instruments; (3) buying or receiving stolen property; (4) unlawful entry of a 61

§ (a)  

building; (5) aiding escape from prison; (6) jostling (Penal Law, Sec. 722, subd. 6); (7) loitering, soliciting of men, (Penal Law, Sec. 722, subd. 8); (8) endangering life or health of a child (Penal Law, Sec. 483); (9) carnal knowledge of a child 10-16 years old (Penal Law, Sec. 483, subd. b); (10) indecency (Article 106, Penal Law); (11) sodomy or rape, as a misdemeanor; (12) sale or possession of amphetamine, or derivatives, or sale and possession of hypodermic syringes and needles (Penal Law, Sec. 1747, subdivisions c and d); (13) violation of the Public Health

Law with respect to narcotic drugs (Article 33, Public 

Health Law.) Justices of the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, it is specially provided, may admit to bail any defendant held for or charged with a misdemeanor in that court. 

Sec. 29(a). Bail to Appear for Examination. If the defendant's offense or offense plus prior record bring him within the scope of Section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, bail can only be obtained from the authority therein stated. 

If the defendant does not come within the foregoing section, then he may be admitted to bail, to appear for examination, pursuant to Section 550 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure: (1) by the magistrate who issued the warrant or before whom the same is returnable, or in case both of said magistrates are incapacitated or are absent from the jurisdiction, and in case the amount of bail shall have been fixed by one or other of them, any other magistrate of like jurisdiction or (2) by any Justice of the Supreme Court, or (3) by any Judge of the Court of General Sessions, or (4) by any County Judge.

In addition to the foregoing, Section 554 of the Code of Criminal Procedure makes it mandatory, on the part of police officers of the grade of sergeant and up, to take bail for the appearance of a prisoner arrested for a misdemeanor between eleven o'clock and eight o'clock the next morning. See, also, Vehicle and Traffic Law, section 70, 62

BAIL § which provides for bail to be taken by certain police officers. 

Sec. 29(b). Bail When Held to Answer. A defendant not within the provisions of Section 552, Code of Criminal Pro cedure, may be admitted to bail when held to answer by the magistrate by whom he is so held; or if he be a Justice of the 

Supreme Court or any judge authorized to preside in a court having jurisdiction to try indictments (Sec. 557, Code of Crim. Proc.). A defendant may be admitted, pursuant to this section, any time before the return of the depositions and statement to the court. However, Section 

559 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that after the record of the preliminary examination and statement is transmitted to the court having jurisdiction to find an indictment, then if the court where the crime is triable is sitting only the judge presiding therein can admit a defendant to bail. If the court where the crime is triable is not sitting, then the defendant may be admitted to bail by the magistrates who could have admitted the defendant prior to the return of the record of preliminary hearing to the court having jurisdiction. 

Sec. 29 (c). Bail After Indictment. When the crime charged in the indictment is a misdemeanor, the defendant may apply for bail before a magistrate in the county where the indictment was issued or in the county where he is arrested. (Sec. 578, Code of Crim. Proc.) When the crime charged in the indictment is a felony, bail may be taken by the judge presiding in the court in which the indictment was found, or to which it is sent or removed, or by any magistrate in the county in a court having jurisdiction to try indictments. 

Sec. 30. Application to Supreme Court. In addition to the foregoing, the defendant has a right to apply directly to the Supreme Court to obtain bail, on a writ of habeas corpus. Sec. 22 (8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure gives 63

§ 

the Supreme Court jurisdiction to "let to bail any person committed before and after indictment and founded on any criminal charge whatever." The attorney should carefully evaluate the advantages of proceeding under this section rather than in the manner set forth in the sections of the Code pertaining to bail (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

550 et seq.). In addition to affording another choice of forum or judge before whom one might desire to make the bail application, a more meaningful right of appeal is conferred by proceeding in this manner. The court, in People ex rel. McManus v. Warden of City Prison, 226 App. Div. 

364, 235 N.Y.S. 112, stated in a case where the relator had sued out a writ in the Supreme Court: "The practice here adopted gives to the defendant a more adequate remedy than is given by applying for bail in the Court of General Sessions from which no appeal lies. An appeal from the order refusing to sustain the writ may be made to this court [Appellate Division] and a review be had both of the exercise of the discretion of the court at Special Term and of the legality of its refusal." 

Sec. 31. Application for Bail. Sec. 560 (1), of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure, provides: "If the crime charged be a felony, all applications for bail either before or after conviction must be made returnable in the judicial district in which the crime was alleged to have been committed or in which the indictment is pending for trial."

This application may be made ex parte or upon notice if the magistrate in his discretion so requires. In the cities of the State the application for admission to bail in felony cases must be on at least two days notice to the District 

Attorney of the county, unless the magistrate by order fixes a shorter time (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 560). The attorney for the defendant should always attempt to shorten the two-day notice requirement, by procuring the 

District Attorney's consent thereto. 

All applications for bail, whether before or after conviction, must recite whether or not any previous applica- 64

BAIL § tion has been made at any time, and a description of the disposition of the application and by whom decided. 

The application must also contain a statement pertaining to the prior criminal record of the accused in this State and elsewhere with a description of the nature of the crimes (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 556-a). The affidavit should succinctly set forth the facts which would move the court to exercise its discretion in favor of admitting the defendant to bail. This necessarily includes those facts which point to the defendant's innocence and the infirmity of the prosecution's case as demonstrated by the preliminary hearings and prior proceedings. The defense counsel, in seeking to obtain bail for his client, should be alert, that in his desire to obtain or reduce bail, he does not give the prosecutor a preview of his defense and the persons through whom he intends to prove his case. Unless the facts set forth will be elicited from the defendant's most reliable witnesses, the facts should be confined to the matters already in the prosecutor's possession. 

Sec. 32. Fingerprints. An applicant for bail charged with a felony or any of the misdemeanors set forth in Sec. 552, Code of Criminal Procedure, supra, in cities or localities that have facilities for the prompt taking and recording of fingerprints will not be admitted to bail until his fingerprints have been taken to ascertain whether he has previously been convicted of a crime. Sec. 552 (a) makes the taking of prints in those cities, having facilities, a condition precedent to the application for bail. This section gives the accused the right, if the charge is dismissed or if there is an acquittal, to have the fingerprints returned to him and all copies thereof destroyed in his presence (Campbell v. 

Adams, 206 Misc. 673, 133 N.Y.S. 2d 876. See, also, Troilo v. Valentine, 179 Misc. 954, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 442).

Sec. 33. Amount of Bail. Article I, Sec. 5, of the New York 

State Constitution prohibits the fixing of excessive bail. 

The determination of what is or is not excessive bail is 65

§ 

entirely subjective and dependent upon a myriad factors. "The amount must be no more than is necessary to guarantee his (the defendant's) presence at the trial.” (People ex rel. Lobell v. McDonnell, 296 N.Y. 109, 71 N.E. 

2d 423.) The object of bail is not to increase the revenue of the State, or to punish the defendant or his sureties, but to combine the administration of criminal justice with the convenience of a person accused but not proved to be guilty. The Court of Appeals, in the Lobell case, supra, said: "The policy of our law favors bail because of the presumption that the prisoner is innocent. 

It is recommended that the District Attorney's assent to bail in a fixed amount should be obtained, if at all possible. Although the District Attorney's consent is not controlling, it is an important guide which the court will usually follow. There is no statutory provision setting forth the factors a court should consider when setting bail, as for example, in the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure. There, Rule 46 (c) provides: "If the defendant is admitted to bail the amount thereof shall be such as in the judgment of the judge will insure the presence of the defendant, having regard to the nature and circumstances of the offense charged, the weight of the evidence against him, the financial ability of the defendant to give bail and the character of the defendant." This has been construed as follows: "The reasonableness of the amount is to be determined by properly striking a balance between the need for a tie to the jurisdiction and the right to freedom from unnecessary restraint before conviction under the circumstances surrounding each particular accused." (United 

States ex rel. Rubenstein v. Mulcahy, 155 F. 2d 1002, 1004.)

Some of the factors and considerations which the courts have recognized as bearing on the amount are: the nature of the offense, the penalty which may be imposed, the probability of the willing appearance of the defendant or his flight to avoid punishment, the pecuniary and social condition of the defendant and his general reputation and character, the apparent nature and strength of the proof 66

BAIL § as bearing on the probability of his conviction (People ex rel. Rothenseis v. Searles, 229 App. Div. 603, 243 N.Y.S. 

15). The nature of the defendant's assets also have a bearing on the probability of flight. For example, the defendant whose assets consist of $100,000 in real property within the jurisdiction would be less likely to abandon this property by fleeing the jurisdiction than would a defendant with $100,000 in cash, which assets do not hold him to the locality.

It will be helpful to examine two cases where the bail was reduced by the appellate court. The Court of Appeals, in People ex rel. Lobell v. McDonnell, supra, held that $250,000 was excessive bail for a defendant charged with thefts and burglaries of $780,000. The prosecutor suggested $100,000, and nothing in the record showed an intent of the defendant to flee the jurisdiction. The court noted, with approval, the quotation of Lord Mansfield, that voluntary surrender was a strong indication that the accused had no intention of absconding from justice. The defendant had business interests in New York City and California and lived in New York City with occasional absences. It is noted that there is nothing wrong, per se, with bail in the amount of $250,000, as the court at about the same time approved bail in exactly the same amount in the case of two material witnesses (People ex rel. Rao v. Adams, 296 N.Y. 231; People ex rel. Gross v. Sheriff, 302 N.Y. 173).

The court, in People v. Gigante, 9 Misc. 2d 881, 173 N.Y.S. 

2d 971, reduced the defendant's bail from $150,000 to $100,000 in a case where the defendant appeared to be of modest means. The accused was charged with attempted murder in the first degree and concealed himself for three months after the crime, until he voluntarily surrendered to the police. The court stated: "While the defendant has ties, these ties were not strong enough to prevent his flight and concealment while he was being sought by the authorities." A bail of $150,000 was sustained in the case of People ex rel. Gagliano v. Warden, 188 Misc. 800, 67 67

§ 

N.Y.S. 2d 220, in the case of a defendant charged with feloniously selling heroin and conspiring to violate the narcotic drug laws. 

Sec. 34. Disposition of Application for Bail. Section 561 

of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires that the determination of the application for bail, either granting or denying, be in the form of an order and if it be granted the order must state the sum in which bail may be taken. Section 562 provides, in addition, that if the application be to a magistrate he issue a certificate in writing granting or denying the application and, if granted stating the sum in which bail may be taken. This certificate must be filed with the clerk of the court to which the depositions and statement are required to be sent.

Sec. 35. Review of Grant or Denial of Bail. Sec. 566 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states: "The decision of the judge presiding in the court in which the crime is triable, granting or denying bail, is final." This section, which precludes an appeal from a decision granting or denying bail, applies both when bail is denied and when bail is fixed in an amount which the accused regards as excessive. In a case where bail is fixed, the defendant's constitutional right, prohibiting the fixing of excessive bail, affords the procedural avenue for a limited review of the court's determination. In the case of People ex rel. Deliz v. Warden of 

City Prison, 260 App. Div. 155, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 435, the constitutionality of this section was sustained and the court reasoned that the defendant's right not to be held in excessive bail was not violated, as he can obtain relief from the Supreme Court under a writ of habeas corpus. 

The review of the amount of bail in which a defendant is held is very limited indeed. The feeling of the judiciary is expressed in People ex rel. Wasmund v. McCloskey, 16 

Misc. 2d 659, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 624, 625, where the court in holding that admittance to bail is a prerogative of the court having initial jurisdiction of the matter, stated: 68

BAIL § "while his determination may be reviewed [on a writ of habeas corpus] it cannot be upset, unless there is a showing that he acted arbitrarily, improvidently or abused his discretion." Thus, the appellate court will confine its power to those instances where there has been a real invasion of the defendant's constitutional rights, and not alter or modify the bail "because of a mere difference of opinion as to amount fixed." (People ex rel. Deliz v. Warden of City 

Prison, 260 App. Div. 155, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 435; People ex rel. 

Rupoli v. McDonnell 277 App. Div. 74, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 182.)

The defendant who is denied bail is likewise precluded from appealing the determination by Section 566 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but must rely upon the more limited review obtained in habeas corpus. Undoubtedly, a defendant denied bail in a misdemeanor case cannot be deprived of his statutory right without reason and such a finding can be assailed. The right to review, again by habeas corpus, a denial of bail in the case of a felony where the admittance to bail is in the discretion of the court, is necessarily more confined. The court, in People ex rel. 

Shapiro v. Keeper of City Prison, 290 N.Y. 393, 398 stated: "the grant by the Legislature to the courts of discretionary power to deny bail in non-capital felony cases, cannot be exercised arbitrarily. Denial of bail is no light matter, and needs to be buttressed by a real showing of reasons therefor *** " 

Sec. 36. Successive Applications. Although the accused may not appeal from a decision granting or denying bail, he may apply for bail to another magistrate. The applicant must set forth new facts to avoid the binding effect of the prior adjudication, and this is in most cases readily accomplished. The Legislature, in recognition of this evil of bail shopping, where an applicant denied bail by one judge applies to other judges, until he strikes the desired sympathetic chord, enacted the following legislation to curtail this practice; in addition to the requirement in Section 

556-a, Code of Criminal Procedure, that a statement about 69

§ 

***" prior applications be made in the application, Section 563 states: "If an application for admission to bail made to a magistrate, be denied, not more than two subsequent applications therefor can be made to other magistrates, except that an application can be made to *** [a judge of the Supreme Court or any judge authorized to preside in a court having jurisdiction to try indictments] if no application has been previously made to [such judge]. Sec. 

565 provides that the above limitation does not limit the power of the judge presiding in the court in which the offense is triable to let the defendant to bail. Sec. 564 contains the sanctions for violation of the foregoing sections. 

A violation is punishable as a misdemeanor, and the admission of the defendant to bail contrary to this section may be revoked by the magistrate who made it, or vacated by the court to which the depositions and statement are or must be sent, or to which, after indictment, the action must be sent for trial.

It is submitted that magistrates should regard previous orders denying bail as presumptively correct. "The practice of overruling one another in matters of purely coordinate jurisdiction not only leads to confusion but tends, in the evil of shopping for bail, to discredit this court in the eyes of the criminal world." (People v. Ackerson, 166 Misc. 

130, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 412.) 

Sec. 37. Right to Bail after Conviction. The right of the defendant, subsequent to conviction and upon appeal, to be admitted to bail is governed by Section 555 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and it is there provided that the defendant may be admitted to bail as a matter of right when the appeal is from a judgment imposing a fine only, providing there is a stay of proceedings. Section 41 of the 

Inferior Criminal Courts Act gives the defendant a right to bail in the case of an appeal from the decision of a City Magistrate, when acting within his summary jurisdiction. 

A defendant may not be admitted to bail if he is convicted of a crime punishable with death or life imprison- 70

BAIL § ment, or is a fourth offender under Section 1942 of the Penal Law, or is convicted of a felony committed while armed with a weapon, or of a felony or one of the following misdemeanors as set forth in Sec. 552

Code Crim. Proc. and has a prior criminal record of a felony or two of such misdemeanors: (1) illegally using, carrying or possessing a pistol or other dangerous weapon; (2) making or possessing burglars' instruments; (3) buying or receiving stolen property; (4) unlawful entry of a building; (5) aiding escape from prison; (6) jostling (Penal Law, Sec. 722, subd. 6); (7) loitering, soliciting of men (Penal Law Sec. 722, subd. 8); (8) endangering life or health of a child (Penal Law, sec. 483); (9) carnal knowledge of a child 10-16 years old (Penal 

Law, Sec. 483, subd. b); (10) indecency (Article 106, Penal 

Law); (11) sodomy or rape, as a misdemeanor; (12) sale or possession of amphetamine or derivatives, or sale and possession of hypodermic syringes and needles (Penal 

Law, Sec. 1747, subds, c and d); or (13) violation of the

Public Health Law with respect to narcotic drugs (Article 33, Public Health Law). 

In all other cases, admittance to bail is a matter of discretion when there is a stay of the proceedings. The statutory design of first limiting the right to bail and secondly absolutely prohibiting bail in certain cases, is consonant with one of the recognized objectives of a bail system, to enable an innocent person to obtain provisional release until his guilt or innocence is determined. Since conviction removes the element of uncertainty of the guilt of the accused, the liberality in granting bail is accordingly contracted. A further reason for limiting the admission to bail after conviction is that the probability of ultimate punishment is now increased, so that the defendant is more prone to escape if released at this point, than he would have been prior to the adjudication of his guilt. 

Judicial authority to admit to bail after conviction is conferred by Section 583 of the Code, which provides that when the defendant may be admitted to bail on appeal, the 71

§ 

order admitting him to bail may be made either by the court from which the appeal is taken or a judge thereof, the appellate court or a judge thereof or by a judge of the Supreme Court. The court or officer to whom the application for bail is made may require such notice as he deems reasonable to be given to the District Attorney of the county in which the verdict or judgment was originally rendered. 

Sec. 38. The Bail or Surety. At common law, only natural persons could act as bail and it was generally required that sureties be relatives, friends, householders or freeholders within the jurisdiction of the court at the time of the undertaking (4 Blackstone Comm., 297). It was felt that because of the personal relation of the bail to the accused, the surety would be enabled to keep close supervision over the defendant and also that because of the personal relationship the defendant would be loath to inflict financial loss on the surety. The Code of Criminal Procedure has extended the types of bail and permits the following to act as surety: (1) a natural person (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

569); (2) a fidelity or surety company authorized by the

State Superintendent of Insurance, through its licensed officers and agents (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 577-a); (3) a professional bondsman, licensed as such by the State 

Superintendent of Insurance. (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 

554-b.) 

Sec. 39. Qualifications of Bail. The qualifications of an individual bail are set forth in Section 569 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The individual must be a resident, and a householder or freeholder within this State and, unless the magistrate otherwise direct, reside within the county, and must not appear upon any official list of undesirable bondsmen. In the City of New York, a member of the Police Department or a keeper or assistant keeper or turnkey of any prison or place of detention for persons 72

BAIL § charged with any criminal offense in said city may not act as surety.

If there is one surety, he must be worth the amount of the undertaking, exclusive of property exempt from execution, and over and above all liabilities; the magistrate may permit more than one person to act as surety if they, in the aggregate, are worth the amount of the undertaking, exclusive of property exempt from execution, and over and above all liabilities. If real estate is offered as security, the assessed value of the real estate, after deducting all charges or liens of any nature, must be at least twice the amount specified in the undertaking, the realty must be at least twice the amount specified in the undertaking and it must not appear upon any official list of undesirable properties. 

Sec. 40. Fidelity or Surety Company. A fidelity or surety company authorized to transact business within this State may give bail. The undertaking shall be executed by one of the officers or its attorney, duly authorized by resolution of its Board of Directors, and a certified copy of such resolution under its corporate seal shall be filed with the undertaking (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 577-a). 

Sec. 41. Professional Bondsman. In recognition of the public's right to have reliable persons of ability and vigilance acting as sureties, the Legislature enacted a licensing statute providing: "No person, firm or corporation shall engage in the business of giving bonds in criminal cases without being duly licensed by the Superintendent of Insurance of the State of New York in accordance with" the 

Insurance Law (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 554 (b), subd. 

3). The court may examine the proposed surety and reject the bond if it is determined that any provision of the section is not complied with. The statute defines as being in the business of giving bail any person, firm or corporation who, within one month prior to the present transaction, made a deposit or gave bail in more than two cases not 1 73

§ 

arising out of the same transaction, and charged a fee. 

The statute regulates the fees which may be charged, limited to 5% on the first $1,000, 4% on the second $1,000 or fraction thereof, and 3% on the excess. If the amount of the bond is less than $200, a minimum premium of ten dollars may be charged.

Sec. 42. Affidavit of Surety. Section 554-c of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure requires every person giving bail to file with the bail bond or other deposit for bail an affidavit setting forth in detail what security, indemnity or consideration has been promised and given the surety and by whom. The surety or sureties must also file an affidavit stating that each of the sureties possesses the qualifications above set forth and required by Section 569 of the Code. 

Sec. 43. Justification of Bail. Except as to a requirement for notice in the cities of the State, the bail may be taken and justified without notice to the District Attorney, unless the court or magistrate requires that reasonable notice be given (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 570). In the cities of the State, in the case of a felony, notice in writing of two days must be given the District Attorney stating: (1) the names, places of residence and occupations of the proposed surety or sureties; (2) a general description of the real or personal property of the surety or sureties in respect to which they propose to justify as to their sufficiency, with the incumbrances thereon, by mortgage, judgment or otherwise, if any. The District Attorney may waive such notice or the court may shorten the two-day requirement (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 571).

Sec. 44. Form of Undertaking. The form of the undertaking is set forth in the statute (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

568, 581). The bail is a written undertaking, executed by the surety and invariably by the defendant, although the statute provides that it is in the discretion of the magis- 74

BAIL § trate whether the defendant execute the undertaking. The undertaking must be acknowledged before the magistrate in substantially the form as set forth by the statute. 

The court is permitted to accept a single consolidated bail bond for the defendant's appearance both before the magistrate and before any court in which the crime or offense with which he is charged is triable (Code of Crim. Proc. sec. 577-b). 

Sec. 45. Deposit in Lieu of Bail. Under the common law, cash would not be accepted as, or in lieu of, bail and in the absence of a statute so providing the magistrate has no authority to accept a deposit of money in lieu of bail (Badolato v. Molinari, 106 Misc. 512, 174 N.Y.S. 512). It is usually the practice to have the bail furnished by a bonding company. However, Sec. 586 of the Code of Criminal

Procedure enables the defendant to deposit with the clerk of the court, or other officials designated in the statute, the amount in cash mentioned in the order of commitment, or a United States bond or treasury certificate, or a New York

State or City bond in the amount fixed by the court. If a person other than the defendant deposits a sum with the court for the defendant's presence, there is a presumption that the money belongs to the person for whose appearance it is held (Finelite v. Sonberg, 75 App. Div. 455, 78 N.Y.S. 

338). This presumption can be rebutted, as in the case of 

Cogliano v. Ippolito, 16 Misc. 2d 95, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 775, where the defendant's sister deposited the money for her brother and creditors of the brother attempted to levy on the sum returned. The court returned the deposited sum to the sister. Section 586, subdivision 4, provides that if the person depositing the money obtain a consent from the defendant, that upon termination of the proceeding the money or other thing of value deposited will be returned to the person who made the deposit. A person depositing money for the benefit of an accused should always obtain this consent. 75

§ 

Sec. 46. Surrender of the Defendant. Although the court retains control over a defendant admitted to bail, upon admission to bail the custody of the accused is reposed in the surety who is regarded as the defendant's jailor, albeit by his own selection. The surety, as such custodian, has the right to terminate the responsibility assumed, by surrendering the defendant to the court. Section 590 of the Code of Criminal Procedure sets forth the manner in which the surety may surrender the defendant, which is essentially a restatement of the prior existing law (Shaul v. Fidelity & Deposit Co. of Maryland, 227 N.Y.S. 163, 131 Misc. 401, aff'd, 224 App. Div. 773 230 N.Y.S. 910), thus: "At any time before forfeiture of the undertaking, any surety may surrender the defendant in his exoneration, or the defendant may surrender himself, to the court in which his case is pending, at the time of the surrender, or to the officer to whose custody he was committed at the time of giving bail, in the following manner: (1) A certified copy of the undertaking of the bail must be delivered to the officer, who must detain the defendant in his custody thereon, as upon a commitment, and by a certificate in writing, acknowledge the surrender, and he must forthwith notify the court in which the case is pending that such surrender has been made. (2) Upon the undertaking and the certificate of the officer, or upon the surrender to the court in which the case is pending, the court in which the indictment or the appeal, or other proceeding, as the case may be, is pending, must, upon a notice of five days to the District Attorney of the county, with a copy of the undertaking and certificate, or certificate of surrender to the court, order that the bail be exonerated; and on filing the order and papers used on application, the bail is exonerated accordingly. 

Since the surety has custody of the defendant, he is permitted to arrest the defendant prior to forfeiture, and can, by written authority indorsed on a certified copy of the undertaking, empower a person of suitable age and discretion to arrest the defendant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 591). 76

BAIL § 

Sec. 47. Forfeiture of the Undertaking or Deposit of

Money. If there is a breach of the condition of the undertaking resulting from the nonappearance of the defendant at the designated time and place, the bail is forfeited. Section 593 of the Code provides that if the defendant neglects to appear, "the court must direct the fact to be entered upon its minutes; and the undertaking of his bail, or the money deposited *** is thereupon forfeited." This section has been interpreted to mean that when the fact of the defendant's failure to appear is spread upon the record, the forfeiture of the bail is complete and the surety is liable, although no formal judgment is entered until afterwards (People v. Bennett, 136 N.Y. 482).

As a practical matter, since the surety is not given notice of the order of forfeiture, the issue of what may be sufficient cause to exculpate or exonerate the surety does not arise until the surety applies to have the forfeiture remitted pursuant to Sections 597 and 598 of the Code. See 

People v. Parisi, 217 N.Y. 24.

Sections 595 and 595-a set forth the method of enforcing the forfeiture. The undertaking and a certified copy of the order of the court forfeiting the undertaking, when filed by the District Attorney with the county clerk, is docketed in the book of judgments as a judgment against the surety for the amount of the undertaking. The undertaking and the certified copy of the order forfeiting the bail constitute the judgment roll. This entry has the same force and effect as if a suit had been commenced and judgment recovered against the surety by the State. Judgment may thus be entered without the commencement of an action (Hoferd v. Oster, 149 Misc. 395, 268 N.Y.S. 227), and there is no requirement or provision for notice to the surety (Re Lexington Surety & Indemnity Co., 272 N.Y. 635). 

Sec. 48. Relief from Forfeiture. The forfeiture of bail is not final, and the court has the authority by reason of the applicable statute to exonerate the surety and relieve the surety of the forfeiture where good reason exists and jus- 77

§ 

tice will be advanced (People v. Sheehy, 204 Misc. 281, 123 

N.Y.S. 2d 720). This power to relieve the surety of the breach of the undertaking is termed the "power to remit." 

Sec. 597 of the Code of Criminal Procedure vests power in the court to remit a forfeiture and specifies the particular courts that can exercise this power, providing: "After the forfeiture of the undertaking or deposit * * * the court directing the forfeiture, the County Court of the county, or in the City of New York, the Supreme Court may remit the forfeiture or any part thereof, upon such terms as are just."

The power to remit the forfeiture is discretionary with the court (People v. Manufacturers Cas. Ins. Co., 208 Misc. 

504, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 282; People v. Cohen, 229 App. Div. 515, 242 N.Y.S. 654, aff'd. 255 N.Y. 530). It has been held that, notwithstanding the broad discretion possessed by the court to remit the forfeiture, such judicial discretion may be reviewed (People v. Di Meo, 181 App. Div. 893, 167 N.Y. 

S. 1118).

Unless the defendant is produced subsequent to the forfeiture, the court will remit only in unusual cases (People v. Parkin, 263 N.Y. 428). It was held in People v. Manning, 8 Cow. 297, that the surety would be discharged when the nonappearance of the defendant has been caused by "an official act of the State, an act of law, an act of public enemy, sickness or injury of the defendant." The court, in People v. Manufacturers Cas. Ins. Co., 208 Misc. 504, 144 N.Y.S. 

2d 282, stated that the criteria for remitting the forfeiture where the defendant is not produced are: (1) if the failure to produce was due to death, insanity or imprisonment on another charge; (2) if the personal surety or indemnitors on the bond suffer extreme hardship as will cause destitution to a family, deprive children of support and education or creditors of their just debts. 

The surrender of the principal in court after forfeiture does not, of itself, vindicate the sureties and warrant a remission (People v. Dellamura, 28 N.Y.S. 2d 584; People v. Licenziata, 230 App. Div. 358, 244 N.Y.S. 731, aff'd, 256

78

BAIL § 

N.Y. 534). Where the defendant is produced within a reasonable time after forfeiture, the remission may be granted if the surety can demonstrate to the court that the People have not lost any rights as a result of the defendant's nonappearance, particularly if the failure to appear was not deliberate and wilful (People v. Fiannaca, 306 

N.Y. 513). The party seeking the remission should obtain a certificate from the District Attorney, that the People have lost no rights as a result of the defendant's nonappearance (People v. Levy, 169 App. Div. 571, 155 N.Y.S. 

512), but, by the same token, additional facts must be presented, as sole reliance cannot be placed upon the certificate of the District Attorney.

Sec. 49. When Application Must be Made. Section 598 of the Code provides: "The application must be made within one year after the forfeiture of such undertaking or deposit is declared, upon at least five day's notice to the District Attorney of the county, served with copies of the affidavits and papers on which it is founded, and can be granted only upon payment of the costs and expenses incurred in the proceedings for the enforcement of the forfeiture."

Since the privilege of remission is statutory, the requirements and procedures set forth must be strictly complied with (People v. Cohen, 229 App. Div. 515, 242 N.Y.S. 654, aff'd, 255 N.Y. 530). The one-year time limitation is strictly enforced and cannot be waived or extended under any circumstances. The court has no discretion to grant the remission of bail on an application made more than one year after forfeiture (People v. Grundy, 218 App. Div. 541, 218 

N.Y.S. 420). Neither can the court grant an extension of time within which to apply for remission (People v. 

Carlino, 179 Misc. 296, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 933). When the time for the application has expired, certification by the District Attorney, that the People have lost no rights, will have no effect (People v. Martin, 255 App. Div. 572, 233 N.Y.S. 643). 79

§ 

In addition to the policy of strictly holding the surety to his undertaking, as one means of encouraging compliance with the bail bond, a special provision is set forth in the 

Penal Law entitled "Jumping Bail" (Penal Law, sec. 

1694-a). This provides that if a person admitted to bail in connection with a charge of a felony fails to appear as required and thereby incurs a forfeiture of his bail, he is chargeable with a felony if he does not appear or surrender himself within thirty days. If the charge was a misdemeanor and the offender does not appear or surrender within thirty days after forfeiture, he is chargeable with a misdemeanor. If the offender does not surrender within fifteen days after forfeiture when admitted to bail in connection with the following offenses, he is guilty of a misdemeanor: jostling, public enemy, vagrancy, prostitution, loitering, professional criminal. The prosecution, to convict under this section, must prove that the defendant's failure to appear was intentional and deliberate (People v. Davis, 168 Misc. 511, 5 N.Y.S. 2d 411).

Sec. 50. Recommitment of Defendant. Section 599 of the 

Code of Criminal Procedure provides for the arrest and recommitment of the defendant: (1) when, by reason of his failure to appear, he has incurred a forfeiture of his bail, or of money deposited. *** (2) when it satisfactorily appears to the court that his bail, or either of them are dead, or insufficient, or have removed from the State. (3) Upon an indictment found in the cases provided in 

Section 306. 

If the reason for the order and the ground recited was the failure of the defendant to appear for judgment upon conviction, the defendant must be committed according to the order (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 603). If the order is for any other cause, then the defendant may be admitted to bail by the magistrate who would have jurisdiction in a similar case to admit to bail upon holding the defendant to answer prior to indictment as prescribed in Sections 80

BAIL § 557 and 558 of the Code, or by any other magistrate designated by the court. The form of the undertaking and the qualifications of bail are the same as those discussed above. 81
