The arraignment of the defendant before the magistrate, after arrest, is not to be confused with the arraignment of the defendant, after he has been indicted by a Grand Jury. Therefore, the proceeding hereinafter referred to, will be called the preliminary examination.

Counsel should appear at the hearing and request an adjourn- 82

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 51 ment to afford him additional time to make a thorough investigation of the case and to inspect or procure a copy of the papers on file. If the defendant is still in custody, bail should be asked for at this time.

As a general rule, a preliminary examination should never be waived. Counsel should utilize every opportunity, instead, to obtain all possible information about the details, and the nature, of the charges filed against his client. He should particularly try to learn all facts known by the prosecution witnesses, which might prove favorable to the defense. To this end, he might consider permitting these witnesses to testify freely, without interposing all the objections available to him by the rules of evidence. He should also forego no opportunity to cross-examine these witnesses. 

The defendant should make no statement at the examination, except where credibility is not an issue, and the proof adduced by the defendant is sufficiently cogent to contravert the prosecution's case and convince the court that he is not guilty of the crime charged. 

Counsel might consider requesting the court to issue subpoenas for witnesses on behalf of the defendant, as court witnesses to preserve their testimony, particularly if they are hostile to the defendant or may be unavailable to appear at the trial. 

Counsel should waive examination if he feels that proof now in control of the District Attorney will not be available to the prosecution at the trial, particularly if some of the witnesses live outside the State or are about to depart therefrom. 

When the prosecution has adduced its entire proof, counsel should move to dismiss on the ground that the People have failed to make out a prima facie case.

At the conclusion of the examination, the magistrate will either discharge the defendant, if he believes the evidence insufficient to connect him with the alleged crime or he will bind him over to the Grand Jury, in the case of a felony. If the magistrate determines that the crime charged is a misdemeanor, he will transmit the papers to the office of the District Attorney having jurisdiction of the case.

If the defendant is held for further prosecution, counsel should request that bail be continued for his client.

Sec. 51. General. After his arrest, the accused person is brought before the appropriate judicial officer-a magis- 83

§ 

trate-for preliminary hearing. In New York City, the magistrate is one of the City Magistrates. Outside of the 

City, it would be a Justice of the Peace, Police Justice, City 

Judge or District Court Judge. Any of these officers, sitting as a committing magistrate, has jurisdiction over the preliminary arraignment, hearing and commitment. This jurisdiction should be distinguished from the trial jurisdiction exercised by these judges. Such trial jurisdiction of New York City Magistrates is very limited, comprising, generally, minor offenses, traffic violations and violations of ordinances. The magistrates above designated, outside 

New York City, have a wider trial jurisdiction, trying, with juries when demanded, misdemeanors as well as minor offenses. In any event, sitting as committing magistrates, they do not try facts or determine guilt or innocence; in such cases the only issues before them are: (1) has a crime been committed?, and (2) is there reasonable cause to believe the accused person committed it? 

Sec. 52. Purposes. The purpose of this preliminary hearing is to bring the arrested person before the court in order to inform him of the charge lodged against him before any further proceedings are had. At one time, the arraignment was known as "calling the prisoner to the bar." He was commanded to hold up his hand as "owning himself to be of the same name by which he was called." However, in our present-day jurisprudence the connotation of the arraignment is to "establish identity, to inform the accused of the charge against him, to ascertain and receive his answer." Arraignment is also commonly known as the pleading. It is in no sense a trial, although in some instances a trial may be demanded immediately upon the completion of the arraignment. Since it is not a trial, any determination thereon is not a binding judgment. On such a hearing, the magistrate merely determines whether a prima facie case is spelled out. Other purposes of arraignment are to keep the witnesses within control of the District Attorney and to preserve all the relevant testimony 84

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 54 and evidence. Bail is usually determined at the time of arraignment.

Sec. 53. Nature of Preliminary Hearing. "The preliminary hearing is not a trial but merely an inquiry after a criminal charge has been initiated to determine whether there is sufficient or probable cause to believe that a crime has been committed and the accused guilty thereof. It is not necessary that all of the essential elements of the crime be proven beyond a reasonable doubt." (People ex rel. Odell v. 

Hall, 204 Misc. 713, 124 N.Y.S. 2d, 289.) If sufficient grounds are found to justify the charges made, the defendant is held until the matter is presented to and passed upon by the Grand Jury. Even though the magistrate discharge the defendant, a subsequent prosecution may be brought for the same offense (People v. Steiger, 154 Misc. 

538, 277 N.Y.S. 602, citing People v. Dillon 197 N.Y. 254).

An accused person is not entitled to a preliminary examination in every case, but only in those required by statute. Generally, such hearing is necessary only when the crime charged is a felony and not a misdemeanor. And 

So, it was held in People v. Mullen, 66 Misc. 476, 124 N.Y.S. 

158, that where the accused was charged with third degree assault, a crime which the Justice of the Peace had exclusive jurisdiction to try, he was not entitled to a preliminary examination. Sections 188, 189 and 190 of the Code, regulating preliminary hearings, relate to proceedings prosecuted by indictment and have no bearing upon misdemeanors prosecuted under Section 56 (People v. Cuatt, 70 

Misc. 453, 126 N.Y.S. 1114). In the City of New York, the accused is held for trial in Special Sessions in misde meanor cases (Section 31, New York City Criminal Courts 

Act).

Sec. 54. Jurisdiction of Magistrate. In the City of New 

York, the Magistrate's Court is a court of limited jurisdiction, set up into various districts, corresponding, as far as practicable, with police precincts. The court is some- 85

§ 

what similar to the Police Courts throughout the State, but with a more limited jurisdiction. A City Magistrate has primary jurisdiction of those violations of law, known as "offenses", as distinguished from misdemeanors and felonies. Certain minor misdemeanors are within its jurisdiction (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, secs. 31, 102). Under Section 

145 of the New York City Criminal Courts Act, a Felony

Court was created in New York, Bronx and Kings Counties. The procedure therein is set forth in Section 147, as follows: "Thereafter, subject to the provisions of the Youth

Court Act, all persons arrested for a felony, or an attempt to commit a felony, or any of the misdemeanors and offenses enumerated in section five hundred fifty-two of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall be arraigned before the Magistrate holding the Felony Court, where such courts are established, and not before a Magistrate having territorial jurisdiction as provided in section one hundred and six. Upon such arraignment the City Magistrate holding such Felony Court shall proceed to examine into the facts so as to determine whether there is sufficient cause to believe the defendant guilty of such felony or other charge and to warrant holding the defendant to answer." 

Outside the City of New York, courts of special sessions are held by Justices of the Peace, Police Justices, City 

Judges and District Court Judges. They have jurisdiction to hear and dispose of traffic violations and misdemeanors and the misdemeanors enumerated under Section 56, Code of Criminal Procedure. They have jurisdiction to try complaints for violations of Sections 1221, 1912 and 1913 of the Penal Law. A Police Justice of an incorporated village, holding a court of special sessions, has exclusive jurisdiction, with or without a jury, subject only to removal proceedings, to try all misdemeanors committed within the village (Village Law, sec. 182; People v. Monahan, 257 N.Y.388). 

Sec. 55. Adjournments. The statute requires the court to allow the defendant a reasonable time to send for counsel 86

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 55 and to grant an adjournment for that purpose. Section 

189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states: "He must allow the defendant a reasonable time to send for counsel and adjourn the examination for that purpose, and must, upon the request of the defendant, require a peace officer to take a message to such counsel in the town or city, as the defendant may name. The officer must, without delay and without fee, perform that duty." The refusal to allow an adjournment in order to obtain counsel is equivalent to a deprivation of the right of cross-examination, and a conviction under those circumstances will be reversed (People v. Sperduto, 221 App. Div. 577, 224 N.Y.S. 529).

Immediately after counsel appear, or if none appear, after waiting a reasonable time, the magistrate must proceed to hear the case unless the defendant waives examination and elects to give bail, in which case the magistrate must admit him to bail, if the crime is bail able. Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states: 

"In the case of a defendant who has reached the age of sixteen years but has not reached the age of twenty-one years, the magistrate shall not proceed in a manner inconsistent with section thirty-three of the Youth Court Act. The magistrate, immediately after the appearance of counsel, or if none appears and the defendant requires the aid of counsel, must, after waiting a reasonable time therefor, proceed to examine the case, unless the defendant waives examination and elects to give bail, in which case the magistrate must admit the defendant to bail if the crime is bailable, as provided in section two hundred ten; and in that case witnesses in attendance or shown to be material for the People may be required to appear and testify, or to be examined conditionally as prescribed in sections two hundred fifteen, two hundred sixteen, two hundred seventeen, two hundred eighteen, two hundred nineteen and two hundred twenty."

The examination must be completed at one session unless the magistrate for good cause adjourn it. Section 191 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states: "The examination 

87

§ 

must be completed at one session, unless the magistrate, for good cause adjourn it. The adjournment cannot be for more than two days at each time, unless by consent or on motion of the defendant." It was held in People ex rel. 

Sidran v. Warden of City Prison, 129 Misc. 327, 220 N.Y.S. 

529, that the magistrate had the power to adjourn the hearing from time to time for periods of two days each while awaiting the arrival of exemplified papers. Section 

192 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states: "If an ad journment be had for any cause, the magistrate must commit the defendant for examination, or discharge him from custody, upon his giving bail to appear during the examination, or upon deposit of money as provided in this Code, to make sure of his appearance at the time to which the examination is adjourned."

Sec. 56. Being Informed of the Charge. Section 188, Code of Criminal Procedure, requires the "magistrate to inform defendant of the charge, and his right to counsel. 

When the defendant is brought before a magistrate upon an arrest either with or without a warrant on a charge of having committed a crime, the magistrate must immediately inform him of the charge against him, of his right to the aid of counsel in every stage of the proceeding, and before any further proceedings are had." The importance of advising the defendant as to his rights before any proceedings are taken was emphasized in People v. Caralt, 135 Misc. 842, 241 N.Y.S. 641, where a defendant was charged with soliciting financial assistance in buildings and offices, and from house to house, without a license as required by the New York Code of Ordinances. The record revealed that on the hearing, after twenty-two pages of testimony had been taken, he was advised by the Magistrate for the first time what the charges were. The Court of Special Sessions, in reversing the lower court, held that the magistrate did not protect the rights of the defendant, as he should, by having the formal charge read to him, and ordered a new trial. 88

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 57 Advising the defendant of his rights must not be done in such perfunctory fashion that he is unable to understand them, or be in a position to avail himself of them. It was held to be a denial of such rights in People v. Berg, 220 

Misc. 203, 105 N.Y.S. 2d 694, where the court attendant informed the defendant of his rights with such rapidity that the defendant was unable to understand him or to assert any of his rights. The Court of Special Sessions, in reversing the lower court, asserted that it was the duty of the Magistrate personally to advise the defendant of his rights and it was not one that he could delegate to a court attendant.

Sec. 57. Communication with Friends, Relatives. Section 

115 of the New York City Criminal Courts Act requires the Magistrate to inform the defendant of his right to communicate with friends, in these words: "At the time of the arraignment of a defendant, the Magistrate shall inform said defendant that he is entitled to communicate with his relatives or friends, by letter or telephone free of charge. The Chief City Magistrate shall investigate the manner and method of the enforcement by the Department of Correction of the provisions of section one hundred seventy-two of this act, and in the event that any of the duties imposed by such provisions are not properly performed, said Chief Magistrate shall promptly report the same in writing to the Mayor. But the failure of the Magistrate to give the warning prescribed herein shall not be deemed a reason to reverse a judgment of conviction unless such failure is shown to have deprived the defendant of a fair trial."

In People v. Griessman, 149, N.Y.S. 63, the court reversed a judgment of conviction for disorderly conduct, where the Magistrate had failed to advise the defendant of her rights pursuant to section 81 of the Inferior Criminal Courts Act (now section 115 of the New York City Criminal Courts Act), even though he had notified her of her right to counsel under Section 188 of the Code of Criminal 89

§ 

Procedure. The court stated: "The notification required by Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has no application to cases where the Magistrates have the summary power of conviction, and is not required in such cases, although, as stated in the opinion of the judges of this court, it is better practice to give such notification. Such notification is required only in cases of preliminary examination of the defendant held for the purpose of discharging him or holding him to answer. On the other hand, the notification required by section 81 of the Inferior Criminal Courts Act is required to be given in all cases where the Magistrates have summary jurisdiction to convict and impose sentence, but is not required where a preliminary examination of the defendant is being held." 

Sec. 58. Right to Counsel. The court, on an application for peremptory mandamus in People ex rel. Steinhardt v. 

Fuller, 68 N.Y.S. 742, 15 N.Y.Cr. 344: "The intention of this section was to guard the rights of the prisoner by making it mandatory upon the magistrate to inform the accused of the charge he is required to answer; and the right to the aid of counsel in every stage of the proceedings is guaranteed to him not only by the section referred to, but by sections of the same Code, as well as by Section 6 of Article 1 of the State Constitution." There was some relaxation of the requirement that the court advise the defendant of his right to counsel at every stage of the proceeding in People v. Begue, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 474, modified on other grounds 1 App. Div. 2d 289, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 791. It held there was no obligation to repeat the advice at every stage of the proceeding when it had been given at the time of arraignment.

Sec. 59. Conduct of the Hearing. When the accused person is brought before the magistrate for arraignment, the attorney should attend and file a notice of appearance. He may then request permission to examine the papers on file and obtain, or make, a copy of the complaint. If a copy of 90

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 60 the complaint has been obtained, the reading of it may be waived when the case is called. Section 194 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure states: "At the examination, the magistrate must, in the first place, read to the defendant the depositions of the witnesses examined on the taking of the information, and if the defendant request it, or elects to have the examination, must summon for crossexamination the witnesses so examined, if they be in the county. He must also issue subpoenas for additional witnesses required by the prosecutor or the defendant."

Sec. 60. Examination of Witnesses. At this point, the at torney for the defendant should determine whether it is to the advantage of his client to proceed with the examination or to waive his right thereto. The waiver of the preliminary examination before the magistrate is a consent that the magistrate hold the defendant to await the action of the Grand Jury or some other officer or body (Armstrong v. Mishkin, 268 App. Div. 864, 141 N.Y.S. 2d 884).

If there is a waiver, and no examination is held, the defendant has no opportunity to ascertain the testimony of the prosecution's witness, which may be useful as a means for cross-examination on the trial or in preparing the defense. There are advantages in a waiver, however. If the witnesses whom the prosecution will need at the trial are non-residents, or may depart from the jurisdiction, or are likely to die before the trial, it is not desirable from the viewpoint of the defendant to have their testimony perpetuated on a preliminary examination. Such testimony can be introduced upon the trial only if the defendant has had an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses (People v. Gilhooley, 108 App. Div. 234, 95 N.Y.S. 636, aff'd. 187 N.Y. 

551. People v. Hines, 284 N.Y. 93). It must be borne in mind, however, that the right to a preliminary examination is not limited to the defendant. The prosecution has a similar right and is not precluded, by defendant's waiver, from examining material witnesses who are present (People v. 

Albero, 119 Misc. 339, 196 N.Y.S. 484). 91

§ 

By availing himself of the examination, the defendant has an opportunity to cross-examine the prosecution's witness at length. He may thus develop testimony favorable to the defendant, or of such inconsistency as to weaken the prosecution's case. A transcript of this testimony, obtained from the court stenographer upon payment of his fees, may be used upon the trial. The defendant is not limited to an examination only of the prosecution's witnesses. He may examine any witness, except where forbidden by statute, whom he deems necessary for his defense 

(People ex rel. Taylor v. Smalley 121 Misc. 331, 201 N.Y.S. 

39).

Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: 

"The witnesses must be examined in the presence of the defendant, and may be cross-examined in his behalf." A deposition used for the issuance of a warrant of arrest may not be used against the defendant on the trial, where he has had no opportunity for cross-examination (People ex rel. Domens v. Warden, 154 App. Div. 728, 139 N.Y.S. 828).

The magistrate, under his judicial authority, and by virtue of Sections 202 and 203 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure, controls the presence of witnesses and other persons on the examination. Section 202 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure requires that witnesses be kept apart, stating: "The witnesses produced on the part either of the People or of the defendant cannot be present at the examination of the defendant; and while a witness is under examination, the magistrate may exclude all witnesses who have not been examined. He may also cause the witnesses to be kept separate, and to be prevented from conversing with each other, until they are all examined." 

Section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides, however, a limitation of the magistrate's right to exclude persons from the examination in the following words: "The magistrate may also exclude from the examination every person except the clerk of the magistrate, the prosecutor and his counsel, the Attorney General, the District 92

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 62 Attorney of the county, the defendant and his counsel and the officer having the defendant in custody."

Sec. 61. Witnesses. Section 215 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure provides: "On holding the defendant to answer, the magistrate may take from each of the material witnesses examined before him on the part of the People, a written undertaking, to the effect that he will appear and testify at the court to which the depositions and statement are to be sent, or that he will forfeit the sum of one hundred dollars." However, if the magistrate is satisfied "by proof on oath, that there is reason to believe that any such witness is an accomplice in the commission of the crime charged, he may order the witness to enter into a written undertaking with such sureties, and in such sum, as he may deem proper, for his appearance as specified in the last section." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 216.) When a witness is thus required to enter into an undertaking to appear and testify, either with or without sureties, his refusal to comply with the order imposes upon the magistrate the duty, mandated by Section 218 of the Code, to commit him to prison "until he comply or be legally discharged."

Section 217 of the Code of Criminal Procedure makes special provision applicable to the commitment of children under sixteen as witnesses. While the magistrate retains the power to commit them as witnesses, he must do so under the restrictions imposed by Section 487 of the Penal Law, requiring that the hearing and examination be held separate and apart from those involving other criminal cases.

Sec. 62. Witnesses for the People-Conditional Examina tion. Depositions of witnesses not actually present at the hearing or trial could not be used at common law, since that was deemed a breach of the defendant's right to be confronted by the witnesses testifying against him. However, by the enactment of Section 219 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure the Legislature has extended to the People the 93

§ 

right enjoyed by the defendant to examine witnesses on deposition. The conditions imposed upon the taking of such examinations and, particularly, those which must be satisfied before testimony so taken is admitted in evidence, give this procedure its name of conditional examination. The examination is allowed by the court after motion made in accordance with the provisions of Section 620, et seq., of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and generally is permitted when the witness is about to leave the State, or is so sick or infirm as to afford reasonable grounds for apprehending that he will be unable to attend the trial. The courts have held that the statutory requirements must be strictly complied with, so that any inexactness or incompleteness in carrying out the provisions thereof vitiates the procedure. Thus, in People v. Sugarman, 248 N.Y. 255, the Court of Appeals reversed a judgment of conviction. and ordered a new trial because depositions used on the trial had not included the original exhibits but only copies thereof.

Section 219 provides: "A witness may be conditionally examined on behalf of the People in the manner and with the effect provided by title twelve, chapter three, Sections 620 et seq. of this Code, for taking examination of witnesses conditionally on behalf of the defendant. A copy of the order and affidavit upon which the application is made, together with notice of the time and place where the examination is to be taken, shall be served on the defendant, and his counsel, if he have any, at least two days before the time fixed for such examination, and the defendant may be present personally upon such examination to confront the witness produced against him, if the defendant have no counsel the order shall contain a provision assigning counsel to him for the purpose of such examination upon whom a copy of said order, affidavit and notice shall be served."

For a more complete discussion of this procedure, see chapter on "Examination of Witnesses, Conditionally," infra. 94

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 65 

Sec. 63. Degree of Proof Required. At the close of the pros ecution's case, the attorney for the defendant may move to dismiss on the ground that a prima facie case has not been made out as a matter of law. If this motion is denied, further examination may be waived. It is to be noted that, in denying such a motion, the magistrate is not passing on the guilt or innocence of the defendant. The court must be satisfied only that a prima facie case is made out (People on complaint of Love v. Schapiro, 77 N.Y.S. 

2d 726). In People on complaint of Schoen v. Bernstein, 95 N.Y.S. 2d 696, the court held that the committing magistrate holding the defendant for Special Sessions, should not require the same degree of proof as would be needed for a conviction, but it should be of such sufficiency that a trial court would not be bound, as a matter of law, to acquit.

Sec. 64. Right to Make Statement. Upon the conclusion of the People's case, the magistrate is required to inform the defendant "that it is his right to make a statement in relation to the charge against him (stating to him the nature thereof); that the statement is designed to enable him, if he see fit, to answer the charge and to explain the facts alleged against him; that he is at liberty to waive making a statement; and that his waiver cannot be used against him on the trial." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 106.)

Sec. 65. Waiver. Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Pro cedure provides: "If the defendant waive his right to make a statement, the magistrate must make a note thereof, immediately following the deposition of the witnesses against the defendant." In People v. Stein, 221 App. Div. 

500, 224 N.Y.S. 667, a judgment of conviction for arson in the second degree was reversed and a new trial ordered, where the trial court had received in evidence statements made by the defendant before the magistrate, there being no record that the defendant had been informed by the magistrate of his right to make a statement, or his liberty 95

§ 

to waive making a statement, or that such waiver could not be used against him. 

Sec. 66. How Taken. If the defendant choose to make a statement, the magistrate must proceed to take it in writing, without oath, and must put to the defendant the following questions only: "What is your name and age? 

Where were you born? Where do you reside and how long have you resided there? What is your business or profession? Give any explanation you may think proper, of the circumstances appearing in the testimony against you, and state any facts which you think will tend to your exculpation." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 198.) Taking the testimony of the accused under oath, without allowing the defendant the safeguards provided by the Code of Criminal Procedure, was condemned in People v. Mondon, 103 N.Y. 

211, and a judgment of conviction for homicide there rendered was reversed. Having, then, either made or waived his statement the defendant may proceed to call his witnesses, if he has any, under the authorization of Section 201 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides: "After the waiver of the defendant to make a statement or after he has made it, his witnesses, if he produce any, must be sworn and examined." 

Sec. 67. Minutes of Hearing. If the statement is given, it must be taken in accordance with Section 199, of the Code, as follows: "The answer of the defendant to each of the questions must be distinctly read to him as it is taken down. 

He may thereupon correct or add to his answer, and it must be corrected until it is made conformable to what he declares to be the truth." The statement is then reduced to writing and authenticated by the magistrate in accordance with Section 200 of the Code, thus: "1. The authentication must set forth in detail, that the defendant was informed of his rights as provided in section one hundred and ninety-six, and that after being so informed, he made the statement; 2. It must contain the questions put to him, 96

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 68 and his answers thereto, as provided in Sections one hundred ninety-eight and one hundred ninety-nine; 3. It may be signed by the defendant, or he may refuse to sign it, but if he refuses to sign, his reason therefor must be stated as he gives it; 4. It must be signed and certified by the magistrate." Testimony of witnesses must also be reduced to writing in accordance with Section 204 of the Code as follows: "The testimony given by each witness must be reduced to writing, as a deposition, by the magistrate or under his direction, and authenticated in the following manner: 1. The authentication must state the name and age of the witness, his place of residence and his business or profession; 2. It must, unless deposition by question and answer be waived by the defendant and the witness, contain the questions put to the witness and his answers thereto, each answer being distinctly read to him as it is taken down and being corrected or added to until it is made conformable to what he declares to be the truth; 3. If a question put be objected to on either side, and overruled, or the witness decline answering it, that fact, with the ground on which the question was overruled or the answer declined, must be stated; 4. The deposition must be signed by the witness, or if he refuses to sign it, his reason for refusing must be stated in writing as he gives it; 5. It must be signed and certified by the magistrate. 6. The foregoing provisions shall apply to preliminary examination in the City and County of New York only when either the defendant or the District Attorney, or the representative of the 

District Attorney shall so elect."

Sec. 68. Stenographer's Minutes. Sect. 221-b of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure provides: "Upon any examination provided by this chapter, by or before any police justice or magistrate by whom an official stenographer shall have been appointed, under provision of law therefor, stenographic minutes of the proceedings and of the examination, depositions of witnesses and statement of the defendant, if any, shall be taken by such stenographer, and such 97

§ 

minutes, when so taken and when certified by the stenographer and by the justice or magistrate who held such examination, shall be regarded as actually taken down in writing by said justice or magistrate and subscribed by the witness or witnesses at such examination and by the defendant, and as fully complying with the requirements of this chapter in reference to the taking and subscribing of such examination, depositions and statement. Where the defendant is charged with a felony and is either held to answer or not so held, upon request of the District Attorney a copy of such stenographic minutes, notwithstanding the provisions of any other law, shall be furnished by such official stenographer to the District Attorney of the county. 

Such stenographer shall be compensated at the rate of ten cents for each folio on such copies furnished, and such compensation shall be a county charge." 

In People v. Cittrola, 213 App. Div. 674, 210 N.Y.S. 21, the Appellate Division reversed a judgment of conviction by a magistrate, sitting as a court of special sessions, where the record did not disclose that any testimony had been taken upon the trial or that any stenographic report of the hearing had been made. The court stated, after setting forth the requirements of Sections 199, 200 and 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: "One convicted of a crime shall not be deprived of his rights to prosecute an appeal because the stenographer cannot produce the minutes of the trial." In People v. Giles, 152 N.Y. 136, the

Court of Appeals stated at page 140: "Our magistrates are invested with important powers. Many offenses of a criminal nature may be summarily tried and disposed of by them. Their determinations, in many instances, involve the liberties and property of citizens. To permit them to exercise these important powers, without keeping any minutes or records of the testimony upon which their determinations can be reviewed, would be contrary to public policy, and would be investing them with autocratic power greater than those possessed by any other officer 98

PRELIMINARY EXAMINATION 

§ 68 of the government. We think that the Legislature never intended to invest them with such powers; that it is their duty to keep, or have kept under their direction, minutes of the testimony taken upon trials, to the end that their determinations as to the facts may be reviewed upon appeal." 

In some courts a stenographer is not regularly employed, and so Section 204-a of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits the employment of a stenographer upon examination on a charge of felony, as follows: "In an examination held in a criminal proceeding upon a charge of felony, in a town or village, the magistrate, unless pursuant to law a stenographer be regularly employed by such magistrate or in the court over which he presides, may, if the defendant be represented by counsel, employ a stenographer to take testimony on such examination. The compensation of such stenographer shall not exceed five dollars per day for each day actually spent in taking such testimony and shall be a county charge." The depositions are then kept by the magistrate, or his clerk, until they are returned to the proper court, as follows: "The magistrate or his clerk must keep the depositions taken on the information or on the examination, and the statement of the defendant, if any, until they are returned to the proper court, and must not permit them to be inspected by any person except a judge of a court having jurisdiction of the offense, the Attorney General, the District Attorney of the county, the defendant and his counsel and the complainant and his counsel." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 205.) Section 206, Code of Criminal Procedure, provides: "If the defendant be held to answer the charge, the magistrate or his clerk having the custody of the depositions taken on the information or examination, and of the statement of the defendant, must, on payment of his fees at the rate of five cents for each hundred words, and within two days after demand, furnish to the defendant, or his counsel, a copy of the depositions and statement, or permit either of them to take a copy." 99

§ 

 Sec. 69. Discharge of Defendant, When and How. The circumstances and manner of the defendant's discharge on preliminary examination are thus prescribed in Section 207 of the Code: "After hearing the proofs and the statement of the defendant, if he have made one, if it appearing either that a crime has not been committed, or there is not sufficient cause to believe the defendant guilty thereof, the magistrate must order the defendant to be discharged, by an indorsement on the depositions and statement, signed by him, to the following effect: "There being no sufficient cause to believe the within named A.B. guilty of the offense within-mentioned, I order him to be discharged." In People v. Weiss, 147 Misc. 595, 261 N.Y.S. 

646, the defendants were discharged after being held on short form affidavits charging them with homicide arising from a criminal abortion. The only evidence adduced was a statement signed by the deceased and testimony of the coroner as to statements made to him by the deceased. The court, holding that these did not meet the requirements of a dying declaration, and thus were inadmissible, stated: "There must, however, be a prima facie case proven, such a case that a trial court would not be bound to grant a motion to acquit at the close of the people's case. There must be a reasonable ground for believing that a crime has been committed and that the defendant is guilty thereof." 

The court further pointed out that sufficient cause for holding the defendant for the Grand Jury required legal evidence, not mere suspicion.

Section 207-a, Code of Criminal Procedure, provides: 

"Whenever a magistrate orders the discharge of a defendant accused of a felony, who has previously been arrested for or convicted of a felony, he shall make in writing a statement setting forth his reasons for such discharge, and he shall append to such statement the complete criminal record of the defendant, and such statement and record shall be filed as a public record in the office of the clerk of the court or if there be no clerk, in the office of the 100

§ 71 magistrate and shall be subject to inspection by any person." 

Sec. 70. Commitment. "If, however, it appear from the examination that a crime has been committed and that there is sufficient cause to believe the defendant guilty thereof, the magistrate must in like manner, indorse on the depositions and statement, an order, signed by him, to the following effect: 'It appearing to me by the within deposition (and statement, if any) that the crime therein mentioned (or any other crime according to the fact, stating generally the nature thereof) has been committed, and that there is sufficient cause to believe the within A.B. guilty thereof, I order that he be held to answer the same."" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 208.) Even if the information is deficient in some respect, it should not be dismissed if evidence before the magistrate proves the commission of a crime (People v. Ehrlich, 14 N.Y.S. 2nd 125). It was held in People ex rel. Willett v. Quiren, 150 App. Div. 813, 135 

N.Y.S. 477: "A committing magistrate is not required to exact the full measure of proof necessary to secure a conviction, but is obliged to hold one accused of crime for trial if there is reasonable ground to believe him guilty.” “If the crime be not bailable, the following words, or words to the same effect, must be added to the endorsement: "and that he be committed to the Sheriff of the County of (or in the counties within the City of New York) "to Commissioner of Correction of the City of New York") (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 209). If the crime be bailable, and bail be taken by the magistrate, he indorses in addition thereto, pursuant to Section 210: “and I have admitted him to bail to answer, by the undertaking hereto annexed."

Sec. 71. Defendant To Choose How He Shall Be Tried. "If the crime with which the defendant is charged be one triable, as provided in subdivision thirty-eight of section fifty-six, by a court of special sessions of the county in which the same was committed, the magistrate, before 101

§ (a)  

holding the defendant to answer, must inform him of his right to be tried by a court of special sessions, and must ask him how he will be tried. If the defendant shall not require to be tried by a court of special sessions, he can only be held to answer to a court having authority to inquire by the intervention of a Grand Jury in cases triable in the county." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 211.) In People v. Lord, 142 Misc. 740, 255 N.Y.S. 409, the defendant moved to dismiss the indictment charging him with violation of Section 1530 of the Penal Law, a misdemeanor which is punishable by imprisonment for one year or by a fine of $500.00, or both; alleging that the crime was triable in the first instance before a Justice of the Peace, sitting as a court of special sessions, pursuant to subdivision 38 of section 56 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In denying the motion, the court held that courts of special sessions are limited to such jurisdiction as is given them by statute. 

Section 56 defines the jurisdiction of courts of special sessions to hear and determine misdemeanors committed within their counties. Where the misdemeanor charged is not one of those enumerated in its various subdivisions, the court may try it as a court of special sessions, pursuant to subdivision 38, if the accused so elect and the misdemeanor is not one which is punishable by a fine exceeding fifty dollars, or by imprisonment exceeding six months. If the case is one which falls under subdivision 38 of section 56 of the Code, the defendant's choice whether he shall go to trial before the justice or go to the Grand Jury determines the procedure of the justice. "If he elects to go to trial, the justice proceeds to try him without any preliminary examination. If the defendant elects to go to the 

Grand Jury, the justice must hold him to answer before a court having a Grand Jury, without any preliminary examination." (People v. Mullen, 66 Misc. 475, 124 N.Y.S. 158.)

Sec. 71(b). Justice's Criminal Docket. Section 220 of the 

Code of Criminal Procedure requires "every Justice of the Peace and every police or other special justice appointed or elected in a city, village or town other than in the City and County of New York," to maintain a "justice's criminal docket," which shall be open for inspection to the public. 

In it, he is required to keep accurate minutes of all criminal actions and proceedings before him, together with the names and places of residence of witnesses sworn by him. 

The failure to make the entries required by this section, or to exhibit such docket when reasonably required, constitutes a misdemeanor and, in addition to the punishment for a misdemeanor, forfeiture of office. 

Sec. 71(c). Magistrate's Return.
