Sec. 87. Wiretapping, Eavesdropping, etc.

Sec. 72. History. The history of the law of search and seizure can be traced rather readily. Two famous English cases form the cornerstone of the development of the right of the people to be protected against unreasonable searches and seizures; the protection extends only against unreasonable actions; the privilege is, of course, not absolute. "The statutes of New York express the principle that 106

§ English law received, as the outcome of the prosecutions of Wilkes and Entick. (Entick v. Carrington, 19 Howell's 

State Trials, 1030; Wilkes' Case, 19 Howell's State Trials, 1045; Boyd v. United States, 116 U.S. 616, 626.) The immunity is not from all search and seizure, but from search and seizure unreasonable in the light of common-law traditions." (People v. Chiagles, 237 N.Y. 193, 195.) The Wilkes case arose in 1762 when Wilkes' home was searched and Wilkes arrested therein, pursuant to a general warrant which had been issued by the Secretary of State and which directed the arrest of certain writers and the seizure of their papers. These writers, among them Wilkes, had engaged in the publication of circulars which were generally critical of the government. After his arrest, Wilkes and the other persons affected sued for false imprisonment and, in the case cited, recovered damages against the persons responsible for the execution of the general warrant, including the Secretary of State. 

The Entick case involved a similar situation and Lord 

Camden stated in his opinion: "*** the law obligeth no man to accuse himself * * * and it shoud seem, that the search for evidence is disallowed upon the same principle.' 

Thus, besides holding general warrants invalid, the decision recognized that searches under invalid warrants violate the privilege against self-incrimination. Later, in 

1766, the decisions of the judges in the Entick case were ratified by the House of Commons, which also adopted a resolution disapproving of the use of general warrants. In an address to the House of Commons urging the adoption of this resolution, Pitt spoke the famous words that embody the principle of the law in this area: "The poorest man may, in his cottage, bid defiance to all the forces of the Crown. It may be frail; its roof may shake; the wind may blow through it; the storm may enter; the rain may enter; but the King of England may not enter; all his force dares not cross the threshold of the ruined tenement." (Cooley, Constitutional Limitations, Vol. 1, p. 611; 8th ed., 1927.)

The restrictions upon general warrants, and against un- 107

§ 

reasonable searches and seizures, were early enacted in State Constitutions and Bills of Rights in the several states after the Revolutionary War. 

The present New York law in this area is codified in the Civil Rights Law, section 8, which originally was contained in the Revised Statutes of 1828 (Pt. 1, ch. 4, sect. 11), and in the New York Constitution, Article I, section 12, which was adopted in its present form in 1938. 

Sec. 73. Constitutional Safeguards. 

(a). State. Article I, section 12, of the New York State 

Constitution provides: "The right of the people to be secure in their person, houses, papers and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no warrant shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.

The right of the people to be secure against unreasonable interception of telephone and telegraph communication shall not be violated, and ex parte orders or warrants shall issue only upon oath or affirmation that there is reasonable ground to believe that evidence of crime may be thus obtained, and identifying the particular means of communication, and particularly describing the person or persons whose communications are to be intercepted and the purpose thereof." Thus, the New York Constitution limits wiretapping also. This area of the law of search and seizure will be treated in a separate section in this chapter, infra. 

The above-quoted section only proscribes those searches and seizures that are unlawful. In Application of Marshall, 17 Misc. 2d 985, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 413, the petitioner applied for an order directing the Police Commissioner to return certain money which had been taken from her by police officers who had entered her home, arrested her, and seized the money without a warrant of arrest or a search warrant. The petitioner had been charged with conspiracy to commit abortion, an information had been filed, and she 108

§ had been acquitted after trial. While directing the return of the money the court stated: "The arrest being unlawful [because made without a warrant; without a claim that defendant had committed or was being arrested for a felony, and without a claim that a crime was being committed in the presence of the arresting officers] and the search having been made without a search warrant or other lawful process, the search was unreasonable and in defiance of the constitutional mandate. *** If a police officer, who enters a home without a search warrant in the course of an illegal arrest, makes a search and then seizes the property of the homeowner, can successfully resist the application of the owner, made after acquittal of crime, for its return, by the unsupported assertion, as made here, that the property of the fruit of criminal activity, the constitutional protection against unreasonable search and seizures will have ceased to exist *** the right of the people to be secure against unreasonable searches and seizures given by the Civil Rights Law (Sec. 8) and now embodied in the Constitution of the State (Article I, Sec. 12) is not violated by a search and seizure incident to a lawful arrest. * * *" For a discussion of the law of arrest, generally, see chapter entitled "Arrest Without Warrant." 

In Schutt v. MacDuff, 205 Misc. 43, 127 N.Y.S. 2d 116, the petitioner unsuccessfully relied upon the above quoted section of the Constitution in an Article 78 proceeding, brought to annul a determination of the respondent Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, who had revoked petitioner's driving license. Petitioner had been arrested for drunken driving, and had refused to submit to a blood test to determine the alcoholic content of his blood. Vehicle and 

Traffic Law, Section 71-a, provided: "Any person who operates a motor vehicle *** shall be deemed to have given his consent to a chemical test of his *** blood *** provided such test is administered at the direction of a police officer having reasonable grounds to suspect such person of [drunken] driving. ***If such person refuses to submit to such *** test the test shall not be given but the 

109

§ 

commissioner shall revoke his license. ***" The petitioner, prior to the institution of the Article 78 proceeding, had been acquitted of the drunken driving charge. In the proceeding, he contended that this section of the Vehicle and Traffic Law was unconstitutional on several grounds. The court considered the various grounds urged by petitioner, and, dealing with the above quoted article of the Constitution, stated that "the guarantee protects only against searches made without a warrant and beyond the terms of a warrant and the papers on which it was issued, or against personal searches made before a legal arrest. This rule in relation to Section 12 was built up while its provisions appeared only in Section 8 of the Civil Rights Law and before it became a constitutional provision in 1938, but the Court of Appeals has held that the enactment as part of the Constitution in that year in no way changed the interpretation of the language previously built up with respect to the statute. * * * Therefore, as a general proposition, a search and seizure of one's person following his lawful arrest, violates no law. Here, the petitioner, being under lawful arrest, could be searched for evidences of the crime for which he was arrested. * * *" The statute was held unconstitutional on other [due process] grounds, the court holding that no test could be made under the statute without the subject's consent.

Pitt's famous phrase, quoted above, was used by the court in People v. Singleton, 117 N.Y.S. 2d 114, where defendant was charged with third degree assault, after the complaining police officer had been injured while defendant was attempting to eject him from his apartment. The officer had entered in the course of an investigation of a disturbance, and had refused to leave when defendant so requested. The court stated, while dismissing the complaint: "There is still a constitutional right against unlawful search and seizure. *** A man's home is still his castle."

The right of the person being unlawfully searched, or whose property is being unlawfully seized, to use a reason- 110

§ able amount of force in resisting such an intrusion is discussed, infra.

In Matter of Matson, 293 N.Y. 476, reversing 182 Misc. 

389, 49 N.Y.S. 2d 598, the search and seizure clause of the

Constitution was held not violated by Mental Hygiene Law, section 51-a, which allowed superintendents of State institutions to apply for court orders to inventory safe deposit boxes of patients. The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division, which had held the section unconstitutional, and stated: "Nor does the statute conflict with the prohibition in the State Constitution against unreasonable searches and seizures. Here, the inspection authorized is in aid of a civil proceeding which was designed to conserve any property which might be possessed by an incompetent. In the circumstances disclosed by the present record such an inspection, as we view it, is not an unwarranted intrusion and is in no sense 'unreasonable'." In 

People v. Carver, 172 Misc. 820, 16 N.Y.S. 2d 268, the District Attorney moved to impound certain corporate books and records, then in the possession of the General Counsel of the State Insurance Fund, for use in a criminal proceeding directed against the bookkeeper of the corporation, charged with forgery of the books involved. The General 

Counsel joined the District Attorney in the motion. Previously, an order had been entered, in an action between the General Counsel and the corporation, directing the General Counsel to return the books to the corporation. The court denied the District Attorney's motion seeking "to be authorized by this Court to seize the said books [from the General Counsel] who was directed to return them to the corporation owning them." The court stated: "A seizure of the property to be used by the District Attorney as evidence in a criminal prosecution is justifiable if effected through the medium of a search warrant. * * * An order of the Court, therefore, purporting to authorize a District 

Attorney to seize property *** belonging to third parties because they contain evidence of crime and without compliance with the statutory regulations prescribed, would 111

§ 

be tantamount to circumventing the provisions of the statute. ***" In effect, the court held that such an order would be an unreasonable seizure of the property in the light of the methods of insuring the reasonableness of seizures prescribed by the statutes regulating the use of search warrants.

The above cases indicate, generally, the New York State constitutional limitations on searches and seizures. Problems concerning the effect of the second paragraph, proscribing wiretapping and related activities, the remedies of one unlawfully searched or whose property has been unlawfully seized, and other problems are discussed below. 

The constitutional limitation may be summarized as prohibiting an "unreasonable" search, the reasonableness of the search depending upon the circumstances. It should however be noted that prior to 1938 the above quoted provision was contained only in a statute (Civil Rights Law, section 8). This status of the prohibition was considered sufficiently significant to warrant mention by Chief Judge Cardozo in People v. Defore, 242 N.Y. 13, the Court of 

Appeals holding that evidence illegally obtained was admissible in New York State criminal proceedings. Prior to the Defore decision, the Court of Appeals had so held in People v. Adams, 176 N.Y. 351, affirmed 192 U.S. 585. After the decision in the Adams case, the United States Supreme Court, in a series of decisions retreated from the position there taken and overruled the Adams case. However, in the 

Defore case, the Court of Appeals noted that it was not bound to follow these later decisions, and stated that in New York the prohibition against unreasonable search and seizure is derived not from the "Constitution, but of statute." 

In People v. Richter's Jewelers, 291 N.Y. 161, the Court of Appeals recognized that "the immunity from unreasonable search and seizure is no longer a creature of statute, for in 1938 the statute was incorporated in the Constitution." The court also recognized the identity of the language of that section with the language of the Federal 112

§ (b) Constitution, but held that because of the long history of decisions in New York, starting with that in the Adams case, holding that illegally obtained evidence was admissible, any change in this rule would have to be initiated by the Legislature. Thus, the Richter case may be noted at this point for its holding that the incorporation in the Constitution of this section did not necessarily, of itself, effect any change in the rules of law that had grown up about the section while it was only a statute. 

Sec. 73 (b). Federal. The language of the Fourth Amend ment of the United States Constitution is identical to that contained in the section of the New York State Constitution quoted above. However the Fourth Amendment does not apply to State action. It is only a limitation upon the powers of the Federal Government. "It has been well settled for years that the first ten amendments apply only to the procedure and trial of causes in the Federal courts and are not limitations upon those in State courts." (Spies v. 

Illinois, 123 U.S. 131, 166; Gaines v. Washington, 277 U.S. 

81, 85.) The question then arose whether the Fourteenth 

Amendment, through its "privileges and immunities" clause, incorporated the Fourth Amendment and afforded its protection to parties affected by State action. In Hague v. C.I.O., 101 F.2d 774, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals held that "unreasonable searches and seizures had occurred and that the prohibitions of the Fourth Amendment had been taken over by the Fourteenth Amendment so as to protect citizens of the United States against such action." However, the Supreme Court held that decision on that point was unnecessary to the decision and modified and affirmed the Circuit Court's opinion on other grounds.

Subsequently, the leading case in this area, Wolf v. 

Colorado, 338 U.S. 25, 93 L. Ed. 1782, was decided. There, the Supreme Court, in a five-to-four decision, held that the Fourteenth Amendment does not require exclusion of unlawfully seized evidence in a State court. In so holding, the 113

§ (b) 

opinion of the court stated: "The security of one's privacy against arbitrary intrusion by the police-which is at the core of the Fourth Amendment-is basic to a free society. 

It is therefore implicit in 'the concept of ordered liberty' and as such enforceable against the states through the due process clause." Mr. Justice Black, concurring, stated that "the Fourth Amendment's prohibition of 'unreasonable searches and seizures' is enforceable against the 

States"; Mr. Justice Douglas, dissenting, stated: "the 

Fourth Amendment is applicable to the States"; Justices

Murphy and Rutledge, dissenting, stated: "the Fourteenth 

Amendment prohibits activities which are proscribed by the search and seizure clause of the Fourth Amendment.'

Despite this language the decision was to the effect previously mentioned. Its basis was apparently that the evidence exclusion rule is a court-created rule of evidence, rather than an interpretation of the Amendment. The opinion of the court stated: "the Fourteenth Amendment does not forbid the admission of evidence obtained by an unreasonable search and seizure * * * though we have interpreted the Fourth Amendment to forbid the admission of such evidence." 

The decision has also been interpreted to mean that the Fourteenth Amendment does not carry over all the rules that have grown up about the Fourth, but only those considered fundamental. The Wolf decision has been widely criticized. The main basis of the criticism is that the decision recognized a right while, at the same time, it denied to the injured party the only adequate remedy for, and prevented imposition of the only adequate deterrent of, future transgressions of the rule-exclusion of the evidence. It is still, however, the law that although portions of the Fourth Amendment may be applicable in state actions, the evidence exclusion rule of the Weeks case, 232 

U.S. 383, 58 L. Ed. 652, is not applicable to State actions.

Thus, for all practical purposes, the Federal Constitution affords no aid to defendants in New York State. New York still has the protection afforded in Article I, section 12, of 114

§ its own Constitution and there need be no reliance on the Federal Constitution to establish the right. Under the 

Wolf case the rights afforded to citizens of the states by the Fourteenth Amendment might be construed to be less than that now afforded under the Constitution of our State.

Sec. 74. Statutory Provisions. Civil Rights Law, section 8, contains language identical to that now found in Article I, section 12, of the New York Constitution. Despite the implication of the Defore case, supra, that no substantive changes were effected by inclusion of the language in the Constitution, it is desirable to cite the Constitution with its greater dignity, rather than the statute, in any argument. 

Sec. 75. Searches Without Warrants. In determining which searches and seizures are unreasonable, the entire law of arrest is called into play, for "The basic principle is this: 

Search of the person is unlawful when the seizure of the body is a trespass, and the purpose of the search is to discover grounds as yet unknown for arrest or accusation (Entick v. Carrington, supra). Search of the person becomes lawful when ground for arrest and accusation have been discovered, and the law is in the act of subjecting the body of the accused to its physical dominion." (People v. 

Chiagles, 237 N.Y. 193, 197.) "*** a search and seizure of one's person following his lawful arrest, violates no law. 

Here, the petitioner being under lawful arrest, could be searched for evidences of the crime for which he was arrested." (Schutt v. MacDuff, 205 Misc. 43, 127 N.Y.S. 2d 

116, 124.)

Where the arrest is lawful, whether made with or without a warrant, a search and seizure incident to such arrest is similarly lawful. Thus in the Chiagles case, supra, the defendant was arrested for a felony and after arrest, was searched and certain letters on his person seized. Defendant moved to compel the return of the letters and the 115

$ 

Court of Appeals held that "the government may search the person of the accused when legally arrested to discover and seize the fruits or evidences of crime." 

In People v. Richter, 265 App. Div. 767, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 751, two inspectors of weights and measures, suspecting a misrepresentation of the weight and quality of a diamond advertised in a shop window, seized the diamond. No arrest was made at that time and, after subsequent examination of the jewel, it was discovered that there had, in fact, been a misrepresentation in violation of Penal Law, section 421. 

A summons was subsequently issued charging false advertising, under the above section, and assault, arising out of the attempted retaking of the diamond by the owner from the inspector. The defendant was convicted and, on appeal, questioned the receipt into evidence of the ring. 

The court, holding the diamond competent evidence despite any unlawful seizure, reversed the conviction of assault. The court noted that the diamond was evidence of a misdemeanor that had been committed, and that arrest of the defendant would have been justified for the misdemeanor had been committed in the inspector's presence. 

However the officers "were not aware of that fact *** they would not be possessed of sufficient information to advise them as to whether to make an arrest until the ring had been examined by an expert. Under the common law a search warrant would not be properly issued merely to procure evidence of a suspected crime. *** The inspectors could not lawfully seize the property in question for the purpose of merely verifying their suspicion. This would not be a reasonable seizure. That a misdemeanor had been committed in their presence would not alter the rule. *** the seizure under the present circumstances, disassociated from an arrest, or without a search warrant, appears to have no support under either the common law or the statutes of this state. *** more than suspicion is required to justify a seizure such as we have here." Thus, the seizure being unlawful the resistance to it by defendant was proper, and his conviction for assault was reversed. 116

§ The case was affirmed in 291 N.Y. 161. Thus the situation must be one not only where an arrest would be lawful, but where an arrest is in fact made, before a seizure without a warrant can be considered lawful. 

Sec. 76. The Area that may be Searched. Even though an arrest has been lawfully made, a search of all of the arrestee's property is not necessarily permissible. In People v. Manko, 189 N.Y.S. 357, affirmed 203 App. 893, 196

N.Y.S. 944, the defendant was indicted and arrested for criminal anarchy. After effecting the arrest, the police officers searched the defendant's coat, which was hanging in a nearby closet, and seized other letters there found. The defendant contended that the right to search his person did not extend to a search of articles of clothing not then being worn by him. The court held that, for the purpose of determining the reasonableness of the search, clothing of the arrested person which had been temporarily laid aside was to be considered on the person of the defendant. In the same case, after defendant's arrest, officers had gone to the defendant's home without a warrant, conducted a search and there seized papers for use in the defendant's trial. These papers were ordered returned. 

In People v. Buchalter, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 621, the court upheld, as reasonable, a search of a defendant's apartment and the seizure of certain papers there found after the defendant's arrest in the apartment. The court cited the Chiagles case in upholding the search as one made incidentally to an arrest. However, in the Chiagles case, the letters seized had been found on the defendant's person. The purposes justifying the search of an arrestee's person are the protection of the arresting officer-the search may uncover weapons hidden on the person-and the preservation of evidence on the arrestee's person and which might be destroyed if a warrant had to be obtained (People v. 

Chiagles, 237 N.Y. 193; United States v. Rabinowitz, 339

U.S. 56). These purposes are not cogent to the search of an arrestee's apartment after his arrest. There is then no 117

§ 

apparent reason why a search warrant cannot be obtained. 

The United States Supreme Court has recently decided several cases which indicate that an officer may search an entire house when making a lawful arrest of the occupant therein. (United States v. Rabinowitz, supra; Harris v. 

United States, 331 U.S. 145.) These cases, both decided by narrow majorities (Harris, 5-4; Rabinowitz, 5-3) have been widely criticized (Moreland, Modern Crim. Proc., sec. 

125 et seq.), but may be cited for the proposition that, despite the ability of the officers to obtain a search warrant if they so desired, "the premises where the arrest was made, which premises were under the control of the person arrested and where the crime was being committed, were subject to search without a search warrant." (United 

States v. Rabinowitz, supra, at p. 63 of 339 U.S.) An annotation in 94 L. Ed. 671 discusses the history of the Supreme Court cases in this area, terminating with the 

Rabinowitz case. Trupiano v. United States, 334 U.S. 699, was reversed and overruled by United States v. Rabinowitz. In the Trupiano case the Supreme Court held that where there was ample opportunity to obtain a search warrant, a search of a still without a warrant, but incident to an arrest, was unlawful. In the above cases, Justice Frankfurter has argued that only the person of the arrestee, and the immediate vicinity thereof, could be searched without a warrant.

There are few New York cases in this area. In Smith v. 

Jerome, 47 Misc. 22, 93 N.Y.S. 202, letters taken from the room and personal effects within the room were held not to have been unlawfully seized. The court stated: "The police have the power and it is also their duty to search the person of one lawfully arrested and also the room or place in which he is arrested, and also any other place to which they can get lawful access." The only authority cited for the above statement was Houghton v. Bachman, 47 Barb. 

388, a very early New York case. The Jerome case has been cited in People v. Richter, 265 App. Div. 767, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 

751, as authority for dictum therein to the same effect. In 118

§ the Richter case, the court quoted, with approval, the statement of the Supreme Court in Agnello v. United States, 267 U.S. 20, 30: "The right without a search warrant contemporaneously to search persons lawfully arrested while committing crime and to search the place where the arrest is made *** is not to be doubted." In People v. Henry, 185

N.Y.S. 644, the defendant was arrested without a warrant for conducting a gambling operation. During the arrest the officers opened defendant's desk and there seized papers pertaining to the gambling business. The court held that possession of the papers by defendant was unlawful, and as the papers were in defendant's "possession" when seized, the seizure was lawful. Fusaro v. McKennell, 120 

Misc. 434, 198 N.Y.S. 719, also cited the Jerome case with approval to uphold a search, apparently without a warrant, of defendant's apartment. Thus, the Jerome case is apparently still recognized in New York and, under that case, a search of the apartment or premises of the arrestee may be made without a search warrant if he has been arrested therein. However, People v. Jakira, 118 Misc. 303, 193 N.Y.S. 306, together with the arguments best expressed in Justice Frankfurter's dissents in the Harris and Rabinowitz cases and in the well reasoned comment on the 

Rabinowitz case in 36 Cornell L.Q. 125, do make a convincing case against allowing a search extending beyond the person of the arrestee. No Court of Appeals cases on this point have been found. 

Sec. 77. Contraband. People v. Defore, 242 N.Y. 13, cert. den. 270 U.S. 657, 70 L. Ed. 784, arose when the defendant was arrested for petit larceny while in the hallway of his boarding house. The arresting officers entered the defendant's room, searched it, and seized a blackjack they there discovered. The defendant was subsequently acquitted of the petit larceny charge, indicted as a second offender for possession of the blackjack and convicted of that offense after a trial in which objections were raised against the receipt of the blackjack in evidence. The defendant con- 119

§ 

tended that the search and seizure had been unlawful. 

The Court of Appeals, while affirming the conviction, noted that the arrest was unlawful as one made without a warrant for a misdemeanor not committed in the presence of the arresting officer. The prosecution contended that the blackjack was contraband, a nuisance subject to destruction under Penal Law, section 1899, and thus justified the seizure. The court replied: "This might have justified the seizure, the abatement of the nuisance, if the weapon had been exposed to view. It might even have justified the refusal to return the weapon, though discovered by unlawful means. It did not justify the search. 

There is no rule that homes may be ransacked without process to discover the fruits or the implements of crime. 

To make such inquisitions lawful there must be the support of a search warrant issued upon probable cause." 

However, the court went on to note that the illegality of the seizure did not make the evidence obtained thereby incompetent.

People v. Milone, 119 Misc. 22, 195 N.Y.S. 488, also involved a weapon seized by officers without a warrant. The defendant operated a duly licensed pool room. During business hours two officers entered and apparently saw defendant attempting to hide a box. Upon questioning, the defendant admitted he had a revolver in the box. The officers seized the revolver, and defendant was subsequently indicted for unlawful possession of a firearm. At the trial, the defendant moved for an order restraining the District Attorney from introducing the revolver in evidence, and requested its return. The court, denying defendant's motion, stated: "whether or not the search was unreasonable *** depends upon the circumstances, and is not influenced by the fact it was without warrant. A search without warrant may be reasonable, and a search with warrant may be unreasonable. It has always been permissible for police officers, in performance of their official function, to follow criminals into their hiding places, and to search the latter for evidence to support conviction. It has never 120

$been required to procure search warrants in all cases of entering upon and searching private dwellings or premises *** the search for and seizure of a concealed firearm, upon reasonable ground to believe that a crime is immediately involved in possessing the same, or otherwise by the person in possession of the searched premises, by duly constituted peace officers lawfully upon such premises [as] *** in the case at bar contains no elements smacking of the abuses which led to the enactment governing unreasonable searches and seizures." The above case has not been cited in any other New York case to date.

People v. Milone, supra, appears to conflict with the reasoning in the Defore case; and with People v. Jakira, 118 Misc. 303, 193 N.Y.S. 306, where officers entered the defendant's apartment without a warrant, and compelling him to open his suitcase, found therein certain weapons. 

The court there granted the defendant's motion for the return of the property seized and prohibited its use as evidence upon the defendant's trial for the unlawful possession of the weapons. The court stated: "the invasion, search and seizure made by the officers in the apartment of the defendant was illegal. The discovery of firearms upon the unlawful search *** did not make the search and seizure lawful." It is true that the Milone case is distinguishable from the Jakira case on several grounds—the entry in Milone was lawful, in Jakira not; the suspicions in Milone were aroused while they were acting lawfully, in Jakira not. However, the two cases, in principle, appear opposed. Under the rationale of People v. Defore, the officers' suspicions of Milone might not have been deemed sufficient to justify the issuance of a warrant and thus should, therefore, not have been deemed to justify a search and seizure without a warrant. However, the case still stands to justify similar action.

In People v. Esposito, 118 Misc. 867, 194 N.Y.S. 326, the court expressed disagreement with the holding and language in the Jakira case. There, the defendant, while walking in the street, was stopped by a police officer who 121

$ 

493 ordered him to throw up his hands and proceeded to search him. The officer found, and seized, a revolver in the defendant's coat pocket and, on the defendant's acknowledgment that he had no permit for the weapon, proceeded to "arrest" him. At the trial, the defendant, charged with unlawful possession of a firearm, moved for suppression of the use of the revolver in evidence, for the return of the weapon, and for dismissal of the proceeding. His motion was, in all respects, denied. The court stated that, despite the officer's characterization of his actions, "it is clear that the arrest happened before, or contemporaneously with, the search. * * * Any restraint of liberty is an arrest. * * * 

If the arrest was unlawful, so was the search. *** If a police officer is in bodily reach of a person then and there actually engaged in the commission of a misdemeanor, and perceiving indications of the offense sufficient to induce reasonable belief of the fact, acting in good faith, intending performance of duty, proceeds to arrest such person, the arrest is lawful as for the commission of a crime in the officer's presence." Thus, the court emphasized the subjective feelings of the officer as furnishing the ground for characterizing the search as lawful. However, this case can be explained upon another recognized basis. Where it is impracticable, or impossible to obtain a search warrant, the courts will not force officers to do so, and searches without warrants in such situations have commonly been upheld. However, the arrest here was made prior to the search.

Another explanation can also be made. Once the arrest has been made, the officer has committed himself; if the arrest is subsequently determined to be unlawful the officer has committed a trespass and will be liable to the arrestee. In People v. Didonna, 124 Misc. 872, 210 N.Y.S. 135, the defendant, while walking on the street, was stopped by police officers and searched, and a revolver found on his person seized. The officers claimed that their attention had been attracted to defendant by his loud and boisterous conduct. The court stated: "It is unlawful for 122

§ any unlicensed person to have a pistol in his possession *** and to require a search warrant before it may be discovered is providing a means for putting the weapon out of the reach of the search warrant. * * * Reasonable search and seizure without a warrant is, in fact, necessary, under proper circumstances, in furtherance of the reign of law and order and for the protection of society and for the preservation of the government itself by the confiscation of contraband *** such search and seizure is not violative of one's civil rights." Thus, the area is still not a clear one in New York. The Jakira case stands, apparently, opposed to the Milone and Esposito cases. Certainly, until a clear 

Court of Appeals decision is promulgated, objection to searches of the character involved in the above cases is warranted. 

Sec. 78. Search Warrants. "A search warrant is an order in writing in the name of the people, signed by a magistrate, directed to a peace officer, commanding him to search for personal property, and bring it before the magistrate." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 791.) The sections of the Constitution and the Civil Rights Law, discussed and quoted above, further require that a warrant not be issued save upon "probable cause supported by oath or information, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized." This requirement is restated in Section 793 of the Code. Section 792 pre scribes the grounds upon which warrants may be issued. 

They are: "1. When the property was stolen or embezzled, in which case, it may be taken, on the warrant, from any 

place in which it is concealed or from the possession of any person in whose possession it may be; 2. When it was used as the means of committing a felony; 

3. When it is in the possession of any person, with the intent to use it as means of committing a public offense, or in the possession of another, to whom he may have delivered it for the purpose of concealing it or preventing its being discovered.' 

123

§ 

Before issuing the warrant, the magistrate must examine, on oath, the complainant and his witnesses and take their depositions, which must set forth facts "tending to establish the grounds of the application; or probable cause for believing that they exist." (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

794, 795.) Section 797 prescribes the form of the warrant, which must be served either by the officer named therein or one acting in that officer's presence and at his request (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 798). The officer executing the warrant is empowered by Section 799 to break open windows, doors, etc., to obtain entrance to the premises concerned or to free any assistant in the execution who might be detained therein (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 800). The magistrate "must insert a direction in the warrant, that it be served in the day time, unless the affidavits be positive that the property is on the person, or in the place to be searched in which case, he may insert, a direction that it be served at any time of the day or night." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 801.) The warrant must be executed within ten days after its date or it becomes void (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 802). Receipts must be given for the property taken (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 803); the property must be delivered to the magistrate, who must deal with it as prescribed by Section 804; and a sworn written inventory must be delivered to the magistrate by the officer who executed the warrant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 805). If there be controversion of the grounds of the warrant, the magistrate must take testimony concerning it (Section 807), which testimony must be reduced to writing and sworn to (Section 808). If the property appears not to be the same as that described in the warrant, or if there "is no probable cause for believing the existence of the grounds on which the warrant was issued," the property must be returned (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 809). Sections 

806 through 809 were declared unconstitutional in their application to a pledgee of the property in People ex rel. 

Simpson v. Kempner, 154 App. Div. 674, 139 N.Y.S. 440, affirmed 208 N.Y. 16, on the basis that there was no oppor- 124

$ tunity afforded, or notice given, to a third party who did not have possession of the property, but who claimed that the property belonged to him. All the writings referred to in the above sections, must be turned over to the County Court having jurisdiction over the offense concerned (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 810). It is a misdemeanor maliously, without probable cause, to procure the issuance and execution of a warrant (Section 811), or for an officer, while executing a warrant, to use unnecessary severity or exceed his authority (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 812). The magistrate may order one charged with a felony searched in his presence if he has reason to suspect the accused to have, on his person, any evidence of the commission of an offense, or to have a weapon on his person (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 813).

Sec. 79. Grounds for Obtaining Search Warrants. A 

search warrant may not be issued to obtain evidence for use in an investigation or a trial. Section 792 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure provides the only grounds upon which a warrant will be issued. "A search warrant cannot be issued for any purpose except as stated." (People ex rel. 

Simpson v. Kempner, 208 N.Y. 16, 20.) In the Kempner case, it was held that a search warrant, and a seizure of property thereunder, followed by the proceedings described in the preceding section, could not be used as a means of trying title to the property concerned. In the 

Chiagles case, supra, the Court of Appeals noted that searches made incidentally to an arrest were not subject to the restrictions imposed upon those made pursuant to a warrant; "defendant *** would restrict the seizure [made incident to an arrest] to things subject to be taken under a search warrant when there is no arrest of the possessor. 

Search is then confined under our statute to property stolen or embezzled, or used as the means of committing a felony, or held with the intent to use it as an instrument of crime. ***We find no support for a like restriction upon 125

$ 

search incidental to an arrest." People v. Chiagles, 237 

N.Y. 193, 196.)

In People v. Roth, 207 Misc. 875, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 122, where defendants were charged with printing and publishing obscene matter, search warrants were ordered vacated and property taken thereunder ordered returned. The warrants had been issued on the basis of an affidavit which stated that "there is probable cause to believe that there is in [defendants'] possession with the intent that it be used as the means of committing public offenses, and with the 

ledgers, payroll records and other papers." The court held the affidavit insufficient as failing to allege the necessary grounds under the statute. See also People v. Carver, 172

Misc. 820, 16 N.Y.S. 2d 268, discussed supra, where the 

District Attorney attempted to obtain certain business records by court order. The court denied the motion, stating that a court order could not be used in place of a subpoena duces tecum and that a search warrant would not issue under the circumstances merely to obtain documentary evidence of cime; "documentary evidence of crime held by parties other than a defendant and whose seizure is not incident to lawful arrest or authorized by 

Section 792 *** is obtainable by the District Attorney through subpoena duces tecum." And in People v. 

Richter, 265 App. Div. 767, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 751, affirmed 291 

N.Y. 161, it was stated: "a search warrant would not be properly issued merely to procure evidence of a suspected crime." While the property is in the custody of the court and the criminal proceeding is pending, it has been held improper for the owner of the property to attempt to regain it in a collateral proceeding, such as replevin. 

It is not yet certain, in New York, whether affidavits upon information and belief are sufficient for the issuance of a search warrant. The majority of the states evidently hold that allegations upon information and belief, without a statement of the sources thereof, are insufficient. An analogous situation is discussed, in the chapter of this 126

§ work entitled "Informations," concerning the sufficiency of informations. A general rule that may be applied in this area was stated by the court in Penn Oil & Supply Co., v. 

Cohn, 131 App. Div. 929, 116 N.Y.S. 124: "when courts and judicial officers are asked to act upon affidavits founded upon information and belief, they must be furnished with the sources of the information in order that they may draw their own conclusions."

Sec. 80. Descriptions in Warrants. The statute requires that the affidavit and warrant "particularly" describe the person or place to be searched, and the property to be seized. In Matter of Graham, 203 App. Div. 172, 196 N.Y.S. 

276, the warrant issued concerned the search of a named person at a certain premises. However, the location description was inaccurate. It held that the search of the premises, at a location different than that described in the warrant, was invalid. The United States Supreme Court has stated the general rule to be that "a description is sufficient if the executing officer can, with reasonable effort, ascertain and identify the person or place intended to be searched." (Steele v. United States, No. 1, 267 U.S. 

498, 69 L. Ed. 757.)

Sec. 81. Automobiles and Similar Vehicles. It is apparent, from the very mobile nature of automobiles, boats, etc., that special rules concerning their search are necessary. 

If warrants were to be required for their search, in all cases where warrants are required for the search of a home, the vehicle might well be without the jurisdiction before the warrant could be obtained. In Carroll v. United 

States, 267 U.S. 132, 69 L. Ed. 543, the Supreme Court stated: "the guaranty from unreasonable searches and seizures by the Fourth Amendment has been construed, practically since the beginning of the government, as recognizing a necessary difference between a search of a store, dwelling house, or other structure in respect of which a proper official warrant readily may be obtained, 127

§ 

and a search of a ship, motor boat, wagon, or automobile for contraband goods, where it is not practicable to secure a warrant because the vehicle can be quickly moved out of the locality or jurisdiction in which the warrant must be sought. ***The right to search and the validity of the seizure are not dependent on the right to arrest. They are dependent on the reasonable cause the seizing officer has for belief that the contents of the automobile offend against the law." See, for cases concerning searches of mobile vehicles, generally, 39 A.L.R. p. 829 et seq. The 

Carroll case involved a violation of the Prohibition laws, and the special procedures applicable thereto. However the general principle quoted is applicable to other situations. 

In People v. Houghtaling, 16 Misc. 2d 459, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 

1015, aff'd without opinion, 6 N.Y. 2d 806, defendants were convicted of third degree assault. An officer, suspecting that the car in which defendants were riding was speeding, stopped the car, and upon approaching it noticed a rifle being carried therein. While the officer was attempting to reach in to inspect the rifle, the defendants resisted him, thus giving rise to the assault charge. In affirming the conviction, the court stated: "a search may be made without a warrant, especially to determine whether or not a rifle in an automobile is loaded when a trooper has stopped a vehicle to determine whether or not a crime has been committed. To hold that under the circumstances an officer must first obtain a warrant, would be almost to scrap all efforts to enforce the criminal law of the State." 

In People v. Fidler, 280App. Div. 698, 117 N.Y.S. 2d 313, the defendants were convicted for resisting an officer in the performance of his duty. The officer had requested the defendants to drive their vehicles upon weighing scales, as required by Vehicle and Traffic Law, Section 69, dealing with overloading of motor vehicles. The drivers refused to do so and were convicted of the offense charged. Upon appeal, their convictions were reversed upon the ground that instructions to the jury had been misleading. The 128

§ court stated: "There would seem to exist a difference in operative constitutional principle between the right of the State to authorize the police to "inspect" a man's house and its right to authorize the police to "inspect" his automobile as to its operation, though the legal effect of "inspect" in this sense is scarcely distinguishable from "search". In the decision the court discussed the Richter case, supra, and the case of People v. Hill, 131 Misc. 521, 227 N.Y.S. 285. The 

Hill case held that a defendant might resist a general search of his automobile where the officers did not have reasonable grounds to believe that defendant committed a crime. But, the court noted, an inspection of an automobile by police acting under a statute authorizing inspection of all vehicles, without a requirement of probable cause, was not the same as the situation there appearing, because there is a "difference between a right to search the person or vehicle after a valid arrest for a crime based on probable cause resting on one theory of law justifying intrusion into privacy; and a right to inspect the safety of a vehicle resting on quite a different theory of law." A recent Supreme Court case (Frank v. Maryland, 79 Sup.

Ct. 804), also affirms the right of the State to make "inspections" without warrants. The Frank case involved the "inspection" of a house. The Supreme Court affirmed the right on the basis of the public need for such inspections in order effectively to enforce health regulations. The court also emphasized the long history of the allowance of such actions. The narrow holding of the case was that the 

Fourteenth Amendment did not prohibit the State's imposition of a small fine upon persons refusing admittance to health inspectors.

Sec. 82. Extent of Search Allowable Under Warrant. As general warrants are invalid (see, supra,) it is obvious that a warrant does not give an officer leave to conduct a general search. Thus, it has been held that officers may not search any place other than that described in the warrant (Rising Sun Brewing Co. v. U.S., 55 Fed. 2d 827), although 129

§ 

an invalid extension of the search will not invalidate the propriety of the search of the area described in the warrant or the lawfulness of the seizure of articles there described. (McCone v. United States, 273 U.S. 95.) Similarly, while the officer is limited to seizure of those articles described in the warrant (United States v. Brunett, 53 F. 

2d 219) if, in the course of executing the warrant, he discovers other property unlawfully there, it is his duty to seize it, particularly if it is "contraband". (United States v. Old Dominion Warehouses, 10 F. 2d 736.) Since the search warrant makes the officer's entrance lawful, a decision as to what he may seize thereafter depends upon the reasonableness of his action. (People v. Jakira, supra.) 

When the officer's entrance is unlawful, as under invalid warrants, a discovery made while in the course of the illegal search will not sustain a subsequent complaint to serve as the basis for another warrant to be used in returning to the premises (People v. Dineen, 192 N.Y.S. 

905). In Re Application for a Search Warrant, 116 Misc. 

512, 190 N.Y.S. 574, concerned such a situation. A warrant had been issued for a search of 52 Front Street, and subsequently the property concerned was discovered at 57, 59, and 61 Front Street. The court stated: "Any seizure made under a search of property other than that described in the warrant is unlawful, and the fact that liquor was found in the place searched does not justify the search or sustain the seizure. *** Peace officers in the execution of a search and seizure warrant must follow strictly the de scription of the premises as contained in the warrant. *** 

A warrant to search a dwelling house of a private person confers authority only to search the house in which the person lives [it does not] authorize the search of a barn. It, however, has been held that a warrant which authorizes the search of a dwelling house and its appurtenances is sufficient to enable the officer to search a stable or outbuildings on the premises, but it will not authorize the search of a building not in the same inclosure." 

130

§ 

Sec. 83. Consent and Waiver. The United States Supreme 

Court has clearly indicated that the rights afforded by the 

Fourth and Fifth Amendments may be waived (Zap v. 

United States, 328 U.S. 624, 90 L. Ed. 1477). The New York cases also sustain this view. In People v. Kalnin, 189 N.Y.S. 

359, the defendants, indicted for circulating seditious pamphlets, apparently consented to the search of their homes by police officers. The court stated: "The court is convinced that defendants consented to the officers' going to their home, and legally waived their rights under sec tion 8 of the Civil Rights Law *** and the Fourth Amend ment to the United States Constitution." It is clear that the right of freedom from unreasonable searches and seizures is a personal right and therefore may be waived. However, as with any other waiver or consent, "The proof to support [it] *** must be clear and positive, must show no duress or coercion, actual or implied, and must be unequivocal and specific, and must be freely and intelligently given." 

(Application of Remy Sportswear, Inc., 16 Misc. 2d 407, 

183 N.Y.S.2d 125, 130.)

The right of one person to consent to the search of another's property derives from the authority, apparent or implied, of the one consenting. In Hook v. State, 15 

Misc. 2d 672, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 621, the wife of the owner of the property consented to a search of a house jointly occupied by herself and her husband. The court, noting the case to be one of first impression in New York, and noting the conflict of authority in other jurisdictions concerning this right, held that "where the officers searching for stolen property were informed that the suspect was attempting to dispose of it, and where they were invited to search the house by the wife who was in charge, in her husband's absence, we cannot say that the search was unreasonable and we find that her consent and invitation to the troopers was a waiver of the requirement that a warrant be procured." The reasoning of the above cases appears correct; society itself is not harmed by an unreasonable search absent coercion by the officers and a disturb- 181

§ 

ance resulting therefrom; the right is for the protection of the individual and is thus waivable. Cases in other jurisdictions hold that a lessor's or landlord's consent is generally insufficient (Kilee v. United States, 53 F. 2d 58); but that one having the joint use or occupancy of the premises may so consent (Duskill v. United States, 281 

Fed. 146); and there is a split of authority concerning an employee's right to consent to a search of his employer's premises (Compare Application of Fried, 68 Fed. 961, with 

United States v. Lagow, 66 F. Supp. 738) and the reverse (United States v. Blok, 188 F.2d 1019, holding an employer could not consent to search of an employee's desk); contra, State v. Zuehlke, 239 Wisc. 111, 300 N.W. 746). It should be noted that the Hook case is the only New York case upholding the power of a wife to consent to a search of the husband's premises. In view of the split of authority on this point, the Hook case should not be regarded as conclusive.

Sec. 84. Remedies of Defendants Unlawfully Searched. 

The right to resist an unlawful search and seizure has been discussed above. The New York rule, allowing unlawfully seized evidence to be introduced at the trial, and the holdings of the Supreme Court that the Fourteenth Amendment does not prohibit such actions in state courts have also been discussed. However there are remedies available whereby one affected by an unlawful search or seizure may, in some circumstances, prevent the use of the unlawfully seized evidence at a trial.

Sec. 84(a). Order for Return Under Article 78. In Applica tion of Silfa, 5 Misc. 2d 375, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 68, aff'd. without opinion, 3 App. Div. 2d 818, 161 N.Y.S. 2d 572, aff'd. without opinion, 3 N.Y. 2d 734, the petitioner applied for an order, pursuant to Article 78 of the Civil Practice Act, directing the District Attorney and the Police Commissioner to return certain property which had been illegally seized from him during the course of an unlawful arrest. 132

§ (a) The court recognized that the illegality of the seizure would not affect the admissibility of the evidence but went on to state: "From this premise the District Attorney concludes that he has a right to retain the prospective exhibits for use at the trial. In 1923 that exact proposition was questioned by our highest court and it declared that it may still be an open question. ** Since then that court has not had occasion to consider the precise question. 

There have been several decisions on the point in courts of original jurisdiction with results not entirely uniform. several seem to confuse the question at issue with whether the evidence so obtained should be suppressed. * * * the fact that the existence of evidence was improperly discovered should and does not prevent proper means of procuring its presence in court. [Compare People v. Dineen, supra.]. Here the property has been unlawfully taken and it is elementary that barring some defect it must be returned. * * * On the other hand it is still admissible evidence and nothing prevents the prosecutor from taking rightful steps to secure its presence in court. It may be argued that * * * return would be the equivalent of suppression because the recipient would forthwith destroy the papers * issue will be met when raised. * * *” The property was ordered returned. * that An Article 78 proceeding was also utilized in Application of Marshall, 17 Misc. 2d 985, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 413. After acquittal, the petitioner there sought the return of certain money seized from him after an unlawful search. The 

Police Commissioner contended that the money was the "fruit of criminal activity", and that the proper remedy was by writ of replevin against the Police Department Property Clerk. The court stated: "The respondent's contention that the proceeding is improperly brought against him was rejected in a closely analogous situation." However, the court noted, "when *** the property has come into [the property clerk's] hands unlawfully, cases such as Costello v. Simmons, 295 N.Y. 807, and Hofferman v. 

Simmons, 290 N.Y. 449, holding the Property Clerk the 133

§ (b)  

799 proper party to the suit, and replevin the proper remedy, are not in point. Where the property has been seized unlawfully the Police Commissioner must be directed to return it for the seizing parties were members of the police force."

The Silfa case was also cited in Application of Remy 

Sportswear, Inc., 183 N.Y.S. 2d 125. Petitioner there moved for the return of certain books and records which had been surrendered to the district attorney after service upon petitioner of a subpoena duces tecum, under the circumstances held invalid. The court stated: "within the exercise of my discretionary power *** I hold that the petitioner is entitled to an affirmative order." There is no indication that an Article 78 proceeding was utilized. It should be noted that inasmuch as the order directing the return of the property in the above cases did not prohibit its use at the trial, once properly obtained by the prosecutor, only temporary relief will be obtained by use of this method. 

Permanent relief will be obtained only if the evidence is to be destroyed upon its return. The ethical problems that arise upon such a course of action are obvious. It is believed that the above cases are the only ones involving a use of an Article 78 proceeding in this area. 

Sec. 84(b). Motion. In Matter of Booth, 200 App. Div. 423, 

192 N.Y.S. 822, the court stated: "The court has inherent power to order the return to the owner of books, papers, or other articles illegally seized or detained by a magistrate or other public officer charged with the administration of the criminal law." The court went on to hold that as the petition was there filed against a Supreme Court Justice, the proper court to hear the application was the Appellate Division. The evidence there had been obtained through the use of subpoenas issued "without warrant of law". Thus, in Matter of Booth, although the court referred to the proceeding as a motion, it was apparently an independent proceeding instituted by a petition for the return of the property. 134

§ (b) In People v. Manko, 189 N.Y.S. 357, affirmed without opinion, 203 App. Div. 893, 196 N.Y.S. 944, the defendant, after papers had been marked in evidence by the committing magistrate, moved for their return because they had been unlawfully seized. The court stated: "If papers have been taken from the defendant by an unlawful search, and are in the possession of officers of the law, the court has jurisdiction to order their return, and a motion made before trial for that purpose is proper procedure." Defendant's motion was granted, the court noting that the Adams case, discussed above, did not apply because "the hearing before the committing magistrate was not a trial". Thus, there is an indication that the court might not have ordered the return if the motion had been made after trial had commenced. In People v. Kinney, 185 N.Y.S. 645, a similar motion was granted. The motion was made after indictment, and before trial. In State v. One Hudson Cabriolet 

Auto, 116 Misc. 399, 190 N.Y.S. 481, a proceeding for the forfeiture of an automobile, which had allegedly been used in the transporting of illegal liquor, had been instituted. 

After the car had been seized, a warrant had been issued. 

The court stated: "Treating the warrant as a complaint, notice of hearing was served upon the alleged owner of the property seized, and upon the return thereof, the claimant filed a document protesting against the jurisdiction of the court, asserting that the search and seizure were unlawful, and requesting that the property be restored. By consent the document has been treated *** as a petition for the return of the goods. *** it is true that the courts have frequently held that in the trial of criminal indictments they will not inquire into the methods by which evidence has been secured, but in cases similar to this, where evidence against the accused has been secured in violation of the constitutional provision relating to search and seizure, and the question has been presented to the court by preliminary motion, or collaterally, the holding is uniform that it is the duty of the court to order the goods and property seized returned to the owner, thus restoring him to the sta- 135

§ (c) 

tus which was his at the moment of the invasion of his constitutional rights." It should be stressed that the above motions were made prior to trial.

Sec. 84 (c). Vacation of the Warrant. Under Code of Crimi nal Procedure, secs. 807-809, after seizure of the property, one from whom the property has been seized, or one who claims that the property is his (People ex rel. Simpson v. 

Kempner, supra) may intervene, controvert the grounds upon which the warrant was issued, and the property may be restored to him. However the attack upon the sufficiency of the warrant and its supporting papers may not be raised in a collateral proceeding, such as by order to show cause (Meegan v. Tracy, 220 App. Div. 600, 223 N.Y.S. 355).

Sec. 84(d). Replevin. As stated above, in the Silfa case, where property is lawfully in the possession of the Property Clerk of the Police Department, or a similar official, and where it is no longer needed in the prosecution of a criminal proceeding, replevin is the proper remedy, and the property clerk the proper party. In Simpson v. St. John, 93 N.Y. 363, the court quoted from Lynch v. St. John, 8 

Daly 143, to the effect that "property in his [the property clerk's] possession might be regarded as in the custody of the law where it *** may be necessary to secure the conviction of the person charged * * * but after his conviction or acquittal the property clerk can have no claim to it as against the rightful owner *** when confronted with the replevin papers, the custodian, if there was any reason why the property for public purposes should remain in his possession, ought to apply to the court." The court, in the 

Simpson case, held that the property should not be returned pending the determination of the criminal proceeding in which it was to be used. 

The replevin action will also not be successful where the property was obtained by the claimant by unlawful means. 

Thus, in Hofferman v. Simmons, 290 N.Y. 449, moneys 136

§ (e) representing gambling winnings, were not awarded to the claimant in a replevin action. The claimant had previously pleaded guilty to a gambling charge. The court did note: "Where the claim is not of wrongful taking, but of wrongful detention, it is for the plaintiff to plead and prove facts showing that the detention is wrongful." Thus, if the taking of the money had been wrongful, as pursuant to an illegal seizure, the problem of the possessor's rights might not be at issue. See the Hudson Cabriolet case, supra. was 

Sec. 84(e). Injunctions. In People v. Jakira, 118 Misc. 303, 

193 N.Y.S. 306, the defendant moved for an order directing the return of certain property which had been illegally seized, and for an order "enjoining the said district attorney and the said police commissioner from using the * * evidence or information derived from said search and seizure, against the defendant." The court distinguished the Adams case, where "the legality of the seizure * * * raised for the first time at the trial. In this case the question of the legality of the seizure was raised before an indictment against the defendant was lodged by the grand jury, on a motion for the return of the property in question." 

The court then held: "papers unlawfully seized * * * be used *** upon the trial, unless seasonable application is made for their return," noted that defendant had raised objections to the use of the evidence at his first opportunity, and granted his motion. In seeking relief by injunction, it must be noted that the applicant will have to contend with all the barriers that equity raises against such relief. See Kalwin v. McLaughlin, 216 App. Div. 6, 214 N.Y.S. 507, for language indicating the court's reluctance to enjoin the police in general. may 

People v. Esposito, 118 Misc. 867, 194 N.Y.S. 326, should be compared with the Jakira case. The court there expressed its disagreement with the Jakira opinion, and stated "that the rule of practice *** to the effect that the defendant in a criminal case should make a preliminary motion in advance of the trial in order to protect himself 137

§ 

against evidence the receipt of which is violative of his rights *** has been virtually abandoned." The court then noted that it should not "direct the restoration of what legislative authority has [called] dangerous public nuisances." The property there involved was a revolver. The court then refused to direct restoration of the revolver to its original possessor on the grounds that it was seized incidentally to lawful arrest. The revolver would be competent evidence in any event. It is submitted that the court could have based its decision on the ground that the revolver was contraband and should not be restored to one unlawfully possessing it, and that a decision on that ground would not have led the court into extending the area of lawful arrests, nor would it have caused the court to disagree with the Jakira decision. A motion for the return of slot machines was denied on the ground that the machines were contraband in People v. Hawkins, 132 Misc. 696, 230 

N.Y.S. 152. However, in People v. Belsky, 177 Misc. 125, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 535, the court denied a motion for the suppression of evidence and, in so doing, refused to recognize any distinction between contraband and non-contraband property. Thus the Belsky case appears to be in accord with the Esposito case. However, until there is a clear decision on this point by the Court of Appeals, attacks upon the use of evidence unlawfully seized may be based upon the 

Jakira case.

Sec. 85. Exclusion of Evidence. Many of the cases in the preceding sections have shown that, in New York, evidence illegally seized may be used in a trial. In 1938, during the Constitutional Convention, Governor Lehman asked that "the State Constitution * * * definitely require that any evidence obtained in violation of the constitutional guarantee shall not be admissible in any judicial or other proceeding." (Record of N.Y. State Constitutional Convention, Vol. I, p. 336.) This provision was not incorporated in the Constitution. The Defore case is the leading case today holding such evidence admissible and, despite many 138

§ criticisms of this rule, it is the law today. See People v. La 

Combe, 170 Misc. 669, 9 N.Y.S. 2d for a discussion of the 

Constitutional Convention proceedings in this area. 

Sec. 86. Habitual Criminals. Section 514 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "The person and the premises of everyone who has been convicted and adjudged an habitual criminal, shall be liable at all times to search and examination by any magistrate, sheriff, constable, or other officer, with or without warrant." 

Sec. 87. Wiretapping, Eavesdropping, etc. The New York

State Constitutional provision concerning wiretapping has been quoted above. Section 813-a and 813-b of the Code provide the rules concerning the granting of orders permitting "eavesdropping". Penal Law, sec. 738 defines eavesdropping, and section 740 provides that one guilty of eavesdropping, except as exempted by Penal Law, sec. 739, is guilty of a felony. Section 739 exempts eavesdropping under a court order obtained pursuant to Section 813-a and 813-b of the Code, from classification as felonious eavesdropping. Under section 813-a, ex parte orders may be issued by Justices of the Supreme Court, County Judges, or General Sessions Judges, upon oath or affirmation of a 

District Attorney, Attorney-General, or any police officer above the rank of sergeant. The application must state that there is "reasonable ground to believe that evidence of crime may be thus obtained, and particularly describing the person or persons whose communications*** are to be overheard *** and the purpose thereof, and, in the case of a telegraphic or telephonic communication, identifying the particular telephone number or telegraphic line involved." It is further provided that the justice may examine the applicant and any other witnesses he wishes in order to "satisfy himself of the existence of reasonable grounds for the granting of such application." Section 

813-b of the Code allows eavesdropping without court order when the law enforcement officer "has reasonable 139

§ 

grounds to believe (1) that evidence of crime may be thus obtained, and (2) that in order to obtain such evidence time does not permit an application to be made for such a court order. * * In any such case an application for a court order * * * must be made within twenty-four hours after such eavesdropping commenced. *** If the application is denied, the eavesdropping must cease immediately." 

United States Code, Title 47, Section 605, prohibits in terception of telephone communications and, together with section 501 of that title, makes divulgence thereof a crime. Evidence procured by wiretapping or eavesdropping is inadmissible in Federal courts. (Nardone v. United 

States, 302 U.S. 379, 82 Law. Ed. 314.) However, the

Supreme Court has stated that section 605 "does not exclude such evidence in state court proceedings", although the introduction of such evidence "would itself be a violation of [section 605] and therefore is a factor for a state to consider in formulating a rule of evidence for use in its own courts." (Schwartz v. Texas, 344 U.S. 199, 201, 97 L.

Ed. 231.) After the above decision, the Court of Appeals decided People v. Saperstein, 2 N.Y. 2d 210, cert. denied, 353 U.S. 946, 1 L. Ed. 2d 856, which held evidence obtained by wiretapping admissible though "requiring a witness to testify as to wiretaps might force him to a criminal violation of the Federal Communications Act."

Subsequently, the Supreme Court decided Benanti v. 

United States, 355 U.S. 96, 2 L. Ed. 2d 126, which held that wiretap evidence procured by New York police, acting under a New York State court order, was inadmissible in a federal court. Thereafter, in People v. Dinan, 7 App. Div. 

2d 119, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 122, aff'd. without opinion, 6 N.Y. 2d 

715, the defendants contended that in view of the Benanti decision the Court of Appeals should reverse or modify the rule set forth in the Saperstein case. The Appellate Division held: "Nothing in the Benanti case can be viewed as casting doubt upon the firmness of the rule in New York." However, the court noted: "It is true that the 

Supreme Court in that case held that the Congress, in 

140

§ ne in enacting the Federal Communications Act *** intended to set forth a comprehensive scheme for the regulation of interstate communications which precludes validity to a State statute that would even under certain circumstances permit wiretapping. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

813-a.) "If indeed a judicial change of the rule ought to be considered, argument should be addressed to the Court of Appeals in an appropriate appeal." The Appellate Division also noted that in Pennsylvania a similar situation prevailed and the highest court of that state held that the Benanti decision did not affect their rule concerning the admissibility of wire tap evidence (Commonwealth v. 

Voci, 393 Pa. 404, 143 Atl. 2d 652). 

In People v. Grant, 14 Misc. 2d 182, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 384, an argument, similar to that advanced in the Dinan case, was also rejected. The court stated: "the failure of Congress to provide a clear enactment regarding the legality of evidence procured by tapping telephone wires for use in a state court, leaves the optional use of such evidence with state courts." However, the Benanti decision has not been completely without effect upon the New York courts. In 

Matter of Interception of Telephone Communications, 9 

Misc. 2d 121, 170 N.Y.S. 2d 84, Justice Hofstadter advised that during his term at Special Term, part II, "no application for a wire tap order will be honored. Under the decision in Benanti, orders authorizing interceptions are contrary to controlling Federal Law. Its authority requires me, therefore, to deny any application for such an order. For all wiretaps, whether 'authorized' or not, in this State are now illegal. In Matter of Interception of 

Telephone Communications of Anonymous, 207 Misc. 69, 136 N.Y.S. 2d 612, I denied an application in the exercise of discretion; any further application would have to be denied because of lack of lawful competence." Thus, although it is now clear that eavesdropping, even under an appropriate court order, issued pursuant to Section 813-a of the Code of Criminal Procedure, is unlawful under the Federal Communications Act, evidence so obtained may 141

§ 

still be admissible in New York State courts. The Grant and Dinan cases were decided after the law developed by the Supreme Court became quite clear and held the evidence admissible. The Court of Appeals affirmed in the 

Dinan case after the Benanti decision.

As this work goes to press (April, 1960), the law on the use of wiretap evidence is completely unsettled. As pointed out, above, the New York courts, while noting contrary Federal judicial holdings and statutory enactments, have generally upheld the use of such evidence, when previously authorized by court order. It has generally been considered that, both by policy and construction, the Federal courts would not assume to control, and the Federal statutes would not be construed to regulate, the practice in the State courts. This was the holding of Federal District 

Judge Bryan, when Burton N. Pugach, indicted in New 

York, sought a Federal injunction restraining the Bronx

County District Attorney from using wiretap evidence at his trial. But an appeal to the Federal Court of Appeals, in the Second Circuit, on February 11, 1960, brought forth an opinion in which Circuit Judge Harold R. Medina clearly indicated that the New York practice was illegal under Section 605 of the Federal Communications Act; a stay pending appeal was granted. The application for a permanent injunction in that case is still pending, but, in the light of Judge Medina's clear statement, Judge Davidson of the New York County Court of General Sessions has publicly announced that he will no longer sign wiretapping orders, under the statute. Several New York Supreme Court Justices, and other judges, have adopted the same policy. The District Attorney of Monroe County has stated that he is delaying the trials of twenty persons prosecuted on the basis of wiretap evidence. New York 

Congressmen have announced their intention to introduce corrective legislation. In the meantime, the final word of the Federal Court of Appeals has not been spoken, and there is always the United States Supreme Court beyond. 142

Courts of Special Sessions Outside the City of New York Sec. 96. New York City Criminal Courts Sec. 97. Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York Sec. 98. Magistrates Courts of the City of New York Sec. 99. Courts of Special Sessions held by City Magistrates Sec. 100. Criminal Jurisdiction of Other Courts PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

The practice, in courts of record and inferior courts, in New York City and outside the city, has been amply covered elsewhere in this work. But it is most important for the practicing lawyer to be familiar with the practice in the inferior courts where minor charges, offenses and misdemeanors are prosecuted against his clients. Either in New York City or upstate, the lawyer will generally first come into the matter after an initial complaint has been made against his client. If the defendant has been brought in by the police, he will be held in the New York City Magistrate's Court under a short affidavit stating in barest outline what he is being held for. On a warrant issued on a private citizen's complaint, 143

there will be a sworn information and statements by the complainant. Out of the city it will be much the same, except that, in the smaller counties, there will be no representative of the District Attorney's office in sight, and the papers may well be drawn in artistically by a lay Justice of the Peace. 

The lawyer's first concern will be to interview his client, if he is in custody, and it will be necessary, generally, that he file a notice of appearance before he is permitted to do so. He will wish, too, to inspect the complaint or information, any depositions and other records on which his client is being held. If necessary and feasible, he will arrange bail and will learn the date set for preliminary hearing. On this preliminary arraignment, the practice will be substantially the same, whether in the New York City Magistrate's Court, or in a special sessions court held by a Justice of the Peace, Village Police Justice, City Judge, Nassau County District Court 

Judge, or other local magistrate. Hearing may be had, or may be waived at the defendants' option. In any event, it will not concern itself with guilt or innocence, but only with a prima facie showing; but it may be most valuable in disclosing to alert counsel how substantial a case the prosecution has.

Either in New York City or outside the city, if this hearing discloses grounds for felony prosecution, the defendant will be held for the Grand Jury on bail to be fixed. If the charge appears to be of a misdemeanor, the City Magistrate will hold the defendant for trial before the Court of Special Sessions, unless he waives and elects to be tried by the Magistrate; the judge outside the City of 

New York will hold the defendant for trial before himself, fixing day and time. In the out-of-City court, this is the time when, pleading not guilty, the defendant must demand a jury trial, which he can have if he asks it, but waives if he does not. The wisdom of moving to dismiss may also appear at this point in the upstate proceedings. Unlike proceedings in New York City, there will not be just a formal short affidavit, or scant information; the sworn information of the complainant, prepared not by the District Attorney's representative, but often by a lay Justice of the Peace on oath of the complainant, is the pleading. It is at this point, too, either in New York City or out of the City, that counsel must decide whether to make an application for a removal of the case to the County Court, for presentation to the Grand Jury. 

In any of the courts, whether courts of record or inferior courts, whether in New York City or upstate, the trial will be basically 144

§ 

the same. There will be juries of twelve in the Supreme and County
