Courts, and juries of six in the courts of special sessions; in the 

Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, or the City 

Magistrate's Court, there will be no juries-three solemn judges in the one, the City Magistrate in the other. The inferior court judges outside of New York, even when they are not the lay Justices of the Peace and Police Justices one may find in remoter areas, are almost invariably more informal and casual in their approach than are those in the higher courts. Particularly in criminal matters, where rights and privileges which are mere technicalities in the civil practice become matters of constitutional privilege and due process in the criminal courts, astute counsel may often make good use of this attitude in the protection and defense of his client's interests.

On appeal, several differences appear, but for the most part the practice is not too different, as between the courts of special sessions out of New York, and the inferior courts in the City. The service and filing of notices of appeal is much the same in appeals from felony convictions throughout the State, and in appeals from the Court of Special Sessions in New York City. Notices of appeal from the New York City Magistrate's Court are only slightly different, in that they are required to indicate the basis of the appeal. 

But appeals from inferior courts to County Courts outside the City do not utilize a notice of appeal, under the practice set forth in the Code. What is called for is an affidavit setting forth all the errors claimed as the basis of the appeal. Served with this, the 

District Attorney often receives what is his first intimation of the case, unless it is one of the more serious matters, because in most situations it has been instituted, tried and disposed of, without representation from, or even notice to, his office. The incidence of such situations varies in different parts of the State, but it is still widely true in minor offenses and violations, and the less serious misdemeanors.

Sec. 88. General Discussion. This chapter will review the structure and jurisdiction of the courts of the State of New 

York having criminal jurisdiction. The first question either in the prosecution or defense of a criminal case is whether the court has jurisdiction. "As has often been pointed out, the legal lexicon knows no word more chameleon-like than 'jurisdiction"." (United States v. Sabella, 145

§ 

272 F. 2d 206.) Professor Beale defines jurisdiction in a broad sense as: "The power of a sovereign to affect the rights of persons by the judgment of a court." (36 

Harv. L. Rev. 241.) Often of greater significance than the law itself, is the determination as to which court has the juridical power to apply and enforce the applicable law. 

The Court of Appeals in Hunt v. Hunt, 72 N.Y., 217, defined the concept of jurisdiction as "the power of the court to hear and determine a case." Implicit in the hearing and determining of a case is the further power to carry into effect the action of the court. 

Jurisdiction or power to act is based upon two components, i.e. jurisdiction of the subject matter of the charge and jurisdiction of the accused person. A court can legally act and render a judgment of conviction if it has jurisdiction of the subject matter (People v. Copit, 187 Misc. 744, 62 N.Y.S. 2d 460), and of the accused person (Francisco v. 

Little Falls Dairy Company, Inc., 163 Misc. 165, 296 N.Y.S. 

956, modified on other grounds, 249 App. Div. 922, 293 N.Y.

S. 282). The jurisdiction of the subject matter of an action includes and may be limited as to the character of the offense committed or the jurisdiction of the territory where the crime is committed.

The initial inquiry prior to determining which particular court has jurisdiction, is whether the State of New York has jurisdiction over the act committed. The courts of New York State have no jurisdiction over crimes committed against the laws of the United States (18 U.S.C., sec. 3231; People v. Conti, 127 Misc. 244, 216 N.Y.S. 442).

New York State retains jurisdiction over areas conveyed and leased to, or operated by, the Federal Government unless jurisdiction is ceded to the United States pursuant to State Law Sec. 52. Thus, in People v. Vendome Service, 

Inc., 173 Misc. 825, 19 N.Y.S. 2d 195, aff'd 284 N.Y. 738, the court held that the State was not divested of jurisdiction over an area purchased by the United States and leased to the defendant until the execution of a deed or release ceding jurisdiction in accordance with State Laws, Sec. 52 146

§ (People v. Bordman, 161 Misc. 145, 291 N.Y.S. 213; 1953 

Op. Att'y Gen., 106).

The jurisdiction of New York State extends beyond the land boundaries of the state to the portion of the Great Lakes lying within the territorial limits of the state, the marginal sea to a line three geographical miles distant from the coast line or a further distance if such is recognized by the United States, and to the high seas to the extent that the United States claims jurisdiction or is recognized as having jurisdiction by international treaty or agreement (State Law, sec. 7a). See Code of Criminal 

Procedure, section 11a.

At common law, jurisdiction of crimes belonged to the court of the state where the crime was completed. The 

Legislature has by statute modified this common law principle to provide for jurisdiction over: "1. A person who commits within the state any crime, in whole or in part; 2. A person who commits without the state any offense which, if committed within the state, would be larceny under the laws of the state, and is afterwards found, with any of the property stolen or feloniously appropriated within this state; 3. A person who, being without the state, causes, procures, aids or abets another to commit a crime within the state; 4. A person who, being out of this state, abducts or kidnaps by force or fraud, any person contrary to the laws of the place where such act is committed, and brings, sends or conveys such person within the limits of this state, and is afterwards found therein; 5. A person who, being out of the state and with intent to cause within it a result contrary to the laws of this state does an act which in its natural and usual course results in an act or effect contrary to its laws." (Penal 

Law, sec. 1930.)

The court, in People v. Zayas, 217 N.Y. 78, held that 

New York State had jurisdiction where false pretenses were made in this state and money obtained in reliance thereon in another state, even though the transaction may not be criminal in the foreign state where the transaction 147

§ 

was completed. Jurisdiction of the courts of New York 

State was sustained where a libelous letter addressed to a foreign country was mailed within the State (People v. 

Bihler, 154 App. Div. 618, 139 N.Y.S. 819, aff'd, 210 N.Y. 

592). In People v. International Nickel Co., 155 N.Y.S. 156, aff❜d. 168 App. Div. 245, 153 N.Y.S. 295, aff'd. 218 N.Y. 644, the defendant's plant emitted smoke, gases and fumes outside of the State, which were carried by the wind into New York State. The prosecution's contention that the defendant came within subdivision 5 of the section, was rejected. 

The court held that the intent required under this section has a higher test than normally imposed, viz. intending the natural and probable consequences of one's acts, but rather the defendant must have had an intent to cause a result contrary to the laws of this State. 

Section 1933 of the Penal Law represents a further at tempt to extend the jurisdiction of the State by providing that a person "who commits an act without this state which affects persons or property within this state, or the public health, morals or decency of this state, and which, if committed within this state, would be a crime is punishable as if the act were committed within this state." The Court of 

Appeals, in People v. Werblow, 241 N.Y. 55, held that it was not within the contemplation of this section to bring within the jurisdiction of New York State every criminal act committed in another State which might affect persons residing within our borders. The court held, however, that this section covers a libel published in another State and later circulated in New York, or a nuisance created in another State and then spread to New York. Sections 735 and 1713 of the Penal Law extend jurisdiction over dueling and prize fighting committed without the state by residents and to non-residents if they leave the State with the intent to engage in this prohibited act outside of the state. 

After determining the jurisdiction of the State, the local jurisdiction of the court within the particular geographical unit of the state must be ascertained. At common law every offense had to be inquired into, as well as tried, in the 148

§ county where the offense was committed (Murtagh v. 

Leibowitz, 303 N.Y. 311; Blackstone Commentaries, 11th ed., Book IV, Page 305). The sections of the Code of Crim inal Procedure relating to each particular court so provide. See infra. Sec. 32 of the New York Criminal Courts

Act provides that all charges of misdemeanor shall be tried in the county wherein the offenses are alleged to have been committed. The statutory scheme of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure is based upon this major premise that the offense must be tried in the county where committed, and therefore certain exceptions are carved out of this general rule as discussed in the following section (People v. 

Hetenyi, 277 App. Div. 310, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 990, aff'd, 301 N.Y.757).

Sec. 89. Counties Having Concurrent Jurisdiction of 

Crimes. "When a crime is committed partly in one county and partly in another, or the acts or effects thereof, constituting, or requisite to the consummation of the offense, occur in two or more counties, the jurisdiction is in either county." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 134.) The county where the preparatory acts for the commission of a crime were conducted has jurisdiction of the matter (People v. Licenziata, 199 App. Div. 106 191 N.Y.S. 619; People v. Thorn, 21 Misc. 130, 47 N.Y.S. 46). Likewise, an indictment for conspiracy may be found in any county where an overt act was committed by any one of the conspirators, though the substantive act was committed elsewhere (People v. Summerfield, 48 Misc. 242, 96 N.Y.S. 502; People v. Vario, 165 

Misc. 842, 2 N.Y.S. 2d 611. People v. Levy, 123 Misc. 845, 206 N.Y.S. 857). It was held in People v. Crotty, 55 Hun 

611, 9 N.Y.S. 937, where the defendant promised to marry in one county and seduced the victim in another, that either county had jurisdiction to inquire and try the crime of seduction under promise of marriage. In homicide cases both the county where the killing occurred and the county in which any part of the victim's body is found, have jurisdiction (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 134-a). 149

§ 

The territorial limit of a county is, in effect, extended for jurisdictional purposes five hundred yards from its boundary, and a crime committed within five hundred yards of the boundary line of two or more counties may be tried in either county (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 135; People v. Davis, 36 N.Y. 77). The terminal boroughs of any bridge or tunnel within the City of New York have concurrent local jurisdiction over all crimes and offenses committed upon such bridges or tunnels (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 135-a). A person charged with deserting or abandoning his family may be charged in either the county where the desertion or abandonment occurred or the county in which the family later resides or acquired a settlement (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 135-b). A crime committed on board a vessel navigating a river, lake or canal is triable in any county through which the waterway passes or on which it borders (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 136). A similar provision governs crimes committed on trains, trucks, airplanes or other common carriers and any county has jurisdiction through which such vehicle passes or has passed or in which such trip terminates, or would terminate if completed (People v. Lowendahl, 108 Misc. 96, 178 N.Y.S. 55).

A prosecution for criminal libel against a resident of the state may be commenced either in the county where the libel is published or in the county where the libeled party resides. The defendant may change the venue to the county where the libel was printed by timely applying for such an order and executing a bond securing the complainant's reasonable expenses of traveling to the place of trial and attending at the trial. If the crime of libel is committed against a non-resident, the defendant must be indicted and the trial had in the county where the libelous paper purports to be published, or in any county where the paper was circulated if the paper does not on its face purport to be published in a particular county (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 138).

Concurrent jurisdiction of a charge of larceny against 150

§ a person charged with misappropriating funds held in trust under the Lien Law (Penal Law, sec. 1302-c) exists in the county in which the improvement is situated, the county in which the defendant resides or in which he has a place for the transaction of business and the county in which the larceny in whole or in part was committed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 138-a, subd. 1). The counties in which the statement was either mailed, served or received all have jurisdiction of a perjury, second degree, in the case of a false verification of a statement made pursuant to the 

Lien Law (Penal Law, sec. 1634; Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

138-a, subd. 2). An accessory to a felony may be indicted, tried and convicted either in the county where he became an accessory, or in the county where the principal felony was committed (Penal Law, Sec. 1934).

Jurisdiction cannot be conferred upon the court by the defendant; a defendant has no power to waive the lack of the courts' jurisdiction over the subject matter of the action. The court, in People ex rel. Pettibone v. Superintendent of New York State Reformatory, 162 Misc. 125, 294 N.Y.S. 255, said: "The defendant could not confer jurisdiction of the offense by consent." It should be noted that the cases holding that a jurisdictional defect in the subject matter of the case may not be waived are inapposite to cases where the defect is caused by the lack of jurisdiction over the person. A defendant can waive the lack of jurisdiction over his person. The issue of jurisdiction may be raised at any time, including the right to raise this objection after pleading, during the trial, in arrest of judgment or on appeal from a conviction. Full discussion of this point proceeds in subsequent chapters. 

The jurisdiction of the court is determined upon the allegations or charges in the indictment (People ex rel. 

Luciano v. Murphy, 160 Misc. 573, 290 N.Y.S. 1011, affirmed 249 App. Div. 879, 292 N.Y.S. 844), or information (People v. Perrin, 170 App. Div. 375, 155 N.Y.S. 698), and is not determined by the facts as ultimately proved or developed. "Jurisdiction of the subject matter is based upon 151

§ 

the authority to hear and determine offenses of the class or grade charged in an indictment and is not dependent upon the facts appearing in the case." (People ex rel. 

Luciano v. Murphy, supra.)

Sec. 90. Classification of Courts. Before proceeding to ex amine in detail the jurisdiction of the designated courts, it may be valuable to establish some of the characteristics or basic criteria for comparing the powers of the various courts of the State.

Sec. 90(a). Original-Appellate Jurisdiction. The first dis tinction is that of courts of original as compared to courts of appellate jurisdiction. Sec. 11 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure provides: "The following are the courts of justice in this state having original jurisdiction of criminal actions: (1). The court for the trial of impeachments. (2). 

The Supreme Court. (3). The county courts in counties other than New York. (4). Local courts of inferior jurisdiction established for cities which are expressly authorized by law to act in criminal matters in cities other than the city of New York. (5). The court of general sessions for the county of New York. (6). The courts of special sessions. (7). The police courts." Some of the above courts also have appellate, as well as original, jurisdiction. The 

Court of Appeals of the State is exclusively a court of appellate jurisdiction.

Sec. 90(b). Constitutional-Statutory Court. A second dis tinction exists between constitutional courts and statutory courts. Although every court owes its genesis to Article VI, the judiciary article of the State Constitution, the courts whose jurisdiction is specifically detailed there and cannot be modified by statute are called constitutional courts. 

Both the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court are constitutional courts. "Any act of the legislature which deprives the court of the jurisdiction it had at the time of the adoption of the constitution or limits or qualifies it is 152

§ (c) 

unconstitutional and void" (People ex rel. Folk v. McNulty, 256 App. Div. 82, 9 N.Y.S. 2d 380). The jurisdiction of the

County Court is dependent upon legislative enactment and subject to any modifications the Legislature deems it proper to make (Gilbert v. York, 111 N.Y. 544).

Sec. 90(c). Courts of Record-Not of Record. A third dif ferentiating characteristic in the distinction between "courts of record," or superior courts and inferior courts not of record. Section 11 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "The courts of special sessions and police courts are deemed inferior courts not of record, within the section of the constitution which provides for the removal of justices of the peace and judges, or justices of inferior courts not of record, and their clerks, by such county, city or state courts as are designated by law, but for no other purpose." The court, in People ex rel. Dunnigan v. Webster, 14 Misc. 617, 36 N.Y.S. 745, affirmed 1 App. Div. 631, 37 N.Y.

S. 1148, stated that by reason of the wording of Section 11, it could be argued that "courts of special sessions * * * are made courts of record except as to the provisions of the constitution providing for the removal of magistrates who may hold such courts." (See, Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 132.)

Section 2 of the Judiciary Law affirmatively establishes that the following are courts of record: "1. The court for the trial of impeachments. 2. A court on the judiciary. 3.

The court of appeals. 4. The appellate division of the supreme court in each department. 5. The supreme court. *** 

7. A county court in each county, except the county of New 

York. 8. The court of general sessions of the county of 

New York. *** 10. The city courts of the cities of Albany, 

Mt. Vernon, New York, Rochester, Schenectady, Troy, Utica and Yonkers. * * *" All courts other than those specified in this section are courts not of record. 

At common law, a court of record was accorded higher status than were courts not of record, because its records were deemed incontestable and it had the power to fine and commit for contempt. The distinction as to contempt is 153

§ (d)  

still retained in that only courts of record are given general power to punish for contempt (Judiciary Law, sec. 750).

While courts not of record also enjoy this power, it is only by virtue of specific legislative grant. (See, for example, N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 102-b; Justice Court Act, sec. 19;

Nassau County District Court Act, sec. 235.) The distinc tion is recognized in many other statutes.

For example, Section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure restricts to courts of record the power to admit to bail in capital cases and those involving crimes which may result in death, and other specified crimes which are considered of special seriousness or concern. (See chapter of this work on "Bail" for fuller discussion; Report of Judicial Council, 1939, p. 240.)

Sec. 90(d). Exclusive-Concurrent. Another jurisdictional distinction is the exclusiveness or concurrency of a court's jurisdiction of specific crimes. As an example, the Supreme 

Court and the County Court, generally, have concurrent jurisdiction of most crimes. On the other hand, subject to removal, courts of special sessions have exclusive jurisdiction of certain specified misdemeanors and offenses (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 56).

Sec. 91. Supreme Court. The first New York Constitution, adopted in 1777, continued the existence of, and provided for, the Supreme Court. This constitutional court has both original and appellate jurisdiction, and has unlimited criminal jurisdiction, including jurisdiction to try felonies with a jury (People v. Washor, 196 N.Y. 104). Although infrequently utilized, its criminal jurisdiction is unimpaired; it has been stated: "It is true that in the recent past, very few cases have been tried in the Supreme Court" 

People v. Fay, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 2), but from time to time felonies are tried in that court, and are often removed there from the County Courts. In the Fay case, supra, where an indictment was filed in the Court of General Sessions and the defendant moved to transfer the matter to the Supreme 

Court, the court said: "The doors of Trial Term, Part I 154

§ 

(Criminal Part) of this court may have rusted at the hinges from disuse, but the doors can still be opened. The power to try criminal cases vested in this court by the State Constitution cannot be divested because seldom employed or because a like power is constantly exercised by another court of limited jurisdiction." 

In 1870, the Supreme Court was organized into its present structure of four judicial departments. Although it sits in every county of the State, and its Justices are elected in ten judicial districts, the court is a single "tribunal of general statewide jurisdiction rather than an aggregation of separate courts sitting in the several counties or judicial districts of the state." (Schneider v. Aulisi, 307 N.Y. 375.)

The process of the Supreme Court may be directed into any part of the State (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 24), and the jurisdiction of the Justices of the court is coextensive with the State (Schneider v. Aulisi, supra). The criminal jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is defined by Section 22 

of the Code (People ex rel. Newton v. Special Term, Part 

1, 193 App. Div. 463, 184 N.Y.S. 193).

Section 22-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure gives the Supreme Court jurisdiction to "inquire by the intervention of a Grand Jury of all crimes committed or triable in the county; but in respect to such minor crimes as courts of special sessions, police courts or city courts have jurisdiction to hear and determine, the jurisdiction of the supreme court attaches only upon removal to the supreme court or presentment of an indictment in accordance with sections fifty-seven, fifty-eight and fifty-nine." The jurisdiction of a Grand Jury empanelled by the Supreme Court is coterminous with the power and authority of the court 

(People v. International Nickel Co. 155 N.Y.S. 156, 218 

N.Y. 644, aff'd, 168 App. Div. 245, 153 N.Y.S. 295). The Supreme Court has jurisdiction of criminal actions only when prosecuted by indictment (People v. Knatt, 156 N.Y. 302; 

Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 222).

Prior to the enactment of Sec. 59 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure, the statute provided that the Supreme Court 155

§ 

had jurisdiction of all crimes and misdemeanors except those which were enumerated in Section 56 of the Code, which were within the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of special sessions. As to such crimes, the jurisdiction of 

Supreme Court could attach only if the defendant obtained a certificate of the County Judge or a Justice of the Supreme Court that the charge be prosecuted by indictment (People v. Gilberg, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 920; People v. Shimko, 11 

Misc. 487, 183 N.Y.S. 893; People ex rel. Morrison v. Pollack, 264 App. Div. 92, 34 N.Y.S. 2d 841, aff'd, N.Y. 600).

In 1944, the Legislature added what is now Section 59 to the Code of Criminal Procedure. Incorporated by reference into Section 22, the jurisdictional section of the Supreme Court, this provides another manner in which the Supreme Court may obtain jurisdiction over misdemeanors otherwise within the jurisdiction of courts of special sessions. In People v. Nicholas, 189 Misc. 218, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 

366, the defendant was indicted for a misdemeanor in violation of Penal Law, Sec. 483, one of the enumerated misdemeanors within Section 56 of the Code. The defendant contended that the court had no jurisdiction until a proceeding was first commenced in a court of special sessions. The court held that although in the first instance a court of special sessions has exclusive jurisdiction of this crime, that "court shall be divested of its jurisdiction to hear and determine misdemeanors if at any time before trial a grand jury shall present an indictment for the same offense. (People v. Rice Associates, Inc., 185 Misc. 473, 56 

N.Y.S. 2d 833.) Section 22, subd. 2, of the Code gives the court jurisdiction to try and determine all crimes which the Grand Jury has the power to indict except that an indictment of a person who is within the jurisdiction of the Youth Court shall be transferred to the Youth Court of the county in which the acts charged were allegedly committed unless the Supreme Court shall be of the opinion that it should be tried therein, and so orders. 

The Supreme Court has jurisdiction to try any indictment found in any County Court or in the Court of General 156

§ Sessions in New York County which is removed by order of the County Court or Court of General Sessions and received by the Supreme Court, or which the court removes from any court into the Supreme Court, if the Supreme Court deems it proper to be tried therein (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 2, subd. 4). The court has the same jurisdiction as a County Court in any matter transferred according to Sections 40 and 41 of the Code (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

22, subd. 5). The authority of the Supreme Court to remove to itself a matter pending in the County Court is based upon case law as well as statutory authority (People v. 

Diamond, 122 Misc. 327, 203 N.Y.S. 836; People ex rel.

Swann v. Court of General Sessions, 115 Misc. 454, 189 

N.Y.S. 780). The court likewise has the power to send or transfer any indictment found in the Supreme Court to the County Court or the Court of General Sessions of the County of New York. In People ex rel. Albanese v. Hunt, 266 App. Div. 105, 41 N.Y.S. 2d 646, affirmed 292 N.Y. 528, the defendant was indicted for arson, second degree, in the Supreme Court, and pleaded not guilty. The matter was transferred to the County Court, where the defendant was convicted of arson, third degree, and the order of transfer was sustained.

The Supreme Court, to confer jurisdiction upon the County Court, must order the matter transferred to the County Court. In People ex rel. Dold v. Martin, 284 App. 

Div. 127, 131 N.Y.S. 2d 12, a defendant was indicted in the

Supreme Court and pleaded guilty before the County Court, withdrawing his prior plea of not guilty. The record did not disclose an order of the Supreme Court in conformity with Sec. 22, subd. 6, of the Code. The court said: "Unless and until, therefore such an order is made, the County Court acquires no jurisdiction of an indictment found in the Supreme Court." The court distinguished the 

Albanese case, supra, where it was held that the mere failure of the clerk to enter an order of transfer actually made did not vitiate the proceedings in the County Court. 

The Supreme Court is the sole arbiter with unlimited 157

§ 

discretion to determine whether a case removed from the County Court should be tried by it or returned to the County Court (People ex rel. Wright v. Klein, 139 Misc. 

353, 248 N.Y.S. 478), and it was held in People v. DePuy, 115 App. Div. 564, 101 N.Y.S. 81, that the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to send to the County Court an indictment which the County Court sent back after the first transfer. 

This inherent power of the court, buttressed by statutory authority, to remove and transfer cases between the Supreme and County Courts, must be distinguished from removal proceedings initiated by either the People or the defendant pursuant to Sections 344-353, of the Code. Those sections provide that the District Attorney or the defendant may make an application for removal on the ground of good cause or to obtain a fair trial. Section 344 of the 

Code requires that such application be made on notice (People v. Fay, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 2). Thus, in People v. Glasser, 1 App. Div. 2d 929, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 596, an indictment in the

County Court was removed to the Supreme Court on the District Attorney's motion without notice to the defendant. The court said: "The requirement of notice now found in Sec. 346 (31), Code Crim. Proc., applies only to transfers 'for good cause shown,' and not to routine administrative transfers from County Court to the Supreme Court in the same county, designed merely to facilitate a speedy trial." (People v. Diamond, 12 Misc. 327, 203 N.Y.S. 

836.) For a fuller discussion of these proceedings, see the chapter on "Change of Venue.' 

99 

Sec. 92. Court To Which Motions Addressed After Trans fer. The question has arisen as to the jurisdiction of the respective courts after the transfer of an indictment from the Supreme Court to the County Court. In Hirschberg v. 

Supreme Court, 269 N.Y. 392, the indictment returned in the Supreme Court was transferred to the County Court. 

The defendant made a motion, addressed to the Supreme Court, to inspect the Grand Jury minutes in that court. 

The court distinguished its authority to permit the inspec- 158

§ 

tion of Grand Jury minutes from other motions, stating that after the indictment is transferred or removed to the County Court, jurisdiction is completely transferred to the County Court, and pre-trial motions, including those directed to the sufficiency of the indictment, must be made to the County Court, to which jurisdiction has been transferred. However, it was there held that a motion to inspect the Grand Jury minutes was appropriately addressed to the Supreme Court, as that court had custody of the minutes rather than the County Court. Subsequently, the 

Legislature in 1939 enacted subdivision 2-a of Section 39 of the Code, which gave the County Court concurrent jurisdiction over the Grand Jury records and proceedings in all cases of indictments sent to the County Court by the 

Supreme Court.

The new statute was applied in People v. Fort, 141 N.Y.S. 

2d 290, where the defendant moved before the Supreme Court to inspect Grand Jury minutes and the court said: "the County Court and Supreme Court have concurrent jurisdiction to hear such a motion." In the case of People v. Zallan, 133 N.Y.S. 2d 167, the defendant made a motion for a bill of particulars in the Supreme Court, to which had been returned the indictment subsequently transferred to the County Court. The court held that all preliminary motions in preparation for trial or directed against the indictment must be made to the County Court, except a motion to inspect Grand Jury minutes and motions incidental thereto. The Court of Appeals has sustained the right of the Supreme Court to stay the proceedings in the County Court, pending a determination of the motion to inspect the Grand Jury minutes (Schneider v. Aulisi, 307 

N.Y.375). The court noted that the right to move to inspect the minutes in the Supreme Court would be rendered futile if the court did not have the incidental power to stay the proceedings.

The Supreme Court has jurisdiction to admit to bail any person committed, before or after indictment on any criminal charge, as conferred by Section 22, subdivision 8 of 159

§ 

the Code. See the chapter of this work entitled "Bail." And exclusive jurisdiction of habeas corpus proceedings is conferred on the Supreme Court, under the stated circumstances, by Section 25 of the Code, which provides: "During the session of the supreme court in any county, no person detained in a county jail of such county upon a criminal charge shall be removed therefrom by writ of habeas corpus, unless such writ shall have been issued by or shall be made returnable before such court." It has been held that such removal, not in conformity with that section, is invalid (People ex rel. Granger v. Foote, 221 App. Div. 

815, 223 N.Y.S.902).

Sec. 93. County Courts in Counties Other Than New York. 

The County Court is a court of special and limited powers, dependent upon the Legislature for its jurisdiction and subject to such modifications or alterations thereof as the 

Legislature may deem proper (Gilbert v. York, 111 N.Y. 

544; People ex rel. Dold v. Martin, 284 App. Div. 127, 131 

N.Y.S. 2d 12). In sixty-one of New York's sixty-two counties, County Courts are established. It should be noted that, unlike the Supreme Court, and although uniformly constituted and regulated outside New York City's counties, these courts are nevertheless "an aggregation of separate courts sitting in the several counties" (Schneider v. Aulisi, 307 N.Y. 375), and each one exists only within its own county. They exist in every county except the County of 

New York, where the counterpart is the Court of General 

Sessions of the County of New York. The County Courts outside the City of New York have civil as well as criminal jurisdiction.

The County Court has jurisdiction, subject to the prior jurisdiction of the Youth Court, to inquire via the Grand Jury, "of all crimes committed or triable within the county; but in respect of such minor crimes, as courts of special sessions, police courts or city courts have jurisdiction to hear and determine, the jurisdiction of the County Court attaches only upon removal to the County Court or pre- 160

§ sentment of an indictment in accordance with sections fifty-seven, fifty-eight and fifty-nine." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 39, subd. 1.) This language parallels that of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, discussed above. 

Like the Supreme Court, the County Court has jurisdiction, subject to the qualifications below, of those crimes not denominated as within the exclusive jurisdiction of courts of special sessions. As to crimes which are, at first instance, within the exclusive jurisdiction of courts of special sessions, the County Court can acquire jurisdiction if the case is removed to the County Court by the certificate provided by Sections 57 and 58 of the Code, or upon the presentment of an indictment in the County Court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 59; People v. Nicholas, 189 Misc. 

218, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 366; People v. Rice Associates, Inc., 185

Misc. 473, 56 N.Y.S. 2d 833.) As pointed out in the section pertaining to the Supreme Court, supra, prior to the enactment of section 59 of the Code, special sessions courts had exclusive jurisdiction, unless the defendant succeeded in obtaining a certificate of removal. The County Court has "jurisdiction to try criminal causes only after indictment by the Grand Jury." (People v. Hopkins, 208 App. 

Div. 438, 203 N.Y.S. 653.)

Every County Court, as well as the Court of General Sessions of the County of New York, has jurisdiction to try and determine indictments returned by the County Court or sent to the court by the Supreme Court in the county, for crimes not punishable by death. Thirty-seven 

County Courts, including the four County Courts of New York City, plus the Court of General Sessions of the 

County of New York, have general jurisdiction concurrent with the Supreme Court over all crimes prosecuted by indictment, including those crimes punishable by death (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 39, subd. 2; People ex rel. Price v. Hayes, 151 App. Div. 561, 136 N.Y.S. 854). The counties having jurisdiction to try indictments for crimes punishable by death are: Albany, Onondaga, Oswego, Rensselaer, Orange, Ulster, Kings, Queens, Bronx, Nassau, 161

§ 

Suffolk, Erie, Sullivan, Richmond, Jefferson, Westchester, Dutchess, Putnam, Monroe, Niagara, Chautauqua, Cattaraugus, Allegany, Wyoming, Genesee, Orleans, Oneida, Herkimer, Lewis, Wayne, Ontario, Steuben, Cayuga, Livingston, Yates, Schenectady and Seneca. Where there is no authority to try a matter where the penalty is death, the County Court must send every indictment found in the county for a capital crime to the Supreme Court (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 40).

The County Court may send an indictment pending in that court to the Supreme Court, and if such indictment is remitted back without trial by the Supreme Court, the County Court may then proceed to trial (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 41). This section is a complement of section 22, which permits the Supreme Court to accept jurisdiction of a matter transferred by the County Court (People v. 

DePuy, 115 App. Div. 564, 101 N.Y.S. 81). As heretofore discussed, the County Court has jurisdiction and control, concurrently with the Supreme Court, over the records and minutes of the Grand Jury in all cases of indictments sent by the Supreme Court, and the jurisdiction to determine any motion for an inspection of such Grand Jury minutes (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 39, subd. 2-a;) People v. Fort, 141 N.Y.S. 2d 290; Schneider v. Aulisi, 307 N.Y.S. 

375; People v. Zallan, 133 N.Y.S. 2d 167).

The County Court has jurisdiction: "6. To review the convictions of disorderly persons actually imprisoned and to execute the powers conferred and duties imposed by law in relation to those persons. 7. To continue or discharge recognizances, undertakings and bonds of persons bound to keep the peace or to be of good behavior, and to inquire into and determine the complaints on which they were founded. *** 10. To let to bail persons indicted therein for any crime triable therein as provided by law, to include for the County Courts of Bronx, Kings, Queens and Richmond Counties, and for the Court of General Sessions of the County of New York, the power of such court of each such county to reduce, increase or change the terms or 162

§ amounts of bail as set by a City Magistrate sitting in the same county. 11. To let to bail persons committed to the prison of the county before indictment for any offense triable in the court, to include, for the County Courts of Bronx, Kings, Queens and Richmond Counties, and for the Court of General Sessions of the County of New York, the power of such court of each such county, to reduce, increase, or change the terms or amounts of bail as set by a City Magistrate sitting in the same county. 12. To discharge persons who have remained in prison without indictment or trial in the cases prescribed by law. 14. To grant new trials in all cases tried therein." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 39.)

The County Court is held by the County Judge, except that in the more populous counties, the Legislature has provided more than one such judge, each of whom sits in a separate part. In addition, where the press of court business necessitates it, a County Judge "of any county outside the City of New York may hold the County Court in any other county when requested by the County Judge of such other county." (Constitution, N.Y., Art. VI, sec. 11.)

And a further provision of the State Constitution authorizes the Governor to designate the County Judge of another county to hold a County Court during the "vacancy, absence, or inability to act" of the County Judge (ibid.). 

The Court of Appeals has characterized the functioning of the County Courts in the following language: "The Constitution envisages a County Court in each of the 62 counties without condition or limitation as to whether its business is conducted in one or more parts. In either event it must be deemed a County Court and, in this respect, is no different than the functioning of the Supreme Court in parts (Matter of Malloy's Estate, 278 N.Y. 429). No contrary conclusion may be drawn from the circumstance that the Legislature has specifically authorized certain County Courts to conduct their business in parts, for to that extent Section 42 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is an act of sanction and, as such, is superfluous. *** Judge Liddle's 163

$

act in holding Nassau County Court while the regularly elected County Judge was neither absent nor incapacitated but, in fact, present in the county and holding Part I, had constitutional authority, and having such, Part III was, therefore, a duly constituted session of the Nassau 

County Court." (People v. Allen, 301 N.Y. 287, 289–290.)

Sec. 94. The Court of General Sessions of the County of 

New York. The Court of General Sessions is a court of limited original criminal jurisdiction (Matter of Ryan, 306 N.Y. 11), comparable in jurisdiction to the County

Courts outside of the County and City of New York and differing, so far as criminal jurisdiction is concerned, in name only. The Court of General Sessions of the County of New York has no civil jurisdiction, as is true of the other County Courts in the City of New York. The jurisdiction and procedure of the Court of General Sessions is governed by the provisions of Sections 51, et seq. of the 

Code of Criminal Procedure (People ex rel. Jerome v. 

Court of General Sessions, 185 N.Y. 504). 

This Court has jurisdiction: "1. Subject to the prior jurisdiction of the Youth Court to determine and punish according to law, all crimes cognizable within said county, including crimes punishable with death or imprisonment in the state prison for life; 2. To exercise, in cases arising in said county, the same powers as are conferred by this code upon county courts in other counties; 3-a. To have jurisdiction and control, concurrently with the Supreme Court, over the records and minutes of the Grand Jury in all cases of indictments sent thereto by the Supreme Court and the jurisdiction to determine any motion for or order of inspection of such Grand Jury Minutes." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 51.)

The process of the Court of General Sessions may be served anywhere within the State of New York, like that of County Courts in general. However, the Court of General Sessions of the City and County of New York has no jurisdiction of an offense committed without the County 164

§ 

of New York. Thus, where the defendants were indicted for concealing and withholding stolen and wrongfully acquired property, General Sessions was held without jurisdiction, since it was not alleged that the criminal act occurred within the County of New York (People v. Fein, 292 N.Y. 10; People v. Bates, 38 Hun. 180, 4 N.Y. Cr. 214).

Sec. 95. Courts of Special Sessions Outside the City of New York. Chapter I of Title VI of the Code of Criminal Pro cedure is entitled:

"The special sessions except in the Cities of New York and Albany." The chapter pertaining to special sessions in the City of Albany was repealed in 1937. The courts known as courts of special sessions outside the City of New York are held by the Justices of the Peace of towns and some cities, Police Justices of villages and local courts in the cities. The courts of special sessions have jurisdiction only as expressly conferred by statute (People v. Henries, 136 Misc. 224, 241 N.Y.S. 127), and are courts which have no stated terms or continuity, but are organized and exist only for the trial of a particular case (People v. Wagner, 45 N.Y.S. 314; People v. Mittleman, 150 Misc. 394, 268 N.Y.S. 819). An information takes the place of an indictment in these courts, and is a condition precedent to the jurisdiction (People v. Pershaec, 172 

Misc. 324, 15 N.Y.S. 2d 215; People v. Perrin, 155 N.Y.S. 698).

The jurisdiction of the courts of special sessions is provided for in Sections 56, 56-a and 56-b of the Code of Criminal Procedure. They have, in the first instance, exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine charges of misdemeanors, offenses, violations of ordinances and infractions committed within their respective counties which are set forth in the statute. As pointed out previously in this chapter, this exclusive jurisdiction is not absolute, as it is provided that such jurisdiction is subject to the power of removal by the County Judge of the county where the charge is pending, or any Justice of the Supreme Court. 

The jurisdiction of these courts is also subject to divest- 165

$ 

ment pursuant to Section 59 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, "if before the commencement of the trial of any person accused of a misdemeanor, a Grand Jury shall present an indictment against the same person for the same offense."

The special sessions was held divested of jurisdiction in a case where the defendant was charged with the misdemeanor of endangering the life or health of a child because the Grand Jury presented an indictment prior to the commencement of any proceedings (People v. Nicholas, 189 

Misc. 218, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 366; People v. Hall, 187 Misc. 1, 62 

N.Y.S. 2d 269; People v. Rice Associates, Inc., 185 Misc. 

473, 56 N.Y.S. 2d 833). Courts of special sessions, being statutory courts, do not have jurisdiction unless the crime charged is one of those provided and specifically conferred by the statute (People v. Mittleman, 150 Misc. 394, 268 

N.Y.S. 819). Section 56 of the Code contains an enumeration of the misdemeanors, over which the courts of special sessions have jurisdiction. 

The jurisdiction of courts of special sessions is broader than indicated upon first analysis of Section 56. Subdivision 37 gives the court "Such other jurisdiction as is now provided by special statute or municipal ordinance authorized by statute." (People v. Hayes, 167 Misc. 18, 4 N.Y.S. 

2d 897.) In People v. Munderback, 108 N.Y.S. 2d 899, the defendant was charged with violating Section 100 of the Penal Law and pleaded guilty. The court held that the City 

Court of Oneida, as created by a special act of the Legislature, was empowered to try all misdemeanors whether or not such offense was enumerated in Section 56. Similarly, Village Police Justices have jurisdiction of all misdemeanors within their villages (People v. Monahan, 257 

N.Y. 388). Specific statutes must, therefore, be consulted as to local courts. For example, see Buffalo City Court Act, Secs. 65-77-a; Mount Vernon City Court Act, Sec. 178; 

Nassau County District Court Act, Secs. 230-235; Rochester City Court Act, Sec. 4(B); Utica City Court Code, Sec. 4. 166

§ Considerable confusion has prevailed as to the jurisdiction of the Police Justices of villages. Section 182, Village 

Law, provides: "The Police Justice of a village may hold a court of special sessions and shall have in the first instance exclusive jurisdiction to hear and try and determine charges of any misdemeanor committed within such village, subject to the jurisdiction of the Youth Court and the rights of removal or divestment provided in the Code of 

Criminal Procedure." In the case of People v. Kraft, 229 

App. Div. 281, 242 N.Y.S. 348, the defendant was charged with maintaining a public nuisance and was held for trial in the Police Court. An application for removal was made in Supreme Court and the Justice denied the application, but stated that the Police Court did not have jurisdiction to try the misdemeanor which was not enumerated in Section 56. The Appellate Division, although holding that the decision of the Supreme Court justice was not appealable, undertook to clarify the law. The court pointed out that prior to the amendment to the Village Law in 1927, such courts had jurisdiction to try misdemeanors "committed within such village and triable by a court of special sessions." The statute, as amended, confers jurisdiction "to hear, try and determine charges of any misdemeanor committed within such village." The Court of Appeals sustained the exclusive jurisdiction of Police Justices to hear all misdemeanors including those not enumerated (People v. Monahan, 57 N.Y.C. 388). Section 183 of the Second

Class Cities Law is identical in language to Village Law, sec. 182 (People ex rel. Folk v. McNulty, 256 App. Div. 82, 9 N.Y.S. 2d, 380).

The courts are loath to remove a case from courts of special sessions, the general feeling being that "sound public policy requires that criminal causes of all grades and classes should be promptly disposed of, and the tribunals having jurisdiction in the first instance be permitted to exercise the same without interference or restraint, unless the interests of justice require otherwise." (People v. Porter, 108 Misc. 100, 177 N.Y.S. 460; People v. Liteer, 153 167

§ 

N.Y.S. 2d 704; People v. Belle, 131 Misc. 610, 227 N.Y.S. 

680; See contra: People v. McClellan 133 Misc. 280, 232

N.Y.S. 9.) The court of special sessions being an inferior court, not of record, its jurisdiction will not be presumed but must affirmatively appear (People v. Freer, 171 Misc. 

478, 12 N.Y.S. 2d, 856). Since the court of special sessions has no stated terms and is organized and exists only for the trial of each particular case, after a judgment the court is without power to entertain any further application (People v. Wagner, 45 N.Y.S. 2d 314).

In People v. Baranowski, 208 Misc. 862, 147 N.Y.S. 2d 

882, the defendant was convicted of speeding but the court reserved decision until a jury rendered a verdict on another charge of driving while the license had been revoked. It was held that the court had lost jurisdiction and that nothing could remedy the action. The court of special sessions has no power to reserve its decision after the hearing of testimony, but must render judgment (People v. 

Pagano, 206 Misc. 717, 136 N.Y.S. 2d 659). It should be noted that the court may adjourn for sentence for a day certain, so as to enable the court to investigate the background of the accused. An appellate court cannot send a matter back to a court of special sessions to remedy a defect because after the termination of the case, the court no longer exists (People v. Mittleman 150 Misc. 394, 268 

N.Y.S. 819). Nevertheless, it has been held that a court of special sessions has the power to act upon a motion to vacate a judgment on the grounds that the judgment was obtained by fraud or other unjust means, and not merely erroneous in law (Matter of Hogan v. Supreme Court, 295 N.Y.92).

Sec. 96. New York City Criminal Courts. The powers and authority of the inferior courts in the City of New York are set forth in the statute entitled New York City Criminal Courts Act. This statute, prior to 1941, was known as the Inferior Criminal Courts Act. The change of name did not change the essential nature of the act, which is to 168

§ 

provide a comprehensive scheme of legislation for the in ferior courts of the City of New York (People v. Formis cio, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 149). This act creates two courts of inferior criminal jurisdiction (People on complaint of Fried v. Santer, 176 App. Div. 733, 163 N.Y.S. 1080). "The inferior courts of criminal jurisdiction of the city of New York shall consist of (1) the Court of Special Sessions and (2) 

the City Magistrates' Courts." (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 

3.) As thus constituted, the Magistrates' Courts are independent of and not a branch of the Court of Special Ses sions (People v. Pray, 87 Misc. 464, 150 N.Y.S. 1061). 

Sec. 97. Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York. 

The Code of Criminal Procedure, secs. 64 and 64-a, contains but a brief reference to the jurisdiction of the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York. The primary source of legislation governing the Court of Special Ses sions is the New York City Criminal Courts Act (People v. Formiscio, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 149; People v. Fuchs, 166 App. 

Div. 811, 152 N.Y.S. 445, affirmed 215 N.Y. 725). The Court of Special Sessions in the City of New York has jurisdiction: "Subject to the prior jurisdiction of the Youth Court, such as is conferred on them by the Greater New York charter and other existing statutes." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 64, subd. 1.) "The Court shall have in the first instance exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all charges of misdemeanor committed within the City of New York, except charges of libel." (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31, subd. 1; 

People v. Samuels, 259 App. Div. 167, 18 N.Y.S. 2d 532, reversed other grounds, 284 N.Y. 410.) The jurisdiction of the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York is analogous to that of Police Justices (Village Law, sec. 182) 

and City Judges (Second Class Cities Law, sec. 183), as distinguished from the narrower jurisdiction conferred on other courts of special sessions by Section 56 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (People v. Kraft, 229 App. Div. 

281, 242 N.Y.S. 348). Section 31 then sets forth the cases 169

§ 

in which the Court of Special Sessions may be divested of jurisdiction, comparable to the provisions of Sections 57, 58 and 59 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Divestiture occurs when an indictment is returned against the defendant (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 1-b), or if before the commencement of trial, a certificate that the case should be prosecuted by indictment is granted by a Justice of the Supreme Court in the department where the trial would be held, or a Judge of the Court of General Sessions of the County of New York, or a County Judge of any county where the crime is triable (People v. Petrulla, 172 Misc. 

853, 16 N.Y.S. 2d 411; People v. McGuinness, 168 Misc. 

849, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 593). As has been previously suggested, the issuance of such certificate of the reasonableness of proceeding by an indictment is within the court's sole discretion (People v. Shattles, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 186).

The court stated, in People v. Petrulla, 172 Misc. 853, 16 

N.Y.S. 2d 411, that "whenever it appears (a) that a case presents intricate and complicated questions of fact, which justify a jury trial; (b) that difficult questions of law are involved; (c) that a property right is affected; (d) that the decision would be far-reaching in its effect and become a precedent which will regulate a matter of general interest; or (e) that the case is of exceptional character and the defendant for some special reason, cannot have a fair trial in the Court of Special Sessions, it would be a reasonable exercise of discretion to grant the applications." It has been held that although the Grand Jury directs the District Attorney to file an information in the prosecution of a misdemeanor, the case may nevertheless be subsequently prosecuted by indictment and the Special Sessions thereby divested of jurisdiction (Dodge v. 

Supreme Court of New York, 276 N.Y. 444).

The words "exclusive jurisdiction" in this section, as in Section 56 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, "was not intended to limit the jurisdiction of courts of general jurisdiction but was intended to define the jurisdiction of the inferior criminal courts established thereby as between 170

§ themselves." (People v. Cooper, 156 Misc. 419, 286 N.Y.S. 

596.) The court may be divested of jurisdiction if, prior to trial, "a person charged with a violation of the motor vehicle law, first offense, or a violation of any law for the prevention of cruelty to animals shall plead guilty in any 

City Magistrates' Court. (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act, Sec. 31, subd. 1-a.)

The court has jurisdiction, where a defendant is charged with a misdemeanor, to accept a plea of guilty to an offense which is not a crime, if such offense can be made out and if the prosecuting attorney so recommends, and the facts and reasons therefore are stated in open court and spread upon the record. (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act, sec. 31.)

The Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York also exercises appellate jurisdiction, to hear appeals from the decision or determination of city magistrates (N.Y.C. 

Crim. Cts. Act, sec. 31, subd. 6), and the power to fix bail pending such appeal (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act, Sec. 31, subd. 

7). It is most important, also, to recognize that the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York has the same power and jurisdiction as the County Courts and Court of General Sessions to send process into any county of the State (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 64; N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act, sec. 31, subd. 4). The Court of Special Sessions, as well as 

Magistrates holding courts of special sessions, have no jurisdiction to try a defendant for any violation of law, unless it is a misdemeanor and hence have no jurisdiction over a violation of the Administrative Code constituting a mere offense (People ex rel. Garafola v. Warden of Rikers 

Island. 186 Misc. 992, 63 N.Y.S. 2d 853; People v. Salerno, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 729).

Sec. 98. Magistrates' Courts of the City of New York. The lowest courts of criminal jurisdiction are the Magistrates'

Courts, which, like other inferior courts, have only the powers conferred by statute (People v. Lamboray, 152 

Misc. 206, 273 N.Y.S. 69). The Magistrates' Courts have jurisdiction to try offenses summarily, and to determine 171

§ 

whether proof presented upon preliminary hearings of misdemeanor or felony, respectively, requires that the person charged shall be held for the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York or for the Grand Jury. The "city magistrates' courts are police courts within the meaning of the provisions of the code of criminal procedure and the penal law, subject to the prior jurisdiction of the youth court." (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act., sec. 102; 

People ex rel. Garafola v. Warden of Rikers Island, 186 

Misc. 992, 63 N.Y.S. 2d 853.) The Magistrates have jurisdiction throughout the City of New York (N.Y.C. Crim. 

Cts. Act, sec. 102). "A city magistrate shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any complaint alleging a violation of any provision of law, rule or regulation relating to vehicular or pedestrian traffic (N.Y. Crim. Cts. Act, sec. 102-a). 

In the case of misdemeanors which are traffic offenses, and thus within the jurisdiction of the Magistrates' Court by virtue of this section, the jurisdiction of the Court of Special Sessions is not divested (People v. Oboler, 276 App. 

Div. 908, 94 N.Y.S. 2d 57). City Magistrates have the "power to try and punish any person charged with violating either section seventeen, two hundred thirteen, two hundred twenty-five, two hundred twenty-seven, two hundred forty-eight or three hundred six of the sanitary code." (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act., sec. 102-c.) A City magistrate also has summary jurisdiction to impose sentence of imprisonment, but only in a limited number of other cases such as disorderly conduct, vagrancy and public intoxication, which were powers possessed by the Magistrates' Courts in 1910 and preserved by statute (Schildhaus v. 

City of New York, 7 Misc. 2d 859, 163 N.Y.S. 2d 201).

Sec. 99. Courts of Special Sessions Held by City Magis trates. The Act empowers City Magistrates in certain misdemeanors to act as courts of special sessions providing the defendant is advised of his right to be tried by the Court of Special Sessions and neither the defendant nor the Dis- 172

§ trict Attorney demands that the trial be held in the Court of Special Sessions (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act., secs. 130, 131).

It has been held that the failure to apprise the defendant of his right to be tried in a Court of Special Sessions, deprives the Magistrate of jurisdiction (People v. Feder, 205 Misc. 8, 126, N.Y.S. 2d 98; People v. Genova, 273, App. 

Div. 496, 78 N.Y.S. 2d 98).

The Magistrate, when trying a matter under Sections 130 and 131, has the same authority as a Court of Special Sessions and has the same power that such court with three justices would have (Hearn v. Parilli, 1 Misc. 2d 201, 147 N.Y.S. 2d 618; People v. Citarelli, 247 App. Div. 53, 286 N.Y.S. 734). Therefore, when a Magistrate sits as a court of special sessions an appeal is not taken to the Appellate Part of the Court of Special Sessions but to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, as are appeals from the three-judge Court (People v. Green, 13 Misc. 2d 

268, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 266). A Municipal Term is established in the Magistrates' Court, which is constituted to try charges of misdemeanor, pursuant to Sections 130 and 131 of the Act, for the violation of any provision of the Administrative Code of the City of New York, or of any local law of the City of New York, or of the rules and regulations of any department, bureau, board or commission of the city, and all such charges for the violation of any statute of the State of New York when the action is prosecuted by or on behalf of any agency of the City of New York, except the Police Department, or by or on behalf of the Department of Labor of the State of New York, or by or on behalf of the Division of Licenses of the Department of State of the 

State of New York (N.Y.C. Crim. Cts. Act, sec. 141; 

Mosher v. Haddock, 181 Misc. 486, 46 N.Y.S. 2d 343, affirmed 268 App. Div. 752, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 802; People v. 

Reisner, 162 Misc. 470, 295 N.Y.S.813).

The Felony Court is a branch of the Magistrates' Court established to examine into cases of persons charged with committing or attempting to commit felonies or one of the misdemeanors enumerated in section 552 of the Code of 173

§ 

Criminal Procedure, as provided in Section 145 of the New 

York City Criminal Courts Act. 

The Women's Court is a part of the Magistrate's Court constituted for the purpose of hearing cases and proceedings within the jurisdiction of that court against women, primarily charges of prostitution and vagrancy. Although created as a night court by Section 109 of the Act, the Board of City Magistrates have since provided that such court is to be held in the day time. The Adolescent Courts, another specialized part of the Magistrate's Courts, created, in the counties other than Kings and Queens, by regulation of the Board of City Magistrates, have jurisdiction of adolescents of the ages of sixteen through twenty. In Kings and Queens, this court exists by virtue of Section 100 of the New York City Criminal Courts Act, with jurisdiction of youths sixteen through eighteen years of age. The Girls' Term Court is a division of the Magistrate's Court having quasi-criminal jurisdiction over females between the ages of sixteen through twenty, who are addicted to drugs or liquor, found in houses of prostitution or ill fame, associate with criminals or prostitutes, live an immoral life or deport themselves so as to injure or endanger the morals or health of themselves or others. 

The Court has jurisdiction of females of sixteen to eighteen years of age who desert or wander from home, or have no one exercising appropriate parental control, whose homes are unfit places to live in, or who are not receiving the necessary care and support (Appendix to New York 

City Criminal Courts Act, secs. 1 et seq.). The action of the

Court pursuant to this Act does not divest the appropriate criminal court of jurisdiction of the matter. 

Sec. 100. Children's Courts. The Children's Courts, estab lished in our State primarily to deal with children under sixteen whose violations, other than capital crimes, are removed from the category of crimes (Children's Court 

Act, sec. 2, subd. 2; Domestic Relations Court Act, sec. 2, subds. 15, 16), are essentially civil courts (Kane v. Necci, 174

§ 269 N.Y. 13). They appear nevertheless to have been vested with a limited jurisdiction over certain misdemeanors dealing with children. Thus, the Children's Court Act, regulating Children's Courts in the fifty-seven counties outside New York City, gives those courts "original jurisdiction to hear, try and determine all cases less than the grade of felony which may arise against any parent or other adult responsible for or who contributes to the delinquency of or neglects any child." (Children's Court Act, sec. 6, subd. 4.) Similarly, the Domestic Relations Court

Act confers on the Children's Court Division of the Domes tic Relations Court of the City of New York "jurisdiction, whenever the issues involving a delinquent or neglected child are before the court similarly to try, hear and determine any charge or offense, less than the grade of a felony, against any parent, or other person in loco parentis to such child, involving an act or omission in respect to such child in violation of any law of the state or ordinance of the city of New York, or which has or is alleged to have contributed to the delinquency, neglect or dependency of any such child." (Domestic Relations Court Act, sec. 61, subd. 2.) 

In People v. Rogers, 248 App. Div. 141, 288 N.Y.S. 900, affirmed 272 N.Y. 612, it was held that the Penal Law, the 

Code of Criminal Procedure and the Inferior Criminal Courts Act (now the New York City Criminal Courts Act) 

were the repositories of the law regulating the manner of prosecuting the commission of crime, and that the Legislature had not intended to transfer to the Domestic Relations Court the power to try misdemeanors. This holding, however, has been distinguished in cases determining that the Children's Court Division has jurisdiction to try offenses of misdemeanor grade and impose sentence if the enforcement of the penal statute is collateral to the Court's primary function to protect children (Humann v. Rivera, 272 App. Div. 352, 71 N.Y.S. 2d 321; Citrin v. Belcastro, 196 Misc. 272, 91 N.Y.S. 2d 275). And it was stated in People v. Phipps, 97 N.Y.S. 2d 845: "When Section 61, subdi- 175

§ 

vision 2, in specific language confers authority and gives power to the Court to punish a person who is the parent of a child or one who stands in loco parentis to a child for contributing to the neglect of the child, the court may not question the authority given nor the power of the State Legislature to give such authority. ***To find a person guilty of contributing to the neglect of a child is in effect convicting such person of the commission of a crime less than a felony." 176

CHAPTER CORONERS' AND  Sec. 101. The Coroner and His Functions 

Sec. 102. Nature of the Inquest 

Sec. 103. Procedure at the Inquest

Sec. 104. The Coroner's Warrant Sec. 105. Coroners and Medical Examiners Sec. 106. The Medical Examiner, His Office and Procedures Sec. 101. The Coroner and his Functions. The office of the coroner, and his functioning in death cases, originated far back in the English common law past. In People v. Jackson, 47 Misc. 60, 67, 68, reversed 121 App. Div. 856, 126 N.Y.S. 

1046, affirmed 191 N.Y. 293, it was pointed out: "The earliest statute defining the duties and powers of the coroner was that of 4 Edw. I [A.D. 1275] stat. 2. This was in affirmance of the common law and is the basis of his modern jurisdiction." And, in the same case, at page 298 of 191

N.Y., it was stated of the coroner: "He is, therefore, a judicial officer *** and, indeed, his duties as an inquisitor, simply, were regarded as 'principally judicial' as long ago as when Blackstone wrote his celebrated commentaries. (1 Blackstone's Comm. 348, Sharswood Edition.)"

The coroner, and his functions in the procedures concerning the investigation of unlawfully-caused deaths, were brought with them to New York as part of the English common law by the colonists. Continuing as part of the State's criminal law establishment after the Revolution, the office of coroner was recognized as a constitutional county office in the earlier State Constitutions and, 177

§ 

with the adoption of the Revised Statutes, was incorporated in the statute law. When the Constitution of 1894 was adopted, it lost its constitutional status, but it remained in operation throughout the State by statutory authority. The omission of the coroner from the listing of county officers in the Constitution of 1894 did not affect its status as a county office (People v. Blair, 21 App. Div. 

213, 47 N.Y.S. 495, affirmed 154 N.Y. 734; see also People v. 

Scholer, 94 App. Div. 282, 87 N.Y.S. 1122, affirmed 179 N.Y. 

602). That omission, nevertheless, made constitutionally possible the substitution of appointed borough coroners for the elected county coroner in the consolidation of the 

City of New York in 1898 (Greater N.Y. Charter, L. 1897, c. 378, sec. 1571), the complete elimination of the office of coroner in Erie County in 1902 (Laws of 1902, ch. 577), and its elimination in New York City in 1915 (Laws of 

1915, ch. 284).

Although he was from time to time invested with other governmental functions which need not here concern us, the coroner's principal task has always been the investigation of sudden or suspicious deaths and suicides. This has been carried out in twofold-by examination of the body itself at the scene of death, with a subsequent autopsy when circumstances indicated its necessity, and by a coroner's inquest or hearing, conducted with or without a coroner's jury, to determine the manner and cause of, the likelihood of criminality in, and the apparent perpetrator of, the death. Section 773 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "Whenever a coroner is informed that a person has been killed or dangerously wounded by another, or has suddenly died under such circumstances as to afford a reasonable ground to suspect that his death has been occasioned by the act of another by criminal means, or has committed suicide, he must go to the place where the person is and forthwith inquire into the cause of the death or wounding. * * *” 

The coroner, usually an elected officer in the county, has never been required to be, and usually is not, a medical 178

§ man. The statute therefore requires that he "summon as a witness a surgeon or physician, who must, in the presence of the jury, inspect the body and give a professional opinion as to the cause of the death or the wounding." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 775.) While the statutes organizing the government in New York City prior to 1915 retained the office of coroner on an appointive borough basis, they called for the appointment of a coroner's physician to serve this purpose in the place of the casually-summoned physician provided for by the Code. 

When circumstances appearing at the inquest indicate the necessity therefor, the coroner orders an autopsy (Penal Law, sec. 2213; Gould v. State, 181 Misc. 884, 46 

N.Y.S. 2d 313), which is performed in accordance with regulations of the State Commissioner of Health. At such autopsy, the surgeon performing the same must "permit the attendance, as a matter of right, of a person, or the medical representative of such person, likely to be the defendant or representative of the deceased person in a civil or criminal action, of which the autopsy and its findings and conclusions may prove to become a part, or in any way affected thereby." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 778-a.) The record of the autopsy, filed with the inquisition or decision on the inquest, becomes a public record available to all. 

Where criminality is indicated, however, it is not open to the public, but it may, in the court's discretion, be made available to a defendant by appropriate order of the court (People v. Preston, 13 Misc. 2d 802, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 542).

Sec. 102. Nature of the Inquest. Extending, as we have seen, far back into legal history, and a part of the statutory system of criminal procedure as long as there has been one in New York, the coroner's inquest is devised as the first formal procedure in death cases. Its purpose is to determine, preliminarily, the cause of death where a person has been killed or dangerously wounded, or has died in the circumstances indicated in Section 773 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as above quoted. When informed of 179

§ 

such death or wounding, the coroner proceeds to hold an inquest "to inquire into the cause of the death or wound" and to determine, if possible, "who is guilty thereof, in so far as by such inquisition he *** has been able to ascertain." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 777.)

The result of the inquest, proceeding with the sworn testimony of witnesses and other familiar indicia of judicial procedure, is "a judicial determination of the manner in which the deceased came to his death; and, if the death be occasioned by criminal means, who is guilty thereof." (Gould v. State, 181 Misc. 884, 46 N.Y.S. 2d 313, 319.) 

Sec. 103. Procedure at the Inquest. The coroner, in conducting an inquest, acts in a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity (Op. Atty. Gen., 1927, 37 St. Dept. 33; see also 1927, Op. 

Atty. Gen. 152), and it was stated in Gibson v. McDonald, 139 App. Div. 51, 52, 123 N.Y.S. 504: "A coroner is, in certain classes of cases, a magistrate with power to hold examinations, issue warrants and commit or discharge a person suspected of crime. ***" The inquest, provided for under the title, "Of Special Proceedings of a Criminal Nature," in Part VI, Title 1 of the Code of Criminal Pro cedure (secs. 773-790), is a “judicial investigation into the cause of death by the coroner. (People v. Coombs, 158 N.Y. 532, 538.) 

The inquest proceeds with the examination of witnesses under oath, and their testimony is reduced to writing. 

Being, however, ex parte in nature, it affords the prisoner no opportunity to produce witnesses or to cross-examine those witnesses who testify. As the court stated in People v. Collins, 20 How. Pr. 111, 115, the coroner "has no power to take testimony to establish the innocence of the prisoner, and then discharge him. * * *” Going on to state the purpose and function of the proceeding, the court in that case wrote that "the inquisition, though taken in the absence of the prisoner and upon the testimony of witnesses he could not cross-examine, settles the question of his guilt, at least 180

§ so far as it concerns the coroner, until the Grand Jury passes upon the case. It justifies the commitment of the prisoner to jail in the same manner that the testimony of witnesses does taken before a Justice of the Peace." 

The coroner summons, as witness, "every person who, in his opinion * * * has any knowledge of the facts" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 775) and, to procure their attendance, he has the power of subpoena, having, in the language of 

People v. Molineux, 168 N.Y. 264, 333, "the right to issue a subpoena *** and to punish him if he disobeyed it." Disobedience to the coroner's subpoena is punishable "as upon a subpoena issued by a magistrate." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 776.) Disorderly, contemptuous or insolent behavior at a coroner's inquest is punishable as a misdemeanor, in the same manner as is similar behavior during the sitting of a court (Penal Law, sec. 600, subd. 2).

The Code still carries the provision that the coroner summon a jury of not less than nine nor more than fifteen to sit with him where the death or wounding occurs in a county in which is situated in whole, or in part, a city having a population of more than 500,000 (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 773). This provision for a jury, however, is now obsolete; there are only two cities of that population class in the State New York and Buffalo-and in both of them the office of the coroner, and coroners' inquests, have long been abolished. This was accomplished in Erie County, which includes Buffalo, by Laws of 1902, ch. 577, sec. 15, a Medical Examiner's office and procedures being established. In the City of New York, the office of the Chief Medical Examiner was established, and the office of coroner as then established was abolished, by Laws of 1915, ch. 284. 

The result of a coroner's inquest is a judicial delineation of the manner in which the deceased came to his death and, if the death was caused by criminal means, of who is guilty thereof (People v. Coombs, 36 App. Div. 284, 55 N.Y. Supp. 

278, affirmed 158 N.Y. 211). The coroner's decision, together with the testimony taken at the inquest, is filed 181

§ 

forthwith in the office of the Clerk of the County Court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 778).

Sec. 104. The Coroner's Warrant. Finding that the death occurred by criminal means, the coroner has the power, and it is his duty, to issue a warrant for the arrest of the person named in his decision as guilty, if such person is not already in custody (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 780; People v. Mondon, 103 N.Y. 211, 216). This warrant is proceeded upon in all respects as is the warrant of arrest issued by a magistrate upon an information (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

782). When the prisoner is brought before one or the other on the coroner's warrant, the coroner or a magistrate must examine the charge in precisely the same manner as is done on a warrant issued by a magistrate (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 783).

Where a person has been injured in one county and, in consequence, dies in another, there being reason to believe that a crime has been committed, the coroner of either county may issue the warrant (1930 Op. Atty. Gen. 309).

But where the deceased lies dead in another State, the coroner is without power or jurisdiction to issue the warrant, regardless of where the wounding or other criminal act occurred (People v. Jackson, 47 Misc. 60, 95 N.Y.S. 

286, reversed other grounds 121 App. Div. 856, 126 N.Y.S. 

1046, affirmed 191 N.Y. 293).

Sec. 105. Coroners and Medical Examiners. The trend has been, for many years, toward the replacement of the ancient office of the coroner, and the archaic procedures of the coroner's inquest (or "crowner's quest," as it was anciently known) by the modern office of the Medical Examiner and his professional procedures. This official, where he has replaced the coroner in the initial investigation of violent and suspicious deaths, is a physician and usually a specialist in post-mortem examinations and autopsies. His investigative procedures, where they have been substituted for the inquest of the coroner, comprise 182

§ "a combination of administrative and quasi-judicial acts which involve the exercise of discretion or judgment and *** the courts may review said acts in order to determine whether the discretion or judgment has been exercised in an arbitrary or capricious manner." (Matter of Merlin v. 

Bradess, 17 Misc. 2d 724, 726, 185 N.Y.S. 2d 430, 432.)

Nevertheless, in the language of Matter of Senior v. Boyle, 221 N.Y. 414, 416: "The duty of such Chief Medical Examiner and his assistants is to investigate the circumstances of all violent and suspicious deaths and to file a written report thereof in his office and to make autopsies if necessary. *** But the characteristic features of the office and power of a coroner (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 773-790) are not retained. The Chief Medical Examiner acts without a jury, holds no inquest, renders no decision, holds no one to answer, issues no warrant of arrest. The ancient office is gone and the ancient duties have largely disappeared with it. Another method of investigating suspicious deaths has supplanted crowner's quest." 

In addition to its abolition in New York City and in Erie County, as we have already indicated, the office of coroner has been abolished in most parts of the State and is on its way out in the others. Section 400 of the County Law now permits its abolition, and the substitution of the Medical Examiner, without further action of the Legislature, merely by the enactment of a County Board of Supervisors and a referendum. A similar option is vouchsafed to counties which have adopted the Option County Government Law, by Section 502 of that statute. As a result, and by virtue of these general laws, a number of counties have availed themselves of this modernization and more are likely to do so.
