In addition, the counties which have had new and modernized forms of government conferred on them by special laws have made this changeover. Nassau County, the first in the State to adopt and effectuate a county charter, made the change by the provisions of Section 2103 of the County 

Government Law of Nassau County (Laws of 1936, ch. 

183

§ 

 879). The Westchester County Charter (Laws of 1936, ch. 

617) also made the same change, which is now effective in that county under the Westchester County Administrative Code (Laws of 1948, ch. 852, sec. 363; Matter of Merlin v. 

Bradess, 17 Misc. 2d 724, 185 N.Y.S. 2d 430). The Suffolk

County Charter (Laws of 1958, ch. 373, effective January 

1, 1960) contains a similar provision. Laws of 1959, ch. 

373, effective November 30, 1959, gave the Board of Supervisors of Monroe County, within which is situated the State's third largest city-Rochester-power to abolish the office of coroner by local law establishing the office of Medical Examiner, upon the appointment and qualification of whom "the terms of office of all coroners elected and holding office in the County of Monroe * * * shall expire ***." (Laws of 1959, ch. 373, sec. 3.)

Though many of the details may differ in different counties, as a result of special statutes and peculiar local conditions, and of the large measure of local control permitted by enabling acts and county charters, all of the Medical Examiners' offices are very much of one pattern, and a generalized consideration of the nature, establishment and functions of the office of the Medical Examiner (in New York City, the Chief Medical Examiner) is clearly feasible.

Sec. 106. The Medical Examiner, His Office and Procedures. 

While devised, essentially, to serve the same purposes as the coroner's-to investigate and establish the apparent cause of violent, suspicious and unnatural deaths, to examine all cases of suspected suicide and all cases where no physician has been in attendance and there is therefore no medical certification of the cause of death-the Medical Examiner's procedures in no respect partake of the nature of a judicial inquisition, being rather administrative in form.

The Medical Examiner holds no inquest, renders no decision, holds no one to answer and issues no warrant of arrest (Matter of Senior v. Boyle, 221 N.Y. 414). He "is not 184

§ bound by those salutary common law rules of evidence which exclude all hearsay and furnish the benefit of the well recognized presumption against suicide." (Matter of 

Merlin v. Bradess, 17 Misc. 2d 724, 726, 185 N.Y.S. 2d 430, 432.) At the same time, it is well to bear in mind, the protection of rights implicit in these restrictions on the coroner are not so necessary in the proceedings of the Medical Examiner, inasmuch as no one can be arrested and imprisoned solely on the basis of the latter's findings and conclusions. Instead, these are provided to the appropriate law enforcement and police authorities, who proceed to prepare the case for prosecution of appropriate court proceedings against those they determine should be charged with the crime.

All of the acts establishing the office make minimum requirements of a professional nature qualifying the Medical Examiner and his assistants. They are usually required to be licensed physicians and surgeons who have practiced as such for at least five years. The enabling act for Monroe 

County provides: "The County Manager may appoint the 

County Health Director as the County Medical Examiner. 

***" (Laws of 1959, ch. 373, sec. 1.) In Lewis County, however, the 1959 amendment to the County Law which eliminated the coroner as a county officer did not substitute a Medical Examiner, as elsewhere; instead it provided that the duties of coroners in that county be transferred to the District Attorney's office, where a Medical Examiner can, presumably, be established as a subordinate of that official (Laws of 1959, ch. 536, sec. 2, effective January 1, 1960).

While we advert, loosely, to the substitution of the Medical Examiner for the coroner, we must always remember that the new office is not subject to the obligations and procedures of the old. As the Court of Appeals stated in 

Matter of Senior v. Boyle, 221 N.Y. 414, 416: “*** the characteristic features of the office and power of a coroner are not retained. *** The ancient office is gone and the ancient duties have largely disappeared with it.” 

An important example of the difference is apparent 185

§ 

when we consider Section 778-a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. That section makes it a matter of right that one likely to be interested in the outcome, or his medical representative, be permitted to attend at an autopsy. This does not apply to an autopsy conducted by a Medical Examiner or his assistant. In People v. Nisonoff, 293 N.Y. 

597, defendants convicted of manslaughter based their appeal on the admission of autopsy findings made by an Assistant Medical Examiner, who had died before the trial. 

This, they contended, was in derogation of the right of confrontation conferred by the Bill of Rights of the State 

Constitution (Article I, Section 6). In the course of an opinion, in which it sustained the procedure followed, the Court of Appeals described the manner in which the autopsy was conducted, which is characteristic of Medical 

Examiners' procedures generally, at page 600 of 293 N.Y., as follows: "The autopsy was performed on November 18, 1942, by the Assistant Medical Examiner. While he was performing the autopsy, he dictated his findings to a stenographer and typist attached to the office of the Medical Examiner. They were subsequently transcribed and a report prepared which was signed by the Assistant Medical Examiner and filed in the office of the Medical Examiner. 

So much of the report as contained the findings was offered and receipted in evidence. The opinion contained in the report was not offered. The Chief Medical Examiner was called to give opinion testimony as to the cause of death, based upon these findings." 

Rejecting the appellants' contentions, the Court of Appeals held that the report of the autopsy, duly filed as prescribed by the statute, was a public record; that, as such, its admission in evidence was proper under one of the recognized exceptions to the hearsay rule, and the reception thereof in evidence was consequently not violative of the defendants' constitutional right of confrontation. 

Despite variations in detail, the statutes generally require the Medical Examiner to maintain an office in which he is required to maintain permanent records, with proper 186

§ indexing, of all deaths examined. A report therein filed is "a report filed in a public office by a public officer for a public purpose embodying facts required by statute to be stated therein." (People v. Nisonoff, 293 N.Y. 597, 604.)

The statutes generally require, as does Section 879 of the New York City Charter, that all of its records shall be open to public inspection except those in which "in the judgment of the Medical Examiner in charge, any indication of criminality" appears. Where there is such indication, the report is required to be delivered to the District Attorney.

The Medical Examiner's report is based on his physical examination of the body and its surroundings and, when he deems it necessary, on an autopsy. He takes and reports the names of witnesses, when they are available, but is under no duty to examine such witnesses formally. He makes no formal inquisition of any kind, although he does report his findings as to surrounding facts and circumstances. Essentially, however, he does not concern himself with who caused the injuries and death, but with what caused them and how. He is, thus, in all respects an administrative investigator, but in no respect whatever a judicial examiner. 187

CHAPTER  Sec. 107. General Discussion 

Sec. 108. Murder and Kidnapping

Sec. 109. Prosecutions Other Than Murder or Kidnapping Sec. 110. Tolling of the Statute Sec. 111. When Prosecution Commenced Sec. 112. Dismissal of Indictment Tolling the Statute Sec. 113. When and How the Plea of Statute of Limitations is 

Raised 

Sec. 114. Amendment of Statute of Limitations 

Sec. 107. General Discussion. At common law there was no limitation of time for the prosecution of offenses, except in specified cases (1 Chitty Crim. Law, 160). The principle has been enunciated that a statute limiting the time within which indictments must be found is a surrender by the State of its right to try and punish criminal offenses at its discretion, without limit as to time. It is, therefore, an act of grace and favor which is to be liberally construed, when construction becomes necessary, in favor of the criminal (People v. Lord, 12 Hun 282; 22 C.J.S. 2241).

Whether a statute of limitation, barring criminal prosecution, is a “statute of repose," as it is in civil actions (Arnold v. Mayal Realty Co., 299 N.Y. 57, 60, and cases there cited), or whether it is a "statute of oblivion” which "destroys the right of action as well as the remedy" (People ex rel. Reibman v. Warden, 242 App. Div. 282, 284, 275 N.Y.S. 59), may make a great difference in its application. Thus if, as in civil actions, only the remedy is barred, the defendant's failure to plead the statute, or his acts indicating waiver thereof, would leave untrammeled the 188

§ court's jurisdiction to try and punish him. This was, in essence, the holding of the Appellate Division, Second Department, in 1939, in People v. Brady, 257 App. Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 789, 790, where three of the five Justices subscribed to the statement in a memorandum by the court that the statute "in criminal causes *** as in civil actions, is a statute of repose." However, although several other authorities are there cited, all of them apparently distinguishable, this does not now seem to be the law. In fact, the very same court some eight years later affirmed without opinion an order in arrest of judgment based on the oblivion concept of the statute (People v. Guariglia, 187 

Misc. 843, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 96, affirmed 272 App. Div. 784, 69

N.Y.S. 2d 759). Although there have been a number of statements of the rule since then in lower courts, the only Court of Appeals authority on the question is but a passing reference, without analysis or study. Because, however, it comports with the great current of authority, and seems borne out by the language of the Code itself, we may accept as the rule and the law in New York, the statement by 

Chief Judge Lehman in People v. Hines, 284 N.Y. 93, 113: "Unlike a Statute of Limitations in a civil case, such a statute in a criminal case creates a bar to prosecution and the time within which an offense is committed becomes a jurisdictional fact which the State must allege and prove." 

Sec. 108. Murder and Kidnapping. "There is no limitation of time within which a prosecution for murder must be commenced. It may be commenced at any time after the death of the person killed." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 141.)

This section, part of our statutory law since the days of the Revised Statutes, was joined, under Laws of 1935, ch. 308, by the following: "There is no limitation of time within which a prosecution for kidnapping hereafter committed must be commenced. It may be commenced at any time after the commission of the crime."

Section 610 of the Penal Law provides that upon the trial of an indictment, a defendant may be convicted of a crime 189

§ 

of lesser degree than that charged, or of an attempt to commit either the crime charged or a lesser crime. The issue has arisen whether a defendant indicted for murder can be convicted of a lesser crime or of an attempt, if the statute would have barred the indictment for such lesser crime or act. People v. DiPasquale, 161 App. Div. 196, 146 

N.Y.S. 523, held that the defendant could not be so convicted of a crime for which he could not have been indicted, citing People v. Miller 12 Cal. 291. The court, in People v. 

Dowling, 1 N.Y.Cr. 529, held that since the indictment was timely, the conviction for the lesser offense was sustained, notwithstanding that an indictment for the lesser offense would have been barred; and in People v. Austin, 63 App. 

Div. 526, 71 N.Y.S. 601, affirmed 170 N.Y. 585, although not deciding on that point, the court stated: "I do not have a right to interpolate into that section providing for conviction of lesser crimes, if such indictment be found within the time prescribed." It would seem that a defendant should not be prejudiced by the fact that the prosecutor chose to indict for murder.

Sec. 109. Prosecutions Other Than Murder or Kidnapping. 

The prosecution for all other felonies (unless a lesser time is prescribed by statute) must be commenced within five years after its commission. The prosecution for any misdemeanor, other than a conspiracy to commit a felony, must be commenced within two years after the commission of the crime; a prosecution for any offense must be commenced within two years after its commission (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 142). A youthful offender proceeding, except where a lesser crime is prescribed by statute, is subject to the same statute of limitations as if the crime involved had been committed by a person twenty-one years of age or older.

It is noted that the statute begins to run from the time of the commission of the crime. However, the statute excepts one group of cases from this rule. A prosecution for larceny committed by a fiduciary in violation of his 190

§ duties may be commenced within five years, if a felony, and two years, if a misdemeanor, after the facts constituting the crime have been discovered by one of the persons injured or defrauded; his natural guardian, if an infant; his legal representative, if an incompetent; or by a successor fiduciary. If the aggrieved person shall have died before the beginning of the period within which the prosecution must be commenced, then the prosecution must be commenced within the above statutory period after the death of the aggrieved party. 

The period of limitation is prescribed in the pertinent sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as set forth above. However, a shorter period of time is provided by the 

Penal Law in two instances. Section 929 of the Penal Law establishes a two-year limitation in prosecutions for falsely personating another person in marrying or pretending to marry or sustain the marriage relationship (Penal Law, sec. 928, subd. 1), and Section 2176 provides a similar twoyear period in which prosecution must be had for seduction under promise or pretense of marriage (Penal Law, sec. 2175).

Sec. 110. Tolling of the Statute. "If, when the crime is committed, the defendant be without the state, the prosecution may be commenced within the time limited therefor, after his return to the state. If, after the crime is committed, the defendant departs from the state, or if he remains within the state under a false name, the time of his absence or of such residence within the state under such false name is not a part of the time limited for the commencement of the prosecution. Only the time during which the defendant is an inhabitant of or usually or publicly a resident within the state or usually or publicly in personal attendance upon business or employment within the state shall be computed as part of the time limited for the commencement of a prosecution." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 143.)

The departure or absence, intended by this section to 191

§ 

toll the statute, does not mean any mere casual absence or an absence on a business or pleasure trip. "The words 'not an inhabitant of' or 'usually resident within' the state require not mere absence from the state but such absence as destroys residence, that is a fixed permanent and established home." (16 Corp. Jur. 228, quoted in People v. 

Guariglia, 187 Misc. 843, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 96, affirmed 272 App. 

Div. 784, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 759.) In the Guariglia case, the court held that the defendant's service in the armed forces outside of the State of New York did not destroy his residence so as to toll the running of the Statute of Limitations and extend the time within which prosecution could be com menced. The Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act (50 

U.S.C. Appendix, secs. 501 et seq.), and the Military Law, sec. 300 et seq., refer only to civil liability and do not affect the running of limitations in criminal prosecutions. 

Sec. 111. When Prosecution Commenced. Section 144 of the 

Code of Criminal Procedure provides that a "prosecution is commenced *** when an information is laid before a magistrate charging the commission of a crime and a warrant of arrest is issued by him, or when an indictment is duly presented by the grand jury in open court and there received and filed." It has been held in People v. Portman, 139 Misc. 544, 247 N.Y.S. 819, that the prosecution was not barred by the Statute of Limitations where the information was laid before the Justice within the statutory period, although the period expired before the filing of the information and the issuance of a warrant (People v. 

Reppin, 126 N.Y.S. 169). The affidavit must be sufficient as a matter of law to constitute an information for the purpose of conferring jurisdiction. In People v. Rapoport, 261 App. Div. 484, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 110, the court held that the prosecution had not been timely commenced by the affidavit of a police officer which did not recite facts but was based on belief of the deponent and another officer. The statute is self-explanatory as to the commencement of a 192

§ prosecution by indictment (People v. Flaherty, 110 N.Y.S. 

154; People v. Herrmans, 69 Misc. 303, 125 N.Y.S. 143).

In the case of a superseding information or indictment, the prosecution is deemed to have been commenced when the first information or indictment is filed. Section 292-a of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that where two indictments are pending against the same defendant for the same offense, or two indictments for the same matter charged as different offenses, the indictment first found is superseded. It was held in People v. Spevack, 253 

App. Div. 683, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 633, modified as to one defendant on other grounds but affirmed, People v. Silverman, 278 

N.Y. 670, that this provision implicitly applies to informations and that the first criminal pleading is determinative of the timeliness of the prosecution (People v. Schildhaus, 15 Misc. 2d 377, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 377). An indictment filed after the statutory period will be sustained if it is in connection with, and related to, preliminary examination which was timely commenced (See People v. Steiger, 154 

Misc. 538, 277 N.Y.S. 602; People v. Rapoport, 261 App. 

Div. 484, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 110).

Sec. 112. Dismissal of Indictment Tolling The Statute. 

Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 144, subdivision 2, states that if a prosecution is timely commenced and, on motion or appeal, the indictment be set aside or dismissed for want of prosecution or otherwise, or a demurrer to the indictment be allowed with directions that the case be resubmitted to the Grand Jury, or a motion in arrest of judgment be granted and the defendant be recommitted to answer a new indictment, the time during which the prosecution was pending shall not be computed as part of the time of the limitation prescribed for the offense, provided a new prosecution for the same offense be commenced within sixty days after the order is entered. The court in 

People v. Steiger, 154 Misc. 538, 277 N.Y.S. 602, confined the meaning of this section to the dismissal of indictments, holding that it does not encompass the dismissal of a com- 193

§ 

plaint. In that case, a proceeding was timely initiated in the Magistrate's Court and the complaint was dismissed. 

The indictment was returned within five years from the dismissal of the complaint but not within five years from the commission of the crime. The court held that the time during which the proceedings were pending before the Magistrate is to be included in the computation of the statutory period.

Sec. 113. When and How the Plea of Statute of Limitations is Raised. Although it is incumbent upon the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt every element of the offense, including the fact that the Statute of Limitations has not run (People v. Smolens, 258 App. Div. 373, 16 

N.Y.S. 2d 731; People v. Guariglia, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 96, 272 

App. Div. 784, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 759), the defense must raise this issue, and it may be waived by a failure to invoke it (People v. Blake, 121 App. Div. 613, 106 N.Y.S. 319, aff'd., 193 N.Y. 616). The court in People v. Bailey, 103 Misc. 366, 171 N.Y.S. 394, stated: "A crime once committed cannot be obliterated by lapse of time. The offender may be protected from prosecution by legislative bar but, if so, that bar is interposed for his protection; and it is he that must raise it. It rests within him to raise it or waive it." There is no burden upon the defendant to show that the failure to prosecute was not due to his absence from the State, or concealment as provided in Section 143 of the Code (People v. Brown, 238 App. Div. 155, 263 N.Y.S. 267).

The defense of the statute of limitations is not raised by way of demurrer (People v. Durrin, 2 N.Y. Cr. 328.) 

It is invoked by a general plea of not guilty. (People v. 

Brady, 257 App. Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 789; People v. 

Brown, 238 App. Div. 155, 263 N.Y.S. 267). The running of the Statute of Limitations is an issue of fact which cannot and should not be disposed of upon affidavit (People v. 

Rutman, 169 Misc. 354, 7 N.Y.S. 2d 718; contra People v. 

Busccolieri, 91 Misc. 156, 152 N.Y.S. 707). See also People v. Reiser, 240 App. Div. 36, 269 N.Y.S. 573, where the de- 194

§ fendant was charged with bigamy, which had been committed ten years prior to the indictment. The court cited 

Section 280 of the Code, providing that the time when the crime was committed does not have to be stated in the indictment unless it is a material ingredient in the crime, and stated that "by reason of the statute of limitations time is a material ingredient in the crime," the absence of which makes the indictment fatally defective. (See People v. Parkinson, 181 Misc. 603, 41 N.Y.S. 2d 331.)

There is no doubt that the defense of the Statute of Limitations should be raised at the trial (People v. Bailey, 103 Misc. 366, 171 N.Y.S. 394; People v. Blake, 121 App. 

Div. 613, 106 N.Y.S. 319, aff'd. 193 N.Y. 616), although it is questionable whether the effect of waiver follows, as held in People v. Brady, 257 App. Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 

789, and People v. Bailey, 103 Misc. 366, 171 N.Y.S. 394.

However, in the case of People v. Rieser, supra, where the issue was first raised at sentencing but before judgment, the court stated: "a general objection that the facts proven do not constitute a crime challenges the existence of every fact necessary to establish a crime, including the timeliness of the prosecution." It is noted that the court, in People v. Rieser, emphasized the fact that the issue of the 

Statute of Limitations was raised at the trial, albeit at the latest stage of the proceeding. The court took cognizance of the cases seeming to hold that it is too late to raise the issue for the first time on appeal (People v. Blake, supra). 

For discussion of the propriety of raising the question after a verdict or plea of guilty, see chapter on "Arrest of Judgment."

Sec. 114. Amendment of Statute of Limitation. After the statutory time has elapsed, within which a prosecution may be commenced, the defense of the Statute of Limitations is one of right and not of grace. It becomes absolute and vested, and the defendant may not be deprived of the right by legislative amendment or extension of the statutory time within which to prosecute (People v. Brown, 195

§ 

238 App. Div. 155, 263 N.Y.S. 267). Such a statute would be ex post facto. A distinctly different principle governs those cases where the statutory period, under Section 142 of Code of Criminal Procedure, has not expired. The State makes no contract with the criminal that after the prescribed time he will not be prosecuted for the crime. Prior to the expiration of the statutory period, the time may be changed, altered, repealed or extended and the prosecution may be initiated within the newly-established period (People ex rel. Reibman v. Warden of County Jail, 242 App. 

Div. 282, 25 N.Y.S. 59; People v. Amann, 159 Misc. 417, 289 

N.Y.S. 316; People v. Hagan, 138 Misc. 771, 247 N.Y.S. 374). 196

Sec. 138. Presentment

Sec. 115. History. The Grand Jury is one of the oldest and most important institutions in our common law system of criminal jurisprudence. Its origin is said to have antedated the Norman Conquest of 1066. The earliest form of what we now recognize as our Grand Jury was the frank pledge 197

§ 

whereby every group of one hundred inhabitants were sureties to the king for the good behavior of each other. 

Annually, the sheriff held a court leet or view of the frank pledge in each hundred, and the offenders were punished. 

This was succeeded by a law providing for an accusing body of twelve knights or freemen of every hundred, a hundred being the territorial division of society, and four men of every township to send in accusations of murder, robbery, larceny and harboring of criminals, arson and forgery (4 Bl. Comm. 301; 1 Pollock and Maitland, History of English Law 137-155X).

These bodies were later selected from the county at large and came to be known as the grand inquests. No witnesses were examined before such bodies and the grand inquests had no power to summon individuals (38 Col. L. 

Rev. 1943, 1948). The presentment was made on the personal knowledge of the jurors. The jurors were summoned therefore in their capacity as accusers of witnesses rather than judges. During the latter thirteenth and early fourteenth century, the grand jurors formed part of the petit jury. Thereafter, the Grand Jury at common law consisted of from twelve to twenty-three persons and undertook to accuse persons of crimes on the basis of evidence presented to them, with twelve persons required to indict (Stephen, A Digest of the Law of Criminal Procedure 199-24). The 

Grand Jury system has been abolished in England since 1933 (Liech, Abolition of Grand Jury in England, 25 

Journ. Crim. L. 623). Most of the continental European nations do not require a Grand Jury and permit a person suspected of a crime to be placed directly on trial at the instance of the prosecutor.

The laws of most jurisdictions within the United States, as does the Constitution of the United States and that of New York State, provide that, "no person shall be held to answer for a capital or otherwise infamous crime *** unless on indictment of a Grand Jury." (United States 

Const., Amend. V; Constitution, N.Y., Art. I, Sec. 6.) The

Supreme Court of the United States held in Hurtado v. 198

GRAND JURY 

§ 116 

California, 110 U.S. 516, 4 Sup. Ct. 111, that the Fifth

Amendment does not apply to a person charged with the commission of a crime by a State and that the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment is not violated by a State's providing for the commencement of a prosecution other than by indictment. Article 1, Section 6 of the New 

York State Constitution further provides: "The power of grand juries to inquire into the wilful misconduct in office of public officers, and to find indictments or to direct the filing of information in connection with such inquiries, shall never be suspended or impaired by law." 

Sec. 116. Purpose and Function. The essential function of a Grand Jury is to determine whether or not there is sufficient evidence to warrant the holding of a trial for an individual charged or about to be charged with the violation of a criminal law. The Grand Jury serves as a filtering or screening process in determining whether a person suspected of criminal activity ought to be released or held for further proceedings. There are two facets to the general objective of determining whether the people have established a prima facie case of the defendant's guilt. One is the bringing to trial of those justly charged and the second, and nonetheless important, is that of exculpating and releasing those against whom there is an unfounded charge. 

Historically, the Grand Jury was organized for the purpose of more efficiently utilizing the power of the King in an age when there was little regard for personal rights. 

It is now recognized that the Grand Jury has a second purpose of equal, and some have urged greater, significance. 

The court stated in Matter of Funston, 133 Misc. 620, 233 

N.Y.S. 81: "The establishment of this inquisitorial body was designed, not only as a means of bringing to trial those accused of public offenses upon just grounds, but had for its primary object the protection of the innocent against unfounded accusations, from whatever source they might originate. The duties imposed by law upon a grand jury are of a dual character, one, to society, to see that persons 199

§ 

justly suspected of crime are held to answer; the other to the citizen to see that he is not subjected to prosecution upon accusations based on envy, hatred or malice." 

The Supreme Court of the United States said in Ex parte Bain, 121 U.S. 7, that the purpose of the Grand Jury is to secure a citizen "from an open and public accusation of crime and from the trouble, expense and anxiety of a public trial before a probable cause is established by the presentment or indictment." The Supreme Court, in Hale v. Henkel, 201 U.S. 43, said that one of the functions of the 

Grand Jury is to "stand between the prosecutor and the accused and to determine whether the charge was founded upon credible testimony or was dictated by malice or personal ill will.”

Sec. 117. Power of Grand Jury. The power of the Grand Jury is set forth in Section 245 of Code of Criminal Pro cedure: "The grand jury has the power, and it is their duty, to inquire into all crimes committed or triable in the county, and to present them to the court." This section is declaratory of the common law (People v. Steiger, 154 

Misc. 538, 277 N.Y.S. 602). Section 253 of the Code sets forth additional powers possessed by the Grand Jury: "The grand jury must inquire, 1. Into the case of every person imprisoned in the jail of the county, on a criminal charge, and not indicted; and 2. Into the wilful and corrupt misconduct in office, of public officers of every description, in the county. 3. The grand jury may inquire into the condition and management of the public prisons in the county." 

The Grand Jury is an inquisitorial, informing and accusing body charged with the duty of investigating infractions of the criminal law occurring within the jurisdiction; its power to submit a statement, report or presentment to the court will be discussed infra. Its primary function is to vote upon the indictment, which is the first pleading by the people in a criminal matter (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

274). The indictment is defined as "an accusation in writing, presented by a grand jury to a competent court charg- 200

GRAND JURY 

§ 118 ing a person with a crime." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 247;

People v. Dumar, 106 N.Y. 502.) The Grand Jury is vested with all authority necessary to a complete inquiry into the subject matter under investigation, which of course includes a liberal power to subpoena witnesses (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 609). The jurisdiction of the Grand Jury is limited by and dependent upon the power of the court to which it is attached, being "coextensive with the powers exercised by the *** Court. (People v. International 

Nickel Co., 155 N.Y.S. 156, aff'd, 168 App. Div. 245, 153 

N.Y.S. 295, aff'd, 218 N.Y. 644; People v. Ruttles, 172 Misc. 

306, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 979.) Thus, it has been held that the grand jury may not inquire into those matters which are not within the jurisdiction of the court to which it is an appendage (People v. Stern, 3 App. Div. 2d, 443, 162 N.Y.S. 

2d 180; People v. Kennedy, 207 N.Y. 533). ***" 

Sec. 118. Stage of Proceeding When Matter Heard by the 

Grand Jury. Most Grand Jury matters are heard after the defendant has been arrested and preliminary hearings held. The complaint and depositions and the magistrate's disposition of the case are then before it, but it must pass upon and evaluate the evidence presented without regard to the magistrate's disposition. Some cases do originate in the Grand Jury without having been passed upon by a magistrate or other preliminary hearing (People v. Diamond, 72 App. Div. 281, 76 N.Y. Supp. 57, affirmed 175 N.Y. 

517). In 1944, the Legislature enacted Section 59 of the

Code, which empowers the Grand Jury to indict for a misdemeanor in the first instance, before the matter is presented to the court of special sessions, Police Court or City Court. Thus, the court in People ex rel. Reis v. Warden of 

Bronx County Jail, 269 N.Y.S. 433, aff'd, 239 App. Div. 

891, 264 N.Y.S. 948, stated that the "Grand Jury has power to inquire into all offenses, felonies or misdemeanors whether there has been a hearing before the magistrate or not." (People v. Nicholas, 189 Misc. 218, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 

366; People v. Edwards, 189 N.Y.S. 2d 39.) 201

§ 

A case may be initiated before the Grand Jury without a prior hearing or examination for any one of a number of reasons. The accused person may be out of the State, with an indictment needed for extradition. The Grand Jury may investigate to determine whether offenses have been committed and, if so, by whom. For example, the Grand 

Jury of Tioga County conducted hearings investigating the meeting of a vast number of persons of reputed criminality who met at the home of Joseph Barbara in Apalachin, New York. In this situation, no individual is accused, and the purpose of the Grand Jury is to inquire and determine whether a crime was committed and the person or persons who committed such crime. A matter may be initiated in the Grand Jury when local authority refuses to act (Prentice v. Gulotta, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 433), or where the

District Attorney does not call the matter to the Grand Jury's attention (People ex rel. Hummel v. Davy, 105 App. 

Div. 598, 94 N.Y.S. 1037, affirmed 184 N.Y. 30). Matters may also be originated before the Grand Jury because the secrecy of the proceedings encourages witnesses to testify more fully than they would if interviewed or if called to testify in a preliminary hearing. 

Sec. 119. Relationship of the Grand Jury to the Court. It is difficult to point out the precise relationship of the Grand Jury to the court. However, the areas of its dependency upon, or independence of, the court, and the control which the court exerts over it, must be explored for full understanding of the power of the Grand Jury. It has been stated that in a sense the Grand Jury is an irresponsible body; nobody can call it to account for its decision, either in favor of an indictment or against an indictment. While an arm or appendage of the court, it is not dependent upon the whim of the court and its authority and power cannot be curtailed by the court, although in certain respects there exists clear dependence (Spector v. Allen, 281 N.Y. 251, reversing 256 App. Div. 902, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 234). To say that the Grand Jury is not a part of the court is "no more 202

GRAND JURY 

§ 120 logical than to say that a petit jury is not a part of the court because a judge may not control its deliberations or determinations or questions of fact submitted upon trial." (Wilson v. United States, 77 F.2d 336.) The court in People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395, stated: "It is neither a regularly organized tribunal, nor yet an entirely informal body. 

While in a certain sense a part of the court in connection with which it conducts its deliberation, it is, for many purposes free from restraint by that court. A Grand Jury is clothed with power to determine both the facts and the law, and its methods of procedure, so far as they are not discretionary are fixed by statute and not by rules of courts." 

In Spector v. Allen, 281 N.Y. 251, reversing 256 App. 

Div. 902, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 234, a defendant was served with a subpoena duces tecum and, on appearing, was told by the foreman to bring additional papers. The defendant refused to produce complete copies of the papers requested by the foreman and was held for contempt. The court held that the defendant was not in contempt because he had not disobeyed a lawful mandate of the court. The court stated: "The Grand Jury is an arm of the court but it is not the court. Its foreman has no authority to issue a mandate of the court." The Grand Jury acts in connection with the court jurisdictionally (People v. Ruttles, 172 Misc. 306, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 979); the legality of the proceeding is determined by the court; the qualifications of the Grand 

Jurors are determined by the court; the Grand Jury's compliance with the law is judged by the court. 

Sec. 120. Relationship of Grand Jury to District Attorney. 

The Grand Jury is not a part of the District Attorney's office, nor is the District Attorney's office an auxiliary of the Grand Jury. Sections 255 through 257, of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure, set forth the statutory authority regulating the relationship and intercourse between the Grand Jury and the prosecuting attorney's office. These sections are each entitled, "When and from whom they 203

§ 

[Grand Jury] may ask advice, and who may be present during their [Grand Jury's] sessions." (See In re District 

Attorney's Relations to Grand Jury, 14 N.Y. Cr. 431.) The 

Grand Jury may ask the advice of the District Attorney or if the advice pertains to crimes against the elective franchise (Penal Law, Article 74), the advice of the Attorney General or his staff (Code of Crim. Proc. sec. 255). 

Sec. 256 imposes a duty upon the District Attorney, when required by the Grand Jury to examine witnesses, to give the jurors legal advice, and to issue subpoenas or other process for witnesses. The same duties are incumbent upon the Attorney General in the case of crimes against the elective franchise (Penal Law, Article 74). Sec. 257 

of the Code permits the District Attorney, and in certain instances the Attorney General, to be present in the Grand Jury room at all times, except that during the expression of the Grand Jury's opinion, or while it is voting on any matter, no one other than the jurors may be present. This section will be discussed more fully subsequently. 

The District Attorney serves as the attorney and counsel for the Grand Jury (People v. Radewitz, 199 Misc. 1058, 103 N.Y. 2d 985), assisting in the general investigation and examination of witnesses, advising as to the admissibility of evidence and proper procedure, giving general information and advice on legal matters, and reviewing the testimony, but, as may any attorney's, his counsel may be ignored. The District Attorney has a duty beyond that of a legal adviser, his duty to the general public. The prosecuting attorney may not properly express any opinion on or off the record concerning the facts of the case or the way in which it should be decided. The credibility of the witnesses, or whether or not the defendant should be prosecuted, is a matter within the jurisdiction of the jury (Attorney General v. Pelletier, 240 Mass. 264, 134 N.E. 

407). This duty imposes an obligation of fairness on the 

District Attorney. He must reveal all of the facts to the 

Grand Jury, for, as the court stated in People v. Rosen, 74 

N.Y.S. 2d 624: "It is the duty of the District Attorney to 204

GRAND JURY § 121 

present to the Grand Jury all of the evidence in his possession relating to a crime even though it may tend to show that the particular individual did not commit the crime. 

It is his duty as a public officer to do that." (See People v. 

Fishgold, 71 N.Y.S. 2d 830.)

The Grand Jury has the power to examine independently into a matter, whether or not the District Attorney calls its attention to the matter. (People ex rel. Hummel v. Davy, 105 App. Div. 598, 94 N.Y.S. 1037, affirmed 184 N.Y. 30.) 

In Prentice v. Gulotta, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 433, the District Attorney had refused to present to the Grand Jury the petitioner's complaint that his wife had removed their children from the State to avoid surrendering their custody pursuant to a court order. On the petitioner's application for an order to compel the District Attorney to present the case, the court held that the District Attorney is not required to present evidence to the Grand Jury if he believes it is not sufficient to indict, the Grand Jury having independent power to find an indictment without having evidence presented by the District Attorney. The Grand Jury is an impartial tribunal standing as a buffer between the prosecutor and the accused person and, in furtherance of this objective, the remarks of the District Attorney must all be made on the record (People v. Benin, 61 N.Y.S. 2d 692).

Sec. 121. Grand Jury Selection. Section 225 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure states that a Grand Jury must be drawn for every term of the Supreme Court, except for the counties within New York City and for extraordinary and adjourned terms or where a term is held where a trial jury is not required to be drawn. The Grand Jury must also be drawn for the Court of General Sessions of New York, and the county courts of the other four boroughs of the City of 

New York. Sec. 226 provides that Grand Juries may also be drawn for every other county court, for any term of the Supreme Court on order of the Justices of the Appellate Division, for an Extraordinary term of the Supreme Court 205

§ 

on order of the presiding Justice, and for any term of the Court of General Sessions or the County Courts in New York City when the judge presiding deems an additional Grand Jury necessary. A special order is not required, when a designation of terms at which a Grand Jury is to attend is made under Section 45 of the Code. (People v. 

Rugg, 98 N.Y. 537.) The order provided in Section 226 must be filed with the County Clerk at least twenty days before the term for which the jury is ordered. (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 227.)

The selection of jurors is governed by the Judiciary Law. 

The general scheme for such selection is that jurors in counties within cities having a population of one million or more are selected pursuant to Article 17 of the Judiciary 

Law. (Sections 590-609.) Article 18 of the Judiciary Law 

(Sections 650-685) governs all counties not within cities having a population of one million or more, and more than 100,000, and those counties having a smaller population whose Boards of Supervisors have elected not to be governed by Article 16 (Sections 500-53.), which otherwise applies to the smaller counties. See Farrington v. Pinckney 

1 N.Y. 2d 74, for the constitutionality of this statutory scheme. The qualifications are basically the same in all three articles and are as follows: The grand juror must be a United States citizen, living or maintaining a dwelling within the county for the greater part of the time between October and the following June. The juror must be not less than twenty-one years nor more than seventy, be in the possession of his natural faculties and not infirm or decrepit, be of good character, approved integrity, sound judgment and able to read and write English. He must be the owner or the spouse of the owner of real or personal property of the value of $250 (Judiciary Law; Secs. 

504, 596, 662). Since 1937, women have enjoyed the right to serve as jurors (People v. Cosad, 189 Misc. 939, 73 N.Y.S. 

2d 890).

The provisions for disqualification of grand jurors are also identical in substance in Articles 16, 17 and 18 of the 206

GRAND JURY 

§ 123 

Judiciary Law. Sections 506, 598, 644, provide that the following are disqualified: Elected officials of the Federal, or 

State government or of any political subdivision of the State, which includes members of the Legislature, judges of courts of record, Surrogates, Sheriffs, under- and deputy-sheriffs, Clerks, Deputy Clerks, and public officers or employees of any government, Federal, State or subdivision thereof, receiving annual compensation in excess of $1000 from the government position. Sections 505, 597 and 663 of the Judiciary Law disqualify persons "in a criminal action where the crime charged is or may be punishable by death, who has conscientious scruples against the death penalty and that such scruples would prevent him from returning an indictment *** of any crime punishable by death."

Sec. 122. Challenge of Panel or Array. The Code of Crim inal Procedure provides that there is "no challenge allowed to the panel or to the array of the grand jury." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 231; People v. Rosen, 251 App. Div. 584, 297 N.Y.S. 877, affirmed 275 N.Y. 627; People v. Fitzpatrick, 30 Hun 493, 1 N.Y.Cr. 425.) However, the court in its discretion may discharge the panel and order another to be summoned if the requisite number of ballots have not been drawn from the Grand Jury box, or if notice of the drawing has not been had in the presence of the officers designated by laws, or if the drawing has not been held at least fourteen days before (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 231; People v. Scannell, 37 Misc. 345, 75 N.Y.S. 500).

The attorney should suggest such discharge under this section at the time of impanelling the Grand Jury and the court's action must be taken prior to the discharge of the panel at the conclusion of its work (People v. Farmer, 194 N.Y.251).

Sec. 123. Challenge to Individual Grand Juror. The Dis trict Attorney may challenge an individual grand juror (Shea v. Swift, 292 N.Y. 110), as may any person held to 207

§ 

EN answer a charge, for one of the following causes only: that he is a minor; an alien; is insane; is the prosecutor of a charge against the defendant; that he is a witness for another party; that such witness cannot act impartially and without prejudice to the substantial rights of the party challenging; that a state of mind exists on the juror's part, either in reference to the case or to either party, making it impossible for him to act impartially and without prejudice to the substantial rights of the party challenging. The statute prescribes that the individual challenging must be "held to answer a charge for crime," hence an individual whose case was under consideration but who had not been held to answer cannot avail himself of the right to challenge. (See People v. Pizzimenti, 13 Misc. 2d 

82, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 935; Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 230, 232.)

A grand juror who is hostile to, or has expressed an opinion of the guilt of, a party whose case would probably come before the Grand Jury, may be objected to (People v. Jewett, 3 Wend 314). The court has great latitude in the exercise of its discretion to determine whether a state of mind exists on the part of a prospective juror warranting the challenge (People v. Luckman, 164 Misc. 230, 297 

N.Y.S. 616, affirmed 254 App. Div. 694, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 864; 

People v. Harris 182 Misc. 787, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 745, reversed 

268 App. Div. 731, 54 N.Y.S. 2d 161, reversed, 294 N.Y. 

424). The grounds set forth are the only grounds upon which an individual grand juror may be challenged (People v. Scannel, 37 Misc. 345, 75 N.Y.S.500).

The challenge exercised pursuant to these sections must be made prior to the indictment and some courts have suggested that such challenge must be exercised before the 

Grand Jury is sworn (People ex rel. Van Slyke v. Wallack, 

6 App. Div. 2d 958, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 821; People v. Pizzimenti, 13 Misc. 2d 82, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 935; People v. Jewett, 3 Wend 

314). The unyielding adherence to this rule is indicated in 

People v. Borgstrom, 178 N.Y. 254, where the court held that an individual grand juror could not be challenged after the indictment, notwithstanding the fact that the 208

GRAND JURY 

§ 125 defendant was in jail and unable to retain counsel. A challenge to individual grand jurors may be oral and must be entered upon the minutes and tried by the court, in the same manner as challenges to trial jurors (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 233). Thus, in People v. Harris, supra, it was held that the court could act from evidence other than the juror's declaration, such as the appearance and demeanor of the juror. The court must allow or disallow the challenge, and the clerk must enter its decision upon the minutes (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 234).

Sec. 124. Appointment and Charge. After the jury is selected, the court appoints a foreman and an acting or alternate foreman of the Grand Jury (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 237). The oath is then administered to the foreman and acting foreman pursuant to Section 238 of the 

Code of Criminal Procedure: "You, as foreman, and acting foreman of this grand jury, shall diligently inquire and true presentment make, of all such matters and things as shall be given you in charge; the counsel of the people of this state, your fellows' and your own you shall keep secret; you shall present no person from envy, hatred or malice; nor shall you leave any one unpresented through fear, favor, affection or reward, or hope thereof; but you shall present all things truly as they come to your knowledge, according to the best of your understanding, So help you God!" This oath is substantially the same language as was employed at common law (People v. Steinhardt, 47 

Misc. 252, 93 N.Y.S. 1026). The grand jurors then swear that they will observe the oath as taken by the foreman (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 239). It is essential to the legal organization of a Grand Jury and to its competency to act that the jurors all be duly sworn. The secretary of the 

Grand Jury is not appointed, but is elected by the jurors after they retire to the Grand Jury room. 

Sec. 125. Charge. The Grand Jury, before retiring to a private room to perform its duties, as provided by Code of 209

§ 

Criminal Procedure, section 242, "must be charged by the court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 241.) The section requires that the charge must include the reading to the jurors of Sections 245 through 260 of the Code, or give "them a copy thereof, and must give them such information as it may deem proper as to the nature of their duties, and any charges and crimes returned to the court or likely to come before the Grand Jury. The court need not, however, charge them respecting violations of a particular statute, excepting when so requested by the District Attorney." The charge must be delivered with the solemnity and dignity appropriate to the seriousness of the occasion. 

However, beyond the statutory mandate, it is within the discretion of the court how to best explain their duties to the grand jurors (People v. Shea, 147 N.Y. 78; People ex rel. Childs v. Knott, 187 App. Div. 604, 176 N.Y.S. 

321, affirmed 228 N.Y. 608). "Beyond the explicit direction to read or deliver to them sections 252 to 267 (now 245 to 260) inclusive, of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the character and scope of the charge is largely a matter of discretion. No exception lies to such a charge and there is no method by which the proceedings of a Grand Jury can be reviewed, except by motion to dismiss an indictment or in arrest of judgment." (People v. Dimick, 107 N.Y. 13.) 

In People v. Both, 118 Misc. 414, 193 N.Y.S. 591, the

Grand Jury did not find a true bill and the jury was called before the judge who stated: "certain facts were brought out which in my judgment were sufficient to warrant the finding of an indictment." This was held to have so far invaded the province of the Grand Jury as to invalidate the indictment. The courts are not prone to set aside an indictment based upon an attack of an improper charge since the regularity of an indictment and the presumption that it was based on legal and sufficient evidence stand unless there is satisfactory proof to the contrary (People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395). In the Glen case, the judge read affidavits which tended to show the commission of the crime upon which the defendant was afterwards indicted. The Court 210

GRAND JURY 

§ 127 

of Appeals held that this did not overcome the presumption that the indictment was based on sufficient legal evidence. Likewise, in People v. Brown, 193 App. Div. 203, 184 

N.Y.S. 165, where the judge had stated in his charge to the 

Grand Jury that it "is a matter of public knowledge that a riot occurred a few weeks ago, at which property was destroyed and many persons brutally beaten by a mob," the Appellate Division held that this was not sufficient to quash the indictment; that the Grand Jury was bound to receive nothing but legal evidence and with no contrary showing it must be presumed that the court would not disregard the direction of the statute. 

Sec. 126. Number. "The Grand Jury must consist of not less than sixteen and not more than twenty-three persons, and the presence of at least sixteen is necessary for the transaction of any business." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 224; 

People v. Herrmans, 69 Misc. 303, 125 N.Y.S. 143; People v. Thomas, 32 Misc. 170, 66 N.Y.S. 191.) At common law, the Grand Jury was composed of not less than twelve nor more than twenty-three men (People v. Blair, 33 N.Y.S. 

2d 182). In People ex rel. Heal v. Foster, 196 Misc. 441, 92 

N.Y.S. 2d, 807, the Grand Jury was composed of twentyfour persons. Although resting its decision on the untimeliness of the application, the court stated that the defendant was not prejudiced where one more grand juror had added his suffrage to the prescribed number 8 (Cokey v. 

People, 1 Abbott 418). For a more detailed discussion, see the chapter of this work entitled "Dismissing and Setting 

Aside Indictments."

Sec. 127. Presence of Persons Other Than Witness Before the Grand Jury. It is the general rule that in the absence of any imperative necessity therefor, it is improper for anyone to be present in the Grand Jury room at any time during the sessions of the Grand Jury, other than the witness undergoing examination and the authorized prosecuting officer and stenographer. Sec. 313, subdivision 2, of the 211

§ 

Code of Criminal Procedure, provides that the indictment must be set aside when "a person has been permitted to be present during the session of the Grand Jury, while the charge embraced in the indictment was under consideration," except as authorized by statute. The District Attorney and an Assistant District Attorney who has properly filed his oath of office and, in the case of a Grand Jury investigating election crimes the Attorney General and his staff, may be present during the session of the 

Grand Jury (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 255–257). Sec. 952, subdivision t, of the Code authorizes the presence before that body of duly appointed and qualified stenographers. 

Section 257 of the Code provides that "no District Attorney, Attorney General, officer or other person shall be present with the Grand Jury during the expression of their opinions or the giving of their vote upon any matter." 

The District Attorney and the foreman of the Grand Jury must be particularly careful to see that this rule is not violated, because the effect of the presence of an unauthorized person before the Grand Jury is ground for the dismissal of the indictment, whether or not there was prejudice to the defendant. In People v. Minet, 296 N.Y. 

315, where two witnesses appeared before the Grand Jury at the same time, the court stated: "We think that historically and on principle, an indictment should be dismissed when two witnesses have been present together while the testimony of one or both was heard by the Grand Jury and that the decision should not be made to depend upon whether or not a defendant was actually prejudiced thereby. *** Except in the clearest situations, it would be practically impossible to show influence or prejudice." 

The court, in People v. Nicholo, 205 Misc. 566, 132 N.Y.S. 

2d 136, held that the indictment would not be dismissed because an interpreter was present to assist the witness, notwithstanding that the witness did not consent to the use of an interpreter. It stated: "The test is whether as a witness she can express herself sufficiently so that justice might be done." A warden of the Grand Jury can stand by 212

GRAND JURY 

§ 128 to prevent the escape of the witness. (See People v. Minet, supra.)

The presence of the Attorney General or his staff, if not authorized by statute, has been held to constitute sufficient ground to set aside the indictment (People v. Hopkins, 182 Misc. 313, 47 N.Y.S. 2d 222). The Attorney General is authorized to appear before the Grand Jury when election violations are being investigated, or violations of Article 22 of the General Business Law, violations of sections of the Tax Law, the Education Law; or when, under Section 

62, subdivision 2, of the Executive Law, the Attorney

General is required by the Governor to attend "any term of the Supreme Court or appear before the Grand Jury thereof for the purpose of managing and conducting in such court or before such jury such criminal actions or proceedings as shall be specified in such requirement." In any other circumstances, the District Attorney must present the matter and the Attorney General's presence is illegal (People v. Dorsey, 176 Misc. 932, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 637; 

Ward Baking Co. v. Western Union Telegraph Co., 205 

App. Div. 723, 200 N.Y.S. 865). These cases have countered the holdings of People v. Kramer, 33 Misc. 209, 68 N.Y.S. 

383 and People v. Tru-Sport Publishing Co., Inc. 160 Misc. 

628, 291 N.Y.S. 449, which had held that the Attorney General's right to be present was as broad as the District Attorney's. The Attorney General has no authority to be present during the Grand Jury's investigation of perjury unless the perjurious statement clearly relates to a matter within the Attorney General's province (People v. Dorsey, 176 Misc. 932, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 637). In People v. Scannell, 36

Misc. 40, 72 N.Y.S. 499, an indictment was set aside because special counsel had failed to take the official oath prior to his appearance before the Grand Jury.

Sec. 128. Evidence. The usual procedure is that the District Attorney presents a written accusation in the form of a bill of indictment and proceeds to support this accusation with evidence. "The Grand Jury can receive none but 213

§ 

legal evidence." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 249.) The statute then more particularly states the manner in which the Grand Jury can obtain such legal evidence. This statute embodies the common law rule that evidence received before the Grand Jury must be competent legal evidence of the same caliber as is proper before the petit jury (People v. Budzinski, 159 Misc. 566, 289 N.Y.S. 656).

This rule is based upon the desire to protect the accused from the embarrassment and expense of prosecutions which could not be proved in accordance with the rules of evidence in the trial court, as well as preventing a waste of the trial court's time (People v. Rauch, 140 Misc. 691, 251 N.Y.S. 454). "To warrant an indictment the Grand

Jury should have legal evidence before them which, when taken together, would be sufficient, if uncontradicted, for a petit jury to convict the accused." (People v. Nicosia, 164 Misc. 152, 298 N.Y.S. 591.) There is not the slightest suggestion of a trend in the New York law toward the holding of the Supreme Court of the United States, in 

Costello v. United States, 350 U.S. 359, where that court sustained an indictment in a tax evasion case where only hearsay evidence was presented to the Grand Jury. The court reasoned that nothing in the Grand Jury guarantee or the historical background of the Grand Jury prevents an indictment from being based on such evidence. "If indictments were to be held open to challenge on the ground that there was inadequate or incompetent evidence before the Grand Jury, the resulting delay would be great indeed. 

The result of such a rule would be that before trial on the merits a defendant could always insist on a kind of preliminary trial to determine the competency and adequacy of the evidence before the Grand Jury."

The Grand Jury inquiry being ex parte, without representation of the defendant, the question arises as to how the exclusion of incompetent evidence may be accomplished. The primary objective of the District Attorney may be to obtain an indictment, but he must observe the bounds of propriety and it is incumbent upon him to con- 214

GRAND JURY 

§ 128 fine his presentation to legal evidence. "In presenting cases to the Grand Jury, the District Attorney should keep in mind that he owes a duty to the persons charged with crime. He should remember that there is a positive mandate that only legal evidence should be presented." (People v. Levis, 96 Misc. 513, 161 N.Y.S. 824.) The problem is made more complex by the fact that grand jurors not aware of, nor trained in, the rules of evidence, have the right to interrogate witnesses appearing before them. The court in People v. Goldenberg, 110 Misc. 556, 181 N.Y.S. 

921, recognized this difficulty and suggested that the District Attorney advise grand jurors that illegal evidence cannot be received and warn the jurors that an indictment so obtained may be subject to dismissal. 

Section 248 of the Code of Criminal Procedure reads: "In the investigation of a charge, for the purpose of indictment, the grand jury can receive no other evidence than, 1. Such as is given by witnesses produced and sworn before them, or furnished by legal documentary evidence; or 2. The deposition of a witness, in the cases mentioned in the third subdivision of section eight." Section 8, referred to, provides in subdivison 3, that, where the charge has been examined by a magistrate and the testimony reduced to deposition in the presence of the defendant, who has either in person or by counsel cross-examined or had the opportunity to cross examine; or where the testimony of a witness for the People had been taken on conditional examination, the witness' deposition may be read upon a satisfactory showing that "the witness is unable to attend by reason of his death, insanity, sickness or infirmity, or that the witness cannot with due diligence be found in the state." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 8, subd. 3.) These are the same conditions for use of the deposition as are imposed for its use on the trial, under Section 631 of the Code, and have been so since the 1958 amendment (Laws of 1958, ch. 

502). Prior thereto, sickness or infirmity was no ground for the use of a deposition before the Grand Jury, the only ones recognized by the statute then being death, insanity or 215

§ 

absence (People v. Pisanti, 179, Misc. 308, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 850).

The Grand Jury may not inspect premises where crimes have been committed, for its indictment must rest upon the testimony of witnesses, papers and documents produced before it (People v. Walsh, 92 Misc. 573, 156 N.Y.S. 

366). The scope of the section has been interpreted and somewhat extended in the case of People ex rel. Sillifanty v. Sheriff, 6 N.Y. 2d 487, where a witness, after being sworn, was given a questionnaire consisting of four pages of simple questions asking details of the witness' and his family's income and the family's assets, to be completed at home and returned to the Grand Jury. The majority of the Judges determined that the use of the questionnaire did not violate Section 248 and 249 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure. Three dissenting Judges found that the "Grand

Jury was without power to employ a financial questionnaire as a deposition in place of the oral testimony of" the witness as prescribed by Sec. 248. 

In People v. Albero, 119 Misc. 339, 196 N.Y.S. 484, the court held illegal, as hearsay, declarations made by the victim of the alleged assault. People v. Levis, 96 Misc. 513, 161 N.Y.S. 824, held that the District Attorney's statement relied on to establish an essential element of an indictment for conspiracy to delay a prosecution was hearsay, vitiating the indictment. (See People v. Baxter, 98 Misc. 552, 164 N.Y.S. 714; People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395.) Similarly, indictments based on the testimony of accomplices are bad because "A conviction cannot be had upon the testimony of an accomplice unless he be corroborated by such other evidence as tends to connect the defendant with the commission of the crime." (People v. Sweeney, 213 N.Y. 37; 

People v. Harris, 182 Misc. 787, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 745, rev'd. 54 

N.Y.S. 2d 161, rev'd. 294 N.Y. 424.) And the testimony of persons who are incompetent to testify subjects an indictment to attack. Thus, where the wife of the defendant testified against her husband, the indictment was set aside under the law which at that time made such testimony 216

GRAND JURY 

§ 128 

incompetent (People v. Moore, 65 How 177; People v. 

Briggs, 60 How 17). An indictment obtained by evidence which would be inadmissible at the trial because of its irrelevancy or highly prejudicial nature may be set aside 

(People v. Nicosia, 164 Misc. 152, 298 N.Y.S. 591; People v. 

Goldenberg, 110 Misc. 556, 181 N.Y.S. 921). An indictment found upon the confidential communication between a patient and physician, or a client and an attorney, will not stand (People v. Sellick, 4 N.Y.Cr. 331). A defendant cannot be cross-examined as to whether he has been previously indicted or charged with a crime (People v. Cascone, 185 

N.Y. 318; People v. Morrison, 194 N.Y. 178). In People v. 

Walsh, 92 Misc. 573, 156 N.Y.S. 366, reliance on newspapers, anonymous letters and the Grand Jury's own knowledge invalidated an indictment. 

Although Section 252 of the Code makes it mandatory for a member of the Grand Jury having knowledge or belief that a crime has been committed, cognizable by that body, to declare this information to his fellow jurors, the Grand Jury can base an indictment on this information only if the juror is sworn (Matter of Gardiner, 31 Misc. 

364, 64 N.Y.S. 760).

There is one further problem which merits consideration in regard to the hearing of "legal evidence," and that concerns the widespread practice of off-the-record comments made to grand juries. The court in People v. Benin, 61 

N.Y.S. 2d 692, noted the prevalence of this practice, and commented at length about the impropriety of the District Attorney's addressing the jury off the record concerning the case for about one hour. The court declined to decide on that ground, but stated: "This practice conflicts with this independence and impartiality, since it permits the representative of the People to say anything he pleases with no opportunity for a check on either its propriety or accuracy ***if the representative of the People sums up to a Grand Jury on the facts or instructs on the law as it may pertain to those facts, he should do so in the presence 217

§ 

of the Grand Jury stenographer and on the record." (See 

Matter of Gardiner, 31 Misc. 364, 64 N.Y. Supp. 760.)

Sec. 129. Quantum of Evidence. In the foregoing section, consideration has been given to the kind of evidence required to be presented to the Grand Jury. The burden of this section will be to analyze the sufficiency of the evidence required to indict, and the effect that the reception of illegal evidence has upon the Grand Jury's action. It is provided: "The Grand Jury ought to find an indictment, when all the evidence before them, taken together, is such as in their judgment would, if unexplained or uncontradicted, warrant a conviction by the trial jury." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 251.)

It is manifest that an indictment based solely and entirely upon illegal evidence, evidence not admissible in the trial court, must be set aside. "If the indictment was found without sufficient legal evidence to sustain it, it is not an indictment in contemplation of law, and cannot stand." (People v. Molineux, 27 Misc. 60, 57 N.Y.S. 936.) The court stated, in People v. Nicosia, 164 Misc. 152, 298 N.Y.S. 591, that this section and Section 249 of the Code, requiring legal evidence, "are protective measures intended to safeguard the defendant's right to the presumption of innocence, and therefore an indictment based extensively on conflicting and hearsay evidence, leading and suggestive questions, and prejudicial testimony affords justification for its dismissal." The language used in the foregoing 

the trial jury", requires evidence sufficient to overcome the presumption of innocence and establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (People v. Mangan, 140 Misc. 783, 252 

N.Y.S. 44; People v. Martinez, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 537). "The defendant is presumed innocent * * * just as much in the

Grand Jury room as elsewhere. The evidence must be of such weight as to clearly overcome the presumption of innocence before an indictment can properly be found." 218

GRAND JURY 

§ 129 (People v. Harris, 182 Misc. 787, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 745, reversed 

54 N.Y.S. 2d 161, reversed 294 N.Y. 424.)

It has been held that the introduction of incompetent or inadmissible evidence before the Grand Jury does not per se vitiate the proceedings and afford grounds for dismissing the indictment. The indictment will not be dismissed if there is sufficient legal evidence upon which a valid indictment could be found (People v. Grout, 174 App. 

Div. 608, 161 N.Y. Supp. 718). The court pointed out in 

People v. Booth, 52 Misc. 340, 102 N.Y.S. 62, that some incompetent evidence is usually received, particularly when Grand Jurors unfamiliar with the technical rules of evidence have as much right to question witnesses as does the District Attorney. The court there stated: "It is not so much a question of whether or not some incompetent evidence was received, as it is whether or not there was sufficient competent evidence to warrant the finding of the indictment."

The real task of the District Attorney is not so much to exclude incompetent evidence as it is to assure that sufficient legal evidence is produced, since the indictment may be dismissed for lack of sufficient legal evidence, but not, except for extreme prejudice, because of the failure to exclude illegal evidence (People v. Leary, 305 N.Y. 793, reversing, 280 App. Div. 679, 117 N.Y.S. 2d 392). In People v. Sexton, 187 N.Y. 495, the testimony of an infant was received in evidence without the required preliminary examination. The court there held that the receipt of this incompetent evidence, in view of the residuum of competent evidence, did not justify quashing the indictment. In People v. Rabinowitz, 301 N.Y. 763, an indictment charging a conspiracy between licensed and unlicensed bondsmen was based in part on hearsay and prejudicial testimony. The court stated that "the illegal evidence before the Grand Jury did not invalidate the indictment in view of the fact there was sufficient other competent evidence." 

Absent a clear demonstration that the illegal evidence was extremely prejudicial and adversely influenced the 219

§ 

minds of the jury, the indictment will not be subject to dismissal (People v. Acritelli, 57 Misc. 574, 110 N.Y.S. 430; 

People v. Barbour, 152 Misc. 39, 273 N.Y.S. 788). The showing of prejudicial effect must be quite cogent, as demonstrated by People v. Smith, 258 App. Div. 800, 15 N.Y.S. 2d 

538, where the dismissal of a manslaughter indictment was reversed and the indictment reinstated, notwithstanding the introduction and admission of evidence that the defendant previously had been charged with larceny, though not convicted, and the criminal record of the brother of the defendant had been improperly introduced. 

The courts are loath to inquire into the sufficiency of evidence presented to the Grand Jury upon the finding of an indictment, properly leaving to the Grand Jury the weighing of the testimony produced (People v. Strong, 1 

Abb. Prac. N.S. 244). "It is the Grand Jury's judgment not that of the court, when there is some competent evidence, whether that evidence is sufficient," to warrant a conviction upon a trial if uncontradicted and unexplained, and therefore sufficient to indict (People v. Buffalo Gravel 

Corporation, 195 N.Y.S. 94). This policy and rule is justified by the presumption that the indictment has been properly found upon legal and sufficient evidence (People v. Sweeney, 213 N.Y. 37; People v. Glasser, 60 Misc. 407, 112 N.Y.S. 321). In People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395, the court reiterated the principle of the presumptive regularity of an indictment, and that "it was based on legal and sufficient evidence stands unless there is satisfactory proof to the contrary." If illegal evidence has been introduced, the cautious procedure is for the District Attorney to resubmit the matter (People v. Brown, 272 App. Div. 972, 71 N.Y.S. 2d 594).

Sec. 130. Witnesses: Power to Subpoena. An investigation by a Grand Jury involves all the powers and incidents necessary to a complete inquiry into the subject matter of the charge. Both at common law (People ex rel. Karlin v. Culkin, 248 N.Y. 465), and by statute (Code of Crim. 220

GRAND JURY 

§ 130 Proc., sec.

609), the power to inquire includes the power of compulsory process or subpoena. The Grand Jury may compel witnesses to attend and testify before it as to any matter within the scope of its power, and examine such witness on any matter relevant to the subject of the inquiry (Matter of Morse, 42 Misc. 664, 87 N.Y.S. 721).

Subpoenas are issued, at the direction of the grand jury, by the District Attorney purusant to Section 609 of the Code, in the form set forth in Sections 612 and 613. 

A witness served with a Grand Jury subpoena may not successfully challenge the authority of the Grand Jury, if it has de facto organization or existence (People v. Doe, 247 App. Div. 324, 286 N.Y.S. 343, affirmed 272 N.Y. 473).

The Grand Jury is under no obligation to reveal to the witness, prior to his testifying, the subject or nature of the inquiry (Application of Inter-City Associates, 207 

Misc. 1012, 142 N.Y.S. 2d 412; Manning v. Valente, 272 

App. Div. 388, 72 N.Y.S. 2d 88). The District Attorney, in some cases, may be willing to discuss the nature of the inquiry, and the attorney for a witness subpoenaed should consult the District Attorney about the proposed testimony, the better to appraise the witness' status and course with respect to pleading his right against self-incrimination. The District Attorney, however, is under no obligation to discuss this, will certainly not do so if he feels it may hinder the investigation. 

"Subpoenas are presumptively valid and can only be challenged by an affirmative showing of impropriety. 

No witness may avoid obedience to the directions of the court without establishing by concrete evidence that the subpoena was issued in bad faith or that it is for some other reason invalid. * * *" The witness is not entitled to have the investigation halted to permit "forecasts of the testimony and nicely balanced arguments as to its probable importance." (Manning v. Valente, 272 App. Div. 

388, 72 N.Y.S. 2d 88.) The courts, sustaining the broad subpoena power as not subject to challenge in the absence of bad faith or patent invalidity, quote the language of 221

§ 

 Chief Judge Cardozo in Matter of Edge Ho Holding Cor poration, 256 N.Y. 374, sustaining the subpoena power of the Commissioner of Accounts of the City of New York. 

The Commissioner's subpoenas, Judge Cardozo reasoned, "will be rendered to a large extent abortive if his subpoenas are to be quashed in advance of any hearing at the instance of unwilling witnesses upon forecasts of the testimony and nicely balanced arguments as to its probable importance. *** Very often the bearing of information is not susceptible of intelligent estimate until it is placed in its setting, a tile in the mosaic."

The Grand Jury is also "entitled to free access, at all reasonable times, to the public prisons, and to the examination, without charge, of all public records in the county." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 254.) It was held however, in 

People v. Doe, 138 N.Y.S. 2d 307, that adoption records, although filed in a public office, absent a showing of dire necessity, are not such public records as may be examined by the Grand Jury. There is a presumption that an inquiry by a Grand Jury is carried on in good faith (Matter of 

Greenleaf 176 Misc. 566, 28 N.Y.S. 2d 28). 

See the chapter on "Subpoenas" for comment on the 

District Attorney's power to subpoena.

Sec. 131. Defendant as a Witness and Evidence On His 

Behalf. "The Grand Jury is not bound to hear evidence for the defendant; but it is their duty to weigh all the evidence submitted to them, and when they have reason to believe that other evidence, within their reach, will explain away the charge, they should order such evidence to be produced; and for that purpose, may require the District Attorney to issue process of the witnesses." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 250, subd. 1.) In People v. Gibson, 16 Misc. 2d 

642, 183 N.Y.S. 2d 52, the defendant's counsel wrote a letter to the foreman of the Grand Jury advising that the defendant was receiving psychiatric care, and offered to have the psychiatrist testify in the defendant's behalf. The court held that the decision of whether to have the psychiatrist 222

GRAND JURY 

§ 131 testify was within the discretion of the Grand Jury. (See 

People v. Prior, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 393, affirmed 283 N.Y. 623.) 

In Morgan v. Null, 117 F. Supp. 111, an action under the

Federal Civil Rights Law, the court construed the New York law to hold that a witness was not denied equal protection of the law when she was not permitted to testify before the Grand Jury about illegal practices in the psychiatric division of a city hospital. 

While the Grand Jury is not bound to hear evidence for the defendant, the prospective defendant himself has a right to appear and be heard before it (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 250, subd. 2; see People v. Blair, 33 N.Y.S. 2d 

183). A person who has reason to believe that the Grand 

Jury is investigating a charge that he has committed a crime has the right to testify before the Grand Jury, upon giving written notice to the District Attorney and the foreman and upon signing a waiver of immunity in accordance with Section 2446 of the Penal Law. 

The defendant or prospective defendant is not entitled to notice that the Grand Jury is investigating a charge against him. This was recognized in People v. Rosen, 74 

N.Y.S. 2d 624. However, the Rosen case presented an atypical constellation of facts where the defendant voluntarily appeared in Felony Court and the facts so patently vindicated his action that the charge was dismissed. The 

District Attorney thereafter presented the matter to the Grand Jury, unknown to the defendant, and an indictment was returned. The court dismissed the indictment, holding that it would have been fair and proper under these circumstances for the District Attorney to tell the prospective defendant of his right to appear before the Grand Jury, as provided in the Code. 

It has been held that after the defendant appears, the examination and interrogation must be conducted in a proper manner. Where the defendant was cross-examined on prejudicial matters not connected with the subject of the charge, the indictment was dismissed, with permission granted to resubmit the matter to another Grand Jury 223

§ 

(People v. Hirschberg, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 861). Similarly, in
