People v. Goldenberg, 110 Misc. 556, 181 N.Y.S. 921, where the defendant was overwhelmed with immaterial and vicious questions, the court dismissed, permitting resubmission to another Grand Jury. In People v. Blair, 33 N.Y. 

S. 2d 183, the court held that the defendant's rights had not been violated, where he had appeared pursuant to this section and was not allowed to give his testimony in narrative form. The District Attorney advised the defendant to answer the questions as posed, first, and that he could later add anything not covered. The court commented that the better practice would have been to permit the defendant to give his uninterrupted version of the story and then submit him to questioning. The District Attorney or the foreman should, in the interest of protecting the defendant's rights and of preserving a careful record, inform the defendant in substantially the following manner: “Mr. 

Witness, you are before this Grand Jury at your own free will and request. You have a right under the Constitution of this State not to be compelled to be a witness against yourself and accordingly you may not be forced to appear or testify. Any statement which you make will be recorded and may be used against you. Do you understand? Do you on your own volition wish to testify?"

In certain situations, it may be advantageous for the accused person to avail himself of the opportunity to testify before the Grand Jury investigating his alleged commission of a crime. If the charge is patently unsubstantiated, he may, by testifying, spare himself the financial expense and stigma of a needless criminal trial. Another instance in which the attorney may consider recommending that his client testify, is where the probability of obtaining the consideration, sympathy or mercy of the Grand Jury is so great that it would probably not indict. 

The following are the countervailing considerations which lead to the recommendation that, as a general rule, the prospective defendant ought not to appear: To avail himself of the privilege of testifying, he will have to execute 224

GRAND JURY 

§ 133 a waiver of immunity and his attorney will, of course, not be present to counsel him during the cross-examination conducted by the District Attorney; in addition to obtaining evidence sufficient for an indictment, the District Attorney will elicit information and testimony which may be used both on the People's case in chief and on cross-examination; as in the cases of any witness' statement, such testimony may produce minor contradictions or inconsistencies, subsequently to plague the defense in the course of trial. If the prosecuting attorney appears already to have formed a conclusion as to the client's guilt, or if there are other indications that an indictment is likely to be found, the client should forego his right to testify before the grand jury.

Sec. 132. Self-Incrimination and Immunity. These aspects are sufficiently important to warrant extended treatment and are fully explored in the next chapter. 

Sec. 133. Secrecy. "Every member of the Grand Jury must keep secret whatever he himself, or any other grand juror, may have said, or in what manner he, or any other grand juror, may have voted on a matter before them." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 258.) The oath taken by the jurors and their foreman (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 238, 239) further implements the privacy of the inquiry. In addition to the sections set forth above, Section 1783 of the Penal Law goes further by making it a crime to disclose Grand Jury proceedings: "A grand juror who, except when lawfully required by a court or officer, wilfully discloses: 1. Any evidence adduced before the grand jury; or 2. Anything which he himself or any other member of the grand jury said, or in what manner he or any other grand juror voted, upon any matter before them, is guilty of a misdemeanor." (See Application of Lundy, 208 Misc. 833, 148 N.Y.S. 2d 

658.) Section 1782 of the Penal Law makes it a misdemeanor for a grand juror to disclose, before the defendant is in custody, that an indictment has been found against 225

§ 

him. At common law, a grand juror was guilty as an accessory or principal to the crime when he disclosed to an accused the evidence presented (People v. Hulbut, 4 Denio 133).

Many reasons are advanced in support of the rule of secrecy of Grand Jury proceedings. The first, and they are not set forth in order of importance, is that if a person is unjustly accused, it would be grossly unfair to make public the fact that he is being investigated for the commission of a crime. The innocent person is thus spared the irreparable injury which would result from being publicly accused of a crime (People v. Kresel, 142 Misc. 88, 254 N.Y.S. 193).

A second reason for secrecy is that witnesses who testify against an individual accused of a crime are rendered more secure from possible retribution by those accused, and witnesses having this assurance and protection are more willing to cooperate with law enforcement officials in appearing and testifying than they might otherwise be. 

A third reason is that the possibility of attempts to influence the People's witnesses is reduced. The identity of the witness is concealed and the testimony given under oath is not publicly set forth to be tampered with. The withholding of what transpired before the Grand Jury reduces the facility with which false testimony may be concocted. 

The fourth advantage of secrecy is the minimizing of the possibility of escape.

The requirements of secrecy apply in all cases, whether or not the accused person has had a preliminary hearing. "It is provided that the proceedings of the Grand Jury must be kept secret, and this is so even in a case in which the accused person has not had a preliminary hearing." (People v. Keavin, 123 Misc. 56, 204 N.Y.S. 193.) Persons other than grand jurors are bound to secrecy. Section 1784 of the Penal Law makes it a misdemeanor for a Grand Jury stenographer to allow anyone other than the District Attorney to have a copy of the minutes or to read any portion of the minutes to one other than the District Attorney, except on court order (Matter of Osborne, 62 Misc. 226

GRAND JURY 

§ 133 

575, 117 N.Y. Supp. 169). It is likewise a misdemeanor for a judge, grand juror, District Attorney, clerk or other officer to disclose, before an accused is in custody, that an indictment has been returned against him (Penal Law, sec. 

1782). The District Attorney has custody of the stenographer's notes and minutes unless they are impounded, "but he shall not permit any other person to take a copy of the same, nor of any portion thereof, nor to read the same, or any portion thereof, except upon the written order of the court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 952-t.) However, note the following statement, in Matter of Osborne, supra: "An attorney, attending under circumstances where he is authorized to attend before a Grand Jury, may, upon leaving the Grand Jury room, lawfully state to anyone and everyone what testimony was given in the 

Grand Jury room while he was there."

There is no legal proscription, either by statute or case law, against a witness' revealing what transpired before the Grand Jury. "There is no secrecy imposed upon a witness before a Grand Jury either as to the fact of his being called before them or as to what he testified to." (People v. 

Naughton, 38 How. 430.) Thus, the court in Matter of 

Osborne, 62 Misc. 575, 117 N.Y. Supp. 169, stated: "A person subpoenaed to attend as a witness before a Grand Jury may, upon leaving the Grand Jury room, state to anybody and everybody what he testified to." It would seem that the reasons for secrecy and the rules effectuating that objective as to grand jurors should be equally applicable to witnesses, as the latter should have no more freedom of disclosure than a grand juror. The power and authority of the court to administer an oath of secrecy to a witness has never been the subject of adjudication in New York State. 

Although the oath of secrecy was not administered to Grand Jury witnesses in England, that was because of the rule that any person present before the Grand Jury was bound by law not to disclose what transpired (1 Chitty 

Criminal Law, 317). Other courts in this country have administered such an oath to witnesses, holding that this is 227

§ 

an inherent power of the court (State v. Fasset, 16 Conn. 

457). The power of the court to administer the oath of secrecy has been sustained in the Federal courts (Goodman v. United States, 108 F. 2d 516; United States v. 

Central Supply Ass'n. 34 F. Supp. 241).

The secrecy of Grand Jury minutes can be invaded under stated circumstances (People v. Miller, 257 N.Y. 54). The statute expressly provides that the testimony may be disclosed by a Grand Juror when required by the court "to ascertain whether it is consistent with that given by the witness before the court" or to disclose the testimony given before them by any person charged with perjury in testifying before the Grand Jury or on trial (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 259; People v. Goodheim, 188 App. Div. 148, 176 N.Y.S. 

468). It has been held that the oath of secrecy is not violated when a grand juror testifies that a witness refused to testify (People ex rel. Hacley v. Kelly, 121 Abb. Prac. 150, aff'd. 24 N.Y. 74).

Section 952-t of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that no one shall have access to the minutes, or the contents thereof, "except upon the written order of the court duly made after hearing the said District Attorney." 

Even on the consent of the District Attorney, the statute nevertheless requires a court order authorizing the release of the custody of the minutes or disclosure of their contents. Pursuant to this section, the court has jurisdiction to direct the release of Grand Jury testimony when the public interest in the secrecy of the proceedings will not be harmed (Matter of Quinn, 293 N.Y. 787). The courts accordingly have permitted Federal and State law enforcement officials to examine Grand Jury minutes (Matter of Sawpit Gymnasium, 60 N.Y.S. 2d 593; Matter of

Attorney General of New York State, 145 Misc. 331, 259 

N.Y.S. 313). In Matter of Attorney General of the United 

States, 160 Misc. 533, 291 N.Y.S. 5, a Grand Jury had investigated the affairs of a title company. The Federal Government, subsequently, applied to see the Grand Jury minutes for the purpose of preparing the trial of a criminal 228

GRAND JURY 

§ 133 case against the title company and some of their principals. 

The court there stated "that reasons which might well preclude an examination of such minutes by private individuals may well be abortive when raised against an inspection by public officials to enable them more efficiently to discharge the obligations of their office." It has been stated that such applications must not only be made in the public interest but must be made by a criminal law enforcement agency. The principle was extended in Application of Scro, 108 N.Y.S. 2d 305, permitting the District Attorney to release the minutes to the Police Commissioner for use at disciplinary proceedings against members of the police force who allegedly had afforded protection to a bookmaker. The court, in Application of King, 188 N.Y.S. 

2d 249, denied the application of the Immigration and Naturalization Service, because its application had not shown the nature and existence of the specific case or cases under investigation.

It is submitted that the relative facility with which the Federal Government can obtain Grand Jury minutes, even where immunity by the State government had been conferred upon those testifying (See Application of King, 188 

N.Y.S. 2d 249), casts grave doubt upon the rationale of the dual sovereignty theory enunciated by the Supreme Court in United States v. Feldman, supra, and followed in 

Knapp v. Schweitzer, supra. Witness' constitutional rights are protected only in the most legalistic sense when testimony before the State tribunal can be used to convict in a Federal proceeding.

Applications of Bar Associations for release of Grand 

Jury testimony have been denied on the ground that the investigation was of a civil rather than a criminal nature and would create precedent for the invasion of the rule of secrecy by other similar groups (Matter of Application of 

Bar Ass'n. of Erie County, 47 N.Y.S. 2d 213; People v. 

Ewald, 145 Misc. 331, 259 N.Y.S. 314). Quite clearly the court has no jurisdiction to place the minutes of the Grand Jury at the disposal of a litigant in a civil action for mali- 229

§ 

 cious prosecution (Dworetzky v. Monticello Smoked Fish 

Co., 256 App. Div. 772, 12 N.Y.S. 2d 270).

Sec. 134. Finding and Presentment of The Indictment. "An indictment cannot be found without the concurrence of at least twelve grand jurors. When so found, it must be endorsed 'a true bill', and the endorsement must be signed by the foreman of the Grand Jury, or by the grand juror designated to act as foreman during the temporary absence or disability of the foreman." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 268.) It has been held that the indictment is sufficiently endorsed in the following manner: "A true bill Geo C. 

Fisher, Foreman." (People v. Peck, 96 N.Y. 650.) "As an outward and visible sign that an indictment has in fact been found by the Grand Jury, the paper purporting to be an indictment must bear the signature of the foreman of the Grand Jury." (People v. Foster, 60 Misc. 3112 N.Y.S. 

706.) The indictment is valid, when properly indorsed by the foreman pursuant to this section, notwithstanding the lack of the signature or indorsement of the District Attorney required by Section 276 of the Code. The signing by the 

District Attorney is a clerical or ministerial act, hence the lack of that signature does not invalidate the indictment 

(People v. Lester, 267 App. Div. 537, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 409). 

An indictment that is regular and valid on its face must be presumed to have been validly returned by the Grand Jury in accordance with the requisites set forth in Sections 

268 and 272 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (People v. 

Smith, 128 N.Y.S. 2d 90, affirmed 283 App. Div. 775, 129 

N.Y.S. 2d 492). Notwithstanding this presumptive validity of the return, if the indictment is in fact not found, indorsed and presented in accordance with the requirements of these sections of the Code, it may be set aside (People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395). The Court of Appeals has held that the mandate of Section 268 does not require the presence of the twelve concurring grand jurors at every session of the Grand Jury, as long as "at least twelve of the Grand Jurors who voted to indict, hear all essential and critical evi- 230

GRAND JURY 

§ 134 dence." (People v. Sapperstein, 2 N.Y. 2d 210, cert. denied, 353 U.S. 946; People v. Brinkman, 286 App. Div. 889, 142 

N.Y.S. 2d 389, affirmed, 309 N.Y. 974.) For extended discussion, see the chapter on "Dismissing and Setting Aside Indictment."

The concept of the secrecy of Grand Jury proceedings does not preclude the defendant from the right to poll the jurors to ascertain whether this section has been complied with (People v. Shattuck, 6 Abb. N.C. 33). An indictment which is found in accordance with the above procedure must be presented by the foreman or acting foreman, in open court, and must be filed with the clerk, and remain in his office as a public record, but cannot be shown to any person other than a public officer, until the defendant has been arrested or has appeared (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 272).

The issue has arisen as to whether a quorum, sixteen persons, must be present when the indictment is presented in open court. In the widely cited case of People v. Herrmans, 69 Misc. 303, 125 N.Y. Supp. 143, the court held that the indictment was invalid because only fifteen jurors were in attendance when the indictment was presented and Sec. 

224 of the Code requires a quorum for the transaction of any business, including the return of an indictment. This case was overruled in People v. Brinkman, supra, where the court stated that the practice is changed so that an indictment need no longer be presented in the presence of the body or quorum of the grand jurors. In People v. Pizzimenta, 13 Misc. 2d 82, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 935, the court noted that Section 272 had at one time provided that the indictment must be presented by the foreman of the Grand Jury "in their presence." The words "in their presence" have since been deleted by amendment, thereby manifesting the legislative intent that the presenting of the indictment would not require the full quorum of sixteen grand jurors. 

The filing of the indictment is directory and omission to file does not avoid it (Dawson v. People, 25 N.Y. 399).

Until the indictment is filed with the court, the vote author- 231

§ 

izing it may at any time be reconsidered, but after it has been filed it is entirely within the control of the court, and the Grand Jury has no further authority over the proceeding. Thus, after the indictment has been returned the District Attorney has no authority to institute a new inquiry for the purpose of obtaining additional testimony to strengthen the case upon which the indictment is based (In re Morse, 42 Misc. 664, 87 N.Y.S. 721). This practice has been indulged in some jurisdictions, particularly where the testimony of an uncooperative witness is desired. The 

District Attorney may, in the course of presenting a matter to the Grand Jury, give consideration to calling a witness who is likely to be uncooperative. 

There is no requirement that the names of the witnesses be indorsed on the indictment, although at one time this was required by Section 271 of the Code. The repeal of this section was probably enacted to encourage witnesses to assist law enforcement by assuring their protection. It is now within the sound discretion of the court to disclose the names of the witnesses who testified before the Grand 

Jury (People v. DiCarlo, 161 Misc. 484, 292 N.Y.S. 252). 

Sec. 135. Grand Jury's Action Upon Failure to Indict. "If twelve grand jurors do not concur in finding an indictment, the depositions (and statements, if any) transmitted to them, must be returned to the court, with an endorsement thereon, signed by the foreman, or by the grand juror designated to act as foreman during the temporary absence or disability of the foreman, to the effect that the charge is dismissed." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 269.) This section together with the preceding section contemplate that the conclusion reached by a Grand Jury will be established as a matter of record whether or not an indictment is found. "If an indictment not be found, the deposition and statement must be returned, indorsed to the effect that the charge is dismissed." (Matter of Osborne, 68 Misc. 

597, 125 N.Y.S. 313.)

A literal and precise reading of Section 269 of the Code 232

GRAND JURY 

§ 136 reveals that it appears to apply only in a case where the defendant is first brought before a magistrate or where depositions and statements exist. Is it therefore a requirement that the court be apprised of the Grand Jury's failure to indict where no depositions or statements are before the Grand Jury? It has become the practice to follow the same procedure in both cases, whether or not depositions and statements are in existence. "Common sense and sound legal practice have, therefore, resulted in the invariable making of a public record when a Grand Jury has not indicted, after hearing. This is good public policy, and provides protection against unjustified repeated submission to a Grand Jury." (Application of Knight, 176 Misc. 635, 28 N.Y.S. 2d 353.) Section 222-d of the Code sets forth another consequence of the Grand Jury's failure to indict. 

That section provides: "within twenty-four hours after the discharge of any Grand Jury by any Supreme or County Court, the court shall cause every person confined in jail on a criminal charge, who shall not have been indicted, to be discharged without bail, unless satisfactory cause shall be shown for his further detention, or if the case may require, upon bail, until the meeting of the next Grand Jury in the county."

Sec. 136. Reconsideration After Dismissal of Indictment. 

A person against whom testimony is considered before a Grand Jury, is not in jeopardy, within the contemplation of the doctrine of "double jeopardy"; therefore, there is nothing within the body of the common law to prevent a Grand Jury or subsequent grand juries from considering evidence against an accused person after a "no-bill" was returned. The doctrine of double jeopardy not applying, nothing precluded the presentation to another Grand Jury after one had returned a no-bill or ignoramus (People v. 

Benson, 208 Misc. 138, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 563; People ex rel. 

Flinn v. Barr, 259 N.Y. 104; 4 Black. Comm. [Wend. ed. 

1854] 305). This principle has been reaffirmed by the

United States Supreme Court, insofar as the regulation 233

§ 

of Federal procedure is concerned (United States v. 

Thompson, 251 U.S. 407, 40 Sup. Ct. 289; United States v. 

Warner, 26 F. Supp. 333).

New York sets forth the effect of a prior dismissal by statute and provides that the dismissal of a charge does not preclude subsequent consideration, providing the proper judge directs that the charge be resubmitted. "The dismissal of the charge, whether it be a felony or misdemeanor, does not, however, prevent its being again submitted to a Grand Jury *** if the County Judge of the county or Justice of the Supreme Court so directs. But without such direction, it cannot be again submitted or further prosecuted." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 270.) "This section is designed to provide a convenient check upon the practice which now prevails of repeated applications to the Grand Jury for an indictment where it has been already dismissed." (Report of Commissioners on Practice and Pleadings, p. 138; Dec. 31, 1849.)

If the District Attorney desires to resubmit the charge to the Grand Jury after it has been dismissed, he makes a motion requesting the court's direction to resubmit the matter to another Grand Jury. This motion is supported by an affidavit of the District Attorney setting forth the facts and reasons why the court should order such resubmission. There is no limit to the number of times the court may order a resubmission, but a new court order is mandatory for each resubmission (People v. Ryback, 3 

N.Y. 2d 467; People v. Lynch 33 Hun 664; People v. Clements, 5 N.Y. Cr. 288). The resubmission of a criminal charge is not a perfunctory action granted and rubberstamped by the court at the request of the District Attorney. In People v. Neidhart, 35 Misc. 191 71 N.Y.S. 591, the court dismissed an indictment returned by a Grand Jury hearing the case upon an order of resubmission predicated upon an affidavit that the prior Grand Jury had misunderstood the law. The court stated: "While the court has power to permit the charges to be again submitted to the Grand Jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 270), such power 234

GRAND JURY 

§ 136 should be sparingly and discriminatingly used. It is a practice that ought not to be encouraged nor granted pro forma. The court should act judicially, and permit such resubmissions only when facts are presented which warrant such action." (People v. Besser, 207 Misc. 692, 140 N.Y.S. 

2d 803.) Likewise, the court in People v. Dziegiel, 140 Misc. 

145, 250 N.Y. Supp. 743, enunciated the principle that the court should not grant permission to resubmit a matter unless there is new evidence or the first Grand Jury hearing has been defective or incomplete because of fraud, mistake, ignorance or negligence. In People v. Both, 118 Misc. 

414, 193 N.Y.S. 591, a Grand Jury had been in session for two months and examined twenty-seven witnesses. The 

District Attorney's affidavit stated in a general manner that additional evidence would be produced through other witnesses, but there was no statement specifying or particularizing the nature of the proposed evidence or additional testimony. The court, granting the defendant's motion to dismiss the indictment, stated: "If the testimony of those witnesses did not satisfy the Grand Jury that there was sufficient evidence against those defendants to justify a prosecution, the matter should have there ended, without further consideration, unless facts were presented which would authorize an order resubmitting the matter to the 

Grand Jury." (See People v. Karlovsky, 147 Misc. 56, 263 

N.Y.S. 293.)

It has been held that this section is intended to indicate a course of conduct for the District Attorney, and was not intended as a limitation upon the court's common law and inherent power to order a resubmission (People v. Besser, 207 Misc. 692, 140 N.Y.S. 2d 195; People ex rel. Besser v. 

Ruthhazer, 3 App. Div. 2d 137, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 803). Hence, the judge to whom the finding of a no true bill had been returned, has the power independently of, and without regard to, Section 270 of the Code, to order resubmission (People v. Lebow, 207 Misc. 762, 192 N.Y.S. 2d 625).

An order of resubmission is not necessary where a record of dismissal was not filed with the court (People 235

§ 

v. Stecker, 141 Misc. 417, 252 N.Y.S. 187; People ex rel. 

Savarese v. Foster, 83 N.Y.S. 2d 583). This section has no applicability when the indictment has been found and quashed by the court (People v. Lenoci, 13 Misc. 2d 789, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 332). An order directing resubmission is not necessary where the charge is different from that considered by a prior Grand Jury, notwithstanding that the both charges may have arisen out of the same underlying incident or transaction. This is consistent with the case law under the doctrine of double jeopardy. Thus, in People v. 

Warren, 109 N.Y. 615, an order for resubmission was held unnecessary where the Grand Jury charged the defendant with manslaughter for the death of a victim, even though the Grand Jury previously had failed to indict for assault. 

In People v. Nelson, 298 N.Y. 272, the court held that the dismissal of a charge of criminal negligence in the operation of an automobile did not preclude a subsequent misdemeanor charge of leaving the scene of an accident, although no order of resubmission had been obtained, and the evidence originally heard may have supported the latter charge. An order of resubmission is not requisite where the matter is not dismissed but is indorsed by the foreman to be prosecuted in a court of special sessions (People v. Kelly, 140 Misc. 377, 250 N.Y.S. 610; People v. 

Ryback, 3 N.Y. 2d 467).

A defendant who is charged with crime by an indictment that has not properly been resubmitted after a prior dismissal, may attack it by a motion to dismiss or may raise the issue of the legality of his detention by writ of habeas corpus (People v. Barr, 140 Misc. 422, 251 N.Y. Supp. 116).

An order granting leave to resubmit is not necessary when the original indictment is not dismissed or set aside but is superseded (People v. Sutherland, 179 Misc. 1020, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 651).

Sec. 137. Power to Return Superseding Indictment. After the Grand Jury finds a bill of indictment and before jeopardy attaches, the Grand Jury, on its own initiative or 236

GRAND JURY 

§ 138 at the suggestion of the District Attorney, has the power both under the common law and under Section 292-a of the Code to return a second indictment for the same offense against the same person (People v. Stafford, 123 Misc. 

488, 205 N.Y.S. 793). This may be done to correct a factual, procedural or legal defect in the first indictment, or the second or superseding indictment may be returned for the purpose of adding other counts to the first bill (People v. 

Benson, 208 Misc. 138, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 563). When the superseding indictment is returned by the same Grand Jury it may be based on the evidence elicited when the prior indictment was considered. A new Grand Jury, however, must hear evidence sufficient to substantiate the indictment.

Section 292-a of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "If there be at any time pending against the defendant, two indictments for the same offense; or two indictments for the same matter, although charged as different offenses, the indictment first found shall be deemed to be superseded by such second indictment, and shall be set aside." (See People v. Farrell, 20 Misc. 213, 45 N.Y.S. 911.)

The defense must move to set aside the first indictment if it is superseded, as Section 292-a is not self-executing (People v. Sloan, 175 Misc. 618, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 381; People v. 

Monroe Oyer and Terminer, 20 Wend. 108).

Sec. 138. Presentment. It has become a common practice for grand juries, upon concluding an investigation or upon final adjournment, to make a report or statement to the court about the character or conduct of public officers, or concerning the condition or situation of the community; such reports have, on occasion, criticized the conduct of named individuals. This statement or report which does not formally charge anyone with the commission of a crime has been called a "presentment." At common law, a presentment was of a distinctly different character. Originally, indictments were of a formal nature initiated at the instance of the King, while the presentment was an in- 237

§ 

formal accusation made by the jurors on their own knowledge and observation, and it was regarded as the instrument upon which a formal indictment was to be later framed (Mack v. People, 82 N.Y. 235; Matter of Funston, 133 Misc. 620, 233 N.Y. Supp. 81; Matter of Osborne, 68 

Misc. 597, 125 N.Y. Supp. 317). The distinction between a presentment, as contemplated at common law, and the indictment has been obliterated in New York. As a matter of practice, the District Attorney draws indictments either before or after the vote of the Grand Jury, and the Grand 

Jury no longer prepares an informal instrument similar to the common law presentment. The term "presentment" is used throughout the Code of Criminal Procedure as indicating the act or process performed in handing up the indictment (See Matter of Osborne, 68 Misc. 597, 125 

N.Y.S. 313).

There is no express statutory authority for rendering a report to the court. In Application of Quinn, 5 Misc. 2d 

166 N.Y.S. 2d 418, it was stated that the failure of the

Legislature to provide for the filing of such report does not negate that power, since the Grand Jury has today all the power it had at common law, absent contrary intention (Constitution, N.Y., Article I, sec. 14), and at common law it had and enforced the power to inquire and report with respect to matters of public interest or concern. (See 

Goebel and Naughton, Law Enforcement in Colonial New 

York 361; Kuh, The Grand Jury "Presentment": Foul 

Blow or Fair Play?, 55 Col. L. Rev. 1110.) The only appellate authority passing upon the power of the Grand Jury to render a report is Jones v. People, 101 App. Div. 55, 92 

N.Y.S. 275. The report in that case, which criticized a

County Board of Supervisors and its clerk for nonfeasance of their duties, was sustained in reliance upon Sections 

253 and 254 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: "The 

Grand Jury must inquire, into the wilful and corrupt misconduct in office of public officers of every description, in the county." The court said: "we may assume that these powers are conferred for some purpose. Official inquiry 238

GRAND JURY 

§ 138 intends either official action or official report." The court held that the report was proper where the investigation revealed inefficiency, carelessness or neglect that required correction but did not justify indictment. The court, in 

Application of Lundy, 208 Misc. 833, 148 N.Y.S. 2d 658, said the Jones decision "remains unimpeached by superior judicial authority, undisturbed by constitutional and legislative authority and not disavowed by the court that decided it." The argument has been advanced that since Penal 

Law, Section 1820, subdivision 77, provides that it is a crime to engage in wilful and wrongful misconduct in public office and the Grand Jury has the power to investigate such matters by reason of Section 223 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the provisions of Section 253 should be read as conferring some additional power beyond that of mere inquiry, i.e. the power to report, so as to give meaning to that section of the code rather than assume that it is surplusage or redundancy (Kuh, The Grand Jury "Pre sentment: Fair Blow or Foul Play?, supra).

The most cogent argument against the power of the Grand Jury to render a statement or report is that contained in the dissent in the Jones case, supra; that is, the danger in permitting a Grand Jury to charge wrongdoing without affording the individual concerned the opportunity to reply or rebut the attack in a judicial forum. The courts of our State have placed some bounds upon the report power of the Grand Jury. The first conclusion one can draw is that the reports are permissible when they relate to public employees and officials (Matter of Healy, 161 

Misc. 582, 293 N.Y.S. 584). See People v. Doe, 176 Misc. 

943, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 648, where a portion of the report was excised because the person criticized was criticized in his capacity as an individual and private citizen. Judge 

Schweitzer, in Application of The Third September, 1958 

Grand Jury, 193 N.Y.S. 2d 553, in a decision analyzing the prior cases on the subject, held that there is no authority to file a report critical of persons in the television industry. 

The Grand Jury in that case did not name specific indi- 239

$ 

viduals; however, it was noted that a report inimical by innuendo is just as injurious and objectionable. "Where private citizens are involved the function of the Grand Jury ends when it determines that no crime has been committed."

The court in Matter of Knight, 176 Misc. 635, 28 N.Y.S. 

2d 353, recognized the Grand Jury's power to report in regard to an individual in a limited situation. Accompanying the return of a "no true bill" was a report stating that the complaint was groundless, and the Grand Jury requested that the report be transmitted to the Appellate Division for their consideration of the attorney who instigated the groundless report. Notwithstanding the Jones' case and Application of Quinn, 5 Misc. 2d 466, 166 N.Y.S. 

2d 418, note the language of Clay v. Wickens, 7 Misc. 2d 84, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 534: "In this judicial district, it has been recognized as the law for twenty-years that when a Grand Jury in the course of investigation into the alleged corrupt misconduct in office of public officials fails to return any indictment, a report criticizing the conduct of such officials is improper as it affords the person so criticized no opportunity to answer the charges made." Other courts have criticized the Jones' case and found other reasons to quash reports. "So long as they are confined to matters of general interest, they are regarded as harmless, even though a waste of time and effort, and after the ephemeral notice of the day has passed they are allowed a peaceful rest." (Matter of Osborne, 68 Misc. 597, 125 N.Y.S. 313; see 

Matter of Heffernan, 125 N.Y.S. 737; Clay v. Wickens, 7 

Misc. 2d 84, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 534. Matter of Woodbury, 155 

N.Y.S. 851.)

Since the primary function of the Grand Jury is to determine whether crimes have been committed rather than to render reports, the authority to render a report or statement exists only if the Grand Jury's investigation was initiated with the objective of ascertaining whether a crime had been committed. The report can then be rendered after the Grand Jury concludes that a crime had not 240

GRAND JURY 

§ 138 been committed, but cannot be rendered if the Grand Jury originally investigates for the purpose of rendering a report. In Application of Schiro, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 423, a report was expunged where the Grand Jury issued a report on its findings after the inspection of a hospital. The court held that the Grand Jury was not charged with the duty of inspecting that institution and such inspection had no relation to an investigation of the commission of a crime. In 

Moore v. Delaney, 180 Misc. 844, 45 N.Y.S. 2d 951, where the Grand Jury sought to render a report on the fiscal affairs of the Legislature, the court said that since the Legislature, as contrasted to the individual members thereof, could not commit a crime, there was no power to report on the fiscal affairs of the legislative body (See 

People v. Talum, 60 Misc. 311, 112 N.Y.S. 36).

If the Grand Jury exceeds its power in rendering a report, the court has the power to refuse to receive the statement (Clay v. Wickens, supra; Matter of Crosby, 126 

Misc. 250, 213 N.Y.S. 86), or the court may receive the report and on motion of the aggrieved party made before the judge who accepted and filed the report, request an order that the report be quashed, set aside or expunged (Matter of Schiro, supra). Although the setting aside of the report removes the official approval or recognition of the contents, it cannot accomplish the retraction or erasure of the effect which such report may have had on the minds and ears of the public.

A third approach is that adopted in application of the 

Third September 1958 Grand Jury, supra, where a report was not received but was impounded and sealed by the court.

CHAPTER 11 THE PRIVILEGE AGAINST SELF- INCRIMINATION AND IMMUNITY Sec. 139. Introduction Sec. 140. Scope of the Privilege Sec. 141. Privilege is Personal as to Testimonial Compulsion Sec. 142. Who is Arbiter of the Claim of Privilege 

Sec. 143. Waiver of Immunity

Sec. 144. Privilege in Grand Jury Proceeding Sec. 145. Immunity Sec. 139. Introduction. Article I, Section 6 of the New York 

State Constitution provides that no person "shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself." 

Section 10 of the Code of Criminal Procedure sets forth the substance of this constitutional right. The reader's attention is directed to the fact that the United States Constitution does not confer the right to refuse to testify in a State tribunal, either by virtue of the Fifth or of the Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution (Adamson v. California, 332 U.S. 46).

Sec. 140. Scope of the Privilege. A witness clearly has the right to invoke this privilege if the testimony sought would itself be incriminating. The witness has a further right, it has been held, to refuse to testify if the answer may lead to incriminating evidence or, in the favored judicial vernacular, if the testimony is a "clue to a link in the chain of guilt." (Doyle v. Hofstader, 257 N.Y. 244; People v. Priori, 164 N.Y. 459; Bradley v. O'Hare, 2 App. Div. 2d 436, 156 242

PRIVILEGE AGAINST SELF-INCRIMINATION § 141 

N.Y.S. 2d 533.) Thus, it has been held that an immunity statute, which must be co-extensive with the privilege, is unconstitutional if it is limited only to the subsequent use of the compelled testimony (Taylor v. Forbes, 143 N.C. 

219; People v. O'Brien, 176 N.Y. 253; See, Counselman v.

Hitchcock, 142 U.S. 547). The non-party witness has no privilege to refuse to be subpoenaed or refuse to take the stand or obey a subpoena, since the privilege does not arise until the questions are asked (In re Weiner, 183 Misc. 267, 49 N.Y.S. 2d 199; Schiffman v. Bleakley, 46 N.Y.S. 2d 353).

The privilege extends to the books, papers and property of the witness (People v. Hunter, 139 Misc. 270, 249 N.Y.S. 66).

Sec. 141. Privilege is Personal as to Testimonial Compul sion. The privilege against self-incrimination has, historically, been one of freedom from testimonial compulsion, i.e. being required by judicial process to give oral testimony and to produce in court under judicial order documents and other objects. Thus the accused may be required without breach of the privilege to be fingerprinted (People v. 

Sallow, 100 Misc. 447, 165 N.Y.S. 915); photographed, physically examined, have blood samples taken (State v. 

Cram, 176 Ore. 577, 160 P. 2d 283); compelled to rise for identification (People v. Gardner, 144 N.Y. 119). See Holt v. United States, 218 U.S. 245, where Mr. Justice Holmes stated: "the prohibition of compelling a man in a criminal court to be a witness against himself is a prohibition of the use of physical or moral compulsion to exact communications from him, not an exclusion of his body as evidence, when it may be material." The privilege is personal to the witness and does not extend to corporations or agents in their behalf (Klein v. Taylor, 52 N.Y.S. 2d 259; Bleakley v. Schlesinger 294 N.Y. 312). Nor may the corporate officer refuse to produce corporate records on the ground that it may incriminate such officer (Application of Inter-City 

Associates, 142 N.Y.S. 2d 412, appeal dismissed, 285 App. 

Div. 1183, 141 N.Y.S. 2d 263, reversed, 308 N.Y. 1044). 243

§ 

 Sec. 142. Who is the Arbiter of the Claim of Privilege? The witness by declining to answer on this ground is the initial arbiter of the legitimacy of the claim; however, the court in a technical sense is the final judge of the good faith of the invocation of the privilege (People v. Forbes, 143 N.Y. 

219. Matter of Cappeau, 198 App. Div. 357, 190 N.Y.S. 452).

In this era of extensive governmental regulations, it is not too broad a generalization to say that any relevant question may tend to incriminate the witness. Since the practice of having the witness produce the possible incriminatory evidence in camera has been regarded as violative of the witness' rights, it has been held that although the court is the judge of the substance or merit to the assertion of the privilege, a presumption exists in favor of the witness' judgment which will be sustained unless it is so "perfectly evident and manifest" that there is no legitimacy to the claim of privilege that all argument is precluded (Matter of Levy, 255 N.Y. 223; Triangle Publications, Inc., v. Ferrare, 4 App. Div. 2d 591, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 128. See Hoffman v.

United States, 341 U.S. 479). The court in People v. Rich ter, 82 Misc. 96, 43 N.Y.S. 2d 114, went behind the witness' assertion of the privilege and held that the claim was remote and without merit.

Sec. 143. Waiver of Immunity. The privilege against selfincrimination, like all personal privileges, may be waived, either expressly or by so testifying about a transaction that further evidence would not be incriminating. A witness, as distinguished from an accused person, as will be discussed hereafter, does not waive the privilege by taking the witness stand, nor is the privilege waived when the witness merely testifies about the subject matter in issue, but only when he gives testimony that actually tends to be incriminating (Southbridge Finishing Co. v. Golding, 

208 Misc. 846, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 911, aff'd, 2 App. Div. 2d 882, 157 N.Y.S. 2d 898). In People v. Forbes, 143 N.Y. 219, the

Grand Jury investigated a death due to the release of gas in a college dining hall. A student who had testified that 244

PRIVILEGE AGAINST SELF-INCRIMINATION § 143 

he had had no connection with the transaction on the evening of the banquet, was held not to have waived the privilege to refuse to answer the question of who placed the gas containers beneath the dining hall, since his prior answers had not been as to incriminating facts (Siegel v. Crawford, 292 N.Y. 651). From the viewpoint of the legal adviser, it serves no purpose to counsel a witness to testify as to parts of a transaction that may be incriminating in the hope that the witness will succeed in halting at the brink of waiver.

Waiver of the privilege is confined to the proceeding in which it is asserted, and it can be reasserted in a subsequent proceeding (Burdy v. Conroy, 182 Misc. 476, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 

871). Thus, a witness may testify before the Grand Jury and assert the privilege as to the same matters when called upon trial. If the witness claims his privilege upon the prior proceeding and then testifies, no comment can be made as to the prior claim of privilege (People v. Luckman, 254 App. Div. 694, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 864). In People ex rel.

Hofsaes v. Warden, 302 N.Y. 403, the witness was a member of the police department who had waived his privilege in the earlier proceeding. He resigned and then attempted to reassert the privilege when subsequently called before another session of the Grand Jury. The court held that the later investigation was ancillary to the first and they would both be regarded as one continuous proceeding, for which the witness had already waived his claim of self-incrimination.

The doctrine of waiver as applied to the accused person is necessarily different from the foregoing because the rights of one accused, in this regard, are unlike the rights of the non-party witness. The accused person has the option not to take the witness stand, and may not be called to the stand by the prosecutor (People v. Chlebowy, 191 

Misc. 768, 78 N.Y.S. 2d 596). The defendant's failure to testify does not create any presumption against him, nor may the prosecutor remark or comment upon such failure 245

§ 

to take the stand (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 393; People v. 

Manning 278 N.Y. 40; People v. Forte, 277 N.Y. 440).

As all defense counsel are keenly aware, the defendant taking the witness stand waives his right to plead the privilege against self-incrimination, both as to inquiries relevant to the charge against him and to questions of other criminal acts which affect the witness' credibility (People v. Casey, 72 N.Y. 393; People v. Tice, 131 N.Y. 

651). The Court of Appeals in People v. Sorge, 301 N.Y. 

198, stated, in a prosecution for abortion where the defendant had been interrogated by the District Attorney about other abortions: "There can, of course be no doubt as to the propriety of cross-examining a defendant concerning the commission of other specific criminal or immoral acts.” 

The People are not foreclosed from inquiry because the offenses or acts are similar in nature and character to the crime for which the defendant may be standing trial. (See 

People v. Brown, 284 N.Y. 753; People v. Jones, 297 N.Y. 

459.) However, there are limitations on inquiry concerning other crimes, as in People v. Redmond, 265 App. Div. 307, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 727, where the District Attorney had probed deeply into other arsons in cross-examining a defendant tried for arson. The court felt that the inquiry was designed to prove that his commission of such acts in the past established the commission of the crime for which he was on trial. (See People v. Shapiro, 308 N.Y. 453.) As is apparent from the foregoing, the decision as to whether a client with a history of prior criminal acts should take the stand is a difficult one, depending upon the facts and personality in each case. If such a defendant does take the stand, defense counsel should elicit in the most innocuous manner, the commission of such crimes on the defendant's direct examination rather than allow the prosecutor on cross-examination to dramatically and more forcefully introduce such testimony. 

Sec. 144. Privilege in Grand Jury Proceeding. It is well settled that one is entitled to the same constitutional and 246

PRIVILEGE AGAINST SELF-INCRIMINATION 

§ 144 statutory protection in a Grand Jury proceeding as at the trial, and such a proceeding is a "criminal case" or "action" within those provisions (People v. Dudish, 5 Misc. 2d 856, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 810; People ex rel. Taylor v. Forbes, 143 N.Y. 

219). A witness who is not the defendant or the subject of the investigation must claim his privilege or he will be compelled to testify, and any testimony elicited may be used against him.

A person who is the subject or target of the investigation, the prospective defendant, is not required to claim his privilege (People v. DeFeo, 308 N.Y. 595: People v. 

Bermel. 71 Misc. 356, 128 N.Y.S. 524). Any testimony given by such subject in violation of the immunity constitutes illegal evidence, which is regarded as so prejudicial that it, in and of itself, is sufficient ground upon which to set aside an indictment. In People v. Singer, 18 Abb. N.C. 96, the defendant was indicted for murder, first degree. After being cautioned by the District Attorney, the grand jurors questioned him. The court held that the witness had been compelled to give evidence against himself, and the indictment was quashed. A Grand Jury investigation, proceeding ostensibly against John Smith but actually aimed at the defendant witness, was held to be a violation of the witness' constitutional right. The court thus held that an indictment for perjury based upon the testimony given in such a hearing was invalid, because the oath could not be legally administered (People v. Gillette, 126 App. Div. 665, 111 N.Y. Supp. 133).

The Court of Appeals, in People v. Steuding, 6 N.Y. 2d 

214, construed the effect of the 1953 immunity statute, Penal Law, section 2447, upon this doctrine. The court held that the mandate of that statute, requiring a witness to plead his privilege to receive immunity does not apply to a defendant or a prospective defendant called as a witness. This constitutionally-conferred privilege is deemed violated even though the witness does not assert the privilege and the right may not be taken away or cut down by 247

§ 

statute. The defendant or target called before the Grand 

Jury in violation of this right does not obtain an immunity for the substantive crime committed, and a Grand Jury other than the one before whom he had been so examined has the power to indict for the substantive crime (People v. Freistadt, 6 App. Div. 2d 1053, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 633; People v. Truesdell, 259 App. Div. 282 18 N.Y.S. 2d 947). But compare People v. Steuding, supra, where the court stated: "Whether it also cloaks him with an immunity, a prosecution for the crime for which he has been indicted is, however, a question with which we are not now concerned. Its answer must await a case in which it is presented." 

The District Attorney, as a matter of practice, usually requests that persons who testify before the Grand Jury, if there is the remotest possibility that they may be defendants, execute a waiver of immunity pursuant to Penal Law, Section 2446. The attorney advising his client as to his right to plead the privilege or to decline to sign a waiver of immunity, should be alert to the fact that certain governmental privileges may be withdrawn from a witness who pleads his right to refuse to answer or waive immunity. Section 22 of the Election Law provides that an officer of a political party who refuses to testify or sign a waiver of immunity loses certain rights, including his disqualification from holding any party or public office for a period of five years. Article 1, Sec. 6, of the New York

State Constitution provides for similar sanctions. See also 

Sections 103-a and b of the General Municipal Law, Gold way v. Board of Higher Ed., 178 Misc. 1023, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 

34; Cohen v. Hurley, 195 N.Y.S. 2d 990, for a discussion of the right of an attorney to plead the self-incrimination privilege or refuse to sign an immunity waiver (Matter of 

Grae, 292 N.Y. 428; Matter of Ellis, 282 N.Y. 435). 

Sec. 145. Immunity. A witness is privileged to refuse to answer questions that may tend to incriminate him unless he is relieved from the risk of prosecution. Then, the reason 248

for the privilege is removed and the claim of constitutional immunity has no merit (Doyle v. Hofstader, 257 N.Y. 

244). The termination of the liability for prosecution may come about after the witness has been convicted, acquitted, or when prosecution has been barred by the Statute of 

Limitations (8 Wigmore, Evidence, Secs. 2279-2281). The constitutional right to refuse to testify on the ground that the evidence sought would be self-incriminating may be divested by the People when, pursuant to statute, the witness is granted immunity from prosecution (People v. 

Sapperstein, 2 N.Y. 2d 210, cert. denied, 353 U.S. 946; Doyle v. Hofstader, supra). Immunity is the exculpation of the witness as to any transaction, matter or thing about which he testifies. The immunity conferred must be coextensive with the constitutional and statutory privilege, and afford absolute immunity from future prosecution for the offense to which the question relates and for any fact or act touching upon which the witness is required to testify (Lewisohn v. O'Brien, 176 N.Y. 253; People v. Riley, 129

Misc. 373; People v. DeFeo, 308 N.Y. 595). The People are precluded not only from using the testimony, but, in addition, the witness cannot be punished for any crime growing out of the matters concerning which he testifies. 

The use of immunity statutes is an important weapon in obtaining evidence "from sources which would otherwise be barricaded behind the privilege of self-incrimination." (People v. Riela, 14 Misc. 2d 213, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 873, affirmed 

9 App. Div. 2d 481, 195 N.Y.S. 2d 558.) It is particularly potent to elicit evidence in the investigation of organized crime or conspiracies, where the mutual silence protected by this right can be an impenetrable shield for the co-conspirators. The People's power to strip a member of the group of this power can be the key to the best source of evidence. In some cases the restraint of the group may be so strong that it will not permit the witness to talk even after the conferral of immunity (People v. Riela, supra). The major objection raised in opposition to the immunity concept is the questionable morality of bargaining with a 249

§ 

criminal, bartering his freedom from prosecution for his testimony against other persons. However, it does not seem wrong to permit public prosecutors to determine the relative importance of the prosecution of certain individuals at the cost of the sacrifice of the conviction of the immunized witness. It clearly is no worse than one of the most effective investigative and enforcement tools-the use of informants, persons whose eyes and ears are closest to the criminal act.

Some object that the witness compelled to testify may be subjected to obloquy or disgrace. There being no constitutional right to decline to answer on this basis, the granting of immunity does not divest the witness of a right previously possessed (People v. Kelly, 24 N.Y. 74). The last objection is the one most deserving of consideration, that is the possibility of the witness receiving immunity and the testimony proving valueless. The prosecutor must be vigilant to this possibility. Immunity is not normally conferred upon a major criminal, but upon an underling who has played a minor role in the transaction, and then only if the prosecutor is convinced by his investigation that the witness' truthful testimony could provide the evidence sought. The possibilities in calling such a witness are: (a) He may tell the true facts and cooperate in the giving of evidence; (b) he may refuse to talk after the tender of immunity, in which case he may be cited for contempt; in this event the witness receives no immunity since he has not given evidence. (People v. Riela, supra); (c) the witness may lie. If the witness testifies, although falsely, he obtains immunity, and the statute provides that he may be prosecuted for perjury (Penal Law, sec. 2447, subd. 2); the initial questioning should be simple, and such that if answered falsely, the prosecutor has the evidence with which to prove a perjury; (d) the more sophisticated witness, rather than testify falsely, will double-talk and so qualify and equivocate that the evidence is of no value to the People. This witness also obtains immunity and remains liable for contempt (Penal Law, sec. 2447, subd. 2). 250

Prior to 1953, the statutes conferring immunity provided that in such cases a witness could not refuse to testify on the grounds of self-incrimination "but no person shall be prosecuted or subjected to any penalty or forfeiture for or on account of any transaction, matter, or thing concerning which he may testify or produce evidence." (Penal 

Law, secs. 380, 381, 554; People v. Sharp, 107 N.Y. 427.)

Under these statutes, the witness, if under compulsion to testify, automatically received immunity by testifying, though he did not assert or claim his privilege and without any affirmative act conferring immunity. One of the difficulties with such legislation was that witnesses were, without choice or option by the prosecution, excused from prosecution.

In 1953, the Legislature revised the immunity procedure and enacted Section 2447 of the Penal Law. This is the comprehensive section governing immunity procedure in regard to all statutes which authorize the granting of immunity. It was enacted to correct the deficiencies in the prior procedure (Report of Crime Commission, 1953 Leg. 

Doc. No. 68). One of its most important effects was to eliminate the automatic and sometimes unintended immunity baths (People v. Feinberg, 193 N.Y.S. 2d 937). The statutes authorizing the grant of immunity were accordingly amended to provide it can be conferred only in the manner prescribed by that section. It is as indispensable for the attorney advising a witness, as it is for the District Attorney, to be conversant with this procedure. 

Immunity can only be granted where authorized "by express provision of statute." (Doyle v. Hofstader, 257 

N.Y. 244.) There are forty-six statutes and two constitutional provisions so providing: Const., N.Y., Art. II, sec. 3 (offer or promise to bribe a public official); sec. 5 (giving of a free pass by a corporation to a public officer); Ag. & 

Mark. L., sec. 33; Banking L., sec. 38; Canal L., sec. 134; 

C.P.A., secs. 789, 1219; Conserv. L. sec. 8, 955; Debtor and

Creditor L., sec. 4, subd. 5 (examination of assignor for benefit of creditors); id., sec. 16, subd. 2 (witness in assign- 251

§ 

ment proceeding); Elec. L., sec. 334, subd. 5 (campaign funds); Exec. L., sec. 295, subd. 7 (discrimination); Gen. 

Bus. L., sec. 345 (monopolies), sec. 359 (security fraud); 

Gen. Corp. L., secs. 131, 170; Indian L., sec. 60; Ins. L. sec. 

25; Justice Court Act, sec. 486; Labor L., sec. 708, subd. 4; 

Penal Law, sec. 81(a) (abortion), sec. 166 (anarchy), secs. 

380-81 (bribery of labor representatives), sec. 395, sec. 

439 (corruption of agents, employees or servants), sec. 

584 (conspiracy), sec. 671, subd. 2 (political contributions), sec. 713 (use of disguises), sec. 737 (dueling), sec. 770 (election offenses), sec. 996 (gambling), sec. 1200 (receiving rebates on life insurance), sec. 1256 (kidnapping), sec. 

1435, subd. 9, sec. 1472 (disturbing the peace), sec. 1716 (prize fighting), sec. 1752, subd. a (narcotic possession), sec. 1787 (resisting process), sec. 1906 (discharging fire arms), sec. 2038 (unlawfully affixing advertising and malicious trespass), sec. 2052, subd. 2 (stealing, mutilating, concealing testamentary instrument), sec. 2097 (riots), sec. 2443 (buying, selling, receiving chose in action illegally), Pub. Serv. L., sec. 20; Real Prop. L., sec. 442 (e) 

(7); Second Class Cities L., sec. 243; Unconsol. L., sec. 

6464(2) (Port Authority). 

The witness must refuse to answer on the ground that his answer may tend to incriminate him. The importance of asserting and claiming the privilege against selfincrimination cannot be overly stressed. This should be done in a precise manner, reciting the constitutional and statutory authority upon which the privilege is invoked. 

Absent the invocation of this specific privilege, the witness will not receive immunity (People v. DeFeo, 308 N.Y. 595; 

People v. Dooling, 14 Misc. 2d 907, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 618). The issue has arisen as to whether the requirement of invoking the privilege applies to a person who is the object of the investigation. As noted above, it was held in People v. 

Steuding, 6 N.Y. 2d 214, that the enactment of Section 2447 cannot be construed as sanctioning the calling of a potential defendant and placing the onus upon such witness to plead the privilege. The defendant has the same right not 252

to be sworn as he did prior to the enactment of the section (People v. Freistadt, 6 App. Div. 2d 1053, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 

633). Clearly, a defendant may be called as a witness pursuant to this section and, if granted complete immunity, his rights are in no way infringed (People v. Feinberg, 193 N.Y.S. 2d 937; Barbuto v. Silver, 186 N.Y.S. 2d 1018; 

Dunham v. Ottinger, 243 N.Y. 423).

The order granting immunity must be made by a competent authority, as defined in the statute (Penal Law, sec. 2447, subd. 3). There are five such competent authorities: (a) a court or magistrate before whom a witness is called, other than in a Grand Jury proceeding, when the prosecuting attorney requests the conferral of immunity; (b) the court before whom a witness is called in a civil proceeding to which the State or a political subdivision, department, agency or officer thereof is a party, when the Attorney General expressly requests the granting of immunity; (c) by the Grand Jury, when the prosecuting attorney expressly requests such an order; (d) by a legislative committee or temporary state commission if a majority of the full membership of such body concurs; (e) by the head of a state department or agency, a commissioner, deputy or other officer, upon twenty-four hours prior written notice to the Attorney General, and to the appropriate District Attorney. The failure or neglect to notify the District Attorney will not deprive such witness of immunity.

The attorney counseling the witness must be sure that the authority conferring immunity has the power so to do and, further, that the proper officers or agencies have either requested the immunity or have been notified thereof. The authority granting the immunity prior to the tender thereof should, beyond complying with any notification required by statute, take the precaution of consulting the District Attorney or attorneys likely to have information about, or an interest in, the witness, such as the District Attorney of the county where the witness resides or may be engaged in illegal activity. The order of immunity 253

§ 

must be as extensive as the privilege. In People v. DeFeo, supra, the foreman of the Grand Jury granted the witness "immunity from the crimes of conspiracy and for the crime of bribing labor officials." The court held that the witness could not be held for contempt because the immunity was not coextensive with and as broad as his constitutional privilege; hence the witness was being compelled to give testimony in violation of his fundamental right against self-incrimination.

A witness cannot decline to answer on the ground of privilege against self-incrimination if granted immunity from State prosecution, by reason that the evidence may tend to incriminate him in a Federal crime, or that of another jurisdiction (Knapp v. Schweitzer, 357 U.S. 371).

The Supreme Court has held that, absent complicity between the Federal and State governments, a defendant is not excused from complying with the order of the court because of the possibility of indictment for a Federal crime, stating: "If a person through immunized selfdisclosure before a law-enforcing agency of the State, facilitate to some extent his amenability to Federal process, or vice versa, this too is a price to be paid for our federalism." The Court of Appeals in People v. Sapper stein, 2 N.Y. 2d 210, cert. denied 353 U.S. 946, sustained a conviction of contempt for the witness' failure to answer questions which might force him to testify as to violations of the Federal Communications Act. In Mills v. Louisiana, 360 U.S. 230, the court extended the doctrine of the Knapp case, supra, to a case where the Internal Revenue Service of the Federal Government was actively investigating the witness tendered immunity in the State proceeding, and such a witness was required to testify. The immunity is likewise sufficient notwithstanding that the evidence might be incriminating in another State (People v. Riela, 9 App. Div. 2d 481, 195 N.Y.S. 2d 558; Commission of Investigation v. Lombardozzi, 7 App. Div. 2d 48, 180 N.Y.S. 

2d 496, aff'd, 5 N.Y. 2d 913).

The testimony obtained under compulsion in a State 254

court is admissible in the Federal court and the defendant's rights are not infringed so long as the State is not in complicity with the Federal Government, using its immunity as an instrument or tool of the Federal Government (Feldman v. United States, 322 U.S. 487). There are harbingers of a change in the Supreme Court's feeling about the Feldman doctrine, in the concurring opinion of Mr. Justice 

Brennan and the dissent of Mr. Justice Douglas in the 

Mills case, supra. The dissent quoted the language of People v. Den Uyl, 318 Mich. 645, 29 N.W. 2d 284: "It seems like a travesty of verity to say that one is not subjected to selfincrimination when compelled to give testimony in a State judicial proceeding which testimony may forthwith be used against him in a Federal criminal prosecution." A holding that the State grant of immunity operate to preclude the Federal Government from prosecution does not resolve the dilemma, as this would be an interference with the powers constitutionally delegated to the Federal Government and would, in effect, confer upon every authorized state officer the power to confer immunity. However, the recognized effort on the part of State and Federal governments to cooperate and coordinate their law enforcement programs should produce an answer to this problem. 255
