Sec. 146. Definition. "An indictment is an accusation in writing, presented by a Grand Jury to a competent court, charging a person with a crime." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

247.) It is the Grand Jury's charge that a person has committed a crime, but it is not an indication of that person's guilt, being based only on the Grand Jury's judgment that reasonable grounds exist to believe that a crime has been committed (People v. Block, 190 Misc. 78, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 

430). However, the Grand Jury's judgment is something more than that of an ordinary group of persons; it is a group selected according to law (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

223-237), sworn (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 238-240), which hears legal testimony and can compel the attendance of witnesses (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 245-254), and which prepares and presents its accusations under the 256

INDICTMENTS 

§ 148 guidance of a public prosecutor. As stated by the Court of 

Appeals in one of the cases arising out of the Murder, Inc., prosecutions: "An indictment must be based upon evidence which in the judgment of the Grand Jury would, if unexplained or uncontradicted, warrant a conviction by the trial jury." (People v. Nitzberg, 289 N.Y. 523, 526, citing 

Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 258, now sec. 251.) An indictment is also the first pleading of the prosecution (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 274), a function which led to a great mass of technical rules surrounding the validity of indictments, and the recently-enacted rules simplifying indictments. 

Sec. 147. Presentments. A "presentment" has been held to be a term that can be used interchangeably with indictment (In re Funston, 133 Misc. 620, 233 N.Y.S. 81, 1929), although in the past the term was used to mean the Grand Jury's notice of an offense inquired into by them without any bill having been presented by the prosecutor. Upon an indictment's being found, the presentment was deemed to merge into it; if no indictment were found the presentment ceased to exist (Application of Bar Association of Erie 

County, 47 N.Y.S. 2d 213). Some courts have used the term "presentment" to refer to a report of censure directed to the conduct of the public officials of the county (In re Jones, 101 App. Div. 55, 92 N.Y.S. 275). In Application of Shiro, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 423, the term was so used, and in Clay v. 

Wickins, 7 Misc. 2d 84, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 534, the court noted that it may refuse to receive such reports or may order them sealed or expunged. See chapter on "The Grand 

Jury," supra. 

Sec. 148. Informations. An information is "the allegation made to a magistrate, that a person has been guilty of some designated crime." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 145.) All criminal prosecutions need not be begun by indictment. 

Article I, Section 6 of the New York Constitution provides: 

"No person shall be held to answer for a capital or otherwise infamous crime unless on presentment or indictment 257

§ 

of a Grand Jury." At common law, and under the Code, indictments are not required for the prosecution of misdemeanors (Matter of Wilcox, 153 Misc. 761, 276 N.Y.S. 117).

The Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 4, subdivision 4, requires prosecution by indictment of all crimes, with certain other exceptions not here material, except those cognizable in Police and City Courts and the courts of spe cial sessions. Article VI, Section 18 of the New York Con stitution, makes misdemeanors cognizable in the courts mentioned above. For present purposes, it need only be noted that an information is the method of instituting a criminal proceeding in cases where an indictment is not required. 

Sec. 149. History. In the early days of the common law, special juries were empaneled to report to the King in answer to inquiries directed to them. These juries, the forerunners of today's Grand Juries, were conducted somewhat similarly to Grand Juries today. After their report, the King would inform his officers, in the counties from which the juries were drawn, of any offenses found by the juries in these counties (3 Holdsworth, Hist. of Eng. 

Law 615 [3rd Ed., 1923]). These notices were the precursors of today's indictments and informations. In those days, grand jurors frequently formed part of the trial or petit jury that later tried the offense. Then the "indictment [was] ***the only document connected with the trial which in all cases [was] *** in writing," and the "history of indictments is a branch of history of the law of special pleading." (1 Stephen, Hist. of Crim. Law of Eng., 274-5.)

Thus, the historical basis of the technical requirements of indictments, which plagued this area until recent years, becomes apparent. As the only written pleading, an indictment had to overcome all the common law objections to pleadings and had to contain within itself almost the complete history of the prosecution. Any technical flaw would void the indictment upon demurrer. Other reasons for the technical, formal requirements of indictments were noted 258

INDICTMENTS 

§ 150 by the court in People v. Gilbert, 199 N.Y. 10, 16, where an objection was made that a murder indictment did not allege that the victim was a human being: "*** technical objections are no longer regarded as serious unless they are so thoroughly supported by authority that they cannot be disregarded.' ***The criminal law is fast outgrowing those technicalities which grew up when the punishment for crime was so serious. * * * When stealing a handkerchief worth one shilling was punished by death, and there were nearly two hundred different capital offenses, it was to the credit of humanity that technicalities should be invoked in order to prevent the cruelty of a strict and literal enforcement of the law. Those times have passed." 

Sec. 150. Purposes. The historical purposes of indictments and informations are, with minor modifications, still valid today. These are to serve as the pleading of the prosecution and initiate the case, to protect the person accused from being prosecuted again on the same charge by precisely recording and limiting the charge, to protect against arbitrary prosecution by requiring the indictment to be scrutinized and approved by a group of responsible citizens of the community, and to notify the accused of the charges against him. The last mentioned reason developed later than the others, for the indictment was originally not shown to the accused, and would have been of little value to him as originally drawn in languages other than English. In People v. Farson, 244 N.Y. 413, 417, the court stated: "The indictment is sufficient if it identifies the charge against the defendant so that his conviction or acquittal may prevent a subsequent charge for the same offense; notifies him of the nature and character of the crime charged against him, to the end that he may prepare his defense; and enables the court upon conviction to pronounce judgment according to the right of the case." And it has also been stated: "Its purpose is to notify the defendant of the charge against him to the end that he may properly prepare his defense and to identify the charge 259

§ 

against him so that conviction or acquittal may prevent a subsequent charge for the same offense." (People v. 

Liebowitz, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 141, 144.)

While the notice functions of the indictment are today in New York largely met by the bill of particulars, the functions of the indictment are not solely historical. The Grand 

Jury still represents the community and is still a protection against arbitrary prosecution. The indictment still notifies the defendant of the charge against him, so that he may properly prepare his demand for a bill of particulars; and it serves as a record of the charge, so that double jeopardy may be prevented. It should further be noted that the purposes of an information are essentially similar to those of an indictment. It is merely a simplified, economical method of accomplishing the same function, although with somewhat less protection to the individual against arbitrary prosecution for a less serious offense. 

Sec. 151. When Necessary. The constitutional requirement that no person may be held to answer for a felony in New York without an indictment by a Grand Jury has been mentioned above. "Until the Grand Jury has found an indictment accusing a person of an infamous crime, no court has jurisdiction to try a charge otherwise made to it or to accept a plea of guilty. The Legislature cannot confer upon the courts jurisdiction which the Constitution commands shall not be exercised by the courts. Since the Constitution commands that no person may be held to answer for a felony, unless on indictment of a Grand Jury, the Legislature cannot authorize a court to pronounce judgment convicting a person of an infamous crime upon the plea of guilty where no accusation has been made by a Grand 

Jury." (People ex rel. Battista v. Christian, 249 N.Y. 314, holding unconstitutional a statute allowing waiver of indictments.) Similarly, a court may not be authorized to amend an indictment to include an accusation of a criminal act independent of those acts charged in the indictment (People ex rel. Wachowitz v. Martin, 291 N.Y. 361). In the 260

INDICTMENTS 

§ 152 Martin case, the accused had been indicted for third degree burglary and, in a second count, for criminally receiving stolen property. After an initial plea of not guilty, the defendant had pleaded guilty to attempted second degree grand larceny, in the presence of his counsel, in response to the second count of the indictment. He was convicted, sentenced, and remanded to jail. Later, by writ of habeas corpus, he challenged the validity of the sentence. The lower courts held his sentence invalid on the ground that the conviction was for a crime not "necessarily included" within the crime charged in the indictment, as required by Code of Criminal Procedure, section 445. The Court of 

Appeals agreed with this finding, but held that the proper method of attacking the conviction was by appeal, not habeas corpus, as the judgment was not a nullity but based upon an erroneous conclusion of law.

The Federal constitutional provisions of the Fifth 

Amendment apply only to prosecutions in the Federal courts and thus a prosecution for a capital offense in a State court, commenced by information, has been held not violative of the due process clause of the Fourteenth 

Amendment (Hurtado v. California, 110 U.S. 516).

Sec. 152. Time To Find Indictment. "When a person has been held to answer for a crime, if an indictment be not found against him, at the next term of the court at which he is held to answer, the court may on application of the defendant, order the prosecution to be dismissed, unless good cause to the contrary be shown." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 667.) However, once an indictment is found, the defendant may not rely upon this section to move for its dismissal: "the injustice which the section is designed to remedy [is] purged by the finding of the indictment." (People v. Pearsall, 6 Misc. 2d 40, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 932, 934.) "The objection not having been raised prior to *** conviction, it cannot be raised years thereafter as a ground for vacating the judgment." (People v. Begue, 1 App. Div. 

2d 791, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 791, 795.) The application for dis- 

261

§ 

missal of the charge may be made only by the defendant. 

However, where there is a statutory method available by which defendant can force the prosecution to proceed, he should first utilize that method. In People v. Gearns, 14 

Misc. 2d 1010, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 875, the court noted that the statute applies only where the defendant is being held to answer a charge for which he has not yet been indicted, and that a defendant then serving a sentence under another charge is not within its scope. The court stated that the section refers to one being held to answer by a 

Magistrate for Special Sessions or the Grand Jury. The remedy of a defendant in prison on another charge is a motion under Code of Criminal Procedure, section 669-a, subdivision 1 (a), which provides for the request by defendants in prison on other charges for final disposition of charges pending against them.

The application for dismissal under Section 667 of the Code should be made to the court in which the charge is pending (People ex rel. McGowan v. Warden, 155 App. 

Div. 484, 140 N.Y.S. 864). An order of dismissal under this section is not a bar to further prosecution for the same offense if a felony, subject to the exceptions contained in the "Agreement on Detainers" entered between New York and other States, codified in Sections 669-b and 673 of the Code. There are two sections, both numbered 673, which provide that an order of dismissal, as above mentioned, is a bar to further prosecution if the offense is a misdemeanor, and bar felonies only when dismissal is ordered under Sections 668, et seq., of the Code (Vahey v. Court of 

Special Sessions, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 974; People v. Wilson, 182 

N.Y.S. 2d 842). 

Sec. 153. Waiver. A statute enacted in New York, providing for waiver of indictments by defendants, was held unconstitutional in People ex rel. Battista v. Christian, 249 

N.Y. 314. This holding does conflict with cases decided in other States, and in the Federal courts, but is no longer open to question in New York. Amendment of an 262

INDICTMENTS 

§ 154 indictment in court with the consent of defendant's counsel was held erroneous in People v. Miles, 289 N.Y. 360, where the amendment added a new count. The court stated: "Nor did the consent by appellant's trial counsel serve as a waiver of defendant's right *** waiver is not permitted where a question of jurisdiction or fundamental rights is involved." In 1945, the Code was amended to allow amendment of "simplified indictments" in certain cases. 

This provision is discussed infra, in the chapter entitled "Amendment of Indictments."

It has been stated that the defendant may lose his right to challenge the sufficiency of the indictment "where the finding of guilt by a trial jury gives the same or greater assurance against oppressions and prosecutions as an indictment based on sufficient evidence is intended to give before trial." (People v. Nitzberg, supra, at p. 530 of 289

N.Y.) Thus, while defendant may not waive the requirement of an indictment, his right to attack its sufficiency on certain grounds may be lost by failure to exercise it at the proper time.

Sec. 154. Short Form Indictments. In 1929, with the enact ment of Chapter III-A of the Code, much of the previous law concerning the requisites of indictments became outmoded. The chapter is entitled "Simplified Indictments" and provides the rules for a new type of indictment. Indictments valid under the old rules are still sufficient (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 295-a), but the new form of indictments need contain only the title of the action, the name of the court in which presented, the names of the parties, a statement of the specific crime with which the defendant is charged, containing the name of the crime, perhaps a reference to the statute defining the crime, and in the case of misdemeanors a description of the crime as set forth in the statute. Amendments of indictments are now allowed in cases in which they were not previously allowable. The chapter also provides for the furnishing of a bill of particulars of the crime to the defendant. This bill now con- 263

§ 

tains the detailed description of the crime and performs many of the functions previously performed by the indictment itself. The leading case of People v. Bogdanoff, 254 N.Y. 416, upheld the constitutionality of this new form of indictment, the court noting that the bill of particulars became part of the record, and was to be read together with the indictment, and that the furnishing of such bills to the defendant was made mandatory where a simplified indictment was used. Therefore, the court held that the constitutional rights of the defendant were sufficiently protected by the provisions of this new chapter. 

See also People v. Berkowitz, 14 Misc. 2d 384, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 119. 

Indictments may contain more than the minimum required by the new chapter, but an indictment in the statu tory form charging "Second Degree Manslaughter con trary to the Penal Law of the State of New York" is no longer demurrable (People v. Farley, 277 N.Y. 617).

A discussion of the history of the simplified indictment is contained in the Berkowitz case, supra. There, the defendants were indicted for "aiding and abetting [each] other of the crime of obscene prints and articles, contrary to Penal Law, Section 1141," and, in a second count, "of the crime of conspiracy, contrary to Penal Law, Section 580." Defendants demurred to the indictment. Section 

1141 proscribes publishing, printing, distributing, selling and possessing obscene prints and articles, which articles may be either pictures, books, magazines, newspapers, records, motion pictures, or paintings. The court noted that, under the indictment, "The defendant is neither advised of the nature of the charge against him nor of the facts which may be proved on the trial. Is he charged as a mere possessor or with distribution? Which of the articles found in his possession are deemed obscene?" Similar objections were noted to the second count. Therefore, the indictment would be insufficient under Sections 275 and 284 of the Code, pertaining to indictments other than simplified indictments. After discussing the Bogdanoff and 264

INDICTMENTS 

§ 154 Farson cases, supra, and after quoting from the Farson case the statement quoted above, the court stated: “* * * in the case of simplified indictments * * * it must also be clear that the indictment and bill of particulars read together do not subject the defendant to actual danger of a trial upon a charge upon which he has not been indicted." 

The constitutional questions, in each instance to be determined are: (1) Does the indictment violate the constitutional mandate that the Grand Jury, not the District 

Attorney has the power to accuse? (2) Does the indictment comply with the minimum requirements of procedural due process in that it sufficiently informs the defendant of the nature of the charges against him to enable him to prepare his defense and adequately protect him against possible double jeopardy? An indictment must contain not only a description of the crime charged but also a statement of the facts by which it is constituted. In a simplified indictment, the bill of particulars may provide such a statement of facts. But there must be certainty that the bill of particulars describes the same crime for which the 

Grand Jury indicted. Procedural due process requires that the defendant be advised by the indictment and the bill of particulars of each essential, but not every, element of the crime (People v. Berkowitz, supra). The court went on, in the Berkowitz case, to note that it had been shown the Grand Jury minutes and that they did not disclose which of the actions proscribed by Section 1141 defendants had committed, nor which of the articles of obscene material was involved. Defendant's demurrer was allowed, the indictment dismissed, and the District Attorney directed, pursuant to Section 327, to resubmit the matter to the 

Grand Jury.

The above case gives a fair example of the difficulties defendants may encounter with simplified indictments and the results of objections thereto. The court noted that in a previous case (People v. Newman, 190 Misc. 143, 72 N.Y.S. 

2d 626), it had inspected the Grand Jury minutes and the proposed bill of particulars to determine if defendant 265

§ 

could prepare his case and protect himself against double jeopardy by use of all these documents and, where it was determined that he could, a demurrer to an indictment was not allowed even though the indictment alone, or possibly the indictment and bill of particulars read together, would not perform this function.

Sec. 155. Long Form Indictments. Sections 275 and 284 of the Code state the requirements for long form indictments. 

Section 275 states that indictments shall not allege that the defendant had previously been convicted of any crime or offense unless such conviction affects the degree of the crime charged in the indictment or is an element of such offense. The basic function of an indictment today is to give notice to the accused. This function is served, and therefore an indictment is not invalid, even if it contains surplusage (People v. Joseph, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 125, where the first count ran three printed pages); or if there is a lack of clarity which can be remedied by a bill of particulars (People v. Williams, 243 N.Y. 162, where the subjects of certain adjectives in an indictment were ungrammatically described). The courts' attitude toward technical attacks upon indictments today is described in People v. Opalka, 204 Misc. 791, 792, 125 N.Y.S. 2d 790: "Where the defendant believes the indictment does not contain reasonable information as to the nature and character of the crime charged, he may, upon arraignment, or at any later stage of the proceedings, request that the court direct the District Attorney to file a bill of particulars of the crime charged." 

In People v. Fox, 205 Misc. 258, 128, N.Y.S. 2d 9, the defendant demurred to an indictment for "Endangering the 

Life or Health of a Child, in violation of Section 483, Para graph 2 of the Penal Law." Defendant claimed the indictment was insufficient because alleged in the disjunctive, but the demurrer was not allowed. See also People v. 

Thompson, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 459, where an indictment containing a conspiracy count was held sufficient against a 266

INDICTMENTS 

§ 155 demurrer despite its lack of the allegation of a specific, overt act committed in furtherance of the conspiracy. The court there noted that the allegation that the defendants had aided and abetted each other in committing the crimes alleged in other parts of the indictment, when read together with the bill of particulars, sufficiently alleged the act.

In the light of the above cases, an extended discussion of the numerous rules and technical requirements of indictments which prevailed until recent years is unwarranted. For the general rules concerning these formalities see Joyce, Indictments, pp. 207-737 (2d Ed., 1924). Section 

284 of Code of Criminal Procedure states that indictments are sufficient if: (a) “entitled in a court having authority to receive it, though the name of the court be not accurately stated"; People v. Peck, 96 N.Y. 650, held an omission of the statement of the court not reversible error if the record otherwise indicated the authority of the court and the omission did not injure the substantial rights of the defendant; (b) "found by a Grand Jury of the county"; defects in the selection or formation of the Grand 

Jury which do not affect the substantial rights of the defendant are not grounds for dismissal of the indictment 

(People v. Carter, 4 App. Div. 2d 879, 167 N.Y.S. 2d 441, defect in issuance of precept by sheriff; People v. Scannel, 37 Misc. 345, 75 N.Y.S. 500, two jurors who did not take part in proceedings not residents of county; but where the 

Grand Jury's selection was regulated by the District Attorney, rather than by lot, the jury was held not lawfully constituted and its indictment dismissed in People v. Harris, 182 Misc. 787, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 745, affirmed 294 N.Y. 424) ; (c) "the defendant is named, or if his name cannot be discovered, that he is described by a fictitious name, with the statement that it has been found impossible to discover his real name"; so an information charging Sol O. Strauss,

Inc., with an offense was held insufficient to try Sol O. 

Strauss personally in People v. Strauss, 272 App. Div. 1022, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 522; (d) "the crime was committed at some 267

§ 

place within the jurisdiction of the court," except where the act, though committed elsewhere is made there triable by statute; (e) "the crime was committed at some time prior to the finding of the indictment"; see cases under "Time", below; (f) "That the act or omission, charged as the crime, is plainly and concisely set forth." 

Intent. Penal Law, section 3, subdivision 5, which provides the general rules for the construction of pleadings and indictments, provides: "where an intent to defraud constitutes a part of a crime, it is not necessary to aver or prove an intent to defraud any particular person." One early case held that an indictment for forgery in the second degree must allege an intent to defraud (People v. D'Argencour, 95 N.Y. 624). The later cases hold, generally, that intent need only be alleged when it is a specific requisite of the crime (People v. Weiss, 252 App. Div. 463, 300 N.Y.S. 

249, reversed on other grounds 276 N.Y. 384). 

Judicial Notice. Indictments and informations need not allege matter of which judicial notice will be taken (People v. Reseniti, 191 Misc. 719, 81 N.Y.S. 2d 338; Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 286). 

Jurisdiction. "Facts constituting the jurisdiction, in indictments concerning judgments of courts of special jurisdiction, need not be set forth at length, only the conclusory fact need be asserted although the facts must be proved at the trial." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 287.) Inspection of

Grand Jury minutes to ascertain these facts will not be allowed (People v. Turkett, 193 Misc. 799, 85 N.Y.S. 2d 196).

Time. Section 280 of the Code reads: "The precise time at which the crime was committed need not be stated in the indictment; but it may be alleged to have been committed at any time before the finding thereof, except where time is a material ingredient of the crime." At common law, indictments had to charge the exact date of the commission of the offense, and indictments failing to do so, were invalid (People v. Parkinson, 43 N.Y.S. 2d 690). Even under the statute, it has been held that an indictment 268

INDICTMENTS 

§ 155 charging that a crime has been committed after the date of the indictment was invalid (People v. Guiley, 222 N.Y. 

548), and a guilty plea does not waive this defect (People v. Schweizer, 160 Misc. 23, 289 N.Y.S. 964). Indictments may be amended under Section 293 of the Code to cure a variance between the date alleged and the time proved, as long as the time proved is not subsequent to the date the indictment was found (People ex rel. Archer v. Brophy, 43 N.Y.S. 2d 311; People ex rel. Russo v. Jackson, 7 App. 

Div. 2d 672, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 153). In the Jackson case, the court also noted that any attack upon the allowance of such an amendment was to be made on appeal from a conviction, not before. As long as the indictment can be understood to charge that the crime alleged was committed prior to the date of the finding of the indictment, it will be held sufficient (People v. Thompson, 12 Misc. 2d 907, 177 

N.Y.S. 2d 459).

Names of Persons Injured. Section 281 of the Code provides that an "erroneous allegation as to the person injured or intended to be injured, is not material" where the indictment sufficiently describes the act. People v. Devinny, 227 N.Y. 397, held it necessary to name the person, or to allege an excuse for the failure to do so, where the crime alleged was unlawfully practicing medicine upon a certain party. The indictment may be amended to rectify an error in the allegation of the name (People v. Cruz, 285 App. Div. 

1076, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 722; People v. Lamm, 292 N.Y. 224).

Statutory Language in Indictment. While it is generally sufficient to allege a crime in the language of the statute defining it (People v. Dillard, 163 Misc. 146, 298 N.Y.S. 

296), if that does not sufficiently describe the crime, or would not properly inform the defendant of the crime with which he is charged, greater particularity may be required (People v. Farson, supra; People v. Berkowitz, supra) although, as previously stated, the bill of particulars may suffice to serve this purpose (People v. Carter, 4 App. Div. 2d 879, 167 N.Y.S. 2d 441).

Negativing Exceptions. When a long-form indictment 269

§ 

is used, and the statute defining the crime provides that the crime will not be deemed committed under certain circumstances, the "exception" thus created must be negatived in the indictment. However, if the condition is considered a "proviso" rather than an "exception," it need not be so negatived (People v. Smith, 299 N.Y. 707). In the

Smith case, the act alleged was driving at a speed in excess of fifty miles per hour. Vehicle and Traffic Law, Section 

56, subdivision 3, made such action illegal, except where permitted by the State Traffic Commission. It was held that this was an "exception" rather than a "proviso," and thus must be negatived. If the condition is contained in a subsequent statute, or in a clause other than the enacting clause, it is considered a "proviso" and therefore a matter of defense which need not be pleaded in the indictment (People v. Willi, 194 App. Div. 946, 184 N.Y.S. 943). "The two classes of provisions-exceptions and provisos—frequently come closely together and the rule of differentiation ought to be so applied as to comply with the requirements of common sense and reasonable pleading." (People v. Devinny, 227 N.Y. 397, 401.)

Miscellaneous Matters. Sections 289, 290 and 291 of the 

Code provide the requirements for indictments for libel, forgery, perjury and subornation of perjury, if long-form indictments are used. They all have the effect of dispensing with the technicalities of common law indictments and of avoiding the effects of variances not prejudicial to the defendant's rights.

Any one or more of several defendants indicted under one indictment may be convicted or acquitted (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 292). If two indictments are returned against one defendant for the same offense or matter, although they might be charged as different offenses, the latter indictment supersedes the earlier one which may be set aside (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 292-a). This was merely a procedural change (People v. Benson, 208 Misc. 138, 143 

N.Y.S. 2d 563) and applies to indictments only before the commencement of trial on either (People v. Sloan, 175 270

INDICTMENTS 

§ 156 

Misc. 618, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 381). Either party may move for dismissal of the prior indictment. 

Sec. 156. Joinder of Offenses. Although the commission of any one of numerous acts referred to in an indictment would constitute a crime, the indictment is not invalid if all the acts are grouped together in a single count. A conviction is valid if based on proof of any one of the acts. In 

People v. Engel, 200 Misc. 60, 102 N.Y.S. 2d 166, the indictment charged a conspiracy to violate New York City Charter, section 896, which proscribed the commission of many acts, but was held valid. 

Section 279 of the Code, as amended in 1936, effected a change in the rules concerning the consolidation of offenses: "*** under the old Section 279, only one crime, and in one form, could be charged in an indictment, except where the acts complained of constituted different crimes, in which event such crimes would be charged in separate counts; under the present Section 279 different crimes committed at different times and at different places may be consolidated in one indictment, but in separate counts thereof, provided such crimes are 'connected together' or constitute parts of a 'common scheme or plan' or if the acts constituting the crimes are 'of the same or a similar character." (People v. Vario, 165 Misc. 842, 2 N.Y.S. 2d 611.)

The section, as amended, is constitutional (People v. Erickson, 302 N.Y. 461), and the court has discretion, reviewable as are other discretionary acts, to determine if a defendant may be included in a trial under an indictment which charges some crimes with which he is not connected (People v. Nickel, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 791).

The possibility of abuse in such actions is evident. The court may, in its discretion, order the trial in one proceeding of several acts of a similar nature, even though it does not appear that they are part of a common scheme (People v. Luciano, 277 N.Y. 348). Thus, a defendant's motion for severance of a second degree rape count from other counts, alleging incest with the same person, was denied (People 271

§ 

v. Haymer, 198 Misc. 101, 97 N.Y.S. 2d 64). However, where one of several defendants was charged with having joined with the others in the commission of one robbery, and another defendant with having individually committed another robbery on another date, and there was no evidence that the acts were related, the trial court's denial of a motion for a severance was held an abuse of discretion where the movant had, allegedly, participated only in the joint robbery (People v. Pepin, 6 App. Div. 2d 

992, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 15).

The provisions of Section 279 of the Code apply to both long-form and simplified indictments (People v. Thompson, 14 Misc. 2d 670, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 319).

Sec. 157. Election Between Counts. The joinder of several offenses in one indictment has been discussed above. The practice of charging the same offense in many ways, in different counts of the same indictment, is long established. 

However, "After the commencement of the trial, the People shall not be required to elect between the counts of any indictment, except that for good cause shown, and in the interest of justice, the court may, in its discretion, require an election as to one or more counts." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 279-a.) The note to the law, as enacted, provided that the section would apply to indictments and informations. 

It had been held, prior to the 1936 enactment of Section 279-a, that the prosecution could not be required to elect upon which count of an indictment, containing several counts charging the same offense in different forms, it would proceed (People v. Austin, 1 Parker Crim. Rep. 

154). Other early cases had indicated that it was within the court's discretion to require such an election, but they had held only that the denial of a motion to compel the election was not error (People v. Armstrong, 70 N.Y. 38, People v. Wilson, 109 N.Y. 345). Where the indictment charged more than one offense, it was generally held that the requirement of the election was within the court's discretion (People v. Davis, 56 N.Y. 95). 272

INDICTMENTS 

§ 157 

In People v. Rosen, 251 App. Div. 584, 297 N.Y.S. 877, the defendant had been charged with second degree arson, in violation of Penal Law, section 222. The defendant moved to compel the District Attorney to elect the subdivision of that section under which he would proceed. Citing section 

279-a, the court stated that the District Attorney was not bound to so elect, and noted that the trial court had charged the jury in such manner that only one subdivision of section 222 was under consideration. 

In People v. Beyer, 163 Misc. 890, 297 N.Y.S. 913, the defendant was indicted upon two counts, one charging a misdemeanor and one a felony. The defendant moved to compel an election and the court ruled: "this seems to be a discretionary matter with the court and one which in a case similar to the case at bar the District Attorney might be unable to determine, at this time, which count of the indictment would be sustained by the facts. I decline the request." 

In People v. Goggin, 256 App. Div. 995, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 586, affirmed 281 N.Y. 611, the defendant had been convicted upon both counts of an indictment charging first degree rape and second degree assault. The court stated: "Although both counts charged the same crime, the District Attorney was not required to elect upon which he would proceed, and denial of a motion to compel him to do so was not erroneous. *** The defendant, however, could be sentenced on but one of the counts *** under such circumstances, this court is empowered to annul a sentence or sentences imposed on more than one count."

When the same actions constitute more than one offense or crime, it is not necessary that the prosecution elect to proceed upon the lesser offense. In People ex rel. Corkum v. 

Wilson, 263 App. Div. 1046, 33 N.Y.S. 2d 682, the defendant contended that he should have been prosecuted for the lesser offense. The court stated: "Apparently appellant might have been prosecuted either for attempted rape, second degree, or for the carnal abuse of a child. *** The

People were not obliged to choose the lesser offense." 273

§ 

 Sec. 158. Attacking Indictments. The law and procedure affecting attacks upon indictments are sufficiently important to warrant an extended treatment thereof and this material will be discussed, infra, in the chapters entitled "Demurrers," "Inspection of Minutes" and "Motion to Dismiss Indictment.”

Sec. 158(a). Youthful Offender Procedures. The trend toward separate consideration, classification and treatment of young people enmeshed in the toils of the law shows no indication of abating. Beginning with the series of enactments which removed completely from the scope of the criminal law the otherwise criminal acts of very young persons, and created a new category of "juvenile delinquency" cognizable in Children's Courts, there have been and will undoubtedly continue to be many and varied procedural enactments dealing with antisocial behavior by the young. It is not the function of this work to go into these. It is within its scope, however, to consider the procedures in this direction which affect the procedural aspects of the criminal law of New York. We proceed with this discussion after considering the indictment, because it is at the point where an indictment has been found, that the youthful offender procedure, if applicable, is initiated. 

Before we analyze the youthful offender procedures, applying to minors who have "reached the age of sixteen years" but have not "reached the age of nineteen years" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-e), established in Part 6, Title VII-B (Sections 913-e through 913-r) of the Code, we must make clear their distinction from juvenile delinquency proceedings, on the one hand, and from proceedings under the proposed Youth Court Act (Laws of 1956, ch. 838) which, although enacted, has never been put into effect and may never be.

Juvenile delinquency, in so far as it includes acts which would be considered criminal if perpetrated by one over sixteen years of age, is not considered a crime (People v. 

Lewis, 260 N.Y. 171). The delinquent is not "convicted"; in 274

INDICTMENTS 

§ 158 (a) 

the proceeding in the Children's Court, the "proper title is not 'The People of the State of New York against *** [It is] commenced and carried to judgment under the correct title of 'In the Matter of ***, a child under the Age of Sixteen Years.' * *** The distinction is not without significance." (People v. Lewis, supra.)

Conversely, as the court pointed out in the remarkable exposition included in People v. Shannon, 1 App. Div. 2d 

226, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 550: "We do not doubt the beneficent purpose of the youthful offender statutes *** which expressly provide that no youth shall be denominated a criminal by reason of an adjudication that he is a youthful offender, and that such a determination shall not be deemed a conviction. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-n). The fundamental point, however, with respect to such an adjudication, is that it may be made only in a criminal action, and may not be made unless it be found that the defendant, so adjudged, has committed a crime (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-e.) The adjudication may only follow an indictment found or an information laid in a court of criminal jurisdiction. The youth accused of the offense is required to plead guilty or not guilty to the charge made against him (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-g). If a plea of not guilty is entered the adjudication may be made only after a trial at which it must be found that the defendant committed the acts charged against him in the indictment or information (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 913-h, 913-j). Those facts, in our opinion must be proved in the same way as if the charge were made against an adult, by competent and sufficient evidence. (People v. Fitzgerald, 244 N.Y. 307.)”

While the youthful offender proceedings proceed in a separate part of the criminal court, they are not exclusive; the defendant cannot be compelled against his consent to be tried under these procedures if he chooses to stand trial in the conventional manner, and they are not followed unless the Grand Jury or the District Attorney recommends, or the court on it own motion initiates, “examinations, investigation and questioning" of the defendant to 275

§ (a)  

determine whether he shall be tried as a youthful offender (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-g). On direction of the court, thereafter, the defendant "shall be tried for the purpose of determining whether he shall be adjudged a youthful offender. The trial shall be held by the court without a jury." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-h.) The Youth Court provisions, on the other hand, contemplate a separate court and separate procedures, although organizationally appended to the County and General Sessions Courts, and supersede the provisions of the Code and the practice relating to criminal actions generally, where applicable. No further discussion of these provisions will be here undertaken, as it appears doubtful whether these provisions will ever be put into effect except in form and details quite different than those heretofore enacted but several times deferred in application. In youthful offender proceedings, no statement, admission or confession of the defendant to the court or on the investigation above referred to "shall ever be admissible as evidence against him or his interest, except that the court may take such statement, admission or confession into consideration at the time of sentencing ** **" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 913-i.) The proceedings are private (id., sec. 913-k), and result in the defendant's being, if he pleads guilty or is found guilty of committing the acts charged, adjudged "to be a youthful offender and the indictment or information shall be considered a nullity and of no force or effect." (id., sec. 913-j.) No determination made "shall operate as a disqualification of any youth subsequently to hold public office, public employment, or as a forfeiture of any right or privilege or to receive any license granted by public authority; and no youth shall be denominated a criminal by reason of such determination, nor shall such determination be deemed a conviction (id., sec. 913-n). 

Commitment, suspension of sentence, suspension of the execution of sentence, and probation for a period not exceeding, with permitted extensions, five years, are provided for (id., sec. 913-m). All records, fingerprints, photo- 276

INDICTMENTS § 158 (a) graphs and physical descriptions of the defendant, taken in the course of the proceedings, are barred to public inspection, and may be opened to inspection only by the court, in its discretion (id., sec. 913-0). 277

CHAPTER 13  Sec. 159. History and Definition Sec. 160. Time of Amendment Sec. 161. Simplified Indictments, Addition of Counts Sec. 162. Long Form Indictments, Addition of Counts Sec. 163. Amendments Allowable Sec. 164. Defendant's Consent Sec. 165. Necessity of Amendment Sec. 166. Attacking Amendments Sec. 159. History and Definition. "At common law the court was powerless to order an indictment to be amended." (People v. Van Emery, 222 N.Y. 74, 78.) Early in the development of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 293 was enacted, providing: "Upon the trial of an indictment, when a variance between the allegation and the proof in respect to time, or in the name or description of any place, person or thing, shall appear, the court may, in its judgment, if the defendant cannot be thereby prejudiced in his defense on the merits, direct the indictment to be amended, according to the proof, on such terms as to the postponement of the trial, to be had before the same or another jury, as the court may deem reasonable." The section was held constitutional in People v. Johnson, 104 N.Y. 213. 

Section 295-j of the Code allows amendments to simplified indictments, upon the same conditions concerning prejudice to the defendant's rights and the postponement of the trial, "by adding thereto new counts, where it is made to appear that the crimes to be charged therein relate to the transaction upon which the defendant stands indicted." 278

§ Where an amendment under Section 295-j is allowed, a note of the order allowing it should be indorsed upon the indictment (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 295-k). Section 295-j does not apply to long-form indictments (People v. Ercole, 308 

N.Y. 425; People v. Thompson, 14 Misc. 2d 670, 178 N.Y.S. 

2d 319).

Section 293, quoted above, applies to proceedings in Police Courts and in courts of special sessions (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 62). Informations may be more easily amended than indictments (People v. Kramer, 10 Misc. 2d 

473, 175 N.Y.S. 2d 508), for the reasons discussed in the sub-section entitled "Time" in the chapter on “Informations."

Sec. 160. Time of Amendment. Section 293 refers to an amendment "upon trial." Thus, an amendment proposed by the District Attorney at the arraignment was held premature and not allowable (People v. Trepel, 207 Misc. 98, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 513; People v. Goyette, 282 App. Div. 980, 125 N.Y.S. 2d 510, where the same rule was applied to simplified indictments under section 295-j). The specific time during the trial when the amendment may be made has not been limited by the courts, although the section applies "when a variance * * * shall appear," thus indicating that the amendment should await variant proof. In 

People v. Lewis, 132 App. Div. 256, 116 N.Y.S. 893, the court allowed the District Attorney to move to amend, and ordered the amendment, at the opening of the prosecution's case. However, in that case, the District Attorney's motion was made at that time at the court's suggestion, after the District Attorney had announced his intention to make the motion after proof had been put into evidence. 

The variance concerned the time of the commission of the crime, and the court noted that it was an immaterial variance and that the defendant did not claim surprise or request a postponement of the trial. The court also held that the crime had been completed at the time charged in the indictment. 279

§ 

Other courts have indicated that amendments will be allowed before proof of the variance where the defendant does not claim surprise, and that if the defendant does so claim a postponement of the trial will be ordered. In 

People v. Hamm, 5 App. Div. 2d 696, 169 N.Y.S. 2d 513, an indictment charging forgery in January, 1955, was amended to charge that the crime had been committed one week later. Notification of the proposed amendment was given defendant's counsel by the District Attorney two days prior to the trial in December, 1955. The indictment was amended on the first day of the trial. The court noted: "Appellant made no claim that the motion to amend was premature because no proof had yet been submitted which showed * a variance *** and, on the appeal, makes no claim the motion was premature ***. In our opinion, the defense on the merits was not prejudiced' *** and reversal is not required, since the prosecution could have adduced its proof * * * without requesting that the indictment be amended, and a conviction could have been sustained without an amendment or the request for one." None of the above cases contains a square holding that an amendment may be allowed, over defendant's objection, prior to a variance appearing in the proof. 

In People v. Ercole, 284 App. Div. 974, aff'd. 308 N.Y. 

425, 429, the Appellate Division reversed a judgment of conviction "on the ground that an amendment to an indictment under Section 295-j of the Code can be granted only after the formal introduction of proof, and that section *** does not permit an amendment to conform to evidence which has not been introduced and which, according to the express prohibition of a statute, could not have been introduced upon the indictment as found by the Grand Jury." 

The affirmance in the Court of Appeals, however, was based upon other grounds. 

In People v. Cruz, 285 App. Div. 1076, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 722, an indictment which had been dismissed was ordered reinstated. The District Attorney had moved to amend the indictment, which charged sodomy and assault, by sub- 280

§ stituting the correct name of the victim. The indictment had correctly described the victim as a child, but had mistakenly used the name of the child's mother. In reversing the dismissal of the indictment by the trial judge, who had acted sua sponte while denying the motion to amend the indictment, the court stated, at page 723: "While it may be that the proof submitted by the People was not sufficient, at the time when the motion to amend was made, to justify, or require, the granting of the motion, it was, nevertheless, error to dismiss the indictment of the court's own motion."

It appears, on the basis of the above cases, that if an amendment to an indictment is ordered prior to a variance developing in the proof, an objection thereto pressed by the defendant with proper exceptions taken, may possibly be the basis for a reversal, if the amendment does not solely concern immaterial allegations. In any event, there has not yet been a clear holding that such action, objected to by defendant, would not be error. Amendments made after the trial to conform to the proof have been held ineffective (People v. Wolf, 216 App. Div. 771, 215 N.Y.S. 95, aff'd. 243 N.Y. 565). Compare People v. Pleasant, 122 

N.Y.S. 2d 141, sustaining such amendment in a prosecution by information.

Sec. 161. Simplified Indictments: Addition of Counts. As above stated, Section 295-j of the Code allows the amendment of simplified indictments by the addition of new counts, if the crimes charged in the new counts "relate to the transaction on which the defendant stands indicted." 

In People v. Miles, 289 N.Y. 360, the defendants were indicted on four counts, three of which charged bribery of police officers on May 9, 1938, and one violation of the lottery laws on May 3, 1938. At the conclusion of the prosecution's case, the District Attorney moved to amend the indictment by adding a new, fifth, count charging violation of the lottery laws on May 9, 1938. The amendment was ordered by the court, the defendant's counsel inter- 281

§ 

posing no objection. The Court of Appeals granted permission for an appeal from an affirmance of the conviction of one of the defendants. The conviction was reversed, the 

Court of Appeals stating, at page 363 of 289 N.Y.: “The change in the Grand Jury's indictment wrought by the amendment on the trial accused the appellant of a crime separately identified by the court for the jury's consideration as being independant of the remaining four counts. 

The date of the crime with which the appellant was charged by the added fifth count differed from the date of the crime charged in the fourth * * * such a change did not relate to the form of the charge, nor to *** the description of the offense. The change went to the substance of the accusation. *** As such it was not an accusation by a Grand Jury as required by the constitutional provision quoted above. Nor did it, in our opinion relate to the transactions upon which the defendant stood indicted. *** Nor did the consent by appellant's trial counsel serve as a waiver of the appellant's rights." 

In People ex rel. Prince v. Brophy, 273 N.Y. 90, an indictment had originally been filed as charging defendants with first degree robbery, second degree assault, petit larceny and criminally receiving stolen property. Two of the defendants, after pleading not guilty, were permitted to plead guilty to second degree grand larceny. After conviction and parole, and revocation of parole following another offense, one of the defendants sought his discharge under the first sentence by habeas corpus, alleging that the judgment of the court, and his plea of guilty, had both been void. The court noted that the indictment, on its face, was insufficient as a second degree larceny indictment. However, after quoting sections 293 and 295-j, the court stated that "the indictment could have been amended so as to contain a count * * * which would include the crime of larceny in the second degree, the defendant in requesting that such a plea might be accepted, in effect, waived any objection that the indictment did not contain such a count. An amendment, which he could have consented to or which in 282

§ the discretion of the court could have been made without his consent, cannot be pleaded as a defect depriving a court of jurisdiction when he and his counsel specifically asked the court [therefor] *** and the court complied with his request." 

Sec. 162. Long-Form Indictments: Addition of Counts. In 

People v. Ercole, 308 N.Y. 425, the Court of Appeals, in a four-to-three decision, held that the provisions of Section 295-j of the Code were not applicable to long-form indictments. The indictment contained one count of grand larceny in the first degree, and three counts of petit larceny. There was no allegation of false representations or pretenses, as required under Penal Law, Section 1290-a, subdivision 1, for the introduction of evidence of such false representations or pretenses. The trial court allowed amendment of the indictment by the addition of four new counts, including allegations of false representations and pretenses, so evidence thereof could be introduced. The 

Court of Appeals held such amendment improper under Section 293 of the Code. It held also that Section 295-j is applicable only to simplified indictments. Thus, until the minority opinion in Ercole becomes a majority, and Section 295-j is held applicable to all indictments, new counts may not be added to long form indictments by amendment. 

Sec. 163. Amendments Allowable. Time. In People v. Van 

Emery, supra, the defendant was indicted on February 8, 1915, the indictment charging commission of a crime on October 17, 1915. The defendant first pleaded not guilty, then withdrew his plea and moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that it did not comply with the requirements of Sections 280 through 284 of the Code. The motion was denied and the defendant excepted to the denial and demurred, contending that the indictment did not state facts sufficient to constitute a crime. The demurrer was not allowed, and the court permitted amendment of the indictment to change the date alleged from 1915 to 1914. 283

§ 

On appeal, after the defendant's refusal to plead further and his conviction, the conviction was reversed and the defendant ordered discharged. The court stated: “the crime was charged as having been committed months subsequent to the finding of the same by the Grand Jury, an impossible date, and as a matter of law cannot be regarded as charging a crime. * * * While the precise time at which a crime was committed need not be stated in an indictment, it is essential *** that it disclose that the crime was committed before the finding of the indictment by the Grand 

Jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sections 280, 284, subd. 5)." The

District Attorney had argued that the amendment sufficiently cured the defect in the indictment. This argument was rejected by the appellate court which noted, first, that Section 293 referred only to amendments made upon a trial, and then stated that "the Grand Jury did not charge the defendant with the commission of a crime at any time prior to the finding of the indictment. * * * Such omission was not one of form but of substance. * * * The County Judge, however, sought by an amendment of the indictment to make good an invalid indictment and thus exercise the functions of the Grand Jury without legal proof that defendant had ever committed a crime. Such practice cannot be sustained." Compare People v. Kramer, supra, where an amendment similar to that held invalid in the Van Emery case was upheld in a prosecution by information. 

In People ex rel. Archer v. Brophy, 43 N.Y.S. 2d 311, a first degree robbery indictment was amended, during trial, to change the date of the alleged crime from August 1 to 

August 31, 1935. See, similarly, People v. Jones, 195 N.Y. 

547. In general, it appears that the indictment can be amended to cure an erroneous allegation of a date as long as the crime charged remains the same, and as long as the date of the crime originally alleged in the indictment, was prior to the date the indictment was found. 

Identity of Offense. In People v. Kuehn, 5 App. Div. 2d 

516, 173 N.Y.S. 2d 366, the defendants were indicted upon a count of second degree assault in a long-form indictment. 284

§ The trial court, at the close of all the proof, after the defendants' motion to dismiss the indictment for want of a prima facie case, directed that the indictment be amended "to conform to the proof" by adding a count of third degree assault. The defendants were convicted of third degree assault after the court dismissed the original count of assault in the second degree. Their conviction was reversed, the Appellate Division noting that it was immaterial that the defendants could have been convicted of third degree assault, a lesser included offense, without amendment. Since a long-form indictment was used, the addition of the new count was not authorized by section 295-j (People v. Ercole, supra), and dismissal of the original count left no further charge open. 

The statement in People ex rel. Wachowicz v. Martin, 293 N.Y. 361, best describes the present attitude of the courts in this area: "*** the Legislature cannot * * “*** * authorize a court to amend an indictment to include an accusation of criminal acts independent of any accusations presented by the Grand Jury in the indictment." The cases indicate a reluctance, on the part of the courts, to amend indictments by changing the identity of the offense. In 

People v. Fiske, 85 N.Y.S. 2d 240, the court quoted the above statement with approval, in denying a motion by the District Attorney, to amend the indictment to correct what the District Attorney called "inadvertence and mistake *** either in the dictation or in the transcribing." The indictment, as originally filed, had charged first degree forgery, contrary to Penal Law, section 884, subdivision 5, which concerns forgery of stocks, bonds, drafts, checks, etc., rather than subdivision 6, which concerns forgery of indorsements. The court stated: "The court could never amend the identity of the offense, but could only amend the description of the offense." So, also, an amendment was not allowed to change an indictment charging larceny of a check on a certain date, to charge larceny of the proceeds of the check on a different date (People v. Geyer, 196 N.Y. 364). 285

§ 

The minutes of the Grand Jury were used by the court in People v. La Barbera, 159 Misc. 177, 287 N.Y.S. 257, to uphold and amend an indictment against defendant's motion to dismiss it for insufficiency of the evidence submitted to the Grand Jury. The District Attorney had moved to amend the indictment, originally charging first degree murder while engaged in the commission of second degree arson, and, in a second count, second degree arson. The amendment sought to include an allegation that the building burned was within the curtilege of an inhabited building containing a human being, and allegations of intent to prejudice or defraud the insurer of the building. The court held the evidence before the Grand Jury insufficient to uphold the murder count, but allowed amendment of the indictment to include the allegations of fraud and prejudice to the insurer because of evidence on this point appearing in the Grand Jury minutes. The amendment concerning the location of the building was not allowed because the minutes disclosed no such evidence. 

People v. Barsh, 281 App. Div. 1042, 121 N.Y.S. 2d 433, appeal dismissed 306 N.Y. 650, rejected an amendment to an indictment charging criminal receipt of stolen property, which amendment would have charged withholding and concealing stolen property. The court noted that withholding and concealing stolen property were not part of the transaction of receiving stolen property.

Ingredients of Offense. In People v. Oliver, 3 N.Y. 2d 

684, the defendants had been indicted upon two counts, one of first degree burglary, and the other of third degree assault. However the long-form indictment used did not allege that the acts constituting the burglary occurred in the night time, as required by the Penal Law. After the defendants' conviction, reversal and a new trial were granted by the Appellate Division. The Court of Appeals affirmed, stating: "The indictment, being in the long form, is defective insofar as it charges burglary in the first degree by omitting the essential allegation that it occurred in the night time (Penal Law, Consol. Laws, c. 40, sec. 402, 286

§ subd. 4), and, being in the long form, it could not be amended nor the deficiency supplied by a bill of particulars or ignored (People v. Ercole, 308 N.Y. 425). Nevertheless the indictment is not to be dismissed inasmuch as, even if the offense were committed in the daytime, it would be burglary in the second degree." Thus, a long-form indictment has been held not amendable to correct the omission of an essential element of the offense. 

Description of Persons, Places, Things. In People v. 

Cruz, discussed supra, the Appellate Division stated, while reversing a dismissal of the indictment by the trial court for the erroneous allegation of the name of the victim: 

66*** we see no impediment to an amendment of the indictment by the trial court to correct an obvious error in the statement of the name of a person therein referred to, if the amendment is made according to the proof and if the rights of the defendant will not be prejudiced. 

though the name of the person injured should be stated to identify the crime charged, to permit a defendant to prepare his defense, and to prevent double jeopardy it is a detail which serves mainly to describe the crime and does not form a part of the substance or body of the offense charged. *** Allegations as to such details may in a proper case be amended to prevent the escape of guilty persons, and a miscarriage of justice through inconsequential technicalities." 

In People v. Grawunder, 2 Misc. 2d 126, 151 N.Y.S. 2d 

137, a misnomer of the legislation involved was held a defect correctable by amendment. The indictment had referred to a law as part of a city charter when, in fact, it was a city ordinance. See also People v. Langley, 114 App. Div. 

427, 100 N.Y.S. 123, where an indictment was amended to change the allegation of the location of certain property from the State of Virginia to the State of West Virginia. 

People v. Scanlon, 132 App. Div. 528, 117 N.Y.S. 57, held an indictment amendable where the name of a village had been stated incorrectly, and People v. Bromwich, 200 N.Y. 287

§ 

385, allowed an amendment to change the number of the election district concerned. 

One early case, People v. Herman, 45 Hun 175, allowed an amendment to cure a variance which arose when the victim was proven to be an individual, rather than a corporation. Section 277 of the Code allows the indictment of a defendant to be amended at any stage of the proceedings by the insertion of the defendant's true name, where he was originally indicted under a fictitious or erroneous name. Section 281 provides that a misnomer of the victim of an injury is not material if the act is described with "sufficient certainty in other respects." 

Sec. 164. Defendant's Consent. Despite defendant's consent, either personally or through his counsel, defendant's right to challenge amendment of the indictment may be waived only when the amendment is otherwise allowable. 

Thus, in the Brophy case, supra, an amendment to allege a lesser included offense was upheld when the Court of Appeals noted that the amendment could have been made without the defendant's consent. In People v. Miles, 289 

N.Y. 360, counsel's consent to the addition of a new count to a simplified indictment was held not to constitute a waiver of defendant's right later to attack such action. The court emphasized that the action was not proper in any event as the new count did not relate to the transaction upon which the defendant stood indicted and thus was not within the court's power to order. 

Sec. 165. Necessity of Amendment. It is not necessary to amend an indictment to convict the accused of a lesser, included, offense. In People ex rel. Bianculli v. McDonnell, 278 App. Div. 782, 103 N.Y.S. 2d 853, aff'd, 302 N.Y. 922, the defendant, indicted on a one-count indictment charging second degree murder, sought, by habeas corpus, his release from jail after a disagreement of the jury. After the close of the People's case he had moved to dismiss the indictment, alleging insufficiency of proof. The motion was 288

§ granted with respect to murder, but denied with respect to manslaughter. The court indorsed upon the indictment the notation that he had taken the second degree murder question from the jury and left only the manslaughter question for their determination. The jury was so charged and the defendant objected, contending that the dismissal terminated the entire matter as the indictment had originally charged only second degree murder. The Appellate Division held, the Court of Appeals affirming: "No amendment of the indictment was necessary." 

People ex rel. Poulos v. McDonnell, 302 N.Y. 89, should be compared with the above case. They were decided within a few months of each other by the same court and, in the Bianculli case, the defendant contended the Poulos case was indistinguishable. The Poulos indictment contained three counts, first degree rape and two counts of second degree assault. The first degree rape count was dismissed by the court at the conclusion of the prosecution's case. 

The jury acquitted defendants of counts two and three. 

Defendants thereupon moved for their discharge upon all counts of the indictment. The motion was denied and defendants remanded for retrial upon a third degree assault charge which, the trial court stated, was "still pending before the Court *** included within the crimes charged in the indictment by virtue of the Code of Criminal Procedure." Exception was taken and habeas corpus proceedings instituted, defendants charging that they were being subjected to double jeopardy. The Court of Appeals affirmed the order of the Appellate Division, which had granted defendants discharge, stating: "*** the indictment might have been amended by the addition of a new count, namely, assault in the third degree, had the statutory procedure been carried out (Code Crim. Proc. secs. 

295-j, 295-k), in view of the fact that such count would merely be an inferior degree of the same generic crime with which they were already charged-assault (in the second degree)-or, in the words of the statute, it relates 'to the transaction upon which the defendant stands in- 289

§ 

dicted'. *** It does not appear that this was done or even attempted, and the court in effect merely recognized that the third count would sustain a conviction in the lesser degree and charged the jury accordingly. Under such circumstances there can be no question of amendment by implication or waiver *** and it is unnecessary to consider what might have been the effect had the indictment been amended to include the additional count.” 

Sec. 166. Attacking Amendments. In the last discussed case (the Poulos case), defendants utilized habeas corpus to obtain their release. The decision was by a four-to-three majority. In another four-to-three opinion, involving a somewhat similar situation, the court recognized the impropriety of the amendment, but dismissed the writ. There, in People ex rel. Wachowicz v. Martin, 293 N.Y. 361, the defendant had pleaded guilty to second degree grand larceny upon an indictment charging criminal receipt of stolen property. The Court of Appeals stated: "Though the judgment of conviction of the charge of attempted grand larceny is erroneous, the question remains whether it is a nullity and whether a person held thereunder may challenge the lawfulness of his detention by writ of habeas corpus. *** The County Court *** which pronounced sentence has general jurisdiction both of the crime charged in the indictment and of the crime of which [defendant] has been found guilty, and had jurisdiction of the person 

*** An analogous question is presented when a defendant moves for arrest of judgment, on a plea or verdict of guilty, on the ground that the facts stated in the indictment do not constitute a crime. Error there may be corrected by appeal, but the judgment entered upon an erroneous determination of a question of law by a court of competent jurisdiction is not a nullity, and may not be challenged by a writ of habeas corpus." Thus, the court held that habeas corpus was not the proper remedy. However, People v. Miles, 289 N.Y. 

360, cited by the dissent in Martin, contains language indi- 290

§ cating that habeas corpus might be the proper remedy in a similar situation. There, the indictment was amended to charge an additional crime, not necessarily included within the crime originally charged, and the court held that the error was fundamental and the conviction a nullity, although the case arose by appeal and not on habeas corpus. 

See, also, People ex rel. Grace v. McCollom, 100 N.Y.S. 2d 

124, where the court, citing the Martin case with approval, stated: "the court's right to permit an amendment may not be raised by habeas corpus. *** If the court's ruling in granting the amendment was erroneous, such error of law may only be corrected on direct appeal from the judgment of conviction." That method would appear, in view of the decision in the Martin case, to be the only effective alternative. 291
