Sec. 168. Need for a Demand 

Sec. 169. Time to Demand

Sec. 170. Form of Bill Sec. 171. Amendment of the Bill Sec. 172. Bill of Defendant Sec. 173. Contents of Bill of District Attorney Sec. 174. Theory of Prosecution Sec. 175. Identification of Joint Defendants Sec. 176. Elements of the Crime 

Sec. 177. Discretion of the Court

PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

Most applications for bills of particulars are denied. A bill of particulars should ALWAYS be asked for whenever the indictment pleads in the alternative, in order to avoid surprise at the trial. At no time should counsel move for a bill, if the items demanded point to some vital phase of the defense, which would otherwise go unnoticed by the prosecution.

Bills of particulars should only be requested if the information called for will assist your client in his defense. Never should counsel demand a bill merely for the purpose of asking for one. If the allegations in the indictment are sufficiently explicit to enable him to prepare his defense, he should forego making this motion. 

Sec. 167. General. Bills of particulars are mentioned in the

Code of Criminal Procedure, primarily in Chapter III-A, which concerns "Simplified Indictments." Section 295-g reads: "Upon the arraignment of the defendant, or at any later stage of the proceedings, the court shall, at the re- 292

§ quest of the defendant, direct the District Attorney to file a bill of particulars of the offense charged." In People v. 

Bogdanoff, 254 N.Y. 16, it was held that where a simplified indictment is used, it is mandatory that the court order the furnishing of a bill upon defendant's request. In so doing, the Court of Appeals indicated that a conviction upon a simplified indictment, without a bill of particulars, would deprive the defendant of constitutional rights, assuming the indictment did not otherwise meet the standards of common law indictments. Referring to past practice, prior to the enactment of the new chapter when only long-form indictments were used, the Court said that "bills of particulars might at times be granted in the discretion of the court, but constitutional rights cannot be made dependent upon the favor of the court. They may be asserted as a matter of right. Even when a bill of particulars was granted, it did not become part of the record. *** In the new chapter *** the Legislature has provided a new method of protecting the rights of an accused. No longer may the court grant or withhold a bill of particulars in its discretion. *** It must state such particulars as may be necessary to give the defendant and the court reasonable information as to the nature and character of the crime charged."

Even today, when the long-form indictment is used "there is no such obligation imposed on the court. This does not mean that there are no instances in which this application for a bill should be granted. Where justice demands a party be apprised of charges with greater particularity (People v. Stedeker, 175 N.Y. 57), or where there is doubt as to some particular of the offense charged, the proper remedy is a motion for the bill of particulars (People v. Schubert, 140 Misc. 689, 251 N.Y.S. 390). And, since the granting of the application is discretionary, if the court be satisfied with the affirmative allegations in the moving papers, it may decide that there is a sufficient ground for granting the relief sought and direct the filing 293

§ 

of such bill." (People v. Keohane, 201 Misc. 597, 115 N.Y.S. 

2d 492, 495.)

Sec. 168. Need for a Demand. It is not always essential that the defendant demand the bill for, as the court stated in 

People v. Berkowitz, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 119, 128: "I have no doubt that despite the failure of the defendant to demand a bill of particulars, I may order same to be served upon him." Of course, reliance upon the court to order service of a bill would not be prudent protection of defendants' interests. "Appellant also contends that the indictment found against him was insufficient to charge the crime of murder in the first degree in that it gave no particulars of the crime charged and did not name the alleged victim. 

It was a short-form indictment as permitted and prescribed by Section 295-d of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and was a sufficient written accusation to comply with the re quirements of the State Constitution. * * * If further par- ticulars were desired the District Attorney would have been obliged to furnish them upon demand * * * but in the absence of such a demand there was no duty resting on the District Attorney to furnish them, especially when the defendant was represented by able counsel. The voluntary failure to make such a demand is a weak foundation for the claim that defendant was deprived of a constitutional right." (People v. Williams, 7 App. Div. 2d 826, 180 N.Y.S. 

2d 955.) The above reasoning would apply, a fortiori, where a long indictment is used, and the granting of the bill is discretionary. See also, People v. Opalka, 204 Misc. 

791, 125 N.Y.S. 2d 790, where defendant's claim, similar to that in the Williams case, was denied by the court upon similar grounds. 

Sec. 169. Time to Demand. The statute specifically states that the bill may be demanded at any stage of the proceedings, commencing with the arraignment. No cases have been found which in any way limit this right. Of course, 294

§ the sooner the bill is acquired, the better will be the preparation of the defense.

Sec. 170. Form of Bill. "The bill of particulars must con tain: 

1. The title of the action, specifying the name of the court to which the indictment is presented, and the names of the parties; 

2. A statement, in ordinary language, without stating items of evidence or necessarily setting forth all the elements of the crime, of such particulars as may be necessary to give the defendant and the court reasonable information as to the matter and character of the crime charged." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 295-h.) Section 295-i gives a form of bill and provides that it "should be signed by the District Attorney."

Sec. 171. Amendment of the Bill. Section 295-j of the Code, providing for the amendment of indictments, discussed in detail in the chapter on that subject, also provides: "The court may likewise, upon the same terms and under similar circumstances, direct the bill of particulars to be amended according to the proof, when a variance between the bill of particulars and the proof shall appear." Notation of the amendment should be indorsed upon the bill in the same manner as in the case of an indictment (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 295-k). No cases concerning amendments of bills have been found and, therefore, reference should be made to the cases on amendments of indictments, contained in the chapter on that subject, for the applicable rules. Since the bill used with a simplified indictment becomes part of the record, there appears to be no valid reason for distinguishing treatment of bills from that afforded indictments on this point. 

Sec. 172. Bill of Defendant. Section 295-1 of the Code re quires the defendant to file a bill, upon the request of the 

District Attorney, stating the details of any "alibi" defense 295

§ 

defendant intends to prove at the trial. The bill must contain a list of the witnesses defendant intends to call to establish his presence elsewhere than at the scene of the crime at the time of the commission of the crime, together with their addresses, names and places of their employment. If the defendant does not furnish the bill, testimony tending to prove the alibi may, not must, be excluded by the court. If the court decides to allow such testimony it must, upon the request of the District Attorney, grant an adjournment of the trial up to three days in length. The bill may be demanded by the District Attorney up to eight days before the trial, and the defendant must furnish the bill within four days after receipt of the demand. Both the bill and the demand therefor must be served upon the opposing party, and a copy filed with the court. 

The defendant may, pursuant to Section 393 of the Code, testify in his own behalf concerning the alibi; Section 295-1 only restricts his right to introduce testimony of witnesses other than himself (People v. Rakiec, 289 N.Y. 306). In

People v. Schade, 161 Misc. 212, 292 N.Y.S. 612, Section 

295-1 was held constitutional against the defendant's attack based, primarily, upon the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. Defendant had moved to set aside the District Attorney's demand for a bill. The court denied this motion, and in answer to defendant's contention that the section "compelled" the defendant to be a witness against himself, stated: "it is still evident that there is no compulsory force about Section 295-1, inasmuch as it merely gives the District Attorney the right to demand certain information * * * certain it is that there is nothing about the section which compels the defendant to incriminate himself, nor is there anything which compels him to give any information to the District Attorney unless he voluntarily and for his own benefit intends to use an alibi defense." An oral demand by the District Attorney has been held ineffective. Service of a written demand was held necessary before the court would direct the defend- 296

§ ant to file a bill (People v. Kamps, 4 Misc. 2d 518, 161 

N.Y.S. 518).

Sec. 173. Contents of Bill of District Attorney. 

Time and Place. In general, where the details requested are immaterial, such as time where such element is unessential under Section 280 of the Code, a bill will not be ordered (People v. Rogers, 150 Misc. 753, 270 N.Y.S. 63).

The interrelation of Sections 295-g and 295-1, discussed in the preceding section, has been recognized by the courts. 

As stated in People v. Wright, 172 Misc. 860, 16 N.Y.S. 2d 

593: "The statutory requirement in regard to alibi witnesses has made it more necessary than before that the defendant be advised with exactitude as to the time and place of the commission of the alleged crime.” There the defendant, indicted under a simplified indictment for second degree rape, pleaded not guilty and demanded a bill containing a description of the acts constituting the offense. The bill served contained the approximate date ("on or about September 12, 1939"), the name of the alleged victim and the name of the town in which the acts were, allegedly, committed. The defendant then moved for a further bill containing the hour, the particular place, and the exact date of the act. The court directed that these particulars be furnished, and noted that the defendant "may have had some sexual intercourse with the prosecutrix at many times and places"; but rape was not a continuing offense and, if the defendant wished to introduce alibi evidence, more than the particulars contained in the first bill would be needed. In so holding, the court noted its disagreement with the decision in People v. Gilbert, 96 

Misc. 660, 118 Misc. 825, 162 N.Y.S. 126, which denied the defendant particulars of the exact place of the commission of the offense. The court noted that Section 295-1 had been enacted after the decision in the Gilbert case.

Similar reasoning was adopted by the court in People v. 

Kamps, supra. There, the defendant was indicted under a 297

§ 

simplified indictment upon five counts-second degree burglary, second degree assault, attempted first degree rape, first degree robbery, and second degree grand larceny. Defendant pleaded mistaken identity and indicated that he would attempt to establish an alibi defense. 

In his demand for a bill, he requested details of a fairly exact nature concerning the date, place, etc. The court, citing the Wright case, directed the District Attorney to furnish the exact date of the occurrences, an accurate location description of the places involved, including street and house numbers, the approximate hours of the acts, and the name of the injured party. The prosecution had claimed that all the acts had been committed during one incident. 

See also People v. Jordan, 283 App. Div. 759, 128 N.Y.S. 2d 

457, where the court noted that although, generally, only the county in which the offense was committed need be supplied, in some cases such as murder, a more exact description may be required.

Generally, the location of the commission of the crime is considered evidentiary matter and need not be supplied by the bill, particularly where the offense is continuing, such as conspiracy (People v. Keohane, 201 Misc. 597, 115 

N.Y.S. 2d 492). The same rule applies to time and date.

However, where the crime alleged was extortion, and the date of commission between December 1, 1938 and January 13, 1939, and the indictment was found approximately four years later, the court directed the defendants to be furnished more specific dates (People v. Parkinson, 181 Misc. 

603, 41 N.Y.S. 2d 331). In the Parkinson case, however, the defendants were not successful in their attempt to obtain more specific details of the place of commission of the crime; the allegation that the crime was committed "in the County of New York" was held sufficient. 

In People v. Hayner, 198 Misc. 101, 97 N.Y.S. 2d 64, the defendant was indicted for second degree rape with a named female, and in four other counts of the same indictment for incest in the same acts on the same dates with the same person, who was alleged to be the defendant's 298

§ daughter. Defendant moved for a bill containing the date, time of day, and location where each act allegedly occurred, and the motion was granted by the court without discussion. In People v. Rogers, 150 Misc. 753, 270 N.Y.S. 63, where defendant was indicted upon two counts of second degree forgery, his motion for a bill giving the time, place, and manner of the forgery was denied, the court stating that the simplified indictment used was sufficient and that "Only in case of doubt should particulars be granted. Evidentiary facts should not be given." 

Sec. 174. Theory of Prosecution. "Before a bill of particulars is ordered, the court should be satisfied that the District Attorney is not thereby practically compelled to make an election of the theory of his case. He should not be placed in the position of determining in advance of the trial, to the peril and embarrassment of the prosecution, what the jury must determine as a fact after the trial. * * * A bill of par- ticulars and the indictment in a case *** must be read together and constitute the written accusation * * * Ever 

a felony was made murder in the first degree, it has been the practice, in prosecutions for that crime, to submit the case to the jury in both aspects, premeditated and deliberate design to take life and killing in the commission of a felony." (People v. Florence, 146 Misc. 735, 262 N.Y.S. 775.) 

Reference can be made to Code of Criminal Procedure, secs. 279, et seq., which provide that the same acts may be alleged in an indictment as constituting "the same crime alleged to have been committed in a different manner" and that "the people shall not be required to elect between the counts of any indictment, except *** for good cause shown, and in the interest of justice." (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 279-a, discussed, supra, in the chapter entitled "Indictments"). These sections evince recognition by the Legislature of the right of the prosecution to proceed upon alternate theories; a right not to be limited by forcing the prosecution to limit itself, in a bill of particulars, to one 299

§ 

theory upon which it will prosecute the case. This rule was recognized by the court in People v. Jordan, 283 App. Div. 

759, 128 N.Y.S. 2d 457, where the court stated: "The other items requested represent the People's evidence and also, in effect, request the District Attorney to state in advance upon what theory under the indictment he intends to try the People's case. The defendant is not entitled to such evidence or a disclosure of the People's theory of trial." However, where the crime charged in the indictment is identified by reference to a section of the Penal Law, which section has several subdivisions, the District Attorney may be required to specify upon which subdivision he is relying (People v. Gallo, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 282).

Sec. 175. Identification of Joint Defendants. Where there are joint defendants, all charged with the same degree of the jointly-committed offense, it is not necessary that the District Attorney identify in a bill of particulars which defendant committed which portion of the offense. Thus, in People v. Keohane, supra, the defendants, indicted for conspiracy and extortion, sought to obtain a bill of particulars identifying each defendant as having committed some specific portion of the offense. The court noted that all the defendants were charged as principals and stated: "The crimes charged and acts done were continuing and it is not necessary that the People identify each defendant separately as to each and every act, for all were charged as principals and the naming of a particular defendant might well be an empty formality." In People v. Florence, 146 

Misc. 735, 262 N.Y.S. 775, the defendants were indicted for first degree murder in a long-form indictment. The defendants moved for a bill particularizing which of the defendants actually shot the victim, killed in the course of the commission of a felony by the defendants. The court directed the District Attorney to furnish these particulars but, on reargument, this direction was eliminated. The court noted that both were charged as principals, that the killing was alleged to have occurred in the course of a 300

§ felony, and "that it is unimportant, for purposes of this motion, which of the two defendants fired the shot *** and to require the furnishing of this particular in such case would be an empty formality." The court did indicate that in a proper case, such as where the defendants were charged with different degrees of the offense, or where one was to attempt to prove an alibi defense, the District Attorney might be required to furnish such particulars. 

However, where so doing would force the prosecution to elect the theory upon which the case is to be prosecuted, such a requirement will not be imposed. 

Sec. 176. Elements of the Crime. It has been held unnecessary that the bill of particulars, or the bill and the indictment together, set forth all the elements of the crime. Only the Code requirements concerning the sufficiency of indictments, such as discussed in the chapter on Indictments, must be met (People v. Bloodgood, 251 App. Div. 593, 298 

N.Y.S. 91). In determining whether these requirements have been met, the bill and the indictment will be read together, in the case of a simplified indictment (People v. 

Opalka, 204 Misc. 791, 175 N.Y.S. 2d 790; People v. Bogdanoff, supra). However, where a long-form indictment has been used, the omission of an essential allegation in the indictment cannot be cured by the discretionary bill (People v. Oliver, 3 N.Y. 2d 684, 171 N.Y.S. 2d 811). In the

Oliver case, the long-form indictment used to allege first degree burglary omitted the requisite allegation that the act had been committed in the night time. 

Sec. 177. Discretion of the Court. As above stated, the granting of a bill of particulars to the defendant is mandatory only when a simplified indictment is used. In other cases where a long-form indictment has been used, it lies within the discretion of the court (People v. Florence, supra). In the Florence case, the court did note that the lack of a preliminary examination was a factor tending toward a decision to grant the bill. However, even under 301

§  

such circumstances, the court will not direct a bill to be furnished which will contain matter otherwise improper, such as evidentiary matter (People v. White, 188 N.Y.S. 

2d 585). The failure of the court to order the furnishing of a bill, after defendant's request therefor, will be considered on appeal if exception has been taken, and will be deemed error only if the court has abused its discretion. 302

Sec. 188. Special Sessions and Police Courts Sec. 189. New York City Courts PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

In a previous chapter it was noted that the preliminary examination before the magistrate is frequently referred to as the arraignment. The discussion that follows will be confined to the arraignment that takes place after an indictment has been found and presented. If the defendant is free on bail he, or his counsel if notice of appearance has been filed, will be informed of the date of arraignment. If no preliminary examination has been held, a bench warrant will be issued for his arrest and he will be brought to the court in which the indictment has been found, or to which it has been removed for trial, and asked to plead to the indictment. 

If the defendant is in prison on a prior conviction, the court in which the indictment is pending is empowered to issue a writ of habeas corpus, for the purpose of securing the attendance of the prisoner at the arraignment.

Counsel should ask for a copy of the indictment or make the necessary arrangements to procure one. Pleas to the indictment will be treated in a subsequent chapter. Unless the defendant 303

§ 

intends to plead guilty, counsel should request additional time to prepare motions addressed to the indictment or a demurrer. If the plea of not guilty is interposed at this time, counsel should be certain to obtain the permission of the court to withdraw the plea, in order to move or demur at a later date. 

Sec. 178. Definitions. The Code of Criminal Procedure treats arraignments in two separate chapters. The arraignment of the defendant, in advance of the trial, is treated in Chapter IV of Title 5 (Sections 296-312), and we will consider it in this chapter. The arraignment of the defendant for sentencing after trial, dealt with in Section 480 of the Code, is not within the purview of the present chapter, but is treated in the subsequent chapter titled "Sentence, Judgment and Execution." "To arraign is nothing else but to call the prisoner to the Bar of the court to answer the matter charged upon him in the indictment." (4 Blackstone Comm. 322.) "The arraignment must be made by the court, or by the clerk or District Attorney, under its direction, and consists in stating the charge in the indictment to the defendant, and in asking him whether he pleads guilty or not guilty thereto. 

If the defendant demand it, the indictment must be read, or a copy thereof furnished to him before requiring him to plead." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 309.) Some authorities have considered the "arraignment" to consist only of that part of the proceeding described in the first portion of the above section, and have considered the plea of the defendant as another proceeding, separate and distinct from the arraignment by the court. "It is true that *** what is called an arraignment, generally includes the pleading of the accused; but I think the more strict meaning of the word is confined to the action of the court." (Whitehead v. 

Commonwealth, 19 Gratt. [Va.] 640.) Compare People v. 

DiMedicis, 39 Misc. 438, 80 N.Y.S. 212: "the arraignment is what is commonly referred to as the 'pleading'." Inasmuch as the defendant's plea is treated in a separate chapter herein, the arraignment discussed in this chapter, 304

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 178 except where otherwise noted, is intended to apply to the action of the court only, not the response thereto by the defendant. This is consistent with Blackstone's definition, quoted above, and with the definition of the Virginia court in the Whitehead case, supra.

The arraignment of the defendant is to be distinguished from the preliminary examination. Preliminary exami nations are treated in Chapter VII of Title 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Sections 188-221-b), and in a separate chapter of this work. The distinction between the two procedures is that the preliminary examination is conducted before a magistrate following the arrest of the defendant (Code Crim. Proc., secs. 188, 190); arraignments are had before the court in which the action is to be tried and follow the indictment (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 296). 

It is the first opportunity of the defendant to have the indictment formally presented to him. It leads to the next step--the defendant's plea; any discharge must await the plea, or motion, and may be considered a separate procedure. The procedures themselves, moreover, are dissimilar. In preliminary examinations, depositions and examinations of witnesses are taken; in arraignments, there is no occasion for such examinations. 

There is no similarity between the essential purposes of the two procedures. The sole object of the preliminary examination "is to ascertain sufficient reasons to justify the holding of the accused, until the matter has been presented and passed upon by the Grand Jury. Even the discharge of the magistrate is in no degree final and effective." 

(People v. Steiger, 159 Misc. 538, 277 N.Y.S. 602.) "The purpose of arraignment is to inform the defendant of the crime of which he is charged and to obtain his plea to the indictment." (People v. Schwartz, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 741.) It has also been stated that another object of the arraignment is to establish the identity of the accused (Parker v. Frost, 5 Parker Cr. 52). Since the arraignment, by definition, occurs after an indictment has been found there is no question of establishing sufficient reason for holding the 305

§ 

accused in such a proceeding. One desired end, served by both procedures, is the implementing of the command of the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution: 

"In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall *** be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation." Article 

I, section 6, of the New York State Constitution contains identical language.

Sec. 179. Right to Speedy Arraignment. Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure reads: "The defendant must in all cases be taken before the magistrate without unnecessary delay, and he may give bail at any hour of the day or night." Some confusion may arise concerning the applicability of this section to arraignments as we have defined them. Since, under Section 296, the defendant must be arraigned before the court in which the indictment was found, or the court to which the indictment has been sent or removed, Section 165 seems inapplicable to arraignments after indictment, for no magistrate is involved. 

In People v. Bardall, 4 Misc. 2d 945, 160 N.Y.S. 2d 167, the defendant sought, in a proceeding in the nature of coram nobis, to vacate and set aside a judgment convicting him upon his guilty plea. The application was based upon Section 165, and alleged a three-day delay after his arrest, before arraignment. The court, denying his petition on the ground that no unreasonable delay had taken place, stated: "When the cases cited under Section 165 are examined, it is found that the section covers cases of an officer making an arrest for a crime committed in his presence or where an information has been laid and a warrant issued by a magistrate. In these and similar instances the defendant should be taken before a magistrate without unnecessary delay. *** The petitioner herein was originally arrested on an indictment charging a felony. Section 296, Code of 

Criminal Procedure, states that this arraignment must take place before the court in which the indictment was found or before the court to which it was sent or removed. 306

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 179 The prisoner was arraigned in accordance with that section. *** I am convinced that there was no unreasonable delay in petitioner's arraignment." 

The Bardall decision, on its facts, does not so hold but the language of the court indicates an awareness of the distinction between the requisites of arraignment after indictment, under Section 296, and after arrest, under Section 165. In many cases the defendant will have been arrested prior to the indictment, and the arraignment before a magistrate under Section 165, will already have occurred. 

The purposes of requiring a speedy "arraignment," in the Section 165 sense, also indicate a ground of distinction. One of the reasons for Section 165's requirement of a speedy arraignment is to prohibit the detention of the prisoner by the police for an indefinite time, prior to hearing. After an indictment has been returned, the arraignment will not affect this.

In People v. Spano, 4 N.Y. 2d 256, the defendant surrendered after he had been indicted and a bench warrant had been issued. He reported to the police precinct with his counsel to surrender on February 4, 1957 at 7:15 P.M. He was questioned until midnight, and then booked. The questioning continued until 3:30 A.M., when he confessed. The next morning he was arraigned before a County Judge. 

There was no claim that the defendant had been physically or psychologically coerced into making the confession. The defendant contended that he had been denied a prompt arraignment and the benefit of counsel. The Court of Appeals stated, while denying his contention: "The rules of criminal procedure requiring prompt arraignment are designed in the main to guarantee that a person will not be detained except upon a clear showing of probable cause, and to provide the defendant with the opportunity of procuring legal counsel. * * ** Here there is evidence that these objectives had in effect been met. The indictment is, of course, a determination that probable cause existed for believing defendant to be guilty of the crime charged. 

307

§ 

24 As for the opportunity to procure counsel, the record shows that defendant did have the benefit of counsel and counsel's instructions preliminary to his surrender." 

In People v. Muro, 115 N.Y.S. 2d 318, the court stated: "The appellant's counsel's argument as to the illegality of his arraignment is based on Section 296 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure. * * * Section 296 * * * refers to ar raignments when an indictment is filed and concededly such an arraignment must be held in open court. However an arraignment before a magistrate as provided in Sections 165 and 188 of the Code *** does not require an arraignment in court. The provisions of Section 165 * * * 

requiring an arraignment before a magistrate, without unnecessary delay, constitutes a compelling reason for not requiring an arraignment before a magistrate or a judge of a court of special sessions, to be held in the evenings, on holidays, at hours when court would ordinarily not be in session. From time immemorial it has been the practice and custom to arraign defendants before Justices of the Peace and judges of courts of special sessions at their homes, places of business or wherever they may be reached so that the defendant would not be denied his right to bail and arraignment without unnecessary delay as provided by law." Insofar as speedy arraignment is designed to prevent the prisoner's being held incommunicado, or subjecting him to pressures designed to force a confession, a speedy arraignment would be desirable in all cases. Similar reasoning applies to one thereby being prevented from obtaining bail. If the prisoner has been arrested pursuant to a bench warrant, then, according to the terms of the warrant, he must be brought before the court or judge there named as soon as possible after the arrest. In general, although the language of Section 165 might not appear applicable to one arrested after indictment, the purposes of that section, and the constitutional guarantees of a speedy trial, and the protection afforded by habeas corpus, should protect a defendant from undue delays. 308

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 180 

Sec. 180. Necessity of Arraignment. "The authorities are quite numerous to the effect that in a criminal case an arraignment and plea are essential and necessary prelimi naries to a legal trial upon an indictment. *** Section 296 

*** declares that when the indictment is filed the defendant must be arraigned thereon. The defendant on arraignment may either demur or plead to the indictment (Sec. 

221) and the plea makes the issue of law or fact to be tried. 

The object of the arraignment is to inform the defendant of the charge against him and have him answer to the indictment. *** A formal plea of not guilty is not necessary to put the defendant on trial. Under the Revised Statutes (2 R.S. 730, sec. 70) a demand of trial by a defendant was declared to be an equivalent to a plea of not guilty. It is sufficient, we think, to constitute an issue that the defendant on his arraignment informs the court that he denies the charge or that he demands a trial." (People v. Bradner, 170 N.Y.1.)

In the Bradner case, where defendant had pleaded not guilty, then was permitted to withdraw the plea to move to dismiss the indictment which motion was denied, the court considered the withdrawal to have been only for purposes of the motion and deemed the subsequent proceeding with trial by all parties as having evidenced their adoption of that interpretation. The court further indicated that the failure to renew the plea formally, under the circumstances, was merely a formal defect. Thus, it was not held ground for reversal under Section 285 of the Code as it did not prejudice the substantial rights of the defendant. In People v. McHale, 61 Hun 618, 15 N.Y.S. 496, the court allowed an arraignment in the midst of the trial, when it appeared that there had previously been none. That court also cited Section 285 and noted that the defendant had not suffered by reason of the delay in arraignment, as he had been permitted to produce all his evidence and make any motions and objections desired.

In Matter of Rudd v. Hazard, 266 N.Y. 302, it was held that a Special County Judge, acting in chambers in the 309

§ 

absence of the County Judge, could not allow an arraignment, accept a change of plea, and impose sentence upon an indictment. The defendant had previously been arraigned in court and had pleaded not guilty. The County 

Judge had thereafter adjourned the term to his chambers at a later date. In the interim, the rearraignment, change of plea to guilty of a lesser offense, and sentencing occurred. The prisoner thereafter brought mandamus proceedings to compel the expunging of the proceedings from the record and to compel a trial upon the original notguilty plea. The court stated: "the proceedings before the 

Special County Judge *** could be had only at a session of a regular or adjourned stated term. These proceedings consisted of arraignment, plea and judgment. An arraignment must be 'before the court'. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

296.) A plea of guilty must be put in 'in open court' * * * judgment must be pronounced while the court is in session. *** Publicity, not secrecy, in arraignment, plea and judgment is part of our tradition. *** Only at stated terms where the general public is advised of the time and place of sessions, both regular and adjourned, is such publicity possible. Since the matter is one of jurisdiction, the fact that all parties went voluntarily before the Special 

County Judge does not change the result."

Federally-Based Rights. In Crain v. United States, 162 

U.S. 625, 40 L. Ed. 1097, the Supreme Court held "that in a 

Federal court no valid trial could be had without the requisite arraignment and plea, and that such must be shown by the record of conviction." Under that reasoning objections could be raised in a State court based on due process grounds. However in Garland v. Washington, 232 U.S. 642, 58 L. Ed. 772, the Court overruled the Crain case, and stated: "If a legal trial cannot be had without a plea to the indictment, duly entered of record before trial * * * such omission in the present case requires a reversal of the judgment of conviction, because the prisoner has been deprived of due process of law. Technical objections of this character were undoubtedly given much more weight 310

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 180 

formerly than they are now. Such rulings originated in that period of English history when the accused was entitled to few rights in the presentation of his defense. * * *

Under that system the courts were disposed to require that the technical forms and methods of procedure should be fully complied with. [Now] any reason for such strict adherence to the mere formalities of trial would seem to have passed away." The court went on to quote, with approval, the dissenting opinion of Mr. Justice Peckham, in the Crain case: "Here the defendant would not have been injured by an inadvertence of this nature. He ought to be held to have waived that which, under the circumstances, would have been a wholly unimportant formality. A waiver ought to be conclusively implied where the parties had proceeded as if defendant had been duly arraigned, and a formal plea of not guilty had been interposed, and where there was no objection made on account of its absence until, as in this case, the record was brought to this Court for review." Thus, due process does not require a formal arraignment when the defendant goes to trial under a not guilty plea, or a course of action equivalent thereto. Compare: ❝* * * in this state *** failure to arraign a defendant who subsequently proceeds to trial is not an omission which tends to prejudice his rights. See People v. Towers, 63 Hun. 

624, 17 N.Y.S. 395, 396, affirmed in 135 N.Y. 457, N.E. 145." (People v. Schwartz, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 741.)

However where a situation such as that involved in the Rudd case, supra, occurs-the lack of an arraignment, or a secret arraignment, plus a guilty plea-it is doubtful whether the reasoning of the Garland case would apply. 

There the recognized purpose of an arraignment, informing the accused of the charge against him, would not adequately be served by other procedures, as in the case of a not-guilty plea. Thus where defendant is not represented by counsel and enters a guilty plea after an improper arraignment, his conviction may be set aside. (People v. Koch, 299 N.Y. 378). 311

§ 

 Sec. 181. Requisites and Sufficiency of Arraignment. If the defendant has counsel, and that counsel has filed a notice of appearance in the court in which the indictment is returnable, "the District Attorney must give at least one day's notice to such attorney of the time and place of the defendant's arraignment on such indictment." (Code 

Crim. Proc., sec. 296-a.) The defendant must be personally present for the arraignment unless he has been indicted for a misdemeanor, in which case he may appear by coun sel (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 297). Under Sec. 335 of the 

Code, pleas of guilty may be entered only by the defendant personally in open court, except in certain cases involving Vehicle and Traffic Law offenses which are treated in Section 335, subdivision 2. Section 297 applies only to courts of record. Arraignments in special sessions courts, or 

Magistrate's Courts, are treated separately, infra. 

If the defendant is in custody at the time the arraignment is to take place, the court may direct his personal production for the arraignment (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

298), and, if necessary, may issue a writ of habeas corpus to bring him into court if he is in custody (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 298, subdivisions a and b). 

Sec. 182. Right to Counsel. "If the defendant appear for arraignment without counsel, he must be asked if he desire the aid of counsel, and if he does the court must assign counsel." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 308.) Section 308 goes on to provide for payment of the assigned counsel in cases involving possible imposition of the death penalty, and for payment at county expense to expert witnesses who may be required in such cases, where the defendant is financially unable to pay therefor, and for the supplying of copies of the daily testimony to the defendant. The courts have always had the power to assign counsel to destitute defendants (People ex rel. Acritelli v. Grout, 87 App. Div. 

193, 84 N.Y.S. 97), but, prior to the enactment of Section 

308, they had no power to award compensation to such counsel (People v. Medicis, 39 Misc. 438, 80 N.Y.S. 42). 312

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 182 The right of the accused to counsel, and to be advised of his right to counsel, is a vital one for obvious reasons, and failure of the courts to comply with the requirements of the law in this area will, usually, entitle the defendant to vacation of a judgment of conviction on writ of error coram nobis. Both the United States Constitution (Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments) and the New York State

Constitution (Article I, section 6) grant such rights to de fendants. Section 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that a defendant in a criminal action "is entitled *** to be allowed counsel as in civil actions, or he may appear and defend in person and with counsel." Section 188 of the Code also states that on the prisoner's being taken before a magistrate, after arrest, the magistrate "must immediately inform him of the charge against him, and of his right to the aid of counsel in every stage of the proceedings, and before any further proceedings are had." 

In People v. Hunt, 258 App. Div. 24, 16 N.Y.S. 2d 19, it was stated: "While Section 308, except in the heading, does not specifically state that a person who has been indicted and appears for arraignment without counsel shall be informed of his right to counsel, it would nevertheless seem that such would be the requirement at common law. It might be argued that it should be assumed that Section 188 has already been complied with before the indictment of defendant when he was brought before the magistrate, and that it would be unnecessary to again inform him of his right to counsel at the time of his arraignment. This does not follow. In many cases indictments are found before arrest and defendants are brought up for arraignment upon indictments without ever having been before examining magistrates." In this respect, the discussion in the preceding section of this chapter concerning the use of the term "arraignment" to apply to the defendant's appearance before the magistrate should be noted. In the lower court's opinion, as stated by the Appellate Division in the Hunt case, the County Judge "compares the provi sions of Sections 308 and 188 of the Code of Criminal Pro- 

313

§ 

cedure, and concludes, as I take it, that a prisoner is not entitled to be informed of his right to counsel, upon arraignment after indictment but only when he is taken before a magistrate after arrest." This distinction between the two proceedings was held unwarranted, at least as it applied to the right to be advised of the right to counsel. 

The United States Supreme Court has held that the failure, actual or in effect, to assign counsel in a capital case is a violation of due process of law. See Johnson v. 

Zerbst, 304 U.S. 455, 82 L. Ed. 1461, where the Court stated that habeas corpus was the proper remedy if "from all of the evidence *** petitioner has sustained the burden of proof resting upon him and that he did not competently and intelligently waive his right to counsel, it will follow that the trial court did not have jurisdiction to proceed to judgment and conviction *** and he will therefore be entitled to have his petition granted." This statement was quoted with approval by the Appellate Division in the Hunt case, which went on to state: "it seems to me to necessarily follow that a plea of guilty could not logically be taken as a waiver of the constitutional requirement that he be informed of his right to counsel." "The proffer [of counsel] should be unequivocal and unconditional." (People v. Hinsch, 3 App. Div. 2d 915, 162 

N.Y.S. 2d 602.) In the Hinsch case, defendant, free on bail, was advised of his right to counsel and stated that he understood that if he asked for counsel his bail would be revoked, to which the court replied: "I don't know that it is so, but if you are prepared to proceed without counsel you may do so." It was held that he had not, effectively, been offered counsel. See also People v. Koch, 299 N.Y. 378, for a similar result in a similar situation. Compare People v. Crimi, 303 N.Y. 749, where it was held that the defendant's personal interpretation of the proffer of counsel, to the effect that he would be required to pay assigned counsel, was not a ground for the relief sought by him. 

In summary: "not only is it the duty of the court to comply with the procedural formalities and requirements 314

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 183 of advising a defendant of his right to counsel, but that it is the further and clear duty of every court to see to it that if a defendant refuses the aid of counsel, that such waiver is a competent and intelligent waiver, and furthermore, that the court be convinced that the defendant intelligently understands the meaning and consequence of his plea of guilt." (People v. Carroll, 112 N.Y.S. 2d 227.) "It is settled that a defendant upon his arraignment must be advised not only of his right to counsel, but also of his right to a postponement of the proceedings in order to enable him to obtain and consult with counsel, and, of course, he must be given a reasonable opportunity to ask for counsel and such adjournment before being required to plead to the charge against him. * * * And, to render the applicable statutory provisions meaningful and effective, this court recently declared in the Marincic case (2 N.Y. 2d, at page 

184,) the judge presiding must 'make it clear' that such are the defendant's rights." (People v. Banner, 5 N.Y. 2d 109.)

The accused person does not have the right to have counsel assigned at the time of sentence, if he has been represented during the trial (People v. Hasenstab, 283 App. Div. 433, 

128 N.Y.S. 2d 388), but a court is authorized to appoint counsel at any time before trial, or at the trial (People ex rel. Acritelli v. Grout, 87 App. Div. 193, 84 N.Y.S. 97). 

Sec. 183. Time to Answer Indictment. "If, on the arraignment, the defendant require it, he must be allowed until the next day, or such further time as may be allowed him as the court may deem reasonable, to answer the indictment." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 311.) If the defendant has been indicted without any preliminary examination, certain courts have held that he should, therefore, be allowed to inspect the Grand Jury minutes prior to being required to plead to the indictment. (See People v. Molineux, 27 Misc. 

60, 57 N.Y.S. 936.) It has also been held that prior to arraignment a motion to set aside the indictment may not be heard (People v. Equitable Gas Light Co., 5 N.Y.S. 19). 315

§ 

Sec. 184. Motions to be Made at Arraignment. For a more extensive discussion of the time to move to set aside or dismiss indictments, see chapter on "Motion to Dismiss Indictment." It should be noted that some cases have held that such motion will not be heard prior to arraignment (People v. Equitable Gas Light Co., supra). There, a corporation attempted, through counsel, to appear specially for the purpose of moving to set aside an indictment on the ground that Sections 675-682 of the Code had not been complied with. Those sections govern proceedings against corporations. The court denied the motion, noting that "defendant has not appeared by counsel, and has not been arraigned upon the indictment, and it follows that the motion to set it aside cannot be entertained. It is true counsel have appeared and have moved to set aside the indictment; but he expressly stated to the court that he appeared only for that purpose, and that he did not appear generally, for the defendant, nor did the defendant appear except for the purpose of the motion." See also Section 313 of the

Code, which provides that a motion to set aside indictments, on the grounds there enumerated, "must be [heard] by the court in which the defendant is arraigned." In People ex rel. Jannicky v. Warden, 231 App. Div. 131, 246 

N.Y.S. 194, affirmed without opinion 255 N.Y. 623, the court noted the District Attorney's argument that the writ of habeas corpus applied for should not be entertained because made in a court other than that in which the defendant was arraigned, being based upon a ground within the scope of Section 313, "which provides that an indictment may not be set aside except in the court of arraignment," but based its decision on other grounds. 

Sec. 185. Bench Warrants. If, after the indictment, a defendant who has previously been arrested, and who has been discharged on bail, does not appear to be arraigned at the time set therefor, "or if the defendant be for any cause absent when his personal attendance is necessary, the court, in addition to the forfeiture of any undertaking 316

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 185 of bail, or, of any money deposited, may direct the clerk to issue a bench warrant for his arrest." (Code of Crim. 

Proc. sec. 299.) The form of the warrant is prescribed by Section 301 of the Code, and under Section 300 the bench warrant may be issued by the clerk, on application of the District Attorney, at any time after the order has been entered. The warrant may also be issued by the District 

Attorney himself at any time after the indictment.

The bench warrant commands that the peace officer executing it bring the defendant before the court in which the indictment was found, or to which the indictment has been sent or removed, or, if the court has been adjourned for the term, to deliver the defendant to the custody of the Sheriff of the county or to another appropriate custodian. 

District Attorneys, when issuing bench warrants, need not follow the form prescribed by Section 310 (People v. 

Mead, 64 How. Pr. 41, affirmed 92 N.Y. 415). A bench warrant will be considered sufficient even if not exactly in the statutory form, if it states clearly the offense for which the defendant has been indicted, and the place and court in which the indictment is pending (People v. Mead, supra).

If the offense for which the defendant has been indicted is a misdemeanor, the bench warrant must contain a direction that, if the defendant require it, the peace officer executing the warrant must take him before a magistrate in the county in which he was arrested, or in the county in which the indictment is pending, so that he may give bail. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 302). The warrant may contain the issuing court's direction of the amount of the bail to be allowed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 303).

If the defendant has previously given bail, the court to which the indictment is presented, sent, or removed for trial, may order the defendant committed without bail, or may order increased bail after the indictment is filed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 306). If the defendant is not present when the order is entered, a bench warrant may be issued to secure his presence; if the defendant is then pres- 317

$

ent he may be committed at that time. See the discussion of bench warrants in the chapter of this work titled "Arrests With Warrant."

Sec. 186. Insanity. Under Section 336 of the Code, treated in greater detail in the chapter on "Pleas to Indictment," pleas of insanity may be interposed at the arraignment, as a specification of a not guilty plea. 

Sec. 187. Traffic Violations. Sections 335, 335-a and 335-b of the Code provide, generally, the rules governing arraignments upon traffic violations. The instructions to be given by the court to the violator are there prescribed, together with the method of accepting guilty pleas, and of accepting waivers of the right to arraignments in these cases.

Sec. 188. Special Sessions and Police Courts. Section 699 of the Code prescribes the proceedings to be had in courts of special sessions and Police Courts in counties outside of New York. The section provides for notification by the magistrate, directed to the defendant, "of the charge against him and of his right to the aid of counsel in every stage of the proceedings and before any further proceedings are had, together with provision for the allowance of time to the defendant to procure counsel, the reading of the charge to the defendant, and a requirement that before a court accepts a guilty plea (except to Vehicle and Traffic Law offenses, which are treated under Section 335) advice be given to the defendant of the possible effect of prior convictions upon the severity of his sentence.

Sec. 189. New York City Courts. The New York City Crim inal Courts Act, sections 101 through 107, provides the rules applicable to arraignments in City Magistrates' Courts. Section 101 provides for the hours and dates of holding such courts, including the provision for the holding of court on Sundays, Saturdays and holidays for 318

ARRAIGNMENTS 

§ 189 arraignments. Under Section 103, City Magistrates are, generally, given the same powers as General Sessions 

Judges and County Court Judges concerning the allowance of bail, with, however, certain limitations upon their power to reduce bail previously set. Section 106 provides that City 

Magistrates shall first ascertain, upon an arraignment, whether the offense was committed within their territorial jurisdiction before proceeding further, with exceptions in the case of defendants who are unable to be taken to the court which has territorial jurisdiction over the offense. 

Under Section 107, the holding of the defendant on bail or in custody for a period of up to 48 hours is allowed if at the arraignment an affidavit made by an officer is produced, stating that the evidence is not yet complete or that the complainant is absent because of physical injury, disability or some other unknown reason. Section 115 requires that the defendant be notified at the arraignment of his right to communicate with friends or relatives without charge.

New York City Criminal Courts Act, section 31, provides that the procedures provided for in the Code of Criminal Procedure, "consistent with this act regulating and controlling the practice and procedure of the Court of General Sessions of the Peace in the City and County of New York shall apply as far as may be, to the practice and procedure in the Court of Special Sessions, and shall regulate and control the practice and procedure of the said court, in so far as its jurisdiction and organization will permit." 

There being no specific statutory provision relating to arraignments in the Court of Special Sessions, this conformity statute is applicable and the provisions of the Code relating to arraignments after indictment generally apply to that court. 319
