Counsel should forego no opportunity to attack the indictment if the grounds therefor exist. 

The usual sequence of steps is to move to dismiss the indictment, and if the motion is not granted to enter a demurrer. If the demurrer is not sustained, defendant will plead to the indictment. In a subsequent chapter, another available remedy, motion in arrest of judgment, will be considered. 

A motion based on the technical grounds enumerated in Sec. 

313 of the Code must be made at the arraignment, or counsel must preserve this right by securing the permission of the court to make it at a later date. The objections raised by this motion are pre- 320

§ sumed waived if not made at the arraignment or at the adjourned date.

However, a motion based on the insufficiency of the indictment, or the proof adduced before the Grand Jury to obtain it, may be made at any time up to the time of the trial, or even at the trial itself. These grounds are discussed in the instant chapter. 

It is made on a notice of motion and affidavits setting forth the facts relied on. As indicated in the next chapter, this application is frequently combined with a motion to inspect the minutes. If the defendant makes an affidavit, matter should be excluded therefrom that may prejudice him at the trial. The better practice would be for the attorney to make the affidavit, on information and belief. 

Counsel may well believe that a motion attacking the sufficiency of the indictment or the evidence supporting it should not be made at too early a date. He will merely call the defects to the attention of the District Attorney and enable him to correct them. He may well consider allowing the testimony at the trial to point up the defects in pleading and proof, and move to dismiss the indictment at the conclusion of the People's case. 

Sec. 190. Compared with Demurrer. There are different means of attacking indictments. One of these is the demurrer, which assumes for the purposes of the attack that the facts stated in the indictment are true but posits that nevertheless a fatal defect is apparent. Demurrers raise only issues of law; a motion to dismiss may raise issues of fact, and may rely upon defects not apparent upon the face of the indictment. While the terms "set aside" and "dismiss" are used interchangeably in this area, Chapter V of 

Title 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Sections 313320) is entitled "Setting Aside the Indictment." Thus, that term will be used here. 

Sec. 191. Grounds. The grounds upon which motions to set aside indictments may be based can, generally, be grouped as follows: attacks based on defects in the procedure of the Grand Jury which found the indictment (such as in the finding, filing, or endorsement of the indictment); attacks based on the quality or quantity of the evidence upon which 321

§ 

the Grand Jury acted; and, attacks based upon violation of an accused's constitutional rights by the Grand Jury's action (such as indictments which violate defendant's right not to be subjected to double jeopardy). Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that the indictment must be set aside by the court in which the defendant is arraigned and upon his motion, in either of two cases but in no other.

The first ground provided by Section 313 is that the indictment is not found, endorsed and presented as prescribed in Sections 268 and 272. Section 268 requires the concurrence of twelve grand jurors and endorsement as a "true bill" by the foreman. Section 272 requires the indictment's presentment by the foreman in court and filing, and imposes a prohibition against its exhibition until the defendant has been arrested or appears.

The second ground under Section 313 is that a person has been permitted to be present during the session of the Grand Jury while the charge embraced in the indictment was under consideration, except as provided in Sections 255 through 257. These sections prohibit persons other than those duly authorized, such as the District Attorney, stenographer, etc., from attending Grand Jury sessions.

These grounds will be considered in detail below. However, despite the seeming exclusion of Section 313, attacks upon indictments by motion to set aside upon grounds other than those enumerated in that section are permissible. 

This principle was established in the leading case of People v. Glen, 173 N.Y.395.

In the Glen case, the defendant, indicted for embracery (influencing a juror unlawfully), after the overruling of his demurrer moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that the Grand Jury had received certain illegal evidence. The Court of Appeals, while considering the case upon an appeal from defendant's conviction, recognized that the basis of the motion "is not one of the grounds specified in Section 313." Thus the court was first faced with the question of whether a motion by a defendant to 

322

§ dismiss an indictment against him can be entertained on any other grounds than those specified in Section 313. The court's answer to that question was yes. In so holding, the court stated: "it is *** clear that no legislative enactment can be permitted to deprive the citizen of any of his constitutional rights. From time immemorial our commonlaw courts have exercised the power to set aside and quash indictments on motion, not only for defects in form, but for irregularities and errors that were proved by extrinsic 

our courts have also always asserted and exercised the power to set aside indictments whenever it has been made to appear that they have been found without evidence, or upon illegal and incompetent testimony *** a power which the Legislature can neither curtail nor abolish, and, to the extent that legislative enactments are designed to effect either of these ends, they are unconstitutional. *** So far as said Section 313 is intended to regulate only matters of procedure which involve no constitutional rights, it is valid and must be obeyed by the courts; but to the extent that it may *** affect the constitutional rights of a defendant it has no force and is void." The nonstatutory, constitutionally-based, grounds for motions to set aside indictments are also discussed in greater detail below. The most common ground is the one mentioned above, the insufficiency of the evidence before the Grand 

Jury to sustain the indictment.

The indictment is presumed to be based upon adequate, competent evidence, and the proceedings of the Grand Jury are presumed to be in accordance with the statutory requirements (People v. Howell, 3 N.Y. 2d 153). Thus the defendant will have the burden of proof, and of coming forward with evidence, to rebut these presumptions. 

Throughout this area of the law it will be found that many cases, deciding whether an indictment should be dismissed, have been initiated by a motion to inspect the minutes of the Grand Jury. These motions are discussed in detail in the chapter so entitled. Similarly, many cases discussed in that chapter were initiated by contemporaneous motions 323

§ 

to inspect the minutes and motions to dismiss. As stated in that chapter, the only purpose of a motion to inspect the minutes is to lay the foundation for a motion to set aside the indictment. When such a motion is made the courts may, and frequently do, inspect the minutes to determine if, in fact, there is a basis for a motion to set aside the indictment. When a defect is found by the court, it will often then set aside the indictment without waiting for the defendant to make the motion. The applicable principles are the same in both cases except where otherwise noted. 

Sec. 192. Irregularity in Grand Jury Proceedings. The first subdivision of Section 313 requires the indictment to be found in conformity with the provision of Sections 268 and 272. Section 268 of the Code requires the concurrence of at least twelve grand jurors for the finding of an indictment. 

Section 224, not specifically referred to in Section 313, requires the presence of at least twelve grand jurors before any business can be transacted. In People v. Herrmans, 69 

Misc. 303, 125 N.Y.S. 143, the court set aside an indictment, on defendant's motion under Section 313, because fewer than 16 jurors were present when the indictment was presented in court. However, as in People v. Brinkman, 205 

Misc. 337, 340, 126 N.Y.S. 2d 495, 500: "Our practice has changed so that now, the indictment need no longer be presented in the presence of the body of grand jurors." This change in procedure was also recognized in People v. Pizzimenti, 13 Misc. 2d 82, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 935, so that the Herrmans case is no longer valid in its holding on this point. 

However, attacks may be made under Section 313, based on the lack of a quorum of grand jurors at the sessions when the evidence was being presented, or the lack of a sufficient number of grand jurors having voted to find the indictment. In the Brinkman case, supra, the court stated, after referring to the Herrmans case: "the concern for faithful attendance is even more evident." The defendant 

Brinkman had moved for inspection of the minutes, and the attendance records of the Grand Jury, alleging that 324

§ these records would show that "there were not at least 12 who had heard substantially all of the evidence adduced in connection with the crimes charged to defendant." The court examined these records, found defendant's contention to be true and stated: "The court finds from the attendance records and the Grand Jury minutes that there were not twelve who had heard all of the evidence, and concludes that the indictment should be set aside for that reason." 

However, the dismissal was reversed by the Appellate Division (286 App. Div. 889, 142 N.Y.S. 2d 389), which reversal was affirmed by the Court of Appeals in 309 N.Y. 974, where the Court stated: "At least twelve of the grand jurors, who voted to indict heard all essential evidence including the testimony of the defendant. Based on such evidence the Grand Jury was privileged to return an indictment. * * * The only testimony not heard by at least twelve of the jurors was of an incriminating nature but was not necessary to the finding of the indictment as it was merely repetitious." Thus motions to set aside may be made if less than twelve jurors concur in the finding of the indictment (People v. Shattuck, 6 Abb. N.C. 33), or if less than a quorum were present when at least all the evidence tending toward proof of the innocence of the accused was heard. However, under Brinkman, the minimal number need not be present at all sessions, if twelve or more heard evidence sufficient to indict. 

The fact that certain jurors were not qualified, thus reducing the number of qualified jurors to less than the amount required for a quorum, is not a proper ground for a motion to set aside an indictment. "There is no provision in the Criminal Code for the right of anyone indicted to challenge a grand juror. * * * *** after the finding of an indictment there can be no challenge to the individual grand jurors." (People v. Pizzimenti, supra.) In the Pizzimenti case, the service of two non-qualified persons on the Grand 

Jury was held not to invalidate the indictment. See also 

People v. Farmer, 194 N.Y. 251, 87 N.E. 457, concerning the methods of objection to grand jurors (Code of Crim. 325

§ 

Proc., secs. 238, 239). However, where the challenge is to the panel, or to the method of selecting the Grand Jury, other problems arise.

It has been held that the invalidity of the statute under which the Grand Jury was selected may not be attacked by a motion to set aside the indictment (People v. Hooghberk, 96 N.Y. 149). As stated by Chief Judge Lehman, concurring in People v. Prior, 294 N.Y. 405: "The court has, however, no inherent or statutory power to set aside an indictment found by a Grand Jury because there were errors in applying the statutory method of procuring an impartial jury where the jury as impanelled conforms to the traditional concept of a Grand Jury and consists of a qualified group of men and women who represent a fair cross section of *** impartial citizens." Although Section 

231 of the Code provides that no challenge to the panel of Grand Jurors is permitted, if the defect alleged is the systematic exclusion of a class of persons from Grand Juries, the holding of the Supreme Court in Pierre v. Louisiana, 306 U.S. 354, 83 L. Ed. 757, would appear to require dismissal of any indictment found by such a jury. In People v. Harris, 182 Misc. 787, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 745, reversed 268 App. 

Div. 731, 54 N.Y.S. 2d 161, reversed 294 N.Y. 424, the Pierre case was cited with approval, and an indictment dismissed on analogous grounds. 

Sec. 193. Presence of Unauthorized Persons. In People v. 

Dorsey, 176 Misc. 432, N.Y.S. 2d 637, the defendant moved to inspect the minutes, alleging that the subsequent motion to set aside the indictment would be based upon the unauthorized presence of an Assistant Attorney General during the Grand Jury sessions. The indictment returned was signed by the Assistant Attorney General "In Charge of the Kings County Investigation," although the indictment was found in Queens County. The court stated that the descriptive words after the signature were surplusage and could be disregarded. The court noted a conflict in the decisions concerning the powers of the Attorney General 326

§ to conduct criminal prosecutions, and held that in New York he is limited to those powers granted in the State Constitution and in Statutes. The court then found that in the case being considered none of those powers was involved, therefore his presence was unauthorized, and the defendant's motion was granted. 

In People v. Minet, 271 App. Div. 345, 66 N.Y.S. 2d 391, the defendant, on appeal from a judgment of conviction of a charge of rape of a fourteen year old girl, raised the question of the propriety of an order, made before trial, denying his motion to set aside the indictment. That motion was based on the presence of the complainant's older sister during the Grand Jury sessions at which the complainant had testified. The District Attorney had contended that the sister did not herself testify, nor did she influence the testimony of the complainant in any way. The lower court noted that the record did not indicate that the sister was present when the Grand Jury was discussing the testimony or voting, and that the defendant made no claim that she was. The Appellate Division held that because the sister's presence had not been prejudicial, the motion had been properly denied. However, on appeal, the Court of Appeals unanimously reversed in 296 N.Y. 315, there stating: "We think that historically and on principle an indictment should be dismissed when two witnesses have been presented together while the testimony of one or both was heard by the Grand Jury and that the decision should not be made to depend upon whether or not a defendant was actually prejudiced thereby." This case has been cited in 

People v. La Breque, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 843, to require dismissal of an indictment when the mother of a complaining witness was present in the Grand Jury room, while her daughter was testifying. Thus it is now clear that no one, other than aides of the Grand Jury, duly authorized by statute, such as stenographers, interpreters, etc., should be present during the sessions and that the presence of anyone else will require dismissal of the indictment. 

It should be noted that in some cases, defendants, after 327

§ 

arrest or conviction, have attempted to use writs of habeas corpus to obtain their release, claiming that the presence of unauthorized persons invalidated the indictment. The courts have held that the remedy provided by Section 313 is exclusive and have denied these writs. See People v. Truesdell, 261 App. Div. 824, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 392; People ex rel. 

Childs v. Knott, 228 N.Y. 608.

Sec. 194. Insufficiency of Evidence Before Grand Jury. As above stated, although not listed in Section 313, the insufficiency of the evidence presented to the Grand Jury may be a basis for setting aside the indictment. Section 251 of the 

Code, the only statutory provision concerning the evidence needed to support an indictment, provides: "The Grand 

Jury ought to find an indictment, when all the evidence before them, taken together, is such as in their judgment would, if unexplained or uncontradicted, warrant a conviction by the trial jury." The word "evidence" in the above section means legal, competent, evidence (People v. 

Molineux, 27 Misc. 60, 57 N.Y.S. 936; People v. Grout, 85 

Misc. 570, 147 N.Y.S. 391). However, "The introduction of other evidence, improperly received, does not justify 

the asserted errors were not material ones." (People v. 

Leary, 305 N.Y. 793, 796.) "The presumption is that an indictment is based upon legal and sufficient evidence until there is a satisfactory proof to the contrary." (People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395.) The proof of the insufficiency of the evidence before the Grand Jury will usually be obtained by inspection of the Grand Jury minutes. The general rule in New York now seems to be that "contrary to the holdings in most States, the court has the power to weigh the evidence before the Grand Jury and pass on its sufficiency but its power to dismiss exists only where the evidence is so clearly insufficient as to indicate that the indictment was found in willful disregard of the defendant's rights. *** In all other cases the presumption of sufficiency and legality shall prevail. *** However 328

§ the courts have also held that where the evidence before the Grand Jury is insufficient as a matter of law as distinguished from a matter of weight, then the indictment must be dismissed." (People v. Porter, 54 N.Y.S. 2d 3.)

In the Porter case, four defendants, three of them under the age of sixteen, were indicted for first degree murder.

They moved for dismissal of the indictment contending that the indictment charged at most a felony murder, of which persons under the age of sixteen may not be convicted under Penal Law, Sec. 1044, subd. 1, and Sec. 1046.

The court agreed with defendants' contention in this respect and examined the evidence of intent to kill. It found insufficient such evidence concerning two of the under-age defendants and dismissed the indictments as to them. Discussing the rules concerning the requisite evidence to support an indictment, the court stated: "when the only evidence before the Grand Jury is illegal evidence such as the testimony of the defendant compelled to be a witness against himself, in violation of his constitutional rights, *** or testimony of accomplices uncorroborated as required by law, or the *** testimony of a prosecutrix in a 

rape case or a confession of a defendant without the additional proof of the corpus required by law, such evidence is as a matter of law insufficient and it is the duty of the court to dismiss the indictment. *** The same rules of law would apply where there is an absolute failure of proof of any essential element of a crime *** an indictment for rape should be dismissed where there has been an absolute failure of proof of penetration. * * * In the same manner the absolute failure of proof of a "breaking" in a burglary charge or the use of "force or violence" in a robbery charge, would make the indictment legally insufficient. And the same rule of law is equally applicable *** when an essential element of a crime is a state of mind or a specific intent *** such as intent to inflict grievous bodily harm in certain assault cases or design to kill in murder cases."

The above statement is a valid summary of some of the rules, concerning extremes and absolute failures of proof. 329

§ 

At the other extreme, it is of course recognized that the court should not substitute its judgment of guilt or innocence for that of a jury in close cases. It is in the middle area, as in most other fields of law, that the problems arise. 

In People v. Martinez, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 537, the court stated: "The test to be applied upon a motion to dismiss an indictment for failure of proof before the Grand Jury is the same that governs upon a motion to dismiss the indictment at the close of the People's case upon a trial." This test would require the Grand Jury to find, for a valid indictment, that on the evidence before them a prima facie case of the guilt of the accused has been established, and that, upon that evidence if it remains uncontradicted or unexplained, there is no reasonable doubt as to defendant's guilt and the presumption of innocence has been overcome (People v. Ledwon, 153 N.Y. 10; People v. Phillips, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 

804). In People v. Sclafani, 8 Misc. 2d 986, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 

713, the above quoted words of the court in the Martinez case were repeated with approval. The court stated: "It follows therefrom that the rules of evidence as to overcoming the presumption of innocence and as to sustaining the burden of proof to make out a prima facie case, prevail in the Grand Jury room as elsewhere." Thus the court, convinced of the fact that on the evidence before the Grand 

Jury "a prima facie case *** has not been established," dismissed the indictment.

Sec. 195. Circumstantial Evidence. Indictments may, of course, be based upon circumstantial evidence as may convictions, for "such evidence is not to be discredited simply because of its nature, it often has more reliable elements than eyewitness testimony which depends upon memory and may be influenced by passions and prejudices." (People v. Eckert, 2 N.Y. 2d 126.) In the Eckert case, the defendant was indicted for criminal negligence in the operation of an automobile resulting in death. Evidence, including testimony of the defendant's doctor, indicated that the defendant had been affected by an epileptic seizure while 330

§ driving the car, and that the defendant had prior knowledge of his susceptibility to such seizures. The court recognized that "the evidence relied upon to connect the accused with the crime charged, as well as that relied upon to establish that the crime was committed while the accused was undergoing an epileptic seizure, is wholly circumstantial." However, the court noted, this by itself did not warrant dismissal of the indictment, for "The legal sufficiency of the evidence is measured by two standards: the facts from which the inferences of accused's guilt are drawn must be satisfactorily established; and they must not only be inconsistent with innocence, but must exclude to a moral certainty every other reasonable hypothesis but guilt. 

In this instance that determination was for the Grand Jury in its capacity as arbiter of credibility and of the weight to be given to the evidence. * * * That a trial jury might not convict on this evidence is not our concern. The Legislature has specifically relegated the question of whether a trial jury would return a conviction to the judgment of the Grand Jury." The indictment was sustained. 

Sec. 196. Illegal or Incompetent Evidence. As long as the record contains sufficient legal or competent evidence to sustain the indictment, the receipt of some illegal or incompetent evidence by the Grand Jury will not invalidate it. Thus, in People v. Leary, 305 N.Y. 793 (reversing 280 

App. Div. 679, 117 N.Y.S. 2d 392, which had dismissed an indictment), the Court of Appeals stated: "The record contains legal evidence which, taken together, might, if unexplained or uncontradicted, result in a conviction by the trial jury. Accordingly, the finding of an indictment against defendant was warranted. *** The introduction of other evidence, improperly received, does not justify setting aside the indictment *** particularly when, as here, the asserted errors were not material ones." Of course if there is doubt that the legal, properly received, evidence would sustain the indictment by itself, as implic- 331

§ 

itly recognized by the court in the above case, the indictment should be set aside. 

Sec. 197. Charge of Wrong Degree of Crime. People v. 

Wasserback, 185 Misc. 67, 54 N.Y.S. 2d 302, involved a situation brought about by the prosecution's tenacity, and one which may arise in similar situations where, after failure successfully to prove a greater crime (and where no problem of double jeopardy is present), the District Attorney attempts to reindict for a lesser offense. Defendant was indicted for rape and the indictment was dismissed because of the lack of corroborating evidence. Subsequently, the defendant was indicted for attempted rape and assault with intent to commit rape, for actions arising out of the same occurrence. The defendant moved to set aside the indictment alleging that the only proof showed a completed rape and that that proof was uncorroborated. 

The court, while dismissing the indictment, stated: "Where the evidence before the Grand Jury clearly establishes that a rape has been consummated, a motion to dismiss an indictment for an attempt to commit rape must be granted. ***The defendant is not deprived of his right to move to dismiss an indictment which charges him with an attempt where the evidence before the Grand Jury conclusively establishes that the crime was consummated. It is clear however that if he permits the trial to continue without objection or proper exception to the charge, he should not complain that he has been convicted of a lesser crime than is established by the evidence." The order of dismissal was reversed and the indictment reinstated in 271 App. Div. 

756, 64 N.Y.S. 2d 703.

Despite the ultimate outcome in the Wasserback case, supra, the reasoning of the court as to indictments for attempts, where proof shows the crime was consummated, is still valid. Thus, in People v. Manwaring, 3 App. Div. 2d 

952, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 548, the court, in dictum, stated: "While the charge of attempted rape on which the defendant was ultimately sentenced does not require corroboration *** 332

§ the indictment had charged the crime of rape and that required corroboration. *** Hence, it may be that, upon a timely challenge to the indictment, it would have been dismissed for lack of corroborating evidence before the Grand 

Jury. ***" However, in the Manwaring case, the defendant had attempted to raise the issue by coram nobis after his conviction, a proceeding termed inappropriate by the court. Since the reasoning of the Wasserback case has not been disapproved by the Court of Appeals, similar objections may well be raised in similar situations. 

Sec. 198. Double Jeopardy. The claim of double jeopardy may be presented by a motion to set aside the indictment as a non-statutory, constitutional, objection (People v. 

Tarum, 143 Misc. 7, 256 N.Y.S. 586; People v. Murray, 168 

Misc. 737,5 N.Y.S. 2d 953).

Sec. 199. Self-Incrimination. The contention that the de fendant's constitutional right not to be compelled to give evidence against himself has been violated, by his being compelled to do so while before the Grand Jury, is a proper ground for a motion to set aside the indictment (People v. 

Buffalo Gravel Corporation, 195 N.Y.S. 940; People v. Seaman, 174 Misc. 793, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 917). Of course, a valid waiver of the right will vitiate this argument (People v. 

Grant, 85 Misc. 570, 147 N.Y.S.591).

Sec. 200. Dismissals for Want of Prosecution. Chapter VII of Title 12 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Secs. 667 

through 673) provides the rules for dismissals of actions for want of prosecution. Section 8 of the Code reads: "In a criminal action the defendant is entitled 1. To a speedy and public trial." The United States Constitution, Sixth

Amendment, also provides that "in all criminal prosecutions the accused shall enjoy the right to a speedy trial,' but that amendment is applicable only to Federal courts 

(People v. Jelke, 308 N.Y. 56). Section 667 provides for the dismissal of a prosecution, upon defendant's application 

333

§ 

when a defendant is held to answer for a crime, if an indictment is not found against him at the next term of the court at which he is held, unless there is good cause for the delay. However, the defect is cured by the finding of an indictment (People v. Pearsall, 6 Misc. 2d 40, 165 N.Y.S. 

2d 932). After an indictment has been found, defendant's remedy lies either under Section 8, quoted above, or Section 668, which provides: "If a defendant indicted for a crime whose trial has not been postponed upon his application, be not brought to trial at the next term of the court in which the indictment is triable, after it is found, the court may, on application of the defendant, order the indictment dismissed, unless good cause to the contrary be shown."

The defendant's failure to object to delay, or proceeding to plead guilty to the charge, waives it (People v. Knowles, 7 Misc. 2d 222, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 293). However, the defendant need not affirmatively move to have the trial brought on; his waiting for action on the part of the prosecution is not a waiver (People v. Exeter, 4 Misc. 2d 651, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 

60; People v. Bishop, 2 Misc. 2d 541, 153 N.Y.S. 2d 961). The leading case in this area is People v. Prosser, 309 N.Y. 353, in which the defendant, in 1946, pleaded not guilty to five indictments. On his trial, he changed his pleas to guilty to two of the indictments and was thereupon sentenced as a fourth offender. Six years later, the courts found that he had been improperly sentenced as a fourth offender and he was returned, pursuant to the court's direction, for resentencing and re-arraignment on one of the three indictments to which he had pleaded not guilty. Defendant then moved for dismissal of the indictment on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to a speedy trial. The 

Court of Appeals held, on appeal from the judgment of conviction, that the indictment should have been dismissed and it reversed. Noting the conflict among the States concerning what constitutes a waiver by the defendant of the right to a speedy trial, the Court stated: "the mere failure of the defendant to take affirmative action to prevent delay may not, without more, be construed or treated as a 334

§ waiver." However, the court noted that there may be a waiver where "the prosecution and defense agree or stipulate for a postponement [or when]* *** the defendant, although present in court, interposes no objection to a postponement sought by the District Attorney." 

It is within the court's discretion to order a continuance of the prosecution from time to time for good cause shown (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 669). Section 669-a gives defendants who have been imprisoned the right to demand trial within 180 days after said demand of any untried indictments, informations, or complaints, pending against them. 

If, after defendant's demand, trial within the prescribed time is not had, the pending action shall be dismissed with prejudice. This constitutes a bar to further prosecution for the same offense, if it is a misdemeanor. All of the other dismissals treated in that Chapter VII of Title 12 of the Code, where felony is involved, do not bar future prosecution for the same offense unless jeopardy has otherwise attached (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 673). 

Sec. 201. Time for Motion. Section 314 of the Code provides: 

"If the motion to set aside the indictment be not made, the defendant is precluded from afterward taking the objections mentioned in the last section." Section 315 reads: "The motion to set aside an indictment must be heard at the time of arraignment, unless, for good cause the court postpone the hearing to another time." It would thus appear that failure to make the motion at the arraignment would constitute a waiver of the right to object. However, it was early recognized that this was not true of the nonstatutory, constitutional grounds of objection, not enumerated in Section 313. In People v. Phifer, 59 Misc. 339, 112 N.Y.S. 285, the defendant moved to inspect the minutes after he had been arraigned and he had pleaded not guilty. 

The prosecution objected to the motion as not timely. The indicated ground of objection to the indictment was the insufficiency of the evidence before the Grand Jury. The court stated, referring to Sections 313 through 315: "These 335

$ 

sections, with respect to the matters embraced in them, are indeed controlling regulations of procedure, as was said in the Glen case [People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395]. *** They are not, however, regulations of procedure governing motions to set aside indictments based upon alleged violations of a defendant's constitutional rights predicated upon grounds not mentioned in Section 313. Respecting such motions the

Code of Criminal Procedure contains no regulation. In the 

Glen case a similar motion was made and entertained, not merely after the defendant had demurred to the indictment, but after the issue of law raised by the demurrer had been tried by the court."

However the above rule does not mean that the indictment can be attacked by motion, even on constitutional grounds, at any time. The Court of Appeals has stated: "The Legislature has provided that a motion based upon objections to an indictment which appear on the face of the indictment must be made before or at the time when the defendant is called for judgment (Code Cr. Pro., secs. 323, 331, 467, 469). Though a motion to dismiss the indictment on the ground that it is based upon insufficient evidence is not within the scope of these statutory provisions, literally construed, we have held that the court may properly deny such a motion made after judgment has been entered upon a verdict untainted by any reversible error at the trial (See People v. Giordano, 231 N.Y. 633). The right to challenge the sufficiency of an indictment may be lost where the finding of guilt by the trial jury gives the same or greater assurance against oppression and persecution as an indictment based on sufficient evidence is intended to give before trial has been had." (People v. Nitzberg, 289 N.Y. 

523,530.) In the Nitzberg case, the defendant, who had been convicted in a previous trial, and whose conviction therein had been reversed and a new trial ordered because of an error in the charge to the jury, was held entitled to dismissal of the indictment in the second trial because of the lack of sufficient evidence before the Grand Jury, although he had not made such objection at the previous trial. 336

§ 

In People v. Pizza, 51 N.Y.S. 2d 488, app. dismissed 53 

N.Y.S. 2d 469, cert. denied, 326 U.S. 747, the court followed the rule above stated, and held: "By failure to challenge the sufficiency of the indictment before his conviction, the defendant lost the right to attack the indictment while he was detained by virtue of such judgment of conviction." 

The defendant had contended that the evidence before the Grand Jury had been illegally procured. In People v. 

Wurzler, 184 Misc. 224, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 601, four years after the defendant had been sentenced on his guilty plea he moved to vacate the judgment of conviction and for dismissal of the indictment as procured through fraud, and on insufficient evidence before the Grand Jury. The court first noted that the defendant had failed to establish that the indictment had been obtained through fraud, and then stated, concerning defendant's claim of insufficiency of the evidence: "Even if such evidence was not sufficient, and even if the defendant's version of what took place is correct, I am, nevertheless, of the opinion that the court may not grant the relief herein sought. *** There is no pro vision in the Code of Criminal Procedure authorizing * * * 

an attack upon the sufficiency of the evidence underlying the indictment long after sentence has been pronounced upon the defendant's plea of guilty. ***Even though the motion to dismiss the indictment is not barred by statute because it rests upon constitutional grounds, the right to make it is clearly something that may be waived or lost by laches." Discussing the Nitzberg case, supra, the court went on to state: "A plea of guilty constitutes an admission of the allegations contained in the indictment. It establishes the guilt of the defendant *** uncontrovertibly as a verdict of a jury after a trial. * * * This being so, it must naturally follow on the authority of the Nitzberg case, *** that the motion to dismiss the indictment in the instant case must be dismissed as not timely made. Another obstacle presents itself. *** a plea of guilty had been interposed. The plea must first be withdrawn before a motion to dismiss can be entertained. * * * In the instant 337

§ 

case judgment has long since been pronounced, and consequently the plea of guilty may not now be withdrawn. 

Since the plea may not now be withdrawn, it follows that the indictment may not be attacked."

The question of the proper time to make the motion was also discussed in People v. Van Allen, 275 App. Div. 181, 89 N.Y.S. 2d 594, where, after a guilty verdict but before the imposition of sentence, the defendant moved for dismissal of the indictment, alleging insufficiency of the evidence before the Grand Jury. The court stated: "When the procedural scheme of the Code is viewed in its entirety, it would seem to have been the legislative intent that the time the defendant is 'called for judgment,' Section 469, fixes the terminal point in time for all attacks upon the sufficiency of the indictment and that the judgment puts the question at rest." The court then cited the lower court opinion in the Giordano case (114 Misc. 62, 186 N.Y.S. 651) for the proposition that a "motion addressed to the indictment on constitutional grounds comes too late if made after judgment", but noted that the Appellate Division had not considered that question. The court went on to state: "There seems to be no instance in the reported authorities where any court has actually allowed an attack upon an indictment based on constitutional infirmities to be initiated after judgment of conviction." (Compare People v. 

Foster, 182 Misc. 73, 42 N.Y.S. 2d 831, discussed below.) It then cited the Nitzberg case for the holding that "When a motion showing constitutional infirmities growing from inadequacy of proof underlying an indictment is made before a trial, it will be granted even though upon the trial, as the appellate court is able to see on reviewing the judgment, the infirmity is fully corrected and the verdict of guilty is properly reached." 

People v. Foster, 182 Misc. 73, 42 N.Y.S. 2d 831, noted above, was cited by the court and distinguished in People v. Wurzler, 184 Misc. 224, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 601. The defendant had been indicted, had pleaded guilty and had been sentenced. After his parole, he was found guilty of another 338

§ crime and was resentenced. After twelve years of imprisonment on the combined terms, he moved for dismissal of the first indictment on the ground that the property stolen by him was not of sufficient value to constitute the crime of grand larceny. His allegation was supported by the record, and recognized as valid by the court, which stated: "A plea of guilty may not be substituted for the crime itself. Without the crime first, a plea of guilty thereof is a nullity." The court then granted the defendant's motion. In the Wurzler case, the court attempted to distinguish the Foster case by noting that there the District Attorney had conceded the insufficiency of the evidence; that the defendant had there pleaded guilty to a greater crime than that committed, and that the equities were on defendant's side in the Foster case. Then, the court stated: "If the cases were not distinguishable on these grounds, and if the decision in the Foster case *** enunciates a principle that the evidence supporting an indictment is forever subject to attack, and that constitutional rights in criminal matters remain inviolate, regardless of circumstances, lapse of time and confessions of guilt, then I must respectfully dissent." The Foster case has since been cited only for the proposition that a confession of guilt cannot be substituted for the crime itself; not for its holding concerning the time to attack indictments.

It has also been held that where the defendant's counsel had not learned of the violation of Section 313 until after arraignment, the motion to set aside the indictment would be entertained, even when made on a statutory ground (People v. Minet, 296 N.Y. 315). In the last-cited case, the objection was based on the presence of an unauthorized person during Grand Jury sessions, but the motion was made before trial. See also People v. Fuller, 156 Misc. 404, 282 N.Y.S. 28, for a similar decision in a similar situation.

In People v. Lee, 151 Misc. 431, 272 N.Y.S. 817, the court held that a motion to dismiss an information for failure to charge a crime could be made after arraignment and plea. The same principles applicable to motions based on 339

§ 

the insufficiency of the evidence before the Grand Jury, would be applicable to other cases of objections made on constitutional, non-statutory grounds, such as that there raised. However, the defect charged is one that should be raised by demurrer, or motion in arrest of judgment under Section 331 of the Code (People v. Chester, 4 Misc. 2d 949, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 829).

In summary, although the attitude of the courts appears to be that "Questions as to the sufficiency of the indictment must be raised before judgment" (People v. Parker, 8 App. 

Div. 2d 863, 186 N.Y.S. 2d 787), the Foster case is still authority in situations where an attack is contemplated after judgment. There is language in several decisions of the Court of Appeals indicating agreement with the last quoted statement; however that court has not yet definitely fixed any terminal point for such an attack. Therefore, while if possible the attack should be made prior to trial, an attack made thereafter is not necessarily bad. 

Sec. 202. Resubmission of the Indictment. Section 317 of the Code provides: "If the motion be granted, the court must order that the defendant, if in custody, be discharged therefrom, or if under bail, that his bail be exonerated, or if he have deposited money instead of bail, that the money be refunded to him, unless the court direct that the case be re-submitted to the same or another Grand Jury." However, as was stated in People v. Lenoci, 13 Misc. 2nd 789, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 332: "This section requires a court order directing the re-submission of the evidence if it is desired to retain the defendant in custody pending the re-submission." The court there also stated: "Where the dismissal of the indictments was not in consequence of a demurrer, but was the result of a motion to set the indictments aside, based on the Grand Jury minutes, there is no requirement that an order be first obtained prior to submitting the case to another Grand Jury." Thus, it appears that the only purpose of Section 317 is to allow the retention of the defendant in custody. The situation wherein a motion to set 340

§ aside the indictment is granted "must be clearly distinguished from the situation which would arise whenever a demurrer to an indictment is sustained. On a successful demurrer, without further order of the court, the judgment allowing the demurrer is final and a bar to any sub sequent prosecution (Section 327, Code of Criminal Pro cedure).

Another situation to be distinguished is that dealt with by Section 270 of the Code. That section applies where the 

Grand Jury dismisses a charge, and it requires that a court order be obtained prior to resubmission by the prosecutor. It has also been held that dismissals of indictments on the constitutional, non-statutory grounds discussed above are not within the purview of Section 317, which applies only to dismissals upon the grounds enumerated in 

Section 313. Thus, in People v. Roth, 128 Misc. 550, 220 N.Y.

S. 167, an indictment was set aside on defendant's motion because of insufficient evidence before the Grand Jury. 

The District Attorney moved for an order allowing a resubmission, which motion was denied by the court "on the ground that the Grand Jury has jurisdiction to indict again without an order of resubmission." The court there considered Sections 313, 317, 318, and 320 and then stated: "But all this is beside the question, because the indictment was not dismissed by virtue of these provisions * * * and by their express terms they have no application to another situation." The Roth case was cited in People ex rel. Grossman v. Warden, 172 Misc. 185, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 245, where, after dismissal of an indictment because founded on insufficient evidence, defendant was reindicted. The defendant attacked the second indictment on the ground that no order directing a resubmission had been obtained. The court replied: "The difficulty with this contention is that this section is concerned only with a resubmission after the indictment has been dismissed upon motion for one of the technical grounds enumerated in Section 313. *** Where, however, the dismissal was by reason of the fact that the indictment was found on illegal and insufficient evidence, 341

§ 

an order or resubmission is not only unnecessary but will be a nullity."

Nor is the defendant placed in double jeopardy by the reindictment. "An order to set aside an indictment as provided in this chapter, is no bar to a future prosecution for the same offense." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 320.) Under the Roth case reasoning, this section, too, would not apply to dismissals on non-statutory grounds. However, “The courts have held repeatedly that the dismissal of an in dictment under Section 313, Code of Criminal Procedure, or because of insufficient evidence before the Grand Jury under the inherent power of the court, does not bar a subsequent indictment for the same offense." (People v. 

Richter, 182 Misc. 96, 43 N.Y.S. 2d 114.) And it has been stated: "if the indictment is set aside on motion, it is not a bar to a further prosecution, although the defendant is entitled to be discharged from custody, 'unless the court direct that the case be re-submitted to the same or another 

Grand Jury'." (People v. Rosenthal, 197 N.Y. 394, affirmed 

226 U.S. 260, 57 L. Ed. 212.)

However, when an order of resubmission is granted, the new indictment must be found "before the next Grand Jury of the county is discharged, [or] the court must, on the discharge of such Grand Jury, make the order prescribed by Section 317." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 319.)

As in the case of demurrers, the Statute of Limitations is tolled pending the prosecution, "Provided a new prosecution for the same offense be commenced within 60 days after the order is entered." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 144-a.)

Sec. 203. Multiple-Count Indictments. As noted in chapter on demurrers, Section 323 was amended in 1945 to allow demurrers to "any count" of a multiple-count indictment. 

Section 313 was not so amended. At common law, it was held that demurrers to indictments would not lie if any count of the indictment was valid (People v. Rosenheimer, 209 N.Y. 115). Language in some cases indicates that some 342

§ courts have applied that same rule to motions to set aside indictments. "It is nevertheless a matter of law that though an indictment may have defective counts, the presence of one good count bars dismissal." (Tyson v. People, 116 N.Y. 

S. 2d 394). In People v. Kupperman, 175 Misc. 650, 24 N.Y.S. 

2d 445, the court stated: "Until the legislature amends *** the Code of Criminal Procedure so as to provide for a demurrer to a part of an indictment [which has now been done], or to permit a motion for the dismissal of a single count of a multiple indictment under Section 671 of the Code [which section allows a court to dismiss an indictment in the interest of justice and is a statutory enactment of the former power of nolle prosequi, People v. Quill, 11 

Misc. 2d 512, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 380] at a time other than at the trial of a case, and establishes beyond doubt the practice and procedure permitting a defendant to do so, I am obliged to hold that there is no authority *** to allow an attack upon a part of this indictment." During trials, courts have exercised the power to allow dismissal of certain counts of multiple-count indictments (People v. 

Mullins, 298 N.Y. 606; People v. Manuel, 113 N.Y.S. 2d 

415). Thus, some courts, at least, will not permit a motion to set aside only certain counts of multi-count indictments before trial. 

Sec. 204. Appeals. Defendant. As noted in the cases discussed previously in this chapter, the lower court's decision upon a motion to set aside the indictment will be reviewed by the appellate courts upon appeal from a judgment of conviction (People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395). 

Prosecution. It should first be noted that there is no specific authority allowing the People to appeal from an order allowing a motion to set aside or dismiss some, but not all, of the counts of a multi-count indictment. Subdivision 1 of Section 518 of the Code allows the people to appeal from a judgment for the defendant "on a demurrer to the indictment," thus encompassing judgments on demurrers to whole indictments, or to any counts of multi-count in- 343

§ 

dictments. Subdivision 3, pertaining to dismissals of indictments, is worded differently. Thus, if the defendant has been successful in a motion to set aside only some of the counts of a multi-count indictment, this distinction applies to any attempt on the part of the People to appeal. 

Subdivision 3, quoted above, was amended in 1942 to overcome the effect of the decision in People v. Reed, 276 

N.Y. 5, which held that the People did not have the right to appeal from a dismissal of the indictment ordered at the end of the trial, and prior to submission of the case to the jury, as a matter of law because the indictment did not state a crime. The court also held that subdivision 5, quoted above, did not give the People any rights, for a defendant would not have the right to appeal from a judgment of acquittal and thus the People would not have that right. 

Thus, as stated by the court in People v. Nikiel, 152 N.Y.S. 

2d 953: "this language grants no right at all. The defendant may only appeal from a judgment of conviction and the language of this section, which also permits the People to appeal from a judgment of conviction means nothing, since the People would have no occasion to appeal from such disposition of the case." Dismissals of informations are also appealable under subdivision 3 (People v. Malmud, 4 

App. Div. 2d 86, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 204). For a full discussion of the law and practice on appeal, see the chapter of this work on "Appeals."

Sec. 205. Proof of the Defect. It is clear that on a motion to set aside the indictment, "irregularity or error in the finding of the indictment may be established by extrinsic evidence." (People v. Harris, 182 Misc. 787, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 745, 761, reversed 54 N.Y.S. 2d 161, reversed 294 N.Y. 424.)

However, it has been stated that "Motions to dismiss indictments for lack of evidence should be decided upon the Grand Jury minutes without the aid of supporting affidavits." It would seem that if the Grand Jury minutes disclose a prima facie case of violation of the penal statute involved, the indictments should be sustained, since a ques- 344

§ 

tion of fact has been raised. The matters contained in supporting affidavits may be proven on the trial as a defense. In other words, a decision on a motion of this character does not go to the merits, but simply determines whether or not proper evidence was presented to the Grand Jury making out a prima facie case of violation.' (People v. Mangan, 140 Misc. 783, 252 N.Y.S. 44.) Thus, again a distinction is made between motions to set aside based on the statutory grounds, in Section 313, which deal with the procedural irregularities, and those founded on the constitutional ground of insufficiency of the evidence. 

While it is true that courts should not usurp the functions of the trial jury in weighing evidence, the above distinction does not appear to be well founded. Irregularities in the proceedings, as well as the insufficiency of the evidence, should be apparent from the minutes (unless the claim is that the minutes were incorrectly kept). At least some of the cases discussed previously in this chapter considered extrinsic evidence in determining whether illegal evidence had been received by the jury. 

In People v. Martin, 87 App. Div. 487, 84 N.Y.S. 823, the

Appellate Division, in dictum, stated that an affidavit submitted by defendant's counsel, alleging the receipt of illegal evidence by the Grand Jury, would not suffice where the deponent was not personally aware of what occurred before the Grand Jury. Thus the court, inferentially, intimated that an affidavit by one with personal knowledge might be considered. In People v. Molineux, 36 Misc. 435, 73 N.Y.S. 806, the court stated: "I know of no practice that permits a motion to be made for a dismissal of an indictment upon affidavits alleging what did occur or what might have occurred in the Grand Jury room." Thus, the court indicated its agreement with the Mangan case, supra. 

However, the Molineux court cited the case of People v. 

Sebring, 14 Misc. 31, 35 N.Y.S. 237, to support its statement. 

But, in the Sebring case the court stated: "the affidavit of the defendant as to what occurred before the Grand Jury, except so far as it is within his personal knowledge, cannot 345

§ 

be accepted and acted upon this motion." Thus, that court was holding only that allegations based on hearsay or opinion could not be used to overcome the presumptions of regularity, a holding that is clearly correct. 

In 1878, in People v. Shattuck, 6 Abb. N.C. 33, the court held that affidavits of grand jurors, submitted by defendant to support a motion to set aside the indictment, were admissible in determining whether there had been a proper vote on the indictment. In accord is People v. Briggs, 60 

How. Pr. 17. Compare People v. Hulbut, 4 Denio 133, which held that the testimony of grand jurors was inadmissible on the trial. The situations are, of course, distinguishable, but the reasoning of the courts, and some of the language in the Hulbut opinion, indicate that that court would have reached a result contrary to that reached in the Shattuck case. Thus, it appears that some courts may not accept affidavits on motions alleging the lack of sufficient evidence before the Grand Jury, although little basis appears for such a result. The Shattuck case, holding that an attack on the procedure of the Grand Jury may not be supported by affidavits, is apparently based on an erroneous reading of the Sebring case. Certainly, affidavits should be considered available now in these motions. However, it is equally certain that affidavits not based on personal knowledge will be considered insufficient. 346
