Sec. 213. Where Motion Must be Made PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

It has become the practice to make this motion in the conjunctive, or in the alternative, with a motion to dismiss the indictment; that is, a motion to inspect the minutes, and upon such inspection, to dismiss the indictment. In theory and in law, it is a composition of two distinct applications since the remedies they seek are separate. But since most courts presently inspect the minutes on their own volition, the two motions in effect become joined into one. 

Counsel himself should make the affidavit on information and belief. The danger exists that if the defendant makes it, any statements therein could be used by the District Attorney as a basis for cross-examination at the trial.

The motion will not be granted merely to enable counsel to prepare for trial. The affidavits adduced must set forth the belief that evidence that was illegal or insufficient to justify this finding of an indictment was presented to the Grand Jury. The danger that the District Attorney will use this motion as a means of correcting his pleading or his proof exists, as it does when any application is made in a criminal case. 347

§ 

Sec. 206. History. "At common law no written record of the proceedings of Grand Juries was kept. It was in the 

1827-1828 revision of the Revised Statutes that authority was first given to keep a written record. *** In 1881 the provision was incorporated in the Code of Criminal Procedure in mandatory form in substantially the language in which it now appears." (In re Attorney General of the 

United States, 160 Misc. 533, 291 N.Y.S. 5.) Section 243 of the Code of Criminal Procedure now provides: "The Grand 

Jury must appoint one of their number as clerk, who is to preserve minutes of the proceedings (except of the votes of the individual members on a presentment or indictment), and of the evidence given before them." 

Title XIV of Part 6 of the Code (sections 952-p through 952-x) provides the rules concerning the employment and duties of stenographers, who are to be appointed by District Attorneys. These stenographers are responsible for the recording and transcription of Grand Jury minutes. 

The predecessor of this title was enacted in 1885. Prior to its enactment there were no reported cases in which the court allowed an inspection of the minutes of a Grand Jury (People v. Steinhardt, 47 Misc. 252, 93 N.Y.S. 1026). "While attempts were made prior to that time to obtain an inspection of Grand Jury minutes, no reported case has been found in which such an application was successful.” (In re Attorney General of the United States, supra.) As stated by the court in that case: "The proceedings before 

Grand Juries from time immemorial have been secret." It is still a criminal offense for a stenographer to violate his duties concerning the preservation of the secrecy of the minutes (Penal Law, sec. 1784), or for a Grand Juror to willfully disclose "1. Any evidence adduced before the 

Grand Jury; or 2. Anything which he himself or any other member of the Grand Jury said, or in what manner he or any other Grand Juror voted." (Penal Law, sec. 1783.) "Every member of the Grand Jury must keep secret whatever he himself, or any other Grand Juror, may have said, or in what manner he or any other Grand Juror, may have 348

§ 

voted, on a matter before them." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

258.) However, Section 952-p does state that the minutes taken by the stenographer "shall be for the exclusive use and benefit of the District Attorney, unless otherwise ordered by the court, or otherwise agreed upon by the District Attorney.", and Section 952-t states that the stenographer shall not permit anyone, other than the District Attorney, to take a copy of the minutes "except upon written order of the court duly made after hearing the said District Attorney." The predecessor of this section was said to be "the first statutory recognition of the control of the court over the written record of the proceedings before a Grand Jury. Before this statute the courts had, and since its enactment have, uniformly declared that inspection is not accorded as a matter of right, but as a matter of judicial discretion." (People v. Steinhardt, supra.) There is no other statutory recognition, or regulation, of the inspection of Grand Jury minutes. 

Sec. 207. Purposes. "The object of such a motion is not to supply an accused with evidence prior to trial but to lay the basis for a motion to dismiss the indictment." (People v. 

Teetsel, 12 Misc. 2d 835, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 612.) The reasons underlying the rule of the secrecy of Grand Jury minutes are commonly recognized, and were stated by the court, in Commonwealth v. Mead, 12 Gray (Mass.) 167, 71 Am. 

Dec. 741, as follows: "One is that the utmost freedom of disclosure of alleged crimes and offenses by prosecutors may be secured. A second is that perjury and subornation of perjury may be prevented by withholding the knowledge of facts testified to before the Grand Jury, which if known, it would be for the interest of the accused or their confederates to attempt to disprove by procuring false testimony. The third is to conceal the fact that an indictment is found against a party, in order to avoid the danger that he may escape and elude arrest upon it, before the presentment is made." This statement of purposes was quoted with approval in People v. Steinhardt, 47 Misc. 252, 93 N.Y.S. 349

§ 

 1026, and in People v. Dunbar Contracting Co., 82 Misc. 

174, 143 N.Y.S. 337. A fourth purpose that has been suggested is the "protection of the reputation of an innocent accused from public knowledge that charges are being prepared against him." (Orfield, Crim. Proc. from Arrest to 

Appeal, p. 171.)

Against these factors, which weigh in favor of maintaining the secrecy of the minutes, may be arrayed those factors urged by defendant, in the Steinhardt case, supra, as warranting allowance of an inspection: "to enable a defendant to prepare for trial; to make known to the defendant the precise nature of the accusation he is called upon to meet; and to enable the defendant to move to set aside the indictment upon one or more of the grounds permissible by law." At this point, it should be noted that once an indictment has been found, the third and fourth factors urged in favor of the secrecy of the minutes become moot. 

The fact of the indictment is then public knowledge, any injury to defendant's reputation will have already occurred, and the defendant will already have appeared in the proceeding before he may move for the inspection of the minutes.

The area for policy conflict is obvious. However desirable secrecy may be, it is the defendant's right that the indictment and the bill of particulars sufficiently identify the charge against him so that he may prepare his defense. 

The only manner of enforcing this right requires an examination of the minutes. Unless this is made available, there is no check upon possible abuse by the Grand Jury or the District Attorney, or both. "It is well settled that the purpose of an inspection of the Grand Jury minutes is to ascertain whether or not grounds exist for a motion to dismiss the indictment." (People v. Kresel, 141 Misc. 593, 253 N.Y.S. 372, 380.) And, in People v. Dunbar Contracting 

Co., 82 Misc. 174, 143 N.Y.S. 337, the court stated: "defendants are not entitled to the minutes to enable them to prepare for trial *** the only ground upon which a motion of this kind can be granted is to enable the defendants to 350

§ move to set aside the indictments upon one or more of the grounds given by the statute for such a motion." The grounds upon which a motion to set aside the indictment can be based are discussed in the previous chapter. They can be summarized: "whenever it appears that [indictments] have been found without evidence or upon illegal or incompetent testimony" and "if unauthorized persons have been permitted to be present during Grand 

Jury sessions. *** The court will not allow an inspection of the minutes of the Grand Jury to enable a defendant to ascertain whether or not grounds exist for a motion to dismiss an indictment, but only to support a motion that may be made upon grounds shown by the moving papers to actually exist or facts from which a good ground may reasonably be inferred." (People v. Dunbar, supra.) 

Sec. 208. Time for Motion. In most cases, the motion to inspect is made immediately after arraignment. Its only purpose is to lay the foundation for a motion to dismiss the indictment, which must be made at the time of arraignment unless the court postpone the hearing for good cause shown; failure to move for dismissal then constituting waiver of objections under Section 313, the motion to inspect should be made at the arraignment if it is to be made at all.

It is true that motions to set aside indictments may be heard, and may be granted, regardless of the rules of Sections 313-315, "whenever it has been made to appear that they have been found without evidence, or upon illegal and incompetent testimony." (People v. Glen, 173 N.Y. 395, 400.) Thus in People v. Nitzberg, 289 N.Y. 523, the court "implied *** that if both the indictment and the verdict are not well founded a motion to dismiss the indictment may be properly entertained and granted even after judgment." (People v. Van Allen, 275 App. Div. 181, 89 N.Y.S. 

2d 594, 600.) In People v. Giordano, 114 Misc. 62, 186 N.Y.S. 

651, the defendant, after his conviction and while an appeal therefrom was pending in the Court of Appeals, 351

§ 

moved to inspect the minutes in order to lay the foundation for a subsequent motion to dismiss the indictment. The defendant relied on the Glen case in his argument that as his constitutional rights had been violated there had been no waiver of his right to move to dismiss the indictment. 

The court held that "defendant has waived his right to make this motion by not doing so prior to the imposition of final judgment. *** While it has been held that a defendant cannot waive a constitutional objection to the power or jurisdiction of the court to try him* * other constitutional rights may be waived *** as well as statutory rights.

While this motion is not for the dismissal of the indictment, but for inspection of the minutes of the Grand Jury, yet, as it is made upon the sole ground that it is for the purpose of subsequently moving to dismiss, it would be futile to grant the motion if the subsequent motion to dismiss must inevitably be denied." An appeal by defendant was dismissed in 231 N.Y. 633.

It is interesting to note that in the Nitzberg case the defendant's objection was the same as that in the Van Allen case, the presence of uncorroborated accomplice evidence only before the Grand Jury. In People v. Nitzberg, supra, the Court of Appeals said that it had held, in the Giordano case, that "the court may properly deny such a motion made after judgment has been entered upon a verdict untainted by any reversible error at the trial." Judge Conway, dissenting in the Nitzberg case, cited the Giordano case as having held that defendant had waived his right to object to the sufficiency of the indictment, or to move for the inspection of the minutes, by not doing so prior to judgment. In People v. Van Allen, supra, the court distinguished People v. Giordano, supra, on the ground that the 

Court of Appeals had there held that denials of motions for inspection of the minutes are discretionary and not subject to review. In any event the rule, as developed, now appears to be as stated in People v. Van Allen, supra: "the time the defendant is 'called for judgment' *** fixes the terminal point for all attacks upon the sufficiency of the 352

§ indictment and that the judgment puts the question at rest." See also People v. Bowers, 3 Misc. 2d 688, 156 N.Y.S. 

2d 82. 

In People v. De Bernado, 199 Misc. 563, 106 N.Y.S. 2d 

515, modified other grounds 282 App. Div. 920, 125 N.Y.S. 

2d 641, the court stated: "Although judgment has heretofore been imposed upon the defendant, and despite the restrictions of Section 314 and 315 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, this court, nevertheless, has inherent power to entertain an application for an inspection of the Grand Jury minutes for the purpose of ascertaining whether the Grand Jury's determination was founded with due regard for the constitutional rights of the defendant." Thus, it appears now that a motion to dismiss may be made, on the non-statutory constitutional grounds, at least until the time of judgment. Therefore, motions to inspect based on these defects should also be allowed until that time. In 

People v. Miller, 257 N.Y. 54, the Court of Appeals held that where the prosecution, on the trial, uses the minutes of the Grand Jury for cross-examination, fairness and due process require that such minutes be made available on demand to the defendant.

It is to the defendant's advantage, and common practice, for the defendant to request on arraignment an adjournment and reservation of rights to move. This is usually expressed: "Adjourned to (date) for all motions."

During this period, if defendant ascertains some ground for an attack upon the indictment, he then moves for inspection of the minutes. One writer has indicated that by so doing, where the suspected defect is the foundation of the indictment upon illegal or incompetent evidence, he will forewarn the prosecution against the use of such evi dence (Black, How to Conduct a Criminal Case, pp. 217219). However, failure to do so may, as above mentioned, constitute a waiver. Waiting until the offer of the evidence will help little if the prosecution has discovered other competent evidence which might sustain the conviction. 

Decision upon this question of trial strategy must, as al- 353

§ 

ways, depend at least in part on an evaluation of the prosecution's available case.

Sec. 209. Grounds. As stated, the court will allow a motion to inspect the minutes only to enable the defendant to lay the basis for a motion to dismiss the indictment. Upon defendant's motion, the court will "examine the moving papers on this motion, to ascertain whether they indicate that an inspection of the minutes will reveal any legal basis for a motion to dismiss." (People v. Steinhardt, supra.) 

The affidavits submitted in support of the motion should set forth facts indicating the ground for the contemplated motion. If the court, upon reading the affidavits and the affidavits in opposition submitted by the prosecution and the minutes, determines that there is no basis for a subsequent motion to dismiss, the motion to inspect will ordinarily be denied (People v. Steinhardt, supra). In People v. Kresel, 141 Misc. 593, 233 N.Y.S. 372, 380, the court stated: "I am not satisfied that on all the papers submitted to me any statutory grounds have been disclosed why the indictment *** should not stand; and by an examination of the minutes of the Grand Jury handed to me * * * I find that no illegal evidence was received by the Grand Jury.” 

The moving papers should specifically allege the supposed defect. Thus, in the Steinhardt case the defendant's affidavit alleged, among other things, that three persons were improperly present at the Grand Jury session. 

The court noted that "It is not alleged *** that any of these persons were present when the jurors were expressing their opinion or voting * * * or even when other witnesses were testifying, and there is nothing to indicate that they were present in any other capacity than as witnesses, except the mere omission of their names from the list of witnesses indorsed on the indictments." The motion was granted, but upon other grounds.

The grounds upon which motions to dismiss, or set aside, indictments can be made are discussed in detail in our chapter on that subject. The discussion here will not attempt www 354

§ to cover these grounds comprehensively but will only discuss the application of some of them in the consideration of motions to inspect the Grand Jury minutes. In People v. 

Lyndaker, 116 N.Y.S. 2d 195, the court stated that on a motion to inspect the minutes "certain prerequisites must appear in the moving papers. The first requirement is that a reasonable effort has been made to ascertain what has been testified to before the Grand Jury and what was learned, and the correlative of that requirement, what information has not been obtained and the reasons therefor. (2) What the defendant surmises was the testimony before the Grand Jury; the ground therefor and the reasonableness of such surmises. *** 3) That the defendant intends in good faith to move to set the indictment aside. *** (4) That the defendant intends to so move, because his constitutional rights have been invaded. * * * (5) That the inspection would not work to the prejudice of the people or serve or tend to defeat the ends of justice." 

Sufficiency of the Evidence. In People v. Duby, 114 

N.Y.S. 2d 510, the defendant, indicted for first degree manslaughter, moved to inspect the minutes, alleging lack of sufficient legal evidence to justify the Grand Jury's finding of the indictment. As the court noted: "The People depend entirely upon defendant's 'confession' for an account of what occurred immediately preceding the time of the fight. *** That account includes facts which may well show affirmatively *** that the homicide was justifiable. *** defendant should be allowed to test the sufficiency of the evidence by motion addressed to the indictment and for that reason the motion to inspect the Grand Jury minutes is granted."

Where the court finds that the ground alleged by defendant for his contemplated attack upon the indictment is reasonably supported in the record, the motion will be granted. People v. Lyndaker, 116 N.Y.S. 2d 195, involved a motion in a case in which defendant was indicted for criminal negligence in the operation of an automobile. The court noted that a coroner's inquest had been held and, 355

§ 

therefore, it was reasonable for defendant to assume that the witnesses before the Grand Jury were the same as those before the inquest. The court stated: "On the argument of the motion, the District Attorney conceded that but one other witness testified as to the speed of the deceased's motorcycle some time and distance from the scene of the accident *** it becomes evident that the ends of justice will be best served by allowing an inspection of the 

Grand Jury minutes." Again the reason for the allowance of defendant's motion was the reasonableness of the grounds of his surmise of the defect, coupled with a reasonable expectation of success in the contemplated motion to dismiss. 

In People v. Hess, 207 Misc. 520, 141 N.Y.S. 2d, 804, the defendant made two motions contemporaneously, one to dismiss the indictment and the other to inspect the minutes. The indictment was for bigamy which, the defendant contended, was committed without the State. The defendant also contended, on the motion to inspect, that testimony of the wife of the bigamous marriage was improperly received in evidence because she had not been advised of her right to refuse to testify, and without such evidence there was insufficient evidence to support the indictment. The court denied the motion to inspect, stating: "The court has examined the minutes of the Grand Jury and concludes that, if it is found that it is proper to indict for bigamy committed in another State, the legal evidence before the Grand Jury is adequate and sufficient and the motion to inspect the minutes of the Grand Jury is denied." The court later decided that it did not have jurisdiction over the crime and dismissed the indictment. 

In People v. Salvato, 12 Misc. 2d 88, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 698, defendant moved simultaneously to inspect the minutes and to dismiss the indictment. The Grand Jury had heard testimony given by an eight-year-old girl. The court, quoting Section 392 of the Code, which provides that no person shall be held upon the unsworn testimony of a child under 12 years of age unless the court is of the opinion that the 356

§ 

child is "possessed of sufficient intelligence," held that that section also applies to grand juries, and that as the minutes did not reflect any investigation of the girl's intelligence or qualifications, a reasonable opportunity should be afforded defendant to question the sufficiency of this evidence.

In summary, the statement of the Court of Appeals in 

People v. Howell, 3 N.Y. 2d 672, may be quoted: "motion to dismiss an indictment for insufficiency of the evidence before the Grand Jury *** is granted only upon a clear showing to that effect, in view of the presumption that an indictment is based on legal and sufficient evidence. *** 

It is enough to justify the granting of a motion for inspection if acts be shown from which there is reason to believe that the evidence before the Grand Jury is insufficient or illegal." And the statement of the court in People v. 

Martinez, 15 Misc. 2d 821, 183 N.Y.S. 2d 588, is an excellent summary of what motivates the court: "the granting of a motion to inspect the minutes of a Grand Jury is a matter of discretion which is not to be exercised arbitrarily nor without good reason shown by the moving party based on fact and not mere assumption. * * * Surmise is not enough."

Improper Grand Jury Procedure. Other grounds, relat ing to the requisite number of Grand Jurors and the presence of improper persons at Grand Jury sessions, may be the basis for motions to dismiss the indictment (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 313). These grounds may also serve as the basis for a motion to inspect. In People v. Brinkman, 126 

N.Y.S. 2d 486, the defendant contended that the indictment had been found without the lawful concurrence of the requisite number of grand jurors, and moved for inspection of the Grand Jury attendance lists, etc., to support a motion to dismiss to be made upon that ground. The District Attorney contended that "the indictment imports absolute verity until impeached by satisfactory evidence to the contrary, nothing short of a showing of vitiating facts can justify an inquiry into the matter and since no such facts are here alleged, the defendant should be denied ac- 357

§ 

cess to the records in question." The court recognized that "In some quarters, the defendant's ignorance which prevents him from sufficiently alleging and showing the facts has been regarded as an insurmountable obstacle to favorable action on his preliminary motion. *** In another quarter a less rigid view is taken that where the defendant shows some basis for belief that the proceedings underlying the indictment are fatally defective and shows also that he has neither the knowledge nor the means of securing knowledge of the matter, considerations of substantial justice and due regard for the safeguarding of constitutional rights may require that the preliminary motion be granted. ***Still others have treated a sort of "reasonable surmise" as sufficient warrant for granting it, provided the defendant has made reasonable but unsuccessful effort to learn what transpired. * * * In recent times, too, the District Attorney's failure to deny an allegation upon information and belief, as to the existence of a fatal defect has at least been treated as significant. *** Finally there are courts which have reviewed the record themselves, either in deciding the sufficiency of the legal structure on the merits ** or in aid of a decision on the right of the moving party to examine the record." The above quotation presents a comprehensive collation of the New York law on this point. No distinction should exist, save in the time when the motion must be presented, between motions to inspect based on a supposed defect in Grand Jury procedure, and a motion based on insufficiency of the evidence (People v. Klaw, 53 Misc. 158, 104 N.Y.S. 482). However, it is doubtful that any clarification of the above, apparently conflicting, theories will be made. The court's decision on this motion is discretionary and, therefore, the Court of Appeals will have no opportunity to review it on appeal except as the exercise of the discretion may be deemed a denial of due process.

Sec. 210. Effect of Lack of Preliminary Examination. In 

1899, People v. Molineux, 27 Misc. 60, 57 N.Y.S.

936, was 358

§ 

decided. In that case the court stated that "the fact that the defendant was indicted without having had a preliminary examination before a magistrate furnishes a strong inducement to the court to look upon the application with favor." Other factors were also present in that case tending toward a granting of the motion, and the court did allow the inspection. However, the court did stress the one factor and the ignorance of defendant of the testimony before the Grand Jury. In People v. Steinhardt, supra, the court indicated its disagreement with this reasoning. Some subsequent cases indicated a favorable attitude of the courts to the Molineux reasoning (People v. Foody, 38 

Misc. 357, 77 N.Y.S. 943; People v. McDonald, 177 App. Div. 

806, 165 N.Y.S. 41), while others have tended to follow, and cite with approval, the Steinhardt decision on this point (Matter of Montgomery, 126 App. Div. 72, 110 N.Y.S. 793; 

People v. Gassett, 112 N.Y.S. 555; People v. Jakeway, 88 

Misc. 124, 151 N.Y.S. 651; People v. Marin, 1 Current Ct. 

Dec. 30). The latest case in point is, apparently, People v. 

Pryor, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 393, affirmed 283 N.Y. 623, where the court, citing the Gassett case, supra, stated: "Inspection of the minutes of the Grand Jury can never be had as a matter of right and does not depend upon whether or not a preliminary examination has been had." Thus the matter now stands. Again it must be stated that it is unlikely that any further clarification will be had. If the only purpose of the motion is to lay the ground for a motion to dismiss, it would seem that the absence of a preliminary examination is not too important. All that the defendant would there learn would be further details of the case. However, the above cases can be relied on to support an argument based on the lack of such an examination. 

Sec. 211. Persons Entitled to Inspection. The defendant is, of course, the one primarily interested in obtaining the inspection. However, on occasion, others have attempted to obtain the minutes and some have been successful. In Matter of Martin, 170 Misc. 919, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 607, a former 359

§ 

judge, who had earlier granted a defendant's motion to inspect and thereafter dismissed the indictment on that defendant's motion, had himself been subsequently indicted for bribery, allegedly arising out of his actions in that previous case. The petitioning former judge asserted that an inspection of the minutes was necessary for the preparation of his defense to the bribery charge. The court denied the motion, stating: "The rule adopted by the courts is almost universal not to grant an inspection except to a defendant named in the minutes sought to be inspected and for the reason above stated [to lay the foundation for a motion to dismiss]". The court did recognize that on occasion, persons other than the defendant had obtained permission to inspect the minutes (as in Matter of Attorney 

General of the United States, 160 Misc. 533, 291 N.Y.S. 5), but "in all of these cases the courts acted with the consent of the District Attorney and, as stated*** no private interest was sought to be served and the information derived by the inspection was not intended to aid a private litigant. The underlying principle is one of public policy requiring the courts to cooperate with public officials entrusted with the administration of our criminal laws rather than to deter [them] ***" The court also refused to accept the petitioner's argument that because the minutes had been inspected in a previous trial, the "veil of secrecy" had, for all time, been broken. In Matter of Crain, 139 Misc. 799, 250 N.Y.S. 249, a motion to inspect made by a Special Commissioner, appointed by the Governor to investigate charges against a District Attorney, was granted over the objections of the subject of the investigation. No cases were cited in support of the court's action. However, the Crain case was cited in 

Application of the Bar Ass'n. of Erie County, 182 Misc. 

529, 47 N.Y.S. 2d 213, wherein a county bar association moved, over the District Attorney's objection, for inspection of the minutes of a Grand Jury which, allegedly, had been investigating the conduct of certain judges in the county. The Court denied the application, noting that the 360

§ bar association was not a "duly organized and existing law enforcing agency or *** endowed with powers similar thereto."

Matter of Special Report of the Grand Jury of Erie 

County, 77 N.Y.S.

2d 438, concerned an application to in spect made by the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles. The 

Commissioner wished to inspect the testimony of a certain witness who had refused to testify before the Motor Vehicle Department on the same subject matter as the 

Grand Jury's report. The Grand Jury report recommended that the subject matter be investigated by the Motor Vehicle Department, and the District Attorney interposed no objection to the Commissioner's motion. The court denied the application, stating that the District Attorney had not acquiesced or consented to the application and that "no reported decisions permitting without the consent of the District Attorney or the Attorney General, an inspection of the Grand Jury minutes in a non-criminal investigation or proceeding" had been found. Thus, more than the tacit consent of the District Attorney was required by the court. See also People ex rel. Sawpit Gymnasium, 60 

N.Y.S. 2d 593, and Dworetsky v. Monticello Smoked Fish 

Co. et al, 256 App. Div. 772, 12 N.Y.S. 2d 270, where a plaintiff suing for malicious prosecution was held not entitled to Grand Jury minutes of his prior indictment, which indictment thereafter dismissed was the basis for his civil suit. 

Sec. 212. Appeals. The apparent dilemma faced by defendants in this area in New York State caused by the rules concerning criminal appeals, was recognized by the dissenting judges in People v. Howell, 3 N.Y. 2d 672. The opinion of the court there stated the recognized rule as: "If the motion to inspect the minutes is denied, the order is not appealable in the absence of a statute authorizing appeal. If the motion for an inspection is granted, frequently the judge announces it at the same time that the indictment is dismissed *** the granting of a motion to 361

§ 

dismiss * * * upon this ground signifies that the discretion of the court has been exercised to reveal the Grand Jury minutes and that then, upon the basis of the minutes, the indictment has been dismissed. *** If the motion to inspect is denied, the Grand Jury minutes are not before the court on the motion to dismiss the indictment. On appeal from a conviction the Court of Appeals has no power to review the exercise of discretion in the denial of motions for inspection of the Grand Jury minutes (People v. Sweeney, 213 N.Y. 37, 41)." While the above stated rules are undoubtedly the present rules of law in this area, Judge Desmond, dissenting in the Howell case, pointed out the difficulty these rules engender. He there stated that it is unquestionably true that the Court of Appeals has jurisdiction to review denials of motions to dismiss indictments, which motions may be made on the ground that the evidence before the Grand Jury was insufficient to sustain the indictment. Therefore, the decision of the majority, that the court could not utilize the Grand Jury minutes on such an appeal if the motion to inspect made below had been denied, had the effect of denying to the court "the use of the only other method of passing on the sufficiency of the Grand Jury proof. We cannot in one breath announce the defendant's right not to be indicted except on adequate proof and in the next breath announce our refusal to look at the evidence to see if it was adequate." Judge Fuld, also dissenting in that case, noted that since the County Court had looked at the minutes, he would also do so. There have been no other cases on this point decided by the Court of Appeals to date. Thus the rule of the Howell case is still the law.

Sec. 213. Where Motion Must be Made. The motion to in spect the minutes should, if possible, be made in the court in which the indictment was found and is pending. In 

People v. Avery, 9 Misc. 2d 141, 169 N.Y.S. 2d 552, the defendant had been indicted by a Grand Jury empaneled by order of a County Court, in which court the indictment was 362

§ pending. However, the defendant moved in the Supreme 

Court for an order dismissing the indictment for insufficient evidence or, in the alternative, for an order permitting inspection of the Grand Jury minutes. He argued that as the Supreme Court had general and unlimited Statewide jurisdiction, it had jurisdiction to grant the relief sought by him. The court indicated its belief that "to attempt to assume jurisdiction in this case, in the absence of any statutory authority, would be an abuse of discretion and tend to disrupt and interfere with the orderly administration of justice. * * * A motion for inspection must be made in the court in which the proceedings were had and the testimony was taken (People ex rel. Hirschberg v. 

Supreme Court, 269 N.Y. 392; Schneider v. Aulisi, 307 N.Y. 

376)." The motion was denied.

However, if the indictment was originally found in one court and thereafter removed to another, the motion may be made in the court in which the indictment was originally found, by reason that the minutes are part of its record. In the Hirschberg case, cited by the court, above, the defendant was indicted in the Supreme Court. The indictment was thereafter transferred to the County Court where the defendant demurred, then after the overruling of his demurrer pleaded not guilty and moved for and obtained a bill of particulars. Subsequently, the defendant moved in the Supreme Court for inspection of the minutes. 

The District Attorney, appearing specially, challenged the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, and applied to the Appellate Division for an order prohibiting the respondent Supreme Court Justice from proceeding further with respect to the inspection of the minutes. The order was granted but was later reversed by the Court of Appeals, which dismissed the application. The Court of Appeals stated that by the removal of the prosecution "the County Court acquired jurisdiction to try and determine the indictment. *** That jurisdiction is complete and includes motions directed to the sufficiency or validity of the indictment and other motions preliminary to the trial. A 363

§ 

motion to inspect the minutes of the testimony given before the Grand Jury which found the indictment, is not such a motion. The proceedings of the Grand Jury were in the Supreme Court, and the justice, presiding in that court, charged the jury, received its indictments when found, and, in general, was responsible for its conduct. That court remains in possession and control of the records of the proceedings held there. The [removal] order * * * did not remove to the County Court the records and minutes of the proceedings of the Grand Jury previously completed in the Supreme Court. They form no part of the indictment. *** Nothing in the statute suggests that the court to which the indictment was transferred should have control of the records of proceedings in the original court, or jurisdiction to order the inspection of such proceedings."

In 1939, after the Hirschberg decision, Section 39 of the Code was amended by the addition of subdivision 2-a, which gave the County Courts "jurisdiction and control, concurrently with the Supreme Court, over the records and minutes of the Grand Jury in all cases of indictments sent thereto by the Supreme Court, and the jurisdiction to determine any motion for an order of inspection of such 

Grand Jury minutes."

Schneider v. Aulisi, 307 N.Y. 376, concerned a similar situation. The indictment, found by a Herkimer County 

Grand Jury, had been removed to the Herkimer County Court from the Supreme Court. While the indictment was there pending defendant moved, in the Supreme Court in Montgomery County, for inspection of the minutes, dismissal of the indictment, and a stay of the trial in the County Court pending the determination of the other motions. The District Attorney then applied, in the Appellate Division, for an order prohibiting the Supreme Court Justice to whom the defendant had made the above application, from proceeding further on the motion. The 

Court of Appeals cited the Hirschberg case and stated the issue confronting them to be "whether a motion for inspection addressed to the Supreme Court may be made only 364

§ at a term of that court in the same county in which the indictment was found." The Court then held that "The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear and determine such an application, though in a county and judicial district other than that in which the indictment was found, may not, therefore, be doubted." However, the court went on to note that the practice of "moving for an inspection before a Justice of the Supreme Court in a county other than that in which the indictment is pending" was not to be encouraged.

Thus, the defendant, after removal, has a choice. He may move in the court in which the indictment was found, or in the court to which it was transferred. However, if he desires to move in the court in which the indictment was originally found, and from which it has been transferred, he may not thereafter move for a dismissal in that court for, after removal, "jurisdiction of all proceedings connected with the disposition of the indictment, whether before or after trial, is vested exclusively in the County 

Court." People v. Saleem Al Hateem, 194 Misc. 97, 88 N.Y.S. 

2d, 114, held the same reasoning applicable where the transfer had been from General Sessions to Special Sessions. 365
