PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

After a motion to dismiss the indictment has been made and denied, or has been waived, counsel should consider the next tactical step, that of demurring to the indictment. This should be done at the arraignment, or at some adjourned date that the court has designated for that purpose. If a plea has been previously entered, permission to withdraw it must be secured before interposing a demurrer. Tactics with regard to pleas will be discussed in the next chapter entitled "Pleas to Indictment".

Five objections to the indictment are permitted to the defendant by Sec. 323 of the Code. Grounds 2, 3 and 5 will have to be urged by demurrer, at this time, or the right to do so will be forever waived.

Grounds 1 and 4 are not waived by failing to demur, since they are of a jurisdictional nature. Counsel may consider it wise to preserve defendant's rights thereunder until a future date. These objections may be raised at the trial under a plea of not guilty. They may even be interposed in the form of a motion in arrest of judg- 366

DEMURRERS 

§ 214 ment after the trial and before judgment. (See chapter on “Arrest of Judgment".)

Sec. 214. Definition. The only pleading on the part of the defendant is a demurrer or a plea (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 321). A demurrer may be interposed to an indictment or any part thereof on any of the grounds set forth in Section 323 of the Code. Prior to 1945, several cases had indicated that no demurrer would lie to only one count of a multi-count indictment, and that if any counts thereof were valid the demurrer would not be allowed. In 1945, the 

Code was amended to allow demurrers to any count. 

The grounds stated in Section 323 are: (1) That the 

Grand Jury, by which it was found, had no legal authority to inquire into the crime alleged; or (2) That the indictment does not conform substantially to the requirements of Sections 275 and 276; or (3) That more than one crime is charged in the indictment within the meaning of Sections 278 or 279; or (4) That the facts stated do not constitute a crime; or (5) That the indictment contains matter, which, if true, would constitute a legal justification or excuse for the acts charged, or other legal bar to the prosecution. 

Section 275, mentioned in subdivision 2, requires inclusion in an indictment of the title of the action, the names of the parties, the name of the court, and a plain and concise statement of the act constituting the crime. Section 276, also mentioned in subdivision 2, requires the signature of the District Attorney to the indictment. Section 278, mentioned in subdivision 3, requires that indictments charge but one crime, except as provided in section 279, which is discussed at length in the chapter on Indictments, under section entitled "Joinder of Offenses."

The Code covers "the entire subject, and especially as to the practice to be pursued when a defendant has been taken into custody under an indictment, and has challenged its sufficiency by demurrer, and *** with the interposition of the demurrer the court becomes possessed of the whole 367

§ 

case, and must determine whether the alleged case against the defendant is to be allowed to go before a jury; it being expressly given the power in a proper case to sustain the demurrer, and to make that determination a bar to further prosecution for the same offense. After the court has obtained the jurisdiction *** there is no provision in the law which permits the same or any future Grand Jury to deprive the court, [thereof]. *** If the demurrer be allowed, then the defendant must be discharged, and the judgment *** is a bar to another prosecution for the same offense, unless the court orders the case be resubmitted. *** A demurrer is a trial upon issues of law." (People v. 

Bissert, 71 App. Div. 118, 75 N.Y.S. 630, 633, affirmed 172 N.Y.643.) "Section 321 *** set forth that the 'only pleading on the part of the defendant is either a demurrer or a plea.' The language ‘either' 'or' is exclusive, presumably because the demurrer raises an issue of law, while the plea raises an issue of fact and the two are not interchangeable. 

Both are required to be put in at the time of arraignment 'or at such other time as may be allowed to the defendant for that purpose.' ***the demurrer must be in the form prescribed by statute. The function of a demurrer * * * is to defeat the indictment in its entirety, or portions thereof *** without a trial. * * * a demurrer must be in writing distinctly specifying the grounds of objection.' 

It must also be signed by the defendant or his counsel. ***The law, in its zeal to protect the rights of an accused, determined not to limit his right to challenge the indictment on certain stated grounds, to the use of a single weapon, but placed at his disposal others by which a like end result might be achieved. If he failed to demur he might still move to dismiss during the course of the trial if the exception existed, or he might even elect to wait and move in arrest of judgment. Each method is to be used in a certain stage of the proceedings. The demurrer before trial, the regular motion before or during trial, and the 368

DEMURRERS 

§ 216 motion in arrest of judgment after conviction or plea." (People v. Meyers, 119 N.Y.S. 2d 474.)

Sec. 215. Time of Demurrer. "Both the demurrer and the plea must be put in, either at the time of the arraignment, or at such other time as may be allowed to the defendant for that purpose." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 322.) As stated by the court in the Meyers case, in the quotation reproduced above, the demurrer must be used "before trial." 

Sec. 216. Effect of Failure to Demur at Proper Time. "A 

demurrer must be interposed (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 

315, 332) at the time of arraignment, or the objections are waived or precluded, except that certain objections, within the purview of Section 331 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, may be urged at the trial. The record, here, discloses that the defendant entered a plea of 'Not Guilty' at the time of his arraignment. A demurrer may not be entertained while the 'Not Guilty' plea stands. * * * The courts have overlooked technical defects in procedure. 

Since the notice of motion [for an order dismissing the information on the ground that the statute defining the crime was unconstitutionally vague] also seeks 'such other and further relief,' this court, too, will overlook the defects in procedure, here, and will consider the present application as one seeking relief by way of demurrer." (People v. 

Dill, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 286, 288.) Technical defects, such as the defendant's failure to demur at the proper time, were also overlooked in People v. Chester, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 829. There, the defendant moved to dismiss an indictment, contending that the facts stated did not constitute the crime charged. 

The court stated: "Preliminarily it might be observed that defendant['s] * * * challenge to the indictment is in the nature of a demurrer. *** the proper procedure for challenging the sufficiency of an indictment is by a demurrer, and a demurrer cannot be interposed while, as here, a plea of not guilty stands. *** The court, however, has decided 369

§ 

to overlook any technical defects in the procedure." See 

People v. Rohn, 10 Misc. 2d 482, 172 N.Y.S. 2d 459, where the court refused to treat a motion to dismiss an information as a demurrer, although the court did note that if it had been so treated, the information would have been upheld.

In People v. Kahn, 155 App. Div. 821, 140 N.Y.S. 618, the defendant, after pleading not guilty, orally moved for the dismissal of a count of the indictment. An order was entered by the court, noting the making of the motion and its denial. Defendant appealed therefrom, and his appeal was dismissed as being taken from a non-appealable interlocutory order. However, while so holding the court stated: "the defendant had pleaded not guilty, and, while that plea stood, could not demur." This last statement was not the essential ruling of the case; it does express the established law in this regard. In People v. Kupperman, 175 Misc. 650, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 445, 448, the court stated, in denying defendant's motion to strike out counts of an indictment: "I must agree that under the circumstances here, so long as a plea of not guilty stands, a demurrer cannot be entertained. 

This, though, could be easily eliminated by permission to withdraw it and by entering a substituted plea. As is commonly done in many cases of pleading in this court, time is allowed by the court, as was done in this instance, within which to withdraw the plea for all purposes, and substituting a demurrer within the time fixed." The above statement indicates the court's universally-utilized method of utilizing a demurrer after a plea of guilty has been entered. In one case the court's granting leave to demur was considered on appeal as the equivalent of withdrawal of the plea (People v. Williams, 213 App. Div. 571, 211 N.Y.S. 244, reversed other grounds, 243 N.Y. 162).

In Matter of DeWitt v. McNamee, 232 App. Div. 88, 249 

N.Y.S. 31, the defendant was indicted in fifty-nine indictments and, upon arraignment, pleaded not guilty to each. 

His counsel requested an extension of time within which he might examine the indictments and prepare motions 370

DEMURRERS 

§ 216 and demurrers. A day, less than one week later, was fixed upon which motions and demurrers would be heard by the court. On that day the defendant's counsel requested another extension of time, which request was denied by the court, stating: "the plea of not guilty will stand. The time for withdrawing the plea and interposing a demurrer has passed." The Appellate Division, while denying a motion for a prohibition order commanding the respondent Supreme Court Justice to refrain from proceeding further with the case, stated "In our view [the above quoted] statement was arbitrary and may be prejudicial to the rights of defendant if left without comment." Quoting

Section 322 of the Code, the court went on to say: "If later application be made to the Supreme Court * * * for leave to withdraw the plea and demur to these indictments or any of them, the aforesaid statement would not so bind the justice then presiding that he must deny the application. *** A Justice of the court has not jurisdiction to place a limitation on the right to apply for leave to demur which is not placed by the statute and which may embarrass another Justice when called upon to act." Therefore, it appears that defendant is not limited to one extension of time to withdraw his plea and demur, where the extension originally granted was inadequate to permit protection of the defendant's rights.

The recognized procedure is to demur at the arraignment if possible. If more time to consider the matter is necessary, an application for an extension of time, under Section 322, should be made. However, even if a plea has been entered, the court will, if the interests of justice demand it, permit withdrawal of the plea and interposition of a demurrer. Even if no request for such an extension is made at the arraignment, it may thereafter be requested. 

But such request must be more than a mere request for favor. It is addressed to the court's judicial discretion, which must be motivated by a showing that reason and justice demand it. 371

§ 

 Sec. 217. Preserving Objections in Disallowed Demurrer. 

Section 330 of the code provides: "If the demurrer be disallowed, the court must permit the defendant, at his election, to plead; which he must do forthwith, or at such time as the court may allow. If he do not plead, judgment must be pronounced against him, if the crime charged is a misdemeanor, otherwise a plea of 'not guilty' must be entered." Section 331 reads: "The objections mentioned in section three hundred and twenty-three can only be taken by demurrer, except that the objection to the jurisdiction of the court over the subject matter of the indictment or that the facts stated do not constitute a crime, may be taken at the trial, under the plea of not guilty, and in arrest of judgment." The failure to demur for lack of jurisdiction or for insufficiency is thus no bar to the defendant's later raising these objections. Nor is it necessary to renew objections asserted and disallowed on demurrer by way of the motions permitted during and after trial. 

The order disallowing the demurrer is one of the intermediate orders renewable on appeal from conviction regardless of the reassertion of its objections. In People v. 

Wilson, 151 N.Y. 403, the Court of Appeals stated: "The

Code of Criminal Procedure does not seem to require that the objections once taken by demurrer to the indictment should be also raised in some form after trial has been entered upon. It was before the Supreme Court, upon the defendant's appeal, and as its judgment must be deemed to comprehend the review of the determination upon the demurrer, that question is also before us upon this appeal." 

Nor is it required that an exception be taken to the disallowance of a demurrer. This is not the practice, and early authorities hold such exception improper. In People v. Reagle, 60 Barb. 527, the court stated that exceptions are to be taken only on the trial, and not to the ruling of the court upon a demurrer before the trial was commenced. People v. Gardiner, 6 Parker Cr. 143, holds to the same effect. In any event, no appeal lies from an order disallowing a demurrer, except as an incident of an appeal 372

DEMURRERS 

§ 218 from adjudgment of conviction (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

517; People v. Ciegel, 282 App. Div. 747, 172 N.Y.S. 2d 638,

People v. Oliver, 214 App. Div. 804, 210 N.Y.S. 562; People v. Flaherty, 206 App. Div. 733, 199 N.Y.S. 940). See the chapter of this work entitled "Appeals."

Sec. 218. Waiver: Effect of Failure to Demur. In People v. 

Caron, 121 N.Y.S. 2d 404, the defendant, after pleading guilty to second degree grand larceny, attempted to secure his release from prison by writ of error coram nobis, contending that the value of the property alleged to have been stolen was less that the statute required for the crime charged. After discussing the procedure made available to defendant by Sections 323, 331, 467, and 469 of the Code, the court stated: "The defendant has waived his right to make this motion by not doing so prior to the imposition of final judgment. While he may not waive his constitutional objection to the power or jurisdiction of the court to try him, other constitutional, as well as statutory rights, may be waived."

In People v. Meyer, 123 Misc. 243, 205 N.Y.S. 713, the defendant, after conviction, applied for a certificate of reasonable doubt on the ground that the indictment did not state facts sufficient to constitute the crime of which he was convicted. The court, quoting People v. Willett, 213 

N.Y. 368, stated: "Unless a motion founded upon the indictment and the insufficiency thereof is made before or at the time when the defendant is called for judgment, the objections thereto are waived.' It not appearing that any such motion was made, the claim that the indictment is insufficient in law may not be considered upon the appeal from the judgment of conviction." 

In People v. Dileo, 194 App. Div. 793, 186 N.Y.S. 156, it was held that the objection that an information charged more than one crime "would only be taken by demurrer, and would be waived, if not so taken." The Code has been amended to permit such an indictment since that case was decided. See the section on "Joinder of Offenses" in the 373

§ 

 chapter entitled "Indictments." People v. Valentine, 147 

App. Div. 31, 131 N.Y.S. 733, affirmed without opinion 205 

N.Y. 556, held that the defendant's failure to demur waived any defect in the indictment concerning the allegation of intent, required under the statute. The court noted that the facts alleged were sufficient to charge a crime under another subdivision than the one alleged and that the misnumbering had been waived. In People v. Grutz, 212 N.Y. 

72, the defendant's objections to an indictment for arson, for not stating the location of the building burned or the name of the person within it, required for the degree charged, were held waived by failure to demur and therefore were not considered on appeal. See also People v. 

Weichers, 94 App. Div. 19, 87 N.Y.S. 897, affirmed 179 N.Y. 

459, holding that the objection on the ground that the indictment charged more than one crime had been waived by failure to raise it prior to appeal.

In People ex rel. Fryer v. Brophy, 149 Misc. 562, 267 

N.Y.S. 735, aff'd per curiam 241 App. Div. 653, 269 N.Y.S. 

985, the defendant, after pleading guilty to an indictment charging a fourth offense, sought release on writ of habeas corpus on the ground that his third conviction was upon an information for a misdemeanor in California. In dismissing the writ, the court stated that his conviction would be upheld on two grounds, one being that defendant "having entered a general plea of guilty to the ** ** indictment which charged *** that *** he was in due form of law convicted of a felony * * * without having demurred to the form of the indictment and the substance thereof, and not having made a motion in arrest of judgment, waived any objections thereto."

However, failure to demur was held not to constitute a waiver in People v. O'Neill, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 945, where defendant's objection was to the jurisdiction of the Grand Jury which found the indictment. The defendant had been indicted upon a charge of carnal abuse of a child "of the age of ten years," under Section 483-a of the Penal Law.

Section 483-b prohibited such action directed against chil- 374

DEMURRERS 

§ 218 dren "of ten years and over and less than sixteen years."

All parties conceded that the child involved had been ten years and ten months old. After pleading not guilty on arraignment, the defendant moved to dismiss the indictment. 

The court, while dismissing the indictment, stated: "The 

District Attorney ** argues that the defendant having plead 'not guilty' to the indictments upon his arraignment and having failed to demur thereto, waived all rights to attack the indictments for any cause whatsoever, and therefore is precluded from attacking them at this time. He cites 

Sections 321, 322 and 323 of the Criminal Code." The court quoted Section 331 of the Code and then stated that the "defendant did not waive his right to object to the jurisdiction of the grand jury, although he pleaded not guilty' on arraignment. Such question may be raised at any stage of the proceeding.' 99 However, attacks based on the lack of local jurisdiction of the court may be waived by failure to move. In People v. Bowers, 3 Misc. 2d 668, 156 N.Y.S. 2d 82, the defendant, indicted for abandoning a pregnant woman, contended that the crime had been committed in another county although the record indicated that on his arraignment he had stated otherwise. The court refused the writ of error coram nobis sought by the defendant, and stated that defendant's not guilty plea, coupled with his failure to demur, had waived any objections to the indictment. 

In People v. Quinn, 161 N.Y.S. 2d 977, the defendant pleaded guilty to second degree larceny, although no larceny count was included in the indictment. The court noted that second degree larceny was a "necessarily included" crime (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 445), and further stated: "It follows *** that even if it be assumed that the facts pertaining to the larceny plea herein do not fit the specified robbery count, defendant is nonetheless foreclosed by a waiver from raising an objection thereto." In 

People v. Scott, 3 N.Y. 2d 148, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 707, defendant, after pleading guilty to a charge of drunken driving pursuant to a traffic summons, appealed, contending that 375

§ 

the summons was legally insufficient as an information because it was not verified. The court stated: "We turn now to the question of whether defendant has waived his objection to the lack of an information by his plea of guilty. 

It is well settled that by such a plea he waives his objection to the form of the information. *** However, objection to the jurisdiction of the court is not waived, nor is the objection that the information does not state a crime." The absence of the verification was held jurisdictional, and the defendant's conviction reversed. 

In summary, defects in the form or in the contents of an indictment will be considered waived absent a demurrer, or motion to set aside the indictment, or a motion equivalent thereto, made at or before the trial. Major defects such as want of jurisdiction in the court, failure of the indictment to set forth facts sufficient to state a crime, or want of the Grand Jury's jurisdiction, will not be considered so waived. "An indictment cannot be attacked upon appeal unless some foundation was laid therefor before final judgment was rendered. An accused person may take advantage of a defective indictment by demurring thereto before the trial, by objecting thereto during the trial, or by a motion in arrest of judgment made after the trial. The function of a demurrer *** is to defeat the indictment without a trial, whenever it appears on the face thereof that it is subject to one or more of the five objections named in the statute. *** These objections can be taken only by demurrer. If a defendant, with all these chances open to him omits to question the indictment before the trial, during the trial or after the trial, and makes no objection to the form or sufficiency thereof until the argument of an appeal from a judgment of conviction, he cannot then be heard upon the subject." (People v. 

Weichers, 179 N.Y. 459, 461-462.) Thus, even the objections which are waived by failure to demur before trial must be raised prior to conviction and appeal or they will be considered waived, and defendant's right to attack the indictment's sufficiency foreclosed. 376

DEMURRERS 

§ 219 

Sec. 219. Form of Demurrer. Section 324 of the Code pro vides: "The demurrer must be in writing, signed either by the defendant or his counsel, and filed. It must distinctly specify the grounds of objection to the indictment, or it may be disregarded." Cases have been discussed above, in the section under "Time to Demur," in which motions to set aside indictments were treated as demurrers, thus indicating the court's willingness to look through the form of the motion to what, substantively, is sought therein. The courts are, naturally, reluctant to disregard valid substantive arguments in criminal cases because presented in the wrong, formal, manner. Thus, in People v. McCormack, 68 Misc. 430, 125 N.Y.S. 68, the defendant demurred on the ground that the facts alleged "are insufficient to constitute any crime against the laws of the State of New York," and that the indictment "does not fully and fairly inform the defendant *** and is evasive, uncertain and does not conform to the requirements of the code." The court noted: "The demurrer does not follow the language of the Code, and does not as distinctly specify the alleged grounds of objection to the indictment as it would have done had it followed such language. It, however, uses to the extent hereinafter stated equivalent language, and to such extent it cannot be disregarded under [Section 324]." The demurrer was subsequently disallowed after the court compared the grounds alleged therein to the equivalent grounds mentioned in the statute.

In People v. Knatt, 156 N.Y. 302, the court noted: "The scope and effect of a general demurrer at common law has not been changed by the Code, unless it be to enlarge it. 

That statute greatly simplified the forms of pleadings in criminal cases, but an indictment or other pleading, which was good at common law, is good still. It may, indeed, be in a much more simple form, but it is not objectionable if it comes up to the standard of accuracy prescribed by the common law." Thus the demurrer will test the sufficiency of the indictment, whether drawn in common law or statutory form. In 1945, Section 323 of the Code was 377

§ 

amended to allow demurrers to any, or all, counts of an indictment. Prior cases, holding that demurrers would not be allowed if any of the counts of a multi-count indictment were valid are no longer pertinent.

Of course not all defects in form will be overlooked, and not all motions to dismiss indictments which are based on grounds which should be raised by demurrer will be treated as demurrers. This is true, particularly, if the indictment attacked is valid "on its face" (People v. Rehn, 172 N.Y.S. 2d 459), or if a not guilty plea stands while the motion or demurrer is interposed. In People v. Meyers, 119 

N.Y.S. 2d 474, the question presented was whether the court had the power to direct the resubmission of a previously dismissed indictment to another Grand Jury. The defendants argued that the dismissal of the indictment, upon their motion after trial, was equivalent to the allowance of a demurrer and that the court had power to direct a resubmission only within the terms of Section 327 of the Code, at the time of the dismissal of the indictment. But the court, noting that a demurrer is required to be in writing and signed, and may not be interposed while a not guilty plea stands, held defendants' oral motion not equivalent to a demurrer for the purposes mentioned. 

Sec. 220. Grounds for Demurrer. There are several general principles applied by the courts in considering demurrers upon any ground. "The demurrer *** serves only to raise objections which appear upon the face of the indictment." (People v. Gutterson, 244 N.Y. 243, 247.) The facts alleged in an indictment must be taken as true upon consideration of a demurrer (People v. Squillante, 12 Misc. 2d 514, 173 

N.Y.S. 2d 749), or upon a motion to dismiss the indictment upon grounds similar to those set forth in Section 323 (People v. Chester, 4 Misc. 2d 949, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 829).

Similarly, all that can be reasonably implied from the facts alleged in the indictment will be deemed true (People v. 

Wright, 12 Misc. 2d 961, 173 N.Y.S. 2d 160).

Grand Jury's Jurisdiction. The first ground, set forth 378

DEMURRERS 

§ 220 in Section 323, for a demurrer is "That the Grand Jury, by which it was found, had no legal authority to inquire into the crime charged." In People v. Lopez, 5 Misc. 2d 1054, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 1001, the defendant demurred to an indictment on that ground, alleging in support thereof that the Grand Jury had no authority to act because selected under an unconstitutional statute. The court disallowed the demurrer, stating: "Section 323 of the Code provides that the defendant may demur to the indictment *** when it appears on the face thereof. "The demurrer serves only to raise objections which appear on the face of the indictment' *** Although a Grand Jury was selected under an invalid statute the defendant's constitutional rights were not violated." The invalidity of the statute not appearing on the face of the indictment, the demurrer was thus not allowed. 

Prior to 1945, Section 323, subdivision 1, contained the words: "by reason of its not being within the local jurisdiction of the county." These words were omitted in 1945, but even prior to that time, it had been held that the jurisdiction of the Grand Jury, other than in a geographic sense, could be attacked by demurrer (People v. Newman, 141 

Misc. 429, 253 N.Y.S. 72). The court reached that result by adopting the reasoning of the Knatt case, supra, to the effect that general demurrers at common law, which did raise questions of general jurisdiction, were still valid under the Code. In the Newman case, the defendant was indicted for "petit larceny, second offense," a crime for which there was no statutory definition. The court noted that jurisdiction over petit larceny offenses was vested exclusively in special sessions and, therefore, the Grand Jury had had no jurisdiction to find the indictment. The demurrer was allowed. This defect, upon the face of the indictment, was thus susceptible of demurrer, distinguishable from the defects in the Lopez case, supra, or in People v. Joseph, 4 Misc. 2d 463, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 125. In the

Joseph case, the defendant alleged, while demurring, that prosecution for the crime charged was required to be ini- 379

$ 

tiated by the Attorney General. The court held that as the restrictions upon the power to initiate proceedings did not appear on the face of the indictment, the demurrer could not be allowed. In any event, the court also noted that defendant's contention was without merit. 

In People v. Foster, 60 Misc. 3, 112 N.Y.S. 706, however, the court noted the absence of an allegation in the demurrer which would have contradicted the allegations of the indictment, stating: "the circumstance that the crime was not within the local jurisdiction of the county, is not alleged in the demurrer. It affirmatively appears upon the face of the indictment that the crime was committed in [the proper] *** county. *** It is therefore established that the *** grounds of the demurrer are without merit."

It is doubtful whether the court meant, by this statement, to indicate that if the demurrer did contain allegations contradicting those of the indictment, it could be sustained. 

One early case held that a demurrer would not lie to an indictment where the deficiency alleged was the failure of the requisite number of Grand Jurors to agree. This defect would not appear upon the face of the indictment (People v. Thomas, 32 Misc. 170, 66 N.Y.S. 191). The proper remedy would now appear to be a motion to set aside the indictment under Section 313. Only when the Grand Jury lacks jurisdiction over the crime will a demurrer lie; when the defect can be discovered by inspection of the Grand Jury minutes, a demurrer will not be allowed. 

Improper Form of Indictment. The second ground, set forth in Section 323, is: "That the indictment does not conform substantially to the requirements of Sections [275 and 276] ***” As previously discussed in the chapter on "Indictments," supra, Section 275 requires the indictment to contain "The title of the action, ** the name of the court to which the indictment is presented, and the names of the parties," and "A plain and concise statement of the act constituting the crime, without unnecessary repetition." Section 276-b prohibits the inclusion in the indictment of defendant's prior criminal record unless it affects, 380

DEMURRERS 

§ 220 or is an element of, the crime charged. Section 276 states that the indictment may be signed by the District Attorney, and may be substantially in the form there provided. The proposed form of a simplified indictment is given in Section 295-d. It should be noted that Section 323 requires only "substantial" conformity with Sections 275 and 276 and does not specifically refer to Section 276-b which was enacted after Section 323. 

In People v. Joseph, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 125, the defendants demurred on several grounds; the first, as to the jurisdiction of the Grand Jury, has been discussed in the preceding section. The second ground alleged was that the indictment did not meet the requirements of subdivision 2 of Section 323 in that it was overly long and repetitious. 

The court stated that the purpose of an indictment "is to notify the defendant of the nature of the charge against him to the end that he may properly prepare his defense and to identify the charge against him. * * * If the indictment meets the aforesaid requirements, it will suffice. ***

This indictment could easily have been shortened by eliminating certain descriptive and conclusory phrases contained therein, but none of them are prejudicial to a degree that a trial court will not be enabled to amply protect the defendants. *** Surplusage will not vitiate an otherwise valid indictment. *** the Court has examined this indictment to determine whether or not on the face thereof, the facts stated constitute a crime. Stripped of all the several repetitious, conclusory and descriptive phrases, there are sufficient allegations remaining in the indictment which *** constitute a crime. The demurrer is overruled."

At this point reference should be made to Section 684 of the Code, which sets forth: "Neither a departure from the form or mode prescribed by the Code, in respect to any pleadings or proceedings, nor an error or mistake therein, renders it invalid, unless it have actually prejudiced the defendant, or tend to his prejudice, in respect to a substantial right." Similarly, Section 285, which refers specifically to indictments, reads: "No indictment is insuffi- 381

§ 

cient, nor can the trial, judgment, or other proceedings thereon be affected, by reason of an imperfection in matter of form, which does not tend to the prejudice of the substantial rights of the defendant, upon the merits." These sections, together with the above quoted language of the courts, clearly indicate the problems met in attempting to demur to indictments for lack of compliance with the formal requisites of subdivision 2. In People v. Cadle, 7 

App. Div. 2d 65, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 576, 577, the court, reversing the allowance of a demurrer stated: "Upon a demurrer the facts stated in the indictment must be assumed to be true as well as everything that can be implied by fair and reasonable intendment from these facts. *** The indictment is to be construed liberally rather than in a technical or impracticable manner. So long as no substantial right of the defendant is prejudiced, the court should take a liberal approach and look to the realities of what the indictment alleges." 

The failure of the District Attorney to sign the indictment has been held merely formal (People v. Foster et al, 60 Misc. 3, 112 N.Y.S. 706). It has been held that this defect is waived by the defendant unless raised at the arraignment and, even if raised then, may be cured by reference of the indictment back to the Grand Jury for signature by the District Attorney. One court indicated that the failure of the foreman of the Grand Jury to sign the indictment might be disregarded in the same manner as the District 

Attorney's (People v. Rice Associates, 185 Misc. 473, 56 

N.Y.S. 2d 833).

Omission of the designation of the court in which the indictment was found has also been held not fatal (People v. Peck, 96 N.Y. 650). In the Peck case, however, the name of the court appeared in other parts of the record. The court in that case further stated that omission of the title of the action would not be a fatal defect upon a demurrer. 

It has been held in Massachusetts that omission from the body of the indictment of the name of the defendants was not fatal where the name of the defendants appeared in the 382

DEMURRERS 

$220 title of the indictment (Downey v. Hale, 67 F. 2d 208). A misstatement of the degree of the offense (first, rather than second degree burglary being alleged) has been held not fatal (People v. Oliver, 3 N.Y. 2d 684). Error in the caption of the indictment was early held immaterial (Niles v. People, 4 Amer. Law J. [N.S.] 507, the caption being held not part of the indictment proper; People v. Myers, 2 Hun 

6). Errors in the commencement and conclusion of the indictment were also early held not material and, in any event, not to be corrected by the court, if in substantial conformity with the statute (People v. Peck, supra; People v. Conger, 1 Wheeler Crim. Cases 448).

However, the requirement stated in Section 275, that the indictment contain a "plain and concise statement of the acts constituting the crime", is not merely formal. The statement may, as discussed above, be overly long and repetitious, but it must be included in a long-form indictment. 

The requirements of the statement are discussed in the chapter on "Indictments."

Duplicitous Indictments. Subdivision 3 of Section 323 

sets forth, as demurrable, that "more than one crime is charged in the indictment within the meaning of Sections [278 and 279]' ***"The cases on joinder of offenses in an indictment are discussed in the chapter on "Indictments." 

Objections based on misjoinder of offenses in an indictment are waived, unless presented by demurrer (People v. Dileo, 194 App. Div. 793, 186 N.Y.S. 156). And, "if more than one crime is charged, except as permitted by section 279 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 'the proper and only remedy is by demurrer'." (People v. Goldner, 70 Misc. 

199, 178 N.Y.S. 375.) People v. Thompson, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 

319, held that a demurrer on this ground did not lie to a multi-count simplified indictment because Section 279, allowing joinder of offenses in stated circumstances, applied to both simplified and long-form indictments. 

If one of the counts of the indictment does not allege a crime, a demurrer will not lie under subdivision 3, even though the acts alleged in that count are unrelated to the 383

§ 

acts alleged as constituting crimes in the other counts. 

Thus, in People ex rel. Weeks v. Platt, 173 App. Div. 451, 159 N.Y.S. 920, the court noted that one count of the indictment contained allegations that were "oppressively injurious by suggestion," but "legally meaningless." Because that count did not allege a crime, the demurrer was not allowed under Section 323, subdivision 3. If the indictment alleges that certain acts were jointly committed, a demurrer will not be allowed on the ground that the acts were really several, and thus a misjoinder resulted from their inclusion in the indictment. The ground for disallowance of the demurrer there is, of course, that the demurrer admits the facts alleged to be true; therefore it admitted the allegation that the actions were jointly perpetrated and defendant could not argue that they were not (People v. Schmidt, 19 Misc. 548, 44 N.Y.S. 607). However, where it was apparent on the indictment that the acts alleged were committed separately, and there was no allegation that they had been part of the same transaction, a demurrer was allowed even though the several crimes were charged in one count of an indictment (People v. Saltwell, 192 

N.Y.S. 559; People v. Goldner, supra).

In People v. Hartwell, 166 N.Y. 361, the defendant was indicted for "knowingly receiving stolen property" and, in the same count, for "concealing and withholding" the aforesaid property. A demurrer was interposed and, reversing the conviction, the court stated: "Under subdivision three of Section 323*** a demurrer may be interposed when 'more than one crime is charged in the indictment within the meaning of Sections 278 and 279.' It may be that *** one crime stated by different means in the same count is not demurrable although prohibited by these sections." 

However the court allowed the demurrer upon other grounds. In 1936, Section 279 was amended and liberalized so that the applicability of many of the cases decided prior to that date may be limited. The rules concerning permissible joinders are discussed in the chapter on "Indictments." 

In considering demurrers on this ground it need be remem- 384

DEMURRERS 

§ 220 bered that the objection of duplicity "not only may, but must be taken by demurrer" (People v. Klipfel, 160 N.Y. 

371), and that if the demurrer is sustained the matter will, generally, be resubmitted for correction of the error in a new indictment (People v. Trepel, 207 Misc. 98, 139 

N.Y.S. 2d 513). 99 

Sufficiency of Facts Alleged. Subdivision 4 of Section 

323 allows a demurrer to the indictment on the ground that "the facts stated do not constitute a crime." Under 

Section 331, this objection may also be raised "at the trial, under the plea of not guilty, and in arrest of judgment.' 

Thus, this objection is not waived by failure to demur 

(People v. Caron, 121 N.Y.S. 2d 204). While some courts have indicated that this objection is not properly raised by motion to set aside the indictment under Section 313 (People v. Kahn, 155 App. Div. 821, 140 N.Y.S. 618), others have treated such motions as demurrers. The cases deciding the requisites of indictments in this area are discussed in the chapter on "Indictments," supra.

An objection that the standards of guilt set by the statute defining the crime are too vague, or are being misapplied to the facts in the case concerned, may not be raised by demurrer, "but properly should be presented to the trial court, in arrest of judgment." (People v. Dill, 165 N.Y.S. 

2d 286.) The bill of particulars may supply deficiencies in the allegations made in a simplified indictment, but not in a long-form indictment. However, where more specific allegations are desired, application should be made for a discretionary bill of particulars; a demurrer should not be used (People v. Weiss, 210 N.Y. 546). Where the demurrer alleges a crime, but of a lower degree than that intended to be charged by the indictment, a demurrer will not be allowed (People v. Cooper, 3 N.Y. Crim. 117). 

Constitutionality of Statutes. In People v. Peck, 112 

N.Y.S. 2d 379, the defendant demurred on the ground that it was "unconstitutional and unreasonable," apparently meaning that the ordinance which he was charged with violating was unconstitutional. The court considered the 385

$ 

"9 argument, decided that the ordinance involved was constitutional, and did not allow the demurrer. The language used by the court in the Dill case, supra, indicates a difference of opinion concerning the propriety of the use of a demurrer to raise this objection. See also People v. 

Estreich, 272 App. Div. 698, 75 N.Y.S. 2d 287, where the court stated: "The principal question presented for determination arises upon defendant's contention, properly raised below on his motion in arrest of judgment" *** that the facts alleged in the indictment do not constitute a crime and that [the penal statute] *** is unconstitutional.' 

While neither of the above courts discussed the time when the constitutionality of the statute should be challenged, both appear to be correct decisions. In the Dill case, the court stated, on reargument of a motion to dismiss an information because the statute "did not set forth sufficient standards of guilt so as to meet constitutional requirements": "We held, and still hold, that the question urged by defendant 'properly should be presented to the trial court' *** and the Butler case [352 U.S. 380] * * * 

supports our view." In People v. Reed, 276 N.Y. 5, the defendants, indicted for violating the gambling laws, moved to dismiss for insufficiency on the ground that the statutes cited in the indictment were, in effect, nullified by other statutes. The trial court dismissed at the close of the case, although the defendants' motions had, advisedly, been made at the commencement of the case. The Court of 

Appeals indicated the impropriety of such action at that time, stating that jeopardy had attached, and the People had no right to appeal from such an order; the appeal from the order was dismissed. The Court of Appeals compared the motion made to a demurrer and indicated that, like a demurrer, the ruling should have been made at the commencement of the trial so that the People could have appealed. However, the rationale of the Reed case has been vitiated by the 1942 amendments to Section 518 of the Code, which now allows an appeal by the People from "an order *** made at any stage of the action setting aside or dis- 386

DEMURRERS 

§ 220 missing the indictment on a ground other than the insufficiency of the evidence." See the chapter of this work on "Appeals."

Justification, Excuse and Bar to Prosecution: Statute of Limitations. Subdivision 5 of Section 323 provides, as a ground for demurrer: "That the indictment contains matter which, if true, would constitute a legal justification or excuse for the acts charged, or other legal bar to the prosecution." Confusion has arisen as to the Statute of 

Limitations, and whether it is properly a defense, to be raised at the trial under a not guilty plea, or whether it is a proper ground for demurrer. In People v. Brady, 257 

App. Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 789, while reversing an order dismissing an indictment, the court stated: "The Statute of Limitations in criminal cases *** is a statute of repose." .”*** It may be raised as a defense at the trial, under a plea of not guilty *** but it may be waived by failure of defendant to invoke it *** on the ground that the Statute of Limitations was not sufficiently raised at the trial. Since there may be a waiver, an indictment which on its face shows the statute has run is not invalid." The defendant had made a motion to dismiss the indictment on the ground that there was insufficient evidence before the Grand Jury in that the Grand Jury minutes showed that the indictment was found without the statutory period. The District Attorney had opposed the motion on the ground that the Statute of Limitations "can only be interposed under a plea of not guilty and at the end of the People's case." (10 

N.Y.S. 2d 395, 396.) The Appellate Division apparently agreed with the District Attorney's contention, although the case does not hold, in the narrow sense, that the defense could not be interposed by means of a demurrer. 

In People v. Steiger, 154 Misc. 538, 277 N.Y.S. 602, a motion to dismiss an indictment was granted where the indictment revealed that it was found without the statutory period. The court stated: "where the prosecution claims that the defendant comes within any of the exceptions of the statute of limitations, it is incumbent upon the 387

§ 

people to allege it in the indictment. *** The indictment in the case at bar contains no allegation whatsoever. * * *

This is a defect in a substantial particular." To the contrary is People v. Amann, 159 Misc. 417, 289 N.Y.S. 316, where the court stated: "the objection that on the face of the indictment the statute of limitations has run against prosecution for the crime cannot be availed of on motion, but must be interposed under the general plea of not guilty. 

See the well considered opinion in People v. Bailey, 103 

Misc. 366, 171 N.Y.S. 374.”

The above cases did not consider the propriety of a demurrer, but are in point, for if a motion to dismiss would not lie because the defense must be raised at the trial under a not guilty plea, a demurrer would similarly not lie. People v. Kaplan, 143 Misc. 91, 256 N.Y.S. 874, did consider the propriety of a demurrer in this area. There "The defendants argue that since it appears on the face of the indictment that more than two years have elapsed since the commission of the crime of conspiracy—a misdemeanor the Statute of Limitations *** is properly raised by de murrer. The weight of authority is to the effect that the 

Statute of Limitations is a defense and cannot be raised on demurrer; * * * nor by special plea in bar; * * * but can be raised only upon the trial under the general issue." The court then cited the adverse cases and adopted the "general rule" as understood by it. The judgment of conviction in the Kaplan case was affirmed by the Court of Appeals, without opinion, in 264 N.Y. 675. The New York case, cited by the court in People v. Bailey as being contrary to the general rule, is People v. Busccolieri, 91 Misc. 156, 152

N.Y.S. 707, which held a demurrer proper where the face of the indictment indicated the passage of the statutory period. That the Statute of Limitations would prevent the finding of a new indictment was held not a valid reason for upholding an otherwise invalid indictment upon demurrer in People v. Goldner, 70 Misc. 199, 128 N.Y.S. 375.

In this connection, it should be noted that the cases holding that the Statute of Limitations in criminal cases is a 388

DEMURRERS 

§ 220 "statute of repose," as it is in civil cases, and can be waived by the defendant's not raising it on the trial, seem to have been discredited. See the chapter of this work on "Arrest of Judgment." The Court of Appeals in People v. Hines 284 

N.Y. 93, 113, stated: "such a statute in a criminal case creates a bar to prosecution and the time within which an offense is committed becomes a jurisdictional fact which the State must allege and prove." The very Appellate Division, which in a 3-2 decision in People v. Brady, 257 App. 

Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 789, stated that the statute is one "of repose," eight years later affirmed without opinion an order arresting judgment on the theory that the People's failure to negative the running of the limitation period was a jurisdictional defect (People v. Guariglia, 187 Misc. 843, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 96, affirmed 272 App. Div. 784, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 

759). If, indeed, it is to be held that the statute "destroys the right of action as well as the remedy" (People ex rel. 

Reibman v. Warden, 242 App. Div. 282, 284, 275 N.Y.S. 59), and is jurisdictional, and cannot be waived, as can a civil Statute of Limitations, it should follow that the question of limitation is a proper ground for demurrer. Apparently, we have yet to see the adoption of a definitive New York rule on this question.

Effect of Demurrer upon the Statute. If a demurrer to an indictment is allowed, and the court directs resubmission to a Grand Jury, the Statute of Limitations is tolled for the period during which the prior prosecution was pending, provided the new prosecution is commenced within sixty days after the entry of the order allowing the demurrer (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 1445a; People v. 

Fuller, 156 Misc. 404, 282 N.Y.S. 28). 

Former Jeopardy, Conviction or Acquittal. "Where the facts are not in dispute, a plea of double jeopardy presents only a question of law" (People ex rel. Kammerer v. 

Brophy, 255 App. Div. 34, 7 N.Y.S. 2d 34, 35), and it would appear that an objection to an indictment on this ground should properly be raised by demurrer. However the cases indicate that this objection is most often interposed by a 389

§ 

plea under Section 332, subdivision 3, of the Code, which allows, as a plea to an indictment, "former judgment of conviction or acquittal of the crime charged which may be pleaded either with or without the plea of not guilty." (See, for example, People v. Papaccio, 140 Misc. 696, 251 

N.Y.S. 717.) In People v. Thrum, 143 Misc. 7, 256 N.Y.S. 

586, the defendant moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that he had previously been placed in jeopardy for the same offense. While granting the motion, the court stated: "There is no statutory authority for this motion. 

There having been no judgment of conviction or acquittal in the lower court, no adequate plea is provided for under 

[Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 332]. ***The relief sought herein is not included in the grounds of demurrer enumerated in [Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 323]." Thus, the court intimated without holding, a demurrer on this ground would not lie. 

In People v. Oliver, 214 App. Div. 804, 210 N.Y.S. 562, an appeal from an order overruling a demurrer was dismissed, primarily on the ground that it was not an appealable order, but the court stated: "The claim that defendant has been once put in jeopardy for the offense charged, and acquitted or convicted, must be raised by plea to the indictment *** Code Cr. Proc. Sec. 332. It was not before the court on the demurrer." (People v. Smith, 172 N.Y. 210, 227.) Of course, if defendant had not been acquitted or convicted, but merely placed in jeopardy, then, as the court, noted in the Thrum case, a plea under Section 332 would not lie. However, as stated by the Court of Appeals in People ex rel. Brinkman v. Barr, 248 N.Y. 126, 129: "Where the defendant charged with crime, has once been placed in jeopardy, he may not again be tried for the same offense. 

Of his right to this defense upon his second trial he may not be deprived *** even, if he may not always bring up the matter by a plea (Code of Crim. Proc. Sec. 332), an objection on the record, or a proper motion which raises the issue, is sufficient."

It would appear to be most desirable to have the validity 390

DEMURRERS 

§ 222 of the indictment, challenged on purely legal rather than factual grounds, settled prior to trial (People v. McCann, 151 Misc. 792, 273 N.Y.S. 839). However, as has been noted, some of the cases indicate that this objection may not be properly raised by demurrer. One early case, People v. 

Krummer, 4 Parker Cr. 217, does indicate that it is available on demurrer. In view of the lack of convincing authority, it would appear to be in defendant's best interest to raise the question of former jeopardy as early as possible by demurrer or by a motion to dismiss, and by plea under Section 332, thus insuring that this defense is not deemed waived. People v. Cignarale, 110 N.Y. 23, indicates that this defense is waived by failing to plead it. 

The Report of the Commissioners on Practice and Plead ings, p. 170 (1849), commenting upon Section 334, providing the form of the plea under Section 332, stated: "These forms are given (and especially the last) [concerning a plea of former conviction or acquittal] to obviate the necessity of demurrer, if the plea, as it might be drawn under the existing rules, should not be substantially sufficient." This statement further indicates the original intention of the legislators that this defense should be interposed as a plea, and not by demurrer. 

Sec. 221. Hearing of Demurrer. After the demurrer is filed, the court sets the date on which the argument will be heard (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 325). The defendant may waive hearing upon the demurrer, and stipulate for decision upon written briefs to be submitted to the court (People v. 

Luckman, 164 Misc. 230, 297 N.Y.S. 616, affirmed upon other grounds, 254 App. Div. 694, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 864). 

Sec. 222. Judgment upon Demurrer. After hearing the argument upon the demurrer the court must give judgment thereon, its order being entered upon the minutes. 

If the court allows the demurrer, no further action is required, and the indictment stands dismissed (People v. 

Whitman, 126 N.Y.S. 1080). If the demurrer is overruled, 391

§ 

the indictment is sustained and trial proceeds. The order is usually a simple one, endorsed upon the indictment by the clerk and initialed by the judge. A formal defect in the order overruling a demurrer will not vitiate the court's decision, nor will it be deemed an allowance of the de murrer (People v. Meola, 193 App. Div. 487, 184 N.Y.S. 

353; People v. Canepi, 181 N.Y. 398). A copy of the "minutes of the plea or demurrer" becomes part of the judgment roll, on judgment of conviction (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 485). Since an intermediate order, such as the disallowance of a demurrer, will be reviewed on appeal only when it is part of the judgment roll (People v. Rudnick, 255 App. Div. 813, 7 N.Y.S. 2d 349), this section has the effect of insuring that rulings on demurrers to indictments may be reviewed on appeal (People v. Canepi, 181 N.Y. 

398), even if no further objection is made during, or after, the trial (People v. Wilson, 151 N.Y. 403). 

Sec. 223. Effect of Allowance of Demurrer. Section 327 of the Code provides: "If the demurrer be allowed, the judgment is final upon the indictment demurred to, and is a bar to another prosecution for the same offense, unless the court, being of opinion that the objection on which the demurrer is allowed may be avoided in a new indictment, direct the case to be resubmitted to the same or another grand jury." A somewhat similar provision, applicable to the allowance of motions to set aside indictments, but with different consequences, is found in Section 317.

The order directing the resubmission must be made by the judge who sustained the demurrer (People v. Zerillo, 146 App. Div. 812, 131 N.Y.S. 500; People ex rel. Grossman v. Warden, 172 Misc. 183, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 243). Such restrictions are not necessarily imposed upon orders of resubmission under Section 317, applicable to motions to set aside indictments. In People v. Meyers, 119 N.Y.S. 2d 474, it was held proper for a court to add to its original order at a later time and direct resubmission. And it has been stated: "Where the dismissal of the indictments was not in conse- 392

DEMURRERS 

§ 223 quence of a demurrer, but was the result of a motion to set the indictments aside, based on the Grand Jury minutes, there is no requirement that an order be obtained prior to resubmitting the case to another Grand Jury. The only requirement for such an order under these circumstances is * imposed by Section 317*** if it is desired to retain the defendant in custody pending the resubmission.” (People v. Lenoci, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 332.) 

An order directing resubmission is not necessary unless the defendant has been placed in jeopardy by the first indictment. In People v. Rosenthal, 197 N.Y. 394, defendant was indicted but, before any plea or motion had been made by him, the court ordered the charge resubmitted to the Grand Jury upon application therefor by the District Attorney. A second indictment, substantially the same as the first, was found and the defendant moved to quash it before trial and, after pleading guilty to one count thereof, moved in arrest of judgment. After denial of that motion, he appealed. The Court of Appeals stated: "The People take nothing from the order of resubmission, which was a nullity. No order to resubmit, however, was necessary, for the Grand Jury had jurisdiction to reindict without one. The defendant was not put in jeopardy by the first indictment, as he was not arraigned thereunder, nor did he demur or plead thereto. If he had demurred and the demurrer had been sustained, a second indictment could not have been lawfully found without an order of resubmission. *** By the express command of the statute a judgment sustaining a demurrer is a bar to further prosecution for the same offense unless such an order is made." Thus, regardless of the attachment of jeopardy, the allowance of a demurrer will prevent a further prosecution absent a resubmission order.

In People v. Zerillo, 200 N.Y. 443, the defendant sought to appeal from an order directing resubmission of an indictment, made more than one year after allowance of a demurrer to the indictment. The Court dismissed the appeal, holding that no statutory basis for it could be found, 393

$

at the same time stating: "There appear to be two ways, however, in which the defendants can raise the question of the validity of the order to resubmit, which was made so long after the determination of the demurrer and by another judge. They could treat the allowance of the demurrer unaccompanied by any order for a resubmission of the case as equivalent to an acquittal and could interpose to the second indictment the plea of former acquittal. *** On the other hand, upon the trial of the new indictment, the defendants, if convicted, might move in arrest of judgment upon the ground that the prosecution was barred *** and if that motion were denied, could review the action of the trial court upon appeal." 

Sec. 224. Appeals. As previously stated, a defendant may not appeal specially from an order disallowing a demurrer; it is an intermediate order and may only be reviewed as part of the record on an appeal from a judgment of conviction (People v. Flaherty, 206 App. Div. 733, 199 N.Y.S. 

940, People v. Siegel, 282 App. Div. 747, 122 N.Y.S. 2d 638).

Section 518 gives the prosecution the right to appeal from "a judgment for the defendant, on a demurrer to the indictment," and from "an order of the court, made at any stage of the action, setting aside or dismissing the indictment on a ground other than the insufficiency of the evidence adduced at the trial." The latter ground covers the situation where indictments were dismissed upon motions held to be equivalent to demurrers. That a resubmission of the indictment has been allowed, under Section 327, does not affect the prosecution's right to appeal under the above quoted sections (People v. Bink, 151 App. Div. 271, 135 

N.Y.S. 733). See the chapter of this work entitled "Appeals." 394
