Sec. 236. Pleas of Guilt to Lesser Offenses

Sec. 237. Effect of Plea PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

After a motion to dismiss the indictment has been denied or waived, and a demurrer has been overruled, the defendant must plead to the indictment. 

Good practice dictates, however, that counsel enter a plea of not guilty when defendant is first arraigned. Before any plea is interposed, counsel should be certain that he either reserves his right to withdraw the plea or secures the permission of the court to withdraw the plea at a later date, for the purpose of moving or demurring with respect to the indictment. 

Never permit a client to enter a plea of guilty at this time. Such a plea, even if later withdrawn, may be introduced in evidence by the District Attorney as an admission against the defendant at a subsequent trial.

We have already considered the various ways to attack the indictment. If all such moves fail, defendant will have to decide whether or not to go to trial. If the probability of his conviction 395

§ 

on the instant charge is great, especially if he has a previous criminal record, he may well consider pleading guilty. Counsel should ask the District Attorney to consent to a plea on a lesser charge. Courts will invariably be guided by the prosecutor's recommendation in this regard.

Sec. 225. Definitions. After the indictment has been filed, the defendant is arraigned thereon and must respond. His response may take the form of a motion, a demurrer, the interposition of any one, or a combination of, the authorized pleas, or a refusal to respond which the law treats, in effect, as a plea. Motions directed to the indictment and demurrers are fully treated and discussed in other chapters of this work appropriately entitled. This chapter concerns itself only with the defendant's plea to the indictment, and is further restricted to pleas other than that of double jeopardy, or former conviction or acquittal, which is treated in the succeeding chapter. 

Some of the objections to indictments, now raised in New York by motion, were formerly raised by plea and are still so raised in other jurisdictions. Traditionally, pleas were classified in three groups: pleas to the jurisdiction; pleas in abatement and pleas in bar. Pleas to the jurisdiction were written pleas, based upon an alleged lack of jurisdiction in the court trying the indictment. Now, in New 

York, such objection is raised by demurrer or motion, and the plea defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure does not raise that objection. Pleas in abatement were also written and, generally, were of a formal nature based upon alleged defects in the constitution or procedure of the Grand Jury which had returned the indictment. They were frequently of a dilatory nature. In People v. Scannell, 36 Misc. 483, 73 N.Y.S. 1067, the defendant attempted to plead, after his arraignment, that the indictment was void because a nonresident of the county had served on the Grand Jury. The court stated the question posed to be "whether a plea described as a plea in abatement is admissible under our present procedure." After noting that "My attention has 396

§ not been called to a case, nor have I been able to find one, where a plea in abatement has been entertained in our state since the adoption of the Criminal Code," the court held that "a plea in abatement has been eliminated from our criminal procedure."

Sec. 226. History. In the early days of the common law the only plea a defendant was allowed to interpose was a denial of the charge (2 Pollock & Maitland, pp. 607-620 [1915 ed.]). As the law developed other pleas were permitted. Pleas of the benefit of clergy were allowed after conviction (4 Blackstone Comm. 26), and pleas of sanctuary were also allowed (3 Holdsworth, History of English Law, 303). Pleas in abatement, directed to the failure of the indictment to meet the strict standards required by the common law, became common (id., at p. 615). Blackstone states: "[a] plea in abatement is principally for a misnomer, a wrong name, or false addition to the prisoner." (4 Blackstone Comm. 328.) The various pleas in bar, similar to those used today, also developed. Pleas were generally oral. The early special pleas were abolished with the advent of the modern rules concerning simplified indictments, and the relaxation of the rules regulating the amendment of indictments, and pleas in abatement "for an error of form" have been rendered obsolete by the powers given to amend indictments (Orfield, Criminal Proc. from Arrest to Appeal, p. 271). Thus, except for the abolition of those pleas based upon the lack of the required formality of the indictment, or the proceedings leading to the finding of the indictment, "arraignment, plea and issue *** stand fundamentally as in the fourth book of Blackstone." (Pound, Criminal Justice in America, p. 109.) One distinction between the common law and the modern procedure lies in the rights of defendants, today, to plead over after an unsuccessful demurrer; at common law, frequently, it was held that such action was not permissible. 397

§ 

 Sec. 227. Types of Pleas. Section 332 of the Code provides: 

"There are three kinds of pleas to an indictment: 1. A plea of guilty. 2. A plea of not guilty. 3. A plea of former judgment of conviction or acquittal of the crime charged, which may be pleaded either with or without the plea of not guilty." The plea of former conviction or acquittal, treated in the succeeding chapter, will not be discussed herein. 

Under Section 336 of the Code, a plea of insanity may be presented by persons in confinement at the time of arraignment as a specification under a not guilty plea. 

Res Adjudicata. In People v. Cryan, 123 Misc. 358, 205 

N.Y.S. 852, the defendant moved to dismiss the indictment under the principle of res adjudicata, contending that the same issue had been decided in his favor in another proceeding. The question presented, as stated by the court, was "whether a judgment in a proceeding in rem of a penal nature, involving the precise issues raised by an indictment, permits the interposition of a plea of res adjudicata in a criminal prosecution." The court noted the prosecution's contention "that the Code of Criminal Procedure contains a provision with regard to a plea of former judgment of conviction or acquittal of the crime charged and is silent upon the subject of res adjudicata, and that therefore no such plea can be entertained, unless the defendant has either been acquitted or convicted of the crime charged", but held that contention untenable. The court upheld the defendant's plea, and dismissed the indictment. Of course, an adjudication in a civil suit, with its different burden of proof, will not prevent a subsequent adjudication on the same point. 

Sec. 228. How Plea Interposed. "Every plea must be oral, and must be entered upon the minutes of the court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 333.) Section 334 prescribes the form of the plea, and requires only a simple statement that "the defendant pleads "Pleas of former conviction or acquittal are discussed in the succeeding chapter. Pleas of guilty may be entered only by the defendant personally, 398

§ in open court, except in cases involving corporations, which may plead guilty by their counsel, and in cases concerning certain offenses under the Vehicle and Traffic Laws, which are treated in Section 335-a of the Code. If the defendant stands mute, or refuses to plead to an indictment, a plea of not guilty will be entered by the court on his behalf (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 342). As noted by the court in the Scannell case, supra, under the common law pleas to the jurisdiction and pleas in abatement were required to be in writing, and the requirement of the Code that all pleas be oral supersedes and abolishes the old, written, pleas.

Sec. 229. When Plea Interposed. After the defendant has been arraigned, "he must be allowed until the next day, or such further time may be allowed him as the court deems reasonable, to answer the indictment." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 311.) "In answer to the indictment, the defendant may either move to set the same aside, or may demur or plead thereto." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 312.) As noted above, it was frequently held at common law that defendants were not permitted to plead over, after unsuccessful interposition of a demurrer. Now, in New York, the defendant is allowed to move to set the indictment aside, and Section 316 of the Code allows, and requires, after an unsuccessful demurrer that the defendant "answer the indictment, either by demurring or pleading thereto." 

Further, Section 332 of the Code provides: "The demurrer and the plea must be put in, either at the time of the arraignment, or at such other time as may be allowed to the defendant for that purpose." Then, under Section 330, we find: "If the demurrer be disallowed, the court must permit the defendant at his election, to plead; which he must do forthwith, or at such time as the court may allow." If the defendant refuses to plead at that time, as in other cases, under Section 342, a plea of not guilty will be entered for him if the crime is a felony. However, in misdemeanor cases, Section 330 requires imposition of judgment against 399

§ 

the defendant if he refuses to plead after an unsuccessful demurrer. Thus, the common law rule on this point has been specifically abrogated by statute. 

The problem of the omission of a formal plea is considered elsewhere. See discussion of People v. McHale, 64 

Hun 618, 15 N.Y.S. 496, in the chapter of this work on "Arraignment." There, the defendant had been arraigned and permitted to plead not guilty after the close of evidence, the trial having previously proceeded as if a not guilty plea had been entered; the defendant was held not prejudiced by the lack of previous entry of a formal plea. 

A plea of guilty may be entered before the date set for hearing on the charge (People v. Henderson, 134 Misc. 

228, 235 N.Y.S. 173). In the Henderson case, the trial date had been adjourned, at defendant's request, and prior to the adjourned date, the defendant had appeared and pleaded guilty. The court held that the plea and sentence were valid.

Code of Criminal Procedure, section 357, provides: 

"after his plea, the defendant is entitled to at least two days to prepare for his trial, if he require it." Failure to allow this time to the defendant is a ground for reversal of any conviction resulting from the trial (People v. Phelan, 222 

N.Y.S. 594; People v. Harper, 139 App. Div. 344, 124 N.Y.S. 

12.) In the Harper case, the District Attorney contended that the defendant's demurrer was a plea to the indictment, and therefore after its disallowance the trial could proceed "forthwith." The court did not accept this contention, noting that under Section 321 of the Code a distinction is drawn between demurrers and pleas, and that under Section 357 the defendant is granted absolutely the right to a two-day interval between plea and trial if he requests it. 

The court further stated that the question of the defendant's need for the interval was immaterial. 

Sec. 230. Withdrawal of Pleas. Guilty Pleas. "The court may in its discretion, at any time before judgment upon a plea of guilty, permit it to be withdrawn, and a plea of not 400

§ guilty substituted." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 337.) In 

People v. Longe, 269 App. Div. 474, 57 N.Y.S. 2d 337, the

Appellate Division reversed the County Court's order denying a motion, made after judgment but before execution, for permission to withdraw a guilty plea and to plead not guilty. That was held an abuse of discretion, and in so holding the Appellate Division indicated that its decision was influenced by the trial judge's expressed doubts whether all necessary elements of the crime had been committed. Compare Dodd v. Martin, 248 N.Y. 594, where the

Court of Appeals stated: "After the judgment on a plea of guilty and the beginning of the term of imprisonment the court was without jurisdiction to permit the defendant to change his plea." A withdrawn plea of guilty may, however, be used in evidence upon the trial (People v. 

Steinmetz, 240 N.Y. 411, 148 N.E. 597). 

In People v. Farina, 2 App. Div. 2d 776, 154 N.Y.S. 2d 501, affirmed, 2 N.Y. 2d 454, the defendant applied for permission to withdraw a guilty plea made in reliance upon the court's promise of a sentence of ten to twenty years. He had been sentenced to fourteen to twenty years. The promise and the sentence were undisputed. The trial court denied defendant's application, except that it treated the application as a motion for vacation of the sentence, which it granted and then reimposed a sentence of ten to twenty years. On appeal, this was reversed, the Court of Appeals stating: "Defendant should be given the right either to withdraw his plea and stand trial or else to let his plea stand and accept the sentence originally promised. *** appellant objected to imposition of the sentence originally promised and insisted on his right to withdraw his plea and stand trial. As he was entitled to withdrawal of his plea, the resentence was without legal basis and, consequently, was unauthorized." Thus where a guilty plea is interposed, based upon a misunderstanding or misrepresentation, it may be withdrawn, at least prior to sentencing. If defendant has been sentenced thereunder, but the sentence was then determined to be invalid, and a re- 401

§ 

arraignment or resentence has been ordered, the defendant may withdraw his guilty plea at that time, as he is then entitled to be returned to the status he enjoyed prior to the original sentencing (People v. O'Neill, 7 App. Div. 2d 997, 184 N.Y.S. 2d 74). Where there is no evidence of any misunderstanding, or of any improvidence on the part of the defendant in pleading guilty, the application for withdrawal of the guilty plea may be denied (People v. 

Marchese, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 554). The court cannot, however, of its own motion and without the defendant's consent, set aside a plea of guilty (People ex rel. Jeimerson v. Freiberg, 137 Misc. 314, 243 N.Y.S. 590).

Section 337 of the Code does not prevent courts from vacating the sentence and plea in situations not described therein (Matter of Lyons v. Goldstein, 290 N.Y. 19). In the

Lyons case, the court stated: "The section is permissive *** It merely authorizes the court, in its discretion, at any time before judgment upon a plea of guilty, to permit it to be withdrawn for any cause or for no cause at all and a plea of not guilty substituted. It does not purport to exclude jurisdiction of a competent tribunal to correct mistakes in its own judgments, or to investigate and * * * set them aside at any time if they are based upon trickery, deceit, coercion, or fraud and misrepresentation." The court noted that at common law such powers were exercised in criminal cases through the writ of error coram nobis and stated: "If the judgment may be reviewed and set aside on the ground that it was procured by fraud, no reason presents itself why the court may not then permit the withdrawal of a plea of guilty because the record is then the same as if no judgment had ever been rendered. ***to deny a person an opportunity to be heard on proof that he was defrauded or coerced into pleading guilty *** would impair a constitutional right." See chapter of this work entitled "Coram Nobis."

Section 335 of the Code was amended in 1959 by the addition thereto of subparagraph b, to require the court to warn defendants (other than those charged with Vehicle 402

§ and Traffic Law offenses, who are governed by Section 335-a) charged with crimes for which a different or additional punishment is provided for second offenders, that any previous conviction may be shown after his conviction or guilty plea and that the additional or different punishment may be imposed. This warning must be given upon arraignment, before the court accepts the plea. 

Not Guilty Pleas. There may be occasions when the defendant may desire to withdraw his not guilty plea, and enter a plea of guilty. One such occasion arose in People v. Benson, 208 Misc. 138, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 563. The defendant had been indicted for manslaughter and arraigned, and offered to plead guilty. Upon the advice of the court at the arraignment, the defendant withheld this guilty plea and pleaded not guilty. The arraigning judge's advice was based upon a practice of not accepting guilty pleas to lesser offenses until the case had been assigned to a trial part, prescribed by the calendar rules of the court. Before the indictment was assigned to a trial part, and without the court's knowledge, another superseding indictment for first degree murder was then returned. The defendant moved to dismiss the later indictment, indicating his desire to plead guilty to the earlier one. The court held that defendant's pleading not guilty upon the advice of the arraigning judge did not waive his right to plead guilty to the first indictment, and stated: "It would be a gross abuse of discretion *** to deprive the defendant now of his right to withdraw his plea of not guilty and substitute his plea of guilty." The power of the court to permit withdrawal of a not guilty plea, and entry of a guilty plea, was also recognized, in dicta, in People v. Dolac, 3 App. Div. 2d 351, 100 N.Y.S. 2d 911, affirmed without opinion 3 N.Y. 2d 945. 

See also People v. Fuller, 156 Misc. 404, 282 N.Y.S. 28, holding that allowance or refusal of the withdrawal of a not guilty plea rests in the discretion of the court. 

Sec. 231. Amendment of Pleas. It has been held error for the court to refuse to allow the defendant to amend his 403

§ 

plea of not guilty so as to include a plea of former conviction (People v. Brinckman, 193 App. Div. 691, 184 N.Y. 

S. 365). The defense of insanity may be utilized without a plea to that effect (see succeeding section) and, therefore, the need for amendment thereof does not come into play.

Sec. 232. Insanity. The Code of Criminal Procedure pro vides, in Section 336: "Whenever a person in confinement under indictment, desires to offer the plea of insanity, he may present such plea at the time of his arraignment, as a specification under the plea of not guilty." However, failure to interpose such a plea at the time of the arraignment will not prevent proof of the insanity at the trial (People v. Joyce, 233 N.Y. 61; People v. Draper, 303 N.Y. 

653). If the insanity of the defendant has been concealed from the court, a defendant who has been imprisoned after his guilty plea may have the judgment of conviction vacated by writ of error coram nobis (People ex rel. Rose v. Addition, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 561). The issue of insanity must be decided by a jury, not by the court (People v. Krautzer, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 377).

Sec. 233. Statute of Limitations. The expiration of the period limited by statute for the prosecution of a criminal offense may be raised as a defense under a plea of not guilty (People v. Brody, 157 App. Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 

789; People v. Brown, 238 App. Div. 155, 263 N.Y.S. 267).

Some cases have held that this defense may be availed of by motion to set aside the indictment (People v. Komar, 190 Misc. 255, 71 N.Y.S. 2d 660). It has been held properly the basis of a demurrer (People v. Busccolieri, 91 Misc. 

156, 152 N.Y.S. 707). So, too, a motion in arrest of judgment, after conviction, has been granted when made on this ground (People v. Guariglia, 187 Misc. 843, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 

96, affirmed 272 App. Div. 784, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 759). The

Statute of Limitations and its procedural effects and ap- 404

§ plications are considered and discussed in chapters of this work entitled "Statute of Limitations," "Motion To Set 

Aside Judgment," "Demurrers," and "Arrest of Judgment." 

Sec. 234. Capital Cases. Pleas of guilty are not permissible in cases where there is a possibility of the death penalty being imposed. "A conviction shall not be had upon a plea of guilty where the crime charged is or may be punishable by death." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 332.) However, one indicted for a capital offense may plead guilty to a lesser, included, offense and be sentenced thereunder. In People v. Smith, 28 N.Y.S. 912, the defendant, indicted for first degree murder, pleaded guilty to second degree manslaughter. The court held Section 332 was not violated thereby. 

Sec. 235. Joinder of Pleas. Under the early common law, as previously discussed, the only plea allowed to a defendant was not guilty. Under the later common law, after the development of the other pleas that were allowed defendants, the defendant was entitled to only one plea (United States v. Shorey, Fed. Cas. No. 16280). However, as above stated, the only "pleas" allowable today, in New York, are guilty, not guilty, former judgment of conviction or acquittal. Joinder of a guilty and a not guilty plea is, by definition, impossible. It was early recognized that defendants could join the pleas of not guilty and former conviction or acquittal, and that where both pleas were interposed they should be disposed of in one trial, before one jury, with "The order in which the issues should be disposed of * * * a matter in the discretion of the court, which had power to direct them to be tried separately or together." (People v. Connor, 20 N.Y.S. 209, affirmed 142 

N.Y. 130.) The defendant had asked for a separate determination of the questions, and for an examination of the jury, after trial upon one of the issues, to determine if they 405

§ 

had been prejudiced by the proceedings had upon the preliminary trial of the issue of former conviction or acquittal. 

The denial of defendant's motion was held not error. 

Sec. 236. Pleas of Guilt to Lesser Offenses. In People v. 

Simmons, 130 Misc. 821, 226 N.Y.S. 397, the defendant, indicted for second degree grand larceny as a second offender, pleaded guilty to second degree grand larceny as a first offender, with the District Attorney's consent. The court stated: "The court had the inherent power to accept the compromise plea of guilty as a first offender. That power has been exercised ever since the early days of common-law jurisprudence, and where wisely controlled, is a valued adjunct to the administration of criminal law." 

In Stebbins v. Sherwood, 148 Misc. 763, 266 N.Y.S. 830, the court stated: "the County Court had no power, on the facts in this case, to change the charge of crime against the accused from assault in the first degree to assault in the second degree, and to accept a plea of a crime not charged in the indictment over the objection of the District At torney. * * * The Grand Jury charged the defendant with assault in the first degree, and the defendant saw fit to plead not guilty. The indictment and the plea were the pleadings, and by these the issue was formed. The County 

Court was without power to alter this issue over the objection of either of the parties."

The question considered by the court in the Sherwood case was before the Court of Appeals in McDonald v. Sobel, 297 N.Y. 679, affirming without opinion 272 App. Div. 455, 72 N.Y.S. 2d 4. There, the Appellate Division had stated the issue posed to them to be a "challenge to a County Judge's assertion of power to receive, over the objection of a District Attorney, a plea of guilt to a lesser offense than that set out in an indictment." The defendant, who upon arraignment had pleaded not guilty to an indictment charging third degree burglary and petit larceny, was permitted to withdraw that plea when the case was called 406

§ for trial, and to plead guilty to unlawful entry, a lesser included offense. No formal order was entered, nor did the 

District Attorney consent to the change of plea. The Appellate Division found that the County Judge had no such power.

Section 342-a of the Code provides: "In any case where the court, upon the recommendation of the District Attorney, and in furtherance of justice, accepts a plea of guilty to a crime or offense of a lesser degree or for which a lesser punishment is prescribed than the crime or offense charged, it shall be the duty of the District Attorney to submit to the court a statement in writing in which his reasons for recommending the acceptance of such plea shall be clearly set forth. Such statement shall be filed by the court with the other papers in the case and shall be a public record subject to inspection by any person." This section, added in 1936, was held by the court in McDonald v. Sobel, supra, not to have conferred on the District Attorney any new power. It merely was a "repetitious declaration of a power previously conferred on the District Attorney, with a new requirement that his recommendation be in writing." The court held, however, that where the written statement required by that section was not filed, the court was without power to accept the lesser plea. 

Note should be made of the provisions of Section 671, which grants to the courts the power to dismiss an action or indictment. That section, the court stated in McDonald v. Sobel, supra, "constituted a transfer to the court of a power, in substance, to nolle prosequi upon an indictment, which power was formerly possessed by the Attorney General and later, to a limited degree, by the District Attorney." However, the court went on to hold that Section 

671 did not also grant a court the power to accept a plea of guilty to a degree of crime lower than that charged in the indictment, over the objection of the District Attorney. 

Failure to file the written statement required by Section 407

$ 

342-a, through mistake or inadvertence, which failure was later rectified by the District Attorney upon its discovery, has been held merely a procedural irregularity, and not a ground for vacating the judgment of conviction (People v. Schoenhardt, 206 Misc. 946, 135 N.Y.S. 2d 730). 

Sec. 237. Effect of Plea. Not Guilty. "The plea of not guilty is a denial of every material allegation in the indictment.' (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 338.) "All matters of fact tending to establish a defense, other than [former conviction or acquittal] *** may be given in evidence under the plea of not guilty." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 339.) This has been held to include the defense of the Statute of Limitations (People v. Hagan, 235 App. Div. 784, N.Y.S. 887), insanity (People v. Joyce, 233 N.Y. 61), and the objection that the indictment does not charge a crime (People v. 

Pierson, 80 App. Div. 415, 81 N.Y.S. 2d 214, reversed on other grounds 176 N.Y. 201). Thus, other than the formal objections which may be waived by defendant's failure to raise them prior to pleading, the plea of not guilty puts in issue all facts necessary to prove the guilt of the accused and the commission of the offense. 

Guilty. "It is well settled that by *** a [guilty] plea [defendant] *** waives his objection to the form of the information, or where it is based on information and belief without disclosing the source thereof. *** However, objections to the jurisdiction of the court are not waived, nor is the objection that the information does not state a crime. ***The requirement that a prosecution for a misdemeanor be based upon a sworn information is an essential guarantee to the defendant of a fundamental right, namely, that he be not punished for a crime without a formal and sufficient accusation, and this right may not be waived by a plea of guilty. *** The Legislature in 1955 

*** amended Sections 335 and 669 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure so as to allow a defendant to waive his rights in cases involving certain traffic infractions only * (People v. Scott, 3 N.Y. 2d 148, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 707.) 408

§ In summary, a plea of guilty constitutes an admission of all well pleaded facts in the indictment or information, and waives all defects in the proceedings, or in the indictment or information, except jurisdictional ones. 409

CHAPTER 20 DOUBLE JEOPARDY Sec. 238. Definitions 

Sec. 239. History

Sec. 240. How Defense Raised and Waiver by Inaction Sec. 241. Offenses Against Two Governments Sec. 242. Identity of Offenses Sec. 243. Effect of Prior Discharge by Habeas Corpus 

Sec. 244. Identity of Parties

Sec. 245. Res Adjudicata Sec. 246. Effect of Reversal or Dismissal of Prior Proceedings 

Sec. 247. Discharge of Jury 

Sec. 238. Definitions. One of the three pleas authorized by the Code of Criminal Procedure in Section 332 is "A plea of a former judgment of conviction or acquittal of the crime charged, which may be pleaded either with or without the plea of not guilty." In Section 9, the Code provides: "No person can be subjected to a second prosecution for a crime for which he has once been prosecuted, and duly convicted or acquitted." Article I, section 6, of the New 

York State Constitution, provides the fundamental statement of the right protected by that plea, providing: "No person shall be subject to be twice put in jeopardy for the same offense", and the Constitution of the United States guarantees this right against Federal action in these words of the Fifth Amendment: "Nor shall any person be subject for the same offense to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb." 

Penal Law, sec. 32, provides: "Where a person is acquitted or convicted, he cannot thereafter be indicted or tried for the same crime, or any other degree, nor for 410

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 238 an attempt to commit the crime so charged, or any degree thereof." Penal Law, sec. 1938, is also pertinent, prescribing: "An act or omission which is made criminal and punishable in different ways, by different provisions of the law, may be punished under any of those provisions, but not under more than one, and a conviction or acquittal under one bars a prosecution for the same act or omission under any other provision."

The differences in wording between the statutory and constitutional provisions above quoted are not without meaning. Section 332 of the Code contemplates former jeopardy which has fully ripened into conviction or acquittal, the constitutional provision prior subjection of the defendant to "jeopardy," involving risk or danger thereof which may never have been consummated in either conviction or acquittal. The prior conviction or acquittal is easily determined; it is a matter of a specified procedural point reached in a prior prosecution. Ignoring for the moment problems of convictions or acquittals for lesser included crimes, the concept of a conviction or acquittal is an obvious one. "If the defendant were formerly acquitted on the ground of a variance between the indictment and the proof, or the indictment were dismissed upon an objection to its form or substance, without a judgment of acquittal, it is not deemed an acquittal for the same offense." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 340.) "When, however, the defendant was acquitted on the merits, he is deemed acquitted of the same offense, notwithstanding a defect in form or substance in the indictment on which he was acquitted." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 341.) Thus, barring acquittals based upon a decision of a court sustaining a defendant's objection to an indictment or other action of the court which is not on the merits, all acquittals bar further prosecution of the defendant for the same, or an included, offense.

Determination of when one has been placed in "jeopardy" is more difficult; the term is not self-defining. A former conviction or acquittal clearly indicates that one 411

§ 

has been previously in jeopardy. However, something less than such action may also place one in jeopardy. The filing of an information or indictment has been held not to constitute jeopardy (People v. Kelley, 230 App. Div. 249, 243 

N.Y.S. 613). Similarly, a surrender and giving of bail, after the filing of an indictment, do not place one in jeopardy (People v. Sloffard, 123 Misc. 488, 205 N.Y.S. 793).

However, "If a person accused of crime is placed upon trial therefor upon an indictment duly found and sufficient in form and if he pleads thereto and proceeds with the trial before a jury duly sworn to try the issues so joined, he is placed in jeopardy within the constitutional provisions", stated the Court of Appeals in People ex rel. 

Stabile v. Warden, 202 N.Y. 138, noting, however, that defendant's prior jeopardy in this sense could not be asserted as a plea. "Although discharge of the jury [in the prior proceeding] was not in form an acquittal of the defendant, it was in effect such an acquittal. It was not, however, a judgment of acquittal within the express provisions of Section 332. *** A former conviction or acquittal which may be pleaded in bar is a conviction or acquittal on the merits." (Ibid.) Nevertheless, as the court said in People ex rel. Brinkman v. Barr, 248 N.Y. 126 "Even if he may not always bring up the matter by a plea *** an objection on the record, or a proper motion which raises the issue is sufficient." And, in the Stabile case, a writ of habeas corpus was held a proper means of raising the question. 

Sec. 239. History. Under the early common law, juries in capital cases could not be discharged without a verdict. "Afterwards, however, in the reigns of the latter sovereigns of the Stuart family, a different rule prevailed, that a jury in such a case might be discharged for the purpose of having better evidence against him at a future day; and the power was exercised for the benefit of the crown only; but it is a doctrine so abhorrent to every principle of safety and security that it ought not to receive the least countenance in the courts of this country. [Later] * * the 412

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 240 was doctrine came under examination, and the rule *** revised with this addition, that a jury should not be discharged in a capital case unless for the benefit of the prisoner ***." (State v. Garrigues, 2 N.C. 241.) The above principles were the basis for the present rules. As Blackstone stated: "The plea of autrefois acquit, or former acquittal, is grounded on this universal maxim of the common law of England, that no man is to be brought into jeopardy of his life more than once, for the same offense. 

And hence it is allowed as a consequence, that when a man is once fairly found not guilty upon any indictment, or other prosecution, before any court having jurisdiction of the offense, he may plead such acquittal in bar of any subsequent accusation for the same crime." (Blackstone Commentaries, p. 335.) See also Vaux's case, 4 Co. Rep. 44a: "the life of a man shall not be twice put in jeopardy, for one and the same offense, and that is the reason and cause that autrefois acquit or convict is a good plea." See, generally, for a discussion of the history of this concept, and the background of the adoption, by the American colonies, of the prohibition against multiple prosecutions, the dissenting opinion of Mr. Justice Frankfurter in Green v. 

United States, 355 U.S. 184, 2 L. Ed. 2d 199.

The purpose of the prohibition, as stated by the majority in Green v. United States, supra, "is that the State with all its resources and power should not be allowed to make repeated attempts to convict an individual of an alleged offense, thereby subjecting him to embarrassment, expense and ordeal and compelling him to live in a continuing state of anxiety and insecurity, as well as enhancing the possibility that even though innocent he may be found guilty." 

Sec. 240. How Defense Raised, and Waiver by Inaction. In 

People v. Taft, 174 Misc. 1033, 22 N.Y.S. 2d 484, the defendant moved in arrest of judgment on the ground that he had been twice placed in jeopardy. The court stated: "As to the second motion *** the defendant did not plead a former judgment of conviction or acquittal. * * * However, the 413

§ 

question is involved in other cases. We, therefore, consider the motion on its merits." The motion was denied on its merits, but the quoted statement indicates that court's belief that the defense should be raised by plea, rather than by motion in arrest of judgment. In People v. Oliver, 214 

App. Div. 804, 210 N.Y.S. 562, the court stated: "The claim that defendant has been once put in jeopardy for the offense charged, and acquitted or convicted, must be raised by plea to the indictment. It was not before the court on the demurrer." Compare People ex rel. Pulko v. Murphy, 244 

App. Div. 382, 280 N.Y.S. 405, where the court stated, after noting that the facts supported the defendant's contention that he had previously been in jeopardy for the same offense: "* * *the court had no jurisdiction to try the defendant a second time for the offense charged, and in doing so deprived him of his constitutional rights. The defendant's ignorance of his rights, or the poverty which prevented the employment of adequate counsel who would interpose his evident defense on the second trial for escape, or make the proper motion in arrest of judgment, would not give the court jurisdiction, nor would they constitute a waiver of his rights under the Constitution. *** Habeas corpus will lie in such circumstances." The right to utilize habeas corpus was also recognized in the Stabile and 

Brinkman cases, supra, but the question in those cases arose prior to the second trial. 

In People v. Cignarale, 110 N.Y. 23, the Court of Appeals stated: "It would be a complete answer to this claim [of prior jeopardy] in point of law, that the defense of former acquittal must be pleaded, and that, in the absence of a plea setting it up, the question cannot be raised. This was the rule before the enactment of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and is recognized by that statute. *** But in a capital case, if it was made to appear that there had been a former acquittal, we shall deem it our duty *** to take notice of the fact, although not presented by a formal plea." The Cignarale case was cited with approval by the court in People v. Zendano, 136 N.Y.S. 2d 106, stating: "It is 414

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 240 apparent from an examination of the cases on the subject that the protection of the provision against double jeopardy is personal and may be waived by the person entitled thereto. The defendant, in requesting a mistrial and consenting thereto, must be deemed to have waived any claim to double jeopardy by reason of the granting of his request."

It would appear more accurate to express it not in terms of a waiver of the right to claim protection from double jeopardy, but rather that the defendant's affirmative act in bringing about the mistrial prevented jeopardy from attaching. Although there is no doubt that such action will prevent the defendant from thereafter claiming the benefit of the defense, calling it a waiver implies that mere failure to raise the objection at the proper time might also prevent future utilization of the defense. At least that would be the common conclusion based on the usual conception of "waiver." However, it is not clear under the decided cases that inaction will prevent future use of the defense. 

See the Murphy, Taft, and Cignarale cases, supra. Another case implying that waiver may be found is People ex rel. 

Hornbeck v. Jackson, 7 App. Div. 2d 689, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 315, where the court stated, in response to defendant's contention that double jeopardy arose on his plea of guilty to both rape and sodomy: "The record before us does not demonstrate double jeopardy; and where there has been a plea of guilty to separate crimes such a question would be deemed waived."

Section 334 of the Code requires that the plea of former conviction or acquittal be entered "in substantially the following form: "The defendant pleads, that he has already been convicted (or acquitted, as the case may be), of the crime charged in the indictment, by the judgment of the court of. (naming it), rendered (naming the place), on the "This section applies only to pleas of former conviction or acquittal. As above stated, when the defendant claims that he was previously in jeopardy for at of day 415

§ 

the same offense (although not convicted or acquitted thereof) some courts have held it proper to raise the objection by motion, objection or plea (People ex rel. Brinkman v. Barr, 248 N.Y. 126), and, of course, the above quoted form would not be applicable. "The guarantee against twofold jeopardy, however, being a constitutional right, any objection on the record which clearly raises that issue at the outset of the second trial is sufficient as a plea in bar." (People v. McGrath, 202 N.Y. 445.)

Sec. 241. Offenses Against Two Governments. Where an act is proscribed by both the laws of the State and the Federal Government, both sovereignties may prosecute and punish. "A single act which violates both Federal and 

State criminal laws is generally held to result in distinct offenses against the two separate governments. Each government in determining what shall be an offense *** is exercising its own sovereignty, not that of the other. It follows that an act denounced as a crime by both national and State sovereignties is an offense against *** both and may be punished by each." (People ex rel. Niss v. Superintendent, 282 N.Y. 115.) There are exceptions, of course, to this statement. The Niss case involved one of these ex ceptions. There, the State statute (Public Health Law, sec. 

445) proscribed prosecution of one who had been acquitted or convicted under the Federal narcotics laws for the same act or omission.

Section 139 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that where New York and another State have concurrent jurisdiction over an offense, a conviction or acquittal in the other jurisdiction will bar a later prosecution therefor in this state. Penal Law, sec. 33, contains a related provision, and prescribes that when it appears that the offense was committed in another State or country, and that the defendant has been convicted or acquitted on the merits in such other jurisdiction, such action will constitute a sufficient defense to a later prosecution in this State based upon the same acts or omission. Another exception to that 416

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 242 rule was involved in Pennsylvania v. Nelson, 360 U.S. 497, 100 L. Ed. 640, where the Supreme Court held that where 

Federal legislative enactments have pre-empted the field of law in a given area, State governments may not intervene therein. Thus, although not decided upon a narrow double jeopardy basis, the theory involved may be of value in similar situations where, but for the Federal Government's assumption of power over the area, a prosecution for the same act or omission by the State government could follow a prosecution by the Federal Government. 

Sec. 242. Identity of Offenses. Both in the area of double jeopardy, and in the related one of determining whether there has been a former conviction or acquittal of the same offense, the question of what constitutes the same offense arises. Several early cases indicated a strict attitude on the part of the courts in construing what offenses were identical. Thus People v. White, 32 N.Y. 465, held that a prosecution for assault upon a named person was not barred by a prior prosecution for assault upon an unnamed person. 

Similarly, where the same acts were involved, a charge that the acts were committed with the intention of killing X, was held not to be barred by a prior charge of the same acts as having constituted the crime of killing Y (People v. 

Warren, 1 Parker Crim. 335). However, where the indictment described the same time and place, and the act charged was unlawful sale of liquor to Y, a prior prosecution for the unlawful sale of liquor to "X" and to "other divers persons" was held to bar the subsequent prosecution (People v. Satchwell, 61 App. Div. 312, 70 N.Y.S. 307). "Where the offenses are distinct crimes, though part of one transaction, a conviction or acquittal of one is not a bar to a prosecution for the other." (People v. Faden, 271 

N.Y. 435.) However, “* * * when one offense is a necessary element in, and constitutes an essential part of, another offense and both are part of one transaction, a conviction or an acquittal of one is a bar to the prosecution for the other." (People ex rel. Kwiatkowski v. Trenkle, 169 Misc. 

417

§ 

687, 9 N.Y.S. 2d 661.) In People ex rel. Moskoff v. Weinstock, 55 N.Y.S. 2d 330, the defendants had previously been charged with abortion. The charge had been dismissed as against one defendant, and the other had been found not guilty. Both were subsequently prosecuted for practicing medicine without a license and the court found that "the very proof essential to sustain the accusation of abortion is relied upon to sustain the information charge of practicing medicine without a license." The court then held that the misdemeanor was "but a component part of the integrated offense constituting the alleged abortion", and sustained defendant's writ of habeas corpus.

The tests to be applied in determining whether offenses are identical have been stated to be: "(a) whether the offenses are the same in fact and in law, (b) whether they are of the same legal character, (c) whether the same evidence will support both charges." (People v. Spitzer, 148 

Misc. 97, 266 N.Y.S. 522.) Where the later prosecution will require the proof of additional facts, there is no bar. In 

People v. Bevins, 74 Misc. 377, 134 N.Y.S. 2d 212, it was held that a prior prosecution for public intoxication did not bar a later prosecution for disorderly conduct, based upon some of the same actions, for one can be drunk without being disorderly and, therefore, different facts would have to be proved at the second trial. Where the same acts on the part of the defendant are alleged to have constituted the crime: (a) A prior conviction for disorderly conduct will bar a subsequent prosecution for third degree assault (People v. Afarian, 89 N.Y.S. 2d 820). (b) An acquittal of a prior charge of practicing medicine without a license upon X will bar a subsequent prosecution for commission. of an abortion upon X (People ex rel. Moskoff v. Weinstock, 55 N.Y.S. 2d 330). (c) An acquittal of a charge of robbery of X's property bars a prosecution for larceny of the same property (People v. McGowan, 17 Wend. 386). (d) A conviction for impairing the morals of a minor, by means of sexual intercourse with that minor, bars a subsequent prosecution for second degree rape based upon the 418

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 242 same act of sexual intercourse (People v. Lavopa, 198 

Misc. 85, 101 N.Y.S. 2d 740). An acquittal of assault and battery charges bars a prosecution for rape based upon the same actions (People v. Piercell, 16 N.Y.S. 199). "Where the difference between the two offenses consists solely in the intention of the criminal * * * the People cannot convict the defendant upon a certain state of facts alleging a certain intent and then try the defendant in a subsequent indictment, upon the theory that the defendant employed the same means, upon the same person and occassion, with a different design." (Restell v. People 1 N.Y. 

379, as quoted in People ex rel. Kwiatkowski v. Trenkle, 169 Misc. 687, 9 N.Y.S. 2d 661.)

Continuing Crimes. Where the offense is of a continuing nature, generally a conviction or acquittal based upon the commission of the act during one period of time will bar prosecutions based upon the commission of the same acts at some time within the period covered by the first charge (People ex rel. Seligson v. Anderson, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 856; 

People v. Farson, 244 N.Y. 413). However, where the statute makes each act a separate offense, it has been held that an acquittal or conviction of the act or omission on one date will not bar a later prosecution for commission of the offense prior to the date charged in the prior prosecution (People v. Sinell, 131 N.Y. 571).

Conspiracy. Conspiracy to commit a crime and the commission of the crime itself are two distinct offenses, and acquittal or conviction of one will not bar a later prosecution based upon a charge of the other (People v. Taft, 174 

Misc. 1033, 22 N.Y.S. 2d 484).

Lesser Crimes Charged. A prior conviction or acquittal of a lesser degree of the crime charged in the first indictment will bar the later prosecution of the defendant for all higher degrees of the crime that were encompassed in that indictment (People v. Cignarale, 110 N.Y. 23). Howif the defendant has been convicted of a lesser offense than that charged in the indictment, and if he secures a reversal of that judgment, he may thereafter be tried for any ever, 419

§  

offense, including those of a higher degree than that of which he was previously acquitted (People v. McGrath, 202 N.Y. 445; People v. Palmer, 109 N.Y. 413). Generally, a prosecution for a greater offense will bar a subsequent prosecution for a lesser offense included therein, where, under the prior indictment, the defendant could have been convicted of the lesser offense. Thus, in Woodford v. People, 62 N.Y. 117, it was held that a prosecution for burning a building barred a subsequent prosecution for burning the contents of the building.

Sec. 243. Effect of Prior Discharge by Habeas Corpus. A 

discharge upon a writ of habeas corpus relates only to the imprisonment and may not be deemed an acquittal of the crime charged. Civil Practice Act, section 1269, provides that a final order in a habeas proceeding is a bar to a subsequent imprisonment, restraint, or retention in custody of the prisoner for the same cause. However, it is not deemed to be the same cause if the discharge was for a "defect of proof or for a material defect in the commitment," and the defect is corrected and he is thereafter "committed by a lawful mandate for the same offense"; or if he is afterwards committed for the same offense, by the lawful order or other mandate of the court wherein he was bound by recognizance to appear or in which he has been indicted or convicted of the same offense." "This is so, even though the defendant has served a part of the sentence imposed upon him [in the prior proceeding] ***." (People v. Mittleman, 150 Misc. 394, 268 N.Y.S. 819.) 

Sec. 244. Identity of Parties. The defendant is, of course, not protected from a subsequent prosecution based upon a crime against persons other than those involved in the prior proceeding, even though the defendant committed all the acts in one transaction (People v. Rodgers, 184 App. 

Div. 461, 171 N.Y.S. 451, affirmed 226 N.Y. 671). There must be an identity of parties in each prosecution. It is clear that when the defendant injures many by one act he 420

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 246 may be prosecuted separately for the offense perpetrated upon each victim (People v. Florio, 301 N.Y. 46). 

Sec. 245. Res Adjudicata. The general principle is that judgments in civil matters "would not and could not be binding as res adjudicata or even as stare decisis in a subsequent prosecution where guilt must be established beyond a reasonable doubt." (Reed v. Littleton, 275 N.Y. 

150.) That result is required, obviously, by the difference in the quantum of proof. However where, as in People v. 

Cryan, 123 Misc. 358, 205 N.Y.S. 85, the quantum of proof required in the prior proceeding is the same, the basis for the distinction does not exist. See also People v. Aulbach, 168 Misc. 239, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 249, which held that proceedings against the husband, under that provision of the disorderly persons statute relating to failure to support, may be barred by an order of the Supreme Court entered in a matrimonial action relating to the same transaction. People v. Kleinman, 168 Misc. 920, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 246, held that prior decisions in defendant's favor in a perjury case, based upon the same point as that involved in a later conspiracy prosecution "creates an estoppel limited to points actually decided in the [prior] action." There, as the later conspiracy indictment encompassed other points also, the defendant's motion to dismiss was denied. However, the court did recognize that if the same issues were involved in both proceedings, the motion would have been granted. 

Sec. 246. Effect of Reversal or Dismissal of Prior Proceed ing. "It is well settled law in this State that when a defendant procures a reversal of his conviction and sentence for legal error at trial, he may not plead the former proceedings in bar to a second trial for the same offense. Upon reversal, the defendant is deemed to be in precisely the same position as though there had been no trial. *** He may be retried upon the original indictment even as to those higher degrees of crime of which he had been acquitted by the jury at the first trial. *** The ground upon 421

§ 

which the reversal is placed is not material. * * In almost every case where a reversal is followed by a second trial the defendant had previously been exposed to valid indictment and trial. But this is not former jeopardy in the eyes of the law. An appeal in a criminal case is a matter of statutory favor. *** When a defendant accepts it for the purpose of vacating his conviction, he is deemed to ask for a just re-examination of the question of his guilt." (People v. Ercole, 4 N.Y. 2d 617, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 649.)

Where the prior trial is terminated without defendant's consent, after jeopardy has attached, a second trial is barred (People ex rel. Stabile v. Warden, 202 N.Y. 138;

People ex rel. Blue v. Kearney, 272 N.Y. 679). In People ex rel. Ostwald v. Crover, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 748, after the defendant's conviction, the District Attorney moved for a new trial upon learning that one of the jurors was not a United States citizen. The motion was granted, defendant's sentence vacated, and thereafter defendant sought by habeas corpus to obtain his release on the ground that the new trial would place him in double jeopardy. The writ was granted, the court noting that "If [defendant] had secured a new trial after conviction upon his own application, he thereby would have voluntarily placed himself again in jeopardy and would not have been able to invoke the Constitution in his behalf for immunity. *** Such is not the case here. The motion to set aside the verdict of the jury for a new trial was made by the People." 

Sec. 247. Discharge of Jury. In People ex rel. Blue v. 

Kearney, 181 Misc. 981, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 691, Section 400 of the

Code of Criminal Procedure was held unconstitutional so far as it empowered the court to order the discharge of a jury, and to suspend proceedings pending another indictment for a higher offense, when testimony at the trial indicated that the facts might prove a more serious offense. 

The court also noted the general rule that the causes for mistrial, not violative of the double jeopardy rule in subsequent proceedings, are those that "arise without motive," 422

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

§ 247 and that occurrences with motive (such as those contemplated by Section 400, the obvious motive of which was to prosecute the defendant for a higher crime), commonly are held to bar a subsequent prosecution. "When a jury is arbitrarily discharged in a criminal case without the defendant's consent and where no circumstances existed warranting the declaring of a mistrial and the discharge of a jury, the defendant is, by reason of the trial coming to a sudden end, placed in jeopardy within our constitutional provisions." (People ex rel. Epting v. Devoe, 206 Misc. 278, 133 N.Y.S. 2d 129.) Section 428 of the Code delineates three grounds upon which the jury may be discharged before agreement, after they have retired to consider their verdict, and Section 430 allows the case to be retried in the event of a discharge under those circumstances. The grounds are injury or casualty to the defendant or a juror, consent of both the prosecutor and the defendant, and the declaration of the jury that they are unable to agree upon a verdict after the expiration of a reasonable time for consideration. In People v. Fishman, 64 Misc. 256, 119 N.Y.S. 89, the court noted that at common law courts were authorized to discharge the jury for these reasons if the cause arose prior to the jury's retirement, and held that Section 430 was not intended to curtail that common law power.

The rule is that the court may discharge the jury "for a legal and justifiable cause" and "cannot act arbitrarily, but must do so with discretion, and when the discretion is abused, the defendant is placed in jeopardy." (People ex rel. Epting v. Devoe, supra.) In People v. Niff, 122 App. Div. 

335, 106 N.Y.S. 749, the court discharged the jury after defendant's counsel objected to the jurisdiction of the court. The Appellate Division held such discharge lawful, and within the court's discretion, so that a subsequent prosecution for the same offense was not barred. See also 

King v. People, 5 Hun 297, where, on discovering that the defendant had not been arraigned and had not pleaded, the court ordered the jury discharged and, upon appeal, such 423

§ 

discharge was held not a bar to a subsequent prosecution. 

However, publication of a newspaper article which allegedly prejudiced the defendant was held not sufficient cause for the granting of a mistrial, and a subsequent prosecution for the same offense was held barred in People ex rel. Totalis v. Craver, 174 Misc. 325, 20 N.Y.S. 2d 533.

A conviction or acquittal procured by the defendant by fraud or collusion, without proper notice to the State or the proper prosecutor, is no bar to a later prosecution for the same offense. Thus in People v. Cuatt, 126 N.Y.S. 1114, after the alleged offense, an assault, had occurred, the defendant voluntarily went before a Justice of the Peace and "appeared and complained of himself." The court held: "The purpose of that appearance before the Justice and that proceeding was not to punish the defendant for the assault, but to enable him to escape the full consequences of his wrongdoing. It was a fraud on the court. *** The general rule is that a former conviction or acquittal procured by fraud of the defendant is no bar to a subsequent prosecution." The reason behind this rule is obvious and needs no rationalization.

A discharge ordered by a magistrate at a preliminary hearing will not bar a subsequent prosecution for the same offense (People v. Dillon, 197 N.Y. 254; People v. Steiger, 154 Misc. 538, 277 N.Y.S. 602). Prosecution under an invalid indictment or information will not bar a subsequent prosecution (People v. Smith, 266 App. Div. 57, 41 N.Y.S. 

2d 512), and prosecution in a court without jurisdiction over the matter will not place a defendant in jeopardy so as to bar a subsequent prosecution (People ex rel. Meyer v. 

Warden, 269 N.Y. 426), nor will a trial in an illegally constituted court (People v. Connor, 142 N.Y. 130). In general, the prior proceeding must have been valid, and must have proceeded to the point of the introduction of evidence to bar later prosecution. 424
