INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT Sec. 248. Definitions 

Sec. 249. History

Sec. 250. Proceedings to Determine Sanity Prior to Indictment Sec. 251. Insanity of Indicted Defendant Before or During Trial, or After Conviction

Sec. 252. Insanity of Defendants Under Death Sentence Sec. 253. Remedies of Allegedly Mentally Incapable Defendants Sec. 254. Proceedings Under Mental Hygiene Law Sec. 255. Degree of Insanity Required 

Sec. 248. Definitions. "It is now a fundamental principle in all civilized countries that this defense [insanity] when established, shall furnish to the accused not only a protection against conviction for crime, but a sufficient reason why he should not be tried or sentenced, or if tried and convicted, why the judgment of the court should not be executed; and this rule has, for a long time been a part of the statutory law of this State." (People v. McElvaine, 125 

N.Y. 596, affirmed 142 U.S. 55.) The problems raised by alleged insanity are, primarily, of two types: the first, as to the accused's mental condition at the time of the trial; the second, the defendant's mental condition at the time of the commission of the alleged criminal act. The former determination will result in finding the defendant capable of pleading and being tried, or sufficiently sane to be sentenced after trial, or sane enough to receive punishment after the sentence. The latter will result in finding the defendant "guilty" or "innocent" of the crime charged. This chapter will be concerned, mainly, with a discussion of the procedures set forth in the Code to determine these ques- 425

§ 

tions and will discuss only in a summary manner the substantive question of what constitutes sufficient proof of the insanity of a defendant at any of the above stages, and what tests are to be applied in determining whether one suffering from some mental disability should be held responsible for his actions.

Sec. 249. History. In the early common law, present insanity did not preclude a defendant's prosecution (2 Pollock and Maitland, Hist. of Eng. Law, 479). It was later recognized that an accused should not be required to plead or defend against a criminal charge when he was mentally incapable of understanding the proceedings and preparing, or assisting in the preparation of, his defense. This reasoning is equally applicable to the imposition of sentence and punishment for one not mentally competent who cannot intelligently respond to the question that must be asked prior to sentencing: whether there is any reason why sentence should not be pronounced (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 480; People v. Nesce, 201 N.Y. 111), and who cannot understand the reason for his punishment. This right of mentally-ill persons not to be forced through such proceedings was early recognized by Coke (3 Co. Inst. 4), and Blackstone (4 Blackstone Commentaries 24). See, also,

Bateman's Case, 11 How. State Tr. 467 (1685). To impose sentence upon an insane person, said Coke, would not act as a deterrent to others, but would be only "a miserable spectacle of extreme inhumanity and cruelty." (3 Co. Inst. 6.)

It was also recognized early that different issues were presented in the determination of whether one was sane enough to stand trial and accept punishment than those in a determination of whether one was sane enough, at the time of the commission of the criminal act, to be held accountable for his actions. In an early New York case, Freeman v. People, 4 Denio 9, this distinction was recognized by the court which stated: "If, therefore, a person arraigned for a crime, is capable of understanding the nature 426

INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT § 250 

and object of the proceedings going on against him; if he rightly comprehends his own condition in reference to such proceedings, and can conduct his defense in a rational manner, he is, for the purpose of being tried, to be deemed sane, although on some other subjects his mind may be deranged or unsound." Thus, the court held, the "right and wrong" test, applicable in determining whether one should be held accountable for a criminal act, was not applicable in deciding whether one was sane enough to stand trial. See also 

People v. Nyhan, 171 N.Y.S. 466, holding that one may be deemed responsible for his allegedly criminal actions, and yet not capable of standing trial. The Freeman case also contains an extended discussion of the history of the law on this subject.

Sec. 250. Proceedings to Determine Sanity Prior to Indictment. Title IV of Part 6 of the Code (Sections 870 through 

876) concerns proceedings to determine the sanity of one charged with a crime or offense, but not under indictment therefor. Section 870 allows the court or magistrate having jurisdiction, on its own motion or on motion of the District Attorney or the defendant, to order the defendant's examination to determine his sanity "If at any time it * * * appear *** that there is reasonable ground to believe that such defendant is in such state of idiocy, imbecility or insanity that he is incapable of understanding the charge or proceeding or of making his defense."

The procedure to be followed is set forth in Sections 659 through 662 of the Code, which sections are hereafter discussed in detail. The District Attorney is to be notified of any order entered by the court, and if the two appointed psychiatrists do not agree in their findings provision is made, in Section 870, for the appointment of a third psychiatrist. If, prior to the filing of the psychiatrist's report, the defendant is indicted, the report shall be forwarded to the court in which the indictment or information is triable, and it shall thereafter be treated as if it were a report 427

§ 

ordered under sections 658 et seq. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 871).

If no indictment or information is filed, and if the two appointed psychiatrists find the defendant not sane enough to stand trial, notification of this finding shall be given to the court, the District Attorney, and the proper public health officer (as defined by Mental Hygiene Law, sec. 81, subdivisions 1 and 2.) That health officer shall then apply for the certification of the defendant as insane and for his commitment to the appropriate State institution under Mental Hygiene Law, secs. 74, et seq. The court in which the original charge has been filed is to be notified of the result of the certification proceedings and, upon a determination in such proceedings that the defendant is not sane enough to stand trial, the criminal proceedings shall terminate. This termination is without prejudice to the right of the District Attorney to reopen the matter or to present evidence against the defendant to a Grand Jury. If the defendant is then indicted, or an information filed against him, all further proceedings shall be conducted as if the defendant had been indicted prior to the institution of the commitment proceedings (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 872).

If the defendant is found sane enough to stand trial, either by the appointed psychiatrists or in certification proceedings under the Mental Hygiene Law, the proceedings against the defendant shall continue as if there had been no examination (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 874).

If the defendant has been charged with an "offense" which is not a crime, or with a misdemeanor over which special sessions courts outside of New York City have exclusive jurisdiction, and if the two appointed psychiatrists report that the defendant is not sane enough to stand trial, and if he is not ordered committed in the certification proceedings, the court may within its discretion dismiss the charge, or order the defendant discharged, or make such other order as it deems appropriate within its powers. 

Upon the psychiatrists' finding that the defendant is not sane enough to stand trial, the appropriate health officer 428

INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT § 250 (in New York City, the Director of the Psychiatry Division of Bellevue or Kings County Hospital) may, if he deems it for the defendant's benefit to receive treatment, notify the court and the appropriate State health officers of that fact so that commitment proceedings may be instituted (Code of Crim. Proc. sec. 873). Thus, in the case of a defendant charged with an offense not a crime, or with certain misdemeanors, the last cited section gives the court power to dismiss the charge, even if the defendant is not committed. The section also provides that any commitment of such a defendant shall be deemed a "final disposition of the offense or misdemeanor charged."

Section 875 of the Code gives to Special Sessions Courts in New York City powers similar to those given other courts in the last cited section. Section 876 provides the above sections supersede any inconsistent provisions of any other laws, specifically including the Mental Hygiene Laws. The above sections were held constitutional in People ex rel. Anderson v. Superintendent, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 84.

Jurisdiction of Courts. Justices of the Peace are con sidered magistrates within the above sections (Application of Waldau, 125 N.Y.S. 2d 793), as are the Judges of 

Children's Courts (Application of Eaton, 196 Misc. 648, 92 

N.Y.S. 2d 461, affirmed 279 App. Div. 1038, 113 N.Y.S. 2d 

279), and the Judges of the Court of General Sessions (People v. Roiter, 180 Misc. 914, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 620).

Offenses within Section. The offenses which are not crimes, mentioned in Section 870, include such charges as disorderly conduct and public intoxication (Application of 

Eaton, supra), and in Application of Waldau, supra, the court noted that traffic offenses might be so considered. 

However, in that case, the only point at issue was whether a proceeding initiated by an information under Section 84 of the Code (threats to commit crimes) was within the coverage of the section. The court held such a proceeding not one in which the accused may be subjected to imprisonment on the primary judgment, and therefore not an "offense" within the meaning of Section 870. The defendant, 429

§ 

who had been ordered committed to a mental hospital, was released and his writ of habeas corpus granted. 

Grounds for Proceedings. "Before the procedure authorized [by Section 870] is adopted, it must appear that there is reasonable ground and the Court must exercise discretion. *** It cannot be done arbitrarily or merely because of the nature of the charge." (People ex rel. Apicella v. 

Superintendent, 173 Misc. 642, 18 N.Y.S. 2d 523, holding that Magistrate's commitment, apparently ordered solely because defendant was charged with loitering and soliciting men to commit sodomy, or other lewdness, was an abuse of discretion.) See, also, State v. Omelanowicz, 162 Misc. 

396, 294 N.Y.S. 741, holding that evidence of defendant's insanity at a time other than that of the commission of the offense, or the time of the trial, was not a valid ground for the commencement of Section 870 proceedings. 

Sec. 251. Insanity of Indicted Defendant Before or During Trial, or After Conviction. Code Sections 658 through 662-f prescribe the procedures to be followed in determining the sanity of indicted defendants. As above mentioned, Sections 870 through 876, applicable to defendants not under indictment, incorporate some of these procedures by reference. Section 658 empowers the court on its own motion, or on motion of the District Attorney, to order the examination of any indicted defendant, "If at any time before final judgment it shall appear that there is reasonable ground for believing that such defendant is in such state of idiocy, imbecility or insanity that he is incapable of understanding the charge, indictment or proceedings or of making his defense, or if the defendant makes a plea of insanity to the indictment." As noted in the chapter entitled "Pleas,' 

Code Section 336 allows confined defendants to enter a plea of insanity as a specification under a not-guilty plea, although it is not necessary to plead insanity at the time of arraignment to it at the trial (People v. Joyce, 223 N.Y. 61). 99 Section 659 of the Code prescribes the persons who may 430

INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT § 251 

conduct the examination; outside of New York City, the person in charge of a State Hospital, certified as having adequate facilities for the conducting of such examinations, shall designate two qualified psychiatrists from his staff. If two such qualified psychiatrists cannot be found there, he may designate any psychiatrists in the State. In 

New York City, the appointment is to be made by the Director of the Division of Psychiatry of the Department of Hospitals. Section 659 has been held constitutional (People ex rel. Klescitz v. Mills, 179 Misc. 58, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 185).

The court is to be notified of the psychiatrists appointed, and those psychiatrists must file the necessary qualifying oaths, prescribed by the Civil Practice Act for referees (People v. Pershaec, 172 Misc. 324, 15 N.Y.S. 2d 215). Section 660 describes the method of examination to be followed, and provides that the examination may be held in the place where the defendant is detained or, in the event the person in charge of the hospital who has designated the psychiatrists recommends such treatment, the court may commit the defendant for a period not to exceed thirty days to another place or to a hospital designated. 

The psychiatrists may examine witnesses, administer oaths, compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of relevant books and records. They may request the clerk of the court to issue subpoenas to compel such attendance and production, and they may receive such information as may be necessary to determine defendant's sanity (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 661).

At the completion of the examination, the report of the psychiatrists' findings is transmitted to the court. In the event of a disagreement between the two psychiatrists who conducted the examination, they may request the appointment of a third psychiatrist. The report submitted is not a public record, and Section 662 of the Code prohibits the receipt of the report in evidence upon the trial. This prohibition does not require exclusion of hospital records of the defendant during his stay in the hospital, although the final report may not be introduced nor may the sub- 431

§ 

stance of the report be placed before the jury by the prosecutor in an indirect manner (People v. Draper, 278 App. 

Div. 298, 104 N.Y.S. 2d 703, affirmed, 303 N.Y. 653).

Copies of the report must be furnished the prosecutor and the defendant, and either party may controvert the findings (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 662-a). In People v. 

Kurtz, 2 Misc. 2d 88, 155 N.Y.S. 2d 764, the court held that it was not necessary that notice be given to the defendant of his right to controvert the report prior to the time of entry of the order of commitment. Section 662-b empowers the court to order the defendant committed to an appropriate institution of the Department of Correction if, after giving both sides an opportunity to be heard, it is of the opinion that the defendant is not sane enough to stand trial. If the defendant is so committed, any bail he has deposited shall be exonerated and any money deposited by him returned (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 662-d). The criminal proceedings against the defendant are suspended during the period of such commitment, and that period shall last as long as the defendant remains incapable "of understanding the charge against him or of making his defense thereto." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 662-a.) When the defendant regains his mental ability, the court which ordered him committed is to be notified of that fact, and the defendant shall be returned to stand trial.

It should be noted that throughout all of the above described proceedings, the reports of the psychiatrists are merely in aid of the court, and are not conclusive upon the issue of the defendant's sanity (People v. Pershaec, supra; 

People ex rel. Vallaro v. Travis, 72 N.Y.S. 2d 804). If the defendant is found sane enough to stand trial, the proceedings against him shall be resumed as if no examination had been ordered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 662-c). If the defendant had asserted insanity at the time of the act, the determination of that question is, of course, for the finder of fact (the jury, in most cases). The jury must be instructed to state specially in its verdict if the acquittal is based on defendant's insanity. If the court then deems the 432

INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT § 252 

defendant's discharge to be dangerous to the public safety, it must order him to be committed to a state hospital until he becomes sane (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 454). The defendant may, thereafter, institute habeas corpus proceedings to have his sanity determined, and to obtain his release (People ex rel. Peabody v. Chanler, 196 N.Y. 525). 

Costs. Any costs incurred in the examination including the psychiatrist's fees, when approved by the court, are a charge upon the county in which the defendant is being tried, although such county has a claim over therefor against the defendant's estate or responsible relatives (Code of Crim Proc., sec. 662-e). 

Sec. 252. Insanity of Defendants Under Death Sentence. 

Any defendant, imprisoned and awaiting execution under a death sentence, who appears to be insane, may, if the Governor so chooses, have his execution deferred until his mental status is determined and, if he is found insane, until his mental ability is regained. The Governor may order a commission of not more than three persons to examine the defendant; this section does not require that the examiners be psychiatrists. The examiner must also take the oath required of referees (Civil Practice Act, sec. 

26), and the District Attorney of the county in which the criminal act was committed must be given at least seven days' notice of the examination and may attend it and call and examine witnesses there. Counsel for the defendant should also be given notice of the examination, for he may also attend and take part therein. At the conclusion of the examination, the commissioners must report their findings to the Governor who may, in his discretion, order the defendant committed to a state hospital for insane convicts until he is cured of his insanity. When, in the opinion of the superintendent of the hospital, the defendant regains his sanity, this fact is to be reported to a Justice of the Supreme Court in the district in which the hospital is located and, after determination of the truth of the Superintendent's opinion, he shall certify that fact to the Clerk 433

§ 

of the court which sentenced the defendant, and order the defendant returned to the prison from which he was committed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 495-a). A copy of the 

Justice's certificate must be forwarded to the Governor. 

Commitment of the defendant under this section tolls the running of the period within which the defendant may appeal (People v. Liebman, 218 N.Y. 625; People v. Swisky, 213 N.Y. 151). The time of the execution of sentence is suspended until the warden of the prison to which the defendant is sentenced receives a warrant from the Governor directing execution (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 498).

After the Governor receives the certificate of the Supreme Court Justice attesting the defendant's return to sanity, the Governor must issue a warrant directing the disposition of the prisoner, appointing a time and place for the prisoner's execution, or pardoning the prisoner, or commuting his sentence. 

Sec. 253. Remedies of Allegedly Mentally Incapable De fendants. If a defendant can establish that he is without mental competence to stand trial or intelligently waive his right to counsel or understand the ramifications of his plea of guilty, he may raise the question, after judgment, by writ of error coram nobis (People v. Boehm, 309 N.Y. 

362). "However *** it requires more to sustain such a writ than merely showing that [defendant] applied for psychiatric examination when he pleaded guilty. Even if he did so apply, it would have been in the discretion of the court to determine whether or not his application should have been granted. ***The exercise of discretion by the trial court would have been final unless abused. * * * [Defendant] is not entitled to a hearing in the absence of some evidence that he was insane when he pleaded guilty and sentence was pronounced. He might not be barred by not having raised the issue at the time of his arraignment, if he could show that he was then mentally incapable of understanding the charge and of conducting his defense. 

He must demonstrate that such was the case [by] *** 434

INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT § 254 

evidence in his petition or other moving papers." (People v. Smyth, 3 N.Y. 2d 184, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 737.) So, too, one who claimed that her insanity was fraudulently concealed from the court could secure her release by coram nobis after commitment on her plea of guilty (People ex rel. 

Rose v. Additon, 189 Misc. 102, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 561). 66 Upon Judgment. Under Code Section 480, when the defendant appears for judgment he must be asked whether he has any cause to show why judgment should not be pronounced against him. See chapter on "Sentence." One response to the question, and a statutorily-recognized 'cause, against the judgment, [is] 1. That he is insane; and if, in the opinion of the court, there be reasonable ground for believing him to be insane, the question of his insanity must be tried as provided by the Code." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 481.) If the defendant is found sane, judgment will then be pronounced against him; if insane, "he must be committed to the State lunatic asylum until he becomes sane; and when notice is given of that fact, he must be brought before the court for judgment." (Ibid.) It has been held that the defendant's insanity is not properly shown in arrest of judgment, but rather is a cause for deferring the imposition of judgment until a later date (People v. Craig, 295 N.Y. 116). Even after conviction, if the defendant then shows, for the first time, signs of insanity which, in the opinion of psychiatrists, indicate his lack of sanity during the trial, a new trial may be ordered and defendant's application therefor is not barred by his failure to raise the issue of sanity during the trial (People v. Wolfe, 102 N.Y.S. 2d 12).

Sec. 254. Proceedings Under Mental Hygiene Law. Sec tions 662-f and 876 of the Code both provide that the provisions of their respective titles of the Code supersede any inconsistent provisions of the Mental Hygiene Law. The 

Mental Hygiene Law contains provision for the commitment of mentally defective persons, either voluntarily or through certification proceedings. The applicable sections 435

§ 

refer to persons "not in confinement on a criminal charge." (See, e.g., Mental Hygiene Law secs. 70, 124.) A discussion of the complete statutory scheme for the treatment of mentally ill persons is found in People v. McDermott, 179 

Misc. 89, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 69, in which the defendant, charged with malicious mischief, was committed for observation by the Magistrate after arraignment and hearing. The examining psychiatrists directed the Department of Hospitals to initiate certification proceedings. That department reported that it would not initiate such proceedings because a criminal charge was pending against the defendant, and requested the City Magistrate's Court to enter the necessary order of commitment. The court held that it had such power under Sections 659, 662-c and 870 of the Code and discussed the various statutes applicable. "General jurisdiction over insane persons is one of the general powers of the Supreme Court, in this State. (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1356.) *** However there are many other courts *** which have been entrusted * * * with power to adjudge a person insane and to commit him. *** The general legislative scheme appears to be that in the case of persons against whom any criminal proceeding is pending, the power to adjudge insane resides in the court having jurisdiction for the time being over the defendant." In the case of a person not in confinement on a criminal charge, alleged to be mentally defective, the application lies within the scope of Mental Hygiene Law, sec. 

124, subd. 1. 

If the person alleged to be insane is a prisoner in a State prison, serving an unexpired sentence for felony, he may be transferred to Dannemora State Hospital for the Criminal Insane upon the certificate of a physician or psychiatrist (Correction Law, sec. 383). If, at the expiration of his term he is still in the hospital and still insane, an application for the extension of his commitment shall be made by the Superintendent of that hospital to a judge of a court of record (Correction Law, sec. 384). If the person alleged to be insane is a prisoner serving a 436

INQUIRY INTO INSANITY OF DEFENDANT § 255 

2 sentence of a year or less, the application shall be made by the warden to a judge of a court of record (Correction Law, sec. 408). If a defendant has been indicted the court having jurisdiction of his person may proceed to determine whether or not he is insane (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 658). If a defendant alleged to be insane, has not been indicted, and is charged with a felony, misdemeanor or offense, then the court to whose jurisdiction he is subject, may decide the question of his sanity (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 870). To exercise the function thus required of it, specific jurisdiction has been conferred, as it must on an inferior court, upon the Court of Special Sessions in the City of New York to "inquire into the insanity of a defendant." (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31, subd. 4.) 

Sec. 255. Degree of Insanity Required. As noted above, the degree of insanity that will prevent a defendant from being tried, sentenced or punished differs from the degree required to absolve a defendant of responsibility for the criminal act. Penal Law, sec. 1120, provides: "An act done by an idiot, imbecile, lunatic or insane is not a crime. 

One cannot be tried, sentenced * * * or punished for a crime when he is incapable of understanding the proceeding or making his defense. 

A person is not excused from criminal liability except upon proof that, at the time of committing the alleged criminal act, he was laboring under such a defect of reason as: 1. Not to know the nature and quality of the act he was doing; or 2. Not to know that the act was wrong."

The statutory rule is a codification of the rule enunciated in the famous English case, M'Naghton's Case, 8 Eng. Rep. 718. Penal Law, sec. 34, which should be read together with the above section, provides: "A morbid propensity to commit prohibited acts, existing in the mind of a person, who is not shown to have been incapable of knowing the wrongfulness of such acts, forms no defense 437

§ 

to a prosecution therefor." This section, in effect, negatives any application of the "irresistible impulse" doctrine in New York (Flanigan v. People, 52 N.Y. 467).

The defendant has the initial burden of coming forth with proof of his insanity as "A person is presumed to be responsible for his acts." (Penal Law, sec. 815.) However, once some such proof has been adduced by the defendant the prosecution has the burden of proving defendant's sanity beyond a reasonable doubt (People v. Egnor, 175 

N.Y. 419; compare People v. Nino, 149 N.Y. 317, indicating that the prosecution need only prove such status by a preponderance of the evidence).

Discussion of the rules applicable in determining defendant's responsibility for his actions belong, properly, in works on the substantive criminal law, and will be fully dealt with in the text on that subject which is included in the series of which the present work is a part. 438
