Sec. 256. Definition. A change of venue is the change of the place of trial. As so defined it includes all of the changes provided for in Section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. However, if venue is defined as the neighborhood, place or county, in accordance with its historical meaning, distinction should be drawn between the type of change allowed by paragraph 1 of Section 344, to a court in the same county, and the change allowed by paragraph 2, to a court of similar jurisdiction in another county. The change of the geographic locality of a trial to another county is the common concept of a change of venue. The other change, of a "vertical" nature, to a court in the same geographical area, has been called a "removal of prosecu- tion." Distinction between these kinds of changes is preferable, as different grounds are prescribed for the respective changes, and different procedures apply. The common usage of the term change of venue to refer to a "horizontal" change of locality to another court of similar jurisdiction will be used in this chapter. Whenever a "vertical" change to a court in the same locality is considered, it will be so described. 

Sec. 257. History. At common law, the general rule was that crimes were inquired into and tried in the county or neighborhood in which the crime was committed. Section 

355 of the Code now reads: "An issue of fact must be tried in the county in which the indictment was found, unless the action be removed, by order of the court, into another county, as provided in the second subdvision of section three hundred and forty-four." This rule was first codified in New York in 1895.

Since the enactment of the above section, it has been held that changes of venue can be made only in accordance with its terms, although cases decided prior to that time had indicated that the Supreme Court had power, as part of its constitutionally-granted general jurisdiction, to remove cases from one county to another. In the absence of statutory authority, the prosecution was held unable to apply 440

§ for a change of venue. In Murphy v. Extraordinary Special and Trial Term, 294 N.Y. 440, the court stated that the

Legislature's depriving the prosecution of the right to apply for a change of venue was not an unconstitutional restriction of the Supreme Court's general jurisdiction. 

The statute has since been amended to allow the prosecution to apply for a change of venue, but the Murphy case is still authority for the proposition that, in the absence of constitutional limitatons, the right to a change of venue is statutory and subject to the Legislature's regulation. 

Prior to the enactment of the Code, changes of the place of trial were effected by writ of certiorari. At common law, the Court of Kings Bench always has had power by such writ to remove indictments to it from lower courts. On such "vertical" removal of the prosecution, trials were had before juries drawn from the county in which the crime was committed, or the indictment found. (4 Blackstone 

Comm. 365). Later, the power of the court to direct a "horizontal" change of venue to another county was developed. Dicta concerning this power of the court are found in early cases but, in the Murphy case, supra, the Court of Appeals stated that it had found no instances of the exercise of this power in the pre-Code cases. The first such statutory authority in New York was 2 Revised

Statutes, Sec. 1, p. 733 (1828). In 1881, with the passage of the Code, the use of writs of certiorari was abolished in these cases (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 343), and Sections 

346 to 348 of the Code now provide the procedure. 

Sec. 258. Purposes. The removal of a prosecution to a higher court within the same county, as allowed by Section 344, subdivision 1, of the Code has been allowed since the early days of the common law, where the novelty or gravity of the legal questions presented warranted decision by a higher court having, presumably, greater stature than the court in which the indictment was found (1 Holdsworth, History of English Law, p. 213). Similarly, where persons of great reputation or social stature were 441

§ 

involved, the need for a trial before a court of equally great stature is evident. The higher the court, the less the chance of its being influenced by the reputation of the defendant. Similarly, the higher the court, the more likely its decision on novel or important legal questions will be widely publicized and followed, not only by the community but by other courts as well.

In this connection, it should be noted that the removal of a trial from the County Court (or General Sessions, in New York County) to the Supreme Court in the same county, under subdivision 1 of Section 344, is not a removal "to a higher court" in the sense we have discussed. 

The realization of this is important to counsel in stating grounds for his application to establish the "good cause shown," required by the statute. The Supreme Court is of coordinate jurisdiction and the trial will be had in the same place, and before local jurors. It is, in effect, a "horizontal" change most frequently required where there is no other judge available in the County Court to obviate the objections to, or disqualification of, the judge who would normally conduct the trial.

The purposes of changing the venue of a trial on a "horizontal" level to a court of similar jurisdiction in another county are quite different. A removal of a trial to a different geographic area does not add weight to a decision; it merely aids in obtaining the desired dispassionate judgment. In cases where public opinion has reached a stage where it appears doubtful that a fair trial can be afforded, a change of venue, interposing distance between the neighborhood where the crime was committed, and therefore where the feelings of the community are the most violent, and the place of the trial, can only add to the objectivity of the forum. Here, too, the removal from the 

County Court of one county to the Supreme Court in another is not a removal to "a higher court." Each County 

Court exists and has jurisdiction only in its own county; the Supreme Court is the only court existing outside its 442

§ county which has jurisdiction to try offenses committed therein.

Sec. 259. Defendant's Right to Apply. By the provision of Section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the de fendant is given the right to apply for a removal of the prosecution to the Supreme Court in the same county or in another county. A motion by the defendant to transfer a case from the Supreme Court to the Court of General Sessions was granted in People v. Hyde, 146 App. Div. 633, 131 N.Y.S. 567, although there is no statutory authority for such a motion, the Appellate Division holding the granting of the motion not reversible error.

Sec. 260. Effect upon Co-Defendants. Where a change of venue to another county has been granted, as to one defendant in a case, it has been held that the change should affect all his co-defendants as the local prejudice constituting the basis for the change probably affected all the defendants involved (People v. Jackson, 114 App. Div. 697, 100 N.Y.S. 126; People v. Baker, 3 Parker Cr. 181). If one of the defendants succeeds in effecting removal because he is a public official, or has some special social standing in the community, prejudice in the community might easily be directed against his co-defendants if their cases were not also removed. So, too, a judge's prejudice might be directed against co-defendants in the event the original object of the prejudice succeeded in having his prosecution removed. The economic advantages of having all trials removed together are also apparent. 

Sec. 261. The Prosecution's Right to Apply. In 1953, Section 

344 was amended to allow application by the prosecution for removal of the case to the Supreme Court in the same or another county. Previously, in the absence of such statutory authorization, it had been held that removal could not be had on the application of the People (People v. 443

§ 

Farini, 239 N.Y. 411; Murphy v. Extraordinary Term, 294 N.Y.440).

Sec. 262. The Court's Right to Remove Causes. Code of 

Criminal Procedure, section 41, permits a County Court to send a pending indictment to the Supreme Court for trial. 

If the indictment is returned by the Supreme Court without trial, the County Court must then proceed with the trial. Section 22, subdivision 6, provides that the Supreme 

Court may, by order entered in its minutes, send any indictment triable by a County Court or the Court of General Sessions of New York County to such County Court or 

Court of General Sessions. 

The Supreme Court may also, as the court stated in 

People v. Glasser, 1 App. Div. 2d 929, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 597: "remove to itself as a pure matter of routine, indictments pending in other courts in the same county." There the defendant's failure to receive notice of the removal of his indictment from a County Court to the Supreme Court was held not reversible error. The court noted that the notice requirements of Section 346 of the Code apply only to removals on application of the parties and not to routine transfers by the courts. This power of the courts is codified in Section 22, subdivision 4, of the Code. 

There is no statutory authority in New York for any court, on its own motion, to order a change of venue to another county. Under the strict interpretation rule of the Murphy case, it is doubtful that such action would be held constitutional. Several States have statutes allowing such action. In one case, arising in Oregon without such a statute, court action of this type was held unconstitutional. In State v. Black, 131 Ore. 218, 282 Pac. 222, trial had proceeded in the original county after a change of venue application had been denied. After the jury had been unable to agree upon a verdict, the court ordered a change of venue over the defendant's objections, this was held error. The texts also differ upon this point. Compare 

Corpus Juris Secundum, Criminal Law, Sec. 198: "It seems 444

§ that the court has no power of its own motion to change the venue unless such power is conferred by statute,” with 

Wharton on Criminal Procedure, sec. 1514: "At common law a criminal court of general jurisdiction has power to change the venue."

It is doubtful whether a court would ever be placed in the situation of having to change the venue on its own motion for, usually, one of the parties will make the motion when the situation demands such action. Apparently, the only 

New York case in point is People v. Mather, 3 Wend. 431 (Supreme Court, Albany County, 1830), where an indictment was found and tried in Orleans County, and the defendant acquitted. The District Attorney subsequently found that a rule (i.e., an order) had been entered in the minutes, directing the trial to be held in Monroe County, and appealed from the judgment on the ground that the Orleans County Court had had no jurisdiction to try the case. Neither party had asked for the rule, and the court stated that it "gave no direct order for its entry." In affirming the judgment, the Supreme Court stated: "There is no such thing as changing the venue in a criminal case though under certain circumstances the place of trial may be changed which however cannot be done by a mere direction of the court." 

Sec. 263. Necessity of an Indictment. The application for a removal of the trial, under Section 344 of the Code, from the County Court to the Supreme Court in the same county (subdivision 1), or from the County Court or Supreme

Court in one county to the Supreme Court in another county "on the ground that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had in the county" (subdivision 2), is, of necessity, limited to an action "prosecuted by indictment", as only such criminal actions are tried in the named courts. Application cannot be made under this procedure for such removal of a criminal action prosecuted by information; however, there are statutes providing for the removal from inferior courts, by means of a certificate that it is 445

§ 

reasonable that the matter be prosecuted by indictment before the Supreme Court or the County Court, instead of on information in special sessions. 

Section 57 of the Code, which applies to courts of special sessions outside the City of New York, provides for the divesting of the exclusive jurisdiction of the magistrate holding such court over the misdemeanors set forth in Section 56 by "filing with the magistrate *** a certificate of the County Judge of the county, or of any Justice of the Supreme Court, that it is reasonable that such charge be prosecuted by indictment, and fixing the sum in which the defendant shall give bail to appear before the Grand Jury. 

Similarly, Section 31, subdivision 1 (c), of the New

York City Criminal Courts Act provides that the exclusive jurisdiction of misdemeanors vested in the Court of Special Sessions may be divested when "before the commencement of any such trial, a Justice of the Supreme Court in the judicial department where the trial would be had; or *** in the County of New York, a judge authorized to hold a Court of General Sessions *** or * * * in another county, a County Judge shall certify that it is reasonable that such charge shall be prosecuted by indictment." 

As to applications made under Section 57 of the Code, the court in People v. Lane, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 769, 771, pointed out: "The defendant-applicant has the burden of showing that it is 'reasonable' that the charge should be prosecuted by indictment. See People v. Currao, 166 Misc. 374, 2 N.Y. 

S. 2d 513; also People v. Katzowitz, 150 Misc. 63, N.Y.S. 

748." The opinion in that case then proceeded to "spell out the formula upon which transfer of cases may be granted. 

The application should establish that the case presents intricate questions of fact, rendering a jury trial proper, or, it presents difficult questions of law, or that a property right is involved, or that a far-reaching decision of general interest is at issue, or that for some special reason the defendant cannot have a fair trial in the court of special sessions. *** it has been held in People v. Hassan, 113 446

§ N.Y.S. 2d 108, that where the defendant could fully protect herself as to all questions of law in trial before the local magistrate and would have the remedy of appeal in the event of errors of law, the fact that intricate questions of law involving the validity of an ordinance might be involved, would not require granting of certificate under 

Section 57 of the Code." 

In People v. Ryan, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 806, the defendants, informed against in the Court of Special Sessions for conspiracy to become a common gambler, conspiracy to keep a place for gambling and conspiracy to engage in bookmaking, applied for a certificate under 

Section 31, subdivision 1 (c), of the New York City Crimi nal Courts Act, transferring the case for prosecution upon indictment. They alleged that their arrest and prosecution had resulted from a personal and persistent campaign instigated and carried out by the Mayor, who had the power to appoint and reappoint the judges of the court in which the information would be tried without à jury. The 

Justice of the Supreme Court to whom the application was made stated, at page 810 of 38 N.Y.S. 2d: "Hence, though the court does not share in the petitioners' doubt of the fairness of a trial in the Court of Special Sessions, it considers it its duty to dispel their doubt by a transfer of the case to a court where the petitioners may probe the minds of the triers of the facts and accept their verdict without 

challenge. presents not only a legal question of first impression but a type of case that is customarily not tried in the Court of Special Sessions. That, too, warrants a transfer, for, as it was said in a recent case (People v. Schulman, 175 Misc. 157, 159, 22 N.Y.S. 2d 

429, 431): 'As I view it, such motions should be determined by the type of case. If it is not the type of case that appears on the Special Sessions calendar frequently, that is, if it is exceptional, if it is a serious criminal case, or if the case has been widely commented upon or is linked to other notorious cases, it is not a typical Special Sessions case.' 

447

§ 

 Sec. 264. Youthful Offenders. People v. Giaccio, 198 Misc. 

1092, 96 N.Y.S. 2d 912, held that defendants consenting to be tried as youthful offenders cannot thereafter make application for the removal of the prosecution to another court. Citing Murphy v. Extraordinary Special and Trial 

Term, 294 N.Y. 440, and Application of Knight, 178 Misc. 

972, 36 N.Y.S. 2d 985, the court stated at page 919 "*** strict application of Sec. 344 [had been decreed] and the inherent right of the Supreme Court had been curtailed by that provision."

Sec. 265. Waiver. Irregularity in the removal of a prosecution can be waived by failure of timely objection thereto. 

In People v. Washor, 196 N.Y. 104, the defendant was indicted in General Sessions and, after a plea of not guilty, the case was removed to the New York County Supreme Court for trial. A verdict of guilty was returned and the defendant appealed. The Court of Appeals, noting the lack of a record showing the removal procedure, stated that defendant's failure to raise this question at his trial constituted a waiver of his right to raise it on appeal. See also 

People v. Martin, 264 App. Div. 928, 36 N.Y.S. 2d 124, reversed on other grounds 289 N.Y. 471, in which defendant pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court to second degree robbery, after he had pleaded not guilty in the County Court, from which the case had been removed, to first degree robbery. The defendant's right to object to the removal was held waived, the Court citing the Washor case as controlling. 

Sec. 266. Grounds: Removal to the Supreme Court. As was stated in People v. Sessions, 10 Abb. N.C. 192, 197, and quoted and reaffirmed in People v. Fay, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 2, 4-5: 

66*** every application for removal must rest in the sound discretion of the court or judge who is to determine it and the reasons must be as various as the surroundings of each case in which it is attempted." And the decision is not re- 448

§ (c) 

viewable on appeal (People v. Fay, 268 App. Div. 135, 50 

N.Y.S. 2d 1; People v. Faricchia, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 269).

Sec. 266 (a). Novel and Grave Legal Questions. Section 344, subdivision 1, of the Code specifies only that removal may be ordered from a "County Court to a term of the Supreme Court held in the same county, for good cause shown." This has been recognized by the courts as "elastic, not capable of exact definition." (People v. Fay, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 2, appeal dismissed 268 App. Div. 135, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 1.) The presence of novel and weighty questions of law does not warrant removal, for there is "absolutely no basis for an assumption that a weighty or difficult question cannot be adequately resolved in the Court of General Sessions and such questions on topics familiar and unfamiliar are constantly being disposed of there." (Slater v. Hogan, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 164, 165.) Thus is reaffirmed the concept that such removalfrom a County or General Sessions Court to the Supreme Court-is not deemed a removal to "a higher court," as is removal from special sessions to a court of record. 

Sec. 266 (b). Great Public Interest. In People v. Fay, supra, the defendants were charged with extortion and conspiracy arising out of their activities as labor leaders. Extraordinary Grand Juries to investigate the matter had been convened by two Governors. Publicity had been widespread and the court recognized the possibility that in the proceedings "labor itself will be on trial" and that the "repercussions of this trial may affect both labor and capital in [two] States." The defendants' motion was granted and the prosecution removed to the Supreme Court, largely by reason of the State-wide jurisdiction of the Supreme Court as contrasted with the county-limited General Sessions jurisdiction. 

Sec. 266 (c). Familiarity with the Field of Law. One early case emphasized the need for a decision by a court familiar 449

§ (d)  

with the field of law involved in its decision on a motion for a removal to a higher court. In People v. Clark, 15 

N.Y.S. 79, removal to the Supreme Court of an indictment for violation of laws pertaining to the heating of railroad cars was ordered on the ground that the Supreme Court was more familiar with railroad law. This would hardly be the view today, as witness the statement of the court in Slater v. Hogan, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 164, 165, quoted above.

Sec. 266 (d). Public Standing of the Defendants. In People v. Sessions, 62 How. Pr. 415, a State Senator was indicted for bribing an Assemblyman to vote for a specific person for United States Senator. The case was widely publicized and the District Attorney had postponed the trial for several months because of the heat of public excitement on the matter. The defendant moved to remove the case from the Albany County Court of Sessions (then held by county judiciary) to the Albany County Court of Oyer and Terminer (then presided over by a Supreme Court Justice) on the grounds that the official public standing of the parties and the difficulty and gravity of the legal questions warranted such a change. The court, unable to find any precedent defining the "good cause" required by the statute stated: "*** a motion of this character should be granted ***whenever the situation and official standing of the accused party, the widespread and clearly divided line of popular opinion, and the circumstances of the alleged crime, as well as the important legal questions which it presents, so magnify the importance of the case, as to justify its removal." (Id., at p. 420.) 

Sec. 266(e). Calendar Delay in Original Court. Delay, caused by a crowded calendar in the court of original jurisdiction, is not sufficient reason to warrant a removal to another court (People v. Stewart, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 189). The proper remedy, in such a case, is a motion to dismiss the indictment for lack of speedy prosecution. 450

§ (a) 

Sec. 266(f). Prejudice of the Judge Below. The alleged prejudice, or involvement in the matter to be tried, of the judge scheduled to hear the case below has been held good cause for the removal of the case. In People v. McDermott, 180 Misc. 247, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 456, the defendants moved for removal from the County Court to the Supreme Court, asserting that they intended to call the County Judge as a witness. The application was granted. 

In People v. Faricchia, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 269, the defendant procured a removal of his retrial on robbery charges from the County Court where it would have been tried by the judge who had presided at his previous trials. One of these trials had resulted in a jury disagreement and the other in a reversal of a conviction on the basis of prejudicial instructions given by the very County Judge. The County 

Judge had refused several applications to assign the case to another judge. The Court granted the application, citing People v. Dorfman, 180 Misc. 160, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 266.

In the Dorfman case, the removal of a retrial was granted, the court noting the statement of the County 

Judge upon sentencing, that defendant was the "pliant tool of racketeers and gangsters." The court stated that though it would not be impossible for the County Judge to hold an impartial trial, the danger of prejudice resulting from his former opinion existed. In People v. Rockower, 51 N.Y.S. 2d 185, an application for removal of a retrial was denied, after arrangements had been made for a different County Judge to preside over the retrial. In denying the application, the court also noted that the District Attorney had assured the court that the trial would be moved before the newly assigned judge.

Sec. 267. Change of Venue. 

Sec. 267(a). Convenience of Witnesses. The only form in which a change of venue is authorized in criminal cases is by removal to the Supreme Court in another county (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 344, subd. 2). Changes of venue will not 451

§ (b)  

be granted for the convenience of witnesses or the parties. 

In People v. Baker, 3 Abb. Prac. 42, a change of venue from 

New York to Suffolk County, requested by the prosecution, was granted over defendant's objection that the cost would be prohibitive. The court directed payment of the added expenses by New York County. Such arrangement for defraying these added expenses has now been embodied in Section 344 of the Code. In People v. Harris, 4 

Den. 150, the defendant swore that he intended to call eighty-nine witnesses, all of whom resided in Chenango and the adjoining counties. The indictment had been found in New York County. The defendant's application for a change of venue was denied. 

In People v. Mitchell, 168 N.Y. 604, the Court of Appeals stated: "* * * the power to change the place of trial for the convenience of witnesses, upon the application of the defendant, should be conferred upon the proper court in all criminal actions, where the indictment alleges that the crime was committed partly in one county and partly in another." However, this statement is dictum, and is a recommendation which the Legislature has not seen fit to adopt. Nor has the Court of Appeals or any other court, as far as research discloses, attempted to effectuate it by judicial fiat. Sec. 267(b). Religious or Racial Prejudice. In the only two 

New York cases found involving allegations that religious or racial prejudice precluded a fair or impartial trial, changes of venue were granted. In People v. Lucas, 131 

Misc. 664, 228 N.Y.S. 31, a negro defendant obtained a change of venue from the prevalently white community where the crime occurred, and where he had been attacked in newspaper articles. In People v. Ryan, 123 Misc. 450, 205 N.Y.S. 664, a Roman Catholic defendant obtained a change of venue in a murder case where the victim was a member of the Ku Klux Klan, and the defendant was able to show that the Klan was a popular movement in the community. However, there appears to be no reason to dis- 452

§ (d) tinguish these cases from the body of cases involving community prejudice derived from other factors. The same considerations are present and the same factors should influence the court's decision whether the prejudice results from racial or religious prejudice or from prejudice engendered by extensive newspaper campaign. 

Sec. 267 (c). Public Officials. The fact that a defendant is a public official accused of malfeasance in office will not, of itself, justify a change of venue. Thus, a motion by the defendant City Treasurer, who had been indicted for bribery, for a change of venue, was denied in People v. 

Hyde, 75 Misc. 407, 133 N.Y.S. 306, affirmed 149 App. Div. 

131, 133 N.Y.S. 780. The court held other evidence of prejudice must be shown. To the same effect, see People v. Sharp, 5 N.Y. Cr. 155, where an Alderman was the defendant. 

The fact that the defendants are public officials, and that their official acts leading to their indictment might have roused a feeling of resentment in the community, weigh in favor of the granting of removal when added to other evidence of community prejudice (People v. Frankel, 140 

Misc. 195, 266 N.Y.S. 360). Active interest in the prosecution by community civic groups and the press were factors which influenced a court in granting a change of venue to a police precinct captain (People v. Diamond, 36 Misc. 

71, 72 N.Y.S. 179). Similarly, where a bank official's larceny of bank funds in a small community was widely thought to be the cause of the bank's insolvency, with resultant financial loss to many in the area, a change of venue was granted (People v. Georger, 109 App. Div. 111, 95 N.Y.S. 790).

Sec. 267 (d). Fair and Impartial Trial. The common ground for requesting a change of venue, and the only one mentioned in the Code, is "that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had in the community where the indictment is pending." (Code of Crim. Proc. Sec. 344, subd. 2.) The factors 453

§ (e)  

mentioned above are merely variations on, and detailed indications of, this ground. 

Sec. 267(e). Newspaper and Similar Publicity. The most common cause alleged for prejudice in the community is newspaper publicity. 

People v. Brindell, 194 App. Div. 776, 780-781, 185 

N.Y.S. 533, 535-536, includes language which most accurately describes courts' reactions to such applications: "Everyone knows the ephemeral nature of opinions derived from reading the public prints. The community is fed on horrors daily, almost hourly, and each sensation crowds out the previous one. 

articles furnished ground for removal, no defendant could ever be tried in this county for a spectacular crime. 

If the defendants' fears in the case at bar are justified, we would not know to what county this trial should be transferred, as our metropolitan press circulates through the entire State. The busy residents of this city are too much interested in their own offices to be so impregnated with casual news accounts as to render them unfit for jury duty." In another case it was noted that there is "a marked distinction between a widespread opinion unfavorable to defendant, based on newspaper articles, and a hostility and prejudice so deep as to create an unconscious prejudice in the minds of potential jurors." (People v. Sollazo, 106 

N.Y.S. 2d 600, 601.)

Where the prosecution moved for a change of venue, alleging that the community had been hostile to the investigation leading to the indictments, which concerned gambling activities in Saratoga County, and that the defendant was being benefited by local political connections and by the local press, the motion was denied, the court noting that the newspaper concerned had a comparatively small circulation and that the people of the community were not all politically of the same mind (People v. Gren- 

284 App. Div. 657, 134 N.Y.S. 2d 676). However, where newspaper articles widely circulated in the community nan, 454

§ had, over a period of five years, contained headlines describing the defendant as a "Fake Doctor" with an "Unsavory Record" and as a "Prenatal Sex Control Faker” and where the defendant's criminal record had been widely publicized, his motion for a change of venue was granted 

(People v. Lucas, 131 Misc. 664, 228 N.Y.S. 31). Similarly, where for a period of two years articles had been published concerning defendant's alleged murder victim and containing defendant's picture, the contents of his purported confession, and a statement that the victim had identified the defendant on her deathbed, the defendant's motion for a change of venue was granted (People v. Mleczko, 193 

Misc. 253, 83 N.Y.S. 2d 821). The principle applied in these cases would be in point in television and radio publicity, where the initial effect of the story might be greater but the period of retention of the contents less. 

Sec. 268. Burden of Proof. "Defendant has the burden to establish clearly that he cannot obtain a fair and impartial trial." (People v. Sollazo, 106 N.Y.S. 2d 600.) Defendants, charged with corrupting basketball players on teams of the three largest colleges in New York City were unsuccessful, in the Sollazo case, supra, in their attempt to have the venue changed to a county not less than 100 miles from New York County. The court noted that although the prosecution engendered "a sizeable volume of newspaper clippings," a lapse of three months from the date of the latest article led the court to believe that a fair trial could be had. The party seeking to remove the trial from the original county has the burden of proof and "only the most compelling reason could justify trial by a jury not drawn from the vicinage." (People v. Murphy, supra.)

Sec. 269. When to Apply. Section 344 permits application 

"at any time before trial." However, one early case held that issue must first be joined (People v. McCraney, 21 

How. Pr. 749). While in one case it was held that defendant's failure to exhaust peremptory challenges militated 455

§ 

against the defendant's contention that an impartial jury could not be obtained (People v. Warder, 231 App. Div. 

215, 247 N.Y.S. 60), such action has been held not requisite to the application (People v. Ryan, 123 Misc. 450, 205 

N.Y.S. 664; Budge v. Northam, 20 How. Pr. 248).

Sec. 270. Before Juror Sworn. Section 353 of the Code provides: "An order for the removal of the action is of no effect, unless a certified copy thereof be filed *** before a juror is sworn to try the indictment." Though counsel had stipulated that either party might remove a juror previously sworn before going to trial, and the court had noted this on the record, it was held that swearing in the juror precluded defendant from later attempting to remove the prosecution from the County Court to the Supreme Court (Application of Hanold, 106 N.Y.S. 2d 326, appeal dismissed, 278 App. Div. 1023, 106 N.Y.S. 2d 1005).

Sec. 271. To Whom Application Made. Section 346 sets forth the courts to which the application must be directed. 

An application for removal to the Supreme Court in the same county must be made to a Special Term of the Supreme Court in the judicial district where the action is pending. Application for removal to the Supreme Court in another county must be made by motion in the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the department in which the action is pending. 

Sec. 272. Notice. Either motion must be made on notice of at least five days to the District Attorney, or to the defendant or his attorney on the People's motion. The motion made at Special Term must be made returnable "at the next special term within the said district, after the motion papers are served." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 346, subd. 

1.) In the Appellate Division, it must "be returnable during the term in which the moving papers are served or the next term thereafter at which such motion may be heard." (id., sec. 346, subd. 2.) In addition to notice of motion, there 456

§ must be served at the same time "a copy of the affidavits or other papers on which the application is founded." (id., sec. 346, subd. 3.) 

Sec. 273. Stays. In the event the trial of a case is scheduled to commence prior to the return date of the motion, Section 347 of the Code authorizes the granting of a stay of the trial, not exceeding thirty days, until the application can be decided. Application for the stay is made to a Supreme Court Justice residing, or holding a term of the Supreme Court, in the district in which the indictment is pending or to a Justice of the Appellate Division of that department. The order granting a stay cannot be vacated by another justice of similar jurisdiction (People v. Mc- 

Laughlin, 150 N.Y. 365). The stay will be granted for "good cause," as where the defendants show a probability of removal granted (People v. Page, 182 Misc. 10, 48 N.Y.S. 

2d 342). Once application for a stay has been denied, another application may not be made to another judge 

(Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 349; People v. McCarthy, 250 

N.Y. 358), and violation of Section 349 is made a contempt of court by Section 350 of the Code. 

The court's decision upon the application for a stay is to be endorsed by the court upon the papers and forwarded by the court to the clerk of the court in which the indictment is pending (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 350). There is no provision for postponement of the trial pending determination of the removal application beyond the thirty day period mentioned above. 

Sec. 274. Moving Papers. In addition to the customary notice of motion and affidavits of the parties, it has been held that extensive and detailed proof should be submitted to the court. Thus, the court will consider all the facts that tend to show prejudice in the community, including affidavits of residents (People v. Sandgren, 190 Misc. 810, 75 

N.Y.S. 2d 753) and newspaper articles (People v. Hyde, 75 457

§ 

Misc. 407, 133 N.Y.S. 306, affirmed 149 App. Div. 131, 133 

N.Y.S. 780).

Sec. 275. The Order of Removal. If the application for an order of removal is granted, the moving party must prepare a certified copy of the order and file it with the clerk of the court in which the indictment is pending. Once the order is so filed, the original court has no further jurisdiction to proceed with the case. Thus, where an order removing a case from a County Court to the Supreme Court had been filed, it was held that the County Court had no further jurisdiction to decide motions which had previously been made for the inspection of Grand Jury minutes and for dismissal of the indictment. The court did note that the motions could be renewed in the Supreme Court (People v. Friss, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 603). The order need not be proved or introduced in evidence in the court to which the action was removed to establish jurisdiction there (People v. Jennings, 230 App. Div. 871, 245 N.Y.S. 41). The order of removal must include provision for the physical transfer of the defendant's custody from the officer holding him to the Sheriff of the county to which the action has been removed (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 352). 

Sec. 276. Appeals. The decision upon a motion for removal lies within the court's discretion (People v. Marinelli, 37 

N.Y.S. 2d 321; People v. Hines, 168 Misc. 453, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 

15; People v. Fay, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 2, appeal dismissed, 268 

App. Div. 135, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 1). The Fay case held the order denying a request for removal from General Sessions to the Supreme Court was not appealable. Since the decision in People v. Zerillo, 200 N.Y. 443, holding the appellate jurisdiction of New York courts in criminal cases to be purely statutory, it is doubtful whether any appeal from these orders may be heard. See People v.

Mordeno, 93 N.Y.S. 2d 369 and People v. Nentarz, 235 App. 

Div. 660, 255 N.Y.S. 214, holding orders denying motions for changes of venue to be intermediate orders, and thus 458

§ not specifically appealable. Reargument of the motion may always be sought if timely application therefor is made 

(People v. Fay, supra). 

After conviction, the effect of an order denying a change of venue can be considered as part of the appeal from the judgment. The constitutional implications of such denial, discussed above, may also be raised at this time. See chapter of this work, entitled "Appeals." 459

CHAPTER 23 SUBPOENAS AND COMPELLING THE ATTENDANCE OF WITNESSES Sec. 277. Definition and Discussion Sec. 278. Power of District Attorney to Issue Subpoenas Sec. 279. Power of  to Issue Subpoenas Sec. 280. Power of Magistrate to Issue Subpoenas 

Sec. 281. Service 

Sec. 282. Witness Fees

Sec. 283. Compelling Attendance of Witness Outside of Subpoena ing State

Sec. 284. Material Witnesses Sec. 285. Challenge and Quashing of Subpoena 

Sec. 277. Definition and Discussion. A subpoena is "the process by which the attendance of a witness, before a court or magistrate is required" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 607), the disobedience of which constitutes contempt (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 619). The power of subpoena, both on the part of the defendant and the prosecutor, is indispensible to the proper administration of criminal procedure. Although the subject of subpoenas is treated summarily, if at all, in most criminal procedure texts, the prompt issuance of a valid subpoena in accordance with the statutory and case law can in many instances mean the difference between success or failure in a criminal case.

Subpoenas are of two types: the subpoena ad testificandum, the more common process commanding the witness to appear and give testimony (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

612), and the subpoena duces tecum, which requires the witness to bring books, chattels, papers or documents (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 613). The books or papers pro- 460

SUBPOENAS 

§ 278 duced in obedience to a subpoena duces tecum remain under the control of the person producing them, and he cannot be required to deposit or leave them with the examining party, but they must be returned to him after such use or examination as may be necessary and proper. The material sought in a subpoena duces tecum must be sufficiently described for it "is well settled that the power to compel the production of books and records by a witness is limited to a proper case. * * * The subpoena duces tecum *** is per mitted *** where the books, records and documents to be produced are material and relevant to the issue and where they have been described with reasonable precision." (Application of Sun-Ray Cloak Co., 256 App. Div. 

620, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 202.)

Although five days' notice is specifically required only in the instance of a subpoena duces tecum served by the defendant upon a State office or official, or subdivision thereof, it is the better practice to give such notice in all cases. See Matter of Atlas Lathing Corp., 176 Misc. 959, 29 

N.Y.S. 2d 458. The courts' distaste for a forthwith subpoena duces tecum was also indicated in Application of 

Remy Sportswear Inc., 16 Misc. 2d 407, 183 N.Y.S. 2d 125. 

Sec. 278. Power of District Attorney to Issue Subpoenas. 

It is the duty of the District Attorney, pursuant to Section 256 of the Code, to issue subpoenas when required by the Grand Jury, and Section 609 provides that the District 

Attorney has the power to subscribe and issue subpoenas "in support of the prosecution or for such other witnesses as the Grand Jury may direct, to appear before them,' upon an investigation pending before that body. The District Attorney may issue subpoenas in support of "an indictment, to appear before the court at which it is to be tried." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 610.) This has been interpreted as also including the power to issue subpoenas to appear at the trial of an information. 

The Code of Criminal Procedure thus authorizes the 

District Attorney to issue subpoenas in but two instances, 461

§ 

דין i.e., for the purpose of compelling witnesses to testify before the Grand Jury and to testify at trial. However, District Attorneys have, on occasion, used the subpoena power for the purpose of examining a witness in their own offices rather than before a Grand Jury or upon trial. There is no authority for the issuance of such a subpoena, custom to the contrary notwithstanding. Under certain situations the attorney may deem it advisable to permit the questioning of his client as a witness in the District Attorney's office, providing the witness' counsel is present. This enables the witness' attorney to determine the witness' status or role in the investigation so that advice can be given accordingly. This practice can be of benefit to the prosecutor, too, since the attorney, present with the client, may counsel the witness to give information which might not be given in the Grand Jury room, where the witness would claim his privilege rather than chance waiving his constitutional rights. Some District Attorneys issue the so-called "askto-see subpoena," which rather than commanding the witness to appear, reads: "You are requested to appear ***"As the form indicates, such a subpoena is not obligatory upon the witness and the course of procedure followed should be the same as with the subpoena valid in form for appearance in the District Attorney's office.

The prosecutor issuing the "ask-to-see" subpoena, or interrogating a witness in his office, is cautioned to the danger in such practice if the witness may be or becomes a target of the investigation. The witness may claim that his rights are violated, because of statements or admissions which were made either under the influence of fear as a result of threats, or promises of immunity made to the witness. If the witness may become a target, conservative practice would dictate that the witness be warned of his rights, which warning with the interview should be transcribed. If a subpoena is issued by the Attorney General, or other agency or department commanding the witness' appearance other than at trial or before the Grand Jury, the attorney should check the specific statutory 462

SUBPOENAS 

$279 authority authorizing the issuance of such process.

For example, Section 352 of the General Business Law author izes the Attorney General or his designated officers to subpoena witnesses and take their oaths in an investigation pertaining to fraudulent practices in stocks, bonds or securities. General Business Law, Section 343, establishes similar subpoena power in an investigation of monopolies (Matter of Atlas Lathing Corp., 176 Misc. 959, 29 N.Y.S. 

2d 458).

When a witness is subpoenaed to appear before the Grand Jury and the proceeding is adjourned either before or after the witness has begun testifying (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 610-a), a new subpoena should be issued directing the witness to appear on the adjourned date. In Application of Mullen, 177 Misc. 734, 31 N.Y.S. 2d 710, the subpoena had had imprinted upon the side the usual words: "Should the case not be called on the day mentioned in said subpoena, you are directed to attend from day to day until it is discharged," but the court held that the oral direction of both the foreman of the Grand Jury and the District Attorney were not valid directives upon which to predicate an order of contempt. The court stated that the only enforcible manner of compelling attendance of a witness is in conformity with Sections 606-618 of the Code, and that, "if further attendance is required, the law provides the means of obtaining it, the issuance and service of another subpoena." This caveat can become most important where the witness is given immunity and the examination is adjourned, as the prosecutor must take every precaution not to lose jurisdiction over such individual. 

The powers and authority of the Grand Jury to issue subpoenas and compel the attendance of witnesses is discussed and considered in the chapter of this work entitled "Grand Jury," under the section thereof: "Witnesses:

Power To Subpoena." Sec. 279. Power of Attorney For Defendant to Issue Sub poenas.

The power of compulsory process is a vital right 463

§ 

which the defendant possesses. This right is afforded in the following sections of the respective statutes. Section 12 of the Civil Rights Law provides: "In all criminal prosecutions, the accused has a right *** to have compulsory process for obtaining witnesses in his favor." (People v. 

Wells, 272 N.Y. 215.) In addition, Code of Criminal Procedure, sec. 8, subd. 3, reiterates this. Section 610-b, the section most frequently cited in support of this right, provides that the defendant may issue subpoenas and subpoenas duces tecum. A defendant has a right to subpoena a witness notwithstanding the possibility that the witness may assert the privilege against self-incrimination (People v. 

Wells, supra; see People v. Pindar, 159 App. Div. 72, 148

N.Y.S. 937). This section provides that Sections 410 through 414 of the Civil Practice Act govern the issuance of subpoenas duces tecum to any office, department, bureau or agency of the State, or any of its subdivisions, or to any officer of such governmental body. 

Unless otherwise ordered by the court, transcripts or photographic reproductions of the entries or records of a hospital or of a department or bureau of a State or municipal body is deemed sufficient compliance with a subpoena duces tecum (Civ. Prac. Act, sec. 142). A subpoena duces tecum served on such government body must be served at least five days in advance of the date of production except that during the trial or hearing the judge may, in his discretion, authorize shorter notice. If the attorney desires the attendance of a particular officer of the government, a separate subpoena, without the duces tecum clause, must be served upon that officer to assure his personal attendance. Unless such separate subpoena is issued, any competent subordinate or employee is authorized to appear and identify the books and records. The clerk of the court in which an indictment is pending, must at all times and without charge, issue as many blank subpoenas as may be required by the defendant. They are issued under the seal of the court and subscribed by the clerk. The clerk, or a magistrate, may be compelled by an Article 78 proceeding 464

SUBPOENAS 

§ 280 in the nature of mandamus to issue the subpoenas (Trombetta v. Van Amringe, 156 Misc. 307, 280 N.Y.S. 480).

Where a witness is required to attend out of the county where he resides or in which he is served with the subpoena, a Justice of the Supreme Court or judge of a court of record must endorse on the subpoena an order for the attendance of the witness, based upon an affidavit of the prosecutor or District Attorney, the defendant or his counsel, stating that the individual believes that the evidence of the witness is material, and his attendance at the trial or examination is necessary (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 618; see 3 Op. State. Compt. 130).

Sec. 280. Power of Magistrate to Issue Subpoenas. When an information is heard by a magistrate, he possesses the power to issue subpoenas on behalf of both the defendant and the People. The subpoenas must be subscribed by the magistrate (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 608). The right of the defendant to subpoena witnesses through the magistrate cannot be denied. In Danaher v. Harris, 236 App. 

Div. 481, 260 N.Y.S. 22, a magistrate refused to subpoena the witnesses because of his belief that the witnesses sought, persons of importance, did not have knowledge of the facts. It was there held that the magistrate could not refuse to subpoena the witnesses, even if it seemed unnecessary; his function is comparable to that of the clerk of the court. In Trombetta v. Van Amringe, 156 Misc. 307, 280

N.Y.S. 480, the court stated that although there is a right to the issuance of a subpoena ad testificandum, the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum is within the discretionary power of the magistrate. The magistrate's power to subpoena is dependent and predicated upon a valid information before him. The information, to provide the foundation for the issuance of a subpoena, must show reasonable ground to believe that a crime has been committed, and by a particular person or persons (People ex rel. Livingston v. Wyatt, 186 N.Y. 383; Gaffney v. Kampf, 465

§ 

268 App. Div. 308, 52 N.Y.S. 2d 1.; People v. Quinn, 150 

App. Div. 813, 135 N.Y.S. 477).

In courts of special sessions outside the City of New York, the magistrate issues the subpoenas, as provided in Sections 608 and 729 of the Code. In the Court of Special 

Sessions, within the City of New York, the clerk issues subpoenas (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 744). 

Sec. 281. Service. A subpoena which is issued by any officer of any court of record of this state, a District Attorney or a County Clerk may be served within any county of the State (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 618). The court of Special Sessions within the City of New York has the same power to send subpoenas into any part of the State (N.Y. 

Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31, subd. 4). The Magistrates within the 

City of New York may issue subpoenas for service within the city (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 101). As noted above, if the person served is required to appear in a county other than where he is served or where he resides, the County Judge of the county where the subpoena is returnable, a Justice of the Supreme Court or a judge of a court of record must endorse an order on the subpoena for the attendance of the witness. The order is supported by an affidavit of the attorney that the evidence of the witness is material and that the attendance at the trial or examination is necessary. A peace officer or any other person may serve the subpoena (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 614). The sheriff has the duty of serving subpoenas upon witnesses residing in the county, when sent to him by the District 

Attorney (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 615-a).

The service of the subpoena is effected either by delivering the original to the witness or, preferably, by showing him the original and delivering a copy, personally (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 615). A written return of service by an officer or an affidavit by the private server, must be promptly filed, stating time and place of service. A subpoena must be served personally, as substituted service is invalid (Broderick v. Shapiro, 172 Misc. 28, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 466

SUBPOENAS 

§ 282 542). There is no provision for substituted service upon a witness, but the following procedure was sustained in 

Application of Barbara, 7 App. Div. 2d 340, 183 N.Y.S. 2d 

147. The officer went to the petitioner's residence and was refused admittance. Observing the prospective witness, he told him and showed him the subpoena through an enclosure. The witness' wife refused to admit the officer. The officer fastened the subpoena and the witness fee to the door of the witness' house, and then announced through an amplifier which was audible for a considerable distance that the subpoena and fees were on the door, and repeated the announcement a number of times.

Sec. 282. Witness Fees. A person subpoenaed by the People in a court of record is entitled to the same witness and mileage fee as a witness in a civil action. Section 1539 of the Civil Practice Act, the applicable section, fixes this at fifty cents for each day's actual attendance in the case of a subpoena ad testificandum and one dollar in the case of a subpoena duces tecum, and if the witness resides more than three miles from the place of attendance he is entitled to receive eight cents for each mile, to the place of attendance, with nothing additional for returning. Actual attendance means personal presence, and prior to the amendment allowing fees to material witnesses held in custody it was held that the period of detention was not regarded as attendance entitling the witness to a fee (People v. Sharp, 78 Misc. 528, 139 N.Y.S. 995; People ex rel. Troy v.

Pettit, 19 Misc. 280, 44 N.Y.S. 256). It is noted that Section 

616 of the Code provides that fees are payable to the People's witnesses only in a court of record. Section 731 of the 

Code provides that no fees are payable to a witness in a court of special sessions, outside the City of New York 

(3 Op. State Compt. 130 [1947]). 

The court has the power to order payment of a further sum for reasonable expenses. The clerk of the court issues a certificate to the County Treasurer based upon the witness' affidavit stating that he attended at the request or 467

§ 

subpoena of the District Attorney, the number of miles. traveled and the days in attendance. There is no statutory fee prescribed for witnesses subpoenaed by the defendant; however, the court may in its discretion pay a reasonable sum for expenses to witnesses attending in behalf of the defendant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 617). No such fee is permitted in courts of special sessions (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 731).

Sec. 283. Compelling Attendance of Witness Outside of 

Subpoenaing State. In 1936, the Legislature substantially adopted the Uniform Act to Secure the Attendance of Witnesses from Without a State in Criminal Proceedings (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 618-a). This statute has been adopted in over forty states and a witness can only be compelled to attend in such adopting State whose statute is reciprocal to that of New York. 

For the reference of the attorney who may be faced with the problem of subpoenaing out-of-State witnesses, the following are the States which have adopted the Uniform Act to Secure the Attendance of Witnesses from Without a State in Criminal Proceedings (9 Uniform Laws An notated):

A Justice of the Supreme Court, or a County Judge of a county in which the individual is present, may issue a subpoena commanding a witness to appear in one of the States which has adopted the reciprocal, uniform legislation if the following requirements are met: A judge of a court of record of the State desiring the witness' attendance must certify under court seal that: (a) there is criminal prosecution pending in such court or that a Grand Jury investigation has commenced or is about to com- 469

§ 

mence, and (b) that the prospective witness' testimony is material, and (c) the number of days that the witness' presence will be required.

Upon presentation of such certificate, the justice or judge in the witness' State will fix a time and place for a hearing, at which time it is to be determined whether the witness is material and necessary, whether it will cause undue hardship on the witness to attend in the other State, and that the laws of the other State will afford the witness protection from arrest and the service of civil and criminal process. The issuing judge's certificate is prima facie evidence at the hearing as to the recited facts. Upon determination that the statutory requisites are met, the subpoena is issued, with a copy of the certificate attached, directing the witness' attendance at the desired place. In 

Matter of Costello, 279 App. Div. 908, 111 N.Y.S. 2d 313, where the State of New Jersey requested the appearance of a witness, the New York court found the certificate defective in that it did not state that the witness' testimony was material. 

In Matter of Mayers, 9 Misc. 2d 212, 169 N.Y.S. 2d 839, the court refused to command a witness to appear in the State of California, because it questioned the good faith of the requesting State, it appearing that the witness might be made a defendant in the proceeding. The court has the right to commit the witness, after hearing, to the custody of the requesting State, in lieu of issuing the subpoena.

The witness is entitled to receive in advance a witness fee of ten cents a mile for each mile traveling to and returning from the court, together with five dollars for each day that the witness is required to travel and attend. 

The identical procedure is applicable when a witness in another state is requested to testify in this State (Code 

Crim. Proc., sec. 618-a, subd. 3). A witness coming into this State in obedience to a subpoena directing him to attend is immune from civil or criminal process in matters arising prior to his entrance into this State pursuant to 470

SUBPOENAS 

$284 the subpoena. The power of the State to direct the attendance of a witness in another jurisdiction has been held constitutional (Commonwealth of Mass. v. Klaus, 145 

App. Div. 798, 130 N.Y.S. 713; People of New York v. 

O'Neill, 359 U.S. 1). The duty to give evidence and the correlative power to compel it is not limited to causes pending in the courts of the State, particularly in view of the safeguards, including an opportunity for the witness to be heard (People of New York v. O'Neill, supra).

Sec. 284. Material Witnesses. A judge of a court of record has the power to require a witness for the People to post an undertaking to assure the witness' presence at a pending criminal action or proceeding. Upon the witness' failure to execute such undertaking, the judge may order the witness incarcerated until he is discharged. Section 618-b requires that the judge be satisfied, by proof on oath, that the witness is necessary and material for the People. The court held in People ex rel. Nuccio v. Eighth District 

Prison Warden, 182 Misc. 654, 45 N.Y.S. 2d 230, that a

Grand Jury proceeding is within the purview of the section requiring a witness to post bond. The Grand Jury proceedings must be pending to justify the holding of an individual as a material witness. In Matter of Prestigiacomo, 234 App. Div. 300, 255 N.Y.S. 289, it was held that the witness could not be held for a future Grand Jury. (See People ex rel. Scalise v. Warden, 176 Misc. 816, 29 

N.Y.S. 2d, 277).

The witness must be afforded the opportunity to appear before the judge in opposition to the order requiring him to enter a written undertaking. In this hearing, the witness is not required to be advised of a right to counsel, but if he requests permission to consult counsel his request must be honored. This proposition was established in People ex rel. Fusco v. Ryan, 204 Misc. 861, 124 N.Y.S. 2d 690, where two brothers were sought to be held as material witnesses; one requested permission to consult his attorney and was told that his attorney could see him in jail. 471

§ 

The other made no request. The court held, as above indicated, that while as a general rule witnesses are not entitled to counsel, in this situation the witness has such a right if he duly demands it. 

The "proof on oath" that the witness is necessary and material does not mean that legal evidence is required, as was held in People ex rel. Ditchik v. Sheriff, 171 Misc. 248, 12 N.Y.S. 2d 341, affirmed 256 App. Div. 1081, 12 N.Y.S. 2d 

232. There, an individual was held as a material witness where the proof consisted of conclusions and opinions by the prosecutor that the witness would not appear and testify when required, because the persons against whom he might give evidence would influence him against testifying.

The factors to be considered in the fixing of the amount of the undertaking include the seriousness of the crime. under investigation; the penalty that may be imposed; the character, background and criminal record, if any, of the prospective witness, and his pecuniary and social condition and general reputation; his relationship to others against whom he may be called to testify; the probability of the witness' willing appearance, or the possibility of his flight to avoid giving testimony; the difficulty, if not impossibility, of procuring his return if he does leave the State (People ex rel. Rao v. Adams, 296 N.Y. 231; People ex rel. 

Fusco v. Ryan, supra). It has been held that a witness may be committed as a material witness, notwithstanding that he has been arraigned in a court of special sessions on misdemeanors similar to those being investigated before the 

Grand Jury (People ex rel. Gross v. Sheriff, 302 N.Y. 

173). It was held in the Gross case, that since the time spent in jail bore an intimate relationship to the crime for which he was subsequently convicted, he was entitled to credit for the period of his confinement prior to conviction and sentence (Application of Gross, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 403. See Bernoff v. Amoroso, 188 Misc. 845, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 810, affirmed 

271 App. Div. 925, 67 N.Y.S. 2d 701).

It was held in People ex rel. Rao v. Adams, supra, and in 472

SUBPOENAS 

§ 285 

People ex rel. Gross v. Sheriff, 302 N.Y. 173, that a $250,000 undertaking was not unreasonable. See People v. Warden, 277 App. Div. 87, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 173, where the court held that a $100,000 undertaking should be reduced to not more than $10,000. The witness may obtain relief from an excessive undertaking by writ of habeas corpus (People ex rel. 

Ditchik v. Sheriff, supra; People ex rel. Weiner v. Collins, 22 N.Y.S. 2d, 774, affirmed 260 App. Div. 806, 22 N.Y.S. 2d 775). 

A judge may allow up to three dollars to the witness for each day of detention, paid after he has testified; payment of one-half the sum due at the time of the order may be directed on proof that the witness is destitute. 

Sec. 285. Challenge and Quashing of Subpoena. A subpoena is presumptively valid and can be challenged only by an affirmative demonstration of the impropriety or invalidity of the process (Manning v. Valente, 272 App. Div. 388, 72 N.Y.S. 2d 88; People v. Doe, 176 Misc. 943, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 

648). It has been held that a subpoena issued by a Grand 

Jury is presumed executed in good faith (Matter of 

Greenleaf, 176 Misc. 566, 28 N.Y.S. 2d 28). See discussion of subpoenas issued by the Grand Jury in the chapter of this work on "Grand Jury."

The attorney whose client has been served with a subpoena subject to attack must determine which procedural course is most desirable. The witness can choose to disregard the subpoena, await a contempt order, and then seek relief by habeas corpus (Matter of Turecamo Con tracting Co., 260 App. Div. 253, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 270). The court in that case indicated that such might be the best course of action since the denial of a motion to quash the subpoena would not be an appealable order (Application of LeFener v. Attorney General, 6 App. Div. 2d 998, 176 

N.Y.S. 2d 728). The Court of Appeals in Matter of Ryan, 306 N.Y. 11, held that there was no right to appeal from the denial of a motion to quash a subpoena issued out of the Court of General Sessions, because there was no jurisdic- 473

§ 

tion to hear such appeal in a criminal matter. The court indicated, however, that had the witness chosen to commence civil proceedings to quash the subpoena, his right of appeal would have been preserved. The court took jurisdiction of such an appeal in Inter-City Associates v. Doe, 308 

N.Y. 1044, holding that it was a civil application in the 

Supreme Court and not a motion in the criminal action. 

The Ryan case was discussed, and an appeal from a motion in the Supreme Court was sustained, in Norris v. Doe, 13 

Misc. 2d 998, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 426. The attack by way of a civil proceeding independent of the criminal action is preferable to the risky course of awaiting a contempt order. 

The least desirable method of attack is by making the motion to quash in the court of criminal jurisdiction in which the criminal action is pending and from which no appeal lies.

Disobedience of a subpoena is punishable as a criminal contempt, as provided in the Judiciary Law (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 619). The matter of contempt of a subpoena is treated in full in the chapter entitled "Immunity and Privilege Against Self-incrimination." 474
