The writ of habeas corpus is a sum mary direction by judicial authority, backed by all the sanctionary power of the court, directed to any person, official or not, who is detaining another person. It commands such person to produce the body of the person detained at a stated time and place, to explain the time, the cause and the claimed authority of the alleged detention, and to submit to and receive whatever the court or judge issuing the writ shall determine and direct. It is a common law remedy preserved by the Constitution (Constitution, N.Y., Art. I, sec. 4), and vested in the Supreme Court by 475

§ 

virtue of its general original jurisdiction (People ex rel. 

Tweed v. Liscomb, 60 N.Y. 559).

As a statutory civil proceeding, habeas corpus procedure is regulated by the Civil Practice Act. "A person imprisoned or restrained in his liberty, within the State, for any cause or upon any pretense, is entitled, except in one of the cases specified in the next section, to a writ of habeas corpus *** as prescribed in this article, for the purpose of inquiring into the cause of the imprisonment or restraint, and, in a case prescribed by law, of delivering him therefrom." (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1230.) Excepted from its availability by Section 1231 of the Civil Practice Act are persons who have "been committed or *** de- tained by virtue of a mandate issued by a court or judge of the United States, in cases where such courts or judges have exclusive jurisdiction under the laws of the United States or have acquired exclusive jurisdiction by the commencement of legal proceedings in such a court" and persons who have "been committed or *** detained by virtue of the final judgment or decree of a competent tribunal of civil or criminal jurisdiction." These exceptions are discussed in greater detail below. 

The only other statutory mention of the uses, or purposes, of the writ is contained in Civil Practice Act, section 1251, which prescribes the procedure upon the return of the writ, and which requires the prisoner's release "if no lawful cause for the imprisonment or restraint or for the continuance thereof is shown; whether the same was upon a commitment for an actual or supposed criminal matter or for some other cause." One of the leading New York cases treating habeas corpus was People ex rel. Tweed v. 

Liscomb, 60 N.Y. 559, where the court, in determining questions concerning the "office and effect of the writ of habeas corpus," discussed the history of the writ and its development in New York.

The form of the writ is prescribed in Civil Practice Act, section 1237, and the writ itself commands the person detaining the prisoner "to have the body of [prisoner] by 476

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 286 2 P you imprisoned and detained, as it is said, together with the time and cause of such imprisonment and detention *** before [the court, or a justice thereof] at * * * on ***" Thus, the writ performs a simple function. It commands that the prisoner be produced before a judge, or a court, at a certain date, at which time the lawfulness of the detention within certain limits as to the scope of the inquiry will be determined. The scope of the inquiry, in summary, has been delineated by the Court of Appeals in 

People ex rel. Carr v. Martin, 286 N.Y. 27: "An order or judgment of a court acting without jurisdiction is entirely void and a person imprisoned by virtue of such an order or judgment may obtain his release by habeas corpus proceedings. A final order or judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction, though erroneous, is not void if the court had jurisdiction of the person of the accused and jurisdiction to try the charge made against him." See also Matter of 

Siebold, 100 U.S. 371: "The only ground on which this court, or any court, without some special statute authorizing it, will give relief on habeas corpus to a prisoner under conviction and sentence of another court is the want of jurisdiction in such court over the person or the cause, or some other matter rendering its proceeding void." 

Compared with Certiorari. Civil Practice Act, section 

1230, pertains to both writs of certiorari and writs of habeas corpus. Before we examine the writ of certiorari, considered as an alternative to habeas corpus, we must be clear in our minds that we are not referring to the writ of certiorari to review, which was a writ for the review of official acts and determinations, and which has been abolished and merged into the consolidated "proceeding against a body or officer," commonly known as an "Article 

78 proceeding" (Civil Practice Act, secs. 1283 et seq.). The writ of certiorari to inquire into detention is a distinct remedy, dealt with in Article 77 of the Civil Practice Act (secs. 1230 et seq.), and was not abolished when the writ of certiorari to review was (People ex rel. Vallaro v. Travis, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 684). 477

§ 

Besides distinctions based on the effect of the use of one, rather than the other, of these writs, the writs are separate and distinct in their application and form. Civil Practice 

Act, section 1261, provides: "Where an application is made for a writ of habeas corpus, as prescribed in this article, and it appears to the court or judge upon the petition and the documents annexed thereto that the cause or offense for which the party is imprisoned or detained is not bailable, a writ of certiorari may be granted instead of a writ of habeas corpus." The writ of certiorari itself, in the form prescribed by Section 1238, directs only that the person detaining the prisoner produce, before the court, the record of the prisoner's detention, not the body of the prisoner himself. Thus, habeas corpus will be used for bailable offenses, certiorari for non-bailable offenses. "Under the writ of habeas corpus, the body of the person must be produced. *** If the offense is not bailable, there is no necessity of the presence of the detained prisoner upon the argument, and a writ of certiorari may be issued, which calls for precisely the same return from the custodian, but does not bring the body of the detained person. Under that writ, then, the same questions arise, the same facts appear for determination and the same limitation rests upon the power of the court as upon the writ of habeas corpus. (People ex rel. Taylor v. Seaman, 8 Misc. 152, 29 N.Y.S. 

329.) In People ex rel. Semenoff v. Nagler, 118 Misc. 476, 194 

N.Y.S. 602, it was said: "*** the writs of habeas corpus or certiorari provided for *** may be sued out in the alternative to meet the situation of the relator, and * * * in some cases each may be resorted to after the failure of the other to accomplish the desired end." 99 Sec. 287. History. In an article concerned mainly with the history of the writ of habeas corpus, Justice Simmons stated: "The scholars of the subject all seem to agree that the origin of the writ is lost in antiquity." (The Writ of 

Habeas Corpus, 41 A.B.A.J. 413 [May 1955].) The Magna 

Carta provided that no "free man shall be seized, or im- 478

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 288 4 

prisoned excepting by the legal judgment of his peers, or by the laws of the land." From that date on, various writs, some in the nature of habeas corpus, were developed, designed to secure the release or the production before a court of persons seized or detained. Some of these writs were the writs of "de homine replegiando," "mainprise," and "de odio et atia." Habeas corpus "was in use before

Magna Carta, and came to us as part of our inheritance from the mother country, and exists as a part of the common law of the State. It is intended and well adapted to effect the great object secured in England by Magna Carta, and made a part of our Constitution, that no person shall be deprived of his liberty 'without due process of law'." (People ex rel. Tweed v. Liscomb, 60 N.Y. 559.)

In 1679, in England, the Habeas Corpus Act was passed. 

This Act, according to Holdsworth, "made the Writ of 

Habeas Corpus ad subjiciendum the most effective weapon yet devised for the protection of the liberty of the subject, by providing both for a speedy judicial inquiry into the justice of any imprisonment on a criminal charge and for a speedy trial of prisoners remanded to await trial. It seems to have made *** the only form of writ used for the purpose of protecting liberty." (9 Holdsworth, History of

English Law, p. 118.) The uses of the writ and the practice were quite similar to that now prevailing. The writ was deemed so necessary for the protection of liberty that, when the United States Constitution was adopted, Article 1, section 9, was included to insure that "The privilege of the Writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in cases of Rebellion and Invasion the public safety may require it." Similar provisions are found in almost all 

State constitutions, including New York State Constitution, Article I, section 4. 

Sec. 288. Uses of the Writ. The uses of the writ of habeas corpus are so varied that a comprehensive discussion of all possible situations cannot possibly be included here. 

Therefore, the following discussion will limit itself to the 479

§ (a)  

most common and important situations which might arise in a criminal prosecution. The subsections will attempt to deal with situations as they arise, in chronological order, in such a prosecution, commencing with the use of the writ to challenge the validity of an arrest, and concluding with its use to secure the release of one imprisoned after a trial and conviction. Its use in civil matters, and in cases concerning infants, will not be treated here. 

Sec. 288(a). Habeas Corpus to Test Validity of Arrest. As stated in the chapter on "Arrest Without Warrant," if a defendant has been unlawfully arrested without a warrant, the court is not thereby deprived of jurisdiction over him as long as some other action has been taken which does give the court such jurisdiction (People v. Dennis, 132 Misc. 510, 230 N.Y.S. 510). "It is too late after an information has been duly filed in the proper court to review the commitment of a magistrate by a writ of habeas corpus." (People ex rel. Smith v. Barr, 223 App. Div. 167, 227 N.Y.S. 614.) In the Smith case, the court did indicate that if the defendant had not pleaded to the charge stated in the information, thereby waiving his objection to the illegality of the arrest, he might have been able to attack the method by which he was being detained by use of the writ of habeas corpus. However, as stated by the court in People ex rel. Mertig et al v. Johnston, 186 Misc. 1041, 62 N.Y.S. 2d 429: "While the 'foundation for the jurisdiction of the magistrate' over the subject matter is the information, jurisdiction over the person of the defendant is acquired when he is brought before the court and charged with the offense. *** It does not matter if he is arrested illegally." This holding follows from the principle that the writ may be used only to test the illegality of the detention at the time application for the writ is made. 

The fact that the detention was originally illegal will not warrant release, so long as the applicant at the time of the writ's return is being lawfully held. Prior to the filing of any information, one arrested without a warrant 480

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 288 (a) who has not waived his right to object to the manner of his arrest may test the validity of the arrest by habeas corpus. "In the case of an arrest without warrant, the duty is * * * to take the arrested party before some officer who can take such proof as may be offered, or if the circumstances will justify it, hold the suspected party for further examination. If this is not done with reasonable diligence, the party arrested can apply for a habeas corpus, calling on the officer to show cause why he is detained, and with the return to the writ, the rule is that where the arrest is upon suspicion, and without a warrant, proof must be given to show the suspicion well founded." (In re Henry, 29 How. Pr. 185.)

Where a warrant of arrest has been issued, and defendant has been arrested thereunder, "If the facts shown did not warrant an inference by the magistrate of the existence of probable cause to believe that the crime charged had been committed, he was without jurisdiction to cause the arrest of the relator and the latter was entitled to resort at once for his protection to the writ of habeas corpus. *** The arrest of the relator was an actual restraint of his person, and he was not obliged to await an examination before the magistrate. *** He could waive these proceedings. *** The question, always, must be whether the magistrate acquired jurisdiction to cause an arrest of the person and the court, upon the habeas corpus proceeding, will look back of his warrant and see if the facts stated in the depositions of the prosecutor and his witnesses support his warrant." (People ex rel. Perkins v. Moss, 187 

N.Y. 410.) Compare People v. Smith, 186 Misc. 48, 61 N.Y.S. 

2d 315, which indicated that where no motion to dismiss the information had been made, writs of habeas corpus would not be sustained.

In the Smith case, the question presented was the information's sufficiency, as a matter of law, in its allegation of facts and whether these facts constituted a crime. The language of the Smith case appears contrary to a long line of other cases in accord with the Moss case. In People ex 481

§ (b)  

rel. Coletti v. Morhead, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 78, for example, the court considered the complainant's preliminary examination to determine if sufficient cause appeared therein to justify his commitment to await the action of the Grand Jury. The court found such cause lacking and sustained the writ. In general, where the detention is under a magistrate's warrant of commitment ordered, the arrestee may seek in habeas corpus a determination of the existence of probable cause. This does not determine his guilt or innocence for conflicts in evidence will not be weighed in the habeas corpus proceeding (People ex rel. Jacobs v. Mc- 

Gurr, 39 Misc. 471, 80 N.Y.S. 171).

If there has been an unreasonable delay in arraigning the arrestee, such as proscribed by Section 165 of the Code, the defendant is being imprisoned unlawfully (Pass v. 

State, 196 Misc. 177, 192 N.Y.S. 2d 42), and a writ of habeas corpus will, apparently, lie. However, since an arraignment at any time makes the imprisonment lawful from that point on, this remedy would appear to be effective only to bring about such an arraignment. Sec. 288 (b). After Preliminary Examination. After a preliminary examination has been conducted by the magistrate, pursuant to the provisions of Section 207 of the Code, "if it appear, either that a crime has not been. committed, or that there is no sufficient cause to believe the defendant guilty thereof, the magistrate must order the defendant to be discharged." The defendant may raise the question of the sufficiency of the evidence adduced at the examination if he has been committed by the magistrate after such examination (People ex rel. Coletti v. 

Morhead, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 78; People ex rel. Agnello v. Mc- 

Donald, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 743). However, "It is too late after an information has been duly filed in the proper court to review the commitment of a magistrate by a writ of habeas corpus, the sufficiency of the evidence upon which a defendant was held by the committing magistrate is not then open for examination." (People ex rel. Smith v. Barr, 223 482

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 288 (c) 

App. Div. 168, 227 N.Y.S. 614; People ex rel. Reed v. Hendrickson, 160 Misc. 825, 290 N.Y.S. 101.)

If the warrant of commitment, issued under Section 214, which is the "sole authority for the confinement"—that is, if no information or other process has been filed-contains an erroneous description of the crime, or other serious error which in effect voids the commitment warrant, the prisoner may obtain his release from imprisonment by habeas corpus (People ex rel. Haney v. Warden, 207 N.Y. 

354; People ex rel. Allen v. Hagen, 170 N.Y. 46). However, minor errors and irregularities in the warrant will not be cause for such release. A warrant of commitment issued after conviction may be corrected at any time, for so long as there is a valid judgment of conviction to support the imprisonment, the warrant performs merely a ministerial function (Wright v. District Attorney, 85 N.Y.S. 2d 387).

As a valid warrant may be issued at any time, it is doubtful that habeas corpus proceedings will be of much value in securing the permanent release of a prisoner. This, perhaps, is the reason that the Haney and Allen cases, cited above, have not been cited in other cases to date. 

Sec. 288 (c). After Indictment or Information Filed. After the filing of an indictment or information, different principles apply concerning the scope of the review of the prior proceedings in habeas corpus. Thus, the Smith case, supra, might be reconciled with the other cases mentioned on this basis, although the language of that decision does not indicate such basis of reconciliation. "If every question regarding the sufficiency of an indictment were reviewable by habeas corpus, the practice as outlined in the Code of Criminal Procedure would soon be a nullity. There may be cases where the crime charged or the facts stated are so clearly beyond the jurisdiction of the court or so manifestly innocent as to justify the resort to habeas corpus." (People ex rel. Childs v. Knott, 228 N.Y. 608.) "The basis of the magistrate's jurisdiction, however, is the information *** and when the information is insufficient, it can- 483

§ (c)  

not confer jurisdiction." (People ex rel. Prudhomme v. 

Superintendent, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 563.) The Prudhomme decision ruled that a plea of guilty did not waive the failure of the information to allege facts sufficient to constitute a crime. The court stated: "Ordinarily, the writ will not be granted where there is a remedy by appeal, but there is an exception where the facts upon which the writ is sought are unquestioned, and where it appears by these facts that a relator is improperly deprived of his liberty." Thus, where, as in the Prudhomme case, there was a guilty plea, only one basis exists for the court's jurisdiction to impose sentence the information-and the court therefore considered its sufficiency. Compare People ex rel. Timmons v. 

Jackson, 285 App. Div. 1202, 140 N.Y.S. 2d 514, where nine years after conviction upon a guilty plea, the relator sought to attack his conviction on the ground that the indictment was based upon perjured testimony, and that the value of the property he allegedly had stolen was less than the amount required to constitute a felony. The court refused to allow the writ.

It has been held that, generally, "where an indictment is valid upon its face, the remedy of the person indicted is in the court where the indictment was found. *** the sufficiency of the indictment and the sufficiency of the evidence before the Grand Jury to uphold it may not be inquired into in a proceeding upon a writ of habeas corpus." 

(People ex rel. Jannicky v. Warden, 231 App. Div. 131, 246 

N.Y.S. 194.) "But where *** the facts before the court cannot be materially changed, qualified, or explained, it has been held, in rare and exceptional cases, that the writ may be resorted to *** even though the question might be raised by a motion in arrest of judgment, this could be only after trial and conviction. *** But if, in the meantime, the accused is unlawfully restrained of his liberty, and the evidence upon this is undisputed, why should he not have resort to this summary remedy?" (People ex rel. Bullock v. Hayes, 166 App. Div. 507, 151 N.Y.S. 1075.) In People ex rel. Lichtenstein v. Langan, 196 N.Y. 260, a writ of 484

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 289 habeas corpus was sustained on the ground that the indictment did not charge a crime. The indictment charged defendant with "oral betting on horses"; the only crime proscribed by statute was operating a gambling establishment. Failure to raise objection to the sufficiency of an indictment until late in the proceedings may also constitute a waiver (People v. Weichers 179 N.Y. 459). 

Sec. 289. Right to a Speedy Trial. "The contention that the prisoner did not have a speedy trial is a matter which must be raised at the trial and may not be raised years after the trial by writ of habeas corpus." (People ex rel. Lee v. Jackson, 285 App. Div. 33, 135 N.Y.S. 2d 345, affirmed without opinion, 309 N.Y. 676.) In the opinion below (131 N.Y.S. 

2d 278), the court cited Matter of Klein, 17 Misc. 107, 39

N.Y.S. 873, where a writ of habeas corpus had been sustained before the relator had been brought to trial. As discussed elsewhere, the right to a speedy trial may be waived (People v. White, 2 N.Y. 2d 219). However, absent a waiver, the Lee case would not preclude resort to the writ to secure a prisoner's release while he is being held for trial. 

In People ex rel. Morgan v. Jackson, 3 App. Div. 2d 48, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 365, dismissal of a writ was sustained where, though relator had objected to the lack of a speedy trial at his trial, he had not appealed from the judgment of conviction. The court stated: "It would seem that he is in no better legal position, so far as habeas corpus is concerned, than if he failed to raise the issue at all." Thus, the writ should be applied for prior to the trial to avoid a denial based on the above cases; waiting until after trial, even if proper objections are made during trial, may raise grave doubts concerning issuance of the writ under the above cases, The Klein case has not been cited recently and, in fact, was criticized in People ex rel. Burke v. McLaughlin, 77 Misc. 13, 136 N.Y.S. 172. However, it has not been overruled, and no cases have declined to follow it on the same facts. In People ex rel. McManus v. Warden, 226 App. Div. 485

§ 

364, 235 N.Y.S. 112, an unreasonable delay in the setting of a trial date was considered a valid basis for sustaining the writ, even where the relator had not applied for bail. 

Sec. 290. Constitutionality of Statute Under Which De fendant Held. A defendant detained to await trial upon a charge of violating a statute, may attack its constitutionality in advance of trial by writ of habeas corpus (People ex rel. Moskowitz v. Jenkins, 202 N.Y. 53). The constitutionality of municipal ordinances and regulations may also be thus attacked. "Habeas corpus may be resorted to in advance of trial and judgment to resolve the question." 

(People ex rel. Pinello v. Leadbitter, 194 Misc. 481, 85 N.Y. 

S. 2d 287, affirmed 275 App. Div. 864, 89 N.Y.S. 2d 924 affirmed, 301 N.Y.695.) 

Sec. 291. Amount of, or Admission to, Bail. It has been held that "an order denying bail is non-appealable (Code of 

Crim. Proc., secs. 517, 566, supra) and so any attack on such a denial of bail must be by other means. The method is by resort to the prisoner's separate and different right to test, by the ancient remedy of habeas corpus, the legality of the denial of bail, as to whether or not the denying court has abused its discretion by denying bail without reason or for reasons insufficient in law. *** It does not follow ***that the court which entertained the writ could exercise an independent discretion as to bail. *** Being no more than a second application to a different judge for the fixation of bail in a case where the first judge had, on the same facts, used his discretionary powers to deny bail, the second application was properly denied." (People ex rel. Shapiro v. Keeper, 290 N.Y.393.)

In People ex rel. Lobell v. McDonnell, 296 N.Y. 109, the 

Court of Appeals stated: "After relator had been indicted *** and had pleaded not guilty, his bail was fixed by the

County Court at $250,000. Thereupon he sued out the writ of habeas corpus, in the Appellate Division, to get the bail reduced. The Appellate Division unanimously dismissed 486

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 292 the writ, and relator appeals here as of right.

that the appeal is properly here." The Court of Appeals reversed the order of the Appellate Division, and remanded the proceeding for a reduction of the bail. 

Section 22 (8) of the Code gives the Supreme Court jurisdiction to let to bail persons committed before indictment, and Section 555 gives the same power, after conviction and judgment (People v. Wirtschafter, 305 N.Y. 

515). Under Section 422, a court may, after a defendant's appearance for trial, commit him pending the trial and judgment or further order of the court. The discretion to order such a commitment "is absolute and may not be interfered with by this court. *** It therefore follows *** a writ of habeas corpus does not lie." (People v. Koson, 6 Misc. 2d 960, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 344.) However, a revocation of bail prior to defendant's going to trial, not being within the purview of the above section, is subject to attack by writ of habeas corpus (People ex rel. Rupoli v. Mc Donnell, 277 App. Div. 74, 98 N.Y.S. 2d 182). In summary, in the usual case, "The determination of the question of whether or not the prisoner should be admitted to bail is the prerogative of the court having jurisdiction of the matter. * While his determination may be reviewed [by habeas corpus] it cannot be upset unless there is a showing that he acted arbitrarily, improvidently, or abused his discretion ***." (People ex rel. Wasmund v. McCloskey, 16 Misc. 

2d 659, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 624.) 

Sec. 292. Defects in Grand Jury Procedure. If the Grand 

Jury did not have jurisdiction to indict for the crime charged, one imprisoned by virtue of such indictment may obtain his release by writ of habeas corpus (People ex rel. 

Morrison v. Pollack, 264 App. Div. 92, 34 N.Y.S. 2d 841, affirmed 289 N.Y. 600). And it has been indicated that habeas corpus would lie to secure release of one imprisoned under an indictment unlawfully re-submitted to the Grand 

Jury (People v. Barr, 140 Misc. 422, 251 N.Y.S. 116). Minor defects in the Grand Jury's procedure are not, usually, 487

§ 

sufficient grounds for relief in habeas corpus.

Thus, in 

People ex rel. Hamway v. Truesdell, 261 App. Div. 824, 24 

N.Y.S. 2d 392, the relator's allegation that an unauthorized person had been present during a session of the Grand Jury, while the charge embraced in the indictment was under consideration, was held insufficient to warrant the granting of the writ. The court stated: "If, in fact, there was an unauthorized person present during the session of the Grand Jury while the charge embraced in the indictment was under consideration, the relator is relegated to the remedy afforded pursuant to Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure."

In People ex rel. Van Slyke v. Wallach, 6 App. Div. 2d 

958, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 821, where, in dismissing a writ of habeas corpus on relator's claims that the Grand Jury was illegally drawn and constituted and that he had been denied opportunity to challenge the Grand Jury, the court stated: "As to the first complaint, the record shows that the Grand Jury was properly drawn. *** As to the second complaint the challenge to an individual grand juror must be made before the Grand Jury is sworn or in any event before the indictment is found. The relator * * * was represented by counsel *** at all times. *** No motion was made to dismiss the indictment, no motion in arrest of judgment. There was no appeal from the judgment. No question was timely raised as to the validity of the indictment. No contention is made that any grand juror was disqualified and there is no showing of any possible prejudice therefrom." Whether the above language indicates that affirmative replies to the questions posed would warrant granting of the writ is not stated. Certainly there is language in several cases indicating that a writ would not lie. "By a writ of habeas corpus the relator seeks * * * to review virtually all the proceedings heretofore had from the time the Grand Jury convened. This, of course, the court may not do. It is forbidden upon the return of such a writ to inquire into the legality or justice of any mandate, decree or formal order of a competent tribunal. * * * The 

1 488

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 293 purpose of a writ of habeas corpus is to determine the right of the custodian to hold the petitioner in custody; it is not available as a revisionary remedy for the correction of errors of law or fact." (People ex rel. Seaquist v. Mederer, 33 N.Y.S. 2d 114.) The reasoning of these decisions is that the disqualification of grand jurors does not destroy the jurisdiction of the court, if the court has jurisdiction of the crime and of the person of the defendant. An indictment returned by an illegally drawn Grand Jury may be voidable; it is not void. The court in which the indictment is returned has jurisdiction to decide questions relating to the organization of the Grand Jury, and if objection to these decisions is properly taken they may be reviewed on appeal. 

See People ex rel. Mizell v. Wilson, 262 App. Div. 1057, 30 N.Y.S. 2d 293, where the court held habeas corpus not a proper remedy for one imprisoned after conviction who sought to vitiate the proceedings by claiming that members of his race had been systematically excluded from the Grand Jury which indicted him. However, see the discussion, infra, concerning the use of a Federal habeas corpus writ to attack the validity of the constitution of a Grand 

Jury. The leading case of Pierre v. Louisiana, 306 U.S. 354, 83 L. Ed. 757, involved an attack upon a conviction where the indictment had been returned by an illegally-selected Grand Jury. While habeas corpus was not the method used there to raise the question, it appears likely that such means may be so utilized. Certainly, the right to an impartial Grand Jury is one of the rights guaranteed by the 

Federal Constitution. 

Sec. 293. Extradition. The use of the writ of habeas corpus in extradition proceedings is also discussed in the chapter entitled "Extradition." Habeas corpus is the proper remedy to obtain the release of a prisoner detained under an arrest on an extradition warrant, to test "the foundation upon which the warrant rests for its author- 489

§ 

ity." (People ex rel. Luciano v. Morhead, 68 N.Y.S. 2d 769.) 

In People ex rel. Goldfarb v. Cullen, 59 N.Y.S. 2d 745, it was stated: "The relator is sought to be extradited on the basis of a warrant issued by the Governor of the State of New York, predicated upon the warrant of the Governor of the State of Massachusetts, to answer to an indictment. *** He has sued out a writ of habeas corpus to test the legality of the proceedings. *** In this proceeding, the following questions may be determined: (1) Whether the papers upon which the warrant was issued by the Governor of the asylum State are sufficient. (2) Whether the indictment charges a crime under the laws of the State seeking extradition. (3) Whether a crime was committed in the demanding State under its laws. (4) Whether the accused was in the demanding State on the day when the crime is alleged to have been committed. (5) The identity of the alleged fugitive. (6) Whether the person sought to be extradited is a fugitive from justice." "It is open to the relator to show by conclusive evidence that he was not in [the demanding State] *** at the time the crime was, if ever, committed." (People ex rel. Gottschalk v. Brown, 237 N.Y. 483.) For a more complete discussion of the questions that may be raised in a habeas corpus proceeding to test the merits of the extradition proceeding, including cases where it is held not necessary to show that the demanded person was in the demanding State when the crime was committed, see chapter on "Extraditions." Habeas corpus is the normal method of testing extradition proceedings. 

Sec. 294. Federal Habeas Corpus. The possible utilization of the Federal Courts to obtain the release of one imprisoned, after trial in a State court should not be overlooked. However, this area belongs to the field of Federal criminal procedure and will not be discussed in detail herein. In general, Title 28, section 2241 (c) (3) of the

United States Code vests power in Federal courts and 490

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 295 judges, to issue writs of habeas corpus "within their respective jurisdictions." However, where a prisoner claims that one of his Federally-granted constitutional rights is being violated by a State, resulting in his detention by the State, and where the procedural requisites concerning the granting of such writs have been complied with, the Federal courts will grant writs of habeas corpus.

The alleged defect need not be lack of jurisdiction in the State court, although several earlier cases limited their inquiries to such issues (See, e.g., Knewal v. Egan, 268 

U.S. 442). Thus, the use of coerced confessions (Leyra v. 

Denno, 347 U.S. 556); the use of a jury panel from which certain groups were systematically excluded (Brown v. 

Allen, 344 U.S. 443); the conducting of the trial in an atmosphere of mob domination (Moore v. Dempsey, 261 

U.S. 86); the denial of appellate review of the conviction (David v. Cook, 340 U.S. 206); and the denial of counsel (Wade v. Mayo, 334 U.S. 672), have all been held bases for the granting of such writs by Federal courts.

Prior to petitioning for the issuance of a writ of habeas corpus in the Federal courts, absent unusual extenuating circumstances, the applicant must first pursue, to their conclusion, appropriate State remedies available to him so that he has obtained, so far as possible, an adjudication of the merits of his claim by the highest State courts (28 U.S.C. sec. 2254). The applicant should then attempt to obtain a review of the highest adverse State court decision by the United States Supreme Court. An excellent discussion, with a summary of almost every case in which such a writ has been granted, is contained in an article in 108 

U. of Pa. Law. Rev., p. 461 (Feb. 1960), Reitz, "Federal

Habeas Corpus, Postconviction Remedy for State Pris oners." Other extended discussions are available (97 L. 

Ed. 543; 55 Col. L. Rev. 196; 13 U. of Chi. L. Rev. 266). 

Sec. 295. Former Jeopardy. If a prisoner has once before been placed in jeopardy for an offense, and is subsequently arrested or indicted for trial upon the same offense, he 491

$

may have recourse to the writ of habeas corpus. "Where the defendant, charged with crime, has once been placed in jeopardy, he may not again be tried for the same offense. Of his right to this defense upon his second trial he may not be deprived. *** 'If there is no authority to again place the defendant upon trial upon the indictment, there is no right to restrain him of his liberty.' (People ex rel. Stabile v. Warden, 202 N.Y. 138.) If, thereafter, the defendant is unlawfully in custody with no right to appeal from the mandate under which he is confined, he may, if he so chooses, seek a remedy by means of the writ of habeas corpus. There is no reason why, entitled to his freedom, he should be imprisoned, until his case is again moved for trial." (People ex rel. Brinkman v. Barr, 248 N.Y. 126.) "There is ample authority to the effect that the writ may be employed to test the legality of the detention of a defendant held for retrial after he has once been placed in jeopardy for the same offense. *** ** Upon such a writ the court has not the power to review the legality of the decision on the procedure of a court of competent jurisdiction. *** The court does have the right, however, in such a proceeding, to inquire into the power of jurisdiction of the court before whom the relator appears, to proceed further and pronounce the judgment." (People ex rel. 

Hunt v. Warden, 201 Misc. 406, 107 N.Y.S. 2d 136.) For further discussion, see chapter entitled "Double Jeopardy." 

Sec. 296. Illegal or Erroneous Sentence. Ministerial errors, irregularities, or defects in the sentence of a prisoner do not render a sentence void. Consequently they are not subject to attack by writ of habeas corpus (People ex rel. La 

Pierre v. Heacox, 231 App. Div. 652, 247 N.Y.S. 424). "Though a defendant fails to appeal from a judgment of conviction embodying an incorrect sentence, he may raise the question later by habeas corpus proceedings *** or by an application for a re-sentence in the trial court. *** In the case at bar, however, defendant sought a re-sentence, 492

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 296 not because of any claim of illegality in the sentence, but to review the conduct of the proceeding before sentence was imposed. An examination of such proceeding could be obtained only by an appeal from the judgment of conviction." (People v. Mellon, 261 App. Div. 400, 25 N.Y.S. 2d 650.) 

The courts will not sustain a writ of habeas corpus because of the alleged excessive severity of a sentence. "While there were circumstances which might make it appear that the sentence which [relator] received was somewhat severe, that was a matter wholly within the jurisdiction of the court fixing the sentence and the act being jurisdictionally correct, the court should not interfere with its exercise." (People ex rel. Ling v. Morhous, 40 N.Y. 

S. 2d 49.) If the prisoner has been sentenced for a period in excess of the maximum allowable under the statute, and if the portion of time of the sentence which was validly imposed has expired, the prisoner may obtain his release by means of a writ of habeas corpus (People ex rel. Tweed v. Liscomb, 60 N.Y. 559; People ex rel. Brooks v. Warden, 175 Misc. 663, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 931). But an application prior to the expiration of the validly imposed portion of the sentence will not be granted, for at the time of the application the prisoner will not be entitled to his release 

(People ex rel. Young v. Martin, 270 App. Div. 1069, 63 

N.Y.S. 2d 672; People ex rel. Fishwercher v. Snyders, 183 

Misc. 549, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 850). "The legality of a sentence may be tested in a habeas corpus proceeding. When an order in such a proceeding directs the sentencing court to resentence the relator, such court is under the necessity of resentencing him within a reasonable time." (People ex rel. Prosser v. Martin, 306 N.Y. 710.)

In People ex rel. Tweed v. Liscomb, 60 N.Y. 559, the court stated: "A party held only by virtue of judgments thus pronounced, and therefore void for want of jurisdiction, or by reason of the excess of jurisdiction, is not put to his writ of error but may be released by habeas corpus.'

Thus, in People ex rel. Hauser v. McDonnell, 99 N.Y.S. 2d 

493

§ 

501, the court sustained a writ of habeas corpus, where the sentencing judge's remarks indicated his belief that the defendant could not be rehabilitated, while the sentence imposed to the New York City Penitentiary-could not be lawfully imposed, under Correction Law, section 203, except for rehabilitation. The court stated: "Upon finding that the defendant was not subject to rehabilitation the court's power was limited to imposing sentence under the provisions of the Penal Law, section 1937, which provides for a maximum term of one year. The defendant has been confined in excess of that maximum and his further detention is illegal." See also People ex rel. Mummiami v. Lewis, 258 App. Div. 643, 17 N.Y.S. 2d 748, where the court sustained a writ of habeas corpus on the ground that the record did not disclose that the defendant had been armed when he committed the crime, thus casting doubt upon the court's power to impose sentence under a provision of the Penal Law concerning armed crimes. People ex rel. Savercool v. Jackson, 196 Misc. 833, 96 N.Y.S. 2d 352, sustained a writ of habeas corpus where there was no allegation of intent in the indictment to which defendant had pleaded guilty, and where the sentencing judge had, apparently, imposed a sentence based upon his belief that the crime involved was committed with intent.

In summary, the language of the Court of Appeals, in 

People ex rel. Carollo v. Brophy, 294 N.Y. 540, may be quoted: "We do not agree with the Attorney-General's assertion that the relator may not invoke the writ of habeas corpus to challenge a sentence, which, according to relator's claim, exceeds statutory limits. If the relator's sentence is for a term longer than authorized by statute it is not a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction even though the sentencing court had power to try the offense and fix the penalty."

Sec. 297. Review of Parole Proceedings. Errors in the computation of the time of imprisonment of parolees upon revocation of parole are not reviewable in habeas corpus 494

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 298 proceedings until an absolute right to release accrues (People ex rel. Jackson v. Morhous, 286 App. Div. 939, 143 

N.Y.S. 2d 280; N.Y. State Department of Correction v. 

Satterfield, 3 App. Div. 2d 629, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 109). "The action of the Parole Board, in the exercise of its discretion, revoking a prisoner's parole and ordering him returned to prison, is not subject to review by habeas corpus so long as the Board does not act in contravention of law. habeas corpus proceeding the petitioner must assume the burden of proof of overcoming the presumption of legality and regularity." (People ex rel. Mahon v. Warden, 144 

N.Y.S. 2d 837.) Of course, where the maximum time prescribed by statute within which the Parole Board may cause the detention has passed, and the relator is still imprisoned, habeas corpus is proper (People ex rel. White v. Commissioner, 193 N.Y.S. 385, reversed other grounds, 190 N.Y.S. 471). In People ex rel. Stumpf v. Graig, 79 Misc. 

98, 140 N.Y.S. 652, the parolee had been discharged, and then arrested, upon a warrant issued upon an information filed by a Parole Officer charging parole violation without alleging facts constituting such violation. The parolee applied for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. The court held that there should, at least, have been an examination upon the information before the warrant was issued, and that the information was lacking in the essential facts.

Sec. 298. Restrictions Upon Issuance of the Writ. In Mat ter of Morhous v. New York Supreme Court, 293 N.Y. 131, the Court of Appeals noted that in the Federal courts the use of habeas corpus had been extended beyond "the bare legal review that seems to have been the limit of the common law practice," and stated: "No such extension has been made by Constitution, statute or judicial decision in this State." The court went on to state that such an extension might be made by the courts of this State, "if a case should arise where a person restrained of his liberty under a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction alleges in 495

§ 

his petition facts sufficient, if established, to show [failure] *** to satisfy the requirements of due process on grounds for which the State has provided no other corrective procedure. *** An appeal to a higher court is ordinarily the appropriate corrective process for error at the trial and appearing in the record; a motion to vacate the judgment is ordinarily the appropriate corrective process for defects not appearing on the record or where for any other reason an appeal would not furnish a remedy. These proceedings are open to an accused in this State. For those reasons this court denied to relator permission to appeal from the order dismissing the writ and thereafter dismissed the appeal." 

See also, People ex rel. Sedlak v. Foster, 299 N.Y. 291, dismissing a writ of habeas corpus where the petitioner claimed denial of his right to counsel; the dismissal, apparently, was on the ground that coram nobis was the proper and exclusive remedy available.

In People ex rel. Stevens v. Morhous, 269 App. Div. 461, the court dismissed the writ of habeas corpus, after noting defendant's failure to take appropriate steps to remedy defects by other means, and stated: "The test is not whether he has an available remedy now, but rather whether corrective process was available before. Unquestionably, the Court of General Sessions had jurisdiction of respondent and of the offenses with which he was charged. It was therefore competent to pronounce judgment. Its judgment cannot now be set aside, more than fifteen years later, by another court without appellate jurisdiction, and by way of habeas corpus, regardless of respondent's allegations that his constitutional rights were invaded, or of any proof in support thereof, in view of the fact that respondent failed to avail himself of other and appropriate process." The statements quoted above are but a few of many wherein courts have indicated that habeas corpus will not lie, where other corrective process is available, and where the defects alleged are other than jurisdictional. However, since nonjurisdictional defects will usually not warrant the granting of the writ in any 496

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 299 event, it is doubtful whether the statements mean anything more than the writ will not be granted in other than the proper cases. See People ex rel. Stabile v. Warden, 202

N.Y. 138 (habeas corpus granted where motion in arrest of judgment available); People ex rel. McManus v. 

Warden, 226 App. Div. 364, 235 N.Y.S. 112 (motion to dismiss available); People v. Brooks, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 516 (appeal available).

Habeas corpus is not available where the detention is voluntary (People ex rel. Posner v. Vollmer, 2 Misc. 2d 575, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 468). A detention is considered voluntary for this purpose if the prisoner can obtain his release by payment of a fine (People ex rel. Schildhaus v. Dros, 178 

N.Y.S. 2d 656). 

Sec. 299. Procedure. "Applications for the writ must be made by a written petition, signed either by the person for whose relief it is intended or by some person in his behalf." (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1232.) The procedure governing the granting of writs of habeas corpus is found in the Civil Practice Act, rather than in the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the remedy is essentially civil in nature. Applications for the writ may be directed to a Special Term of the Supreme Court within the judicial district in which the prisoner is held, or to any Justice of the Supreme Court within the State, or to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court within the department wherein the prisoner is held, or to an officer within the county in which the prisoner is held who is authorized to perform the duties of a Justice of the Supreme Court at chambers (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1232). If such an officer is unavailable, or if no such judge within the proper county will grant the writ, the last cited section allows application to be made to such judges in the adjoining county upon proof of the unavailability of the judge within the county in which the prisoner is held.

The contents of the petition are prescribed by Section 1234, which also requires verification of the petition. It 497

§ 

must state, in substance, the name of the prisoner; the fact and place of his imprisonment; the name or description of the person detaining him; the cause of the imprisonment, showing also that it is not for a purpose excepted by Section 1231; the manner in which the imprisonment is illegal; whether any previous applications for the writ have been made and, if such prior applications have been made, a description of the proceedings had and a statement concerning any new facts adduced since the prior hearing; a description of any appeals from decrees of imprisonment which may have been taken, and the writ desired-habeas corpus or certiorari. A copy of the mandate, by virtue of which the prisoner is detained, must be annexed, or if no copies are available, a statement of the unavailability and the reasons therefor should be included in the petition.

After the petition has been presented to the court or judge, that court or judge "must grant it without delay *** unless it appears from the petition itself or the documents annexed thereto that the petitioner is prohibited by law from presenting the writ." (Civil Practice Act, sec. 

1235.) The act of issuing the writ is ministerial, not judicial (Nash v. People, 36 N.Y. 607). The writ must be issued under the seal of the court awarding it, and it is issued in the name of the People upon the relation of the petitioner or, if issued pursuant to a request of the Attorney General or the District Attorney, it is issued in the name of the People alone (Civil Practice Act. Sec. 1260). 

Absence of a seal is not a fatal defect and may be cured by an amendment of the writ (People ex rel. Herkimer & 

McKaw v. Assessors, 6 Civ. Proc. 297). Defects in form will also not void the writ (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1246).

The writ may be made returnable at any time except on Sunday before any person authorized to grant it in the county of imprisonment, if it was issued in another county. 

If the writ is directed to an agent, director, etc., of a State institution, the writ must be made returnable in the county of imprisonment (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1239). The writ 498

HABEAS CORPUS 

§ 299 may be served at any time, including Sunday (Civil Practice Act sec. 1242), and after service the person to whom the writ was directed, and upon whom the writ was served, must file an answering pleading, called a "return" to the petition. The return will describe the justification for the detention; and the contents thereof are prescribed, generally, by Section 1245 of the Civil Practice Act. It has been held that a return to the writ is essential to the jurisdiction of the court and, therefore, a court may not proceed further until the return has been made (People ex rel. 

Gamaldi v. Warden, 160 App. Div. 480, 145 N.Y.S. 1064).

However, the return may be filed nunc pro tunc (Sacket v. 

Billinghurst, 7 Cow. 520), and if the person to whom the writ was directed fails to make a return, Sections 1248 through 1250 give the court power to imprison that person until a return is made. In Mellon v. Kinkley, 201 App. Div. 

619, 194 N.Y.S. 732, no return was made but the court held that there was, in effect, a demurrer to the petition. The court treated the petition as if it had been demurred to, accepted its allegations as true, but nonetheless dismissed the writ. In People ex rel. Jenkins v. Kuhne, 57 Misc. 30, 107 N.Y.S. 1020, affirmed 127 App. Div. 907, 111 N.Y.S. 

1136, the court indicated that objections to the manner of service of the writ, or to other similar defects which in effect voided the writ, should be raised by a motion to quash the writ. 

Notice must be given the District Attorney of the county from which the petitioner was committed, and also to the District Attorney of the county in which the prisoner is detained (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1258, subd. 4). Absent such notice, the court may not order the relator discharged (People ex rel. Carollo v. Brophy, 294 N.Y. 540). Upon the return of the writ, the person to whom it was directed must produce the prisoner unless, by reason of sickness, etc., such production would endanger the prisoner's life. 

The facts stated in the return, made by the person detaining the prisoner, are deemed true unless controverted by the relator in a reply (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1259; People 499

$ 

Fi ex rel. Moore v. Holmes, 151 App. Div. 257, 135 N.Y.S. 467).

Facts alleged in such a reply, however, are not deemed true, even if not denied (People ex rel. Moore v. Holmes, supra). 

Upon the return day the court or judge conducts a hearing and an immediate examination into the case (Civil 

Practice Act, sec. 1251). Under Section 1257, the court or judge before whom the prisoner is brought may make such orders concerning the prisoner's detention as the circumstances require. 

After the hearing, and a determination of the issues, a final order will be made by the court holding the hearing (Civil Practice Act, sec. 1268). This order may require the discharge of the prisoner absolutely or on bail, or it may remand him to custody. If the People wish to appeal from an order discharging the prisoner, the prisoner must, nonetheless, be discharged pending the appeal (People ex rel. Sabatino v. Jennings, 246 N.Y. 258). Section 1269 provides, in effect, that a discharge is merely from custody, not from the penalty; it therefore does not constitute an acquittal, nor does it bar a subsequent indictment or imprisonment after another trial (Sutton v. Butler, 74 

Misc. 251, 133 N.Y.S. 936, affirmed, 151 App. Div. 894, 135 

N.Y.S. 1145). 

Appeals from orders in habeas corpus proceedings are, generally, permitted by C.P.A., sec. 1274. See however, People ex rel. Curtis v. Kidney, 225 N.Y. 299, indicating that an appeal as of right to the Court of Appeals does not exist in such cases where the decision of the Appellate 

Division is unanimous. See, for discussion of appeals in habeas corpus, the chapter of this work entitled "Appeals." 500

CHAPTER 25 EXAMINATION OF WITNESSES, CONDITIONALLY Sec. 300. Nature of Examination Sec. 301. Conditional Examination by the People Sec. 302. The Application Sec. 303. The Order Sec. 304. The Examination and Deposition Sec. 305. Compelling Attendance and Testimony of Witnesses Sec. 306. Reading in Evidence Sec. 307. Suppression or Exclusion of Deposition Sec. 308. Objections to Questions and Answers PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

Although Section 620 of the Code prescribes this right only for the defendant, under Section 219, by incorporation by reference, the application is made available to the People as well. This examination is seldom employed by either side. 

Since the interrogation is an open one, in the sense that the District Attorney has the right to be present, and put his own questions to the witness, counsel may well forego this examination if the testimony to be elicited is only cumulative. But if the person sought to be examined is the only witness, or is in possession of information vital to the defense, the opportunity to hold this examination should not be overlooked. 

Sec. 300. Nature of Examination. Pre-trial examinations are made available in criminal cases by the Code, but under more restrictions and in far more limited circumstances than those in civil actions under the Civil Practice Act and the Rules of Civil Practice. They are, consequently, much less frequent than in the examination-ridden civil practice, 501

§ 

99 and judicial authorities construing the applicable statutes are few and far between. It often becomes necessary, therefore, both for us when we seek to examine the import of the statutes controlling our criminal practice, and for the courts when they seek to interpret and apply them, to rely on analogous authorities in civil practice. Thus, for example, Judge Bronson in Barron v. People, 1 N.Y. 386, 391: "I am of opinion that the rule which governs the reading of depositions taken in civil cases should be applied to depositions taken under the New York criminal statutes.'

Our criminal procedure knows no pre-trial examination of parties, in the manner of the civil practice. It is obvious why, with constitutional protection against self-incrimination and other long-cherished rights of persons accused of crime, this should be so. Nevertheless, the protection of the defendant's rights and the tradition of making available to him the means to produce and examine his witnesses and establish his defense dictate provisions whereby he can produce available testimony of persons who cannot attend, and can not be compelled to attend, at the trial. 

Accordingly, there have been established two forms of pre-trial examination, the first of which we know as conditional examination of witnesses. This is provided for in 

Title 12, Chapter III of the Code (Sections 620-635), and is roughly analogous, although differing in specification, to the examination under Section 288 of the Civil Practice 

Act "of any other person, which is material and necessary, where such person is about to depart from the state, or is without the state *** or is so sick or infirm as to afford reasonable grounds of belief that he will not be able to attend the trial *** " The likelihood of unavailability of the witness at the trial is the basic rationale of the remedy, and all the specifications of what must be shown to obtain it are made with that in mind. But the condition from which it gets its name, and on which the examination is based and its product permitted to be read in evidence, is that this unavailability continue and be proved to exist as of the time of the 502

CONDITIONAL EXAMINATION 

§ 301 trial. It is clearly a substitute for examination of the witness in open court on the trial, but only if that cannot be had.

Sec. 301. Conditional Examination by the People. Condi tional examination is made available to the People, as well. 

Section 219 of the Code assimilates the practice thereon to that prevailing on defendants' examinations, providing that the prosecution may examine "in the manner and with the effect provided by title twelve chapter three of this Code, for taking examination of witnesses conditionally on behalf of the defendant. 

In Matter of Fitzgerald, 182 Misc. 684, 49 N.Y.S. 2d 570, the constitutionality of this provision was questioned on an application for a writ of prohibition. It was there claimed that the right of confrontation of witnesses granted in the 1938 Constitution (Article 1, Section 6) was impugned by the provision authorizing the People's examination of witnesses before trial and using the deposition on the trial. In this connection, it should be remembered that the right of confrontation had not, prior to 1939, been constitutionally granted or guaranteed in New York State, but had only been recognized in the Civil Rights 

Law (People v. Reese, 258 N.Y. 89).

The court, however, at page 685 of 182 Misc., page 571 of 49 N.Y.S. 2d, held otherwise, by reason of "the absence of debate in the Constitutional Convention or report by any committee thereof, and in view of the long established right to such pretrial examinations. (People v. Fish, 125 

N.Y. 136.)"

The holding of the Court of Appeals in People v. Ni sonoff, 293 N.Y. 597, sustains this view despite the surface plausibility of the argument advanced in the Fitzgerald case. In the Nisonoff case, the same Bill of Rights, newly added to the Constitution of 1938 after years of embodiment only in the Civil Rights Law, was advanced as requiring the reversal of a manslaughter conviction because it was based on the admission in evidence of autopsy find- 503

§ 

ings by the Assistant Medical Examiner. The defendants contended that the right of confrontation of witnesses now embodied in the Constitution precluded this. Affirming the judgment of conviction, the Court stated, at page 601 of 293 N.Y.: "The right of confrontation imports and confers the right of cross-examination. When that right was added to our State Constitution, there was eliminated the possibility of its deprivation by legislative act. When we interpret that addition to the Constitution, we must do so in the light of the law as it existed at the time of the change. 

Any exceptions to the right of confrontation or crossexamination existing prior to the adoption of the State constitutional provision and not contrary to its spirit, must be respected. (Mattox v. United States, 156 U.S. 237, 243.)"

It would thus seem that the recognition of this procedure prior to the constitutional change, despite the fact that "the right of the accused to be confronted with the witnesses against him has always been a part of the Bill of 

Rights" (People v. Corey, 157 N.Y. 332, 347) contained in the Civil Rights Law (See People v. Sugarman, 248 N.Y. 

255), requires its recognition under the Constitution as it now stands.

Section 219 specifically preserves the defendant's right of confrontation and cross examination on the examination itself, providing: "* * * A copy of the order and affidavit upon which the application is made, together with notice of the time and place where the examination is to be taken, shall be served on the defendant, and his counsel, if he have any, at least two days before the time fixed for such examination, and the defendant may be present personally upon such examination to confront the witness produced against him ***." It goes even further in this direction by making provision that "*** if the defendant have no counsel the order shall contain a provision assigning counsel to him for the purpose of such examination upon whom a copy of said order, affidavit and notice shall be served."

The examination so taken on behalf of the People may be 504

CONDITIONAL EXAMINATION 

§ 302 used on the trial, in the same manner, and under the same conditions, as an examination of the defendant's witnesses. 

In addition, it may also be received before the Grand Jury, where there is a satisfactory showing to the Court that the witness "is unable to attend by reason of his death, insanity, sickness or infirmity, or that the witness cannot with due diligence be found in the State." (See Code, secs. 

8, subd. 3(b); 248, subd. 2.) 

Sec. 302. The Application. During the term, the application must be made before the court in which the matter is pending. If made out of term, it may be made to a Justice of the Supreme Court or the County Judge, when the indictment is pending in the Supreme Court or in a County Court. Similarly, where the indictment is pending in the 

Court of General Sessions, the application may be made out of term to one of the Judges of that Court, or to one of the Justices of the Supreme Court in New York County. 

It should be noted that no specific provision is made for the application where there is no indictment pending, either because the offense for which the defendant is held is not an indictable one, or to cover an application made before the Grand Jury has returned an indictment. This despite the broad availability of the remedy under Section 620 which provides for this examination "When a defendant has been held to answer a charge of crime * * * either before or after indictment." When the application is made in term, there is apparently no problem-Section 623 merely requires that the application then be made to "the court," which can include any court before which any criminal charge is pending. Applications made out of term, however, are provided for only in cases "When the indictment is pending. ' ***"To find specific statutory authorization where there is no indictment, or where the charge is before an inferior court of limited jurisdiction, a conferring of jurisdiction must be sought in the legislative acts dealing with the specific court.

As an example, the Court of Special Sessions of the City 505

§ 

of New York has jurisdiction, under Section 31 of the New York City Criminal Courts Act, "to order the conditional examination of witnesses ***." It has been held in that court that an application for such an order, made in a proceeding which is criminal in form, is there cognizable, and is "governed by the provisions of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure." (Commissioner of Welfare v. Soto, 5 Misc. 2d 

449, 160 N.Y.S. 2d 263, 265.)

There is no express requirement that the application for an order to examine be made on notice. On the contrary, the provision requiring "proof of the service upon the District Attorney, of a copy of the order, and of the affidavit on which it was granted" (Code, sec. 627), seems to contemplate that there is no service of the affidavit on the application except after the order is signed. It is, of course, always within the discretion of the court or judge applied to to direct such notice, which can be done by way of an order to show cause.

The want of provision for advance notice does not leave the People without protection against abuse of the procedure. Section 628 provides that the District Attorney may, even after the order for an examination is made and served, establish to the satisfaction of the court or judge, by affidavit or other proof or by way of preliminary examination of the witness, that the witness is not about to leave the State, that he is not sick or infirm, or that the application has been made to avoid the examination of the witness on the trial. In such event, the section provides: **the examination cannot take place; otherwise it must proceed."

The content of the affidavit, upon which the application must be made, is indicated in Section 622, requiring that it show: "1. The nature of the crime charged; 2. The state of the proceedings in the action; 3. The name and residence of the witness; and, 4. That the witness is about to leave the state, or is so sick and infirm as to afford reasonable grounds for apprehending that he will be unable to attend the trial." 506

CONDITIONAL EXAMINATION 

§ 304 

Sec. 303. The Order. The court or judge must be satisfied that the requirements of the statute are met and "that the examination of the witness is necessary to the attainment of justice." Thereupon, an order is made, directing that the witness be examined conditionally at a specified time and place. It must also direct that a copy thereof, and of the affidavit upon which it is granted, be served upon the 

District Attorney within a specified time before the date fixed for examination.

The order, when made by the court, may direct that the examination proceed before any judge thereof or before a magistrate of the county, to be named therein. However, when it is made out of term by a Justice of the Supreme Court, a County Judge or a Judge of the Court of General Sessions, it must direct the examination to be taken before the judge who signs it.

Sec. 304. The Examination and Deposition. The examina tion is presided over by the judge or magistrate designated in the order, and is conducted in the customary question and answer form. When the defendant's witness is examined, the People have the right to be represented by counsel and to cross examine. Similarly, as we have already seen, the defendant has the right to be represented, to be physically present, and to cross examine when the People's witness is thus examined, to the extent even that counsel is appointed by the court to represent him for this purpose when he is not otherwise so represented. It should be noted, however, that the defendant's examination of a witness must proceed, even in the absence of counsel for the People, when due service of the order and affidavit on the District 

Attorney has been proved.

In accordance with long-standing custom in examinations before trial, the Code requires that the examination be reduced to written deposition, signed and sworn to by the witness and signed and certified by the judge or magistrate presiding. It must be retained by the presiding judge or magistrate "and filed by him in the office of the clerk 507

§ 

of the court without unnecessary delay." (Code, sec. 630.)

The Court of Appeals, in People v. Bruno, 220 N.Y. 702, 703, indicated in a per curiam opinion what it deemed to be a properly-authenticated deposition, stating: "The deposition was properly authenticated. An official stenographer had been appointed by the magistrate before whom the preliminary examination was taken under proper provisions of law therefor and stenographic notes of the proceedings and of the examination and depositions of witnesses and statements of the defendant, if any, had been taken by such stenographer. Such minutes were properly certified by the stenographer and by the magistrate who held such examination."

Sec. 305. Compelling Attendance and Testimony of Wit nesses. The attendance of the witness at the time and place of the examination, as ordered, is compelled in the same manner as the attendance of witnesses at a trial or other judicial inquiry, by subpoena. The subpoena is subscribed by the judge or magistrate and, where issued by the court, must be under its seal. (Code, sec. 634). 

Section 635 of the Code makes disobedience to the subpoena, or a refusal to be sworn or to testify, punishable by the court or presiding judge or magistrate, as prescribed in Section 619, "as and for a criminal contempt in the manner provided in the Judiciary Law." Section 751 of the 

Judiciary Law, in turn, provides that such punishment "may be by fine, not exceeding two hundred and fifty dollars, or by imprisonment, not exceeding thirty days, in the jail of the county where the court is sitting, or both, in the discretion of the court." The last section also provides: "Such a contempt, committed in the immediate view and presence of the court, may be punished summarily. 

Sec. 306. Reading in Evidence. "The deposition, or a certified copy thereof," states Section 631, "may be read in evidence by either party on trial. *" The importance attached to this language was indicated in People v. Sugar- 508

CONDITIONAL EXAMINATION 

§ 306 man, 248 N.Y. 255, where a conviction was reversed because photostatic copies of the exhibits identified on pre-trial examination were introduced in the place of the originals originally attached to the deposition which had been lost before the trial. At page 260 of 248 N.Y., Judge 

Pound, writing for the Court, stated: "Secondary evidence of the exhibits in connection with the deposition was improperly received. The Code expressly limits secondary evidence of depositions to a certified copy thereof." 

At this point, however, the conditions under which the examination is ordered and held come into play. The problem here is distinguishable from that involved in the initial granting of the order to examine. Then, there must be a showing that the witness will not be likely to be available at the trial for the reasons and on the grounds prescribed. 

Now, before the deposition may be read in evidence at the trial, however, it must be proved that the conditions persist, "that the witness is unable to attend, by reason of his death, insanity, sickness or infirmity, or of his continued absence from the state." (Code, sec. 631.) 

In the dearth of authorities dealing with this subject, we can well rely on the reasoning of those in analogous civil cases, bearing in mind the statement of Judge Bronson in 

Barron v. People, 1 N.Y. 386, 391: "* *** the rule that governs the reading of depositions taken in civil cases should be applied to depositions taken under the New York criminal statute." Baumeister v. Durham Realty Corp. 238 

App. Div. 424, 264 N.Y. Supp. 672, construing Civil Practice Act, sec. 304, setting forth the conditions under which depositions may be read in evidence in civil cases, quoted 

Green v. Middlesex Valley R.R. Co., 31 App. Div. 412, 417, 418, 53 N.Y. Supp. 500, as follows: "The purpose of this condition is quite apparent, and it is this: That while a party may, under certain circumstances, procure the evidence of a witness before the trial of the action, he must nevertheless produce the witness upon the trial, if possible, in order that the jury may have the benefit of an examination conducted in open court, and it is not until he has 509

§ 

shown his inability to thus produce the witness that he is permitted to read his deposition."

No recent cases have been found, going into the question of what must be proved, and how, to permit the reading of the deposition in evidence in a criminal case. The general intent and purpose of the statute, however, is clear and the few reported authorities, even though not recent, amply illustrate it.

Thus, in Barron v. People, 1 N.Y. 386, the Court of Appeals held that a deposition should not have been received in evidence where the only foundation laid was the testimony of an assistant that he went to two hotels where, the District Attorney had informed him, the witness was accustomed to stop when he came to the city; that he inquired of the bartenders in both these hotels and they told him that to their knowledge the witness was not there and that they knew he did not live in the city; and that he was not expected. 

Similarly, in People v. Hadden, 3 Denio 220, the appellate court held that a deposition had been improperly received where it was admitted on the basis of the testimony of the Assistant District Attorney, who had attended at the taking of the deposition of the complainant about one month previously. He testified that the complainant had then said he lived in New Jersey and wished to return home; that after the deposition was taken the complainant left the recorder's office, saying he was going home that afternoon; and that the witness had not seen the complainant thereafter. The court there stated, at page 224 of 3 Denio: "The party who seeks to use such evidence must show the circumstances which make it admissible; the burden is on him, and until those circumstances are shown, the testimony must clearly be rejected." 

In People v. Murphy, 1 N.Y. Cr. 102, the court held that sufficient proof of absence had not been made to justify the reception of the deposition where the only testimony offered was that of a process server who, a few days before the trial, had gone to an address where the witness had 510

CONDITIONAL EXAMINATION 

§ 307 said he was stopping and was told he had not resided there for some two years. He admitted he had made no inquiry at a previous address given by the witness, nor of the surety on the witness' bond, nor at the address of such surety. 

Essentially the same tests must be applied when we determine the admissibility of testimony taken on pre-trial examination as are used for testimony given on a previous trial by a witness who is "unable to attend by reason of his death, insanity, sickness or infirmity, or cannot with due diligence be found in the state." (Code, sec. 8, subd. 3d.) 

Sustaining the admission of such testimony, given on a previous trial by a witness who had since committed suicide, the Court of Appeals, in People v. Hines, 284 N.Y. 

93, quoted the following statement in Young v. Valentine, 177 N.Y. 347, 357: "The fundamental ground upon which evidence given by a witness who afterwards dies may be read in evidence on a subsequent trial is that it was taken in an action or proceeding where the parties against whom it is offered or their privies have had both the right and the opportunity to cross-examine the witness as to the statement offered."

In the Hines case, supra, the court made another holding which may well be applicable when the testimony of a witness since deceased is read into evidence from a pretrial deposition. At page 115 of 284 N.Y., it was stated: "The law is well settled that a deceased witness whose prior testimony is admitted may not be impeached by showing alleged contradictory or inconsistent statements or alleged declarations that the prior testimony was false. (Hubbard v. Briggs, 31 N.Y. 518, 536, 537; Stacy v. 

Graham, 14 N.Y. 492, 498–501; Mattox v. United States, 156 U.S. 237, 248-250, 39 L. Ed. 409.)"

Sec. 307. Suppression or Exclusion of Deposition. Section 

632 of the Code provides: "The deposition cannot, however, be read, if it appear that the copy of the order and of the affidavit on which it was founded, was not served on 511

§ 

the District Attorney, as directed, or that the examination was in any respect unfair or not conducted as prescribed in this chapter. 99 While the Code makes no specific procedural provision for the implementation of this section by motion to suppress, as does Civil Practice Rule 133 in an out-of-State deposition in a civil action, or Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 32(d), nevertheless it would seem that the court, in its discretion, might grant such a motion under the above section. In any event, the objection can clearly be advanced on the trial on a showing contemplated by the section.

Sec. 308. Objections to Questions and Answers. Section 633 

of the Code provides: "Upon the reading of the deposition in evidence, the same objections may be taken to a question or answer contained therein, as if the witness had been examined orally in court." 

While there seem to be no reported cases construing this section, apparently it reserves every objection which might be made to the questions and answers for determination by the trial court when the same are read in evidence. 

There is no provision in the Code, and none appears to be applicable to pre-trial depositions in criminal matters, similar to that made in Section 305 of the Civil Practice Act which effects a waiver of objections "as to the form only of a question" unless noted upon the deposition. 

By reason that such objections are made specifically to the individual questions and answers, as the section indicates, in the same manner as on examination in open court, the determination that portions of it are incompetent cannot result in the suppression of the whole, only the incompetent portions being rejected. (See Commercial Bank v. Union Bank, 11 N.Y. 203; Valton v. National Fund L.A. 

Co., 20 N.Y. 32; Champney v. Blanchard, 39 N.Y. 111.) The objection that a lay witness is incompetent to express an opinion requiring expert knowledge is one properly reserved for the trial (Kearns Coal Corp. v. United States 512

CONDITIONAL EXAMINATION 

§ 308 

Fid. & Guar. Co., 118 F. 2d 33, certiorari denied 313 U.S. 

579, 85 L. Ed. 1536). Similarly, relevancy of questions and answers is properly raised at the trial (Rost v. Regal 

Warehouse, 182 N.Y. Supp. 816; Kalkhoff Co. v. Russian

Orthodox St. Nicholas Church, 67 Misc. 107, 121 N.Y. Supp. 

713; Dennison v. Brown, 51 Hun 642, 4 N.Y. Supp. 257).

Conversely, however, it has been held that objections to the admissibility of questions, though stated on the examination itself and noted on the deposition, are waived if not renewed at the trial, and cannot thereafter be raised on appeal (Martin v. Silliman, 53 N.Y. 615). 513
