Sec. 317. Reading in Evidence PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

As in the case of examination of witnesses, conditionally, this interrogation is rarely used by the defense in a criminal prosecution. A peculiar quirk of the proceeding is that it is only available to the defendant in the first instance, but once it is used by him it may be likewise employed by the District Attorney. 

Therein lies its danger.

As soon as application is made for an examination on commission, you inform the People of the nature of the testimony you are seeking. The District Attorney now has the right to cross-examine your witness. Furthermore, the door has been opened to him to seek the examination of his own out-of-State witnesses. You are thus enlarging the area from which the prosecution could draw its proof. Counsel should exercise great caution in making application for this examination. 

Sec. 309. Nature and Distinguishing Features. The need often arises, in the course of the prosecution and defense of criminal actions, to procure the testimony of persons 514

§ who are beyond the State's territorial limits, and therefore immune to subpoena and the other ordinary procedures whereby such testimony is procured within the State. The remedy in this situation, universally established in our civil procedure (Civil Practice Act, sec. 302; Rules of Civil 

Practice, Rule 130), in the Federal system, and in the procedures of practically all the States, is the second of our two forms of criminal pre-trial examination-the examination of material witnesses out of the State on commission and interrogatories. It is provided for in Title 12, Chapter IV of the Code of Criminal Procedure, sections 636–657. 

This procedure differs from that we have discussed in conditional examinations, primarily in that it is meant to deal with situations where it is entirely unlikely that the witness will be in the jurisdiction at the time of the trial. 

The conditional aspect of the former procedure, therefore, does not seriously enter into its constitution; the witness resides without the State, is not expected to be available therein, and we must go to him to obtain the testimony he can give.

Examination on commission, as distinguished from conditional examination, is made available only "When an issue of fact is joined upon an indictment." (Code, sec. 636.) 

It cannot, therefore, be availed of in a non-indictable offense, or while the defendant is held prior to indictment. 

It follows, of course, that it is not available to obtain testimony for presentation to the Grand Jury.

The prerequisite of indictment was well illustrated where the defendant, charged with disorderly conduct and resisting arrest, both misdemeanors normally cognizable by courts of special sessions, sought removal from the Police Court and certification for prosecution of the charges by indictment. He established that the only eyewitness who could testify for him was a Pennsylvania resident, and asserted his inability to make a defense without the testimony of that witness. The County Court, to which the application was made, held this to be sufficient reason for granting it, stating in People v. Sheldon, 190 Misc. 156, 515

§ 

74 N.Y.S. 2d 36, 37-38: "It is undisputed that it is only after issues of fact are joined upon an indictment that the remedy of the issuance of a commission is available. 

Witnesses for the prosecution were present at the time of the alleged events but without an indictment the defendant cannot obtain the evidence of the only eyewitness who will testify in his defense."

Further demonstrating the limitations on the availability of this form of examination, an application therefor was denied when it sought a commission to take testimony out of the State for use in an inquiry into the sanity of a defendant under indictment. Pointing out that the inquiry was a special proceeding of a criminal nature, and not a trial of the issues joined under an indictment, the court stated in People v. Haight, 3 N.Y.Cr. 60, 62, 63: "The statute authorizes the testimony of a non-resident witness to be taken for use on a trial, but not in a special proceeding. ***the object of the statute is to authorize a commission to take testimony to be read only upon the trial of an indictment. No provision is made for the case of an inquiry by commissioners into the sanity of a defendant under indictment. The power to issue a commission for any purpose is an innovation upon the common law, and must be strictly pursued. It depends solely upon the statute, and cannot be extended to any case not provided for by the statute." 

And in People v. Morris, 151 Misc. 212, 213, 270 N.Y. 

Supp. 901, the court stated: "There is no provision in the

Code of Criminal Procedure which authorizes the issuance of a commission in aid of a motion for a new trial. A commission can be issued only for the taking of testimony to be used upon a trial when an issue of fact is joined upon an indictment."

It is, under the statute and unlike the provisions for the conditional examination discussed in the previous chapter, indispensable that the witness whose testimony is to be taken is one "residing out of the State" (Code, sec. 

636), and that the commission authorizing the examination direct that it be held at a place outside the State. 516

§ 

Sec. 310. How Available to Defendant and to the People. 

By the statute, this examination is made available to the defendant only, at least in the initiation of the procedure. 

Thus, it is provided that "the defendant may have any material witness * * * examined" (Code, sec. 636), that "When a material witness for the defendant resides out of the state, the defendant may apply ***" (Code, sec. 

637), and that the application may be granted "without notice to the District Attorney, unless the court direct notice to be given." (Code, sec. 642.) Consequently, it is only the defendant who can make an application for an examination on commission. 99 However, after providing for the initial application, and fixing the requirements thereof and limitations thereon, the Code goes on to provide that "an order must be made that a commission be issued to take his testimony, and that the People be permitted to join in the commission, and to examine witnesses in support of the indictment.' (Code, sec. 643.) That this joinder of the People, and the right given them to examine witnesses, is not limited to mere cross-examination of the defendant's witnesses was held in People v. Werblow, 212 App. Div. 445, 456, 209 N.Y. 

Supp. 88, reversed other grounds 241 N.Y. 55, in the following language: "The defendant attempts to construe such statutory provision as merely permitting the crossexamination of such witnesses as the defendant sought to examine by commission. The statute certainly is not susceptible of such narrow interpretation, and when it said that the People were permitted to join in the commission and to examine witnesses the Legislature must have meant that the People were given the right to examine the witnesses generally and not merely to cross-examine the defendant's witnesses."

Although the District Attorney does not have the right to initiate the procedure, once it has been set in motion by the defendant the remedy is fully available to the prosecution. The law in this regard was stated and summarized in People v. Parkinson, 187 Misc. 328, 63 N.Y.S. 2d 903, 517

§ 

905-906, as follows: "The only limitation under the sections of Chapter 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is that the defendant must in the first instance apply for an order that the witness be examined on a commission. If the defendant makes no such application, the People cannot take testimony by commission. If the defendant opens the door by applying for testimony by commission, then the People are permitted 'to examine witnesses in support of the indictment.' The door having been opened by the defendants' application to examine a witness by commission, the People are not limited to an examination of the defendants' witness, nor may the door be closed to deprive the People of the right afforded the District Attorney to examine other witnesses as provided in Section 643 of the Code of Criminal Procedure." Sec. 311. The Commission. The commission under which the out-of-State examination is taken is defined in Section 638 of the Code, thus: "A commission is a process issued under the seal of the court and the signature of the clerk, directed to one or more persons, designated as commissioners, authorizing them to examine the witness upon oath, on interrogatories annexed thereto, and to take and return the deposition of the witness, according to the directions given, with the commission." 

It is this commission which transmits to the commissioners their authority to conduct an examination beyond the boundaries of the State in which it is issued. Without it, or beyond its scope and limitations, they are powerless to act. Thus, where a petitioner sought the production of books and records for use on an examination before trial in an action pending in Florida, and could produce only a commission from the Florida court to a New Jersey commissioner to take testimony in that State, the New York court to which he applied denied his application, stating, in Matter of Hild, 124 N.Y.S. 2d 271, 274: "As stated aforesaid, the production of the records in this case is not sought in connection with any lawful commission or order for the 518

§ 

taking of a deposition in this State. The petitioner merely comes into court and makes the general claim that they are germane to the issue raised * * * Generally, the proper procedure, therefore, would be to obtain from such court the issuance of the necessary commission returnable in this State directed to the obtaining of such records and the necessary testimony in connection therewith." 

Sec. 312. Application for Commission. Application for an order directing the issuance of a commission must be made to the same court or judge as is an application for conditional pre-trial examination. If during the term, it must be presented to the court in which the indictment is pending (Code, sec. 640). If the indictment is in the Supreme 

Court or in a County Court, application may be made out of term to any Justice of the Supreme Court or to a County Judge of the county in which it is pending. Where the indictment is before the Court of General Sessions, any Judge of that Court or one of the Justices of the Supreme Court in New York County may entertain the application out of term (Code, sec. 641).

An affidavit must be submitted, in support of the application, showing facts mandated by Section 639 of the Code, as follows: "1. The nature of the crime charged; 2. The state of the proceedings in the action, and that issue of fact has been joined therein; 3. The name of the witness, and that his testimony is material to the defense of the action; 4. That the witness resides out of the State."

It is not required that the matters as to which the examination is sought deal only with the most essential issues; its materiality must be determined in the light of the rules of evidence and the actual need for its production in the defense of the action. Thus, in People v. Goodman, 43 Misc. 

508, 89 N.Y. Supp. 522, the court held that the District Attorney's concession of the defendant's previous good character obviated the need for examination on commission of character witnesses. The defendant's application in that 519

§ 

case to examine on commission to prove that the complaining witness had been indicted and tried for crime was denied by the court as not admissible in the absence of proof of conviction; the court further pointing out that, although that was not alleged in the affidavit, if the examination should disclose that the complainant had actually been so convicted, the examination still remained unnecessary because "a duly exemplified copy of the record of conviction would be admissible as evidence." Similarly, the same defendant's proposed examination to establish that the complainant had engaged in unconscionable business dealings was held irrelevant although the court conceded that it "possibly may be a subject for further crossexamination of the complaining witness;" nevertheless, the court held that a witness sought to be examined for this purpose could hardly be deemed to be a "material witness" (Code, secs. 636, 637, 639), nor did examination for such purpose appear "necessary to the attainment of justice." (Code, sec. 643.)

Examination on commission was specifically indicated as proper to be utilized for laying the foundation of proof by secondary evidence of a lost paper in People v. Burgess, 244 N.Y. 472, 479, which quoted Kearney v. Mayor, 92 N.Y. 

617, as follows: "It has repeatedly been held that the person last known to have been in possession of the paper must be examined as a witness to prove its loss, and that even if he is out of the State, his deposition must be procured if practicable, or some good excuse given for not doing so." 

The District Attorney need be given no notice of the application, provides Section 642 of the Code, and his right to join in the commission and examine in support of the indictment is automatically provided in Section 643, regardless of any affirmative request on his part. However, when the application is made out of term to a judge or justice, at least five days notice must be given to, and a copy of the supporting affidavit must be served upon, the 

District Attorney. 520

§ 

Sec. 313. Order for Commission. Section 643 of the Code reads: "If the court or officer to whom the application is made, be satisfied that the witness resides out of the State, and that his examination is necessary to the attainment of justice, an order must be made that a commission be issued to take his testimony, and that the People be permitted to join in the commission, and to examine witnesses in support of the indictment."

Both the language and the spirit, as well as the practice and custom on pre-trial examinations generally, bear out the established rule, stated in Rowland v. Stim, 147 N.Y.S. 

2d 876, 877, affirmed 283 App. Div. 942, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 882: "The granting of an examination before trial rests in the exercise of discretion." And in Combes v. Maas, 209 App. 

Div. 330, 204 N.Y. Supp. 440, 441: "The privilege of examining may not be availed of to annoy and worry the adverse party, or to do prospecting, or to speculate. The taking of depositions must be prosecuted in good faith." 

If the court is satisfied that the statutory requirements have been met, no doubt as to the competency or capability of the witness should be permitted to interfere with the granting of the order, as these questions are not properly considered at this point. Considering an order directing the issuance of a commission to examine as a witness an inmate committed to a state mental hospital in another State, the court wrote in Stevens v. State, 272 App. Div. 

642, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 879, 881: "In Hand v. Burrows, 23 Hun 

330, it was held that a commission might issue to take the testimony of one committed to a lunatic asylum in another State and the question of the competency of the proposed witness and the admissibility of his testimony was to be determined at trial by an appropriate examination. We do not find that that ruling has ever been seriously questioned, and the reasons therefor given by the General Term are compelling in the interests of justice. We find no statutory interdiction. We find no rule nor reason for one which precludes the court from directing that such a commission include a preliminary examination, on interrogatories, 521

§ 

respecting the competency of the proposed witness as of and at the time his interrogatories are addressed to him. 

Such a preliminary examination would not be conclusive. 

It would be merely an aid to the trial court in connection. with such further examination as might be deemed necessary or proper to aid in that court's final determination as to the question of competency."

For obvious reasons, Section 644 of the Code mandates the inclusion in the order granting a commission "a direction that the trial of the indictment be stayed for a specified time, reasonably sufficient for the execution and return of the commission." 

Sec. 314. The Interrogatories, and their Settlement. That the interrogatories-the actual questions which the witness will be required to answer on his examination-must be "pertinent" is specifically provided by the Code, but there is no other specification therein as to their content. 

Thus, Section 647 states that "either party may insert any questions pertinent to the issue," and Section 648 makes it the duty of the judge to "expunge every question not pertinent to the issues and modify the questions, so as to conform them to the rules of evidence."

In this regard, the court stated in Matter of Ames' 

Estate, 207 Misc. 746, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 327, 330, affirmed 286 

App. Div. 1010, 146 N.Y.S. 2d 662: "* * * the only objection which may be interposed in connection with the settlement of interrogatories relates to 'pertinency.' *** Interroga- tories may not be disallowed because of objections relating to competency of the witness, for such objections may properly be interposed only upon the trial. Interrogatories may, of course, be disallowed if improper in form, but with these exceptions the court is under a duty to allow all questions pertinent to the issue involved."

Parenthetically, it might be pointed out that the section of the Code we are dealing with, not applicable in the quoted case, specifically requires that the judge "modify" 522

§ the questions to "conform" them to the evidentiary rules; this would, it seems, not permit a judge to disallow an interrogatory for impropriety in form, if he can possibly modify it to make it proper. 

The Ames' Estate case, supra, further quotes Webster's 

New International Dictionary as defining "pertinent” as: "Related to the matter in hand or subject under consideration; relevant; to the point." And, in Matter of Horn, 137 

N.Y.S. 2d 165, 166, the court stated: "Frivolous, immaterial and irrelevant questions should be excluded." 

In Jones v. Jones, 208 Misc. 721, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 820, 824, the court said: "As a general rule, pertinency of the inquiry sought to be made is the only test to be invoked upon the settlement of interrogatories and cross interrogatories. *** This is so because the trial court normally passes upon the competency of a witness or the admissibility of evidence as the case may develop, and the rights of the parties are duly protected at the trial, either by objections or by motions to strike. *** However, an exception to the pertinency rule arises where privilege is claimed; otherwise the forbidden disclosure would result, even though the answers to the interrogatories were ultimately excluded at the trial. The Civil Practice Act, § 354, pro vides that the testimonial privilege arising out of the confidential relationship of physician and patient applies 'to any examination of a person as a witness' unless there be a waiver." 

Inasmuch as the "rules of evidence in civil cases are applicable also to criminal cases *" (Code of Criminal 

Procedure, sec. 392), the provisions as to competency of witnesses contained in "Sections 346 to 354 of the Civil 

Practice Act ** apply to criminal cases with certain added limitations which are not material here." (People v. 

Bevilacqua, 12 Misc. 558, 170 N.Y.S. 2d 423, 429, reversed other grounds 5 N.Y. 2d 867; see also Matter of Abortions in Kings County, 206 Misc. 830, 135 N.Y.S. 2d 381, affirmed 

286 App. Div. 270, 143 N.Y.S. 2d 501.) By the same token, 523

§ 

the rule on questions in the settlement of interrogatories where privilege is asserted, as above enunciated in civil actions, must be considered applicable to the settlement of interrogatories for examination in criminal matters, as well.

After the order is signed, the settlement procedure begins. The defendant serves upon the District Attorney a copy of his proposed interrogatories with two days' notice of settlement. The District Attorney, if he intends to join in the commission and examine his own witnesses thereunder, must likewise serve upon the defendant or his counsel his interrogatories and like notice. Notice of settlement is required to be returnable before a Justice of the Supreme Court or a County Judge of the county, if the indictment is pending in the Supreme Court or in a County Court. If pending in the Court of General Sessions, the notice is to be returnable before a Judge of that Court or one of the Justices of the Supreme Court in New York County (Code, sec. 645). In the same manner, the parties may serve cross-interrogatories, comprising the questions by way of cross-examination, proposed to be annexed to the commission, with like notice of the settlement thereof (Code, sec. 646).

When the interrogatories contain questions as to specific exhibits, a witness cannot be compelled to make an identification of such as are not before the commissioner (Matter of Dittman, 65 App. Div. 343, 72 N.Y. Supp. 886). Accordingly, the proper practice and the safe practice is to annex to the interrogatories and commission such documents and exhibits as are sought to be identified, or referred to in his answers, by the witness (Commercial Bank of Pennsylvania v. Union Bank, 19 Barb. 391, affirmed 11 N.Y. 203).

When the original cannot actually be sent along with the interrogatories and commission, as, for example, when it is a paper filed in the public records, annexing a copy is sufficient, and the exhibit may be produced at the trial, separate from the commission (Jackson ex dem. Woodruff v. Shepherd, 6 Cow. 444). 524

§ re Sec. 315. Execution of the Commission. After the interrogatories are settled, the commission and interrogatories are forwarded to the commissioner therein named, who thereafter proceeds to conduct the examination in accordance therewith. The manner in which the commission is to be executed is carefully enjoined in Section 650 of the Code, a copy of which is required to be annexed to the commission (Code, sec. 651). No better summary of the proper procedures in execution of the commission exists than that given in the section, and it is therefore set forth at length, as follows: "The commissioners, or any one of them, unless otherwise specially directed, may execute the commission as follows: 

1. They must publicly administer an oath to the witness, that his answers given to the interrogatories shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth; 

2. They must cause the examination of the witness to be reduced to writing; 

3. They must write the answers of the witness, as nearly as possible in the language in which he gives them, and read him each answer as it is taken down, and correct or add to it, until it is made conformable to what he declares is the truth; 

4. If the witness decline answering a question, that fact, with the reason for which he declines answering it, as he gives it, must be stated; 

5. If papers or documents are produced before them, and proved by the witness, they must be annexed to his deposition, and be subscribed by the witness, and certified by the commissioners; 

6. The commissioners must subscribe their names to each sheet of the deposition, and annex the deposition, with the papers or documents proved by the witness, to the commission, and must close it up under seal, and address it, as directed thereon. 

7. If there be a direction on the commission, to return it by mail, the commissioners must immediately deposit it in the nearest post-office. If any other direction be made, by 525

§ 

the written consent of the parties, or by the officer, on the commission, as to its return, they must comply with the direction."

While it has been held that parties have the same right to appear by counsel on the execution of a commission for the examination of witnesses as on the trial of an action (Union Bank v. Torrey, 12 N.Y. Super. 626, 2 Abb. Pr. 

269), it has also been held that the presence of counsel on behalf of either of the parties is not necessary at the time the deposition on closed interrogatories is taken (Richter v. 44 W. 175th St. Corp., 162 Misc. 745, 295 N.Y. Supp. 463).

In Matter of Eldridge, 82 N.Y. 161, it was held that where the attorney for one of the parties wrote out the answers to the interrogatories, direct and cross, and read the answers to the direct interrogatories to the commissioners, leaving it to the witness to read the answers to the cross interrogatories he had prepared, such examination did not constitute a deposition or an execution of the commission.

In Greenman-Roth v. Carl Marks & Co., 196 Misc. 156, 

91 N.Y.S. 2d 851, the court denied defendant's motion to suppress a deposition taken on interrogatories in South America, based on the assertion that the United States Consul, acting as commissioner, had acted improperly in permitting the witness to refer to memoranda before answering. This, it was contended, had lost the absent defendant the opportunity to see the memoranda or to insist on exhausting the witness' memory before allowing their use, as could have been done on a trial. Asserting that "that is a vice of closed commissions and does not amount to an irregularity or improper conduct," the court pointed out that the memoranda could at best have been, if seen by the defendant, used for cross-examination. 

Sec. 316. Return of the Commission. After proper signature and authentication, the commissioner must forthwith return it to the clerk or judge, as directed. The direction may be that he return it by mail, or by an agent designated 526

§ in the commission. When it is returned by mail the clerk must open it and file it in his office where it remains, pending other direction of the court (Code, sec. 655). When it is delivered by the commissioner to an agent, he must deliver it to the clerk or to a judge of the court in which the indictment is pending, by whom it may be opened, upon the affidavit of the agent that he received it from the hands of one of the commissioners and that it had not been opened or altered since he had received it (Code, sec. 652). If the agent be dead or be, by reason of sickness or casualty, unable to deliver the commission and return personally, it may be received by the clerk or judge from some other person, upon his making an affidavit that the agent is dead or is unable for the reasons stated to deliver it, that it has not been opened or altered since he received it, and that he believes it has not been opened or altered since it came from the hands of the commissioners (Code, sec. 653). 

After its filing, as provided, the commission must at all times be open to the inspection of the parties. The clerk is mandated to furnish copies thereof, or of any part of the same, on payment of his prescribed fees (Code, sec. 656). 

Sec. 317. Reading in Evidence. Section 657 of the Code provides: "The deposition, taken under the commission, may be read in evidence by either party on the trial, and the same objections may be taken to a question in the interrogatories, or to an answer in the deposition, as if the witness had been examined orally in court." 

This is the only section of the Code which provides for objections, and it indicates and provides that these are to be made precisely as are the objections made to oral testimony offered on trial. There is no provision for suppression of the deposition in the Code, similar to that in Civil 

Practice Act, sec. 304, and Rule 133 of the Rules of Civil 

Practice, or to the provisions of Rule 32(d) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. This does not mean that the court does not have the power to suppress or set aside a deposition improperly taken; in fact, every provision of 527

§ 

the Code prescribing the proper manner of taking and returning the deposition impliedly authorizes the court to take the steps necessary to enforce it and to exclude depositions, or parts thereof, which do not meet its standards. However, the absence of specific provision does mean that the courts must rely on general rather than specific powers, in so far as they may suppress or reject depositions which should be barred because of impropriety or invalidity.

In any event, as the deposition is read on the trial, question by question and answer by answer, objection may be made by either party, and is then and there ruled on by the court. And, as the court stated in Jones v. Jones, 208 Misc. 

721, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 820, 824: "*** the trial court normally passes on the competency of the witness or of the admissibility of evidence as the case may develop, and the rights of the parties are duly protected at the trial, either by objections or by motions to strike; see Irving v. Royal 

Exchange Assurance of London, 122 App. Div. 56, 107 N.Y. 

Supp. 83; Wanamaker v. Megraw, 168 N.Y. 125." 528

CHAPTER 27 EXTRADITION, RENDITION, AND INTERSTATE REMOVAL Sec. 318. Definitions Sec. 319. Constitutional and Statutory Provisions Sec. 320. Grounds for Extradition Sec. 321. Procedure Sec. 322. Attacking the Extradition Sec. 323. Uniform Act to Secure the Attendance of Witnesses From Without a State in Criminal Proceedings 

Sec. 318. Definitions. "Extradition may be sufficiently defined to be the surrender by one nation to another of an individual accused or convicted of an offense outside of its own territory, and within the territorial jurisdiction of the other, which, being competent to try and punish him, demands the surrender." (Terlinden v. Ames, 184 U.S. 

270, 279, 46 L. Ed. 534, 541.) This definition restricts the usage of the term to international, as distinguished from interstate, transactions. Some authorities have preferred to use the word "rendition" in discussing interstate transactions. (See, e.g., Alexander, The Law of Arrest, p. 

769.) However, as the word extradition is more commonly used to refer to both situations, it will be used in this chapter to refer to both interstate and international removals. 

Sec. 319. Constitutional and Statutory Provisions. Federal. 

"A Person charged in any state with Treason, Felony or other crime, who shall flee from Justice and be found in another State, shall on Demand of the Executive Authority of the State from which he fled, be delivered up, to be removed to the State having jurisdiction of the Crime." 529

§ 

enacted the predecessor of Section 3182 of Title 18 of the 

United States Code to implement the constitutional provision. The statute directs, in part; "Whenever the executive authority of any state or Territory demands any person as a fugitive from justice *** and produces a copy of an indictment found or affidavit made before a magistrate of any state or Territory, charging the person demanded with having committed * * * crime, certified as correct by the governor or chief magistrate of the [demanding] State *** or Territory *** has fled shall cause him to be arrested and secured, and notify the executive authority making such demand *** and shall cause the fugitive to be delivered."

The obligation imposed upon the Governor of a State by these constitutional and statutory provisions has been held not legally enforceable; it is a moral duty only (Kentucky v. Dennison, 24 How. 66). It has been held that to be a "fugitive from justice" under the Federal statute and the constitutional provisions above quoted, a person must have been physically present within the demanding State when the crime was committed, and he must have thereafter left that State, although the reason for the departure has been held to be immaterial (Appleyard v. Massachusetts, 203 U.S. 222). Although no legally enforceable obligation is placed upon the States by the Federal enactments upon this subject, it has been held that those provisions do invalidate any State statutes which purport to impose stricter requirements for extradition (People ex rel. Carr v. Murray, 357 Ill. 326, 192 N.E. 198; Ex parte Riccardi, 68 

Ariz. 180, 203 Pac. 2d 627).

It has also been held that States may be less exacting, and may permit rendition in situations where all of the Federally imposed requirements have not been met. Thus, in People ex rel. Faulds v. Herberick, 276 App. Div 852, 93 

N.Y.S. 2d 272, affirmed 301 N.Y. 614, there was upheld, as constitutional, the section of the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act which permits extradition of one only "con- 530

EXTRADITION 

§ 319 structively" present in the demanding state when the crime was committed. In Barton v. N.Y.C. & H.R.R., 245 

U.S. 315, the arrest of a fugitive by the asylum State, prior to any demand having been forwarded by the demanding State, was upheld, and a statute providing for waiver of all the formalities contained in the Federal statute, in cases involving parolees, has been held constitutional (Gulley v. Apple, 213 Ark. 350, 210 S.W. 2d 514).

One of the leading New York cases is People ex rel. 

Matochik v. Baker, 306 N.Y. 32, where the fugitive contended that the provision of the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act allowing extradition upon an "information supported by affidavit" was unconstitutional as the Federal statute, quoted above, provided for extradition only upon indictments or affidavits before magistrates. The demanding State, Vermont, allowed prosecution for burglary, the crime involved, to be initiated by information. 

New York deems burglary a felony and, accordingly, indictable. The fugitive's contention was rejected and the statute upheld by the Court of Appeals, resolving the prior conflict which had existed among the departments of the 

Appellate Division (Compare People ex rel. Lipshitz v. 

Bessinger, 273 App. Div. 19, 75 N.Y.S. 2d 329; People ex rel. MacSherry v. Enright, 196 App. Div. 964, 188 N.Y.S. 

2d 945).

The law of international extradition is regulated solely by Federal statute and treaties. This Federal authority is exclusive and States may not provide for, or regulate, the surrender of persons to foreign governments (People ex rel. Barlow v. Curtis, 50 N.Y. 321; Holnes v. Jennison, 14

Pet. 540). The principles of law applicable to international extradition will not be considered in detail herein. In general, they may be stated to be that no extradition may be had in the absence of an extradition treaty with the demanding government (Valentine v. United States, ex rel. 

Neidecker, 299 U.S. 5), although the fugitive cannot secure his release when he has been illegally taken from the asylum country (Kerr v. Illinois, 119 U.S. 436; Chandler 531

§ 

v. United States, 171 F. 2d 921, cert. denied, 336 U.S. 918).

There is also a right of political asylum, recognized in the international law of extradition which has no counterpart in interstate law on this subject. The procedure to be followed in international extradition is to be found in Title 18 of the United States Code, at sections 3184, 3186, and 3190. A distinction between international and interstate extradition arises out of the requirement of the extradition treaties that to be extraditable, a crime concerned must be either specifically named in the treaty, or it must be a crime against the laws of both nations. (Compare Kentucky v. Dennison, supra, where the Supreme 

Court, referring to interstate rendition, stated that the word "crime," as used in the constitutional provision above quoted, means "any offense * ** which the demanding state, consistently with the Constitution and laws of the 

United States, may have made a crime.")

State. New York, and 41 other States, and Hawaii while still a territory, have enacted substantially all of the Uni form Criminal Extradition Act (9 Uniform Laws An notated). The States which have not enacted that act are Alaska, Kentucky, Louisiana, Nevada, North Dakota, South Carolina and Washington, plus the District of Columbia. The act is contained in Chapter 1 of Title IV 

(sections 827 through 859) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Sec. 320. Grounds for Extradition. Section 829 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "Subject to the provisions of this title, the provisions of the constitution of the United States controlling, and any and all acts of Congress enacted in pursuance thereof, it is the duty of the Governor of this State to have arrested and delivered up to the executive authority of any other State *** any person charged in that state with *** crime, who has fled from justice and is found in that State." However, more than an unsupported charge of crime is required. Under Section 830, demands for extradition shall not be recognized unless 532

EXTRADITION 

§ 320 "accompanied by a copy of an indictment found or by information supported by affidavit in the State having jurisdiction of the crime, or by a copy of an affidavit made before a magistrate there, together with a copy of any warrant which was issued thereon, or by a copy of a judgment of conviction or of a sentence imposed in execution thereof, together with a statement by the executive authority of the demanding State that the person claimed has escaped from confinement or has broken the term of his bail, probation or parole. The indictment, information or affidavit made before the magistrate must substantially charge the person demanded with having committed a crime under the law of that State; and *** must be authenticated by the executive authority making the demand." Section 834 permits, but does not require, the Governor to surrender, in the same manner as provided in other cases, persons charged "with committing an act in this State or in a third State, intentionally resulting in a crime in the [demand

*** would be punishable by the laws of this State, if the consequences claimed to have resulted therefrom *** had taken effect in this State; 

may, in his discretion, make any such surrender conditioned upon agreement *** that the person so surrendered will be held to answer no criminal charges of any nature except those set forth in the requisition *** at least until such person has been given reasonable opportunity to return to this State after his acquittal' *** [or] after he shall be released from confinement. Nothing in this section shall apply to the crime of libel." This is the only one in the Code requiring the act to constitute a crime in both the demanding and the asylum state. 

In Kentucky v. Dennison, 24 How. 66, it was held that the act, in cases of actual physical presence within the demanding State at the time of commission of the crime, need be a crime only under the law of the demanding State. See 

People ex rel. Swanson v. Fitzsimmons, 2 App. Div. 2d 235, 153 N.Y.S. 2d 772, for a comparison of this section with the 533

§  

sections governing the usual situation where the accused was present in the demanding State when the crime was perpetrated. The word "act" in the section has been construed to include an omission also. So, in People ex rel. 

Kaufman v. O'Brien, 197 Misc. 1019, 96 N.Y.S. 2d 401, the defendant was extradited where the acts complained of were his failure to support, and make payments to, a minor, an indictable offense in the demanding state. The defendant there contended that he was not present in the demanding state when he had committed the acts, or omissions, that he had not thereafter fled from that state, and that therefore he was not a fugitive. The court, however, upheld the extradition under Section 834. 

As stated above, it is not necessary for a valid extradition that the crime charged be prosecuted in the demanding State in the same manner as in the asylum State. Nor is it necessary that if the crime is one prosecuted only by indictment in the asylum State, it be so in the demanding State. In People ex rel. Matochik v. Baker, 306 N.Y. 32, the demanding State, Vermont, permitted prosecution for burglary to be initiated by information, and an information was held a sufficient support for the extradition warrant; this despite New York's requirement that burglary, which it regards as a felony, be initiated by indictment. 

As stated, it is not necessary that the crime be recognized as a crime in the asylum State. In People ex rel. Hayes v. McLaughlin, 247 N.Y. 238, Chief Judge Cardozo wrote: "The question is whether 'the fugitive has been in fact, however inartificially, charged with crime in the State from which he has fled.' (Pierce v. Creecy, 210 U.S. 387.) 

A Grand Jury *** has said that what has been charged against him is there a crime. The Governor has said the same. Unless a reasonable basis for what they said is lacking altogether, unless the indictment is so frivolous or contradictory as to be a presentment of innocence rather than of crime, we do not go beyond the documents when flight is once established. Doubt, if there is any, must be resolved in the demanding State. * * * The test is *** whether the 

534

EXTRADITION 

§ 320 substance of criminality is lacking altogether when substance is determined by any standard of penal justice that can rationally be supposed to prevail in the demanding jurisdiction." 

The above case was cited with approval in People ex rel. 

Gellis v. Sheriff, 251 N.Y. 33, where the defendant contended that the complaining affidavit was defective in alleging only that there had been a false representation by the defendant of the value of stock. The defendant claimed that the statement was only an expression of his opinion concerning the value, and thus not a criminal act. The papers supporting the demand alleged that the false representation had been made with intent to defraud and thus constituted a crime in the demanding state. The Court of 

Appeals stated: "The reasonable possibility that the act alleged to be a crime may be such in the demanding State must appear. Nothing more is required. 

is not, however, as to the law of New York but of the law of the demanding State on the subject. *** The test has recently been stated with care and precision by this Court. 

Applying this test, we must ask ourselves whether a sister State may reasonably be assumed to have enacted a statute which punishes as criminal a false representation as to value made with 'intent to cheat and defraud' another. If it would be so unreasonable as to border on the ridiculous to assume * * * that a sister State has departed widely from the general principles of criminal law, we may not be called upon to draw such an inference from the mere fact of a requisition. * * * It is not for this State to apply its own rules. *** It cannot be said that a reasonable basis is altogether lacking for the assertion of the demanding Governor that the acts charged are made criminal in his 

State by statute. * * *” Thus, the crime charged need not be a common law crime, to warrant extradition, even if no statute of the demanding State, showing that the act has there been made a crime by statute, has been placed in the record. 535

§ 

Sec. 321. Procedure. The demand for extradition is required to be in writing. Prior to the enactment of the uniform Act, it was held in Solomon's Case, 1 Abb. Pr. N.S. 

347, that the Governor had no authority to issue a warrant for the arrest of the fugitive, in the absence of a written, duly authenticated demand, and of his receipt of the necessary copies of the supporting papers, such as the indictment. Solomon's Case was cited with approval in People v. 

Hagerty, 261 App. Div. 1049, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 568, to support the proposition that "A proceeding for the rendition of relator could not be commenced except upon *** requisition of the Governor of the [demanding] State." 

Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 842, permits the issuance of a warrant and the arrest of the accused person, prior to the receipt of any demand therefor, upon his being "charged on the oath of any credible person of this State before any justice, judge or magistrate of this State with the commission of any crime in any other State." 

Section 843 further provides for the arrest of any person "without a warrant, upon reasonable information that the accused stands charged in the courts of a State with a crime punishable by death or imprisonment for a term exceeding one year." However, when such arrest is made, the accused person is to be brought, forthwith, before a judge or magistrate; a complaint must then be made against him on oath, and his "answers shall be heard as if he had been arrested on a warrant." Thereafter, the fugitive may be committed, pending the receipt of the extradition requisition, for a period not to exceed thirty days (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 844), subject to extensions of time as provided in Section 846. Code Section 851 provides procedure for the waiver of extradition proceedings, and, under Section 855, one brought into a State after executing such waiver is granted immunity from the service of process in civil actions arising out of the same acts as those involved in the criminal proceeding.

After an extradition demand is received by the Governor of the asylum State, that Governor must investigate the 536

EXTRADITION 

§ 321 demand to determine whether the person sought ought to be surrendered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 831). It has uniformly been held that the accused has no right to a hearing before the Governor during this investigation; the Governor may, as a matter of grace, grant the accused a hearing, if he so desires (Ex parte Cohen, 12 N.J. 362, 96 Atl. 2d 794; In re Murphy 321 Mass. 206, 72 N.E. 2d 413; 

Yaws v. Warden, 166 Kan. 685, 203 Pac. 2d 742). After the investigation is completed, the Governor, deciding that the demand should be complied with, issues a warrant of arrest, sealed with the State seal, which must recite substantially all of the facts necessary to evidence its validity (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 835). Merely formal defects in the warrant, such as misnomer of the accused, will not invalidate the warrant (Matter of Scrofford, 12 N.Y.S. 943), but a substantial defect, such as a completely erroneous description of the crime of which the accused is charged, will have that effect (People ex rel. Swanson v. Fitzsimmons, 2 App. Div. 2d 235, 153 N.Y.S. 2d 772). The Swanson case, while its essential holding lies upon a somewhat narrower ground, did indicate that failure to recite correctly the facts of the crime, and the proceedings thereafter held in the demanding State, would invalidate the warrant.

The Swanson case held that where the demand and the underlying papers showed that the person sought was demanded as one who had committed acts within this State, which acts had an effect in the demanding State, limiting proceedings to the requirements of Section 834, a warrant, reciting that the person was a fugitive from justice and thus extraditable under Section 829, was invalid. The court noted that under Section 834 the Governor had discretion to decide whether to order the surrender while under Section 829 there is no such discretion permitted, and that if the Governor had decided to comply with the demand Section 834 gave him discretion to impose conditions upon the surrender, while under Section 829 no such conditions could be imposed. The court further noted that 537

§ 

under Section 834 the act complained of must be a crime in both the demanding and the asylum State, while under Section 829 there is no such requirement. Thus, a warrant erroneously describing the section under which extradition was sought would, in the case involved, narrow the scope of the Governor's inquiry to the detriment of the accused.

Under Sections 836 and 837, the warrant issued as above stated is to be executed in the same manner as other arrest warrants. Section 838 provides for the production of the arrestee before a judge of a court of record. The arrestee may be confined in jail, when necessary, during his journey to the demanding State (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 840).

Sec. 322. Attacking the Extradition. Code Section 838 pro vides that after the arrest of an accused under a warrant issued by the Governor, the accused shall be taken before a judge of a court of record of this State "who shall inform him of the demand made for his surrender and of the crime with which he is charged, and that he has the right to demand and procure legal counsel; and if the prisoner or his counsel shall state that he or they desire to test the legality of the arrest, the justice or judge of such court of record shall fix a reasonable time to be allowed within which to apply for a writ of habeas corpus. When such writ is applied for, notice shall be given to the prosecuting officer of the county in which the arrest was made and in which the accused is in custody, and to the said agent of the demanding State." The scope of the judicial inquiry in the habeas corpus proceeding has been stated to be "(1) whether the papers upon which the warrant was issued by the Governor of the asylum State are sufficient, (2) whether the indictment charges a crime under the laws of the State seeking the extradition, (3) whether the crime was committed in the demanding State under its laws, (4) whether the accused was in the demanding State on the day when the crime was alleged to have been com- 538

EXTRADITION 

§ 322 mitted, (5) the identity of the alleged fugitive, (6) whether the person sought to be extradited is a fugitive from justice." (People ex rel. Higley v. Millspaw, 281 N.Y. 441, 445.) To the above list should be added, in cases in which it is alleged that the accused committed an act outside of the demanding State which intentionally resulted in a crime in the asylum State, (7) whether the acts complained of would constitute a crime if the effects thereof had been felt in the asylum State.

In the Higley case, the Court of Appeals went on to state: "We may not consider the sufficiency of the indictment as a pleading *** nor the possibilities resulting from the trial *** nor the merits of the defense to the indictment or the motive and purpose of the extradition proceedings." 

There, the relator had been indicted for failure to support his wife and for desertion. The court, inquiring pursuant to Section 391 of the Civil Practice Act, noted that the act charged was a crime under the laws of Maryland. Upon consideration of the affidavits submitted by the relator, and those submitted by the respondent, which papers it held made out a prima facie case for extradition, the court noted: "It then became necessary for the relator to establish by conclusive evidence that he was not in the demanding State when the crime was committed and is not a fugitive from justice." However, it was held that the relator had met this burden and had "overcome the presumption raised by the warrant," and the arrest warrant was declared void. "The extradition warrant issued by the Governor of the asylum State is presumptive evidence of the fact that the act complained of is a violation of the laws of the demand

[But] there is no reason why it should be conclusive. The evidence in a habeas corpus proceeding should be construed liberally in favor of the demanding 

State." (People ex rel. Tumminia v. Police Commissioner, 

178 N.Y.S. 2d 532.) So, in a habeas corpus proceeding in which an attack is made upon an extradition warrant, the arrestee must overcome those presumptions and infer- 539

§ 

ences if he is to prevail. However, "where the basis of the requisition is not an indictment but a complaining affidavit, closer scrutiny is called for to prevent a removal 'merely ignorant or wanton'." (People ex rel. Shurbut v. 

Noble, 4 App. Div. 2d 649, 169 N.Y.S. 2d 181.) Therefore, while there still remains a presumption of regularity attached to the extradition papers, a warrant not based on an indictment, with all its attendant safeguards, will elicit a closer examination of the validity of the extradition requisition; but "the affidavits in support of the warrant need not make such a showing as to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the [accused] was actually guilty of the crime." (Ibid.)

In the Shurbut case, supra, the accused person attacked a warrant of extradition, based upon complaining affidavits filed before a magistrate in Puerto Rico. The act complained of in the affidavits was the fraudulent delivery of checks with knowledge that the maker did not have sufficient funds to cover payment thereof. The checks involved were marked by the bank "Payment Stopped," and the accused person contended that there was insufficient evidence to show that he knew of any insufficiency of funds. The court noted that in certain conditions, under 

Puerto Rican law, the presumption of such knowledge attached and that it could not hold that the situation concerned was one in which such a presumption did not arise. 

The relator further contended that the purpose of the proceeding was to force his payment of a gambling debt, rather than the enforcement of the criminal law. The court held that it could not take cognizance of this, noting that the papers submitted in support of the warrant contained a substantial charge of a crime, and dismissed his writ.

The relator may attempt to prove, in the habeas corpus proceeding, that he was not present in the demanding State at the time of the commission of the crime, except where such proof is immaterial under Section 834 (People ex rel. 

Higley v. Millspaw, supra). This situation should be dis- 540

EXTRADITION 

§ 322 tinguished from an attempt by the accused to prove an alibi defense in the habeas corpus proceeding, a line of attack that will not be allowed, as going to the merits of the charge of crime. In People ex rel. Albert v. Commissioner, 111 N.Y.S. 2d 307, the extradition warrant rested upon an indictment for keeping gambling machines in the demanding State. The affidavits indicated that the accused was not present in the demanding State at the time of the crime. 

However, the District Attorney contended that Section 834 was applicable, and that defendant's sale of the devices in New York to other persons for use in Maryland constituted a crime in both States. The sale was the only act complained of. The court noted that the machines involved had been declared not to be gambling machines in prior judicial proceedings. Thus, their sale was not a crime in 

New York; Section 834 did not apply and the accused was released. In People ex rel. Fazio v. Warden, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 

383, the relator prevailed where the demand alleged that a crime had been committed in the demanding State, the crime involved being desertion of a child. The court noted that the demand was "patently made pursuant to the provisions of Section 831," and ordered his release despite the fact that the facts alleged in the affidavit supporting the demand "clearly" appeared to allege a situation within the coverage of Section 834. 

In People ex rel. Waldman v. Ruthazer, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 

428, a similar result was reached. There, the District Attorney relied upon Section 834 in the proceeding. However, the court noted that the extradition request and the supporting papers, which had been the basis for the Governor's action, relied upon and alleged their authority to be Section 830 and the United States Constitution. 

Therefore, the court held the demands "being predicated on the provisions of the Constitution and the laws of the United States, it is obvious that the relator did not have the benefit of the exercise of the discretion of the Governor of this State provided for in Section 834." In People v. 

Warden, 205 App. Div. 650, 200 N.Y.S. 81, the court refused 541

§ 

to try and hear evidence of an alibi defense, which evidence would have attempted to prove that the accused was not at the scene of the crime. The court noted that only evidence tending to disprove the accused's presence within the demanding State at the date of the crime was admissible. 

It has long been establised that the defendant may raise the issue of his identity in the habeas corpus proceeding. 

Attempts to prove that the relator is not the person named in the foreign affidavits or indictment are, however, met by a presumption that if the relator's name and the name of the person accused in the foreign papers are identical the person named is the person in custody (People ex rel. 

Teitelbaum v. Ryan, 181 App. Div. 404, 168 N.Y.S. 787).

If the accused person is the subject of a pending criminal prosecution within the asylum State, it lies within the discretion of the Governor either to surrender him to the demanding State, or to retain him in the asylum State during the prosecution and for the term of his imprisonment thereafter (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 848; People ex rel. 

Seiler v. Warden, 199 Misc. 570, 102 N.Y.S. 2d 969). The accused cannot claim the right to remain in the asylum State, either in prison or during the prosecution, as the determination on this point is one to be made solely by the 

Governor (People ex rel. Gallagher v. Hogan, 34 Misc. 

85,69 N.Y.S. 475).

The question of the admissibility of evidence of the sanity of the accused, either at the time of the commission of the offense, or at the time his extradition is sought, is discussed at length in a note in 114 A.L.R. 693. After discussing several cases, none of which had been decided by New York courts, it there stated that "There seem to be no actual judicial decisions of a court of last resort upholding the right to consider in extradition proceedings the mental condition of the alleged fugitive." The leading case in this area is Drew v. Thaw, 235 U.S. 432, 59 L. Ed. 

302, which held that whether the accused was insane at the time of the commission of the crime was not a question to 542

EXTRADITION 

§ 322 be determined in the extradition proceeding in the asylum State. 

In Brewer v. Turner, 165 Kan. 330, 194 Pac. 2d 507, the court found that "authority is generally to the effect that where habeas corpus is invoked to defeat extradition, whether the prisoner was insane at the time of the commission of the offense with which he is charged in the demanding State, or is presently insane, is not a question to be decided in a habeas corpus proceedings brought in the asylum State *** and that courts have no authority in habeas corpus proceedings to consider the present sanity or insanity of an alleged fugitive from justice." Since the purpose of allowing one to plead insanity at the time of trial is to assure that he will be able to present his best defense by requiring that he be able to know and understand all that is happening, and since the same reasoning would appear to apply to a habeas corpus proceeding, there appears to be valid ground for the argument that determining insanity then, not at the commission of the offense, would best effectuate the purposes of the rules of law in this area. Certainly until this avenue of argument is foreclosed by judicial decision, it should not be ignored in an applicable situation.

The failure of the affidavits submitted in support of an extradition requisition to meet the requirements of Section 830 may also be a basis for an attack. As stated by the 

Court of Appeals in People ex rel. Martini v. McLaughlin, 243 N.Y. 417: "When extradition is sought on the basis of an affidavit, there is need for closer scrutiny [than when the supporting charge is contained in an indictment]. * * *

The affidavits in this case, when read together, are seen to proceed upon information and belief. * * * The charges are vague, indefinite and general. They are made without specification of the sources of the information or the grounds of the belief. * * * they still omit a basic element of guilt. *** There is room for argument that any one of these grounds of criticism, standing alone, would be adequate." The accused was ordered discharged. The 543

§ 

above statement was quoted by the court in People ex rel. 

Namlik v. Wagner, 205 Misc. 520, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 237, to justify the release of an accused. There, the facts alleged to support the extradition were contained in a warrant issued by a Justice of the Peace of the demanding State, and an "Information for a warrant" containing statements made by a detective in the demanding State. The court noted that the information did not contain direct statements of fact but was made apparently upon information and belief, without oath that the facts stated in the warrant were true. Thus, the court stated, the insufficiency of the warrant was clear under the Martini case. 

Sec. 323. Uniform Act to Secure the Attendance of Wit nesses from Without a State in Criminal Proceedings. Code 

Crim. Proc., secs. 618-a through 618-c, contain the Uniform

Act to Secure the Attendance of Witnesses from Without a State in Criminal Proceedings. This act has been adopted in 43 other states and Puerto Rico. The states which have not adopted it, are Alabama, Alaska, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa and Michigan. It is discussed in the chapter of this work entitled "Subpoenas and Compelling Attendance of Witnesses." 544
