PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

Care should be exercised in the making of this motion. If made at too early a date, the District Attorney will be merely stirred into immediate action. Courts seldom dismiss an indictment unless the reasons therefor are cogent. But the courts will grant the prosecutor additional time and this extended period may be used by him to complete his investigation and prepare his case for trial. 

Before making this application, be certain that the District Attorney has no valid reason for the delay. However, if it is believed that the prosecutor is unable to proceed to trial because of the lack of evidence or the absence of necessary witnesses, counsel should not hesitate to make the motion.

Sec. 324. Definitions. Code of Criminal Procedure, section 

8, provides:

"In a criminal action the defendant is entitled *** To a speedy 

*** trial.” Civil Rights Law, section 12, contains a similar guarantee. Chapter VII of Title 12 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Sections 667 through 673) are the corollary statutory provisions which imple- 545

§ 

 ment these guarantees. The Sixth Amendment of the 

United States Constitution also provides that all defendants are entitled to speedy trial, but that section is applicable only to the Federal Courts (People v. Gearns, 14 

Misc. 2d 1010, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 875), except as it may be deemed to be embodied in the "due process" guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment against State action (In re Sawyer's Petition, 229 F. 2d. 805). The New York State

Constitution contains no similar guarantee. 

There is no absolute time limit within which a defendant must be brought to trial. Prior to the finding of an indictment, the statutes of limitation applicable to all crimes but murder fix the time within which prosecution must be commenced. Code Section 667 also prescribes the period of time, after a defendant is "held to answer" for crime, within which an indictment must be found. Once an indictment has been found, the Statute of Limitations stops running, and the defendant's only protection against an indeterminate period of waiting for trial is found in the above cited sections of the Code. "The speedy trial guarantee is intended to protect the accused, if held in jail to await trial, against prolonged imprisonment; [and] relieve him of the anxiety and public suspicion attendant upon an untried accusation of crime." (People v. Kraemer, 14 Misc. 2d 42, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 425.) Another purpose served by the requirement is "like statutes of limitation, it prevents him from being exposed to the hazard of a trial, after so great a lapse of time, that, 'the means of proving his innocence may not be within his reach'-as, for instance, by the loss of witnesses and the dulling of memory." (People v. Prosser, 309 N.Y. 353.)

The general principle applied by the courts was stated in People v. Winter, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 254: "defendant's right to a speedy trial is not absolute and unyielding, regardless of the circumstances causing the delay. The People's right to effective enforcement of the criminal law requires that allowance be made for a reasonable time to prepare for trial and for reasonable accommodation to the pressures 546

§ and needs of those charged with the duty of administering the law.*** no defendant has a right to complain of delay attributable to his own conduct. His right to a speedy trial is deemed waived if he delays the prosecution by dilatory pleas or motions or if he consents to or fails to object to a postponement sought by the District Attorney. ***

On the other hand, a waiver of the right to a speedy trial is not to be lightly inferred from equivocal circumstances.' 

99 Sec. 325. History. The right to a speedy trial was impliedly recognized in Magna Carta's words: "To no one will we *** deny or delay right or justice." After that, special writs were developed ("gaol delivery") and special judges were appointed to review, twice a year, the cases of all those in jail awaiting trial (II Co. Inst. 43). In 1679, with the passage of the Habeas Corpus Act, it was provided that prisoners indicted for treason or felony were to be tried at the next term of court or else released on bail, unless the prosecution, on oath, could show that its witnesses would not then be available. From this act, and the comparable statutes and constitutional provisions enacted by the States after the Revolution, developed the present law. A more complete history of this area of the law is set forth in Petition of Provoco, 17 F.R.D. 183, 196–199.

Sec. 326. Statutory Provisions. Under Section 667 of the 

Code, one held to answer for a crime may apply for a dismissal of the prosecution against him "if an indictment is not found at the next term of the court at which he is held to answer." The delay which this section seeks to prevent is, clearly, a delay in the finding of the indictment. Once an indictment has been found, an unreasonable delay prior thereto will not affect its validity, the injustice having been purged by the finding of the indictment (People v. 

Pearsall, 6 Misc. 2d 40, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 937). After indictment, the defendant's protection against an unreasonable delay in bringing the case on for trial is provided for in Section 668 of the Code: "If a defendant, indicted for a 547

§ 

crime whose trial has not been postponed upon his application, be not brought to trial at the next term of the court in which the indictment is triable, after it is found the court may, on application of the defendant, order the indictment to be dismissed, unless good cause to the contrary be shown." It is clear, from the wording of the above section, that sufficient notice to the District Attorney must be given so that he may oppose the application. 

The motion must be made in the court in which the indictment is pending (People ex rel. McGowan v. Warden, 155 

App. Div. 484, 140 N.Y.S. 864).

If the prosecution does sufficiently establish good cause for the delay, "the court may order the action to be continued from term to term, and in the meantime may discharge the defendant from custody, on his own undertaking, or on the undertaking of bail for his appearance to answer the charge at the time to which the action is continued." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 669.) If good cause for the delay is not established and the court orders the prosecution dismissed, the court must order the defendant discharged if he is in custody, and the exoneration of any bail that may have been deposited or return of any money deposited by him (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 670).

Section 671 of the Code empowers the court "either of its own motion, or upon the application of the District Attorney, and in furtherance of justice, to order an action, after indictment, to be dismissed." This section requires the filing of a written statement by the court containing the reasons for the dismissal. In effect, the section is a substitute for the power previously reposed in the Attorney General and the District Attorney to enter a nolle prosequi (People v. Quill, 11 Misc. 2d 512, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 

380). Section 672 eliminated this power. The court may order dismissal, under Section 671, upon many grounds such as the lack of evidence before the Grand Jury (People v. Stern, 33 Misc. 455, 68 N.Y.S. 732), among these grounds being lack of prosecution (People v. Nass, 61 N.Y.S. 2d 

229). There are two sections numbered 673 in the Code, 548

§ but both provide that dismissals for lack of prosecution do not constitute a bar to subsequent prosecution for the same offense, unless the offense charged is a misdemeanor or unless the dismissal is ordered after the defendant has initiated the procedures provided by Sections 669-a or 669-b. The last cited sections refer to trials of defendants imprisoned upon other charges either in this State (Section 669-a) or in other States (Section 669-b.) 

Sec. 327. Waiver. The right to a speedy trial is a personal right of the defendant and, therefore, may be waived by him. "Not only is such a waiver spelled out where both prosecution and defense agree upon or stipulate for a postponement, but it may be implied, for example, from the fact that the defendant, although present in court, interposes no objection to a postponement sought by the 

District Attorney." (People v. Prosser, 309 N.Y. 353.) “The contention that the prisoner did not have a speedy trial is a matter which must be raised at the trial, and may not be raised years after the trial by writ of habeas corpus.' (People ex rel. Lee v. Jackson, 285 App. Div. 33, 135 N.Y.S. 

2d 345, affirmed, 309 N.Y. 676.) See, also, People v. Russo, 3 Misc. 2d 916, 155 N.Y.S. 2d 765, holding that the defendant's failure to raise this objection at trial precluded his later application, based on the same ground, for vacation of the judgment of conviction. The Lee case holding, above, does not mean that the defendant is barred from availing himself of the writ of habeas corpus while being held for trial. "While Section 668*** offers a remedy to a defendant to move to dismiss for lack of prosecution in the court where the indictment is pending *** habeas corpus may also be a proper remedy. See People ex rel. Estes v. Warden, (1880) 22 Hunter 18, 11 Weekly Digest 271." (People ex rel. Seiler v. Warden, 199 Misc. 570, 102 N.Y.S. 2d 969.)

It has been held that "Failure of the defendant to act cannot be construed as a waiver on his part." (People v. 

Brandfon, 4 Misc. 2d 466, 157 N.Y.S. 2d 864.) Since the burden of moving the prosecution forward rests upon the 549

§ 

prosecution, "which has the duty of seeing that the defendant is speedily brought to trial * a mere failure of the defendant to take affirmative action to prevent delay may not, without more, be construed and treated as a waiver." (People v. Prosser, supra.) This does not make the defendant's acquiescence, by failure to object to a request for an adjournment by the District Attorney, any the less a waiver. The defendant, being aware of the request and of his right to object, by remaining silent in effect acquiesces in the request for the delay and will not be heard to complain of it afterwards (People v. Prosser, supra). 

Similarly, once the trial has commenced the defendant must raise his objections and not wait for the results of the trial before acting (People v. Romano, 7 Misc. 2d 565, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 301; People v. White, 2 N.Y. 2d 220, 159 N.Y. 

S. 2d 168, appeal dismissed, 353 U.S. 969, 1 L. Ed. 2d 1133; 

People v. Bogue, 1 App. Div. 2d 289, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 791).

As pointed out in People v. Bogue, supra, permitting the defendant to defer the objection to the termination of the trial would leave him an unwarranted option. "He could go to trial when the case is moved and, if the verdict is in his favor, let it stand, but if it is against him, argue that it was too late to try the case and that the indictment should have been dismissed." If the defendant pleads guilty, knowing the nature and consequences of his act and with the advice of counsel, it will be deemed a waiver if the objection of undue delay is not raised prior to sentencing (People v. Knowles, 7 Misc. 2d 222, 159 N.Y.

S. 2d 293). A plea of guilty to a lesser included offense, while a motion to dismiss for lack of prosecution is pending, will also be deemed a waiver of the right to object to the lack of a speedy trial (People v. Bishop, 2 Misc. 2d 541, 153 N.Y.S. 2d 961). Of course, there can be no waiver if the defendant is unaware of the pendency of the prosecution (People v. Prosser, supra). 

Sec. 328. Who May Claim Right. Section 668 of the Code applies, by its terms, to any "defendant, indicted for a 550

§ crime," and the meaning of the phrase is clear. "Its benefits may be claimed * * * by any person under indictment, whether he be imprisoned to await trial on the pending charge, whether he be admitted to bail or whether he be a prisoner already serving a sentence in the same jurisdiction for a different crime. (People v. Prosser, 309 N.Y. 353.) 

Section 667, applicable where an indictment has not yet been found, and designed to insure the speedy finding of indictments or the release of prisoners charged without indictment being found, applies to persons held to answer for crimes. As stated in People v. Gearns, 14 Misc. 

2d 1010, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 875: "The meaning of the words 'held to answer' is to be found in Section 208 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure. * * * It is clear that 'held to answer' refers to situations where the Magistrate holds a defendant either for the Court of Special Sessions or for the action of the Grand Jury." In the Gearns case, the defendant, who had been serving a term upon another charge, was denied his motion to dismiss a charge then pending in the Felony Court division of the Magistrate's Court, it being held that he was not being "held to answer" for the charge he was moving against. 

Sec. 329. What Constitutes Undue Delay. Both Sections 

667 and 668 require dismissal of the prosecution, or indictment, in the event of undue delay in the proceeding, "unless good cause to the contrary be shown." The burden lies upon the prosecution to establish good cause for the delay, once the defendant shows the fact of delay (People v. Mudra, 12 Misc. 2d 438, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 224;

People v. Prosser, supra). The Mudra case also indicated that it will be presumed that the defendant has been prejudiced by the delay; therefore, it is not necessary that the defendant show any prejudice in fact. In accord with the general rule that defendants may not complain of delay caused by themselves are the cases holding that any period of delay attributable to some act of the defendant will 551

§ 

be excluded from the computation of the total period of delay (People v. Martin, 99 App. Div. 372, 91 N.Y.S. 486; time lag caused by defendant's demurrer and appeal from disallowance therof excluded from period).

Court-Caused Delay. Delay caused by the courts, such as delay attributable to a crowded calendar, has been treated in different ways in different jurisdictions. In 

People ex rel. Ianik v. Daly, 142 N.Y.S. 297, the court indicated its belief that the statutory protection afforded defendants against delay was designed to protect against delay caused by the prosecution and that "unless it appears that his detention is due to want of preparation on the part of the People to go on with the trial, coupled with resistance to postponement on his part and a demand for a speedy trial," the defendant may not have the prosecution dismissed. It appears that the last phrase of the quoted statement is no longer valid under the Prosser case reasoning. 

Whether that court's determination that delay caused by the court is not within the period of the delay contemplated is sound, remains unclear. Some cases from other jurisdictions have indicated that delay caused by the courts is not within the period of delay proscribed by the statute. (See, e.g., State v. Kuhnhausen, 201 Ore. 506, 272 Rac. 2d 

225, but compare, for the opposing view, Martens v. Gaffney, 230 Iowa, 712, 298 N.W. 801.) A later New York case, indicating a view in accord with that of the Ianik and 

Kuhnhausen cases, is People v. Winter, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 254.

However, in the Winter case, the court did note that "the People may not rely on the claim of calendar congestion as a cause for delay. For no matter how busy the various trial parts of the court are, such calendar pressure may not be advanced as a reason for delaying a trial of an indictment more than thirty-eight months in one instance, and some twenty-seven months in two other instances where the People have chosen to give the 'right of way' of trial to innumerable other indictments." The court nevertheless indicated that, where the facts do not show such extreme 552

§ dilatoriness and disregard of the customary, though not inflexible, rule that indictments be tried in chronological order, delay caused by calendar congestion would not be considered "undue delay." "Section 668 of the Code of

Criminal Procedure was designed as a safeguard, not against delay in prosecution due to calendar congestion, but rather against delay in prosecution traceable to laches on the part of the prosecution." (People v. Winter, supra.)

That defendant is imprisoned in another State has been held not to be good cause for delay of over thirty months in the prosecution since, under Code Sections 837 and 632, proceedings could have been instituted to secure defendant's presence in this State (People v. Brandfon, 157 N.Y. 

S. 2d 864). 

Sec. 330. Appeals. The lower court's determination of a defendant's motion to dismiss for lack of prosecution is reviewable on appeal from a judgment of conviction. However, no appeal lies specially from the order itself, prior to conviction, because it is intermediate in nature and not appealable under the Code. (See People v. Chierieleison, 3 

N.Y. 2d 170, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 726.) “If * * * the Court erred in denying the motion to dismiss, the error was one of law and was apparent upon the record. Remedy by way of appeal from the judgment of conviction rendered the same day, which would have brought up for review the denial of the motion to dismiss was immediately available to defendant." (People v. Smith, 4 App. Div. 2d 914, 167 N.Y.S. 

2d 129.)

If the defendant is successful in his motion to dismiss, or if the court dismisses the action, sua sponte, under Code Section 671, the People have an appeal from the dismissal (Silver v. Gassman, 12 Misc. 2d 58, 171 N.Y.S. 2d 314, aff'd. 

6 App. Div. 2d 694, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 277; Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 518). For further discussion of rights to appeal and procedure thereon, see the chapter of this work entitled "Appeals." 553

§ 

Sec. 331. Imprisoned Defendants. Under Section 669-a of the Code, a defendant imprisoned in this State may demand that any untried indictments, informations or complaints pending against him be brought to trial. Copies of the demand must be served upon the District Attorney of the county in which the charge is pending and the court having jurisdiction over that charge. The demand must be accompanied by a certificate of the Commissioner of Correction describing the prisoner's detention period, the time remaining to be served, the amount of good-conduct time earned, and the time when the prisoner will be eligible for parole, together with the record of all parole decisions previously made. All the prisoner need do is give written notice of his imprisonment, including therein a request for the trial, to the Commissioner of Correction who is obligated to forward the request to the proper District Attorney and court. If the trial is not commenced within one hundred eighty days after the request is received by the District Attorney and the court, the action must be dismissed, with prejudice, and an order to that effect entered by the court. The court is, however, empowered to grant "any necessary or reasonable continuance for good cause shown in open court, the prisoner or his counsel being present." If the prisoner escapes after making the demand, the request shall be deemed void. In 

People v. Gearns, 14 Misc. 2d 1010, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 875, the court noted that a defendant's failure to utilize this procedure would prevent him from claiming lack of a speedy trial upon the untried charges. However, utilization of the procedure authorized by Section 669-a does not constitute a waiver of the defendant's right, at the trial, to move to dismiss for past delay in the prosecution, under Section 

668 (People v. Segura, 12 Misc. 2d 279, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 218).

Section 669-b of the Code (the interstate "Agreement on Detainers") established a similar procedure for prisoners held in other States, party to the agreement. In general, the agreement provides that prisoners may request. the final disposition of untried charges against them in 554

§ other States which are party to the agreement (the Federal Government is deemed a State for the purpose of the agreement), and that such request operates as a request for the disposition of all untried charges pending in the other jurisdiction and as a waiver of extradition by the prisoner with respect to all such charges. The waiver also concerns any further extradition to the other State after trial, for sentence. It also operates as a consent by the prisoner to be brought into any court where his presence might be required for trial, and as a consent for the prisoner's return to the State of his original imprisonment after the trial. The agreement further provides a uniform and simple method for the States to secure prisoners imprisoned in out-of-State prisons for trial in other States, without resort to special agreements or extradition proceedings. See Chapter entitled "Extradition."

Sec. 332. Re-Indictment. As noted, Code Section 673 provides that a dismissal for lack of prosecution is not a bar to another indictment for the same crime, if the crime is a felony (People v. Schwartz, 6 App. Div. 2d 459, 179 N. 

Y.S. 2d 372). The flaw in this rule is obvious; most of the purposes behind the requirement of a speedy trial may be thwarted if a new indictment can be found after dismissal is ordered. The delay which required dismissal of the first indictment will not necessarily again require dismissal of the new indictment, for the period of the delay is measured from the date of the finding of the indictment (People v. 

Wilson, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 842). Indeed, it is difficult to advance arguments in favor of moving for a dismissal on this ground, at least before the statutory period of limitation has run, for such action will probably only have the effect of spurring the prosecution on in procuring a subsequent indictment and moving that indictment on for trial within the proper period. The Wilson case contains a critique of the provisions of Section 673, the court noting: “Although this court believes that the reasons laid down in People v. 

Prosser, supra, should prevail over the provisions of Sec- 555

§ 

tion 673 *** so as to bar a re-indictment of the defendant for the same crime charged in the original indictment which the Appellate Division saw fit to dismiss on the defendant's motion for failure to grant the defendant a speedy trial, the court is constrained to follow the law of this State which measures the undue delay *** from the time the particular indictment to which the motion is addressed was found. Such a dismissal does not bar the District Attorney from proceeding to obtain a new indictment under Section 673 *** if the offense charged *** be a felony." No cases have been found upholding a due process argument in which it might be contended that the application of Section 673 is unconstitutional. 1 556

CHAPTER 29  Sec. 333. Definitions Sec. 334. History Sec. 335. Motion for Separate Trial of Jointly Indicted Defendants Sec. 336. Motion for Severance of Counts Sec. 337. Grounds for Motion Sec. 338. Grounds for Severance of Counts Sec. 339. Effect of Joint Trial upon Challenge PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

A motion for severance and separate trial, under Section 279, should be made whenever counsel believes that the indictment contains certain counts that might tend to arouse the emotions of the jury or even of the court because of the nature of the alleged crime or the manner in which it was committed. Only in this way would it be possible to obtain fair consideration from the jury on the several counts in the indictment. A defendant is placed in a more favorable position if he is tried for one charge rather than on a combination of charges. However, the danger exists that your client now faces two or more trials instead of one, if the application is granted.

Generally, an accused is assured greater success if he is tried alone than if he is tried together with another defendant. Therefore, a motion under Section 391 should be made for a separate trial where your client is jointly indicted with another. However, there may be occasions when the co-defendant may be made your client's scapegoat or depicted as the real culprit. At other times, your client might be in need of certain information or testimony that could only be elicited from the co-defendant. Under such circumstances, counsel should weigh carefully the advantages to be derived from a joint trial, before considering moving for a separate trial. 557

§ 

 Sec. 333. Definitions. In the chapter entitled "Indictments," 

joinder of several counts in one indictment was discussed. 

Similarly, that chapter discussed the joinder of several defendants in one indictment. The purpose of this chapter is to consider how a defendant, charged in one indictment of more than one count or in several indictments comprising different charges which are to be tried together, may obtain the separate trial of each count; and how a defendant charged with other defendants in one indictment, or to be tried with other defendants in one trial, may secure a trial separate from that of his co-defendants. 

The statute applicable to the joinder of offenses in an indictment is Code Section 279, which allows such joinder when the acts complained of are "connected together or constitute *** parts of a common scheme or plan, or * * * 

constitute *** crimes of the same or a similar character."

The section, however, goes on to provide that "where the charges involve two or more acts or transactions constituting crimes of the same or a similar character which are neither connected together or parts of a common scheme or plan, the court, in the interest of justice and for good cause shown, may, in its discretion, order that the different charges set forth in the indictment or information or indictments or information, be tried separately." 

The power to join several defendants in the same trial is recognized by Section 391, which states: "Defendants, jointly indicted, may be tried separately or jointly in the discretion of the court." The different problems concerning the separate trial of each charge against a defendant, or of each defendant charged, are discussed below. 

Sec. 334. History. At common law, defendants who had jointly committed an offense could be jointly indicted therefor. However, some early cases held that such joinder was permissible only where the act complained of, by its nature, could be jointly committed (Rex v. Weston, 93 

Eng. Rep. 740 [1726]). When a proper joinder of several defendants in the indictment had been effected, "The com- 558

§ mon law had been that where two or more defendants were jointly indicted they were to be tried jointly or separately in the discretion of the court. *** The Revised 

Statutes in 1829 * * * changed the common-law rule by providing that when two or more persons shall be jointly indicted for any felony, any one defendant requiring it shall be tried separately. This remained the law *** until 

*** 1926." (People v. Doran, 246 N.Y. 409.) In 1926, the present section 391 was enacted.

Under the early common law, two or more offenses could not be joined in the same count. But the joinder, in one indictment, of several counts each charging a different offense was allowable if the acts complained of were of the same nature and subject to the same procedures upon the trial (Orfield, Crim. Proc. from Arrest to Appeal, 261). In People ex rel. Pincus v. Adams, 274 N.Y. 447, which upheld, as constitutional, Section 279 of the Code, the Court of Appeals described the history of the law relating to the joinder of offenses in an indictment: "There is nothing unique about a statute which provides that a person may be tried in a single trial for a number of crimes of a similar nature or connected together as part of a common plan. *** Such procedure was not unknown to the common law." As with the joinder of defendants at common law, it appears that the court could, in its discretion, order the prosecution to elect upon which count of the indictment the defendant would be tried if the joinder could adversely affect the defense of the action (Hawker v. People, 75 N.Y. 487).

The rule is now embodied in Section 279, above quoted, and Section 279-a: "After the commencement of the trial, the people shall not be required to elect between the counts of any indictment, except that for good cause shown, and in the interest of justice, the court may, in its discretion, require an election as to one or more counts." Both of these sections were enacted in 1936 when dissatisfaction with the efficacy of the existing sections, in their application to cases involving crime on an organized scale, became wide- 559

§ 

spread.

These sections were based on the Federal statutes, then Section 557 of Title 18, United States Code, now Rule 14, Fed. Rules of Criminal Procedure. (See Bulletin 64, 

Ass'n. of the Bar of the City of New York, Comm. on Crim. 

Cts., Law and Proc. [1936].)

Sec. 335. Motion for Separate Trial of Jointly Indicted Defendants. When and How Made. The motion for a separate trial is directed to the trial court in its discretion (People v. Gaskill, 132 Misc. 318, 228 N.Y.S. 731; People v. Fisher 

249 N.Y. 419). It may be made either by the defendant or the prosecution (People v. Stockholm, 1 Parker Cr. 424), and the burden of establishing the reason for the severance rests upon the movant (Application of Capone, 28 N.Y.S. 

2d 475). The motion should be made upon notice to the District Attorney who will, usually, be allowed to submit affidavits in opposition thereto (Application of Capone, 28 N.Y.S. 2d 435). The motion papers must, of course, contain a statement of the grounds for the application (People v. 

Kassis, 145 Misc. 493, 259 N.Y.S.339).

Review. In People ex rel. Singer v. Rogers, 254 App. Div. 

865, 4 N.Y.S. 2d 905, an application to the Appellate Division for an order prohibiting a Supreme Court Justice from proceeding with a separate trial against the defendant, after severance entered at Special Term, was denied, it being held that the application was in effect, an unlawful appeal from the order of severance. "The discretion given by the statute as to joint trials cannot be exercised arbitrarily and is subject to review by an appellate court which has jurisdiction to pass upon questions of fact.***But the decision of the trial court upon such a motion is merely a ruling during the course of a trial, and as such is reviewable only on appeal." (People v. Buck, 6 

App. Div. 2d 528, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 1007.) In People v. Lombard, 4 App. Div. 2d 666, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 419, the court indicated that failure to move for a separate trial waived the right later to object to joint trial. However, the holding there is upon another point. Although no New York cases 560

§ dealing with the time for such motion decided since the enactment of the present section have been found, the general rule appears to be that failure to move for a separate trial prior to the completion of the swearing of the jury and the commencement of the prosecution's opening statement constitutes a waiver of the right to so move (See 

Little v. State, 173 So. 172 [Ala.]; Moss v. State, 108 S.W. 

2d 782 [Ark.].) In People v. Marcus, 220 App. Div. 697, 222 

N.Y.S. 456, affirmed 246 N.Y. 637, the Appellate Division considered the defendant's motion for a separate trial on the merits, although it was made after the empanelling and swearing of the jury. In People v. Schwartz (1st Dept., Feb. 16, 1960), the Appellate Division reversed a conviction, based on failure to grant a separate trial, where the motion was made after the opening statements. However, in People v. Lashowitz, 166 Misc. 40, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 98, the court indicated that it believed that one of the reasons for the denial of the motion in the Marcus case was the fact that it was made after the jury had been sworn. 

Where grounds for the separate trial do not become apparent until late in the trial, it would appear that the above rule would be unnecessarily harsh in its application. 

See Pointer v. United States, 151 U.S. 396, 402, for the statement of a more reasonable rule applied to the severance of counts. While there have been no decisions found on the point, it would appear clear that the prosecution cannot appeal from an order granting a separate trial.

Sec. 336. Motion for Severance of Counts. Practice. The motion for severance of counts is directed to the trial court, in its discretion (People v. Hayner, 198 Misc. 101, 97 N.Y.S. 

2d 64; People v. Babb, 194 Misc. 5, 88 N.Y.S. 2d 212). While it should be made as early as possible, the Code apparently recognizes that such a severance may be ordered even "After the commencement of the trial" (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 279-a). The motion should be made as soon as the grounds indicating that defendant's rights may be prejudiced by proceeding further are discovered. See 561

§ 

Pointer v. United States, 151 U.S. 396. The rules concerning the practice upon the motion are similar to those applicable in motions for separate trials.

Sec. 337. Grounds for Motion. Separate Trials. The test to be applied by the court in determining whether a separate trial should be ordered has been stated to be: "Will a separate trial impede or assist the proper administration of justice in a particular case and secure to the accused the right of a fair trial?" (People v. Snyder, 24 N.Y. 491.) In the same decision, the court further stated: "The decision of the trial court rendered before the trial is dictated by a reasonable interpretation based on the facts then disclosed. 

The decision of this court rendered upon a review of the trial itself rests upon determination of whether the prophecy has been realized." Thus, the defendant's application upon review of this point is not confined to the facts known at the time the trial court denied the application. 

Some of the circumstances which have been held significant in this determination by the courts follow: "The fact that one defendant has made a confession which will be admissible against himself but not against a codefendant may be a circumstance which enters into the court's consideration of whether a joint trial would be fair." (People v. Snyder, supra; People v. Feolo, 282 N.Y. 276. Compare 

People v. Schemnitzer, 142 Misc. 16, 254 N.Y.S. 480 for an indication of a contrary view.) The surrounding of the defendant by a large group of codefendants having criminal records (People v. Hines et al., 168 Misc. 453, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 

15). "The intensely antagonistic interests of the two defendants," in a case where one of the defendants confessed, charging that the moving defendant was the principal schemer in the planning of the crime, and where, admittedly, the moving party did not actually participate in the killing (People v. Wargo, 149 Misc. 461, 268 N.Y.S. 400).

The fact that one of the codefendants was to be a witness for the prosecution, combined with a confession by another co-defendant (People v. Lashowitz, 166 Misc. 640, 3 N.Y.S. 562

§ 2d 98). The fact that one of the defendants was a prisoner and would have to be brought into court as such (People ex rel. McCarthy v. Kanze, 200 Misc. 907, 112 N.Y.S. 2d 12).

Factors which have been considered not of sufficient import to warrant the granting of a separate trial are: "the criminal activities and history of a co-defendant have been publicized by our daily papers more extensively than [moving defendant's]." (Application of Capone, 28 N.Y.S. 

2d 435.) The fact that one of the defendants was a recentlydisbarred lawyer (People v. Hines, 168 Misc. 453, 6 N.Y.S. 

2d 15).

It should be noted, also, that while the factors above mentioned have been considered of substantial import in their specific cases, the presence of any one or combination of several of these factors in another case does not guarantee a successful appeal from a denial of a motion. for a separate trial. The question on appeal is whether the trial court abused its discretion in the denial of the motion, not whether the appellate court agrees with the trial court's decision (People v. Marcus, 246 N.Y. 647; People v. Doran, 246 N.Y. 409). But where, on appeal, it appears that the conviction would not have resulted save for the introduction of a co-defendant's confession, it has been held that a refusal to grant a separate trial was an abuse of discretion (People v. La Ruffa, 2 App. Div. 2d 765, 153 

N.Y.S.2d 352).

The most recent case concerning this problem is People v. Schwartz, 21 Law. Rep. News, No. 22, p. 3 (1st Dept., Feb. 16, 1960), which reversed a defendant's conviction.

After the opening statements, but prior to the presentation of evidence to the jury, a motion for a separate trial had been made and denied. The moving defendant's counsel had contended that there were indications of a lack of resistance to the prosecution by a co-defendant. The Appellate Division noted that the trial court's decision should not be disturbed, in the absence of abuse of discretion, but it also noted the possibility that the trial court felt at the time of the application that there was insufficient evidence 563

§ 

to sustain the motion. The court noted that "A preliminary inquiry at that stage of the trial would not have been amiss," and also stated that the existence of a confession by a co-defendant would not, alone, warrant a separate trial where the trial court limited its effect by proper instructions. "But when it is apparent that the practical effect of a confession and additional statements made by a cooperative defendant which are received in evidence on the trial is to jeopardize the rights of a co-defendant to a fair trial, or to accuse such co-defendant of the commission of other or additional crimes for which he is not on trial, the conviction thereby obtained cannot stand." 

Sec. 338. Grounds for Severance of Counts. As noted in the chapter on "Indictments," one "may be indicted in separate counts for different crimes, or the same crime alleged to have been committed in a different manner or by different means, arising from the same act or transaction." (People v. Josie, 206 Misc. 704, 134 N.Y.S. 2d 283.) Further, a person may be indicted for different crimes of a related nature in different counts in the same indictment (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 279). The same section also provides for the consolidation of several indictments for trial where the crimes charged are of a similar nature. However, Section 279 further empowers the court to order separate trial of different charges joined together for trial where the crimes charged "are neither connected together nor parts of a common scheme or plan." Section 279-a empowers the court to require the prosecution to elect between counts after the commencement of the trial. 

It is not clear, under the wording of these sections, whether the court has power to direct separate trials of separate charges arising out of the same transaction or part of a common scheme or plan, if a trial of all of such charges at one time would be obviously prejudicial to a defendant's rights. (See People v. Hayner, 198 Misc. 101, 97 N.Y.S. 2d 64.) Compare People v. Babb, 194 Misc. 5, 88 

N.Y.S. 2d 212, where separate trials were ordered of differ- 564

§ ent charges when all the charges were related to defendant's commission of abortions, and the court found: "The indictment does not allege any plan or scheme, merely the commission of several abortions on different people at different times." 

In People v. Luciano, 277 N.Y. 348, the Court of Appeals stated: "Where it does not appear in the indictment that the charges involving acts of a similar nature are connected together or parts of a common scheme or plan, the court has discretion to order them tried separately." This implies that if the charges are so related, no such discretion exists. In People v. Kaplan, 86 N.Y.S. 2d 916, the court held that where the acts were part of a common scheme and of a similar nature, "the court is absolutely barred from exercising any discretion whatsoever." This holding appears correct on the basis of Section 279. However, Section 279-a contains no such limitation. The problem that arises concerns the situations to which Section 279-a applies. Where the indictment charges only one offense, but in different counts alleges that it was committed by different means, it has been held, and it now appears to be the recognized rule, that the right to compel an election in such a case lies within the discretion of the court (People v. 

Kellogg, 105 App. Div. 505, 94 N.Y.S. 617; People v. Wilson, 109 N.Y. 345). It has also been held that where the different counts have been inserted in good faith, to protect the prosecution in the event of a variance between the proof and the indictment, no election will be required of the prosecution (People v. Sullivan, 173 N.Y. 122).

Where the different counts charge different offenses, and it appears that the defendant may be prejudiced by their joint trial, it would appear that Section 279-a would apply and that an election may be required. The section was enacted in 1936; prior to that time the Court of Appeals had stated: "The accused has not a legal right to put the prosecution to an election, when more than one offense is charged upon which he will proceed." (People v. Davis, 56 N.Y. 95.) After that statement, the Court of 565

§ 

Appeals went on to indicate that the decision might lie within the discretion of the court. In People ex rel. Maurer v. Jackson, 2 N.Y. 2d 259, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 203, the Court of 

Appeals stated: "Either a defendant may or may not be prosecuted to a final judgment for several related crimes in a single indictment. Were a prosecutor required to elect on which crime to proceed, the problem would be solved at the outset. New York, however, has chosen to provide otherwise. Section 279 *** authorizes the joinder of re lated crimes in separate counts in a single indictment. Section 279-a expressly provides that 'the People shall not be required to elect between the counts of any indictment' except in the court's defined discretion. Our courts have so held."

It now appears, therefore, that the Court of Appeals would hold that Section 279-a gives the court discretion to order an election wherever the original joinder was proper. 

This rule appears consistent with the language of Section 

279-a and with some early New York cases. See, for example, Kane v. People, 8 Wend. 203, where the court stated: "In cases of felony, where two or more distinct and separate offenses are contained in the same indictment, the court, in its discretion, may compel the prosecutor to elect upon which charge he will proceed." See, also, Peo ple v. Costello, 1 Denio 83; People v. Court of General Ses sions, 13 Hun 395; In re Quin, 6 City Hall Rec. 63. 

In general, however, election will not be required. In 

People v. Wright, 136 N.Y. 625, it was held that no election was required between a charge of attempted rape and one of killing by unknown means. In People v. Moore, 26 

Misc. 168, 56 N.Y.S. 802, no election was required between armed robbery and assault. Compare People v. King, 53 

N.Y.S. 2d 894, where, after defendant had been indicted upon a six-count indictment, he successfully moved for a severance of the counts involving one victim from the counts involving the other. The court noted that the acts, though of a similar nature, were not part of a common scheme, and then stated that the decision, which lay within 566

§ its discretion, had to "be based upon the premise as to whether this defendant will get a fair trial when called upon to defend himself against the indictment as it is now drawn. There is a strong conviction in my mind that regardless of the force of evidence, or the lack of it, in either of the charges, that the jury, in deciding the facts, may *** be swayed into convicting the defendant of both such charges because *** the crimes charged are identical in nature. If the defendant were upon trial for either of the sets of charges herein contained, the other sets would be inadmissible as evidence of intent. * * * However under the indictment as presently drawn, the picture of both sets of crimes would be before the jury. This situation would work as an advantage to the People and incidentally a disadvantage to the defendant. The amendment of 1936 to 

Section 279 was a drastic departure from the forms of pleading theretofore existing. It may be assumed, for that reason, that the Legislature saw fit to incorporate into the statute the remedy to appeal to the court's discretion in cases where unfairness might result." While the case is not a holding upon the effect of Section 279-a, the language quoted indicates arguments that can be advanced in support of a motion for severance under that section. 

In People v. Jack, N.Y.L.J., p. 12 (Mar. 15, 1960), while sustaining the demurrer to an indictment the court indicated that severance of counts was proper. Defendant was charged, in the first count, with conspiracy and, in three other counts, with the commission of substantive crimes twenty-one months prior to the date of the conspiracy. The court held that the conspiracy count "should be tried separately and thus avoid the appearance created by the joinder of an implication of guilt on the part of the defendant as to crimes alleged in counts two, three and four." As all the charges appeared related, this court apparently believed it was not limited, in ordering a severance, to unrelated counts. As above noted, supra, the New 

York Code sections in this area were derived from the Federal statutes. When they were enacted it was intended 567

§ 

that the relevant Federal cases might be precedents in the interpretation of the new Code provisions (Bulletin 64, Ass'n. of the Bar of the City of New York, Comm. on Crim. 

Cts. Law and Proc. [1936]). The test most commonly used under the comparable Federal statute (Rule 14, Fed. Rules of Crim. Proc.) in determining whether a severance of counts will be required, is whether the evidence used to sustain one count would be admissible and relevant to sustain the other. (See, e.g., McNeil v. United States, 85 F. 2d 

698, and cases cited under Rule 14.) Under the Federal rule, election may be required wherever it appears that either the prosecution or defense will be prejudiced by a joinder of counts or defendants. 

Sec. 339. Effect of Joint Trial Upon Challenges. Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 360: "When several defend ants are tried together they cannot sever their challenges, but must join therein." If all defendants do not join in the challenge, the juror will be sworn in (People v. Label, 298 

N.Y. 243). Where several defendants are tried jointly for murder in the first degree (where, ordinarily each defendant would have thirty peremptory challenges (Code Crim. 

Proc., sec. 373), it has been held that all defendants together are entitled to thirty peremptory challenges among them as if there were only one defendant. See chapter of this work entitled "Trial." 568
