Requests to Charge Sec. 361. Conduct of Jurors Sec. 340. Extent of Coverage. The trial, especially in a criminal case, is the heart and the crux of the litigation. 

As such, it involves innumerable details of law and practice, not to mention countless aspects of strategy and tactics. But in this work we must find the space to cover in broad and practical fashion the whole field of criminal 569

§ 

procedure in our State, and to guide and inform the practitioner at every stage of his criminal cause. We cannot, for that reason, be as detailed and precise as in a more specialized work.

The law and the rules of evidence applicable to criminal trials, the fine and detailed points of maneuver which form part of every trial-all these we necessarily leave for future works to deal specifically with those subjects. It is our object and our intention, however, to provide the New York lawyer with a dependable and useful compilation of the basic knowledge indispensable in the trial of a criminal cause in this jurisdiction.

Sec. 341. The Issues and Mode of Trial. The defendant, hav ing been charged by indictment, or by information in an inferior court, raises a triable issue by his plea, which may be either "not guilty" or "former conviction or acquittal of the same crime." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 354.) This issue thus joined, in a proper case for jury trial, must be "tried by a jury in the county in which the indictment was found, unless the action be removed. ***" (Code of Crim.

Proc., sec. 355.) It should be noted that reference to a trial of the issues is not deemed to include hearings on collateral issues. Thus, an inquisition after indictment to determine defendant's sanity, not part of the trial itself, is not such trial as to justify the issuance of a commission to examine witnesses therein (People v. Haight, 3 N.Y. Cr. 60), and a proceeding after conviction, to determine a charge of prior convictions brought under repeater statutes, is merely collateral and not a trial of the issues presented by the indictment (People v. Reese, 258 N.Y. 89, followed 258 N.Y. 557).

The purpose and function of the issue so raised is to determine the guilt or innocence of the defendant, as thereby presented. In reaching this determination, he is entitled to a presumption of innocence "until the contrary be proved; and in case of a reasonable doubt whether his guilt is satisfactorily shown, he is entitled to an acquittal." 570

THE TRIAL 

§ 341 (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 389.) Furthermore, where "there is reasonable ground of doubt, in which of two or more degrees he is guilty, he can be convicted of the lowest of those degrees only." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 390.)

The trial by jury, long preserved as a right, is also a jurisdictional requirement (Cancemi v. People, 18 N.Y. 

128). However, since Article I, section 2, of the State Constitution of 1938 included a novel provision for waiver of a jury in non-capital cases, such waiver may now be effected, as in that section stated, “by a written instrument signed by the defendant in person in open court before and with the approval of a judge or justice of a court having jurisdiction to try the offense." No statute has been enacted to implement this constitutional provision, but it has nevertheless been held to be self-executing, "clear and specific, subject only to the permission granted the Legislature to standardize procedure." (People v. Carroll, 4 App. Div. 

537, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 265, affirmed 3 N.Y. 2d 686.)

The trial must proceed in the presence at all times of the judge presiding, whose temporary absence, at least in felony trials, has been held necessarily fatal to jurisdiction (People v. Silver, 240 App. Div. 259, 269 N.Y.S. 765). As to the defendant's presence, Section 356 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "If the indictment be for a misdemeanor, the trial may be had in the absence of the defendant, if he appear by counsel, but if the indictment be for a felony the defendant must be personally present." In capital cases, the defendant may not waive his right to be present at all times, but in others, it was stated in People v. O'Keefe, 281 App. Div. 409, 120 N.Y.S. 2d 349, affirmed 

306 N.Y. 619: "***a defendant may waive any objection growing out of his absence during a part of the trial." 

The right to a public trial is a "fundamental privilege of the defendant in a criminal prosecution." (People v. Jelke, 308 N.Y. 56, 51; see Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 8; Civil Rights

Law, sec. 12.) This is mandated by Section 4 of the Judi ciary Law, but that section excepts proceedings and trials in cases for seduction, abortion, rape, assault with intent 571

§ 

to commit rape and sodomy, in which, it provides, "the court may, in its discretion, exclude therefrom all persons who are not directly interested therein, excepting jurors, witnesses and officers of the court." It was nonetheless pointed out, in the Jelke case, supra, that a court has inherent power to limit the number of spectators "in the interests of health or for sanitary reasons or in order to prevent overcrowding or disorder" and "may temporarily exclude spectators, where necessary to enable an immature or emotionally disturbed witness to testify." So, also, despite the lack of statutory provision therefor, the Court of Appeals stated in People v. Cooke, 292 N.Y. 185, 191, that a motion to exclude witnesses should, in the court's discretion, "be granted as of course, especially in a capital case." 

There is no fixed rule as to the time, after the plea, when the trial proceeds. This, obviously, depends on calendar conditions, court sittings and many other factors. However, "the defendant is entitled to at least two days to prepare for his trial, if he requires it." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 357.) It should also be noted that criminal actions are allowed a statutory preference over civil actions and proceedings (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 7-a), with the exception of certain civil actions brought on behalf of the People. (C. 

P.A., sec. 139.) Adjournment or continuance of the trial, on either party's motion, rests in the sound discretion of the court (People v. Jackson, 111 N.Y. 362). Denial of such motion, in abuse of discretion, depriving the defendant of due process, has been held to warrant reversal of a conviction (People v. Gordon, 262 App. Div. 534, 30 N.Y.S. 2d 

625) and vacation of a judgment in coram nobis proceedings (People v. McManus, 17 Misc. 2d 247, 181 N.Y.S. 1001). 

Sec. 342. Empanelling the Jury. Where the trial is by jury, the first procedure is the empanelling and swearing-in of the jury. The judge may, when he deems it advisable, direct the calling of not less than one nor more than four "alternate jurors," drawn in the same manner, subject to the 572

THE TRIAL 

§ 342 same challenges as, and seated with, the sworn panel of twelve, ready to substitute for any of the sworn jurors who may die or become otherwise unable to serve before the final submission of the case (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 385-a). 

Elaborate provision for examining, challenging, and trying the challenges of, persons called as trial jurors is made by the Code. The practitioner will find that most of the procedures provided for are rarely used except in the most serious cases-those involving capital offenses and trials which have attracted widespread public interest. In the routine of the day-to-day practice, informality is prevalent and carefully-evolved procedures developed for the protection of the defendant are often waived by usage and acquiescence, if not expressly. Nevertheless, these protective procedures are always available, and even apply to trials of minor offenses in Justices' and Police Courts. (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 62). However rare his need to apply them, the practioner should nevertheless be familiar with, and alert to demand the application of, all these procedures when the situation warrants.

The choosing of the jury centers around the examination by counsel of prospective jurors, challenging of those who are deemed undesirable for legal cause or for strategic or psychological reasons, and the procedure on such challenges. The Code provides two categories of challenges: first, a challenge to the panel, or "challenge to the array" as it was often called at common law; and, second, challenge to individual jurors (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 359). The order in which these challenges is made is prescribed in Section 386 of the Code, as follows: "1. To the panel. 2. 

To an individual juror, for a general disqualification. 3. To an individual juror, for implied bias. 4. To an individual juror, for actual bias. 5. Peremptory." Under this section and Section 385, challenges must first be made by the People and then by the defendant, in the order named, and the People cannot be required to go through all their challenges before the defendant makes a challenge upon any 573

§  

ground, although in practice all the challenges for cause may be grouped (People v. McGonegal, 62 Hun 622, 17 N. 

Y.S. 147, affirmed 136 N.Y. . 62). 

Sec. 343. Challenge to the Panel. "A challenge to the panel is an objection made to all the trial jurors returned and may be taken as well to the panel returned for the term, as to an additional panel ordered to complete the jury.' (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 361.) "A challenge to the panel can be founded only on a material departure, to the prejudice of the defendant, from the forms prescribed by the 

Judiciary Law *** or on the intentional omission * * * * to summon one or more of the jurors drawn." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 362.) It is worthy of note, in the light of occurrences of the last few years, that this challenge is the one which has been commonly used to test the constitutionality and propriety of jury drawing and summoning procedures; in this connection, it must be observed that it will not suffice to test constitutionality in the absence of specific allegation of the respects and details in which unconstitutionality is asserted (People v. Ebelt, 180 N.Y. 470). The challenge to the panel has been the principal procedure used in civil rights cases. (See, for example, United States v. Flynn, 216 F. 2d 354, certiorari denied 348 U.S. 909, 99 L. 

Ed. 713, rehearing denied 348 U.S. 956, 99 L. Ed. 747; 

United States v. Dennis, 183 F. 2d 201, affirmed 341 U.S. 

494, 95 L. Ed. 1137.)

Section 363 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires that this challenge be taken before a juror is sworn (City of New York v. Mason, 1 Abb. Pr. 344), "and must be in writing, specifying distinctly the facts constituting the ground of challenge" (People v. Petrea, 30 Hun 98, affirmed 92 N.Y. 128), although it may thereafter be withdrawn, waived or abandoned by the defendant (People v. 

Borgstrom, 178 N.Y. 254; Cox v. People, 80 N.Y. 500;

Pierson v. People, 79 N.Y. 424), and the objection to its not being in writing may be waived by the People's failure to object (People v. Wilber, 61 Hun 620, 15 N.Y.S. 435). It has 574

THE TRIAL 

§ 344 been held that the written challenge need not be verified (Cox v. People, 80 N.Y. 500).

When the challenge is taken, the adverse party may except thereto as a means of denying the sufficiency of the facts alleged as a ground of challenge, whereupon "the court must proceed to try the sufficiency of the challenge, assuming the facts alleged therein to be true." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 364.) If, on the exception, the court deems the challenge sufficient it may allow the challenge or, if justice require it, permit the excepting party to withdraw his exceptions and deny the facts. In this event, or if no exception has been taken, the adverse party may deny the facts alleged in the challenge (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

365), and the court proceeds to try the questions of fact on the challenge (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 366). The trial of the challenge proceeds with examination of "the officers, whether judicial or ministerial, whose irregularity is complained of, as well as any other persons *** to prove or disprove the facts alleged as the ground of the challenge." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 367.) If the court allow the challenge, either upon the exception or the denial of the facts, the jury must be discharged "so far as the trial of the indictment in question is concerned"; if it disallow the challenge, the court must direct the jury's empanelling (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 368). 

Sec. 344. Challenges to Individual Jurors. "Before a juror is called, the defendant must be informed *** that if he intend to challenge an individual juror, he must do so when the juror appears, and before he is sworn." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 369.) There are two alternative methods of examining and swearing jurors, referred to in People v. 

Fromen, 284 App. Div. 576, 578, 132 N.Y.S. 2d 376, 378–379, appeal dismissed 308 N.Y. 324, as "the full-box method where no juror is to be sworn until the jury is complete" and, alternatively, "to swear each juror separately as he is examined and accepted by both sides." Of their use, the court there stated, at page 578 of 284 App. Div., page 378 575

§ 

of 132 N.Y.S. 2d: "The trial court may determine the practice to be followed in that respect. ***It would seem that one or the other of the two methods of forming the jury may be employed by the trial court but that a combination of the two after the drawing has commenced may not be. 

It is evident that a switch from the full-box method *** to the individual method of acceptance and swearing could be most unfair to a defendant."

The prospective jurors are first examined by both parties. Most commonly, this is done informally, although either party has the right to demand that they be sworn for "voir dire" examination pursuant to the statute.

In the discretion of the court the more formal procedure may be instituted from the start, and this is almost always done in capital cases or those considered of special importance. The parties then may challenge any of the talesmen, either peremptorily or for cause (Code of Criminal Procedure, sec. 370). As we have already indicated, supra, these challenges are made in the order indicated by Sections 385 and 386 of the Code, and must be made before the juror is sworn, although the court's discretion for good cause to set aside a juror before evidence is given is nevertheless preserved (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 371; see People v. Hughes, 137 N.Y. 29; People v. Carpenter, 38 Hun 490, affirmed 102 N.Y. 238). It has been held neither error nor ground for reversal that the court refuse to entertain objections as to a juror's qualifications after the start of testimony (United States v. Rosenstein, 34 F. 2d 630, certiorari denied 280 U.S. 581, 74 L. Ed. 631 and 280 U.S. 

602, 74 L. Ed. 647). 

Sec. 345. Peremptory Challenges. "A peremptory challenge is an objection to a juror, for which no reason need be given, but upon which the court must exclude him." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 372.) "Peremptory challenges shall be allowed in the following number: 1. If the crime charged be punishable with death, thirty for the regular jury; and three for each alternate juror; 2. If punishable with im- 576

THE TRIAL 

§ 346 prisonment for life, or for a term of ten years or more, twenty for the regular jury; and two for each alternate juror; 3. In all other cases, five for the regular jury; and one for each alternate juror." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 373.) "When several defendants are tried together they cannot sever their challenges, but must join therein." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 360.) When two defendants tried jointly did not join in a peremptory challenge, the court's ruling that the juror be sworn was sustained (People v. 

Lobel, 298 N.Y. 243, reargument denied 298 N.Y. 920).

And where more than two defendants were tried together, it was held error to accept peremptory challenges made by a majority vote of counsel, one defendant refusing to evince assent or dissent (People v. Hull, 251 App. Div. 40, 296 N.Y.S. 216). All defendants tried together are permitted only the number of challenges allowed to one and cannot multiply the number allowed by law, as above stated, according to the number of defendants (People v. 

Doran, 246 N.Y. 409; see, also, People v. Kassis, 145 Misc. 

493, 259 N.Y.S. 339). 

Sec. 346. Challenges for Cause. "A challenge for cause is an objection to a particular juror, and is either 1. General, that the juror is disqualified from serving in any case; or 

2. Particular, that he is disqualified from serving in the case on trial." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 374.) General causes of challenges are a conviction of felony, or the want of any of the qualifications prescribed by the Judiciary Law (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 375). The provisions of the 

Judiciary Law thus referred to are Section 504, applying to counties of less than 100,000 population; Section 596, covering New York City; and Section 662, dealing with counties of more than 100,000 population and those smaller counties which have elected to come within Article 18 of the Judiciary Law. Despite certain procedural variations as between the respective articles of the Judiciary Law, all these provisions conform in requiring a juror to be a 577

§ 

citizen of the United States, over 21 and not over 70 years of age, the owner of a minimum of $250 in real or personal property or the spouse of a person who is such owner, a resident of the county, and not to have been convicted of a felony or a misdemeanor involving moral turpitude. 

Certain designated public officers and officials are specifically disqualified by reason of their offices. 

Particular causes of challenge are actual bias, which is defined as a "state of mind *** in reference to the case, or to either party, which satisfies the court, in the exercise of a sound discretion, that such juror cannot try the issue impartially and without prejudice to the substantial rights of the party challenging ***" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

376); and implied bias, including the causes enumerated and set forth in Section 377 of the Code. 

Section 377 includes the following under implied bias: "1. Consanguinity or affinity within the ninth degree, to the person alleged to be injured by the crime charged, or on whose complaint the prosecution was instituted, or to the defendant; 2. Bearing to him the relation of guardian or ward, attorney or client, or client of the attorney or counsel for the People or defendant, master or servant, or landlord or tenant, or being a member of the family of the defendant, or of the person alleged to be injured by the offense charged, or on whose complaint the prosecution was instituted, or in his employment on wages; 3. Being a party adverse to the defendant in a civil action or having complained against, or been accused by him in a criminal prosecution; 4. Having served on the Grand Jury which found the indictment, or on a coroner's jury which inquired into the death of a person whose death is the subject of the indictment; 5. Having served on a trial jury, which has tried another person for the crime charged in the indictment; 6. Having been one of a jury formerly sworn to try the same indictment, and whose verdict was set aside or which was discharged without a verdict after the cause was submitted to it; 7. Having served as a juror, in a civil action brought against the defendant, for the act charged 578

THE TRIAL 

§ 347 as a crime; 8. If the crime charged be punishable with death, the entertaining of such conscientious opinions as would preclude his finding the defendant guilty; in which case he shall neither be permitted nor compelled to serve as a juror."

The procedure on the challenge to the individual juror is the same as that indicated on a challenge to the panel, above (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 383). The challenge may either be excepted to on the ground of insufficiency, or denied on the facts alleged. It may then be tried, on "voir dire" examination under oath of the juror as a witness (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 383). Other witnesses may also be examined, and the rules of evidence applying to a trial are then equally applicable (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 384). 

If the court allow the challenge, the juror must be discharged; if it be disallowed, the juror is accepted on the panel (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 382).

Sec. 347. Order of Trial. The order of the proceedings, where the trial is by jury, has been prescribed by Section 

388 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as follows: "1. The 

District Attorney, or other counsel for the People, must open the case; 2. The defendant or his counsel may then open his defense; 3. The District Attorney, or other counsel for the People, shall then offer the evidence in support of the indictment; 4. The defendant or his counsel may then offer the evidence in support of his defense; 5. The parties may then, respectively, offer rebutting testimony, but the court, for good reason, in furtherance of justice, may permit them to offer evidence upon their original case; 6.

When the evidence is concluded, unless the case is submitted to the jury on either side, or on both sides, without argument, the defendant or his counsel must commence, and the counsel for the People conclude the argument to the jury; 7. The court must then charge the jury." 

These provisions apply in all criminal courts sitting with juries, whether courts of record trying felonies or misdemeanors on indictment, or courts of special sessions try- 579

§ 

ever, ing misdemeanors and offenses on information (People v. Wallens, 297 N.Y. 57). It does not appear that there has ever been an authoritative and specific determination as to their applicability in trials without juries, and there is no specific statute so providing. It must be deemed, howthat they are in such cases equally applicable, saving the specifically inappropriate portions of the statute, in the light of the statement of the Court of Appeals in People v. Koerner, 154 N.Y. 355, 368, as follows: "The provisions of Section 388 are a mere formulation of the rules which formerly existed in regard to the order of proof in civil and criminal cases. But it has always been regarded as within the discretion of the court to vary those rules." 

Sec. 348. Motions Before Trial Proceeds. Of the objections to the indictment which may be raised by demurrer, "the objection to the jurisdiction of the court over the subject of the indictment or that the facts stated do not constitute a crime, may be taken at the trial, under the plea of not guilty ***" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 331.) It has also been stated, as in People v. Reiser, 240 App. Div. 36, 269 

N.Y.S. 573, that "an indictment will be dismissed on grounds other than those specified in Section 331 of the Code of Criminal Procedure when the constitutional rights of a defendant are involved."

The right to make these motions, and to take these objections at any point before the close of the trial, is thus preserved by statute. Generally, it is most appropriate when they are based on the indictment alone that the motions be made before any evidence has been presented. 

It is also proper, at this time, for the People to move to amend the indictment or the bill of particulars, or both, and this may also be done during the course of the trial. 

The bases on which such motions may be made, and amendments allowed, are dealt with in Sections 293 through 295 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and are considered elsewhere in this work, under appropriate chapter titles. 580

THE TRIAL 

§ 349 Sec. 349. Opening to the Jury. After the jury has been empanelled and sworn, Section 388 prescribes: "The District Attorney, or other counsel for the People, must open the case * * *." This requirement, the courts have repeatedly held, is mandatory, and cannot be waived by either or both parties (People v. Romano, 279 N.Y. 392, 395; People v. McLaughlin, 291 N.Y. 480, 483). The People's opening serves as a statement of the charges the defendant will be required to meet, and the defendant's right to such statement is a basic one. Thus, in People v. Levine, 297 N.Y. 

144, 147, while the court conceded that "the reading of a detailed indictment might conceivably serve the purpose of an opening," it nevertheless held, despite the defendant's failure to make appropriate objection, that the People's failure to open was a "defect in the proceedings, which could not be waived or cured, and is fundamental ***." In the case of an indictment charging twenty-two defendants with riot and conspiracy, one of the grounds on which the Court of Appeals based its reversal was that "the District Attorney in his opening of the case should have made some statement as to the part each of the individual defendants played in the alleged crime * * *" (People v. Gray, 303 N.Y. 660.)

Nor is the mandatory nature of this requirement restricted to the trial of felonies in courts of record. In 

People v. Wallens, 297 N.Y. 57, 61, the court stated: “* * * when the accused-as here-demands and has been accorded a trial by jury, the order of trial from then on must follow prescribed procedure, without distinction as to whether the charge is a felony or a misdemeanor." In a trial in special sessions, the procedure on trials under indictments applies "as far as may be" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 62). In one case, it was held that the People's opening statement is mandatory in a non-jury trial in Special Sessions (People v. Sperbeck, 5 Misc. 2d 849, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 

968; but, contra, People v. Barbano, 10 Misc. 2d 847, 176 

N.Y.S. 2d 52, and People v. Macomb, 9 Misc. 2d 1027, 174 581

$

N.Y.S. 2d 330; and, specifically disapproving, People v. 

Duskin, 11 Misc. 2d 945, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 527).

Statements made on the People's opening should be material to the issues, and should not be so presented as to inflame the jury or prejudice the defendant. So, a prosecutor's reference to heinous and revolting acts alleged to have been committed by the defendant, which were foreign to the crime charged, brought about reversal of a conviction (People v. Wolf, 183 N.Y. 464). The latitude to be allowed counsel, however, is within the sound discretion of the trial court and will not be disturbed on appeal unless that discretion has been clearly abused (People v. Stone, 125 App. Div. 250, 109 N.Y.S. 199). It is the customary practice for defendant's counsel to object to improper statements immediately on their making, and for the trial court to rule on them and, where deemed necessary, to admonish and limit the prosecuting counsel. People v. 

Latta, 231 App. Div. 7, 245 N.Y.S. 692, dealt with this question and the court there stated: "While freedom of advocacy must not be held too strictly in check it must not exceed the bounds of ordinary decency and decorum. (People v. Fielding, 158 N.Y. 542, 547.) *** Even in cases of clearest guilt*** it is the duty of the District Attorney to refrain from overzealous advocacy. (People v. Slover, 232 N.Y. 264.) The duty of defending counsel is not less or different.' 99 The court has the power, most rarely used though it be, on motion of the defendant to dismiss the indictment on the People's opening statement. To do so, it must find that the issues are so limited that the proof offered by the People is insufficient to establish the crime alleged, and there appears to be no triable issue of fact (People v. Cory, 124 

Misc. 532, 208 N.Y.S. 768). Such dismissal is based on the rule that the admissions of counsel as to the facts are conclusive, obviating the need for testimony. 

A significant difference appears in the statement of the next order of procedure, the opening by defendant or his counsel (People v. McLaughlin, 291 N.Y. 480, 483). Here, 582

THE TRIAL 

§ 350 in subdivision 2 of Section 388, the word used is may, instead of the must of the prior subdivision. Opening by the defendant is at his option; while most frequently employed it may, for strategic or psychological reasons, be waived. The restrictions on overzealousness and impropriety imposed on the District Attorney apply equally to defendant's counsel (People v. Latta, 231 App. Div. 7, 245 

N.Y.S. 692, quot. supra).

Sec. 350. The People's Direct Case and Defendant's Motions 

Thereon. The openings completed, the District Attorney proceeds with the presentation of his evidence "in support of the indictment" (Code of Criminal Procedure, sec. 388, subd. 3). It is common practice, especially in trials for felony, to move for the exclusion of witnesses from the courtroom to avoid the danger that stories given from the stand may emerge trimmed to those heard. While there is no statutory provision therefor, the Court of Appeals has stated that, in the exercise of the trial court's discretion, this motion should "be granted as of course, especially in a capital case." (People v. Cooke, 292 N.Y. 185, 191.) Witnesses are then called, examined directly and crossexamined in the usual manner. Objections to questions, motions to strike answers and the court's rulings thereon are similar to those in civil cases (Code of Criminal Procedure, sec. 392; People v. Grant, 14 Misc. 2d 182, 179 N.Y. 

S. 2d 384).

The standard rules of competency of witnesses apply, but a special statutory rule affects the testimony of children actually or apparently under the age of twelve years. 

If the child "does not in the opinion of the court or magistrate understand the nature of an oath, the evidence of such child may be received though not given under oath, if, in the opinion of the court or magistrate such child is possessed of sufficient intelligence to justify the reception of the evidence." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 392.) But the statute goes on to provide that "no person shall be held or convicted of an offense upon such testimony unsupported 583

§ 

by other evidence." It was held in People v. Klein, 266 N.Y. 

188, that a child under twelve is presumed to be incompetent to be sworn as a witness until the presumption is overcome by a preliminary examination, as provided by 

Section 365 of the Civil Practice Act. 

On their direct case, without reference to or reliance upon any evidence which may thereafter be adduced by the defendant, the People must establish the defendant's guilt. It therefore is appropriate that the defendant move, at the close of the People's direct case, to dismiss the indictment on the ground that the People's evidence was insufficient (People v. Hendrickson, 264 App. Div. 903, 35 N. 

Y.S. 2d 770, affirmed 289 N.Y. 740). Because the burden imposed on the People in criminal cases is to prove the defendant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 389), the erroneous denial of the defendant's motion does not put him to his proof; he need not produce any proof, whatever, in such a situation. Where the defendant nevertheless took the stand and his testimony tended to establish his guilt, as the People's proof had not, the Appellate Division reversed the resulting conviction (People v. Raubvogel, 217 App. Div. 713, 216 N.Y.S. 891; see People v. Fazio, 5 N.Y.S. 2d 195). 

Sec. 351. The Defendant's Case. Here, again, the next step is optional with the defendant. He "may" offer evidence in his defense, as provided by subdivision 4 of Section 388. On the other hand, if he feels sufficiently confident that the People's case has been insufficient, he may elect not to do so. 

At his own option, the defendant may testify as a witness. 

Failing to do so, "his neglect or refusal to testify does not create any presumption against him." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 393.) However, on taking the stand he may be cross-examined generally, even as to matters about which he has not testified in direct examination (People v. Tice, 131 N.Y. 651), and his conduct as a witness is measured by the same standards as applied to other witnesses (People v. Connolly, 253 N.Y. 330). He thereby subjects himself to 584

THE TRIAL 

§ 352 all presumptions which may arise from what he does, the prohibition against comment on his failure to testify being no longer operative (People v. Leavitt, 301 N.Y. 113), and the District Attorney's reference to any failure on his part to deny guilt becomes proper (People v. Tybus, 219 N.Y. 18).

Although he is under no obligation to disprove guilt (People v. Burlingame, 213 App. Div. 331, 210 N.Y.S. 535, followed 214 App. Div. 793, 210 N.Y.S. 539), it is nonetheless appropriate and desirable that the defendant produce evidence controverting that adduced by the prosecution. 

It is sufficient for acquittal if he can raise a reasonable doubt (People v. Ellmore, 277 N.Y. 397). It is also within the scope of the proof he should present to negative any presumptions of fact upon which the People's case can properly rely. Thus, he may produce proof to show that the case comes within an exception of the penal statute (People v. Tarlow, 249 App. Div. 224, 291 N.Y.S. 918), as when, in a prosecution for violation of a zoning ordinance, defendant was required to prove the pre-existence of the non-conforming use on which he relied (People, on complaint of Lewis v. Kollender, 169 Misc. 995, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 252).

Sec. 352. Objections and Exceptions to Admission of 

Evidence. The practice, with respect to objections and exceptions in criminal trials, despite certain essential substantive differences and constitutional restraints, has been conformed to that in civil actions (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 420-a; Twelfth Annual Report of Judicial

Council, 1946). The basic rule remains that enunciated in 

Section 417 of the Code: "The court must decide all questions of law which arise in the course of the trial." 

Objections to questions asked and evidence offered are available on the grounds that the same is incompetent, irrelevant or immaterial. What constitutes such cannot here be considered, but is more properly the subject of a work on evidence. That the evidence tendered is not within 585

§ 

the acts charged by the indictment, or contemplated by the penal statute (see, for example, Penal Law, sec. 1290-a) is a proper objection. But, by the same token, failure to take such objections, which must be made at the time the question is asked or the proof offered, makes them unavailable (Perry v. People, 86 N.Y. 353; People v. Ramistella, 306 

N.Y. 379, 385). So, also, the objection that the cross-examination is unnecessarily extended to the prejudice of the defendant, while properly addressed to the court's discretion, may be waived if not duly made (People v. Du Byk, 285 

App. Div. 1025, 139 N.Y.S. 2d 577, affirmed 309 N.Y. 833).

While the stated exception to the court's ruling on an objection may be dispensed with, except with respect to the charge and requests to charge (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

420-a), the objection must be stated for the record to be effective.

Motions to strike out unresponsive testimony constitute a familiar part of trial procedure, as are those to strike testimony which is hearsay. In any situation in which the objection to admissibility, not appearing in the question asked, becomes apparent in the course of the answer, the motion to strike should be made (People v. Fisher, 223 N.Y. 

459). It is not erroneous for the court to deny the motion when the objection could have been made to the question itself before the answer was given, but was not (Pontius v. People, 82 N.Y. 339). However, if the answer is only objectionable in part, but the motion is directed to the whole, denial of the motion is proper (People v. Grano, 265 

App. Div. 231, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 668, reversed other grounds 

290 N.Y. 771).

Sec. 353. Rebuttal and Subsequent Evidence. After the presentation of defendant's case, rebutting evidence may be introduced by both sides. In furtherance of justice, the court may also permit either party to reopen its case. But in People v. Smith, 124 Misc. 65, 207 N.Y.S. 555, the court held that permitting the People to reopen their case after submission was a practice which, while not meriting re- 586

THE TRIAL 

§ 354 versal, should not be encouraged. At any rate, the trial court's discretion in this regard has been sustained, even in extremes, as when the Court of Appeals refused to reverse where reopening was permitted after final argument had begun (Wilke v. People, 53 N.Y. 525), and where further examination of a witness was permitted after the jury had been charged and had retired (People v. Ferrone, 204 

N.Y. 551).

Sec. 354. Examination of Witnesses. Examination of wit nesses proceeds, as we have seen, in the prescribed order, subject to modification in the trial court's discretion. Proof in a criminal case is offered and received in any of the manners permitted and provided for in civil trials (People v. Warner, 152 Misc. 607, 274 N.Y.S. 689, affirmed 244 

App. Div. 833, 270 N.Y.S. 639, affirmed 269 N.Y. 597), and the mechanics of examination and rules of evidence, except in a few matters otherwise specifically provided for in the Code, are the same as those in civil actions (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 392).

The oath, or an affirmation when required by the witness' conscientious scruples, is administered in one of the manners provided in Sections 360 to 365, inclusive, of the Civil Practice Act. The examination is conducted in the accustomed question and answer form and, upon completion of direct examination, cross-examination follows. As stated in People v. Ramistella, 306 N.Y. 379, 384: "The right to cross-examine is basic in our judicial system (Alford v. United States, 282 U.S. 687, 75 L. Ed. 624; People v. Becker, 210 N.Y. 274, 304-305; People v. Cole, 43 N.Y. 

508, 512-513), and has been from earliest times (Friedel v. Board of Regents of University of New York, 296 N.Y. 

347, 352). Although in the last-cited case we held that 'once the right has been accorded, the extent of cross-examination rests largely in the discretion of the tribunal, whose exercise thereof is not reviewable if not abused,' such a denial or limitation of cross-examination has been upheld only where it has related to collateral matters, or where 587

§ 

the right itself has been abused (Friedel v. Board of Regents of University of New York, supra, 296 N.Y. at page 

352; People v. Braun, 158 N.Y. 558, 567-569; McGuire v. 

People, 48 How. Prac. 517; White v. McLean, 57 N.Y. 670, 671, opinion in 47 How. Prac. 193; Langley v. Wadsworth, 99 N.Y. 61, 63).'

The criminal trial judge may take an active part in the examination of witnesses where questioning is necessary to elicit significant facts, to clarify or enlighten an issue, or merely to facilitate the orderly and expeditious progress of the trial (People v. Mendes, 3 N.Y. 2d 120). He may properly intervene to clear up obscure points, but this must be done with restraint, being basically in the province of the cross-examination rather than in that of the judge (People v. De Maio, 243 N.Y. 588). It has been held erroneous for a judge to indicate impatience with the defendant (People v. Carlsonakas, 241 App. Div. 232, 272 N.Y.S. 35, affirmed 265 N.Y. 565), to say as matter of law that the defendant's evidence is false (People v. Ohanian, 245 N.Y. 

227), or to interrogate the defendant on a prior hearing before a magistrate (People v. Russo, 251 App. Div. 176, 295 N.Y.S. 457).

Sec. 355. View of Premises. In proper circumstances, and under prescribed supervision, the jury may be given the opportunity to view the place where the crime is charged to have been committed, or in which any material fact occurred (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 411, 412). This procedure, while designed to assist the jury in understanding the matter and arriving at a correct result (People v. 

Thorn, 156 N.Y. 286), is, nevertheless, not considered part of the trial itself (People v. Landers, 264 N.Y. 119). Such view may be ordered, according to Section 411, when "in the opinion of the court, it is proper ***" and is entirely in the discretion of the trial court (People v. Buddensieck, 103 N.Y. 487). Nevertheless, the authority to exercise that discretion is statutory, and there must be substantial com pliance with the statute (People v. Klein, 213 App. Div. 

588

THE TRIAL 

§ 356 

66, 209 N.Y.S. 594). Section 411 enjoins that the jury must be "conducted, in a body, under charge of proper officers" and the officers, it is required by Section 412, "must be sworn to suffer no person to speak to or communicate with the jury, nor do so themselves, on any subject connected with the trial, and to return them into court without unnecessary delay, or at a specified time."

The time, or stage of the trial, when the view may be allowed is not prescribed and a trial court's permitting it after having submitted the case to the jury, to permit them to check up on the testimony of the People's witnesses, was held to be a proper exercise of the court's discretion (People v. Landers, 264 N.Y. 119). Where, however, for all practical purposes the trial was actually permitted to be continued at the scene, the conviction was reversed (People v. Klein, supra). In another case, where the judge purported to reconvene court at the scene, but conducted no proceedings there, it was held irregular, but no fatal error (People v. Pisano, 142 App. Div. 524, 127 N.Y.S. 204). In the language of Section 411, the place must be shown to the jury "by a judge of the court, or by a person appointed by the court for that purpose." A refusal to permit the defendant and his counsel to accompany the jury was held an infraction of the defendant's rights (People v. Palmer, 43 

Hun 397, affirmed 109 N.Y. 413); their presence at the view, however, unlike that at the trial, may be waived by the defendant (People v. Thorn, 156 N.Y. 286).

Sec. 356. Mistrial and Discharge of Jury. At any stage of the trial, when the court, in its discretion, determines that the trial should not with propriety be permitted to continue, it may declare a mistrial and discharge the jury. The traditional device by which this is done, and the expression most frequently utilized in doing it, is "withdrawal of a juror." The practice is a familar one, and of long standing, but is provided for by statute only in certain specified situations; for the rest, and in most cases where the procedure is employed, it finds its authority in the inherent dis- 589

§ 

cretion of the court. It may be effected either on motion of a party or on the court's own motion, and the motion to "withdraw a juror" is the common procedure employed by counsel in raising objection to seriously prejudicial occurrences or conduct deemed to be inimical to a fair trial. In 

People ex rel. Epstein v. Lawes, 164 Misc. 58, 297 N.Y.S. 

386, it was stated: "* * * the general principle may be laid down that the trial court may discharge a jury and order a new trial in the exercise of its discretion during the course of a trial when there is substantial reason therefor." 

Where the jury is discharged on defendant's motion or consent, he cannot thereafter assert an objection, nor claim his rights have been derogated thereby. But his failure to object cannot be deemed a consent (People ex rel. 

Stabile v. Warden, 139 App. Div. 488, 124 N.Y.S. 341, affirmed 202 N.Y. 138). However, where "circumstances have arisen during the trial that warrant the exercise of the court's discretion to use such power, as illness, death, tampering with witnesses, undue contact by the witnesses with the jury, inflammatory and prejudicial remarks by either side" which "clearly show that a fair and unbiased trial could not properly have been had" and "were cumulative episodes that compelled the court to exercise its discretionary power to discharge the jury," it was held that discharging the jury was proper and "did not jeopardize the defendant's right as to bar a second trial." (People v. 

Epstein, 8 Misc. 2d 364, 170 N.Y.S. 2d 577.)

As completely and aptly summed up in People v. Montlake, 184 App. Div. 578, 581, 172 N.Y.S. 102, the law on the subject may be concisely outlined as follows: (1) where the jury is discharged during trial, but before final submission to it: (a) a substantial reason arising, making discharge necessary in the interests of justice, the judge is empowered to do so, and the defendant cannot plead former jeopardy when again placed on trial (People v. Olcott, 2 

Johns, Cas. 301, People v. Goodwin, 18 Johns. 187); (b) if the reason is inadequate and the defendant does not consent, the discharge constitutes a former jeopardy (People 590

THE TRIAL 

§ 356 ex rel. Herbert v. Hanley, 142 App. Div. 421, 423); (2) where the jury is dismissed after submission, it may be done only pursuant to Section 428; in any other event, the defendant may have a plea of former jeopardy or release in habeas corpus (People ex rel. Stabile v. Warden, 139 

App. Div. 488, 124 N.Y.S. 341, affirmed 202 N.Y. 138; see also People ex rel. Brinkman v. Barr, 248 N.Y. 126).

Any occurrence which either makes impossible the legal continuation of the trial, or which prejudices the defendant's right to a fair and impartial trial, is a proper basis for mistrial and discharge of the jury. Inasmuch as it "is undoubtedly true that the judges of a criminal court before which a trial is commenced cannot be changed during its progress" (People v. Bork, 96 N.Y. 188, 198), the death or disability of the judge occurring during the trial impels a mistrial, and a juror's becoming sick and disabled has the same result (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 416; but see provision for alternate jurors, Section 358-a). Improper or unjudicial conduct by the court, in prejudice of defendant's rights, requires a mistrial (People v. Mendes, 3 N.Y. 

2d 120, 121), as do improper statements, prejudicial remarks or improper conduct by the District Attorney (People v. Tasciello, 300 N.Y. 425, 430).

Statutory provision for a mistrial is made in Section 428 of the Code, but this applies only "After the jury have retired to consider their verdict * * * before they shall have agreed thereon," and only where there is an injury or casualty affecting the defendant, the jury or one of them, or the court, where after the lapse of time which seems reasonable to the court they declare themselves unable to reach a verdict, or when with leave of court the parties consent to a discharge. Both as to such statutory mistrials, and also as to those made in the court's inherent power, the reason for the discharge must be entered upon the minutes (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 429) and "except where the defendant is discharged from the indictment *** the cause may be again tried at the same or another term." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 430.) 591

§ 

All of the sections dealing with the discharge of a jury before submission deal with specific situations, rather than with the court's power to do so in general, and were not intended to "limit the power of the court to discharge a jury." (People v. Fishman, 64 Misc. 256, 119 N.Y.S. 89.)

Two of them, however-Sections 400 and 401-have been held unconstitutional. Section 400 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure provides that the court may, where the facts proved constitute a crime of a higher nature than the one for which the defendant has been indicted and tried, discharge the jury, suspend proceedings and hold the defendant to answer any new indictment which may be found for the higher offense. Section 401 requires the court to proceed to try the defendant again on the original indictment where the Grand Jury thereafter dismisses or finds no indictment at or before the next term. These provisions have been held to be contrary to public policy and in contravention of the injunction against double jeopardy contained in Article I, sec. 6, of the State Constitution (People ex rel. Blue v. Karney, 181 Misc. 981, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 691, affirmed 292 N.Y. 655).

Section 402 of the Code provides for discharge of the jury where it appears the court has not jurisdiction of the crime or that the facts charged do not constitute a crime. 

A series of succeeding sections then deals with the proceedings following such discharge. When the offense was committed out of the State, the court may order the defendant discharged or detained until a communication can be sent to the chief executive officer of the jurisdiction where it was committed (Code of Crim., Proc., sec. 403). If it was committed in another county of this State, the court may direct the defendant's commitment for a reasonable time to await a warrant from that county, or admit him to bail (id., sec. 404). In such case the clerk must forthwith give notice to the District Attorney of the appropriate county (id., sec. 405), but the defendant must be discharged from custody or his bail exonerated if he is not thereafter arrested within a reasonable time (id., sec. 406); if he is so 592

THE TRIAL 

§ 356 (a) arrested, the proceedings are the same as upon the arrest of a defendant in another county on a magistrate's warrant (id., sec. 407). If the jury is discharged because of the insufficiency of the indictment, the defendant must be discharged from custody or his bail exonerated, unless the court is of opinion that a new indictment can be framed on which the defendant can be legally convicted, in which event the court may direct that the case be resubmitted to the same or another Grand Jury (id., sec. 408). The latter section, it has been held, does not make it mandatory that the court direct resubmission (People v. Meyers, 119 N.Y.S. 

2d 474), but when it does so, the same proceedings are had thereon as on an original submission to the Grand Jury (id., sec. 409). 

Sec. 356(a). Motions at the Close of the Case. After all the evidence has been received, and all parties have rested, it is appropriate and customary for the defendant to initiate, or to renew, motions to dismiss based on want of jurisdiction, insufficiency of the indictment and insufficiency of the proof. At this time, also, despite its availability to the defendant at any time after the People have completed their case, it is the usual practice to make the defendant's motion for a directed verdict of acquittal. While a verdict of guilty can never be directed (People v. Walker, 198 N.Y. 

329), it is provided in Section 410 of the Code: "If, at any time after the evidence on either side is closed, the court deem it insufficient to warrant a conviction of one or more of the crimes in the indictment or information, it may advise the jury to acquit the defendant thereof and they must follow the advice."

The motion to direct a verdict differs, essentially, from the motion to dismiss based on the failure of the indictment to set forth a crime. The motion is based on the insufficiency of the proof adduced to establish the crime charged; if, indeed, the proof does not so suffice the defendant is entitled, as a matter of law to an acquittal (People v. Kresel, 147 Misc. 241, 264 N.Y.S. 464), and the court 593

§ 

should not avoid its duty by letting the case go to the jury (People v. Fyfe, 6 Misc. 2d 524, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 976). And it has been said: "The court on its own motion may but on motion of the defendant must dismiss all the counts which the evidence does not establish ***" (People v. Wasserbach, 185 Misc. 67, 54 N.Y.S. 2d 302, 312, reversed on the facts 271 App. Div. 756, 64 N.Y.S. 2d 703.) Both the objection to the sufficiency of the indictment and that directed to the insufficiency of the proof should be carefully preserved by appropriate motion and exception; exception to the denial of a motion to direct acquittal, it has been held, will not preserve the right on appeal to raise the question of the sufficiency of the indictment (People v. Weichers, 179 N.Y. 459). Nevertheless, meticulous strictness as regards form is not always enforced in criminal cases, and a motion to discharge the prisoner by reason of the failure of proof was deemed to be intended, and was treated on appeal, as a motion to direct a verdict of acquittal (People v. Bennett, 49 N.Y. 137). So, too, a motion in form to dismiss the indictment was treated, where the circumstances and argument warranted, as a motion to direct (People v. Ledwon, 153 N.Y. 10). And in the Ledwon case, at page 18 of 153 N.Y., the court indicated the substantive rule and test in this language: "The statute has established a standard of proof in criminal cases and the proof must conform to that standard before there can be a lawful conviction. Whenever it is clear that it falls below the prescribed standard the accused is entitled as a matter of law to an acquittal." 

Sec. 357. The Summation. When the presentation of evi dence is concluded by both sides, and all motions have been made and disposed of, the next order of procedure, directed by subdivision 6 of Section 388 of the Code, is that "unless the case is submitted to the jury on either side, or on both sides, without argument, the defendant or his counsel must commence, and the counsel for the People conclude the argument to the jury." Unlike the People's opening, man- 594

THE TRIAL 

§ 357 dated by subdivision 2 as we have already observed, the closing argument is not indispensable and waiver may be elected by either or both sides. Needless to say, this rarely occurs for the summation, or closing argument, is counsel's last, and greatest, opportunity to convey his position to the jury. The time allowed each party is in the court's discretion (People v. Kelly, 94 N.Y. 526), and usually depends on the seriousness of the charges (People v. Mayer, 132 

App. Div. 646, 117 N.Y.S. 520), the length of the trial, the complexity of the issues presented, and other factors. Unreasonable limitation is deemed an abuse of discretion, and may result in reversal (People v. Mayer, supra). 

The limits beyond which counsel may not be permitted to go are determined by "the simple principle of fairness which *** *** pervades those rules which govern the administration of criminal law." (People v. Tassiello, 300 N.Y. 

425, 427.) In the Tassiello case, supra, the Court of Appeals stated, at page 430 of 300 N.Y.: "The assertion by a prosecuting attorney of his personal knowledge of matters which may influence the jury's verdict should have no place in the record of a criminal trial." And it has been stated that the District Attorney is free to employ “all of the traditional forensic arts and wiles of the advocate so long as it may be said that, viewed as a whole, the defend ant had a fair trial ***." (People v. Vollmer, 274 App. Div. 

1011, 85 N.Y.S. 2d 1, 2.) The Court of Appeals disagreed with the Appellate Division's determination that such was indicated and reversed the judgment of conviction, stating: "It was plainly wrong to permit the prosecutor, after cross-examining defendant about his assault conviction some years before, to read to the jury the information in that other case, which contained most prejudicial matter." (People v. Vollmer, 299 N.Y. 347, 350.)

It has been held error to permit the District Attorney to say that the police used remarkable restraint in not giving the defendant his just dues (People v. Mleczko, 298 N.Y. 

153), to state to the jury that should they convict, the court could suspend sentence and provide for supervision of the 595

§ 

defendant in the future (People v. Friedt, 280 App. Div. 

836, 113 N.Y.S. 2d 889), to comment upon the race of the deceased, upon defendant's use of peremptory challenges, and upon defendant's retaining an attorney and paying him a fee (People v. Castellano, 273 App. Div. 978, 78 N.Y.S. 

2d 978), and to urge conviction on the assurance that there would be a soft penalty (People v. Afarian, 202 Misc. 199, 108 N.Y.S. 2d 533). 

Similar restrictions, generally, are imposed upon defense counsel's summation, although it is borne in mind that his statements are not those of "a prosecuting officer apt to carry much weight against the accused when they should properly carry none." (Berger v. United 

States, 295 U.S. 78, 88, 79 L. Ed. 1314.) Thus, a defendant summing up in his own behalf was held properly admonished for stating matters not shown to be facts (People v. 

Gitlow, 195 App. Div. 773, 187 N.Y.S. 783, affirmed 234 N.Y. 

132, affirmed 268 U.S. 652, 69 L. Ed. 1138). It was held, also, that where counsel for the defense oversteps the bounds of propriety in summation, the proper remedy is to punish him for contempt rather than to permit retaliatory vituperation and abuse in the District Attorney's summation (People v. Wansker, 108 Misc. 84, 177 N.Y.S. 295). 

Where opposing counsel makes objectionable statements and remarks to the jury, the remedy is by objection, followed by exception if the court rules adversely. The weight of authority and the common practice permit counsel to interpose such objections immediately, interrupting the argument to do so (People v. Wansker, 108 Misc. 84, 177 

N.Y.S. 295). But even in the absence of such objection, the court is in duty bound to intervene on its own motion, and prevent continuing departures from propriety (People v. Manganaro, 218 N.Y. 9; People v. Migliori, 273 App. Div. 

915, 77 N.Y.S. 2d 707). The court's failure to check the District Attorney's misstatements brought on a reversal (People v. Decker, 143 App. Div. 590, 127 N.Y.S. 1059), and the presiding judge's contenting himself with making mild suggestions that the prosecutor desist was held not 596

THE TRIAL 

§ 358 enough, but rather an accentuation of the impropriety which required reversal (People v. Castellano, 273 App. 

Div. 978, 78 N.Y.S. 2d 356).

Sec. 358. The Court's Charge. The final step in the prescribed procedures is the court's charge to the jury (Code of Criminal Procedure, sec. 388, subd. 7). Section 420 of the

Code provides that the court "must state to them, all matters of law which it thinks necessary for their information in giving their verdict; and must, if requested, in addition to what it may deem its duty to say, inform the jury that they are the exclusive judges of all questions of fact; the court must state to them that in determining the question of guilt they must not consider the punishment, but that it rests with the judge to fix such punishment as may be provided by law." In a criminal libel case, of course, this instruction must be modified in the light of Section 418 which provides: "On the trial of an indictment for libel, the jury have the right to determine the law and the fact." And they must also be admonished that, although their verdict is to be general-"guilty" or "not guilty"including "questions of law as well as of fact," they must, nevertheless "receive as law what is laid down as such by the court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 419.)

The charge, comprising the judge's directions and instructions to the jury, is delivered orally. It must be fair and impartial, and clearly indicate judicial indifference to individuals (People v. Odell, 230 N.Y. 481). Its delivery in an oratorical and fervid manner, especially when its emphasis indicates partiality, is improper and reversible (People v. De Martine, 205 App. Div. 80, 199 N.Y.S. 426).

When it is overly long and unduly prolix it may defeat its purpose of clarification, and a charge occupying 163 pages of the printed record, requiring more than eight hours for delivery, was held prejudicial (People v. Kresel, 243 App. 

Div. 137, 277 N.Y.S. 168). The language in which it is couched should be such as the judge deems most intelligible to the jury, but his refusal to put it in the language of an 597

§ 

elementary writer is not error (People v. Wayman, 128 

N.Y. 585).

The judge "should not as a rule limit himself to stating good set terminology from the reports. Jurors need no legal definitions merely. They require instruction as to the method of applying such definitions after reaching their conclusions on the facts." (Judge Pound, in People v. Odell, 230 N.Y. 481, 487-488.) The court may discuss and comment on the facts, as long as it does not presume to decide them (People v. Walker, 198 N.Y. 329), or give positive expressions of opinion thereon (People v. Barbieri, 149 

N.Y. 256). And, in applying the requirements of Section 

420 of the Code, Judge Dye wrote in People v. Salemi, 309 

N.Y. 208, 213: "While this statute emphasizes that the court shall charge the jury on all matters of law, it does not follow that the charge on the law shall be given with only slight reference to the facts. The better practice for the court in a capital case, as we long ago pointed out, even when uninvited by the defendant to do so, is to present to the jury the case on trial in all its phases in which the jury ought to consider it."

The court's formal set charge is not the only occasion when he gives instructions to the jury. The jury may request further instruction, even after they have retired and begun deliberation (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 427). Such further instructions are deemed part of the charge (Maurer v. People, 43 N.Y. 1). When such request is made, as was pointed out in People v. Miller, 6 N.Y. 2d 152, 156, the court has no discretion as to whether or not to answer a proper question (People v. Gonzales, 293 N.Y. 259, 262), but his failure to answer is reversible error only if there was serious prejudice to the defendant's rights (People v. Cooke, 292 N.Y. 185, 188; People v. La Marca, 3 N.Y. 2d 

452, 461). 

Sec. 359. Exceptions to Charge. A party's objection to the charge as given by the court, in whole or in part, is made by way of exceptions. The practice with regard to excep- 598

THE TRIAL 

§ 360 tions is now conformed in criminal cases to the civil practice (Twelfth Annual Report of the Judicial Council, 1946), by operation of Section 420-a of the Code. While, by its provisions, specific exceptions need not be taken to rulings "either before or after the cause is finally submitted" as long as the party has made his position thereon known to the court or judge, it is otherwise with respect to the 

an exception to the charge given to the jury by the court or any part thereof and to the granting or refusal of a request to charge, shall not be deemed to have been taken unless expressly noted by the party adversely affected before the jury have rendered their verdict.' 99 The objection and exception must be specific. A general exception is unavailing where any part of the matter so objected to is correct (People v. Guidici, 100 N.Y. 503). 

Generally, such objections as that the court failed to submit a fact to the jury and call their attention thereto (People v. Truck, 170 N.Y. 203; People v. Ferone, 120 App. Div. 

323, 105 N.Y.S. 448, affirmed 196 N.Y. 522; People v. Richardson, 223 N.Y. 103), or that it omitted to charge on a particular proposition of law (People v. Rosino, 168 App. 

Div. 920, 152 N.Y.S. 628), are not available by way of exception in the absence of a request to charge. 

Sec. 360. Requests to Charge. Requests to charge are customarily submitted orally by counsel after the court has completed its charge. Their function, differing from that of the exceptions usually stated at the same time, which state objections to the matters contained in the charge, is to request that the court include in its charge matter not already therein stated, or inadequately stated. The defendant is not entitled to select the phraseology of the instructions, as long as the thought desired to be presented, has been fairly stated by the court (People v. Radcliffe, 232 N.Y. 249), and a refusal to charge in the words of the request, where otherwise fully and fairly covered, is not error (People v. Katz, 209 N.Y. 311; People v. Williams, 599

§ 

92 Hun 354, 36 N.Y.S. 511, affirmed 149 N.Y. 1). A charge in abstract language, not made applicable to the evidence, may be properly refused (People v. McCallam, 35 Hun 

663, affirmed 103 N.Y. 587). A request for instruction defining punishment for the crime charged, under the provisions of Section 420 of the Code, is held properly rejected (People v. Ryan, 55 Hun 214, 8 N.Y.S. 241). Any objection that the court failed to call the jury's attention to a fact which must be considered must be embodied in a request to charge (People v. Truck, 170 N.Y. 203), as must the objection that the court failed to charge a particular proposition of law which counsel deems necessary (People v. 

Rosino, 168 App. Div. 920, 152 N.Y.S. 623).

Sec. 361. Conduct of Jurors. Innocence or guilt of the de fendant must be determined solely upon the evidence presented and, accordingly, if a juror have personal knowledge of any fact in issue at the trial it is his duty to make this known to the court and be sworn and examined as is any other witness. This was the prior rule (People v. 

Zeiger, 6 Parker Cr. 355), and is now the statutory rule declared by Section 413 of the Code. That section further imposes upon the jury the duty of returning to the court if, after it retires, one of the jurors declares knowledge of a fact which could have been evidence in the cause. 

Before submission, it is within the court's discretion to permit them to separate or to require them to be kept together in the charge of proper officers. Such officers must be sworn to keep them together, to permit no discussion of the case, and not to do so themselves (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 414). The jurors must at each adjournment be admonished not to discuss the matter, or form or express any opinion, until the case is finally submitted to them (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 415). The conduct of the jurors and their procedures, after submission, are regulated by Part 

4, Title 7, Chapter II (secs. 423-432) of the Code. 

After hearing the charge, the jury may decide in court, but this is so rare as to be virtually unknown. If they retire, 600

THE TRIAL 

§ 361 one or more officers must be sworn "to keep them together in some private and convenient place, and not to permit any person to speak to or communicate with them, nor do so themselves, unless it be by order of the court, or to ask them whether they have agreed upon a verdict, and to return them into court when they have so agreed, or when ordered by the court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 421.) They may be permitted, on consent of the parties, to take with them any paper or article received in evidence. (id., sec. 

425.) They may also take with them notes of the testimony or other proceedings, taken by themselves or by any of them, but none taken by any other person (id., sec. 426). 

After retiring, they must require the officer to conduct them back into court if they disagree as to any of the testimony, or desire to be informed of a point of law, which is given to them after notice to counsel and, in cases of felony, in the presence of the defendant (id., sec. 427).

Though the court may proceed to other business, or adjourn, in the absence of the jury, it is deemed open until the verdict is rendered or the jury discharged (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 431). The discharge may thereafter take place by reason of accident or casualty, by consent of the parties on leave of the court, or upon their declaring their inability, after a reasonable time, to agree upon a verdict (id., sec. 428). Final adjournment, whether on a verdict or otherwise, discharges the jury, but it is provided that the stated term may be extended to finish a trial or receive a verdict (id., sec. 432). 601
