Sec. 362. Definitions. "Verdict", derived from the Latin vere and dictum, means philologically a "true saying". It could mean the decisions of any fact-finding body but, in law, it has been restricted to the determination of a jury on matters of fact in issue in a specific case. At common law, two kinds of verdicts were permissible in a criminal case, a general verdict and a special verdict. Both are now permitted in New York under the Code (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 436). The general verdict is the one almost always used. Where the trial has proceeded on the defendant's plea of not guilty, that verdict "is either 'guilty'; or 'not guilty', which imports a conviction or acquittal of the offense charged in the indictment." If, however, the plea has been former conviction or acquittal, the general verdict is either "for the People" or "for the defendant." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 437.) Special verdicts make findings of fact only, and are stated in terms of conclusions of fact. No judgment relating to the guilt of the accused is contained therein; that is left to the court after hearing argument upon the findings of fact (Code of Crim. Proc., 602

VERDICT § 364 

secs. 438-442). The intendment of a special verdict is the presentation of all the ultimate facts to the court which, in turn, shall draw the necessary legal conclusions therefrom.

Sec. 363. History. In the early days of the common law, it was the general and established practice of the courts to coerce juries into finding verdicts. Juries were kept without food, light, or heat until a verdict was found (3 Blackstone Comm. 414). A leading New York case was one of the first in this country to criticize this practice (People v. Olcott, 2 Johns. 301). It was also the practice to punish juries for finding false verdicts. Therefore, jurors early sought to avoid such punishment by restricting their findings to determinations of the facts at issue, for it was recognized that there was a greater probability of error if the jurors attempted to draw legal consequences from the facts. Thus the special verdict came into being (Morgan, A Brief History of Special Verdicts, 32 Yale L. J. 575, 590). 

The right of the jury to return a general verdict was first clearly recognized in Rex v. Shipley, 21 How. St. Tr. 847.

Today, the special verdict is seldom used and, with the development of rules concerning new trials and the setting aside or arresting of judgment there is no longer the need for juries, in their own self interest, to restrict their findings to determinations of fact. 

Sec. 364. How Verdict Given. "When the jury have agreed upon the verdict, they must be conducted into court by the officer having them in charge. Their names must then be called, and if all do not appear, the rest must be discharged without giving a verdict. In that event, the cause may again be tried, at the same or another term." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 433.) No cases have been found upholding the constitutionality of this section against the claim of double jeopardy. Some authorities have indicated that the provision allowing a retrial is of doubtful validity (See Report of the Commission on Administration of Justice in 603

$ 

New York, p. 139 [1936]). If the defendant has been tried for felony, he must be present in court when the verdict is rendered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 434). This right, and obligation, is not waivable (People v. La Barbera, 274 N.Y. 

339). However, defendant's counsel need not be present unless it appears that the defendant may be prejudiced by his absence (People v. Wilson, 109 N.Y. 345). When the jury appears, the court or the clerk will ask if they have agreed upon a verdict and, if the foreman replies that they have, they must then declare the verdict (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 435). If the jury reports that they are unable to agree upon a verdict, and the court orders their discharge under Section 428 of the Code, it is not necessary, if the defendant has been indicted under a multi-count indictment, to ask the jury if they have reached a verdict under any of the counts submitted to them. "What is contemplated by Section 435 is that, before a jury is asked to state what its verdict is, some effort should be made to establish that they have, in fact, reached a verdict." (People ex rel. Polakowski v. Silberglitt, 13 Misc. 2d 

21, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 563.) The verdict must be received by the court which tried the case (Hinman v. People, 13 Hun 266). 

If the verdict is for an acquittal, the court cannot direct the jury to reconsider it. However, if a verdict of conviction is returned, and the court believes that the jury has mistaken the applicable law, the court may explain to the jury the reason for its opinion to that effect, and may direct the jury to reconsider its verdict. If the same verdict is thereafter returned it must be entered (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 447).

If the verdict returned is defective in form (People v. 

Bush, 3 Parker Cr. 552), or if it appears to be neither a general nor a special verdict, or when it cannot be clearly understood from the verdict whether the jury intended to render a special or general verdict, the court may direct the jury to reconsider and may give additional instructions concerning the applicable law at that time (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 449). If the jury continues to return an "in- 604

VERDICT 

§ 365 1 formal" verdict, one in improper form, if "it can be clearly understood, that their intention is to find in favor of the defendant, upon the issue" the court must adjudge the defendant acquitted, and the verdict must be entered in the terms in which it is found. No judgment of conviction, however, can be entered upon such informal verdict (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 449).

Sec. 365. Polling the Jury. After the verdict has been given by the foreman, but before it is recorded by the clerk, either party may demand that the jury be polled (People v. Hoffman, 288 N.Y. 538). The polling consists of asking each juror, individually, whether the verdict rendered is his. If a negative answer to this question is given by any juror, resubmission of the case to the jury is required (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 450). The court may, sua sponte, order the polling of the jury where it suspects some fault in the finding of the verdict (People v. Orr, 138 Misc. 535, 246 

N.Y.S. 673). The polling consists only of asking each juror: "Is this your verdict?" (Leighton v. People, 10 Abb.

N.C. 261, aff'd. without discussion of this point, 88 N.Y. 

117.) Where a multicount indictment was under consideration, and a general verdict was returned, an early case held that the jury could be asked upon which count the defendant had been found guilty (Noah's Case, 3 City Hall Rec. 13). The right to obtain a polling of the jury is waived by a failure to request it at the proper time (People v. 

Schneider, 154 App. Div. 203, 139 N.Y.S. 104; People v. Allgood, 2 App. Div. 2d 931, 156 N.Y.S. 2d 791).

Where there had been no roll call of the jury (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 433), and no express waiver of that requirement, and the record failed to indicate that the clerk had recorded the verdict, read it, and asked the jury, collectively, if it was their verdict (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

451), it was held that the substantial rights of the defendant were injured, judgment of conviction was reversed and a new trial was ordered (People v. Light, 285 App. Div. 

496, 138 N.Y.S. 2d 262). In People ex rel. Mault v. Jackson, 605

§ 

3 App. Div. 2d 688, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 359, the court held that counsel's silence after the required roll call of the jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 433), together with his failure to request a poll of the jury, under section 450, constituted a waiver of the right to a poll. The distinction between the above cases is that, in People v. Light, there had been no record of compliance with either section 433 or 451. In the 

Mault case those sections had been complied with, and there was adequate protection of the defendant's rights. 

In People ex rel. Mault v. Jackson, supra, the court also held that the inquiry contemplated by Section 451 is a collective one, addressed to the jury as a whole, and is satisfied by a collective response, as distinguished from the inquiry under Section 450, where the question is posed to each, individual, juror. This holding appears clearly correct, based upon the wording of the sections. Also, as the court noted, if both sections required an individual inquiry, there would be needless repetition. If all the jurors give affirmative responses to the questions put to them on the poll, "the verdict is complete, and the jury must be discharged from the case", but "If any juror disagree, the fact must be entered on the minutes and the jury again sent out ***" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 451.)

After the verdict has been entered, and if the judgment is of acquittal, based upon a ground other than a variance between the proof and the indictment, the defendant must then be discharged, in the absence of any other legal cause for his further detention. However, if the acquittal is based upon a variance between the proof and the indictment, and a re-indictment may be obtained, the court may order the defendant's continued detention (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

452). Note that Section 293 allows the amendment of the indictment, during trial, if a variance appears, where the defendant will not be prejudiced in his defense thereby. 

The constitutionality of Section 452, in its authorization of the continued detention of a defendant after an acquittal on the ground of a variance, has not been decided. The 

Commission on the Administration of Justice in New York, 606

VERDICT 

§ 366 in its report in 1939, at page 158, indicated doubt as to its validity as against an attack based on double jeopardy, or on a writ of habeas corpus.

If the verdict is of conviction upon a general verdict, or if a special verdict has been rendered, the defendant must be remanded (or, on bail, committed) to await the judgment of the court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 453). The court will appoint a time for judgment (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 471), at least two days after the verdict if the court is to remain in session that long, or if not, "as remote a time as can reasonably be allowed ***." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 472.)

Sec. 366. Special Verdicts. New York juries may render either "a general verdict, or when they are in doubt as to the legal effect of the facts proved, they may, except upon an indictment for libel, find a special verdict." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 436.) The special verdict "must present the conclusions of fact, as established by the evidence, and not the evidence to prove them; and these conclusions of fact must be so presented, as that nothing remains to the court, but to draw from them conclusions of law." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 438.) A special verdict must be written, either by the jury or in its presence (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 439), but there is no prescribed form established in the 

Code, save the requirement that it must "present intelligently" the required findings (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 440).

Once the verdict has been rendered, agreed to by the jury, and entered upon the minutes of the court, it may be brought to argument by either party upon five days' notice to the other. The defendant has the right to close the argument to the court upon the verdict (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 441). If the special verdict does not find facts sufficient to enable the court to give judgment upon it, or if evidence rather than conclusions of fact is given in the verdict, a new trial must be ordered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 443).

If a satisfactory special verdict has been entered, the 607

§ 

court, after hearing argument upon it, must give judgment. If the defendant has pleaded former conviction or acquittal, the court must either convict or acquit upon the facts found. If the defendant had pleaded not guilty, and the facts establish guilt of the crime charged, or of any inferior degree of that crime, or of an attempt to commit that crime, or of any "necessarily included" charge, the court must give judgment accordingly (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 442).

Sec. 367. Multi-Count Indictments. Where the indictment charges several crimes in different counts, the defendant may be convicted or acquitted upon any one or more of the counts and the foreman of the jury, when delivering the verdict, must state each crime of which the defendant is convicted. An acquittal of any one count is not deemed an acquittal of any other count (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

443-a). See chapter entitled "New Trial" for a discussion of the effect of such action on a retrial of the defendant upon any of these counts. If there has been a joint trial of several defendants, the jury may return a verdict as to those defendants upon whom they agree, and the rest of the defendants may be retried before another jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 446). It has also been stated that a jury could, after rendition of such a verdict, return again to their deliberations to consider the remainder of the defendants (People v. Cohen, 273 N.Y. 406). An early case held that failure of the jury to find on certain counts of a multi-count indictment is deemed an acquittal as to the undecided counts (People v. Dowling, 84 N.Y. 478). However, in People ex rel. Polakowski v. Silberglitt, 13 Misc. 

2d 21, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 563, the court held that the jury's discharge on failure to agree, despite affidavits of jurors that all jurors had concurred in finding the defendant not guilty of first degree murder, required the defendant's retrial upon that count. The District Attorney had submitted controverting affidavits of other jurors. The distinction between People v. Dowling and the Polakowski case is that 608

VERDICT 

§ 368 there had been no verdict at all rendered in the Polakowski case and thus no finding by the jury; in the other, there was a specific verdict of guilty of certain counts, with silence upon other counts. 

Sec. 368. Verdicts upon Different Degrees of Crime. The problems that arise upon consideration of the offenses of which one indicted may be convicted necessarily affect double jeopardy, also. See chapter so entitled. New York follows the common law doctrine that, provided the wording of the indictment covers the offense, one indicted upon one charge may be found guilty of a related offense of a lesser nature (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 444, 445; Penal 

Law, sec. 610; People v. Schleiman, 197 N.Y. 383). Thus, if the prosecution fails to prove some necessary element of the crime charged in the indictment, the jury, disregarding this missing element, may find the defendant guilty of an included crime proved upon the established facts. 

Section 444 of the Code, substantially identical to Section 610 of the Penal Law, gives a specific example of this situation: "Upon a trial for murder or manslaughter, if the act complained of is not proved to be the cause of death, the defendant may be convicted of assault in any degree constituted by said act, and warranted by the evidence." 

Problems are born of the duty of the court to instruct the jury concerning conviction of lesser crimes; the determination of the crimes of which the defendant may be convicted; and whether a conviction or acquittal of the crime precludes, as double jeopardy, a later prosecution for a related crime. In general, when conviction of a less serious crime is more clearly warranted by the evidence than that for which the defendant has been indicted, and when the lesser crime is "necessarily included" within the greater crime charged, all of its elements constituting elements of the greater crime, the court must charge the jury upon this point (Dedieu v. People, 22 N.Y. 178). In People v. Jordan, 125 App. Div. 522, 109 N.Y.S. 840, it was noted that failure of counsel to request a charge upon this point may pre- 609

§ 

clude review on appeal of the court's decision. The Dedieu rule, requiring identity of statutory elements, has also been broadened so that an offense may be considered included if all of the lesser crime's elements are alleged in the indictment for the greater offense (People v. Miller, 143 

App. Div. 251, 128 N.Y.S. 549, affirmed 292 N.Y. 618; People v. Zulinsky, 247 App. Div. 573, 288 N.Y.S. 176). The common law rule that one indicted for felony could not be convicted of an included misdemeanor, is not applicable in 

New York (People v. Jackson, 3 Hill 92). 

In People v. Schleiman, supra, 197 N.Y. 383, it was indicated that lesser crimes must be charged unless "there was no possible view of the facts which would justify any verdict except a conviction of the crime charged or an acquittal." However, application of this rule was, until recently, extended only to felony murder cases where the defendant did not commit the act of killing. In People v. 

Clemente, 285 App. Div. 258, 136 N.Y.S. 2d 202, affirmed without opinion 309 N.Y. 890, the principle was extended to a perjury case. In People v. Mussenden, 308 N.Y. 558, the refusal of the court to charge the lesser offense was held not error, the Court of Appeals noting that if the jury believed the prosecution's evidence it could not find the defendant innocent of the crime charged. 

When the defendant is convicted of an offense of a lesser degree than that charged in the indictment and submitted to the jury, though the court fail to submit still lesser offenses for the jury's consideration that is held not prejudicial (People v. Monat, 200 N.Y. 308; People v. Thompson, 41 N.Y. 1). Even if the elements of the lesser offense have not been alleged in the indictment, and although there has been no charge upon that offense, the defendant may nevertheless not subsequently be prosecuted therefor. This follows, because acquittal of the offense with which a defendant is charged bars prosecution thereafter for an offense which is part of the same transaction and was proved in the trial which resulted in acquittal (Penal Law, secs. 32, 1938). 610

VERDICT § 370 Sec. 369. Sealed Verdicts. The use of sealed verdicts, despite the lack of any statutory authorization, is common in civil trials, where they may be ordered even without the parties' consent (Fahey v. South Nassau Comm. Hosp., 197 Misc. 490, 95 N.Y.S. 2d 842, affirmed 277 App. Div. 774, 97 N.Y.S. 2d 711). This practice is thus described: “Where the jury are likely to be absent for some time, and the business of the day is through, it is usual to direct them, when they shall have agreed upon their verdict, to seal it, and to bring it into court the next morning." (Carmody, New 

York Practice, vol. 4, p. 3098, sec. 1340.) However, as we have seen, criminal practice is essentially a statutory practice and there is no sanction for, or even reference to, sealed verdicts in our statutes. The use of sealed verdicts in criminal trials was emphatically disapproved in People v. Pickert, 26 Misc. 12, 56 N.Y.S. 1009, where, although the defendant gave no consent, the court in no respect indicated that the practice would be deemed more acceptable if the parties had consented. 

Sec. 370. Impeachment of Verdict. Generally, the affidavit, deposition or statement of a juror may not be received to impeach his own verdict, or for the purpose of avoiding a verdict to show matters which occurred during the trial or in the jury room which do not entirely inhere in the verdict (People v. McNaspie, 261 App. Div. 657, 27 N.Y.S. 

2d 906). See chapter on "Motion for New Trial," for a discussion of the methods of attacking verdicts because of faults in the jury's conduct while deliberating. 611

CHAPTER 32  

Sec. 371. Definitions

Sec. 372. History Sec. 373. Where, When and How Motion Made Sec. 374. Withdrawal of Motion Sec. 375. Grounds for a New Trial Sec. 376. Appeals PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

Generally, counsel should move for a new trial immediately after the jury has rendered a verdict of guilty. And, as pointed out in the next chapter, it is made simultaneously with a motion in arrest of judgment although they are separate and distinct motions. 

Usually the motion is made orally, based on the minutes of the trial. Notice to the District Attorney and the preparation of formal papers are not required, as a rule. But where the motion is based on grounds dehors the record, affidavits should be presented, setting forth the facts relied on. If the motion is made after sentence has been imposed, on the ground of newly discovered evidence, notice should be given to the District Attorney, and the motion should be based both on the record and on affidavits showing the new evidence relied on.

Sometimes, the making of this motion presents a hazard. There have been instances of defendants indicted for murder, convicted of manslaughter and, on a new trial, subsequently convicted on the original charge of murder. Counsel should carefully assay the risks attendant upon a new trial before making the application. 

Sec. 371. Definitions. After the verdict has been rendered, and the defendant found guilty, certain methods of attacking that verdict are available to him. The most obvious is 612

§ an appeal and another method is by motion in arrest of judgment. Both these procedures are fully discussed in appropriately-titled chapters of this work. This chapter deals with another commonly used method of attacking the proceedings which led to the verdict, the motion for a new trial. In general, the motion is based upon defects in the proceedings prejudicial to the defendant, which are not apparent upon the face of the record. "A new trial is a re-examination of the issue, in the same court, before another jury." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 462.) “The granting of a new trial places the parties in the same position as if no trial had been had. All the testimony must be produced anew; and the former verdict cannot be used or referred to, either in evidence or in argument." (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 464.) The provision last stated applies to any court ordering the new trial; a similar provision applies to cases wherein a new trial is ordered by an appellate court after an appeal (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 544).

The practice of re-indicting or re-trying a defendant after dismissal of a void indictment, or after his acquittal by a court without jurisdiction, should be distinguished from a new trial. In this chapter when reference is made to a new trial, it is intended to refer to a re-trial after the granting of the defendant's motion for such relief, based upon one of the grounds discussed in this chapter. In New 

York, the trial court may not on its own motion order a new trial (People v. McGrath, 202 N.Y. 445). 

Sec. 372. History. The granting of new trials in criminal cases is a comparatively recent development in the law. 

The practice was, apparently, unknown at common law until the end of the Seventeenth Century, when Rex v. 

Haines, 2 Keb. 765, was decided (1 Stephens, Hist. of Crim. 

Law of Eng. 310). However, even then, new trials were not granted in felony cases (1 Holdsworth, Hist. of Eng. 

Law 216), and applications for new trials were not made to the trial court, but to the entire panel of the King's 613

§ 

Bench. (See, generally, Riddell, New Trials at Common 

Law, 26 Yale L.J. 49.) In New York, the first statutory grant of power to order new trials was made in 1859; prior to that time it had been held that the courts had no inherent power to order such action (People v. Rao, 271 

N.Y. 98). Before the Nineteenth Century, even though statutes similar to that later enacted in New York had not yet been adopted in other jurisdictions, the practice of granting trials in specific cases by special act of the Legislature developed (Pound, Criminal Justice in America, 96).

There is no constitutional right to a new trial for, like an appeal, its granting is considered a matter of legislative grace (People v. Lamboray, 152 Misc. 206, 273 N.Y.S. 69; 

State v. McLeod, 8 Kansas 232).

Sec. 373. Where, When and How Motion Made. Where. The motion must be made before the court in which the former trial was had, although they need not be made to the same judge before whom the case was tried (People v. Rao, 271 

N.Y. 98). In the event of a death sentence, when the court before whom the trial was had is not in session at the time of the motion, the application may be made to any Supreme Court Justice, or to any Special Term of the Supreme Court within the Judicial Department wherein the conviction was had (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 466). If the trial court is not in session at the time of the motion, in other than a death case, and it appears that it will not resume sitting until after expiration of the statutory period within which the motion must be made, application may be made to a Supreme Court Justice or Special Term, as in death cases. There is no express statutory recognition of this procedure, although it can be argued that Section 22, subdivisions 5 and 7 of the Code, grant such powers to the Supreme Court. In any event, the above procedure is the established practice (see Housel and Walser, How to Defend a Criminal Case, 413), and no cases have been found disapproving this practice.

When. The motion for a new trial is made after the ver- 614

§ dict and before judgment, except where the application is based upon the discovery of new evidence in which case it may be made within one year after the date the judgment was entered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 466; People v. Pratowski, 127 N.Y.S. 2d 263). The taking of an appeal by the defendant does not extend this period (People v. 

Marano, 120 Misc. 696, 200 N.Y.S. 256), and, in the event of a death sentence, the motion may be made any time prior to execution (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 466).

How Made. The manner of moving for a new trial depends, in part, upon the ground for the motion. Where it is based on an alleged misdirection or refusal to instruct the jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 465, subd. 5), or a verdict contrary to law or against the weight of the evidence (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 465, subd. 6), the motion is made upon the minutes of the trial and record of the testimony. 

Where the basis for the motion is the discovery of new evidence, the statute requires that affidavits be used to establish that, and further authorizes the court to "compel the personal appearance of the affiants before it for the purposes of their personal examination and cross-examination, under oath, upon the contents of the affidavits which they subscribed." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 465, subd. 7.) Affidavits have also been held admissible to prove that a juror was unqualified to serve, because of pre-existing prejudice against the defendant's race, and a new trial granted based on such papers (People v. Leonti, 262 N.Y. 256). 

In People v. Spiegel, 149 Misc. 439, 267 N.Y.S. 512, with the permission of the court, oral testimony was heard to substantiate the defendant's assertions of a juror's misconduct, and subpoenas were issued to compel the attendance of necessary witnesses. In general, therefore, the motion itself should be supported by whatever proof the defendant's counsel believes most convincing and appropriate. If it is believed that oral evidence should be given, application should be made to the court for permission to introduce such evidence. While there is no statutory basis 615

§ 

for such action, the last cited cases provide authority in support of the application. 

Sec. 374. Withdrawal of Motion. A motion for a new trial may be withdrawn prior to decision thereon (People v. 

McGrath, 202 N.Y. 445). See chapter on "Sentence," for a discussion of the effect of failure to permit such a withdrawal.

Sec. 375. Grounds for a New Trial. Section 465 of the Code of Criminal Procedure sets forth the grounds upon which new trials may be granted. They are: 1. Where a defendant, indicted for a felony, has not been present during the trial. 2. Where improper evidence has been received by the jury out of court. 3. Where there has been an improper separation of the jury after their retirement, or where the jury has committed acts interfering with a fair consideration of the case. 4. Where the verdict has been arrived at by improper means, such as by lot or chance. 5. Where the court erroneously instructed the jury, or erroneously refused to instruct them, and the defendant expected to such action. 6. Where the verdict is contrary to law or against the weight of the evidence. 7. Where newly discovered evidence has been found since the trial, if such evidence is not merely cumulative, and where the failure to produce the evidence at the trial was not due to the defendant's lack of diligence. A more detailed discussion of this ground follows. However, it should be noted that none of the occurrences discussed above is, of itself, ground for the granting of a new trial unless the defendant's "substantial rights have been prejudiced" thereby. 

It should also be noted that an appellate court, finding error in the proceedings leading to a conviction, will usually reverse the conviction and remand the case for a new trial. This may be done on grounds other than those enumerated in Section 465. So, in People v. McLaughlin, 291 

N.Y. 480, a new trial was ordered on reversal because of the denial, in effect, of the defendant's right to counsel. 616

§ Section 528 of the Code authorizes the Court of Appeals to order a new trial in a death case "if it be satisfied that the verdict was against the weight of the evidence or against law, or that justice requires a new trial." Thus, the law is completely different, both substantively and procedurally, as to new trials granted on motion to the trial court under Section 465 and those on reversal by an appellate court, as witness Section 528. There is no reason nor need for attempting to reconcile the holdings under one with those under the other. As to the rule in appellate grants of retrials, the language of People v. Becker, 210 N.Y. 274, reversing a conviction for murder in the first degree, is instructive. The Court stated: "The fundamental demand of our law is that the accused shall have a fair trial, and that if that right has been infringed, not in respect of mere technicalities but in substantial matters *** he shall have another opportunity to meet his accuser and establish his innocence." On the other, the power of the trial court to order a new trial on motion under Section 465 was well characterized in People v. Frangipane, 171 Misc. 610, 13 

N.Y.S. 2d 429, thus: "The power to order a new trial is created and measured by the statute *** and cannot be exercised by the court after judgment unless the defendant comes within the scope of its provisions." 

Statements by appellate courts have seemed, at times, to indicate a different view: "When the court is not satisfied with the verdict, and the justice of the case makes it clear there should be a new trial, the judge may exercise his discretion accordingly." (People v. Scarlione, 298 N.Y. 

305.) Apparently contrary statements have also been made by trial courts: "It is the duty of the court, in the interests of justice, to order a new trial when convinced by an examination of the entire record that the same should be done." (People v. Groom, 174 Misc. 250, 20 N.Y.S. 2d 683.) But, generally, the trial court will not grant a new trial except upon a ground or grounds within those listed in Section 465. In People v. Groom, supra, the basis was procedure in the jury room; in the Scarlione case, a verdict apparently 617

§ 

against the weight of the evidence. While it is not intended to infer that counsel should not, as an advocate, assert grounds other than those listed in that section, relying on appropriate statements in applicable cases in support of his argument, undue reliance should not be placed upon these cases insofar as they seem to authorize the grant of a new trial upon grounds other than those set forth in the statute. This chapter will concern itself with the statutory grounds. Discussions of other grounds for attacking verdicts will be found in the chapters dealing with appeals, coram nobis, and arrest of judgment. 

Defendant's Absence. The meaning of subdivision 1 of 

Section 465 is obvious. The defendant must be present during the trial, when the verdict is received (People v. 

Perkins, 1 Wend. 91); after the jury has retired, the defendant must be present when the jury returns to the courtroom to have testimony reread. In People v. Shapiro, 3 N.Y. 2d 203, 165 N.Y.S. 2d 14, the court held that the defendant's failure to raise this issue by a motion for a new trial, or to assign it as error on appeal, precluded its consideration on the defendant's application for a writ of error coram nobis. 

Jury's Receipt of Improper Evidence Out of Court. Sec tion 411 provides for the jury's viewing of places concerned, under court supervision. (See the chapter of this work titled "Trial".) If the jury receives any other evidence out of court which results in prejudice to the defendant's substantial rights, a new trial may be ordered. 

However, an unauthorized visit by a juror to the scene of the crime is not, by itself, a sufficient reason for the granting of a new trial. In People v. Kraus, 147 Misc. 906, 265 

N.Y.S. 294, there was no showing of prejudice to the defendant's rights that might have been caused by such view, the court indicating that there had been no change in the scene of the crime, nor had there been any discussion of the view with others. (Compare Eastwood v. People, 3 

Parker Cr. 25, for an indication of an apparently contrary view.) 618

§ 

Jury's Unauthorized Separation or Misconduct. An un authorized separation of the jury, as with other grounds for new trials, is not of itself sufficient for granting a new trial. It must appear that the separation was prejudicial to the defendant (People v. Dunbar Contracting Co., 215 

N.Y. 416). Where the separation was unavoidable, as in the illness of a juror and his visit to a physician in the company of a court officer, a new trial was denied (People v. Hoch, 150 N.Y. 291; People v. Buchanan, 145

N.Y. 1). However, a separation, during which one of the jurors drank some liquor in a bar which he visited alone, was held sufficient reason to grant a new trial in People v. Schad, 12 N.Y.S. 695. Other unauthorized actions of jurors, held to require the ordering of a new trial, have been: The drinking of intoxicating liquor (People v. 

Douglas, 4 Cow. 26. Compare People v. Pscherhofer, 19 

N.Y.S. 483, holding that drinking alone was not sufficient cause, where no effect upon the judgment was shown); the existence of an affidavit related to the defendant's examination by the police, which affidavit had been withheld from evidence (In re Mitchell, 1 City Hall Rec. 147); the receipt of information from a former alternate juror concerning the defendant (People v. Cocco, 279 App. Div. 1129, 112 N.Y.S. 2d 562); discussion, after retirement, with people standing outside the windows of the jury room (People v. Durling, 303 N.Y. 382); the receipt of information from the judge, in the jury room, concerning the charge of which defendant was accused (People v. Linzey, 29 N.Y.S. 560); the presence of an alien on the jury (People v. Bett, 121 

Misc. 380, 201 N.Y.S. 47; compare People v. Thayer, 132 

App. Div. 593, 116 N.Y.S. 821, and People v. Morrisey, 1

Sheld. 295, both cases holding that the presence of overage jurors did not require a new trial); a juror's statement that he would not believe anyone of defendant's race (People v. Leonti, 262 N.Y. 256); a juror's statement, before trial, that he wished to serve on the jury and punish the defendant (People v. Bishop, 66 App. Div. 415, 73 N.Y.S. 226).

Actions held not sufficient, of themselves, to require the 619

§ 

granting of a new trial are: a juror's sleeping during some of the sessions (People v. Morrisey, 1 Sheld. 295); the relation of one of the jurors in the ninth degree to the defendant (People v. Mach, 35 App. Div. 114, 54 N.Y.S. 698); the jury's acquisition, and perusal, of a law book (People v. 

Draper, 28 Hun1), or a copy of the Penal Law and Code of 

Criminal Procedure (People v. Priori, 164 N.Y. 459), or of the penal statutes (People v. Gaffney, 50 N.Y. 416); the jury's acquisition of, and perusal of, a newspaper article concerning the defendant (People v. Lube, 190 App. Div. 

339, 179 N.Y.S. 691, affirmed 229 N.Y. 601); the jury's acquisition, out of court, of the defendant's prior police record (People v. Caputalo, 233 App. Div. 206, 249 N.Y.S. 

930); a juror's examination of a piece of demonstrative evidence in the courtroom, where there was no possibility of his being misled, and where the defendant's counsel knew of the action and did not object thereto (Wilson v. 

People, 4 Parker Cr. 619).

Any conduct of jurors deemed improper must be objected to at the time defendant becomes aware of the act, or the objection will be waived, and a motion for a new trial based thereon denied (People v. Spiegel, 149 Misc. 

439, 267 N.Y.S. 512; People v. Flack, 10 N.Y.S. 475).

Manner of Reaching Verdict. Some of the cases last cited indicate that a juror's preconceived ideas of defendant's guilt, or credibility, will warrant a new trial if the prejudice is discovered after the trial (See, e.g., People v. Leonti, supra, People v. Bishop, supra). Subdivision 4 of Section 

465 of the Code also provides that if a verdict is decided by lot, or other improper means, a new trial should be granted. 

No cases construing this section have been found, however.

Erroneous Instructions by the Court. This ground, which may be urged in support of a motion for a new trial, is necessarily related to the substantive law. Section 420 of the Code requires that the court charge the jury upon "all matters of law which it thinks necessary *** and must, if requested, ***inform the jury that they are the 620

§ 

exclusive judges of all questions of fact; [and that] in determining the question of guilt they must not consider the punishment, but that it rests with the judge to fix such punishment as may be provided by law.” An erroneous instruction, or failure to instruct, is ground for a new trial only if excepted to at the trial. An erroneous charge on an irrelevant matter has been held not valid ground for the granting of a new trial (People v. Robinson, 2 Parker Cr. 235), although that holding appears to be merely a rephrasing of the principle that matters not affecting a defendant's substantial rights are not ground for a new trial. Some examples of erroneous instructions that have been held to warrant a new trial are: on the burden of proof of an alibi (People v. Vaccaro, 288 N.Y. 

170); on the question of whether a witness was an accomplice of the defendant, where such question was properly for the jury to decide (People v. Monacco, 293 N.Y. 867); an erroneous characterization in the charge of the nature of a witness of the defendant, whether a character witness or not, and of certain material testimony, whether uncontradicted or not (People v. Ash, 267 App. Div. 770, 45 N.Y. 

S. 2d 220); overemphasis, by the court in its charge, on its recollection of certain testimony when coupled with error as to the recollection (People v. McEldowney, 270 App. Div. 

949, 62 N.Y.S. 2d 219).

Verdict Contrary to Law or Clearly Against the Weight of the Evidence. This ground, by definition, will depend upon the facts of each separate case. Conflicts in the evidence, of course, are for the jury to resolve and do not, of themselves, warrant a new trial (People v. Shea, 147 N.Y. 78). However, where evidence was erroneously excluded (People v. Stover, 147 N.Y.S. 2d 680), or where there was an improper limitation by the court of the defendant's area of cross-examination (People v. Taurisano, 267 App. Div. 940, 47 N.Y.S. 2d 208), new trials have been granted. In some of these cases, the court felt that the verdict returned was contrary to law, rather than against the weight of the evidence. However, the admission of 621

§ 

incompetent evidence may, certainly, affect the verdict and therefore may properly be considered within this subdivision.

The cases holding that improper conduct of the prosecution warrants a new trial (see, e.g., People v. Brick, 6 

App. Div. 2d 28, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 437, People v. Castellano, 273 App. Div. 978, 78 N.Y.S. 2d 356) may also properly be classified within this subdivision as cases wherein the verdict was contrary to law because influenced by illegal evidence, or influenced by illegal actions. 

Newly Discovered Evidence. The most widely accepted rule, evidence which will warrant the granting of a new trial as newly-discovered, is stated by the court in People v. Sagel, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 741: "The testimony now offered is such as will, if believed, change the result if a new trial is granted, it was discovered after the previous trial, it could not have been produced at the previous trial had due diligence been exercised, it is material, it is not cumulative to the former issue and it is not merely contradictory or impeaching." See, also, People v. Swanston, 13 Misc. 2d 

837, 181 N.Y.S. 2d 397. The above statement does not mean that newly discovered evidence must meet all of the above requirements to be a basis for the motion. All of the cases agree that the evidence must be "newly discovered," and that evidence available at the first trial may not be urged in support of a motion for a new trial (See People v. Sileo, 179 Misc. 366, 41 N.Y.S. 2d 579). "A criminal may not experiment with one defense, and then when it fails him, invoke the aid of the law *** to experiment with another defense, held in reserve for that emergency." (People v. 

Schmidt, 216 N.Y. 324.) In Anonymous v. Anonymous, 13 

Misc. 2d 718, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 183: "When the newly discovered evidence is contradicted by opposing affidavits, and with the other evidence presents questions of fact which, in the judgment of the court, would not change the result, and the court is satisfied that the judgment is just, the motion for a new trial should be denied. (People v. 

Stielow, 161 N.Y.S. 599.)" 622

§ Cases have been decided in which newly discovered impeaching evidence was held sufficient to warrant a new trial. In People v. Kudon, 173 App. Div. 342, 158 N.Y.S. 

817, such new evidence attacked the testimony of an accomplice's mother, the only witness who corroborated the accomplice's testimony. Note, however, that the Kudon case has not been cited again to date in support of the proposition that such evidence is proper in warranting the granting of a new trial. However, it has not been expressly overruled and may be cited in support of such argument until the matter is definitely decided by the Court of Appeals. See, also, People v. Shilitano, 218 N.Y. 161, where evidence of the recantation of a witness was held to be not merely impeaching evidence, but independent evidence which had the effect of destroying previous evidence, and thus ground for a new trial. 

Sec. 376. Appeals. No appeal specially lies from an order denying a motion for a new trial as it is an intermediate order (People v. Trezza, 128 N.Y. 529; People v. Garrini, 249 App. Div. 739, 291 N.Y.S. 672). The decision of the motion may be reviewed upon appeal from the judgment of conviction (People v. Schad, 12 N.Y.S. 695; People v. 

Noona, 14 N.Y.S. 519) and, if the decision upon the motion based upon newly discovered evidence is decided prior to the appeal, it, too, will be reviewed (People v. Priori, 163 

N.Y.99). Compare Hubbard v. Loeb, 125 App. Div. 579, 109

N.Y.S. 1116, indicating that if the motion based upon newly discovered evidence is decided after the appeal from the original judgment of conviction, no appeal will lie from the decision upon the motion. Generally the completion of the judgment roll on the initial appeal from the conviction is the cut-off beyond which subsequent motions for new trials are held not appealable (People v. Antonio, 265 N.Y. 

467; People v. Gersowitz, 294 N.Y. 163; People v. Ramistella, 282 App. Div. 722, 122 N.Y.S. 2d 10).

In 1947, the Code was amended (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

517) to permit appeals from orders denying motions to 623

§  

vacate judgments of conviction, and People v. Greenfield, 275 App. Div. 862, 89 N.Y.S. 2d 344, held that that section allowed appeals from orders denying motions for new trials on the ground of newly discovered evidence. In 1953, the Code was again amended to "restrict the right of review, except on appeal from a judgment of conviction, to appeals from orders denying motions to vacate such judgment on grounds which would make available the remedy of a writ of error coram nobis. *** We find no decision in this state which permits [that] *** *remedy to be invoked for newly discovered evidence." (People v. 

Palumbo, 282 App. Div. 1059, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 381.) See chapter on 'Appeals' for a further discussion of appeals. 624

CHAPTER 33  Sec. 377. Nature and Function Sec. 378. Based on Jurisdictional Grounds Sec. 379. Based on Insufficiency of Indictment or Information Sec. 380. Based on Unconstitutionality of Statute Sec. 381. Based on Defendant's Insanity 

Sec. 382. Based on Double Jeopardy

Sec. 383. Based on Statute of Limitations Sec. 384. Based on Errors and Improprieties in the Trial Sec. 385. Making the Motion Sec. 386. Arrest of Judgment without Motion Sec. 387. Effect of Arrest of Judgment Sec. 388. Arrest of Judgment in Inferior Courts PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

After a verdict of guilty, counsel should always move in arrest of judgment if he feels there are grounds for this motion. It is usually made orally, although occasionally it is made on formal papers. Frequently, a motion in arrest of judgment and a motion for a new trial are made at the same time, although they are not combined since the remedies they seek are separate. 

It is customary for the court to grant counsel's application for additional time to make these motions. However, the attorney should be certain that the record shows that the court has granted permission to make this motion at a later date. 

Sec. 377. Nature and Function. As our examination of criminal procedure from the initial information and arrest through indictment, trial and verdict, has already made apparent, "The Legislature, in adopting the Code, intended to establish a complete system of criminal practice." (People ex rel. Benton v. Court of Sessions, 46 N.Y. 625

§ 

St. 255, 19 N.Y.S. 508.) To make the practice truly complete, it must assure, despite prior opportunities afforded to raise questions of jurisdiction and those of the sufficiency of the indictment and information, that final judgment will not be pronounced, or sentence imposed, until all reasonable likelihood that these fundamental requisites have not been duly considered is obviated. While motions of like import and similar effect can be presented immediately after the indictment is found or the information filed, at the opening of the trial, or during its course, there is still the possibility of oversight or neglect; and against such possibility the practice provides the remedy of arrest of judgment.

This remedy is applied for by the motion defined in Section 467 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, thus: "A motion in arrest of judgment is an application on the part of the defendant that no judgment be rendered on a plea or verdict of guilty, or on a verdict against the defendant upon the plea of a former conviction or acquittal. It may be founded on any of the defects in the indictment mentioned in section three hundred and thirty-one." The available defects, thus incorporated by reference, are stated as follows: "*** the objection to the jurisdiction of the court over the subject of the indictment or that the facts stated do not constitute a crime, may be taken at the trial * * * in arrest of judgment." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 331.)

The first, and basic, consideration is that motions in arrest of judgment cannot be founded on matters of fact or evidence, but, as the court stated in Jacobowsky v. People, 6 Hun 524, affirmed 64 N.Y. 659: "They are made upon supposed defects in the record itself, of which the evidence given upon the trial forms no part." Thus, in People v. 

Kelly, 94 N.Y. 526, the Court of Appeals considered an appeal raising the denial by the trial court of a motion in arrest of judgment, based on an affidavit seeking to establish that the court had improperly communicated with the jury in the absence of the defendant and his counsel. It was 626

§ there stated, at page 530 of 94 N.Y.: "A motion in arrest of judgment must be made for some defect which appears on the face of the record, and cannot be based upon a mere affidavit showing the existence of facts outside the record, and which do not constitute a part of the same." Being limited to objections "to the jurisdiction of the court over the subject of the indictment and that the facts stated do not constitute a crime" (People v. Meakim, 133 N.Y. 214), "such a motion raises only questions of law." (People v. 

Beckwith, 42 Hun 366, 5 N.Y. Cr. 232, affirmed 108 N.Y. 67.)

Most significant, and implicit in its very purpose and function as the last opportunity to raise basic issues of law, is the fact that the motion in arrest of judgment is not an exclusive remedy. This is indicated by the defining statute, in which we have already seen other provisions for other remedies are incorporated by reference (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 467), and certain of the grounds of demurrer to the indictment become the grounds of arrest of judgment. Denying a motion to strike out and dismiss counts of an indictment, in a decision in which it stated that “this is another way of raising the same issues of law which would be presented if a demurrer had been filed," the court stated in People v. Kupferman, 175 Misc. 650, 24 N.Y.S. 2d 

445, 449: "A demurrer is not the exclusive manner of raising the point urged here; it may be the subject of a motion at any stage of the trial or a motion in arrest of judgment." 

And in People v. Weichers, 94 App. Div. 19, 21, 87 N.Y.S. 

897, affirmed 179 N.Y. 459, the court stated: "This question, of course, relates to the form of the indictment, and the claim is that the facts alleged do not constitute a crime, that they allege an executed conspiracy. This question might have been raised by demurrer under subdivision 4 of Section 323 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, or at the trial or in arrest of judgment under Section 331 of said Code." Similarly, in a case in which the objection was jurisdictional, and not based on the insufficiency of indictment or information, it was stated in People ex rel. N.Y. 627

§ 

Disposal Corp. v. Freschi, 173 App. Div. 189, 191, 159 N.Y.S. 

23: "In any event, the question of jurisdiction could be raised either by motion at the commencement of the trial or by motion in arrest of judgment." 

Sec. 378. Based on Jurisdictional Grounds. The court's lack of jurisdiction "over the subject of the indictment" is one of the defects which may be raised by motion in arrest of judgment, we have seen. In People v. Knatt, 156 N.Y. 302, it was held that the objection that the court in which the indictment for a misdemeanor had been found was without jurisdiction, for lack of the certificate required under Section 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to remove a misdemeanor from the exclusive jurisdiction of special sessions, could be properly raised by motion in arrest of judgment.

In People v. Gardner, 78 Misc. 514, 139 N.Y.S. 1013, the defendant, under sixteen years of age, had pleaded guilty to burglary in the third degree. Sentence was suspended and he was placed on probation. On the following day, a motion was made in arrest of judgment, on his behalf, by reason that the statute made an offense committed by one under sixteen juvenile delinquency. The motion was granted and the defendant discharged, the court stating, at page 515 of 78 Misc.: "The motion must be granted, for the reason that the Grand Jury did not have jurisdiction to find the indictment ***" In People ex rel. New York Disposal Corp. v. Freschi, supra, the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York tried the defendant, charged with a violation of the Sanitary Code on an information made before a City Magistrate and transferred to it pursuant to Laws of 1915, ch. 531, sec. 44. The Appellate Division there held that the question of the jurisdiction of Special Sessions could properly be raised on a motion in arrest of judgment. On the other hand, where the motion in arrest was based on the contention that the evidence did not show that the crime had been committed in the county where trial was 628

§ had, it was held that this did not constitute an objection to the court's jurisdiction over the subject matter, but rather one of proof of venue, which should have been raised earlier in the proceedings (People v. Cooper, 58 App. 

Div. 532, 69 N.Y.S. 257).

Sec. 379. Based on Insufficiency of Indictment or Informa tion. In People v. Weichers, 179 N.Y. 459, 461-462, the court stated: "An accused person may take advantage of a defective indictment by demurring thereto before the trial, by objecting thereto during the trial, or by motion in arrest of judgment made after the trial. *** A motion in arrest of judgment is made after a plea of guilty, or after the trial has ended in a verdict of guilty *** If a defendant, with all these chances open to him omits to question the indictment before the trial, during the trial or after the trial *** he cannot then be heard upon the subject." While the statute itself specifically provides, and all construing authorities expressly acknowledge, that the motion in arrest of judgment properly raises the question of the insufficiency of the indictment, judgment will nevertheless not be arrested for minor, unsubstantial or merely technical defects. The defect requiring arrest of judgment must be a "fatal defect” and in the absence thereof "such order in arrest of judgment should not have been granted." (People v. Tripodi, 262 App. Div. 939, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 384.) 

And in People v. Buddensieck, 103 N.Y. 487, the Court of

Appeals referred to the indictment attacked by the appellant as having "no imperfection, therefore, in it, either in form or in substance, and those alleged against it by the appellant, if not wholly unfounded, do in no respect tend to his prejudice so far as substantial rights upon the merits are concerned, and hence they cannot affect either the in dictment or the judgment ***. It follows that the trial court did not err in denying the defendant's motion in arrest of judgment."

It has been held that where "there can be no doubt in 629

$ 

the defendant's mind as to the nature of the charge," even though "the defendant had wished more specific details as to the time and place of the alleged offense" and could have "made application to obtain such information by a motion for a bill of particulars," there was no basis for arrest of judgment, and the defendant's motion therefor was denied (People v. Ross, 11 Misc. 2d 870, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 

519). The test indicated in the Buddensieck case, supra, that the defects asserted must "tend to his prejudice so far as substantial rights upon the merits are concerned," has been frequently applied. 

In a case where the motion was made in arrest by reason that the information alleged the violation of a section other than that of which the defendant was convicted, Judge Van Voorhis, writing for the Court of Appeals in People v. Love, 306 N.Y. 18, 23, stated: "Appellant cannot have been prejudiced by the reference in the complaint * * * even the requisites of an information or indictment are merely that it shall state the offense and the acts constituting the offense ***. It has been held that where an information charges violation of the wrong section of a statute, this may be disregarded as surplusage if the information fully advises the defendant of the acts relied upon to constitute the alleged violation, and if the acts charged are clearly referable to the offense of which the defendant has been convicted ***"

The courts have repeatedly pointed out that technical and unsubstantial errors do not suffice for arrest of judgment, when raised on such motion for the first time. Such mere irregularities are deemed, as was stated in People v. Jacoby, 304 N.Y. 33, 40, to have been "waived by the defendant when he pleaded guilty," and the rationale of such holdings is that expressed in People v. Thompson, 41 N.Y. 

1, 7, as follows: "There is no injustice in closing his mouth now, in this respect, when he chose to keep it closed for such a purpose, at a time when the error might have been corrected, had he called attention to it." 

On the other hand, where a defendant convicted of book- 630

§ making (Penal Law, sec. 986) moved in arrest of judgment on the ground that the information had failed to allege that the offense had occurred elsewhere than on an authorized running or trotting track, the District Attorney opposed, by reason of the defendant's failure to demur or raise the question previously. The trial court denied the motion, but the Appellate Division reversed in People v. 

Silver, 251 App. Div. 309, 296 N.Y.S. 781, holding this was no merely unsubstantial technical error, but the very essence of the offense under the wording of the statute. 

In this connection, it should be borne in mind that although waiver of insubstantial defects has been consistently held to bar arrest of judgment, conviction on a plea of guilty to a crime not charged in the indictment under which the defendant has been charged is violative of Article I, section 6, of the State Constitution. As was stated by Judge Desmond in his dissenting opinion in People ex rel. Wachowicz v. Martin, 293 N.Y. 361, 369: "Relator's plea of guilty *** could not be an effective waiver of his constitutional rights. It could not ‘authorize a substantial change in its fundamental mode of proceeding.' (People v. Giudice, 100 N.Y. 503, 508; see Cancemi v. People, 18 

N.Y. 128, 136)."

Nevertheless, in People ex rel. Wachowicz v. Martin, supra, the majority held that, although the conviction of the relator on his plea of guilty of attempted grand larceny, second degree, when the indictment had been for burglary in the third degree, was "based upon a verdict or plea where the indictment fails to state facts sufficient to constitute the particular crime of which the defendant has been found guilty," his attempt to obtain relief by habeas corpus was not the correct remedy. He should, the court held, have moved in arrest of judgment, and appealed from the judgment if that was denied. 

Sec. 380. Based on Unconstitutionality of Statute. A direct challenge to the jurisdiction of the court is implicit in the assertion of the unconstitutionality of the penal statute 631

§ 

under which the defendant has been convicted. Consequently, such a challenge brings the matter squarely within the appropriate field of a motion in arrest of judgment as an "objection to the jurisdiction of the court over the subject of the indictment." In People v. Estreich, 272 

App. Div. 698, 75 N.Y.S. 2d 267, the defendant had been convicted of criminally receiving stolen property, in violation of Section 1308 of the Penal Law. Moving in arrest of judgment, he contended that subdivision 1, paragraph b, of that section, making "the mere purchase by a second hand dealer of the articles enumerated ** a felony, regardless of his knowledge or intent" was unconstitutional. The Appellate Division, Second Department, held this contention "properly raised below on his motion in arrest of judgment," reversed the judgment and the order which denied the motion, dismissed the indictment, and discharged the defendant. 

Sec. 381. Based on Defendant's Insanity. The alleged insanity of a defendant has been expressly disavowed as a proper ground on which to move in arrest of judgment. 

In People v. Craig, 295 N.Y. 116, 119, Chief Judge Loughran wrote for the unanimous court: "Insanity of the defendant is not a ground for arresting a judgment (Code of 

Crim. Proc., secs. 467, 331), but is rather a legal cause why judgment should not be pronounced against him until he becomes sane. (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 480, 481, 658 to 662f.)" 

Sec. 382. Based on Double Jeopardy. The plea of a former conviction or acquittal is specifically made available to the defendant by way of a motion in arrest of judgment, by the provision of Section 467 of the Code of Criminal Pro cedure. While he thus need not wait until the very point of sentence to raise the question, he may nevertheless rely therefor on a motion in arrest with full statutory authority. As the court stated in People v. Goldfarb, 152 App. 

Div. 870, 138 N.Y.S. 62, affirmed 213 N.Y. 664: "Doubtless 632

§ the defendant would have been entitled to a discharge on a writ of habeas corpus, on being held to answer the second charge * * * but this was not his only remedy, and he was at liberty after conviction to move in arrest of judgment on these facts as he did ***”

Sec. 383. Based on Statute of Limitations. Whether the running of a statutory period of limitation fits into the "no jurisdiction-insufficiency" formula applicable to arrest of judgment depends upon whether criminal statutes of limitation are deemed jurisdictional, barring prosecution after the expiration of the period stated, or, like those in civil actions, are considered merely "statutes of repose" not affecting the right to the remedy but permitting the defendant to make use of them or waive them.

The difficulty here is that our courts appear to have ruled both ways. It is not within the scope of this work to go into this question in the detail of legal scholarship, and we shall make no attempt to distinguish the seemingly contradictory holdings. We must, however, indicate the two lines and their reasoning and leave the practitioner not unwarned of the problem. 

In People v. Austin, 63 App. Div. 382, 71 N.Y.S. 601, affirmed 178 N.Y. 585, it was held that the Statute of 

Limitations could be raised in objection only by proof under the plea of not guilty and appropriate requests to charge; accordingly, where the question was first raised at the close of testimony and thereafter in arrest of judgment, the trial court's denial of the motions was sustained. 

In People v. Brady, 257 App. Div. 1000, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 789, the court stated: "The Statute of Limitations in criminal causes (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 142), as in civil actions, is a statute of repose." The court there cited People v. 

Bailey, 103 Misc. 366, 17 N.Y.S. 394, holding to that effect, and People v. Brown, 238 App. Div. 155, 263 N.Y.S. 267, which held that the mandatory language of Section 142- "A prosecution *** must be commenced within * * *”. might be construed as directory. People v. Blake, 121 App.

633

§ 

Div. 613, 106 N.Y.S. 319, affirmed 193 N.Y. 616, while cited by these cases for the proposition that the defense of limitation might be waived when not raised on the trial, did not so hold on the rationale they adopted, but rather on strictly procedural grounds relating to review on appeal. 

In fact, in the Blake case, supra, though divided as to the result, a majority of the Justices held that the Statute of Limitations in criminal cases is a statute of oblivion and not a statute of repose, as in civil actions. 

Conversely, Chief Judge Lehman, writing for the Court of Appeals in People v. Hines, 284 N.Y. 93, 113, stated: "Unlike a statute of limitations in a civil case, such a statute in a criminal case creates a bar to prosecution and the time within which an offense is committed becomes a jurisdictional fact which the State must allege and prove." 

And in People ex rel. Reibman v. Warden, 242 App. Div. 

282, 284, 275 N.Y.S. 59, it was stated: "A statute of limitations in criminal causes, therefore, differs from one applicable to civil actions, for while the latter bars the remedy only and not the cause of action, a statute limiting criminal prosecution destroys the right of action as well as the remedy." People v. Guariglia, 187 Misc. 843, 65 N.Y. 

S. 2d 96, quoted People v. Smolens, 258 App. Div. 373, 16

N.Y.S. 2d 731: "it was incumbent on the People to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the Statute of Limitations with respect to the various offenses had not run," and cited People v. Hines, supra; it accordingly granted the defendant's motion in arrest of judgment, and was thereafter affirmed by the Appellate Division, Second Department, in 

272 App. Div. 784, 69 N.Y.S. 2d 759, this being the same department in which the seemingly contrary People v. 

Brady, supra, had been decided eight years before.

While the two lines of authority would seem irreconcilably in conflict, the viewpoint that the bar of the Statute of Limitations is both jurisdictional and that its inapplicability must be proved by the People as part of their case seems the better one. Although the only citation given by the Court of Appeals in People v. Hines, supra, was that 634

§ of a text book, and in People ex rel. Reibman v. Warden, supra, the court relied on two New Jersey authorities, there is no gainsaying both the mandatory language of the statute and the general rule in most jurisdictions as to the nature of a Statute of Limitations in criminal cases (C.J.S., Criminal Law, sec. 223). Accordingly, it would seem that the question of statutory limitation may properly be raised by way of motion in arrest of judgment. 

Sec. 384. Based on Errors and Improprieties in the Trial. 

In Jacobowsky v. People, 6 Hun 524, affirmed 64 N.Y. 659, the court stated: "It is insisted that the judgment in this case should have been arrested, because the proof on the trial did not show that the house charged to have been disorderly was situated in the Seventeenth Ward of the City of New York, as it was alleged to be by the indictment. 

This position is clearly untenable, because motions in arrest of judgment are not supported by mere defects of evidence. *** The remedy for defective proof is by way of objection and exception, on that account, upon the trial. 

If that had been taken, the proof could probably have been at once supplied, and the defect, if any in fact existed, corrected." 

In People v. Paterno, 187 Misc. 56, 60 N.Y.S. 2d 813, the court considered the remedies available to a defendant who had been convicted on his plea of guilty of attempted grand larceny, second degree, interposed to an indictment charging the receiving of stolen property. Distinguishing a dictum contained in People ex rel. Wachowicz v. Martin, 293 N.Y. 361, cited supra in the present chapter, the court held a motion in arrest of judgment unavailable because the court had jurisdiction over the subject matter and there was no superficial insufficiency; the error, accordingly, must be reached through other remedies. And in 

People v. Osterhout, 34 Hun 260, 3 N.Y. Cr. 443, the defendant asserted, as error, that while present at his arraignment, he had not been required to and did not 635

§ 

plead; this was held neither to have prejudiced him nor to be available by way of motion in arrest of judgment. 

Misconduct, error or defect in the empanelling, summoning or dealing with juries has frequently been held to constitute no ground for the motion in arrest. Thus, in 

People v. Barrett, 2 Caines 100, arrest of judgment was denied when the proffered ground was that the trial judge had ordered a juror to be withdrawn without the defendant's consent. In People v. General Sessions, 20 Johns. 310, a clerical error in the venire summoning the jury panel, which was in violation of the statute tested out of term, was held to be no ground for the arrest of judgment. And in People v. Smith, 187 N.Y. 836, the court held that improper communications between officers and jurors, not of such character as could have influenced the result, was insufficient ground for an arrest of judgment. 

Sec. 385. Making the Motion. Section 469 of the Code of 

Criminal Procedure reads: "The motion must be made, before or at the time when the defendant is called for judgment. If made before, it must be on notice to the District 

Attorney, or in his presence." As was stated in a concurring opinion in People v. Lee Foon, 275 N.Y. 229: "The rule is laid down in Chitty's Criminal Law (vol. 1, p. 660) that the motion may only be made between the conviction and the sentence, and this ancient rule coming down from King's Bench has not been changed or modified by the pro visions of Sections 467-469 of the Code of Criminal Pro cedure. A reading of those sections clearly indicates that it must be made before sentence is pronounced." 

The motion thus becomes the defendant's last opportunity before sentence to move against the sufficiency of the indictment. As the Court of Appeals stated in People v. 

Nitzberg, 289 N.Y. 523, 529-530: "Though the Legislature may not curtail the right of an accused to challenge the sufficiency of a charge upon which an accused is held for trial, the courts of this State have refused to dismiss an 636

§ indictment upon the motion of a defendant made when the accused is held under a judgment of conviction after a valid finding of guilt by a trial jury. The Legislature has provided that a motion based upon objections to an indictment which appear on the face of the indictment must be made before or at the time when the defendant is called for judgment (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 323, 331, 467, 469)."

The basic rule was laid down in People v. Willett, 213 

N.Y. 368, 375, the court there stating: "Unless a motion founded upon the indictment and the insufficiency thereof is made before or at the time when the defendant is called for judgment, the objections thereof are waived." However, in People v. Lee Foon, 275 N.Y. 229, reversing 250

App. Div. 616, 294 N.Y.S. 872, this rule and requirement were not strictly complied with, the motion actually having been made after judgment was pronounced. Nevertheless, by reason that the whole procedure had taken place in a continuous hearing, at one session, it was held that the objection was of little consequence and the motion was considered to have been made in substantial compliance with the rule.

Sec. 386. Arrest of Judgment Without Motion. While the motion, made on defendant's behalf to arrest judgment after verdict or plea, is the normal and usual procedure, power is vested in the courts, even in the absence of such motion, to protect the defendant and achieve its benevolent result. This is embodied in Section 468 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides: "The court may also, on its own view of any of these defects, arrest the judgment without motion." As the court stated in People v. Reiser, 240 App. Div. 36, 269 N.Y.S. 573: "In the exercise of its inherent power, the court may and should arrest judgment to avoid the results of clear mistake or to avoid a miscarriage of justice." See, also, People v. Fuchs, 71 Misc. 69, 129 N.Y.S. 1012. 637

§ 

Sec. 387. Effect of Arrest of Judgment. Section 470 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: "When judgment is arrested, and it appears that there is not evidence sufficient to convict the defendant of any crime, he must, if in custody, be discharged; or, if under bail, his bail must be exonerated; or, if money has been deposited instead of bail, it must be refunded; and in such case the arrest of judgment operates as an acquittal of the charge upon which the indictment was found; but if there is reasonable ground to believe the defendant guilty, and a new indictment can be framed upon which he may be convicted, the court may order him to be re-committed or admitted to bail anew to answer the new indictment; if there is reasonable ground to believe him guilty of another crime, he must be committed or held to answer therefor; and in no case, when re-committed or held to answer, is the former verdict a bar to a new indictment."

In People v. Loomis, 30 How. Pr. 323, it was held that a defendant who was discharged on his motion in arrest of judgment could not thereafter plead the order and proceedings in bar of a subsequent indictment for the same offense. Similar holdings were reported in People v. Mc- 

Kay, 18 Johns. 212, and People v. Casborus, 13 Johns. 351. 

In People v. Cox, 67 App. Div. 344, 73 N.Y.S. 774, where a conviction for assault under a manslaughter indictment was reversed and judgment arrested because it was without warrant of law under the manslaughter indictment, it was held that the defendant need not be held to answer on another indictment for assault, being a permanent resident of the county and there being nothing to prevent his arrest for that crime. 

A defendant was convicted of manslaughter in the second degree, after trial under an indictment for murder in the second degree. Contending that the indictment was insufficient to sustain judgment under the verdict, and that a new indictment was barred by the lapse of the five-year limitation period, he moved in arrest of judgment and asserted the right to be discharged. It was stated, however, 638

§ in People v. Austin, 63 App. Div. 382, 71 N.Y.S. 601, affirmed 

170 N.Y. 585: "The appellant having voluntarily taken advantage of the verdict, was certainly not entitled to be discharged on an arrest of judgment unless it appears that there was not sufficient evidence to convict him of any crime. *** But the question that the offense of which the accused has been convicted is barred by the Statute of Limitations is not presented on a motion in arrest of judgment."

Sec. 388. Arrest of Judgment in Inferior Courts. For many years, the same procedure on motions in arrest of judgment has been followed in the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York. While trying only prosecutions for misdemeanors under information (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 64; N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31), and therefore not specifically covered by Section 467, which is within Part 

IV of the Code: "Of the Proceedings in Criminal Actions 

Prosecuted by Indictment," it has nevertheless been authorized to employ this procedure by Section 31, subdivision 4, of the New York City Criminal Courts Act, read ing: "All sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure consistent with this act regulating and controlling the practice and procedure of the Court of General Sessions of the Peace in the City and County of New York shall apply, as far as may be, to the practice and procedure of the said court, insofar as its jurisdiction and organization will permit." 

In People v. Cully, 167 App. Div. 332, 153 N.Y.S. 125, where the specific question raised was of the power and practice in this regard, the court carefully summarized and outlined the permissible practice in Special Sessions, in accordance with the provisions of the Code applying to courts trying indictments. Similar power would appear to have been conferred on City Magistrates of the City of New York by the provisions of Section 131, subdivision 3, of the New York City Criminal Courts Act. 

No such power, express or implied, seems to have been 639

§ 

conferred on the courts of special sessions which, outside the City of New York, are held by Justices of the Peace, Village Police Justices, City Judges, District Court Judges and other local magistrates throughout the State. The judicial officers holding such courts, which try misdemeanors and offenses on informations (Code of Crim. 

Proc., secs. 56 et seq.), without or with a jury (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 702; People v. Brodlowicz, 182 Misc. 351, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 86), have no such inherent power for, as was stated in People v. Freer, 171 Misc. 478, 12 N.Y.S. 2d 856, 857: "In all cases, jurisdiction of a court of special sessions must affirmatively appear and, in support thereof, no presumptions will be indulged (People v. McLaughlin, 57 App. 

Div. 454, 68 N.Y.S. 246)."

It would seem, furthermore, that Section 717 of the Code of Criminal Procedure mandates sentence on plea or conviction, without opportunity to interpose any motion in arrest, for it requires that on such plea or conviction "the court must render judgment thereon, of fine or imprisonment, or both, as the case my require." That section was, however, amended by Laws of 1959, ch. 218, sec. 2, effective 

September 1, 1959, in a manner which may have some bearing on this question. Superficially, the new subdivision 2 thereby added, which deals with procedure where the defendant convicted in special sessions has been previously convicted of crime and is therefore liable to additional punishment, is not intended to affect the question of arrest of judgment. Its last sentence, however, may well be construed to do so, its wording being: "Notwithstanding any other provision of any general or local law, this subdivision does not apply where the conviction upon which defendant is to be sentenced is not a conviction of crime." 

The intention of the Legislature, in this wording, was apparently to prevent the treatment of traffic offenses and minor infractions as crimes for the purpose of adding punishment under repeating offenders' statutes (see Law Revision Commission, 1959 Report, Recommendations and 

Studies; 1959 Leg. Doc. No. 65 M.). But it is not specifically 640

§ so limited and seems to empower the court to determine whether "the conviction upon which defendant is to be sentenced is not a conviction of crime." This, it is submitted, is the classic function of the motion in arrest of judgment and it may, possibly, be held to authorize the court's determination as to whether, because of defects in the information or want of jurisdiction, the conviction is not in law valid. Astute counsel will undoubtedly find the occasion to raise this question, and the rulings of the courts should be scanned for construction on this point. 641
