There is much that a lawyer can do for a client after the jury has rendered a verdict against the defendant, and prior to the time of sentence. Immediately after verdict, the defendant's pedigree is taken. If you know that he has a prior felony record you may determine that it is wiser to have your client stand mute. Such silence will not subject the defendant to any additional penalty. 

Where the defendant answers questions addressed to him, in the taking of the pedigree, he may reveal information which is not known to the prosecutor, and thus bring about a more severe sentence. This will apply more forcefully where the defendant has an 642

§ out-of-State rather than an in-State prior record. It must be remembered that fingerprints disclose information that clients do not always reveal to their counsel. 

The defense attorney should discuss the matter as candidly as prudence will dictate with the probation officer, in order to enlist his help and co-operation. The sentencing court will frequently be guided by the suggestions and recommendations of the probation office. Counsel should try to obtain letters favorable to the defendant from persons of good repute and high standing in the community. In fact, all information pointing up the good qualities of the client should be procured. Furthermore, all data in connection with the defendant's health, the dependence of his family upon him, and their economic deprivation in the event of his incarceration, should be assembled. These letters and this information should be available for submission no later than the day of sentence, in order to induce the sentencing court to temper its judgment with mercy.

It may be wise, on occasion, to discuss the matter of sentence with the District Attorney. His recommendation carries great weight. But it is the court and not the District Attorney who imposes sentence. Nothing the District Attorney says can bind the court unless the court is moved to agree with the recommendation. 

Sec. 389. Definitions. After the jury's verdict has been rendered, there must be a judicial determination of conviction if such is the verdict, and the imposition of a penalty. 

Prior to these, appropriate motions may be made, such as for a new trial or in arrest of judgment. This chapter discusses the proceedings to be had after such attack has been made unsuccessfully, or in the event no such motions are made.

Some authorities have drawn distinctions between "judgment" and "sentence" (see American Law Institute, Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 376 and 382), and between "sentence" and "conviction" (State v. McCall, 27 N.J. Super. 

157, 99 Atl. 2d 153). The Report of the Commission on the 

Administration of Justice in New York State (1936), at page 154, while recognizing that "The sentence of the court is the judgment thereof and the terms are used interchangeably in the cases," nevertheless, in its recommen- 643

§  

dations, "separates the judgment and sentence into distinct entities and prescribes the functions of each." "Judgment" was defined as "the adjudication by the court that the defendant has been convicted or acquitted"; "sentence" as "the pronouncement by the court of the penalty imposed on the defendant after judgment of conviction." These recommendations were not adopted and the present Code uses the terms interchangeably. (See Berman v. United 

States, 302 U.S. 211).

This usage may lead to some lack of preciseness in discussion. For example, Section 480 of the Code requires the court to ask the defendant, when arraigned for "judgment," whether he has any legal cause to show why judgment should not be pronounced against him. However, one of the reasons the defendant may then show is that he is then insane (Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 481), clearly relating to suspension of the execution of sentence, rather than to the judgment. In this chapter the definitions, as above quoted, will be used for clarity but, it should be noted, this distinction has no statutory basis at this time in New York. 

There is, in the Code, no requirement that formal judgment be entered upon an acquittal. Section 452 refers to a "judgment of acquittal on a general verdict" and requires the defendant's discharge as soon as such judgment is given. However, Sections 471 and 472 require the judgment to be rendered at a time to be appointed by the court, not sooner than two days after the verdict. This clearly is not intended to cover cases where verdicts of not guilty have been rendered and, in view of the practice, it is apparent that the "judgment" referred to in Section 452 is intended to refer to the verdict of the jury and its recording by the clerk. 

Sec. 390. When and How Judgment Rendered. As noted, the court will appoint a time for the rendition of judgment after a verdict or plea of guilty, or against the defendant on a plea of former judgment of conviction or acquittal. 

The time must be not less than two days after the verdict, if the that d rende may r nounc lie to judg 799). a rel rems 211: 964 whi me cor del de im at de th 644

§ if the court is to remain in session that long, but beyond that date no time limit within which judgment must be rendered is prescribed. One case has held that judgment may not be pronounced on Sunday, that a judgment pronounced on that day is void, and that habeas corpus will lie to secure the release of one imprisoned under such a judgment (People v. Ramsey, 128 Misc. 39, 217 N.Y.S. 

799). However, that release is not final, for in the case of a release after a void judgment the defendant may be remanded for re-sentence (see People v. Nesce, 201 N.Y. 

211; People v. Lipschultz, 5 Misc. 2d 686, 161 N.Y.S. 2d 

964; 9 Harv. L.R. 220).

After the verdict, it is desirable that time elapse within which motions may be made, and within which psychiatric, medical, or other investigations of the defendant may be conducted. Further, Section 472 expressly provides: "any delay [in pronouncing judgment] may be waived by the defendant." The waiver need not be express, but will be implied where counsel is present from a failure to object at the time sentence is pronounced (People v. Nesbitt, 7 

App. Div. 2d 763, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 878). Sentence "may not be deferred or postponed indefinitely. It is incumbent upon the Court * * * to pronounce judgment, either to sentence defendant to a term in prison or to suspend sentence or impose a sentence and suspend its execution." (Hogan v. 

Bohan, 305 N.Y. 110.) It is not required that the time fixed for imposition of sentence be within any specific period. 

In People v. Ryan, 132 N.Y.S. 2d 283, where pronouncement of sentence was deferred until the defendant's release from prison, approximately one year later, the delay was held not unreasonable in the light of the Hogan decision. In People v. Gorney, 103 N.Y.S. 2d 75, the defendant contended a one-year delay, where no definite time had been set for pronouncement of sentence upon his guilty plea, ousted the court of jurisdiction to impose sentence. 

While holding the question not properly before it on defendant's coram nobis application, the court indicated its approval of the holdings in Zerbst v. Nakas, 67 F. 2d 742, 645

§ 

and Miller v. Aderhold, 288 U.S. 206, which it stated: "In the absence of a request by the accused to be sentenced, the court did not lose jurisdiction to impose sentence by reason of the delay." Even if defendant's contentions were correct, the court further held, the error must be remedied in the court which erred or in an appeal from the invalid sentence.

In People v. LaMore, 4 App. Div. 2d 840, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 

477, it was held that sentence less than two days after plea, in violation of Section 422, was an error of law apparent upon the record, and not properly before the court in a coram nobis proceeding. It left unanswered the question "whether a violation of Section 472 is sufficient to warrant the vacating of the sentence in a coram nobis proceeding." (People v. Spencer, 2 App. Div. 2d 930, 156 N.Y.S. 2d 423.) 

People v. Van Cour, 208 Misc. 840, 137 N.Y.S. 2d 167 and

People v. Dalton, 205 Misc. 755, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 222, indicate that failure to comply with Section 272 is only a procedural irregularity. In People ex rel. Miller v. Martin, 1 N.Y. 2d 

406, the Court of Appeals indicated that violation of that section would require a remittal of the case for resentencing, while holding that failure to comply with Section 480 (regarding the "allocutus") did require such a remittal. 

In People ex rel. Ingber v. Jackson, 5 App. Div. 2d 1019, 172 N.Y.S. 2d 358, the court indicated, in dicta, that such an interpretation of the Miller case was warranted. The 

Miller case apparently put at rest the question posed in People v. Dalton, supra, concerning whether Section 472 was applicable to a plea, as well as a verdict, of guilty. 

Sec. 391. Suspension of Sentence. Deferring the sentence, as above discussed, must be distinguished from a suspension of its execution. At common law, courts exercised the power to suspend the imposition of sentence for a time for varying reasons. In Rex v. Rudd, 1 Cowp. 331, suspension was allowed to enable the defendant to attempt to obtain a pardon. The practice was often availed of in the absence of the present broad scope of review in criminal cases. Some previo the p the C Sus has b law, previ of co Div. pens N.Y at c the sen cus bee pr ter off of Se ha th 646

§ 

Some courts also suspended the execution of sentences previously imposed to inquire into the health or sanity of the prisoner (4 Blackstone Comm. 394; 2 Hale, Pleas of the Crown, 412).

Suspension of the time for imposition of the sentence has been discussed. The right of a trial court, at common law, to suspend conditionally the execution of a sentence previously imposed for an indefinite period is the subject of conflict. In People ex rel. Hirshberg v. Seeger, 179 App. 

Div. 792, 166 N.Y.S. 913, it was indicated that such suspension was invalid; People ex rel. Forsyth v. Court, 141 

N.Y. 288, indicated that that power was widely recognized at common law. In New York, Penal Law, section 2188, is the only statute specifically granting the power to suspend sentence in all cases. See chapter on "Probation" for a discussion of that section's grant of power to the courts. 

Suspension is not permitted where the defendant has been convicted of a crime punishable by death or life imprisonment, other than a crime punishable for an indeterminate term up to life; where the defendant is a fourth offender within the provisions of Penal Law, section 1942; where the defendant has been convicted of the commission of a felony while armed, within the purview of Penal Law, section 1944; or where imprisonment under the sentence has commenced. Sentence may not be suspended, nor may the defendant is on probation (Penal Law, sec. 2188; Peoport (mental, including a psychiatric report if such an examination has been previously ordered, criminological, and sociological) has been submitted to, and considered by, the court. Those sentenced to indeterminate terms may not be placed on probation or have their sentences suspended unless a psychiatric examination is conducted in the manner prescribed by Code of Criminal Procedure, sections 659 through 661. Prior to the suspension, the court must give the District Attorney an opportunity to be heard in opposition, and the court may require security if an order directing the defendant to support his children or wife has previously been entered against him. 647

§ (a) 

Sec. 391 (a). Revocation of Suspension. The court may revoke the order of suspension at any time during the period the defendant is on probation (Penal Law, Sec. 2188; People v. Moore, 184 Misc. 444, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 189). If execution of sentence has been suspended, the court may, when revoking the suspension, impose any punishment it might have imposed at the time of the original conviction. Section 483 of the Code also deals with suspensions of sentence and probation. It provides, in summary, that after a guilty plea or verdict "in a case where a discretion is conferred upon the court as to the extent of the punishment, and where there appear to be circumstances in mitigation of the punishment," the court has the power to place the defendant on probation in accordance with the provisions of the Code governing probation procedures, after suspension of the execution or imposition of sentence. It should be noted that it is not mandatory that a defendant whose sentence is suspended be placed on probation. The New York courts hold that they have inherent power to suspend sentence and that statutory regulations concerning the revocation of probation and hearing thereon do not necessarily apply to non-statutory suspensions; this is held even where, in the exercise of such common law powers, the court imposes conditions upon the suspension which make it, in effect, a probation.

However, in People ex rel. Goldberg v. Sheriff, 206 Misc. 

820, 137 N.Y.S. 2d 498, the court indicated that hearings should be granted, even though not required by statute, prior to a revocation of a conditional suspension, based on a violation of one of the conditions. The court sustained a writ of habeas corpus because no such hearing had been granted, although recognizing that the defendant therein had not been placed on probation. In so doing, the court relied upon Ercoe v. Zerbst, 295 U.S. 490, which construed the Federal probation statutes. If the original judgment ordered the payment of a fine and imprisonment until its payment, the court may suspend the execution of the im- JU prison condi defen provi ment suspe acco sions follo If the whi that had 2d N. aff pro the th tic of (་ 648

Any suspension ordered under Section 483 may be revoked in accordance with the provisions of Section 470-a. Suspensions ordered independently may be revoked without following of the procedures set forth therein.

If sentence has been suspended, the court may revoke the suspension at any time within the longest period for which the defendant could have been sentenced, even if that period exceeds the period for which the suspension had been ordered (People v. Kastel, 172 Misc. 784, 17 N.Y.S. 

2d 418; People ex rel. Fellman v. Foster, 184 Misc. 213, 53 

N.Y.S. 2d 255, affirmed 270 App. Div. 877, 62 N.Y.S. 2d 528, affirmed 296 N.Y. 954), or at any time within the period of probation, if such has been ordered, if that period exceeds the aforementioned period. The court, moreover, is given the power to revoke the suspension of imposition or execution of sentence thereafter if the defendant is convicted of the commission of another crime during that period (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 470-a). This is not an unconstitutional deprivation of any right (Ex parte Kuney, 280 N.Y. 

794). If the Court attempts to revoke the suspension order subsequent to that time, habeas corpus will lie to secure the defendant's release (People ex rel. Berman v. Marsden, 3 

App. Div. 2d 980, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 993). The suspensions above referred to are matters within the discretion of the court (People v. Stone, 25 N.Y.S. 2d 94), and when the judge ordering the suspension is succeeded in office during the period in which revocation is allowable his successor in office has the power to revoke the suspension (People v. 

Foote, 144 Misc. 134, 258 N.Y.S. 210). However, once imprisonment has commenced the court no longer has power to order a suspension (People ex rel. Quigley v. Marsden, 188 Misc. 37, 66 N.Y.S. 2d 698). 649

§ 

Sec. 392. Effect of Suspension. For the purpose of imposing sentence as a second offender in a subsequent trial, the prior suspension of imposition or execution of sentence is considered a conviction (People v. Garry, 237 App. Div. 

769, 263 N.Y.S. 288). Such suspensions are also considered convictions for the purpose of impeaching the defendant's testimony in later civil or criminal actions or proceedings (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 470-b). Suspensions of sentence in other states, after convictions there, are also considered convictions for the purpose of imposing sentence as a second offender in a later trial in New York (People v. 

Wengorra, 256 App. Div. 508, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 632). However, suspensions are not considered convictions within the meaning of the fourth-offender statute (Penal Law, sec. 

1942) and, to be considered a third or fourth offender, the defendant's prior prosecutions must have terminated with the imposition and execution of sentence (People ex rel. 

Marcley v. Lawes, 254 N.Y. 249; People ex rel. Bistany v. 

Brophy, 285 N.Y. 839; People ex rel. Lozzi v. Fay, 5 N.Y. 

2d 890, 182 N.Y.S. 2d 835).

Sec. 393. Presence and Arraignment of Defendant at 

Judgment. If the conviction is for felony, the defendant must be personally present for judgment (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 473). His presence may be procured by a bench warrant if he is at large on bail, or by order of the court directed to the officer having him in charge if he is in custody (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 474). Once the defendant appears for judgment the "allocutus" occurs: that is, the judge must ask the defendant whether he has any legal cause to show why judgment should not be pronounced against him (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 480). This requirement is a substantial legal right of the defendant (People v. Dalton, 205 Misc. 755, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 222), applicable only in felony cases (People v. Kaminsky, 208 N.Y. 289), and failure of the court to comply with the requirements of Section 480, while not voiding the conviction (People v. De 

Bernardo, 191 Misc. 563, 106 N.Y.S. 2d 575), does require reversa resent Lipsch

The ment, may a arrest Proc. cause hear for N time othe sent imm sho N.Y has jud fer th ch of re of in 650

§ reversal of the sentence and judgment and remand for resentencing (People v. Nesce, 201 N.Y. 111; People v. 

Lipschultz, 5 Misc. 2d 656, 161 N.Y.S. 2d 964).

The defendant may show, as cause against the judgment, that he is insane (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 481). He may also show that he has "good cause to offer, either in arrest of judgment, or for a new trial." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 481, subd. 2.) If the defendant does show such cause, the court may defer the imposition of judgment and hear the motion to be made. See chapters entitled "Motion for New Trial," and "Motion in Arrest of Judgment." This time is also the proper moment for the defendant to show other mitigating factors, and to plead for leniency in the sentence. So, also, if one has been promised leniency or immunity for cooperating with the prosecution, the court should be made aware of that fact (People v. Reilly, 224 

N.Y. 90).

If, in its discretion, the court decides that the defendant has not sufficient cause to show against the judgment, judgment will be rendered after the court reviews the defendant's previous criminal record and any other reports that may have been made as a result of a "mental, psychiatric or physical examination" of the defendant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 482). Upon such examination of the record, if it appears that the defendant is a previous offender and that fact was not alleged in the indictment, an information will be filed accusing the defendant of such prior conviction and proceedings had thereon. These proceed in the same manner as proceedings upon an indictment for the crime for which sentence is to be imposed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 482). These proceedings are held only after a verdict or plea of guilty, if the previous conviction is not alleged in the indictment, if a different or additional punishment is prescribed for a previous offender, and if no other proceedings are prescribed by law for the same purpose, such as those prescribed in Penal 

Law, sections 1943 and 1751-a. 651

§ 

 Sec. 394. Evidence of Prior Convictions. A copy of the minutes of any prior convictions with the sentence of the court thereon, certified by the clerk having custody thereof, and a similarly certified copy of the previous indictment, are deemed sufficient evidence of a former conviction when the clerk's certificate indicates that no record of judgment upon such conviction has been filed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 482-a). It is not necessary that prior convictions be shown in this manner, for they may also be proved under the rules of evidence (People v. McIntyre 99 

Misc. 17, 163 N.Y.S. 528). Another recognized method of proving prior conviction is by the production of a report of the person in charge of fingerprint records, to the effect that those records show the previous conviction of one with the same fingerprints (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

482-b). This section does not apply to records of out-of- 

State convictions (People v. Reese, 258 N.Y. 89), and it has been held that such records are not, of themselves, sufficient proof of the prior conviction without the production of the original or of an exemplified copy of the record (People v. Fine, 140 Misc. 592, 251 N.Y.S. 187).

Sec. 395. Fines and Remission of Fines. Any court of record except an inferior court of local jurisdiction, or any judge authorized to preside at such a court, has the power, within discretion, to remit any fine or portion of any fine imposed by that court on five days' notice to the District Attorney of the county in which the fine was imposed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 484). County Courts also have such power as to any fines imposed by the inferior courts, excepted from the above section, as has the General 

Sessions of New York County. Section 484 also restricts the imposition of imprisonment until a fine is paid to not more than one day for every dollar of the fine.

Sec. 396. Effect of Jury Recommendations. First degree murder convictions are punishable by death "unless the jury recommends life imprisonment as provided by section 652

$ 1045-a." (Penal Law sec. 1045.) Section 1045-a of the Penal 

Law, applicable to felony murder convictions, provides that the jury may recommend life imprisonment as part of its verdict, in which case the court "may" sentence the defendant to life. In People v. DeRenna, 166 Misc. 582, 25 

N.Y.S. 2d 694, the court held such a recommendation, in a felony murder case, binding upon the court. But in People v. Ertel, 283 N.Y. 519, the Court of Appeals clearly indicated its holding that such a recommendation was not binding, and that must be considered the law. 

Sec. 397. Place of Imprisonment. Penal Law, sections 2180 

through 2187, prescribe the places of imprisonment of convicted defendants, and Section 2180 requires the court to state, in its judgment and sentence, that place. Specification of the wrong place (for example, sentence to a State prison upon a misdemeanor conviction, which is proscribed by Penal Law, sec. 2182, subdivision 2), will not void the sentence, and warrant the sustaining of habeas corpus, but upon the prisoner's application he will be remanded to the custody of the Sheriff for imprisonment in the proper place (People ex rel. Mittelman v. Superintendent, 46 Misc. 131, 93 N.Y.S. 218; People ex rel. Devoe v. Kelly, 97 N.Y. 212). 

Sec. 398. Period of Sentence. Penal Law, section 2189, requires imposition of indeterminate sentences on first conviction of a felony, other than first or second degree murder or kidnapping. For the purposes of that section, one is considered a first offender if he has never before been convicted of a crime punishable by imprisonment in a State prison and is not punishable as a second, third or fourth offender under Penal Law, sections 1941 or 1942.

The sentence shall be for a maximum period of not more than the longest period authorized by law as punishment for that offense, and for a minimum period, where another minimum is not fixed by law, of not less than one year and not more than one half the maximum period (Penal Law, 653

§ 

sec. 2189). Psychiatric examinations of persons sentenced under the above section are required by Penal Law, sec. 2189-a. 

Penal Law, section 2193, provides in detail the methods of calculating the term of imprisonment, including provision as credit for time spent in confinement prior to sentence. Section 2190 provides for those convicted of more than one offense, and requires that sentence imposed for a second offense commence at the termination of the sentence for the first offense. But the court may order one convicted at the same trial for more than one crime to serve the sentences either concurrently or consecutively. 

It has been held that the provision in Penal Law, sec. 2190, subd. 4, allowing the court to decide that matter, is applicable only where the crimes charged were separate and distinct in nature and arose out of different transactions (People v. Savarese, 114 N.Y.S. 2d 816). In other cases, and where no direction to the contrary is made by the court, sentences are to be served consecutively (Becker v. Sinnett, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 872).

Where a crime is punishable under the statute for a period stated to be not less or not more than specified numbers of years, the court has discretion to sentence the defendant for any time less than the maximum, and more than the minimum set (Penal Law, secs. 2191, 2192). In 

People ex rel. Dearborn v. Jennings, 132 Misc. 196, 229

N.Y.S. 281, the court indicated that this rule is not applicable to first offenders, required to be sentenced under the indeterminate sentence provisions of Section 2189. The 

Attorney General, in 1956 Op. Atty. Gen. 175, held that by enactment of Section 2189, "the Legislature intended thereby to abolish determinate sentences upon conviction of a felony," and that the "imposition of an indeterminate sentence appears to be mandatory, whether defendant is a first or multiple offender." In People v. Barry, 273 App. 

Div. 971, 78 N.Y.S. 2d 402, the court had held a determinate sentence proper in the case of a first offender, where the punishment prescribed by statute was not less than a 654

§ (a) 

specified number of years. The Attorney General distinguished the Barry case in his opinion on the ground that it dealt with a sentence imposed prior to the amendments of the sections in 1936. 

Sec. 399. Previous Offenders. Under Penal Law, sec. 1940, prior convictions for rape, sodomy and related crimes, upon subsequent conviction of a felony, empower the court to sentence the defendant to an indeterminate sentence of one day to life. Second, third and fourth offenders, generally, are treated in Penal Law, secs. 1941 and 1942. Punishment of persons who have previously been convicted of a felony, or of an attempt to commit a felony in New York, or who have been convicted outside New York of a crime which would have been a felony if committed in New York, are within the scope of those sections. Where the latter conviction is for an offense punishable for a term less than life, the sentence must be for an indeterminate term, the minimum being not less than one half the maximum term for such crime, and the maximum being twice the longest period for which the crime is punishable if a first offender were involved. Three-time narcotics law felony offenders are to be sentenced for an indeterminate term of fifteen years to life.

Multiple convictions resulting from one trial are considered only a single conviction under these sections. There is no requirement that one be indicted as a prior offender in order to be convicted as such (People v. Gowasky, 244 

N.Y. 451). See section on "Presence and Arraignment of

Defendant at Judgment," above, concerning the proceedings that are to be instituted when it is discovered, prior to sentencing, that the defendant is a prior offender (Penal 

Law sec. 1943).

Sec. 399 (a). Fourth Offenders. Penal Law, sec. 1942, gov erns the sentence that may be imposed after conviction of a felony, other than first or second degree murder, if the defendant is one who has previously "been three times con- 655

§ (a) 

victed within this State, of felonies or attempts to commit felonies, or under the law of any other State, government or country, of crimes which if committed within this State would be felonies." An indeterminate sentence is to be imposed, the minimum term of which shall be not less than the maximum term which could be imposed upon a first offender who had committed the last crime of which the defendant is accused, but in any event such minimum term shall not be less than fifteen years, and the maximum term of the sentence shall be life. The parole of defendants convicted and sentenced under this section shall be in the same manner as the parole of other prisoners serving indeterminate sentences.

Suspended sentences are not considered prior convictions within the meaning of this section (People ex rel. 

Marcley v. Lawes, 254 N.Y. 459). "Although a previous felony conviction upon which sentence has been suspended may be used as the basis for imposing the additional punishment prescribed by Section 1941 in the case of a second felony offender (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 470-b), it is now settled that a person who has been twice convicted of a felony, but who has received a suspended sentence on one of such convictions, may not on a subsequent conviction be classed as a third offender under Section 1941 (People v. 

Shaw, 1 N.Y. 2d 30, 150 N.Y.S. 2d 161), nor may a person on the basis of three previous convictions, on one of which sentence has been suspended, be sentenced under section 

1942 *** as a fourth felony offender. *** the finality of a judgment is necessary to establish each of the previous convictions ***. Where there is a conviction but sentence has been suspended, there is no judgment." (People ex rel. 

Lozzi v. Fay, 6 App. Div. 2d 18, 175 N.Y.S. 2d 236.)

So, also, where sentence has been imposed after the previous conviction but execution of that sentence has been suspended, it is not considered a previous conviction within the scope of Sections 1941 or 1942 (People ex rel. LaPlaca v. Murphy, 252 App. Div. 827, 299 N.Y.S. 336, affirmed without opinion 277 N.Y. 581; People ex rel. Lozzi v. Fay, 656

§ (a) 

supra). Previous convictions of felony by military courts martial are considered prior convictions within these sections (People v. Wilson, 11 Misc. 2d 840, 171 N.Y.S. 2d 

438). The court has no discretion, under Section 1942, as to the sentence to be imposed (People v. Wicklem, 183 Misc. 

639, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 88), although the section does not inhibit the Governor's power to pardon any fourth offender (Scholer v. Rattigan, 204 App. Div. 205, 197 N.Y.S. 847).

A previous conviction for escape is not to be considered a prior conviction in any subsequent sentencing of the prisoner as a second, third or fourth offender (People ex rel. 

Carallo v. Brophy, 294 N.Y. 540). A prisoner sentenced as a previous offender may, in habeas corpus, challenge the propriety of such sentence (People ex rel. Carallo v. 

Brophy, supra). 

If the prior convictions are discovered at any time after sentence or conviction for the last felony, the District Attorney of the county in which that last conviction occurred must file an information accusing the defendant of such prior convictions. The court in which the last conviction occurred shall then bring the defendant before it, and advise him of his right to be tried upon such information, and shall ask him at that time if he is the same person as charged in the information. If the defendant denies being such person, or if he stands mute, a jury must be empanelled to try the issue. If the jury finds that he is that person, or if the defendant acknowledges that fact, then the court shall sentence him under Sections 1941 or 1942, the last conviction shall be vacated, and the new sentence imposed after deducting therefrom all time the defendant served on the vacated sentence (Penal Law, sec. 1943). 

The procedure described need not be followed if the indictment upon which defendant was convicted alleged that the defendant was a previous offender. In that case, the court may impose sentence upon him as a previous offender after the conviction (People ex rel. Smith v. Hunt, 257 App. 

Div. 457, 13 N.Y.S. 2d 919). It should be noted that Section 

1942 does not limit the time within which proceedings 657

§ 

under Section 1943 may be instituted, and that it has been held that the lack of limitation is valid (People ex rel. 

Fernandez v. Kaiser, 230 App. Div. 646, 246 N.Y.S. 309, affirmed without opinion 256 N.Y. 581, cert. denied, 284 

U.S. 631).

Sec. 400. Reduction of Sentences. Correction Law, sections 

230-247, provide for the discretionary reduction of sentences for good conduct (generally ten days off for each month with a maximum of four months off per year), and these reductions are allowable under the rules promulgated by the Commissioner of Correction (Corr. Law, sec. 234).

Sec. 401. Habitual Criminals. Code of Criminal Procedure, secs. 510 through 514, and Penal Law, secs. 1020 through 

1022, concern habitual criminals, and provide that a court may adjudge one previously convicted of any felony, upon a subsequent conviction, a habitual criminal. One five times previously convicted of misdemeanors, upon subsequent conviction, may be so adjudged in addition to, or instead of, the punishment provided for the sixth misdemeanor. 

Unlike the situation prevailing in the case of prior offenders, where it is sought to have the defendant adjudged a habitual criminal it is necessary that the indictment charge the prior convictions (People v. Rosen, 208 

N.Y. 169; People v. Manning, 253 App. Div. 744, 300 N.Y.S. 

836). Code Section 511 requires that the court enter the order adjudging one a habitual criminal in a separate book kept for that purpose, and copies of the entry are to be sent to Police Departments and District Attorneys throughout the State. A habitual criminal is subject to the supervision of magistrates "to the same extent that a minor is subject to the control of his parent or guardian" (Penal Law, sec. 1021); his person and premises are liable at all times to search by any officer, with or without warrant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 514); he is subject to summary arrest without warrant and punishment as a dis- 658

§ orderly person when he is found, without sufficient reason, in possession of any dangerous weapon or criminal tool, or in "any place or situation, under circumstances giving reasonable ground to believe that he is intending or wait- *** to commit some crime." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. ing 512.) 

Sec. 402. The Judgment Roll. After judgment of conviction has been rendered, in this case the term judgment being used synonymously with sentence (People v. La Sasso, 182 

Misc. 538, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 93), the clerk is required to enter it upon the minutes of the court, including therein a brief statement of the offense. If an appeal is to be taken by the defendant, upon service upon the clerk of the notice of appeal he will prepare the judgment roll. See chapter on "Appeals" for a further discussion of the procedures upon an appeal and the contents of the judgment roll. 

Sec. 403. Court's Power to Change Sentence. It is generally held that once a lawful sentence has been imposed, it may not be changed by the court which imposed it after the expiration of the term of court within which it was rendered, or after commencement of execution of the sentence (People v. Elliot, 140 Misc. 685, 251 N.Y.S. 458; People v. Thompson, 251 N.Y. 428; People v. Youell, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 390).

There are cases holding that "The judgment or sentence cannot be changed once rendered." (People ex rel. Walosky v. McDonnell, 116 N.Y.S. 2d 387, affirmed without opinion, 280 App. Div. 914, 115 N.Y.S. 2d 819.) However it has also been held that the court has the power, if exercised within the term within which judgment was rendered, to vacate the original sentence and re-sentence the defendant (Terwilliger v. Eaton, 164 Misc. 776, 299 N.Y.S. 351; People v. 

Meskel, 245 App. Div. 673, 284 N.Y.S. 193). Improper sentences may be corrected, and it has been held that a writ of mandamus lies to effect such a correction (Matter of 

Cropsey v. Tiernan, 172 App. Div. 435, 158 N.Y.S. 948; 

People v. Miller, 169 Misc. 709, 8 N.Y.S. 2d 53). On appeal, 659

§ 

excessive or unreasonable sentences may be reduced (People v. Klepper, 261 App. Div. 1036, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 2).

Sec. 404. Execution of Judgment. After judgment has been pronounced, if the sentence is other than a death sentence, a certified copy thereof will be furnished by the clerk to the officer whose duty it is to execute the judgment (in New 

York City to the Commissioner of Correction; elsewhere to the Sheriff). No other authority is needed to effectuate the sentence (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 486, 488, 489).

Thus, where a warrant of commitment has been issued, its defectiveness has been held immaterial (People ex rel. 

Dauchy v. Pitts, 118 App. Div. 452, 103 N.Y.S. 258). The officer must then deliver the prisoner, together with a copy of the entry upon the court's minutes, to the keeper of the proper prison (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 489).

Death Sentence. Code Sections 491 through 509 pre scribe the procedure to be followed in the execution of a death sentence. When such a sentence has been imposed, a warrant executed by at least a majority of the judges of the convicting court, including the presiding judge thereof, must be delivered to the Sheriff (in New York City the 

Commissioner of Correction), such warrant being directed to the Warden of Sing Sing Prison. The warrant must appoint the week for the execution, and must be delivered to the warden together with the prisoner within ten days after its issuance. The defendant, during the period prior to the execution, must be kept in solitary confinement. Only his counsel, members of his family, and requested religious officials are permitted to see the defendant without court order (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 491). The execution must occur within four to eight weeks after the sentence and no prior announcement of the day, except to the necessary witnesses, shall be made; the choice of the day is left to the discretion of the warden (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

492). Except for insanity or pregnancy of the defendant, only the Governor may reprieve or suspend the execution. 660

§ 

Discussion of pardons and reprieves is contained in the chapter so entitled.

Witnesses are required to be present at the execution, and invitations thereto are given the District Attorney and Sheriff of the convicting county (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 507). After the execution by electricity (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 505), which must take place within the designated prison (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 506), a certificate describing the execution and the post-mortem examination (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 507) is filed by the warden with the clerk of the convicting court. The body of the prisoner, unless claimed by relatives, will be buried within the prison. If the date set passes without the execution occurring and the sentence remains in force, the Court of Appeals, upon the application of the Attorney General or the District Attorney of the convicting county, shall fix a new date for the execution (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 503; 

People v. Lyons, 2 N.Y.S. 604).

Pregnant Prisoner Under Death Sentence. If it appears that a prisoner under death sentence is pregnant, the warden must empanel a jury of six physicians to ascertain the pregnancy and, if pregnancy is found, the execution must be suspended until a new warrant is executed by the Governor, who, after receipt of the information concerning the pregnancy and the subsequent birth, may appoint a new time for the execution or order the sentence commuted to life imprisonment (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 502). 661

Sec. 422. Judgment upon Appeal

Sec. 423. Effectuating the Judgment on Appeal Sec. 424. Entry and Remittitur of Judgment Sec. 425. Appeals in Habeas Corpus Proceedings Sec. 405. Matters Considered. In this chapter we shall con sider the principles and procedures affecting appeals from criminal judgments and orders. While proceedings in habeas corpus are not deemed criminal, being civil special proceedings regulated by Article 77 of the Civil Practice 

Act (People ex rel. Curtis v. Kidney, 225 N.Y. 299), we shall nevertheless deal briefly with appeals therein, by reason of the intimate relation they bear to the subjects of our concern. However, there are some other proceedings 662

APPEALS 

§ 406 which, while having a definite relationship to criminal matters, are also deemed civil special proceedings. Among these are proceedings to test a court's jurisdiction, taken outside the criminal procedure itself by way of prohibition 

(Article 78, Civil Practice Act; Matter of Bayberry-Hun tington, Inc., 137 N.Y.S. 2d 250); summary orders to punish for contempt of court committed in the court's presence (as distinguished from conviction of contempt as a misdemeanor), which are reviewed not by criminal appeal but by way of certiorari (Article 78, Civil Practice Act; Goodman v. Sala, 268 App. Div. 826, 49 N.Y.S. 2d 245, appeal dismissed 293 N.Y. 934; see also Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

515); applications to compel a court to vacate a felony sentence illegally imposed and legally resentence the defendant, when the same is instituted independently of criminal proceedings by a person other than the defendant, held to be in the nature of mandamus (Article 78, Civil 

Practice Act; Matter of Lyons, 271 App. Div. 946, 67 N.Y.S. 

2d 813). These we shall not consider. 

Sec. 406. Criminal Appeals, in General. "It is well settled that appeal is not a matter of constitutional right, and in criminal (noncapital) cases an appeal lies only by virtue of statutory authorization; such jurisdiction can never be assumed, unless a statute expressly authorizes its exercise." (Matter of Ryan, 306 N.Y. 11, 16.) Nor is the right to appeal a necessary part of constitutionally-guaranteed due process of law (People v. Gersewitz, 294 N.Y. 163, certiorari dismissed 326 U.S. 687, 90 L. Ed. 404). It is established "that the appellate jurisdiction of the courts of this

State in criminal cases is purely statutory; and, of course, such jurisdiction can never be assumed, unless a statute can be found which expressly sanctions its exercise." (People v. Zerillo, 200 N.Y. 443, 446.) Even the fact that an identical proceeding, brought in a civil forum, is appealable by provision of the Civil Practice Act, creates no jurisdiction when instituted in a criminal court, if the Code 663

§ 

of Criminal Procedure does not confer appellate jurisdiction (Matter of Clausi, 296 N.Y. 354).

The whole statutory scheme discloses the intention to place definite limitations on the right to appeal in criminal causes. It is the purpose of the statutes (see Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 520) "to limit further appeal following one appeal to an intermediate appellate court," and it is "the presumed purpose of the Legislature to maintain uniformity of procedure in criminal cases." (People v. Hatzis, 297 N.Y. 163, 164.)

Sec. 407. Effect of Appeal on Execution of Sentence. With one exception, the taking of an appeal by a defendant does not, of itself, stay the execution of the judgment appealed from, whether it be an appeal to the Court of Appeals (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 528), to the Appellate Division (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 527), to a County Court from a court of special sessions without the City of New York (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 753), or to the Appellate Part of the New York City Court of Special Sessions (N.Y.C. 

Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 43), except upon appropriate determination of reasonable doubt and appealability, as provided in the respectively applicable statutes, to be discussed farther on in this work. The only exception to this otherwiseuniversal statutory rule is in death cases, where an appeal (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 528), or the granting of a motion. for the reargument of the defendant's appeal (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 528-a), stays the execution "of course."

And it is provided, in Section 526 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure: "An appeal taken by the People, in no case stays or affects the operation of a judgment in favor of the defendant, until the judgment is reversed." 99 

Sec. 408. Who May Appeal, and from What. The defendant may appeal, as of right, from a judgment on a conviction in a criminal action or proceeding. He may similarly appeal, as of right, from an order denying a motion to vacate a judgment of conviction, known also as a motion or appli- 664

APPEALS 

§ 408 cation for a writ of error coram nobis (Code of Crim Proc., sec. 517). The People may appeal, as of right, from a judgment for defendant entered on a demurrer to an indictment; from an order arresting judgment; from an order made at any stage of the action setting aside or dismissing an indictment on any ground other than the insufficiency of evidence adduced at a trial; from an order granting a motion to vacate a judgment of conviction, otherwise known as a motion or application for a writ of error coram nobis; and in any case where a defendant may appeal, except where a verdict or judgment of not guilty has been rendered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 518). 

Section 517, regulating appeals by defendants, provides that "for every purpose of an appeal herein * * * a conviction shall be deemed a final judgment although sentence has been or may thereafter be suspended or otherwise suspended or stayed." Thus, except for this technical exception intended to overcome the common law rule denying appealability where sentence is suspended or stayed, judgments must be final to be appealable. It has, for example, been held that an appeal will not lie from a judgment which has been superseded by an amended judgment 

(People v. Verney, 269 App. Div. 858, 55 N.Y.S. 2d 779, af firmed 295 N.Y. 769). But even a judgment of conviction on a plea of guilty, being a final judgment, is reviewable and appealable to the extent that the sentence is deemed excessive (People v. Collins, 271 App. Div. 511, 67 N.Y.S. 2d 53).

To the extent that there may be an appeal from a judgment on a conviction, "any actual decision of the court in an intermediate order or proceeding forming a part of the judgment roll" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 517) may be reviewed. Accordingly, it has been repeatedly held: "No separate appeal lies from the sentence, the intermediate orders, the denial of motions, the errors of law or the rulings." (People v. Hamm, 5 App. Div. 2d 696, 169 N.Y.S. 2d 

513, 515.) With respect to what orders and proceedings are intended by that statute to be made reviewable as an 665

§ 

incident to an appeal from the judgment, the Court of 

Appeals, in People v. Priori, 163 N.Y. 99, 106, stated that it "is not confined to orders made between the finding of the indictment and the preparation of the judgment roll in the first instance. The word 'intermediate' as thus used means between the finding of the indictment and the completion of the judgment roll by the attachment of the case thereto whenever it is filed. *** if all the papers which the statute says shall be part of the judgment roll are not on file when it is first made up, they become part of it when filed, and the word 'intermediate' is limited only in this way." Consequently, the Court went on to hold in the 

Priori case, supra, that an order denying a motion for a new trial based on newly-discovered evidence, if made before the final filing of the judgment roll, is reviewable on the appeal from the judgment; if, however, the motion and order are made thereafter, it was stated at page 107 of 163 N.Y.: "The right is lost, the same as many other rights in legal proceedings are lost, by delay."

Among the intermediate orders which have been held not appealable separately, but only in connection with an appeal from the judgment, have been an order denying the defendant's motion to dismiss the indictment on the Grand 

Jury minutes (People v. Peetz, 7 App. Div. 999, 184 N.Y.S. 

2d 82), an order denying a motion for a change of venue (People v. Mordeno, 93 N.Y.S. 2d 369), an order overruling a demurrer and denying the defendant's motion for a bill of particulars (People v. Mangano, 264 App. Div. 870, 35 

N.Y.S. 2d 518), orders denying a motion to inspect Grand

Jury minutes and disallowing a demurrer (People v. 

Siegel, 282 App. Div. 747, 122 N.Y.S. 2d 638), denial of a motion to set aside a verdict and for a new trial (People v. 

Savage, 5 App. Div. 2d 795, 171 N.Y.S. 2d 42), and an order denying a motion to amend the minutes of a trial (People v. Huff, 5 App. Div. 2d 795, 170 N.Y.S. 2d 664). 

Section 517's limitation of the right to appeal to "a criminal action or proceeding" has impelled the courts to rule adversely on the appealability of those not made 666

APPEALS 

§ 409 in the course of such. Thus, it was held that an order made in connection with a judicial investigation, neither action nor proceeding either civil or criminal, was not appealable 

(Matter of Judicial Inquiry, 6 App. Div. 2d 1045, 179 

N.Y.S. 2d 301).

Similarly, no appeal lies from an order re voking probation (People v. Capria, 278 App. Div. 748, 103 

N.Y.S. 2d 358), or from one which denies an application to require a District Attorney to preserve Grand Jury minutes on the indictment under which the movant had been convicted (People v. Schectman, 277 App. Div. 783, 97 

N.Y.S. 2d 69), or from an order denying a motion to vacate an order directing movant's commitment as a material witness (People v. Doe, 259 App. Div. 1027, 20 N.Y.S. 2d 608).

Sec. 409. Courts to Which Appeals May Be Taken. An ap peal from a judgment of death is taken directly, as of right, to the Court of Appeals (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

517, subd. 1). Appeals from convictions of every other nature, in the Supreme Court, the County Courts, the Court of General Sessions of the County of New York, and the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, are taken to the appropriate departments of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

517, subds. 2, 3). Convictions by a court of special sessions, Police Court, Police Magistrate or Justice of the Peace, outside the City, are appealed to the County Court of the county in which they were entered (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 517, subd. 3, b). An appeal from a conviction by a City 

Magistrate, in New York City, goes to the Appellate Part of the Court of Special Sessions (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

517, subd. 2, b).

Upon the determination of the initial appeal, either party may take a further appeal provided permission is first obtained, as hereafter indicated and discussed in a subsequent section. In every such instance, the secondary appeal must be taken to the Court of Appeals, inasmuch as only one intermediate appeal is allowed. Such secondary 667

§ 

appeal to the Court of Appeals lies from a judgment or order affirming or reversing a judgment, including an order granting a new trial; from a judgment or order affirming or reversing a judgment for the defendant on demurrer; from an order affirming or reversing an order which sets aside or dismisses an indictment; from a final determination affecting a substantial right of the defendant; and from an order affirming or reversing an order granting or denying a motion to vacate a judgment of conviction, otherwise known as a motion for a writ of error coram nobis (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 519). 

Sec. 410. Appealing as a Poor Person. "There is no constitutional or statutory provision which requires the assignment of appeal counsel to an indigent defendant." This was stated in the majority opinion of Judge Froessel in People v. Breslin, 4 N.Y. 2d 73, 76, and he proceeded to cite 

United States Supreme Court authority holding this no deprivation of due process (Betts v. Brady, 316 U.S. 455, 85 L. Ed. 1595), and a large array of other Federal, New 

York and other authorities, and to rule for affirmance of the conviction.

Section 308 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does provide for the assignment of counsel for an indigent defendant, on arraignment, and for appeal counsel after conviction under a judgment of death or of life imprisonment on recommendation of a jury. No other statute applies (People v. Moylan, 4 Misc. 2d 747, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 479).

Accordingly, as stated in People v. Breslin, supra, at page 

78 of 4 N.Y. 2d: "Unless and until the Legislature acts, the determination of whether counsel should be assigned in post-conviction proceedings in a given case should be left to the court in which the application is made." 

Where the defendant's indigence makes it impossible for him to serve the required return on an appeal from a conviction in an inferior court, the trial court may be required to make and file it on his behalf, without charge (People v. Pride, 3 N.Y. 2d 545). Application for copies 668

APPEALS 

§ 411 of papers to be used on appeal is properly made to the trial court (People v. Hornbeck, 4 App. Div. 996, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 

213; People v. Lewis, 12 Misc. 2d 266, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 136).

A motion for leave to respond to an appeal as a poor person is properly made to the appellate court (People v. Fortson, 167 N.Y.S. 2d 976). A motion to appeal, or to respond to an appeal, as a poor person, will not be granted where there is no merit to applicant's appeal or contentions (People v. 

Morgan, 169 N.Y.S. 2d 938); nor will it be granted where no notice of appeal has been served (People v. Ashe, 164 

N.Y.S. 2d 842); nor where the papers do not precisely classify the crime (People v. Mawbey, 2 Misc. 2d 800, 153 

N.Y.S. 2d 244). Nor will a trial court grant a motion for a transcript of the stenographer's minutes without charge, until the indigent defendant has moved in the appellate court and there received leave to appeal as a poor person (People v. Ford, 8 Misc. 2d 486, 167 N.Y.S. 2d 603; People v. Kasulkas, 4 Misc. 2d 737, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 505; People v. 

Strong, 4 Misc. 2d 748, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 352).

Sec. 411. Taking the Initial Appeal. A defendant's appeal must be taken "within thirty days after the judgment was rendered or service of a copy of the order with notice of entry thereof" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 521), and he must serve "a written notice in duplicate on the clerk with whom the judgment roll is filed, stating that the appellant appeals from the judgment" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

522) and a similar notice on the District Attorney (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 523). Similar service must be made by the District Attorney on the People's appeal, with provision for service by publication where defendant cannot be served with due diligence (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

524). The clerk forthwith transmits the duplicate notice to the clerk of the appellate court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 522). Where the defendant appeals from a judgment of death, the District Attorney must forthwith notify the official in whise custody the defendant is. These prescribed services are mandatory steps; in their absence, or that of 669

§ 

any of them, no appeal is deemed to have been taken 

(People v. Green, 137 App. Div. 763, 122 N.Y.S. 571). Pro vision has been made, however, authorizing the appellate court, in its discretion, to permit the omission to be supplied, or an amendment made, where an act necessary to perfect the appeal or stay judgment has been omitted through mistake, inadvertence or excusable neglect (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 524-a). There was no such power prior to the adoption of the last-cited statute in 1936 (People v. Marano, 243 App. Div. 278 N.Y.S. 431), and it has been held that that section does not affect appeals to County Courts from courts of special sessions (People v. Omans, 306 N.Y. 375; People v. Cornell, 186 Misc. 825, 59 N.Y.S. 2d 835). 

In People v. Taras, 269 App. Div. 694, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 694, affirmed 296 N.Y. 983, certiorari denied 332 U.S. 818, 68

S.Ct. 144, rehearing denied 333 U.S. 839, 68 S.Ct. 602, the defendant failed to serve timely notice of appeal and "his right to review the legality of the prior proceedings to and including the rendition of the verdict was lost by failure to appeal within the time allowed by law from the judgment of conviction entered on the original sentence" (page 

695 of 269 App. Div., page 695 of 53 N.Y.S. 2d). Testing the validity of his sentence in habeas corpus proceedings, he was remanded for resentencing (People ex rel. Taras v. Kirby, 266 App. Div. 872, 42 N.Y.S. 2d 949). After being thus resentenced, he served notice of appeal from the original judgment, and the District Attorney moved to dismiss. The Appellate Division stated: "*** the order which remanded him for resentence did not affect the validity of the prior proceedings, nor did it revive the right*** lost by the failure to appeal. The present appeal brings up for review only the question of the correctness of the amended sentence."

While failure to serve notice of appeal within the limited time thus loses the right, and a notice served thereafter is a nullity and requires dismissal of an attempted appeal (People v. King, 273 N.Y. 646; People v. Friedlander, 278 670

APPEALS 

§ 412 

App. Div. 669, 102 N.Y.S. 2d 673), Section 521-a effects an extension of the time to appeal for sixty days from the death, removal or suspension from practice of a party's attorney, when that occurs within the time fixed. Where an attorney becomes physically or mentally incapacitated within that time, the court from which the appeal is taken may, in its discretion and on such terms as it may direct, permit such notice to be served, on application made within sixty days from the commencement of the incapacity.

Sec. 412. Initial Appeals from Inferior Courts. The pro visions of the Code regulating the taking of appeals, which we have examined, do not apply to appeals taken from a conviction in a court of special sessions outside the City of New York (People v. Omans, 306 N.Y. 375). There are distinct provisions of law relating to appeals from such court to the County Court, contained in Part 5, Title III (Sections 749, et seq.) of the Code. Similarly, appeals from a conviction by a New York City Magistrate, which must be taken to the Appellate Branch of the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, are controlled by Article 

IV (Sections 40-56) of the New York City Criminal Courts 

Act.

The appeal from the City Magistrate's conviction is taken by a notice of appeal served by the defendant "or someone in his behalf" within thirty days after the judgment appealed from was rendered, or order entered, on the City Magistrate or the clerk of the court and upon the clerk of the appellate court in the appropriate county. 

The notice of appeal so required to be served must state that the defendant appeals from the judgment and must specify "the particular rulings alleged to have been erroneous or any other grounds upon which the appeal is taken." (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 42.) An appeal is a nullity, and may be dismissed, where the service of notice is made beyond the 30-day period (People v. Brown, 133 Misc. 732, 234 N.Y.S. 231), and the failure to specify the grounds of 671

§ 

appeal, as required, renders the notice ineffective, except that it has been held that Section 524-a of the Code applies, and permits the appellate court to grant the appellant leave to amend his notice of appeal in this respect (People v. Trimboli, 207 Misc. 200, 137 N.Y.S. 2d 451).

On an appeal to the County Court from a conviction rendered by a local inferior court in a county outside New 

York City (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 749), instead of requiring the usual notice of appeal as in the statutes relating to appeals from other criminal courts, Section 751 of the Code directs the filing "within thirty days after the judgment or after the commitment, where the appeal is from the latter" of "an affidavit with the magistrate or clerk of the court *** setting forth the alleged errors in the proceedings, conviction or commitment." It is further provided that within three days thereafter a copy of the affidavit must be delivered to the District Attorney of the county in which the appeal is to be heard. In People v. 

Omans, 306 N.Y. 375, the Court of Appeals decided, on 

March 11, 1954, that Section 751 was conclusive and that the sections of Part V, and particularly Section 524-a, of the Code did not apply, and affirmed the order of the County Court denying leave to correct by permitting filing of an affidavit of errors. 

On September 1, 1954, Laws of 1954, chapter 806, became effective, and in Section 10 thereof it amended Section 750 of the Code to read in relation to appeals of this kind, as it now does: "An appeal may be taken as provided by sections five hundred seventeen through five hundred twenty ***" At the same time, Section 520-a was added to the Code, providing that Sections 517 through 520 of the Code be deemed to supersede any other provisions of the Code "in conflict with the same." This would seem to remove the basis on which the Omans case, supra, had been decided, the Court there having stated, at page 378 of 306 N.Y.: "Part V provides for a complete system of procedure, independent of that provided for in Part IV, except as otherwise specially provided." There was, how- 672

APPEALS 

§ 413 ever, no change made in Section 751 and its requirement of an affidavit of errors, nor was there a specific extension to appeals from special sessions of the provisions of Section 524-a.

There has been found no Court of Appeals or Appellate Division authority dealing with this matter since the 1954 amendments, but County Court decisions reported still follow the Omans case, supra (People v. Palmer, 5 Misc. 

2d 866, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 231; People v. Capobianco, 10 Misc. 

2d 802, 171 N.Y.S. 2d 726). Until higher authority determines this question, the prudent practitioner will comply with Section 751. It should be noted, however, that the 

Court of Appeals held, in 1949, that a District Attorney's failure to raise the question where an appellant had served a notice of appeal, instead of filing an affidavit of errors, had waived the objection, stating in People v. Belcher, 299 

N.Y. 321, 324: "Section 751 does not relate to defendant's right to appeal (see Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 520), and manifestly is intended only to provide a method of appeal which will insure adequate notice to a District Attorney who may not have participated in the trial (see Seventh 

Annual Report of Ñ.Y. Judicial Council, 1941, p. 254)."

Sec. 413. Secondary Appeals to the Court of Appeals. There is no appeal, as of right or of course, after the determination of the initial appeal. In criminal cases other than those resulting in judgment of death, it is provided by the State Constitution, appeals may be taken "as the Legislature may from time to time provide." (Article VI, sec. 

7.) The Legislature has provided, in Section 519 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that "an appeal may be taken from such determination by any party aggrieved to the Court of Appeals in the following cases, provided such party obtains a certificate granting permission to appeal, as provided in section five hundred twenty: 1. From a judgment or order affirming or reversing a judgment of conviction, including an order granting a new trial; 2. From a judgment or order affirming or reversing a judgment for the 673

§ 

defendant on a demurrer to the indictment; 3. From an order affirming or reversing an order of the court setting aside or dismissing the indictment; 4. From an order affirming, vacating or reversing an order of the court arresting judgment; 5. From a final determination affecting a substantial right of the defendant; 6. From an order affirming or reversing an order granting or denying a motion to vacate a judgment of conviction, otherwise known as a motion or application for a writ of error coram nobis." 

Security is not required to perfect the appeal (People ex rel. Kipnis v. McCann, 200 App. Div. 898, 192 N.Y.S. 944), but the condition imposed is that the certificate be procured, as provided in Section 520, subdivision 1, as follows: "*** if a Judge of the Court of Appeals or a Justice of the

Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the department in which such conviction was had makes a certificate granting permission to appeal and certifying that a question of law is involved which ought to be reviewed by the Court of Appeals, then a further appeal on such question of law may be taken to the Court of Appeals." In subdivision 2, the section proceeds to make a similar provision with respect to direct appeals from orders denying coram nobis in death cases, which may be taken directly to the Court of Appeals only upon similar permission and certificate granted by a Judge of that Court.

Such secondary appeal is timely "if the application for leave to appeal is made within such thirty days [after the judgment was rendered or service of a copy of the order with notice of entry thereof] and if the notice of appeal is duly served and filed within fifteen days after the certificate is granted." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 521.) Service of the notice of appeal is effected in the same manner as on an initial appeal (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 522, 523, 524); the provisions for extension of the time to appeal when an attorney dies, is removed or suspended, or becomes mentally or physically disabled, are equally applicable (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 521-a); applicable, too, is the 674

APPEALS 

§ 415 appellate court's discretionary authority to permit the correction of errors in perfecting the appeal and staying execution on the judgment (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 524a).

Sec. 414. Alternative Methods of Perfecting Appeal. The primary obligation and burden of seeing to the perfection of the appeal, and the preparation and submission of the record and papers which the appellate court must have to undertake a review, is imposed upon the appellant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 458; People v. Gordon, 26 N.Y.S. 2d 

665, 666), except that in appeals from judgments of death, or where a life sentence has been imposed on recommendation of the jury, the burden of preparing the record is imposed upon the clerk (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 485). Two alternative methods of preparing his record are permitted the appellant, who may proceed by way of a case and bill of exceptions, or on the judgment roll (People v. Williams, 213 App. Div. 482, 210 N.Y.S. 363). In either event, "Within thirty days after the service of a notice of appeal, the appellant, except as otherwise provided in section four hundred eighty-five, shall procure to be printed as required by the Rules of Civil Practice the record upon which the appeal is to be heard and cause the same to be filed with the clerk of the court in which the appeal is to be heard duly certified by the clerk of the court in which the conviction was had, or stipulated by the attorney for the party and by the District Attorney to be a true copy of the original." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 458.)

Sec. 415. Procedure by Bill of Exceptions. To perfect his appeal by way of a bill of exceptions, the appellant must "make a case and procure the same to be settled and signed, by the judge or justice, by or before whom the action was tried, as prescribed in the Rules of Civil Practice; or, in the case of the death or disability of such judge, in such manner as the appellate court directs. The case must contain so much of the evidence, and other proceedings upon 675

§ 

the trial, as is material to the questions to be raised thereby, and also the exceptions taken by the parties making the case; and a case where a special question is submitted to the jury, such exceptions taken by any party to the action as shall be necessary to determine whether there should be a new trial, if the judgment be reversed." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 458.)

This procedure has always been found the more advantageous of the two alternatives where only questions of law are presented (Derby v. General Electric Co., 208 App. 

Div. 529, 204 N.Y.S. 224; see Grobert R. Co. v. Dorf Bros., 118 Misc. 856, 193 N.Y.S. 584, dissenting opinion). Under this method, "a case is made by the appellant, to which the respondent may propose amendments, and, if these are not agreed upon by the attorneys for the respective parties, they are settled by the judge who presided at the trial. In this way, as the experience of generations has shown, substantial accuracy is attained, and the case is presented to the appellate court upon as perfect a picture of what transpired at the trial as can well be secured." (People v. Conroy, 151 N.Y. 453.)

Rule 230 of the Rules of Civil Practice requires that the proposed case and bill of exceptions be served on the adversary within thirty days after the judgment appealed from. The party served may propose and serve amendments within ten days thereafter. Within four days thereafter, either party may serve upon the other notice that the proposed case and amendments will be submitted for settlement to the trial judge at a time and place therein designated. This notice is required to be returnable not less than four, nor more than ten, days after its service. "At the time appointed, the judge must settle and sign the bill of exceptions." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 459.) The requirement of settlement by the judge is mandatory; it cannot be dispensed with by stipulation (People v. Bradner, 44 Hun 233, affirmed 107 N.Y. 1; Weed v. People, 31 

N.Y. 465). However, the "time for preparing the case, or the amendments thereto, or for settling the same, may be 676

APPEALS 

§ 416 enlarged by consent of the parties, or by the presiding judge or by a Justice of the Supreme Court, but no other officer. Only one order extending the time shall be granted, except upon notice of at least two days to the adverse party." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 460.)

The importance of meticulous care in settling the case is underlined by the rule that it will be presumed in the appellate court that all the evidence in support of the findings and decisions excepted to is included therein, it being necessarily assumed that if any of it had been omitted by the party making the case, the adversary would have had it inserted by amendment (Perkins v. Hill, 56 N.Y. 87).

The Court of Appeals, it has been held, cannot correct an improper insertion of findings in the original case on appeal (Binghamton O. H. Co. v. City of Binghamton, 156 

N.Y. 651), and that the court below, notwithstanding an appeal to the Court of Appeals, retains the power to make its record reflect the truth as to its judgment, and may amend the same (National City Bank v. N.Y. Gold Exch. 

Bank, 97 N.Y. 645).

The use of the bill of exceptions is subject to the follow ing provisions of Section 461 of the Code: "If the bill of ex ceptions be not served within the time prescribed in section four hundred and fifty-eight, or within the enlarged time therefor, as prescribed in the last section, the exceptions are deemed abandoned. If it be served, and the parties omit, within the time limited by section four hundred and fifty-eight, the one to prepare amendments, and the other to give notice of appearance before the judge, they are respectively deemed, the one to have agreed to the bill of exceptions, and the other to the amendments."

Sec. 416. Proceeding on the Judgment Roll. The appellant need not make a case or bill of exceptions, but may rely on the alternate procedure, in which event "the appeal shall be heard upon the judgment roll including a copy of the minutes of the trial." (People v. Peters, 117 N.Y.S. 2d 882, 883, certiorari denied 347 U.S. 906, 98 L. Ed. 1064.) The 677

§ 

judgment roll upon a conviction must contain the following papers, prescribed by Section 485: "1. A copy of the minutes of a challenge interposed by the defendant to a grand juror, and the proceedings and decision thereon; 

2. The indictment and a copy of the minutes of the plea or demurrer; 3. A copy of the minutes of a challenge, which may have been interposed to the panel of the trial jury, or to a juror who participated in the verdict, and the proceedings and decision thereon; 4. A copy of the minutes of the trial; 5. A copy of the minutes of the judgment; 6. A copy of the minutes of any proceedings upon a motion either for a new trial or in arrest of judgment; 7. The case, if there be one ***"" The clerk must procure the stenographic minutes of the trial, at the county's expense, and file them in his office (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 456). Where the appellant does not elect to make a case on a bill of exceptions, "the appeal shall be heard upon the judgment-roll, including the copy of the minutes of the trial filed as prescribed by section four hundred-fifty-six." The appellant procures the printing of the stenographic minutes and the judgment roll, "the record upon which the appeal is to be heard", which, either certified by the clerk of the trial court or stipulated to be a true copy of the original, must be filed with the clerk of the appellate court within thirty days after the filing of the notice of appeal (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 458). 

Sec. 417. Filing Record in Appellate Court. As we have already noted, the record is required to be filed, after being properly prepared, settled, printed and certified, with the clerk of the appellate court within the thirty days prescribed by Section 458, or within the time "enlarged by consent of the parties, or by the presiding judge, or by a Justice of the Supreme Court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

460.) Failure to so file is the basis for a motion to dismiss the appeal, addressed to the appellate court on four days' notice (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 458), on which motion the court may dismiss or may, for good cause, enlarge the time 678

APPEALS 

§ 417 to file (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 534; People v. Grieco, 265 

N.Y. 505). The most usual disposition of such a motion, in appellate courts generally, unless the appellant indicates abandonment of the appeal by not answering, is to direct the dismissal of the appeal unless filing is completed by a date, or for a specified term, designated in the order. 

Specific requirements as to number of copies required to be filed, number of days before a term or session filing must be made therefor, requirements as to filing and service of briefs and other practice details vary as between the Court of Appeals and the respective departments of the Appellate Division. The variations in practice in the fifty-seven 

County Courts of the State hearing appeals from inferior criminal courts is even greater. No attempt, therefore, will be made here to cover these matters; it is urgent that the prudent practitioner consult the printed rules of the appellate court in which his appeal is to be prosecuted or, lacking these, that he confer with the clerk as to current requirements and practice. In every appellate court, the mandate of Section 538 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is imperative: "*** the appellant must furnish the court with copies of the record upon which the appeal is to be heard, except where the judgment is of death or of life imprisonment following a recommendation ***. If he fail to do so, the appeal must be dismissed, unless the court otherwise direct." “*** In appeals from inferior courts to County Courts, the practice is simpler. After the affidavit of appeal is filed (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 751), the burden is imposed on the magistrate or court rendering the judgment to make a return and file the same in the office of the County Clerk within ten days after the service of the affidavit of appeal (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 756). On the lower court's failure to make the return, the County Court or County Judge may order it to be made within a specified reasonable time and may, by attachment, compel compliance therewith (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 757), and may also order and compel, in the same manner, a further or amended return 679

§ 

when the one made is defective (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

758). The appeal is brought to argument by ten days' notice of argument served by the appellant (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 759), the appeal is heard on the original return, and the appellant need furnish no copy thereof (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 763).

Appeals to the Appellate Part of the Court of Special 

Sessions of the City of New York are also heard on a return made by the Magistrate and filed by him with the clerk of the appellate court. The clerk mails a copy of the return immediately to the defendant or his attorney (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 46). The requirement is that the appeal be brought to argument by notice served by the appellant on the District Attorney within thirty days after the filing of the return, and not less than ten days before the date set. An order of dismissal may be entered, without notice, if the court does not enlarge the time and the appeal is not argued within the period limited (N.Y.C. Cr. 

Cts. Act, sec. 48). Provision is further made for serving and filing a brief or points on appeal at least three days before the argument (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 49). 

Sec. 418. Motions in the Appellate Court. The details of motion practice in appellate courts, including the terms and times at which motions are heard, requirements for service and filing of notice and motion papers, and the form and manner in which these are to be presented to the court, are matters prescribed by the rules of the respective courts and, consequently, vary considerably. Section 533 of the Code of Criminal Procedure makes provision for a motion to dismiss an appeal by the respondent, on five days' notice, "If the appeal be irregular in a substantial particular ***." Similarly, Section 436 provides for a motion to dismiss for failure to file the record, and this and other similar provisions, applying where time limits have not been met, have already been considered. 

Various motions are made in relation to calendar and practice details, amendments and other incidents of the 680

APPEALS 

§ 419 practice. Motions are made for temporary stays, enlargement of time, to compel compliance with requirements, for leave to appeal where required by statute, and for other diverse matters of practice. Motions generally are made either by way of notice of motion or by order to show cause, as in courts of original jurisdiction, and are customarily disposed of by orders, or by rules in the Court of Appeals. Here again, while general statutes and rules of practice may carry us to a certain point in discovering the practice in any court, reference to the specific rules and usages of the court is indispensable. 

Rule 11 of the Rules of the Court of Appeals provides that motions may be noticed for, and will be heard, the first Monday of each session of the court, but they may be submitted without oral argument on any Monday when the court is in session, provided they are submitted by both sides and the papers are filed with the clerk on or before the preceding Friday. If either party demands oral argument, the motion will go over to the first Monday of the succeeding session. Where there is no appearance in opposition to a motion, it will be granted as of course; where the movant does not appear, the opposing party is entitled, on applying to the court at the close of motions for that day, to a rule denying the motion, with costs.
