Sec. 419. Argument and Briefing. Appeals are brought to argument in the Appellate Division under general regulations prescribed by Section 535 of the Code of Criminal 

Procedure. Five days' notice of argument, fixing any day at a term held in the appropriate department, is required. Unless the time is enlarged for good cause shown, the argument must be noticed within ninety days after the last day for which notice of appeal was required. If the time is not enlarged or, if enlarged, notice is not given for argument on a day within the period of enlargement, the appeal is deemed abandoned. When the court is not in session during all or part of the ninety-day period, application for enlargement may be made upon notice served within the 681

§ 

ninety days, to be heard on the first day of the next term following. 

Briefs are prepared, usually required to be printed, and are served and filed in accordance with the rules made by the Appellate Division in each department, which also regulate time allowed each party for argument, and other requirements both as to briefing and argument. All courts are bound by the provisions of Section 540 of the Code, which prescribes: "Upon the argument of the appeal, if the crime be punishable with death, two counsel on each side must be heard if they require it. In any other case, the court may, in its discretion, restrict the argument to one counsel on each side. The counsel for the defendant is entitled to the closing argument."

Provision for bringing on argument in the Court of Appeals, substantially similar to that made for the Appellate Division, is made in Section 536. The argument may be brought on by notice returnable on any day in term, served by either party, and the return must be within ninety days from the taking of the appeal. Enlargement of time may be had on motion, as in the Appellate Division, served within the ninety days, but when heard after the ninety-day period such notice must be returnable not later than ten days after the court shall have reconvened. Rule 9 of the 

Court of Appeals provides: "Appeals in criminal causes may be brought on for a hearing as preferred causes, upon a notice of five days; and it shall be the duty of the clerk to place such causes on the calendar for the day for which they shall be noticed or upon which the cause shall be ordered by the court or stipulated by the parties, to be heard." "The defendant need not personally appear in the appellate court." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 541.) Failure of appearance by the respondent will never result in a reversal by default (People v. Bradner, 44 Hun 233, affirmed 

107 N.Y. 1), which "can only be given upon argument", but affirmance "may be given, without argument, if the appellant fails to appear, or, where the judgment appealed 682

APPEALS 

$ 420 from is of death and it shall not have been brought on for argument within six months from the taking of such appeal, unless the court, for good reason shown, shall have enlarged said time." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 539.)

Procedure on appeals from inferior courts is much more streamlined and is closely integrated with the procedure on return of the appeal to the appellate court. Accordingly, it has been dealt with in the prior section of this chapter relating to filing records in appellate courts. 

Sec. 420. Review of Law and Fact. In appeals from judg ments of death, presented initially in the Court of Appeals, that court's power to review is plenary and is not limited, as in other matters, "to the review of questions of law" (Constitution, N.Y., Article I, sec. 7). Therefore, in capital cases it examines the record to determine whether the evidence is of sufficient weight and credibility to make out a case of murder, or other capital crime, beyond a reasonable doubt (People v. Crum, 272 N.Y. 348). In all other matters, which it reviews on secondary appeal, the Court of Appeals is limited to questions of law. 

The appellate courts, other than the Court of Appeals, are empowered generally to review questions of fact as well as those of law. Referring to the Appellate Division, Section 527 of the Code provides: ***the appellate court may order a new trial if it be satisfied the verdict against the prisoner was against the weight of the evidence or against the law, or that justice requires a new trial, whether any exception shall have been taken or not, in the court below." This power is borne out, also, by Section 

543-a which requires every intermediate appellate court, in its order determining an initial appeal, to "state whether its determination is upon the law, or upon the facts, or upon both the law and the facts." 

Consideration of the facts, and of the weight of the evidence adduced, does not mean that the court will lightly disregard the findings of fact implicit in the verdict or de cision appealed from (People v. Legacy, 4 App. Div. 453, 683

§ 

456, 167 N.Y.S. 2d 93, 96; People v. Farrell, 2 App. Div. 797, 153 N.Y.S. 2d 284). However, the determination of the trial court is not deemed binding on the appellate court (People v. Beck, 205 Misc. 757, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 354) and, where a verdict was found to be against the weight of the evidence because requisite corroborative evidence was "of doubtful value," the Appellate Division reversed (People v. Czyz, 262 App. Div. 1027, 30 N.Y.S. 2d 299). Similarly, where the People's testimony in a non-jury trial was found "so vague, inconsistent and contradictory that it failed to establish the guilt of the defendant beyond a reasonable doubt", a City Magistrate's conviction was reversed (People v. Saldinger, 269 App. Div. 849, 55 N.Y.S. 2d 785). In 

People v. Woodard, 2 Misc. 2d 26, 150 N.Y.S. 2d 366, the court said: "An appellate court must review the evidence to determine if there was proof beyond a reasonable doubt to sustain a conviction."

The distinction between an intermediate appellate court's powers on an initial appeal and those of the Court of Appeals on secondary appeals, was clearly made when it was stated in People v. Jelke, 1 N.Y. 2d 321, 331: "If the verdict were to be set aside as the product of passion or prejudice on the part of the jury, that would have been in the power of the Appellate Division. We have no jurisdiction to decide the case on any issue of fact." However, where a record presents not an issue of truth or falsity, or a question of whether the jury was swayed by passion or prejudice in coming to its verdict, but, instead, indicates no proof at all to establish a necessary element of the charge, the question is not one of fact but of law. Thus, on the ground that there was no individual identification of voices heard in conversation on tapped telephone wires, the Court of Appeals reversed a conviction in People v. 

Abelson, 309 N.Y. 643, 649–650.

Sec. 421. Remittal for Further Proceedings Below. In a proper case, where an appellate court finds that the record below is incomplete in "a matter that must be closely scruti- 684

APPEALS 

§ 421 nized to determine if any of the defendant's rights have been impaired thereby," it may remit the record to the trial court to take testimony or other proceedings necessary to complete the record. This practice has become firmly established in the Court of Appeals (People v. Winship, 309 N.Y. 311; People v. Leonti, 262 N.Y. 256; People v. 

Arata, 254 N.Y. 565; People v. Shilitano, 215 N.Y. 715), and has been followed in other appellate courts (People v. 

Sadness, 275 App. Div. 731, 86 N.Y.S. 2d 829; Leishman v. 

People, 5 Weekly Dig. 413). 66*** 

In People v. Winship, 309 N.Y. 311, the court considered an appeal from a conviction of second degree robbery and sentence as a second offender, which had been affirmed by the Appellate Division. Finding that the trial court had failed to make any disposition of a motion for a new trial before sentence, the court stated, at page 315 of 309 N.Y.: we think further proof should be taken by affidavit or oral testimony in order that the trial court, before passing on the merits of the application for a new trial, and this court, should be fully informed ***", and withheld final determination of the appeal, "so that the defendant may promptly renew in the Supreme Court, Erie County, the motion for a new trial ***. This is in accord with our practice." 

In People v. Durling, 303 N.Y. 385, after a verdict convicting the defendant of first degree manslaughter and before sentence, the defendant's counsel moved for a new trial on the ground of misconduct of the jurors, tendering evidence and requesting a trial on the issues he thus raised. 

The trial court denied the motion and imposed sentence. 

After affirmance by the Appellate Division, the Court of Appeals held "determination of this appeal should be withheld in order that defendant may promptly renew in the 

Seneca County Court his motion for a new trial * * * and so the Seneca County Court may hold a hearing and render a decision thereon." 

In People v. Sadness, 275 App. Div. 731, 86 N.Y.S. 2d 

829, the Appellate Division, Third Department, reviewed 685

§ 

an order denying a motion to vacate and set aside a judgment on a plea of guilty as a second offender. The appellate court found that the record presented an issue as to whether the defendant had made a valid plea of guilty and, "being uncertain whether the record submitted on appeal is a complete record of all that took place at the arraignment," remitted the matter to the County Court for disposition of the issue raised.

On appeals from courts of special sessions to County Courts, where questions are raised as to errors in sentencing, it was held in People v. Mittleman, 150 Misc. 394, 268 

N.Y.S. 819 that the appellate court cannot remit the record for further judgment inasmuch as courts of special sessions are not continuing courts, deemed merely convened for the trial of the matter in hand. This rule, however, was changed, at least in part, by the adoption of Section 764-a of the Code, added in 1953, which provides that such courts be deemed continuing to "correct an illegal sentence at any time."

Sec. 422. Judgment upon Appeal. "After hearing the appeal, the court must give judgment, without regard to technical errors or defects or to exceptions which do not affect the substantial rights of the parties", provides Section 542 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Further, by authority conferred by subdivision 1 of Section 543, the appellate court "may, in cases where an erroneous judgment has been entered upon a lawful verdict, or finding of fact, correct the judgment to conform to the verdict or finding; in all other cases they must either reverse or affirm the judgment or order appealed from or reduce the sentence imposed to a sentence not lighter than the minimum penalty provided by law for the offense of which the defendant or defendants have been convicted and in cases of reversal, may, if necessary or proper, order a new trial." 

The Appellate Division, it was held under this subdivision, could correct the improperly-made judgment and for that purpose could require the defendant to be brought 686

APPEALS 

$ 422 before it for the pronouncement of a proper judgment (People v. Voelker, 220 App. Div. 528, 221 N.Y.S. 760; see, also, People v. Cohn, 252 App. Div. 910, 299 N.Y.S. 834). In 

People v. Davies, 275 App. Div. 726, 86 N.Y.S. 2d 832, affirmed 300 N.Y. 506, the Appellate Division modified a maximum sentence of imprisonment imposed on the defendant, of previous good character and without prior convictions, deeming the original sentence unusually harsh and severe. A sentence in excess of that allowed by law was held, in People ex rel. Miresi v. Murphy, 253 App. Div. 441, 2 N.Y.S. 2d 731, not to void the severable legal and authorized portion of the sentence, leaving open the elimination of the excessive part. Under this subdivision, it has been held that the Appellate Division's jurisdiction is complete to effect a reduction of the sentence (People v. Speiser, 277 

N.Y. 342) and to extend mercy to a defendant (People v. 

Potskowski, 298 N.Y. 299), within the limits fixed.

Similar powers are vested in County Courts, hearing appeals from inferior courts outside New York City, by

Section 764, which authorizes them to "render the judgment which the court below should have rendered *** or modify the sentence." This does not give the appellate court the right to suspend sentence as that is not a "rendition of judgment" (People v. Harco, 292 N.Y. 321), but it does authorize correction of an illegally excessive sen tence (People v. Shaffer, 173 App. Div. 177, 158 N.Y.S. 

824). Reduction of the amount of a fine imposed which, though not illegal, was deemed excessive, is within the power of the reviewing court (City of Rochester v. Drummons, 171 Misc. 13, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 725), as is reduction of the imprisonment imposed (People v. Mulkins, 25 Misc. 599, 54 N.Y.S. 414), even to the extent of reducing it to the time already served and thereby, in effect, permitting the discharge of the defendant (People v. MacKenzie, 69 Misc. 

540, 125 N.Y.S. 1020).

Reversal or affirmance, either by the Court of Appeals or by the Appellate Division, it has been held, is not, in any respect, an expression of opinion as to the propriety of 687

§ 

staying or suspending execution, inasmuch as neither court has jurisdiction to express such opinion with authoritative force; while it is true that the Appellate Division can reduce the sentence, it may never do so below the minimum provided (People ex rel. Woodin v. Ottaway, 247 N.Y. 

493). Where it appears that the defendant had not received a fair trial, a judgment may be reversed in the interests of justice (People v. McGuiness, 7 App. Div. 2d 

685, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 159). And the Appellate Division is without power, as a matter of law, to change the mandatory indeterminate sentence imposed on a defendant guilty of attempted carrying of a dangerous weapon (People v. 

Zuckerman, 6 App. Div. 2d 901, 177 N.Y.S. 2d 554, motion granted 5 N.Y. 2d 789, motion granted 5 N.Y. 2d 850).

Where a sentence of imprisonment seemed excessive, and was in part imposed in fulfillment of a threat to give defendant the maximum for failing to plead guilty, the Appellate Division reduced it by half (People v. Guiden, 5 App. 

Div. 2d 975, 172 N.Y.S. 2d 640).

Further authorization to modify the judgment below is given an appellate court by subdivision 2 of Section 543, applicable where it determines that the record does not sustain the judgment convicting the defendant of a felony but warrants conviction of a lesser degree of the crime, or a misdemeanor. In such case, the court can modify or correct the judgment in whole or in part, and affirm as so modified or corrected. Because of its constitutional limitations, the Court of Appeals, however, may not review the appropriateness of a discretionary sentence (People v. 

Speiser, 277 N.Y. 342) but where, on the intermediate appeal the original judgment had been modified and as modified affirmed, the Court of Appeals must determine whether there is foundation in law for the determination that the original judgment was not, and conviction in a lower degree was, sustained by the record (People v. Rytel, 284 N.Y. 242).

The intermediate appellate court must, in reversing or affirming, state whether its determination is on the law, 688

APPEALS 

§ 422 upon the facts, or on both law and facts; if on the law alone, the order is required also to state whether the findings of fact below have been affirmed or have not been considered. 

These requirements must be met in the order, and not merely in the opinion, and if not stated therein the Court of Appeals will presume that the questions of fact were not considered on the intermediate appeal (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 543-a). When it reverses or modifies the intermediate appellate determination, and it appears or is presumed that the trial court's findings were not affirmed or considered, the Court of Appeals will not base its determination upon the fact findings of the trial court but will remit the matter to the intermediate court to determine the questions of fact raised (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 543-b).

A new trial ordered by an appellate court must proceed in all respects as if no trial previously had been had (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 544), and the courts will give no effect, whatever, to the judgment which has been reversed (People v. Nitzberg, 289 N.Y. 523). Where, however, a jury had been silent on three of four counts and convicted on the fourth, there was an effective acquittal on the first three, and a new trial ordered on a subsequent reversal must be deemed limited to the fourth count only (People v. Migliori, 271 App. Div. 798, 65 N.Y.S. 2d 260). A verdict of acquittal on the new trial ordered on appeal nullifies the effect of the previous conviction (Shields v. Chilton Co., 168 Misc. 745, 6 N.Y.S. 2d 116, reversed other grounds 255 App. Div. 985, 8 N.Y.S. 2d 276), but, by the same token, where a defendant was charged with first degree murder and convicted in the second degree, reversal on his appeal subjects him to retrial for murder in the first degree (People v. McGrath, 202 N.Y. 445). And after a judgment of conviction has been reversed on appeal, the defendant enjoys the same right to attack the indictment that he possessed before his first trial (People v. Mullens, 63 N.Y.S. 2d 486, reversed other grounds 76 N.Y.S. 2d 858, affirmed in part and reversed in part on other grounds 298 N.Y. 606). 689

§ 

 Sec. 423. Effectuating the Judgment on Appeal. Where a judgment of conviction is reversed and a new trial ordered, all procedures with respect thereto become the responsibility of the trial court after remittal to it by the appellate tribunal. Where, however, the appellate court orders no new trial, it must direct, if the defendant be in custody, that he be discharged therefrom, or if admitted to bail that his bail be exonerated, or that money he had deposited in lieu of bail be returned (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 545).

These directions, included with the determination of the appellate court, are remitted with it to the trial court which enforces them.

On an affirmance, the original judgment must be carried into execution as the appellate court directs, and on a corrected judgment the judgment must be executed as corrected (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 546). By express statutory direction, however, the affirmance of a judgment of death by the Court of Appeals requires that court to fix the week during which the original sentence of death shall be executed, and no further authority is required therefor (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 543-c). But where a judgment of conviction, reversed on intermediate appeal, is thereafter reinstated by the Court of Appeals, the original judgment is required to be carried into execution (People v. 

Cornell, 65 Misc. 452, 121 N.Y.S. 972, affirmed 138 App. Div. 

915, 123 N.Y.S. 1134).

The procedures for effectuating judgments of the County Courts on appeals from inferior tribunals are different. Where the County Court affirms a judgment of conviction, it must direct the execution and commit the defendant if he has been discharged on bail pending appeal (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 766). If it reverses the conviction of an imprisoned defendant, the County Court must order his discharge (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 767). And Section 

769 states generally: "If any proceedings be necessary to carry the judgment upon the appeal into effect, they must be had in the County Court." Accordingly, despite the provision of Section 768 that a new trial ordered "may be had 690

APPEALS 

§ 424 in the County Court or in the court wherein the defendant was convicted," it has been held that this confers no discretion on the County Court, and that the new trial must proceed in that court (People ex rel. Watson v. Lamphier, 104 Misc. 622, 172 N.Y.S. 247; see, also, People v. Standish, 149 Misc. 32, 267 N.Y.S. 76), where "it may be had in the same manner as upon an issue of fact on an indictment; and that court may proceed to judgment and execution, as in an action prosecuted by indictment." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 768.)

On appeals from City Magistrates to the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, proceedings "to carry the judgment upon the appeal into effect *** must be had in the Court of Special Sessions." (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. 

Act, sec. 55.) The execution on affirmance and the recommitment of a defendant discharged on bail are under the direction of the appellate court (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 

52), and the discharge, exoneration of bail or return of money deposited in lieu of bail, must be directed by the appellate court on a reversal of the judgment (N.Y.C. Cr. 

Cts. Act, sec. 53). A new trial ordered, however, "shall be had in the Magistrate's Court wherein the defendant was convicted, and it shall proceed in all respects as if no trial had been had." (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 54.)

Sec. 424. Entry and Remittitur of Judgment. The judg ment of an appellate court is entered in its judgment book, and a certified copy thereof is forthwith remitted to the clerk with whom the original judgment roll is filed. If a new trial is directed in another county, the remittitur is to the clerk of that county. When the judgment is rendered in the absence of the defendant, the court may direct that it be retained, not exceeding ten days (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 547). The decision and return, it is provided, shall be remitted to the court below in the same form and manner as in civil cases (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 548; See Civil 

Practice Act, secs. 607-a, 621; Rules of the Court of Appeals, Rule 16). 691

§ 

Only until the certificate of the judgment is remitted does the appellate court retain jurisdiction of the matter, with power to correct its decision or order (People v. Hill, 73 Hun 473, 26 N.Y.S. 331). Once the remittitur has been effected "the appellate court has no further jurisdiction of the appeal, or of the proceedings thereon ***" (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 549.) This is the reason for the direction of retainer permitted under Section 547, supra. Consequently, if it should become necessary thereafter to correct the order, it can be done only by obtaining a return of the remittitur (People v. Mershon, 46 App. Div. 629, 61 N.Y.S. 

1144). Except in judgments of death, under the provisions of Section 543-c, jurisdiction to direct the execution of the sentence and make all necessary orders therefor devolves upon the court of original jurisdiction (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 549). This statutory provision is mandatory and imposes the duty of seeing to the execution of the judgment upon the court to which it has been remitted (People v. 

Lyons, 17 N.Y.St. 766, 2 N.Y.S. 604).

Sec. 425. Appeals in Habeas Corpus Proceedings. The right to appeal, both from orders refusing the writ of habeas corpus and from final orders made on the return of the writ, is granted by the provisions of Section 1274 of the Civil Practice Act. Such appeal may be taken by the relator, where the writ is refused or the final order remands the prisoner or dismisses the proceedings, or by the People of the State of New York, acting by the District Attorney or the Attorney General, where the final order directs the prisoner's discharge (C.P.A., secs. 1274, 1275).

Where the District Attorney sought to appeal from a final order because it directed the prisoner's discharge on bail, and the relator desired to appeal therefrom on the claim that the bail so directed was excessive, the Appellate Division held in People ex rel. Shapiro v. Keeper of City 

Prison, 265 App. Div. 474, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 526, 528: "The final order of the Supreme Court, made upon the return of the 692

APPEALS 

§ 425 writ, discharging the prisoner on his giving bail, was appealable by the People and by the relator." 

It has been held that the statutory authorization of appeal by the People does not violate either the United States 

Constitution (Article I, sec. 9, cl. 2), or the New York State

Constitution (Article I, sec. 4), as affecting a suspension of the protected right to the writ. While Section 1274 of the Civil Practice Act specifically provides: "where the appeal is taken by the People, the discharge of the prisoner upon bail shall not be stayed thereby," the statutes have been construed, generally, to require the immediate release of the prisoner ordered to be discharged, absolutely and without bail, despite the People's appeal. Were it otherwise, it was held in People ex rel. Sabatino v. Jennings, 246 N.Y. 258, the detention of the prisoner, merely because the People had taken an appeal, would be without legal justification and in derogation of the ancient right to the writ.

On the appeal, the procedure followed is that prescribed by the Civil Practice Act, and not by the Code of Criminal Procedure, by reason that habeas corpus is a civil special proceeding (People v. Mucciolo, 269 App. Div. 782, 55 

N.Y.S. 2d 845). The limit of ninety days after appeal taken, which is set for the perfection and argument of criminal appeals in the absence of enlargement in the discretion of the court (Code of Crim. Proc., secs. 535, 536) does not apply. As the court stated in People ex rel. Monroe v. Jackson, 176 N.Y.S. 2d 408, 409: "Since habeas corpus is regarded as a civil remedy the appellant is not required to procure an extension of time within which to perfect his appeal unless a motion is made to dismiss the appeal." 

Similarly, the right to take a second appeal to the Court of Appeals, after a determination of the initial appeal by the Appellate Division, is regulated by the civil, rather than the criminal, appeals practice.

The appeal is taken, as in all civil appeals, by serving on the adverse party's attorney and the clerk with whom the final order appealed from is entered, written notice of ap- 693

$

peal (C.P.A., sec. 562). The initial appeal is taken to the 

Appellate Division, as of right (C.P.A., sec. 631), and notice thereof must be served within thirty days after service on the appellant's attorney of the order appealed from and notice of its entry (C.P.A., sec. 632). However, if "the only question involved on the appeal is the validity of a statutory provision under the Constitutions of the United States or of the State," the appeal may be taken directly, in the first instance, to the Court of Appeals, "and on any such appeal only the constitutional question shall be considered and determined by the court." (C.P.A., sec. 

588, subd. 4.) Where the Appellate Division has determined the matter on the initial appeal, a further appeal may be taken to the Court of Appeals, as of right, if the determination is a final one, where there is directly involved the construction of the Constitutions of the United States or of the State (People ex rel. Richards v. Kirby, 291 N.Y. 75), or where one or more of the Justices of the Appellate Division dissented in the matter, or where the Appellate Division has directed a reversal or modification of the order appealed from (C.P.A. sec. 588). Otherwise, an appeal to the Court of Appeals may be taken on permission of the Court of Appeals or of the Appellate Division, as set forth in Section 589 of the Civil Practice Act. 

While a refusal of the writ is made specifically appealable by Section 1274 of the Civil Practice Act, no other appeal is permissible in a habeas corpus proceeding unless it is from "a final order, made upon the return of such a writ, to discharge or remand a prisoner or to dismiss the proceedings" (C.P.A., sec. 1274), or from "a final order discharging a prisoner committed upon a criminal accusation, or from the affirmance of such an order" (C.P.A., sec. 

1275). Thus, an appeal will not lie from an order refusing to dismiss the writ and continuing the proceeding in force, as not a final order (People ex rel. Duryee v. Duryee, 188 

N.Y. 440). Similarly, it has been held that refusal by the court to set aside an order in a habeas corpus case, on motion, is not reviewable where it was in the lower court's 694

APPEALS 

§ 425 discretion to grant that relief or to leave the appellant to set up the order's invalidity whenever an attempt should be made to enforce it (People ex rel. Brush v. Brown, 103 

N.Y. 684). Similarly, an order directing a further return to a writ of habeas corpus was held not final or appealable (Matter of Larson, 96 N.Y. 381), and it was held that the propriety of the Supreme Court's ordering an infant's general guardians brought in as parties could not be reviewed on the order so directing, but could only be so considered on an appeal from the final order (Matter of 

Vanderbilt, 245 App. Div. 390, 282 N.Y.S. 506, motion granted 270 N.Y. 549).

A person imprisoned on a criminal charge is entitled, as of right, to the allowance of the writ unless he is committed or detained by virtue of a legal order or judgment of a competent tribunal. That question must be determined by the court to which the writ is presented, and its final order thereon is a proper subject of appellate review (People v. 

Mayer, 16 Barb. 362). An order discharging the prisoner cannot be reversed on the law unless all the jurisdictional facts are admitted or conclusively established (Matter of 

Depue, 185 N.Y. 60). However, the appeal from an order denying discharge will be dismissed where it has become academic by reason of the relator's intervening discharge from custody (Matter of Philippovsky, 246 N.Y. 558), or by the superseding of the jurisdiction of the Magistrate who had ordered the commitment by the filing of an information for the same offense in the Court of Special Sessions (People ex rel. Hertz v. Warden of City Prison, 149 App. 

Div. 939, 134 N.Y.S. 443). But it has been held that an appeal from an order quashing a writ will not be dismissed as academic because the relator's term of imprisonment had expired, and he had consequently been discharged in the interim (People ex rel. Robin v. Hayes, 163 App. Div. 

725, 149 N.Y.S. 250, appeal dismissed 212 N.Y. 603). 695

CHAPTER 36  Sec. 426. Staying Execution Sec. 427. Nature and Effect of the Certificate Sec. 428. The Application for the Certificate Sec. 429. Stay Pending Application 

Sec. 430. Grounds on Which Granted

Sec. 431. On Appeal from Conviction on Guilty Plea Sec. 432. Denial of the Certificate 

Sec. 433. Bail Pending Appeal

Sec. 426. Staying Execution. In our consideration of crimi nal appeals, we have already noted that, except in capital cases, the mere taking of an appeal does not stay execution of a judgment. A defendant who, believing himself aggrieved by his conviction and convinced that upon the proper presentation of his case to the appellate tribunal his conviction will be reversed and his conviction nullified, must nonetheless enter upon his term of imprisonment. 

Just at the time he needs all his personal and associational resources most, he may be removed from the county in which he has been tried and in which his counsel, friends and associates are likely to be. The urgent need of provision for this situation, for a procedure to permit staying of the execution of sentence pending appeal and, also, to provide for the prisoner's release on adequate security pending the preparation, processing and argument of his appeal, is apparent. Just as important, however, is the need for safeguarding the society whose precepts he has been convicted of breaching. Certainly, a prisoner who has been properly and lawfully convicted and committed, and whose appeal may be merely dilatory and without indication 696

§ of reasonableness or likelihood of successful prosecution, should not be allowed to exploit or abuse the remedy which may be provided. This, then, protecting both society and the man convicted of abusing it, provides the function and the rationale of the certificate of reasonable doubt. 

When he applies for the certificate we now consider, the prisoner may obtain a temporary stay which will prevent, for the time, his removal from the county jail to the State prison to which he may have been committed (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 529), but that is only an interim remedy and will not serve to permit his release pending his appeal (People ex rel. Hummel v. Reardon, 186 N.Y. 164), for it is not based on the careful judicial consideration which is prerequisite to the certificate of reasonable doubt. The only means available whereby a prisoner may both effect a stay of execution and make possible his release on bail pending his appeal is to apply for that certificate. 

Sec. 427. Nature and Effect of the Certificate. The certifi cate we now consider evidences a determination by proper judicial authority, made in compliance with statutory requirements on careful review of the record and on due judicial consideration, "that in the opinion of said court there is reasonable doubt whether the judgment should stand. *** Such certificate must recite briefly the particular rulings believed to have been erroneous together with any other grounds upon which it was granted." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 527.) By its nature and the terms of its statutory authorization, the certificate cannot be granted until "such conviction was had or such determination was made" (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 527), and this imports not only a verdict or plea of guilty, but the further finality of judgment and sentence (People v. McGregor, 147 App. 

Div. 488, 131 N.Y.S. 783). It serves to stay the execution of a judgment of conviction of crime, but has no application to, and the quoted section authorizes no similar stay on appeal from, the dismissal of a writ of habeas corpus (Ex parte Kuney, 168 Misc. 285, 308, 5 N.Y.S. 2d 644, af- 697

§ 

firmed 256 App. Div. 802, 9 N.Y.S. 2d 403, affirmed 280 N.Y. 794). 

While effective to meet the need for which it has been devised, to stay execution of sentence and to serve as the basis of an application for release on bail pending appeal, this certificate does not affect any of the incidental consequences of conviction not part of, or explicit in the terms of, the judgment itself. Thus, not as part of the judgment of conviction but by provision of a statute independent of the criminal process, a public office becomes vacant on its incumbent's "conviction of a felony, or a crime involving a violation of his oath of office" (Public Officers Law, sec. 30, subd. 5). This consequence of the conviction is not deemed a punishment for the offense but a protection of the office, and constitutes an automatic limitation on the incumbency of one proved unworthy. As a result, it has been held that the granting of a certificate of reasonable doubt pending appeal from the conviction of a Mayor stayed neither the creation of a vacancy nor the right to fill it (Matter of Obergfell, 239 N.Y. 48).

While not constitutionally vested (McKane v. Durston, 153 U.S. 684, 687, 38 L. Ed. 867; People v. Priori, 163 N.Y. 

99), the right to one appeal in a criminal case "is provided and has, indeed, been regarded as fundamental" (People v. Gersewitz, 294 N.Y. 163, 168). But there never has been a disposition on the part of the Legislature or of the courts to permit one who has been removed from contact with society by due process of law to exploit that right as a dilatory means of deferring punishment merited and meted. If there is reason to believe that his appeal has merit, he will not be restrained during the substantial period it takes for the processing and determination of his appeal. His application for the certificate of reasonable doubt does not confer on him the right to appeal (People v. 

Willett, 149 N.Y.S. 390, affirmed 213 N.Y. 368), nor does it in any respect serve as a determination of his guilt or innocence (People v. Sloan, 181 Misc. 822, 42 N.Y.S. 2d 281).

It does submit the record of his prosecution and conviction 698

§ to a judicial officer or body so that a superficial determination of merit may be made. The problem it presents to the court or judge to whom it is addressed "is whether any question of substance has been raised for consideration by the Appellate Division." (People v. Squillante, 185 N.Y.S. 

2d 357, 359.) And it must be remembered that it is not addressed merely to judicial favor or even to the discretion of the court, but that it invokes substantial rights (People v. Hines, 12 N.Y.S. 2d 454).

Sec. 428. The Application for the Certificate. Application may be made for a certificate of reasonable doubt on an appeal to the Appellate Division (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

527), on an appeal to the Appellate Part of the Court of 

Special Sessions of the City of New York (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. 

Act, sec. 43) and, in an analogous but less formal procedure, on an appeal to a County Court from the conviction by a court of special sessions outside the City of New York (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 753). It is also provided for, and serves the same purposes, in appeals to the Court of Appeals (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 528).

Section 529 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides: 

"Upon an appeal on a conviction of felony or misdemeanor an application for a certificate of reasonable doubt made pursuant to section five hundred and twenty-seven of this Code must be heard and determined either by the court in which such conviction was had, provided said court is a court of record, or the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, or by a regularly appointed Special Term of the Supreme Court held within the judicial district in which the conviction was had. An application for such a certificate, made pursuant to section five hundred and twenty-eight of this Code, must be made either to a Judge of the Court of Appeals or to a Justice of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court from the judgment of which the appeal is taken."

On an appeal from the judgment of a New York City Magistrate, application must be made therefor to the "ap- 699

§ 

pellate court, or a Justice thereof" (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts.

Act, sec. 43). Section 763 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, dealing with appeals from courts of special sessions in the fifty-seven counties outside New York City, makes no separate provision for a certificate of reasonable doubt on the appeal to the County Court. Instead, as an incident of the defendant's application for release on bail pending appeal, it provides: "The Judge of the County Court wherein the appeal shall be heard, or a Justice of the Supreme Court, if satisfied that there is a reasonable doubt whether the conviction should stand, but not otherwise, may take from the defendant, a written undertaking 

Thus, it requires the same standard, without requiring the formal application and certificate. ***"" Section 529 provides that the application "must be founded upon the record of the cause and notice of motion duly served on the District Attorney of the county where the conviction was had, or upon such record and an order to show cause granted either by the trial judge or by a Justice of the Supreme Court; the moving papers must contain a formal specification of the particular rulings alleged to have been erroneous and of any other grounds upon which the application is based and at least two days' notice of the time and place for hearing such application must be given the District Attorney of the county in which the conviction was had. 

Similarly, as to appeals to the Appellate Part of the 

Court of Special Sessions, Section 43 of the New York City 

Criminal Courts Act provides: "The application for the certificate must be founded upon the record of the proceedings before the Magistrate and a notice of motion served at least two days prior to the hearing of such application on the District Attorney of the county in which the conviction was had." But in appeals to County Courts, Section 753 of the Code makes no requirement for notice to the District Attorney, or other procedural requirements as on a motion. That an ex parte application is contemplated would seem to be indicated by the fact that the first 700

§ 

express requirement the statute makes for notice to the District Attorney is that in Section 754, requiring the clerk with whom the undertaking bailing the defendant is directed to be filed, to give notice of such filing to the District Attorney within five days after it has been filed in his office. "When an application for such certificate shall have been made to and denied by the court in which such conviction was had or by the Supreme Court or in the case of an appeal to the Court of Appeals, by a Judge of that Court or a Justice of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court, no other application for such certificate shall be made." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 529.) It was stated in People v. 

Carbonaro, 208 Misc. 761, 145 N.Y.S. 2d 417, 418: "There is no authority for making this application without prejudice and, when the court denies the application outright, defendant is precluded from thereafter renewing it before another court, otherwise a defendant could make such application ad infinitum, contrary to the clear intent of Section 527 of the Code of Criminal Procedure." In People v. 

Balcerzak, 2 Misc. 2d 895, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 578, 579, however, the court stated: "While the defendant is not precluded from rearguing the motion, it must nevertheless be made before the Justice who heard the original motion.' 

Sec. 429. Stay Pending Application. Referring to bringing on the application for a certificate of reasonable doubt by way of an order to show cause, which is permitted as an alternative to the usual notice of motion, Section 529 of the Code provides: "The judge or justice granting such order to show cause may in his discretion stay execution of the judgment of conviction until the determination of such application." The discretionary stay thus authorized, as an ex parte incident of the application terminating upon its determination, is merely temporary and casual, and does not constitute the stay prerequisite to the defendant's admission to bail pending his appeal (People ex rel. Hummel v. Reardon, 186 N.Y. 164). It was held in People v. Kay, 701

§ 

191 Misc. 511, 78 N.Y.S. 2d 392, that the inclusion in the order to show cause of both such stay and a provision admitting the defendant to bail was erroneous and unauthorized. 

In People v. Bowles, 280 App. Div. 476, 114 N.Y.S. 2d 

353, the reviewing court took particular note of the practice the trial court had followed. There, upon pronouncing judgment, the court had stayed the execution of the sentence pending an application for a certificate of reasonable doubt while continuing the former bail. The Appellate 

Division stated: "There is no authority for such action. 

Section 529 of the Code of Criminal Procedure authorizes the judge or justice who grants the show cause order for a certificate of reasonable doubt, to stay execution of the judgment of conviction until determination of the application. The duty of the sentencing judge is to comply with Section 487, Code of Criminal Procedure ***. The temporary stay under Section 529, Code of Criminal Procedure, is not the stay of proceedings provided in Section 527 which is effective only when a certificate of reasonable doubt is filed." 

Sec. 430. Grounds on Which Granted. Generally, in evaluating the merits of an application for a certificate of reasonable doubt, the court should be guided by the standards which were well stated in People v. Muller, N.Y.L.J., July 

27, 1953, quoted in People v. Von Cseh, 9 Misc. 2d 718, 170 

N.Y.S. 2d 699, thus: "The issue before me is, of course, not the innocence of the defendant, or even his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Nor is it necessary that I be convinced that there will be a reversal on appeal. It is sufficient that in my opinion there is reasonable doubt whether the judgment should stand, that is, that I be satisfied that there is presented an arguable, substantial question as to a claimed error, which question ought in law and justice be settled by the appellate tribunal before incarceration in pursuance of the sentence." And in People v. Dashnaw, 4 Misc. 

2d 60, 157 N.Y.S. 2d 729, 732, it was stated: "This court is 702

§ of the opinion that, even though the defendant pleaded guilty, it has the power to grant a certificate of reasonable doubt if the sentence may be reduced or modified by the appellate court. However, certificate of reasonable doubt may not be issued as a matter of right or of course, but only where there is reasonable doubt that the judgment should stand."

In People v. Sobieraj, 189 N.Y.S. 2d 9, the defendant had been charged with rape on a specified date, specifically limited by the indictment under which he was tried and convicted. Accordingly, a statement by the trial judge from which the jury could have relied upon the prosecutrix's pregnancy and birth of a child more than eleven months after such date as essential corroboration necessary to conviction, was held to justify the issuance of a certificate of reasonable doubt; so, too, was the defendant's claim that he had been prejudiced by the trial court's refusal to adjourn the trial because of his counsel's engagement in court elsewhere.

In a prosecution for assault in the third degree, the defendant was a policeman. The trial court permitted extensive cross-examination of the defendant based on his record as a policeman, indicating that he had been complained against and tried on a number of departmental charges, all of which he had denied. The judge had, in the course of the cross-examination, interposed a number of probing questions stressing the defendant's bad departmental record and casting doubt on his denials of the charges therein set forth. In People v. Bilanchuk, 199 Misc. 

871, 106 N.Y.S. 2d 330, reversed 280 App. Div. 180, 112

N.Y.S. 2d 414, this was held to have created a situation which might necessitate a new trial, and the application for the certificate was therefore granted. 

In People v. Squillante, 185 N.Y.S. 2d 357, the prosecution and conviction had been for extortion based on conspiracy, and the evidence presented conversations by some, but not all, of the defendants. The trial court had given no instructions limiting consideration of this evi- 703

§ 

dence to the defendants immediately involved therein. The 

Supreme Court granted a certificate of reasonable doubt, holding that the question, of whether more should have been shown than the record presented to establish continuation of the conspiracy to the point where the declarations of one conspirator were admissible against all the defendants, was a substantial one for the consideration of the Appellate Division. 

In a prosecution for sodomy, the prosecutor produced a young woman and two detectives in court, had them stand, and questioned the defendant on cross-examination as to whether he knew them, whether he had gone with one of them to the precinct, whether he had seen them in several places, and whether he had committed upon the young woman an act of sodomy similar to that with which he was then being charged; the prosecutor vigorously refused to accept the defendant's denials as binding. This was held sufficiently indicative of error to justify the granting of a certificate of reasonable doubt in People v. Allen, 64 N.Y.S. 

2d 619.

Sec. 431. On Appeal from Conviction on Guilty Plea. It has been held that the sentence is the judgment of the court (Manke v. People, 74 N.Y. 415, 424; People v. Bork, 78 N.Y. 

346, 350), and accordingly the judgment may be reversed on appeal for error in the sentence (People v. Miles, 173 

App. Div. 179, 183, 158 N.Y.S. 819, 821). Accordingly, a conviction on a plea of guilty, while it might not otherwise present questions reviewable on appeal, nonetheless may be reviewed as to the sentence imposed (People v. Collins, 271 App. Div. 511, 67 N.Y.S. 2d 53). This being so, it has been held that the provisions for stay of execution on certificate of reasonable doubt are equally applicable in an appeal from such a judgment. In People v. Collins, supra, at page 517 of 271 App. Div., page 59 of 67 N.Y.S. 2d, Dore,

J., wrote for the unanimous court: "We hold that in a proper case the Supreme Court has the power under Section 527 to grant a certificate of reasonable doubt when in 704

§ the opinion of the court the sentence is excessive even though the defendant has pleaded guilty. This construction is in conformity with reason and with the language of the statute (Sec. 527), for if the court in its opinion believes that the sentence is excessive and accordingly unwarranted by law, it may state that there is reasonable doubt whether "The judgment should stand.' As the sentence of the court is the judgment of the court and as this court has power in reviewing such judgment to reduce the sentence, the judgment is necessarily modified and therefore does not 'stand' as rendered if, on appeal, sentence is in fact reduced." 

Sec. 432. Denial of the Certificate. Every error in the trial record does not necessarily justify the granting of a certificate of reasonable doubt; to deny the certificate, however, the court to which application is made, must determine that the error complained of could not have prejudiced the defendant (People v. Martin, 91 Misc. 107, 154 N.Y.S. 324, affirmed 172 App. Div. 928, 157 N.Y.S. 1140; see also People v. Horvatt, 144 Misc. 278, 258 N.Y.S. 374; People v. 

Steppello, 141 Misc. 162, 252 N.Y.S. 254). To harbor and to certify a reasonable doubt, it was held in People v. Perlman, 128 Misc. 68, 217 N.Y.S. 662, such doubt must be founded upon 'substantial error,' one which works harm and from which the applicant has sustained injury. However, in People v. Damron, 80 Misc. 114, 140 N.Y.S. 787, it was held that one applying for a certificate of reasonable doubt need not affirmatively show he was prejudiced by the alleged error, but that the court must determine on the record that he was not so prejudiced to be warranted in denying the certificate. 

In People v. Block, 191 Misc. 94, 76 N.Y.S. 2d 886, the applicant urged that the trial court's denial of a motion to dismiss the indictment on the ground that one of the grand jurors, otherwise fully qualified, did not own property as required by law, was error sufficient to justify the issuance of a certificate of reasonable doubt. The court, however, 705

§ 

held that because the defendant had not objected to the panel or to the individual grand juror, he had waived the objection, was not prejudiced by the alleged error, and was not entitled to the certificate. In People v. Wasserberger, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 99, a defendant convicted on four counts charging the exacting of excessive fees for procuring bail bonds, sought a certificate of reasonable doubt on the sole ground that the District Attorney had erroneously failed to open to the jury on several of the counts. 

Holding "that the purposes of an opening were fully complied with and that the petitioner was not prejudiced," the court denied the application. 

In People v. Williams, 198 Misc. 621, 99 N.Y.S. 2d 672, the defendant sought a certificate of reasonable doubt as to his conviction for violations of the Alcoholic Beverage 

Control Law and of Section 973 of the Penal Law, dealing with the keeping of gambling and betting establishments. 

The imposition of sentence on Sunday by a court of special sessions was held neither illegal, nor void, and the fine of $500, or one day in jail for each $10 unpaid, was held neither unjust, in abuse of discretion nor excessive; a certificate of reasonable doubt was therefore denied. 

Sec. 433. Bail Pending Appeal. We have seen that the principal function of the certificate of reasonable doubt, aside from deferring the fulfillment of the sentence until the appeal is determined, is to permit the appellant's release on bail. To determine the conditions under which he may or may not obtain such release, we must refer to Section 555 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which reads: "After the conviction of a crime not punishable with death or life imprisonment a defendant who has appealed, and when there is a stay of proceedings, but not otherwise, may be admitted to bail: 1. As a matter of right, when the appeal is from a judgment imposing a fine only; 2. As a matter of discretion, in all other cases, except that (a) if the defendant convicted is a fourth offender under section nineteen hundred and forty-two of the Penal Law, or, 706

§ (b) if the defendant is convicted of a felony committed while armed with a weapon as provided in section nineteen hundred and forty-four of the Penal Law, or, (c) if the defendant is convicted of any of the crimes or offenses described in section five hundred and fifty-two of this Code and is circumstanced as there described, he shall not be admitted to bail."

The crimes and offenses, described in Section 552 and thus referred to are the following: (a) previous conviction of a felony, (b) two previous convictions of any of the following misdemeanors or one conviction of each of two of them-illegally using, carrying or possessing a pistol or other dangerous weapon; making or possessing burglar's instruments; buying or receiving stolen property; unlawful entry; aiding escape from prison; disorderly conduct under Penal Law, section 722, subds. 6 and 8; violations of 

Penal Law, secs. 483, 483-b and Article 106; sodomy or rape as a misdemeanor; violation of Penal Law, secs. 

1747-c and 1747-d; violation of Article 33 of the Public 

Health Law, relating to narcotic drugs. As to these exceptions, the court stated, in People v. Wirtschafter, 305 

N.Y. 515, 520-521: "Although the Legislature has provided for bail and has designated the public official who may grant it, before and after indictment, even in a case where it appears that the defendant has been previously convicted of a felony or certain specified misdemeanors or offenses (§552), the Legislature has carefully prohibited any public official from admitting to bail anyone who has been twice convicted of a felony (§555).”

The effect of a certificate of reasonable doubt, where the appeal is from a judgment in which only a fine was imposed, was thus stated in People v. Connolly, 88 App. Div. 

302, 84 N.Y.S. 617: "Where a defendant sentenced to pay a fine only, takes an appeal, obtains a certificate of reasonable doubt, and an order is made admitting him to bail, such certificate is, in effect, granted upon condition that the defendant will execute an undertaking conditioned for the payment of such fine, and the collection of such fine is 707

§ 

not stayed until such undertaking is executed, in case the conviction is affirmed."

In courts of special sessions outside New York City, release on bail pending appeal is effected by application to the judge of the County Court wherein the appeal is to be heard or to a Justice of the Supreme Court, who, if satisfied "that there is a reasonable doubt whether the conviction should stand, but not otherwise, may take from the defendant a written undertaking, with such sureties as he may approve, that the defendant will abide the judgment of the County Court upon the appeal, and may thereupon order that he be discharged from imprisonment, on service of the order upon the officer having him in custody, or if he be not in custody, that all proceedings on the judgment be stayed." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 753.)

No prior notice to the District Attorney is specified in the statute, but the undertaking "must be immediately filed" with the County Clerk who must, within five days thereafter, serve notice on the District Attorney of the filing of the undertaking in his office (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 754). It has been held that the notice thus required to be given to the District Attorney constitutes no part of the appeal, and a failure thereof in no respect vitiates the appeal (People v. Palaguay, 216 App. Div. 508, 215 N.Y.S. 

666). Even though the appeal be based, essentially, solely on the excessiveness of the punishment meted out, as where the defendant pleaded guilty, this section has been held to apply and, finding reasonable doubt, the court admitted the defendant to bail (People v. Spinello, 104 

N.Y.S. 2d 586). 708
