PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

The best that can be said about coram nobis was stated by the Hon. Stanley H. Fuld, Associate Judge of the Court of Appeals, when he remarked that it was "the wild jackass of the law." It is a remedy which was revived by the United States Supreme Court in order to secure for defendants rights that they had under the Constitution of our land, but which no longer could be reviewed by our courts either because time to appeal had expired and no appeal had been taken, or the matter to be considered did not appear in the record on appeal. 

Coram nobis has been expanded considerably since the first decision came down some years ago. Its limitations are not clearly defined. This remedy may be used to secure a review of any error in any of the proceedings which has deprived the defendant of substantial justice where such an error does not appear in the record. It has been definitely held that such an error, if affecting a constitutional right, may always be reviewed by coram nobis, but even that principle has its limitations. 709

§ 

Where you believe that the remedy of coram nobis is available to you, be certain that your papers contain assertions of fact which will support the conclusions you draw as distinguished from bald conclusory statements. Bear in mind, also, that where there is a question of fact raised concerning the assertions in your moving papers, you will ordinarily be accorded a hearing, unless the proof offered against you is documentary so that it cannot well be disputed by you.

Sec. 434. Nature and Status. The writ of error coram nobis was anciently a remedy in chancery, devised as all such were to perform a service which could not be provided by the inflexible forms of the common law jurisdiction. In 

New York, it may be said with some justice, this procedure has been only recently rediscovered, having been reactivated for the similar purpose of filling a gap in our statute-inhibited criminal procedure. In this State, it exists as the product of a contemporary common law development for, unlike the Federal jurisdiction, we have not devised and enacted a modern statutory coram nobis procedure. Nevertheless, a 1947 amendment to the Code of 

Criminal Procedure gave this proceeding its first statutory recognition by authorizing appeals therein (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 517, as amended by Laws of 1947, ch. 706, sec. 1; revised and clarified by Laws of 1954, ch. 806, sec. 1).

Previously, a complicated and roundabout procedural device, utilizing proceedings in the nature of prohibition under Article 78 of the Civil Practice Act, had had to be worked out for the purpose (Hogan v. Supreme Court, 295 N.Y.92).

The essence of coram nobis is that it is addressed to the very court which rendered the judgment in which injustice is alleged to have been done. The words coram nobis ("our court") themselves as used in the old chancery practice, in contradistinction to the common law coram vobis ("your court") applied to what we now know as appeals or review by another court, clearly point this up. 

The implications of these words have been broadened and 710

§ extended by the Court of Appeals to limit the remedy to "our courts," in announcing that coram nobis will not be utilized by the courts of New York to correct error in the judicial proceedings of other jurisdictions (People v. Mc- 

Cullough, 300 N.Y. 107, 110).

Coram nobis does not partake, in its approach, of the nature of a separate proceeding. Although it finds its principal concerns in matters which do not appear in the record, and is often utilized long after the entry of the judgment, it is nevertheless more nearly a motion in the original action finding its substance in events of the trial and the subsequent judgment procedures (see People v. 

Gersewitz, 294 N.Y. 163, 168). Despite this, the form in which our courts have developed the procedure, and the statutory appeal treating it substantially as the judgment itself is treated on appeal, would seem to have converted it into a criminal special proceeding in our practice. In its essence, the motion to vacate the judgment in the nature of an application for a writ of error coram nobis is a motion addressed to a court's inherent power to examine and correct its own proceedings in furtherance of justice and due process of law, and has been held to be substantially similar to, and based on the same principles as, motions to vacate judgments addressed to courts of civil jurisdiction (Lyons v. Goldstein, 290 N.Y. 19, 25-26).

Coram nobis proceedings are distinguishable from appeals from the underlying judgment in that they are addressed to the court which rendered the judgment in the first instance, are not severely limited or statutorily restricted in the manners and methods by which they may be instituted, and are generally held to be unavailable where other established remedies or procedures can serve, or might have served, their purpose. They differ from the ancient and constitutionally-guaranteed procedure of habeas corpus, in that they are not limited in purpose to the determination of the judicial warrant of the applicant's detention or to test its legality solely on the face of the record, as is that remedy (People ex rel. Carr v. Martin, 711

§ 

286 N.Y. 27). Unlike the statutory motion to set aside the judgment, they are not subject to the one-year statute of limitation (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 466). And their concept is entirely different from that in which applications for parole, or for executive clemency, find their genesis. 

Although these may, and in many instances do, involve consideration of error or unfairness in the judicial process, they nevertheless are appeals to grace; coram nobis, on the other hand, asserts constitutionally-enjoined and universally recognized rights.

The writ of error coram nobis, as applied in the courts of New York, cannot be defined, for, as Judge Desmond stated in a concurring opinion in People v. Sullivan, 3 N.Y. 

2d 196, 199: "no clear rule or rules exist and each case must be decided according to its own equities." And, as put by 

Judge Fuld in the same case, at pages 199-200 of 3 N.Y. 2d: "it has been employed for the purpose, for which it was designed, of calling up facts unknown at the time of the judgment, facts which affected the validity and regularity of the judgment itself, facts which, if known, would have precluded the judgment rendered. We have expanded the scope of the writ, beyond its original purpose, to include cases in which a second or fourth felony offender asserts the invalidity of a prior conviction even though such invalidity is not ascribable to an error of fact not apparent on the record. See, e.g., People v. Shaw, 1 N.Y. 2d 30; 

People v. Kronick, 308 N.Y. 866. *** It is difficult, if not impossible, to define the precise limits of coram nobis, but there is a general guiding principle at hand. In determining whether or not the remedy may be invoked, we should have in mind *** that the writ is an emergency measure born of necessity to afford a defendant a remedy against injustice when no other avenue of judicial relief is, or ever was, available to him."

Sec. 435. The Court Applied To. The function of the writ of error coram nobis "was and is to call certain matters to the attention of the court in which the case was tried." 712

§ (People v. McCullough, 300 N.Y. 107, 110.) And, conversely, it has been said "that a duly constituted court, even in the absence of express statutory warrant, has the right 'to exercise so efficient a control over every proceeding in an action as to effectually protect every person actually interested in the result, from injustice and fraud.”” (Hogan v. Supreme Court, 295 N.Y. 92, 97.) Continuing, the same court stated: "Due process is lacking unless some corrective process is available to them ***. A remedy there must be. The approach to it must be by the only visible route-by motions addressed to the sentencing court." (Id., at page 97.)

It is required, then, that the application be made to the court which rendered the original judgment. This follows, even though the sentencing judge is no longer sitting, or is disqualified (People v. Amoroso, 8 App. Div. 2d 613, 184 

N.Y.S. 2d 383; People v. Carpus, 2 App. Div. 653, 152 N.Y.

S. 2d 27). In People v. Wurzler, 300 N.Y. 344, it was held that the disqualification of the sole County Judge did not warrant the transfer of the matter to the Supreme Court, but that another County Judge should have been brought in to sit in the County Court, as may be done under the law, and have thus heard the proceeding in the original court. And while County Judges are vested with some of the powers of Supreme Court Justices in appropriate circumstances, it was held erroneous to bring coram nobis in the Erie County Court to set aside a judgment rendered in the Erie County Supreme Court (People v. Vogel, 8 App. 

Div. 2d 770, 186 N.Y.S. 2d 203).

At one point in the development of coram nobis, doubt was asserted as to the powers of inferior courts, and courts not of record, to entertain the proceeding. The essential nature of a court of special sessions is that it is not a continuing court; it is merely a court specially convened by a designated judicial officer for a special purpose. 

But the Court of Appeals soon decided "that the writ of error coram nobis lies in courts not of record-such as a court of special sessions ***" 

713

§ 

N.Y. 658, 659.) And the whole current of authority is re flected in the language of People v. D'Art, 205 Misc. 743, 

130 N.Y.S. 2d 227: "the proceeding must be addressed first to the Police Court in which defendants were tried and convicted" and of People v. Zajkowski, 121 N.Y.S. 2d 586, 590: "Such courts [of special sessions], although having no continuing jurisdiction and not being courts of record, 'have all the powers incidental to the proper discharge of duty,' including motions in the nature of coram nobis." 

A similar question was raised with regard to the powers of a City Magistrate to entertain coram nobis, where a conviction had been had before such Magistrate sitting as a court of special sessions. In People v. Freudenberg, 6 App. 

Div. 2d 8, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 319, 320, reversed on the facts 5 

N.Y. 2d 209, the court stated: "The City Magistrate had jurisdiction to entertain the writ and conduct the hearing. 

Where neither the defendant nor the prosecuting official demands trial in the three-justice Court of Special Sessions, the City Magistrate has all the 'powers and jurisdic tion of the Court of Special Sessions.' (New York City 

Criminal Courts Act, sec. 131, subd. 3.) Nor is it necessary that subsequent proceedings be taken before the same Magistrate as the one before whom the defendant was convicted or pleaded guilty (cf. ibid., subd. 4). This embraces not only the power to sentence (ibid., subd. 4), to grant a new trial (ibid., sec. 131, sub. 3; sec. 31, subd. 8), but, by logical extension, to entertain a writ of error coram nobis."

Sec. 436. Time for the Application. In People v. Richetti, 

302 N.Y. 290, 298, the Court of Appeals, in Judge Desmond's majority opinion, stated: "there is no time limit on such applications. Even if laches could be a defense (which we doubt but do not decide), that defense itself would require a trial." This has been the uniformly asserted rule, in coram nobis matters, starting with forceful assertions by Court of Appeals authority (Bojinoff v. People, 299 

N.Y. 145; Lyons v. Goldstein, 290 N.Y. 19), and repeated 714

§ in the reported opinions of every court. Thus, it is not unusual to find notations of the entertainment of the application twenty-one years after the conviction (People v. 

Gilmore, 16 Misc. 2d 578, 185 N.Y.S. 2d 27), fourteen years thereafter (People v. Glass, 201 Misc. 460, 114 N.Y.S. 2d 

635), and twenty-three years later (People v. Dalton, 203 

Misc. 268, 118 N.Y.S. 2d 263). 

Sec. 437. Initiating the Application. Although there are no statutory prescriptions or standards as to procedure, a very well established common-law practice and procedure have developed in what Section 517 of the Code calls “a motion to vacate a judgment of conviction, otherwise known as a motion or application for a writ of error coram nobis." The very lack of any limiting statute has allowed a certain amount of leeway in this regard, which the courts have not hesitated to recognize in the interests of justice and fairness. It must be assumed as fundamental to the procedure that it cannot be prosecuted, except on notice to the prosecutor (Comstock v. Schoonhaven, 3 How. Pr. 

258; Maher v. Comstock, 1 How. Pr. 175; Smith v. Kingsley, 19 Wend. 620; People v. La Plante, 207 Misc. 546, 137 N.Y.S. 

2d 893).

The length of the notice, calendar practice and filing procedures should be governed by the usual and customary practice in other matters, which obtains in the court in question. Most frequently, the application is instituted by serving copies of the notice of motion and a verified petition on the District Attorney, and filing the originals in the clerk's office. It is most important that the petition set forth all the facts on which the petitioner relies, inasmuch as the insufficiency thereof may result in a dismissal or denial without hearing (People v. Oddo, 275 App. Div. 816, 89 N.Y.S. 2d 708, affirmed 300 N.Y. 649). This formality, however, is not indispensable; it has become a regular and frequent experience for judges of criminal courts to receive informal letters from convicts serving prison sentences, complaining of injustice or irregularity. Should the 715

§ 

facts so informally alleged indicate a possibility of grounds for vacation of the judgment, the judge will notify the District Attorney and schedule the matter for argument. 

Thus, in People v. Sullivan, 4 N.Y. 2d 472, the court, after full hearing, had made an order denying an application coram nobis; some two years later, there was received an informal writing from the prisoner asking that the court reconsider. "The court, despite the informality of the paper, treated the request for reconsideration as a new motion for relief coram nobis. This was quite proper." (Id., at page 474 of 4 N.Y. 2d.)

On the return date, the District Attorney appears and either acquiesces in the application, moves to dismiss it for legal insufficiency, or submits opposing affidavits and requests that a date be fixed for a hearing. It is within the rights of the defendant to due process that such a hearing be held, but only if a dispute of fact is presented by the papers before the court (People v. White, 309 N.Y. 636). If none clearly appears, or if the defendant's contentions are clearly insufficient to afford him the relief he seeks, the application may be dismissed without further proceedings (People v. Oddo, 275 App. Div. 816, 89 N.Y.S. 2d 708, affirmed 300 N.Y. 649; People v. Sullivan, 4 N.Y. 2d 472).

The petitioner, naturally, has a right to be present and to be represented by counsel both on the initial argument and on the subsequent hearing, if one is ordered. 

If the petitioner is in legal custody, he may petition the court for an order directing that he be brought up to testify, under Section 10-c of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Section 10-b, if in the county jail). It was held in 

People v. Gruberman, 183 Misc. 535, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 261 that the prisoner's production in court on the argument "is not a matter of absolute right," and in People v. Seymour, 208 

Misc. 894, 145 N.Y.S. 2d 338, that he had no right to be brought up for the preliminary argument, despite his right to be brought up for the later hearing, if one should be directed. The petitioner may be represented by counsel of 716

§ his own choosing at the argument and hearing, or, on aplication, have counsel assigned to represent him. **" Sec. 438. The Hearing. The hearing fixed by the court where "there is no reasonable probability at all that the defendant's averments are true" (People v. Guariglia, 303 N.Y. 

338, 343), is had when "the statements in the opposing papers conflict with the allegations of the petition, thereby raising questions of fact which can be resolved only after a hearing (People v. Silverman, 3 N.Y. 2d 200, 203.)

This hearing is not a "trial" as contemplated by the Code of Criminal Procedure, which "ends with the verdict" (People ex rel. Steckler v. Warden, 259 N.Y. 430), and therefore the requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 389) does not apply to it. 

A presumption of regularity may attach to the original proceedings which forces the petitioning defendant "to go forward with proof, but once he does go forward, the presumption is out of the case." (People v. Richetti, 302 

N.Y. 290, 298.) Going forward, the defendant must present sufficient proof of the facts justifying the granting of his application to establish the same by a fair preponderance of the credible evidence (People v. Barber, 276 App. Div. 

1040, 95 N.Y.S. 2d 246).

In People v. Richetti, supra, the Court of Appeals dwelt on the incidents of the hearing, at page 297 of 302 N.Y. 2d: "*** it is the practice in trial courts throughout the State to hold formal trials in these matters, whenever the petition exhibits a prima facie case. *** A ‘hearing' or 'trial' of such an issue of fact is an empty form unless it takes place in open court, with the right, on each side, to examine and cross-examine. For centuries a 'trial' of a dispute of fact has meant 'the examination, before a competent tribunal, according to the laws of the land, of the facts put in issue, for the purpose of determining such issue' * * *

A 'hearing' contemplates the right to be present and to put forth one's contentions by proof and argument ***." And, at page 298 of 302 N.Y. 2d, the court stated: "There must 717

§ 

be a trial, as we have indicated, and it will be for the trial judge to pass on all questions of fact, including the credibility of defendant and of any other witnesses on either side."

Sec. 439. Res Adjudicata. It has been held that the strict principles of res adjudicata do not apply with respect to applications in coram nobis (People v. Marra, 1 App. Div. 

2d 545, 152 N.Y.S. 2d 69). Where a defendant's application in coram nobis had been denied in 1944, which denial was not further reviewed because the statute then permitted no appeal, and was thereafter renewed in 1949, when such appeal had become available, the Court of Appeals said: "Ordinarily, a motion may not be renewed without first obtaining permission. *** This, however, is not an ordinary situation. It involves the petitioner's present liberty, of which he is being deprived in reliance upon a void prior conviction." (Bojinoff v. People, 299 N.Y. 145, 151).

Where, two years after his application for relief in coram nobis had been denied on a full, formal hearing, a prisoner informally requested that a reargument or rehearing be afforded him, without adducing any new or other facts, the court treated it as an application for a writ of error coram nobis, with the subsequent approval of the Court of Appeals, which stated in People v. Sullivan, 4 N.Y.S. 2d 472, 474: "Where a second or later application is made, which alleges no new or additional evidence and is in all material respects substantially the same as dealt with in the prior application, there is no reason why a hearing must be conducted on the renewed application. The court, of course, will consider new or additional evidence and in the exercise of his judicial discretion decide whether such evidence is of sufficient merit and substance to warrant a new hearing. If so, he should hold a hearing. When that is done, all that remains for an appellate court to pass on is whether the order as made constituted an abuse of discretion." 718

§ 

Sec. 440. Errors Appearing on the Face of the Record. The writ of error coram nobis cannot be used to correct an error of law which appears on the face of the record. As was said in People v. Sadness, 300 N.Y. 69, 74: "We have also indicated that where an error of law appears on the face of the record coram nobis is not available *** and that the proper procedure to be adopted by the petitioner for the correction of such an error must be limited to the normal appeal, motion in arrest of judgment, or motion to withdraw a plea * * *** " In another formulation of the rule the Court of Appeals stated: "A writ of error coram nobis may be invoked to show an error of law apparent on the face of the record. * * * the defendant's claim was reviewable upon an appeal of the judgment of conviction ***

Therefore, the defendant may not be permitted to forego his right of appeal from the judgment and resort to the remedy of coram nobis * * *. Coram nobis is available only in cases which 'involve the abrogation-without adequate remedy-of fundamental precepts going to the jurisdiction of the court or resulting in the perpetration of a fraud upon the court'." (People v. Sullivan, 3 N.Y. 2d 196, 197198.) 

Similarly, where an alleged error of fact appears on the record and might have been raised on appeal, the general rule has been stated that coram nobis does not lie (People v. Parker, 8 App. Div. 2d 863, 186 N.Y.S. 2d 787; People v. 

Waterman, 5 App. Div. 2d 717, 168 N.Y.S. 2d 819). Nevertheless, it has been the tendency to allow some exceptions to this rule, usually based on the emergency nature of the remedy and its function to assure justice and due process where no other remedy is in fact available, but the Court of Appeals has stated that "each exception to the rule must be justified by special evidence of a denial of due process requiring corrective judicial process. Hence the scope of coram nobis will not be expanded unless the injury done to the defendant would deprive him of due process of law." (People v. Silverman, 3 N.Y. 2d 200, 202–203.) Thus, where two of three defendants appealed through the courts and 719

§ 

ultimately succeeded in being sustained in their claim that the confessions used against them were unlawfully and unconstitutionally coerced, the third co-defendant who had failed to join in their appeals, and was serving a prison sentence, was held unable to avail himself of coram nobis to remedy his equally unjust conviction. Judge Fuld, writing for the Court of Appeals in People v. Caminito, 3 N.Y. 

2d 596, 601, stated: "His failure to pursue the usual and accepted appellate procedure to gain a review of the conviction does not entitle him later to utilize the present day counterpart of the extraordinary writ of error coram nobis. * * * And this is so although the asserted error or irregularity relates to a violation of constitutional right. *** While the scope of coram nobis has been somewhat expanded beyond its original office *** it still remains an emergency measure employed for the purpose for which it was initially designed, of calling up facts unknown at the time of the original judgment.' 99 

Sec. 441. Effect of Determination. The customary and usual result of a determination granting the application coram nobis is to void the judgment attacked ab initio. 

Thus, in People v. Farina, 2 N.Y. 2d 454, the defendant's motion was based on his contention that he had changed his plea from not guilty to guilty of third degree burglary in reliance on the trial court's promise of a sentence of from ten to twenty years. Despite this promise, he was then sentenced to serve from fourteen to twenty years. At the hearing on his coram nobis application, the court conceded the promise and granted the motion, but only to the extent of vacating the sentence, denying the defendant's motion to withdraw his plea of guilty, and resentencing him to the term originally promised. On appeal, this was held error, both in the Appellate Division and in the Court of Appeals; it was stated, at page 455 of 2 N.Y. 2d: "Since the record supports his assertion of improper coercion, simply changing the sentence and imposing the one promised does not meet the necessities of this case. The de- 720

§ fendant is entitled to an order * * * setting aside the judgment of conviction entered on his coerced plea of guilty and directing that there be a trial."

This does not necessarily imply that the outcome of coram nobis must always be a complete vacating of the judgment; the rule must rather be found in the requirement that the outcome "meet the necessities" of the case in the light of due process. Accordingly, and as Judge 

Fuld has stated, "the scope of coram nobis has been somewhat expanded beyond its original office" (People v. Caminito, 3 N.Y.S. 2d 596, 601) to include applications for resentencing (People v. Shaw, 1 N.Y. 2d 30; People v. 

Kronick, 308 N.Y. 866) where multiple-offender sentences were imposed on the basis of errors as to the nature of the prior alleged convictions not appearing at the time of the original judgment. Thus, in People v. Gifford, 2 App. Div. 

642, 151 N.Y.S. 2d 982, a determination in favor of the petitioner who had been sentenced as a second felony offender on the basis of a Vermont conviction, which the court held was only considered of misdemeanor grade in New York, produced an order directing that the defendant be resentenced as a first felony offender. 

Sec. 442. Fraud, Coercion and Duress. Perhaps the classic situations in which coram nobis is used are those in which it is sought to set aside judgments brought about by fraud, duress and coercion. While we cannot here cite all of the numerous cases where this has been the basis of relief, a few characteristic ones culled from the reports should illustrate the use of the remedy. In People v. Picciotti, 4 

N.Y. 2d 340, a defendant who had pleaded guilty to receiving stolen goods on a threat by an Assistant District Attorney that if he did not do so he would be prosecuted under indictments found against him five years before but never prosecuted, was held entitled to relief in coram nobis. 

Similarly, a plea of guilty induced by an Assistant District Attorney's representation that the sentence to be imposed would not exceed five to ten years, after which, on so plead- 721

§ 

ing, he was sentenced to serve from seven and one-half to ten years, was held to require the vacating of a judgment of conviction and permission to defendant to withdraw his plea, in People v. Freeman, 7 App. Div. 2d 960, 182 N.Y.S. 

2d 146. So, too, in People v. Van Nostrand, 4 App. Div. 2d 

913, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 823, coram nobis was granted where the defendant alleged that a confession was extracted from him by police beatings and that he was threatened with prosecution for a murder charge in another county if he failed to state to the court that he did not want counsel assigned.

While fraud and coercion, perpetrated by the court or the prosecution or by police officials have generally, when established, sustained the remedy, it will not generally be allowed "that inducements made by defendant's own counsel, which in many cases must of necessity border closely upon the giving of advice to an accused by counsel, should have the effect of official fraud" (People v. Saladak, 15 

Misc. 2d 506, 183 N.Y.S. 2d 276; People v. Wilkes, 136 N.Y.S. 

2d 662; Crowe v. United States, 175 F. 2d 799).

Sec. 443. Insanity. In People v. Nickerson, 283 App. Div. 

854, 128 N.Y.S. 2d 797, the court stated: "We believe that coram nobis is the proper remedy to raise the claim that the defendant was insane at the time of plea within the meaning of Penal Law, section 1120. * * * That is a ques tion of fact not apparent of record (Leonard v. Barnes, 280 App. Div. 1, 111 N.Y.S. 2d 5, affirmed 303 N.Y. 989).

In contrast to Flora v. People, 281 App. Div. 946, 119 

N.Y.S. 2d 434, affirmed 306 N.Y. 515, where the petition alleged the court's knowledge of petitioner's mental condition at the time the plea was received, the plea of this defendant was received by a court then uninformed of his alleged incapacity." 

Sec. 444. Deprivation of Counsel. Coram nobis has been used in many situations to remedy a deprivation of constitutional rights in the rendering of judgments of convic- 722

§ tion. Failure to advise defendant of his constitutional right to counsel has been held a proper ground for setting aside the judgment (Hague v. Court of General Sessions, 296 

N.Y. 1; People v. McCullough, 300 N.Y. 107). Even when the abridgement of the right to counsel is apparent on the face of the record, although this would ordinarily bar the remedy, it will be granted as an exception because of its importance, where special evidence indicates its necessity (People v. Silverman, 3 N.Y. 2d 200). And the fact that the defendant was a moron with intelligence so low that he was incapable of understanding the proceedings and of intelligently waiving his right to counsel was held to require granting of coram nobis (People v. Boehm, 309 N.Y. 362). 

Another exception to the requirement that the error appear dehors the record seems to be in cases where defendant has been unreasonably forced to trial in the absence of his own attorney, represented by counsel summarily assigned him by the court, as in People v. 

Silverman, 3 N.Y. 2d 200. But alleged incompetence of counsel is, in itself, no basis for the writ (People v. Shapiro, 2 Misc. 2d 462, 153 N.Y.S. 2d, affirmed 3 App. Div. 2d 740, 161 N.Y.S. 2d 564, affirmed 3 N.Y. 2d 203), except "only when the alleged instances of ineptitude are so extensive as to indicate that the entire proceedings were a mockery and a sham resulting in a denial of due process, that coram nobis will be warranted." (People v. Kalmus, 123 N.Y.S. 

2d 411, 415.) 

Sec. 445. Applications for Resentence. One use of the writ of error coram nobis not contemplated when it was first revived in our modern jurisprudence has developed into a most frequently-utilized application of it. This application involves an attack not on the trial or proceedings prior to sentence, but an application for resentencing. It has most frequently been resorted to by convicts serving added sentences under the statutes requiring increased punishment where the defendant is proved to have been previously convicted of one or more felonies. When it is 

723

§ 

subsequently disclosed that the prior convictions, or some of them, were improper or were not actually felonies, the application is made, there being no other form of review therefor. 

In People v. Kronick, 308 N.Y. 866, the defendant had been convicted and sentenced as a fourth felony offender under Section 1942 of the Penal Law. Contending that two of the previous convictions, one in Maryland and one in Delaware, were of such nature under the laws of those States that they did not meet the definition of felony in New York, he applied for a writ of error coram nobis. Reversing the County Court and the Appellate Division (283 

App. Div. 965, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 893), the Court sustained the defendant's contention, and remitted the matter to the County Court "to vacate and set aside the sentence imposed upon defendant as a fourth offender * * * and to resentence the defendant as a second felony offender (Penal 

Law, sec. 1941)." In People v. Shaw, 1 N.Y. 2d 30, the Court, despite a vigorous dissent and the conceded situation that the reduction of the number of felonies charged to the defendant, from two previously to one, by reason that the second one had brought only a suspended sentence, would not necessarily affect the sentence, nevertheless directed the defendant's resentencing as a second, rather than as a third, felony offender. 

In these applications, involving convictions in other

States or jurisdictions, it has been held, our courts will not consider any claims of impropriety in the other jurisdictions, and will treat the convictions as an effective predicate for multiple-offender punishment under Sections 1941 and 1942 of the Penal Law until the courts of the jurisdictions in which they were rendered set them aside (People v. McCullough, 300 N.Y. 107). However, the New York courts will consider, and will give weight to, the contention that conviction of felonies under the laws of other jurisdictions which, under New York law, are not deemed felonies, are improper bases for multiple offender treatment and will resentence accordingly (People v. Olah, 300 724

§ 

N.Y. 96; People ex rel. Newman v. Foster, 297 N.Y. 27).

In these situations, it has been held, the New York courts will ordinarily look to the statute under which the conviction was had to determine whether conviction thereof shall be deemed a prior conviction of felony, and not to the evidence adduced at the trial or other evidentiary and narrative allegations (People v. Benjamin, 7 App. Div. 2d 410, 184 N.Y.S. 2d 1). Thus, for one example, it was held in 

People v. Gifford, 2 App. Div. 2d 642, 151 N.Y.S. 2d 982, a defendant sentenced as a second offender, because of a prior conviction in Vermont of grand larceny, was ordered resentenced without the second offender increment because the Vermont statute makes larceny of a sum in excess of $50 grand larceny, while in New York larceny is not a felony unless the sum is over $100. 725

CHAPTER 38 RIGHTS OF DEFENDANT, COMPENSATION OF COUNSEL, AND COMPROMISE OF CRIMES Sec. 446. Coverage Sec. 447. Right to Counsel and Compensation Therefor Sec. 448. Expert Witnesses Sec. 449. Informing Defendant of Right to Counsel and Waiver of Right Sec. 450. Right to a Public Trial Sec. 451. Right to Produce Witnesses and Confront Adverse Witnesses Sec. 452. Impeachment of Own Witness Sec. 453. Freedom from Undue Restraint Sec. 454. Compromising Certain Crimes Sec. 446. Coverage. This chapter deals with miscellaneous rights of a defendant in a criminal action which, by their nature, do not warrant treatment in a complete chapter. 

These rights are primarily those granted by Code of Criminal Procedure, sections 8 through 10, such as the right to counsel and to be informed of that right; the right to compensation for such counsel and expert witnesses; the right to be free from unreasonable restraint; the right to a public trial; and the right to produce witnesses in one's own behalf. Sections 8 through 10 are termed "preliminary provisions" of the Code and are concerned, mainly, with constitutionally-granted general rights of a procedural nature such as those mentioned above. Some of the rights therein granted are treated in separate chapters herein. 

See chapter on "Double Jeopardy" for a discussion of the 726

COUNSEL AND COMPENSATION 

§ 447 right granted in Code Section 9, the right not to be subjected to a second prosecution for a crime for which one has once been placed in jeopardy, or of which one has previously been convicted or acquitted. See Chapter 28 "Dismissals for Lack of Prosecution", for a discussion of the defendant's right to a speedy trial, and Chapter 11, for a discussion of the privilege against self incrimination. 

Chapter VI of Title 12, Part 4, of the Code (sections 663 

through 666), entitled "Compromising Certain Crimes, by

Leave of the Court," will also be discussed. 

Sec. 447. Right to Counsel and Compensation Therefor. 

The right to counsel in a criminal case is granted by Arti cle I, Section 6, of the New York State Constitution: "in any trial in any court whatever the party accused shall be allowed to appear and defend in person and with counsel as in civil actions." This has been construed, in New York, to mean that defendants are entitled to counsel throughout the various stages of a criminal prosecution. Compare 

State v. Martin, 27 N.W. 2d 158 (Minn.), as an example of the right restricted to less than this period, e.g., to the trial only.

The corollary statutory provisions in Code of Criminal Procedure, are Section 8, subdivision 2, which provides: "In a criminal action the defendant is entitled *** 2. To be allowed counsel as in civil actions, or he may appear and defend in person and with counsel"; Sections 308 and 

308-a, which further implement the constitutional requirement, by requiring the court to inform the defendant of his right to counsel when he appears for arraignment, and also provide for compensation to be paid assigned counsel in certain cases; Section 188, which further guarantees that the defendant be informed of his right to counsel by requiring the magistrate to so inform him before any further proceedings are had, when the defendant is first produced before him after an arrest, prior to the preliminary examination; and Section 699, which imposes a similar requirement in summary proceedings. This last cited section 727

§ 

is similar to Section 308, except that Section 308 is applicable to an arraignment upon an indictment, and Section 188 to arraignments in other cases. 

The Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution also guarantees the right of counsel to defendants, but it is applicable only to proceedings in Federal courts; thus, a defendant's Federally-based constitutional right must arise out of the due process guarantee of the Fourteenth Amendment, which has been held to apply, except in death cases, only on a showing of prejudice (Quicksall v. Multzer, 339 U.S. 660).

The parties protected by Sections 8, et seq., are "defendants," the meaning of which appears clear. However, the right does not extend to parolees or probationers during hearings to determine whether the conditions of their release have been violated, unless the right arises from some other statute. See Chapter 41. In People ex rel. Fusco v. 

Ryan, 204 Misc. 861, 124 N.Y.S. 2d 690, the court held that a material witness, proceeded against under Section 618-b of the Code (under which section material witnesses may be held in substantial bail, or in default thereof, be imprisoned for a number of months), is entitled to counsel if he requests it, but that the court is not required to inform him of that right. Other witnesses, not subject to the strict provisions of Section 618-b, have been held not to be entitled to counsel (People ex rel. McDonald v. Keeler, 99 

N.Y. 463). On the other hand, all defendants, regardless of the seriousness of the charge, are entitled to counsel (City of New York v. Wierzibicki, 137 Misc. 427, 244 N.Y.S. 342).

If the defendant does not have counsel, and desires counsel, the court must assign counsel to him. 

Compensation of Counsel. The counsel assigned by the court is entitled to compensation for his services only in capital cases. In such cases, the court may allow counsel his expenses (upon a verified statement thereof being filed with the clerk of the court) and a fee not in excess of $1,500, or where more than one counsel has been assigned and has appeared, not in excess of $2,000 for each defendant. Pre- 728

COUNSEL AND COMPENSATION 

§ 447 requisite to the granting of such an allowance by the court is the filing of a statement, by or on behalf of the defendant, "showing that he is wholly destitute of means." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 308.) The assigned counsel, upon showing to the court that such is necessary, may also receive a free copy of the daily testimony, after the court enters an order directing such action. However, the court has no power to furnish such free copies for use on appeal after the trial in other than a capital case, unless there was an order, on motion, granting leave to prosecute the appeal as a poor person (People v. Kasulkas, 4 Misc. 2d 737, 162 

N.Y.S. 2d 505; People v. Raymondi, 180 Misc. 973, 43 N.Y.S. 

2d 217, app. dismissed, 268 App. Div. 863, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 678).

But, compare Griffin v. Illinois, 351 U.S. 12, which may sustain the argument, based upon due process grounds, that such copies must be furnished, nevertheless. 

Counsel's allowance may be ordered by the court which finally disposes of the case, or by the trial court, or by the court in which any appeal is determined, or in which the action is suspended or otherwise disposed of. The court has no power to order compensation of counsel in cases other than those provided by statute (Application of Sullivan, 297 N.Y. 190). To become entitled to the fee, counsel must first be properly assigned (People ex rel. Van Doren v. Prendergast, 214 N.Y. 16), although compensation for services rendered after an assignment is not precluded by the same counsel's appearance, on behalf of the defendant, prior to the assignment (People ex rel. Berry v. Berry, 250 

N.Y. 452; Compare People v. Price, 262 N.Y. 450). If counsel assigned continues as counsel on appeal, the court will, generally, allow additional compensation for those services (People v. Ferraro, 162 N.Y. 545; Op. Dept. Audit and 

Control, 38 State Dept. 443 [1929]). However, the appeal must be perfected within the time allowed by statute (People v. Mummiami, 259 N.Y. 8; People v. Cowan, 245 N.Y. 

532), and must not have been taken solely for delay (People v. Triola, 175 N.Y. 407). 729

§ 

Sec. 448. Expert Witnesses. In cases where the defendant may require expert witnesses, on establishment to the court's satisfaction that the defendant is unable to afford such witnesses, the court may direct their employment by the defendant, directing their compensation to be paid by the county in an amount not to exceed $1,000 (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 308). The direction of the court must be by written order, or by a notation in the court's minutes (Reilly v. Berry, 250 N.Y. 456). Although the statute states that experts may be employed "in any case" it has been held that such action is proper only in capital cases (Marcus v. Joseph, 281 App. Div. 336, 119 N.Y.S. 2d 431, affirmed, 308 N.Y. 813). The number of witnesses that may be so employed is limited, by statute, to no more than the number to be used by the prosecution, or, where the defendant has the burden of going forward with the evidence upon the issue, or where there has been no indication of the number to be employed by the prosecution, to no more than two such witnesses.

The procedure followed in applying for the authorization and payment of experts is similar to that applicable in the case of assigned counsel. An affidavit supporting the application is submitted to the court and notice given the District Attorney, and an order should be submitted for the court's signature, directing such employment and payment.

Sec. 449. Informing Defendant of Right to Counsel and 

Waiver of Right. The defendant may waive his right to counsel after he has been duly informed thereof (People v. Fortson, 7 App. Div. 2d 139, 180 N.Y.S. 2d 945). However, the waiver must be made intelligently, and must be specific, and the defendant cannot waive his right to be informed of his right to counsel. In People v. Cole, 6 App. Div. 2d 725, 174 N.Y.S. 2d 398, conviction was reversed and a new trial ordered, where defendant withdrew his plea of not guilty, entered at his arraignment where he had been advised of his right to counsel,and later entered a guilty plea and was 730

RIGHTS OF DEFENDANT 

§ 449 sentenced without any further advice of this right, and where there also had been no proper "allocutus" under 

Section 480 of the Code. 

The court's duty to inform the defendant of his right to counsel is a substantial one and must be obeyed by the court regardless of its opinion concerning the defendant's ability to understand the advice (People v. Wright, 1 Misc. 

2d 711, 178 N.Y.S. 2d 535, where the defendant was found to have been too intoxicated to comprehend the advice, but nevertheless the information dismissed and fine remitted on appeal because of the lack of such advice). 

The right to counsel does not require two defendants, being tried together, to be assigned separate counsel unless, of course, other factors indicate that such an assignment would be proper (People v. Buck, 6 App. Div. 2d 

528, 179 N.Y.S. 2d 1007). Also, counsel's decision not to appeal is not a denial of due process, nor does it show inadequacy on the part of the counsel. "Where the sentence is less than death it may be the wiser course not to appeal." (Ibid.) "The duty of counsel assigned to defend the person charged with murder in the first degree will not end with the judgment of conviction; it will be his duty also to take the necessary appeal within the [time] *** fixed by statute." (People v. Price, 262 N.Y. 410.)

If the defendant replies to the court's question, concerning his desire to have counsel, in the affirmative, it is improper for the court to request that the defendant plead prior to the assignment of, and his consultation with, counsel. However, that error does not necessarily require a reversal of defendant's conviction. In People v. Marincic, 2 

N.Y. 2d 18, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 569, two young defendants pleaded guilty immediately after being informed of their right to counsel, but prior to any assignment. The court's request for, and acceptance of, their plea was held to be reversable error. However, in People v. Dolac, 3 App. Div. 

2d 351, 160 N.Y.S. 2d 911, affirmed, 3 N.Y. 2d 945, 168 

N.Y.S. 2d 315, the defendant pleaded not guilty before counsel was assigned. Thereafter, upon consultation with 731

§ 

counsel, that plea was withdrawn and a guilty plea entered. On appeal, the court stated that the error "in depriving the defendant of his right to confer with assigned counsel before making answer to the indictment *** was cured when later * * * defendant appeared with his counsel in Court, withdrew his plea of not guilty, took no steps to move against the indictment or demur thereto, but pleaded guilty."

Sec. 450. Right to a Public Trial. As above noted, Sec tion 8 of the Code grants to a defendant in a criminal action the right "to a speedy and public trial." The right to a speedy trial is discussed in Chapter 28, supra. The right to a public trial is guaranteed not only by Section 8 and the New York State Constitution, but also by Section 4 of the 

Judiciary Law and Section 12 of the Civil Rights Law. Sec tion 4 of the Judiciary Law provides: "The sittings of every court within the state shall be public, and every citizen may freely attend the same, except that in all proceedings and trials in cases for * * * abortion, rape, assault with intent to commit rape, sodomy ***the court may, in its discretion, exclude therefrom all persons who are not directly interested therein, excepting jurors, witnesses, and officers of the court."

The most recent, and leading case on this subject is People v. Jelke, 308 N.Y. 56, which involved "the power of the trial court to exclude members of the general public, including representatives of the press, from the courtroom during the trial of a criminal prosecution," involving charges of compulsory prostitution because of "The obscene and sordid details *** [and] the offensive obscenity of this already over-publicized trial," in the words of the trial judge. The defendant was permitted to have present, in the courtroom, "any friends or relatives he deems necessary for the protection of his interests." After the defendant's conviction had been reversed by the Appellate Division (284 App. Div. 211, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 662), the prosecution appealed. At the same time, certain representatives of the 732

RIGHTS OF DEFENDANT 

§ 451 press instituted a separate proceeding, in the nature of a writ of prohibition, directed against the trial judge's enforcement of the order excluding them from the trial, alleging that their rights, as members of the public, had been infringed by the order (United Press Association v. 

Valente, 308 N.Y. 71). In an extensive opinion, which considered the history of the right to a public trial, and the purposes of the requirement, the Court of Appeals affirmed the reversal of the conviction and stated: "The statutory requirement of a public trial is not satisfied simply by allowing relatives and friends of defendant's choosing to be present. A trial open to only a limited class of persons may not be regarded as public, particularly if no representative of the press is permitted to attend." The 

Court held that Section 4 of the Judiciary Law, allowing the exclusion of the public in certain cases, was applicable only to the specific cases there mentioned, and that the court's right to limit attendance, for valid reasons such as to prevent overcrowding, etc., or to exclude minors from trials of the nature of the Jelke trial, did not extend to a general power to exclude all but a limited class. "The exclusion of particular spectators or classes of spectators may then be justified, without impairing the essential nature of the trial which remains otherwise open to the public at large." In the United Press Association case, the court held that the fact that defendant had been deprived of a public trial did not warrant a holding that petitioners, as members of the public, had a right to be present. The right to a public trial may be waived by the defendant (People v. Miller, 257 N.Y. 54).

Sec. 451. Right to Produce Witnesses and Confront Ad verse Witnesses. Section 8 of the Code grants to defendants the right to produce witnesses in their own behalf and to be confronted with adverse witnesses, in the presence of the court, except in four enumerated situations, which are: 1. Where there has been a preliminary hearing before a magistrate and the witness's testimony has been 733

§ 

reduced by the magistrate to the form of a deposition in the defendant's presence, and where the defendant had the opportunity to cross examine the witness at the hearing, and where the court is shown, to its satisfaction, that the witness whose testimony is sought to be introduced in deposition form, is "unable to attend by reason of his death, insanity, sickness or infirmity, or that the witness cannot, with due diligence, be found in the state"; 2. Where a deposition containing the witness's testimony has been taken pursuant to Section 219 of the Code (providing for the conditional examination of prosecution's witnesses), and where it is shown that the witness is unable to attend the trial for the reasons quoted in connection with subdivision 1, above; 3. Where the defendant is charged with violation of the Tenement House Law, in which case a duly certified certificate of the proper officer shall be presumptive evidence that the house concerned is a tenement house; 4. 

Where the testimony to be introduced is that of a witness who testified at a previous trial of the defendant upon the same charge, and who is unable to attend the subsequent trial for the reasons quoted in subdivision 1, above. 

The above provisions have been held constitutional (People v. Qualey, 210 N.Y. 202; People v. Vituskey, 115 

App. Div. 139, 140 N.Y.S. 19). In People v. Hines, 284 N.Y. 

93, the court held that the right to confront witnesses necessarily included the right to examine them. To effectuate the defendant's right to produce witnesses, the court cannot refuse defendant the right to subpoena witnesses, even though, in the court's opinion, such action is unnecessary (Danaher v. Harris, 236 App. Div. 481, 260 N.Y.S. 

22), and the refusal of the court to permit the defendant to produce a witness who will deny the prosecution's testimony requires a reversal of any conviction that might result from the trial (People v. Mulcahy, 153 N.Y.S. 912). 

Similarly, if a reasonable adjournment is necessary so that the defendant may produce his witness, a refusal to grant the adjournment may constitute ground for reversal (People v. Brackerton, 89 Misc. 269, 153 N.Y.S. 567; People 734

WITNESSES 

§ 452 v. O'Neil 139 Misc. 529, 248 N.Y.S. 674). The defendant must exert a reasonable effort to produce the witnesses at the adjourned date. People v. Browne, 118 App. Div. 793, 103 N.Y.S. 903, aff'd., 189 N.Y. 528.

The right to confront and examine witnesses may be waived, and a waiver will be implied by the defendant's failure to object to the reading of the testimony of absent, adverse, witnesses (People v. Toledo, 150 App. Div. 403, 135 N.Y.S. 49, affirmed, 206 N.Y. 661). The defendant is not entitled to confront and examine persons who are not witnesses, such as one who was connected with the case but whose testimony was not introduced at the trial (People v. Kendricks, 300 N.Y. 544).

Civil Practice Act, section 392, which codifies rules of evidence, is also deemed applicable to criminal cases, where not inconsistent with other statutes, and thus has some effect upon the defendant's right to examine and be confronted with adverse witnesses. So, in People v. Nisonoff, 181 Misc. 696, 50 N.Y.S. 2d 420, the admission in evidence of official records, primarily autopsy reports, was upheld as within the scope of that section. See also People v. Corey, 157 N.Y. 332 (dying declarations held admissible).

Sec. 452. Impeachment of Own Witness. In 1936, Section 

8-a was added to the Code. That section provides that either party may impeach any witness, including one called as his own or made his own, by showing that prior inconsistent statements had been made by the witness, providing that such statements are in writing, subscribed by the witness, or that they were made under oath. A corollary section to 8-a, but applicable only to civil actions, is Civil Practice Act, sec. 343-2, which was enacted at the same time on the same recommendation of the Judicial Council. These sections' intent was noted as: “limiting prior inconsistent statements to those which are written or made under oath *** and by leaving the procedure for adducing evidence as to general bad character in its pres- ent form." (1936 Rep., Jud. Council, p. 183.

) Thus the rule 735

§ 

enunciated in People v. Minsky, 227 N.Y. 94, to the effect that one cannot impeach his own witness by general character evidence remains in effect. See also Roge v. Valentine, 280 N.Y. 268, holding that the impeaching evidence may be used only to attack the credibility of the witness, and cannot be used as evidence in chief. 

Sec. 453. Freedom from Undue Restraint. Section 10 of the Code contains two guarantees; one, to the effect that the defendant cannot be compelled to testify against himself, has been treated in this work in Chapter 11, while the other is the provision that no "person charged with crime be subjected, before conviction, to any more restraint than is necessary for his detention to answer the charge." The right of freedom from undue restraint has been rarely considered in the cases. 

In People v. Mendola, 1 App. Div. 2d 413, 151 N.Y.S. 2d 

278, reversed on other grounds 2 N.Y. 2d 270, 159 N.Y.S. 

2d 473, the problem did arise. There the defendant attacked his conviction, and the denial by the court of his motion to be freed from handcuffs during the trial. The court stated: "The conduct of a trial with the accused in manacles is highly unusual. Before a trial judge permits such a thing to be done, the necessity therefor should be shown clearly. It is seriously prejudicial to the defendant, for the jury might well conclude that he is a dangerous criminal who cannot be trusted, even under the surveillance of guards. The presumption of innocence could thus be impaired by an appearance of guilt. ***It is the court's responsibility, not the sheriff's to decide whether the defendant should be fettered during the trial." 

In People v. Bryant, 5 Misc. 2d 446, 166 N.Y.S. 2d 59, after an application by the District Attorney for the court to order the defendant restrained during the trial, a hearing was held by the court on the application, without the presence of the jurors, opportunity being given to the defendant to cross-examine witnesses at that hearing and proof taken under oath. After considering the Mendola 736

COMPROMISE OF CRIME 

§ 454 case, the trial court ordered the defendant restrained during the trial, noting that on prior occasions the defendant had attempted to escape by violent means, had shot an officer, and had discharged firearms in a public conveyance; therefore, the court found "reasonable ground for apprehension and evident danger of escape." The holding in the Bryant case appears clearly correct, and the method of conducting the hearing on the application prevented any prejudice to the defendant. 

Sec. 454. Compromising Certain Crimes. Sections 663 

through 666 of the Code provide the method for the compromise of certain crimes, between the perpetrator of the act and the victim, without further criminal proceedings in the courts. The crimes which may be so compromised are those misdemeanors "for which the person injured * * * has a remedy by civil action * * * except when it was committed: 1. By or upon an officer of justice while in the execution of the duties of his office; 2. Riotously, or 3. With an intent to commit a felony." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

663.) Examples of crimes subject to compromise, given by the Commissioners on Practice and Pleading (1849) p. 

339, of their report recommending enactment of the section, are “libels, and simple assault and batteries." 

To effect a compromise the victim must appear before the examining magistrate or the court to which that magistrate must make his return (the County Court, or Supreme Court, or other court as provided by Code Crim. Proc., sec. 

221), and "acknowledge in writing that he has received satisfaction for the injury." In such event the magistrate or court, in discretion, on payment of costs and expenses incurred, may order "all proceedings to be stayed upon the prosecution and the defendant discharged therefrom." The reason for the order must be entered upon the minutes of the court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 664), and the order bars subsequent prosecution for the same offense (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 665). No proceedings other than those mentioned in Section 663 may be compromised, and 737

§ 

an attempt to compromise other proceedings by the payment of money to a complaining witness, may constitute the compounding of a crime (Matter of Hart, 131 App. Div. 

661, 116 N.Y.S. 193).

Some early cases held that a crime could not be compromised, under these sections, after the jury had been sworn (People v. Prince, 1 Wheeler Crim. 32), or after conviction (People v. Bishop, 5 Wend. 111). Further, a compromise effected between the parties, without the interposition of the court and the District Attorney, was held ineffectual to prevent the District Attorney from thereafter bringing the case on for trial (In re Gilmore, 2 City Hall Rec. 29, where the parties appeared before clerk of court, paid costs and obtained a receipt but no court order had been entered). However, if such outof-court settlement is brought to the attention of the court, an order of compromise may then be entered (Cleveland v. Cromwell, 110 App. Div. 82, 96 N.Y.S. 475). Any other procedure, differing from that set forth in the statute, will usually not be effective to prevent the prosecution of the defendant, and any agreement, arising out of a compromise effected by procedures not authorized by the statute, may be held unenforceable and illegal (Hallstrom v. Erkas, 124 N.Y.S. 2d 169: agreement to convey land in consideration of compromise of crime, and in consideration of promise to refrain from prosecution for third degree assault, held unenforceable). 738

CHAPTER 39  IN MISDEMEANOR CASES
