Sec. 455. Introduction Sec. 456. Duty to Advise Defendant of Right to Certificate Sec. 457. Application for Certificate of Removal Sec. 458. Cause for Removal Sec. 459. Effect of Grand Jury's Direction to File an Information Sec. 460. Procedure after Grant or Denial of Certificate PRACTICAL SUGGESTIONS 

Counsel should move for a transfer to a higher court where he believes that his client would receive a more sympathetic hearing by a jury than by the court alone. There are also situations where counsel feels that another court would take a more lenient view of the charges upon which defendant is to be tried than the court where the prosecution is presently pending. 

Sec. 455. Introduction. As previously noted, the courts of special sessions outside of the City of New York have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine the charges of misdemeanors, offenses, violations and infractions listed in Section 56 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and committed within the county. The Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York has exclusive jurisdiction of all charges of misdemeanors committed therein, except libel (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31). The jurisdiction, in either, is subject to divestment if the Grand Jury finds an indictment prior to trial (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 59; N.Y.C.

Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31(1) (b); People v. Nicholas, 189 Misc. 

218, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 366). The court is likewise divested of 739

§ 

jurisdiction to proceed with the charge if a certificate is issued by the appropriate judicial authority determining that it is reasonable that the charge be prosecuted by indictment and the matter therefore be presented to the 

Grand Jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 57; N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. 

Act, sec. 31(1) (c). The law and procedure applicable to such removal outside of the City of New York (Code of 

Crim. Proc., secs. 57, 58), and within the City of New York (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31(1) (c) are the same, except as otherwise noted. 

One of the original purposes of the right afforded the defendant by this section was to permit the accused to obtain a trial in a court of record (People v. Ruttles, 172 

Misc. 306, 14 N.Y.S. 2d 979) and in a court composed of better qualified judiciary. As the court stated in People v. 

Zinke, 170 Misc. 332, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 313, the Court of Special

Sessions was at one time comprised of one lawyer, a butcher and an undertaker. The caliber of the judiciary of this court has been radically changed since that time and it is staffed with qualified jurists, members of the Bar whose ability and background are not essentially different from the judiciary of courts of record. 

The provisions of these sections apply only where the court has exclusive jurisdiction (People v. Supt. of New 

York State Reformatory, 162 Misc. 125, 294 N.Y.S. 255).

It was held in People v. Schacher, 181 Misc. 769, 46 N.Y.S. 

2d 471, that there was no authority to apply for a certificate of removal in the case of an infraction of Federal Office of Price Administration regulations since the New York City Criminal Courts Act provided for removal only in the case of misdemeanors. There is likewise no authority to apply for the certificate of removal until a charge is made against the accused (People ex rel. Seaman v. Hendrickson, 245 App. Div. 838, 281 N.Y.S. 103).

Sec. 456. Duty to Advise Defendant of Right to Certificate. 

There is no doubt that a person charged with a violation 740

§ within the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of special sessions has the statutory right to make the necessary application for removal (People v. Cowie, 88 Hun 498, 34 

N.Y.S. 888; People v. Anschell, 23 N.Y.S. 707). The denial of the right to make this application is reversible error (People v. Barry, 16 App. Div. 462, 44 N.Y.S. 913; see 

People v. Marinelli, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 321).

The next and more meaningful question is whether the accused must be warned or apprised of his right to apply for such certificate. The statute requires that the magistrate inform the accused "of his rights under section fifty seven and this section." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 58.)

This specific statutory direction is not present in Section 31 (1) (c) of the City Act; however, the case interpretation for both statutes has been the same. Although there has been some division in the lower courts, the weight of authority supports the conclusion that the defendant, in addition to the right of applying for the certificate, has the right to be informed of this available procedure. The court in People v. Freileweh, 11 App. Div. 409, 42 N.Y.S. 

373, stated that the "defendant was not told and in ignorance of his rights he cannot be said to have waived them." (People v. Barry, 16 App. Div. 462, 44 N.Y.S. 913.) In People v. Evans, 10 Misc. 2d 409, 175 N.Y.S. 2d 656, the court stated: "a waiver of the defendant's right * *** to have his matter prosecuted by indictment must be made understandingly, completely and intelligently." See People v. 

Berg, 200 Misc. 203, 105 N.Y.S. 2d 694. There are two older cases not specifically overruled, but contrary to the above, which held that the statutory language above referred to is merely directory and that it is prejudicial error only if there is a wilful failure to apprise the defendant of his right to apply for a certificate (People v. Parker, 69 Hun 

136, 23 N.Y.S. 704; People v. McGann, 43 Hun 55). If the defendant pleads guilty, the failure to warn him of the right to a certificate is not error because the warning is important only if the accused is to stand trial (People v. 

Loomis, 65 Misc. 156, 121 N.Y.S. 91). 741

§ 

There is a point at which the defendant, by having committed himself to a trial in the court of special sessions, may be said to have waived his right to make an application for removal pursuant to this section. In People v. 

Brody, 43 N.Y.S. 2d 225, the defendant was arraigned, pleaded not guilty and the matter was adjourned. At the adjourned date, the complainant was sworn on behalf of the People and the defendant then moved for the certificate of removal. The court held that the trial of the case could not be interrupted for an application of removal (People v. Kuzniski, 179 N.Y.S. 739; People v. McGann, 43 Hun 55). In People v. Freileweh, 11 App. Div. 409, 42

N.Y.S. 373, it was held that adjournment of the case twice did not constitute a waiver of the defendant's right to apply to have the case presented to the Grand Jury.

Sec. 457. Application for Certificate of Removal. The ap plication for a certificate that the charge be prosecuted by indictment outside the City of New York may be made before trial to any Justice of the Supreme Court, or to the County Judge of the county where the crime is triable, upon three days' notice to the complainant or to the District Attorney of the time and place of the application therefor 

(Code of Crim. Proc., Sec. 57). In the Court of Special 

Sessions of the City of New York, the application must be made to a Justice of the Supreme Court in the judicial department where the matter is triable, a County Judge in counties other than New York, or to a Judge of the Court of General Sessions in the County of New York, upon at least two days' notice to the District Attorney (N.Y.C. Cr. 

Cts. Act, Sec. 31(1), c).

In the courts outside of the City of New York, the magistrate is required to adjourn the case for at least five, but not more than ten, days to enable the accused to apply for a certificate that the case be presented to the Grand 

Jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 58). See People v. Barry, 16 App. Div. 462, 44 N.Y.S. 913. In New York City, a judge 742

§ authorized to make the certificate, is not required to but may, pending the determination of the application, order the proceedings stayed in the Court of Special Sessions. 

The ordered stay may not exceed ten days. The order should be served upon the clerk of the part of the court where the charge is triable, whereupon all proceedings, except to admit the defendant to bail, are stayed for the time specified (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act, sec. 31 (1), c). The affidavit accompanying the notice must fully set forth the reason or reasons for the transfer in accordance with the following section.

On the return of the motion, oral argument is held and confined to the issue of the reasonableness of the certificate (People v. Hayes, 167 Misc. 18, 4 N.Y.S. 2d 897). The statute under which defendant is charged will not be construed or interpreted at such hearing (People v. Title 

Guarantee and Trust Co., 180 App. Div. 648, 168 N.Y.S. 278, rev'd on other grounds 227 N.Y. 366), nor will the court at that time determine which statute is violated (Application of Knight, 36 N.Y.S. 2d 985). The jurisdiction of the court cannot be challenged at this hearing (People v. Sabourin, 166 Misc. 23, 2 N.Y.S. 2d 728; People v. Lane, 149 

N.Y.S. 2d 769).

Sec. 458. Cause for Removal. The sole stated cause for removal expressed in the statute is if "it is reasonable that such charge be prosecuted by indictment." (Code of Crim. 

Proc., sec. 57; N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act 31 (1), c). Beyond this general test, the statute does not set criteria, hence the court is given great latitude and discretion in granting or denying the certificate (People v. Schulman, 175 Misc. 157, 22 N.Y.S. 2d 429). "Reasonable means just, proper, fair or equitable." (People v. Butts, 121 App. Div. 226, 105 

N.Y.S. 677.) The burden is upon the accused to demonstrate the necessity and reasonableness of the certificate of removal (People v. Currao, 166 Misc. 374, 2 N.Y.S. 2d 513;

People v. Lane, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 769; People v. Liteer, 3 Misc. 743

§ 

2d 505, 153 N.Y.S. 2d 704; People v. Rosenberg, 59 Misc. 

342, 112 N.Y.S. 316).

The leading and often quoted case as to the requisites for the granting of the certificate is People v. Rosenberg, supra, where the following factors were enumerated: "first, that a case presents intricate and complicated questions of fact, rendering a jury trial proper; or, second, that it presents difficult questions of law; or, third, that a property right is involved; or fourth, that a decision may be far reaching in its effect, and may become a precedent which will regulate a matter of general interest; or lastly that the case is of exceptional character, and that the defendant, for some special reason cannot have a fair trial in the Court of Special Sessions."

Although the courts reiterate the language of the Rosenberg case, and most applications for removal liberally adopt and transpose the language of the opinion, an analysis of the cases reveals that the applications are not granted upon all the requisites there set forth and that they are but a guide as to some factors which may warrant a removal. It will be helpful to examine the present legal efficacy of each of these considerations.

The first two grounds, i.e. complicated questions of fact or law are no longer support for the granting of a certificate (Application of Knight, 178 Misc. 972, 36 N.Y.S. 2d 

985). These grounds are no longer persuasive since the qualifications and caliber of the judiciary of the Court of Special Sessions are on a par with the higher courts of record (People v. Zinke, 170 Misc. 332, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 313; 

People v. Lane, 149 N.Y.S. 2d 769). The reason for requesting indictment by the Grand Jury must be something more than the mere preference for a jury trial (People v. Levy, 24 Misc. 469, 53 N.Y.S. 643; People v. Wade, 26 Misc. 585, 57 N.Y.S. 645. See People v. Sheldon, 190 Misc. 156, 74 

N.Y.S. 2d 36; People v. Killorin, 123 N.Y.S. 2d 612). The court, in People v. Hassan, 113 N.Y.S. 2d 108, stated: "the fact that questions of law involving the validity of an ordinance might be involved would not require the grant- 744

§ ing of the certificate. (People v. Satterthwaite, 195 Misc. 

33, 91 N.Y.S. 2d 597.)”

There is one constellation of cases where the nature of the factual disposition is such that the courts have ruled that a jury would afford a more "reasonable" forum for the accused. In obscenity cases where the issue of fact is resolved by the application of the mores and standards of the community, the courts have felt that a jury composed of citizens of the community are in a better position to pass upon the question (People v. Goldman, 197 Misc. 

290, 94 N.Y.S. 2d 535; People v. Morganstern, 134 Misc. 

127, 234 N.Y.S. 211; People v. Herk, 44 N.Y.S. 2d 444).

Also, in the case of People v. Faber, 190 Misc. 29, 73 N.Y.S. 

2d 374, the certificate was granted where the issue of fact was one dependent upon the mores of the community as to whether a certain game was "a game of chance." In People v. Shattls, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 186 the court held that the jury was best qualified to pass on an issue as to whether the public would be deceived by the defendant's activity. This argument cannot be advanced outside the City of New York, where in trials of misdemeanors the right to trial by jury is afforded (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 702). 

The certificate of removal on the ground that the accused will be subjected to severe punishment or loss of a property right has been the most frequently sustained basis for removal. The courts have felt in this instance that although the charge is technically a misdemeanor, the practical effect of the decision will result in consequences just as serious and harmful to the defendant as in felony; therefore the matter should be inquired into by the Grand Jury. A monetary fine is not the type of deprivation of property contemplated by this line of cases (People v. 

Hassan, 113 N.Y.S. 2d 108). If the conviction would result in an automatic revocation or cancellation of a license the certificate of removal will be granted on this ground. 

Thus, where the accused was charged with a crime where the conviction would result in the forfeiture of an alcohol and beverage control license, the certificate of removal 745

§ 

was granted (People v. Hoenig, 86 N.Y. Supp. 673; People v. Gantz, 41 Misc. 542, 85 N.Y.S. 79). In People v. Marinelli, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 321, a certificate was granted where the defendant, a licensed truck driver, was charged with leaving the scene of an accident, the conviction of which would result in a mandatory revocation of his license. 

It has been held that the certificate will issue where the effect of the conviction will be a loss of pension and civil service benefits. This is deemed a loss of property rights which merits the consideration of the Grand Jury (People v. Willis, 59 Misc. 371, 112 N.Y.S. 368; People v. Killorin, 123 N.Y.S. 2d 612; People v. Harrington, 169 Misc. 461, 7 

N.Y.S. 2d 720; People v. Schumann, 146 Misc. 395, 262 

N.Y.S. 486; People v. McGuinness, 168 Misc. 849, 6 N.Y.S. 

2d 593).

It is noted that the above decisions require that the loss of license or position be automatic and the courts have been reluctant to grant the certificate where the license will in all probability be revoked as a result of the conviction, but not mandatorily. In People v. Taffer, 170 Misc. 

688, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 58, two licensed detectives were charged with a conspiracy to obstruct justice. The court denied the certificate on the theory that the conviction might entail a loss of license, but it would not occur as a matter of law (People v. Porter, 108 Misc. 100, 177 N.Y.S. 460). Since an attorney's disbarment is not automatic upon conviction. of misdemeanor, certificates have been denied (People v. 

Speiser, 162 Misc. 9, 292 N.Y.S. 481; People v. Sabourin, 166 Misc. 23, 2 N.Y.S. 2d 728; Application of Knight, 36

N.Y.S. 2d 985). There is a growing body of law upholding the issuance of the certificate if there is a probability of loss of license and livelihood. In People v. Price, 53 N.Y.S. 

2d 47, a licensed booking agent charged with an obscene performance was granted the right to have the matter presented to the Grand Jury. Dentists have been granted certificates on the ground that conviction might entail loss of license (People v. Figur, 21 N.Y.S. 2d 571. People v. 

Shattls, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 186). 746

§ The granting of a certificate on this ground has been extended by some courts to the case where the financial interest of the defendant is substantial, and the loss resulting from conviction merits a trial in a court of record (People v. Faber, 190 Misc. 29, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 374). In People v. Otis, 46 N.Y.S. 2d 423, the accused, the operator of a beauty salon, was charged with unlawfully practicing medicine. The court held that in view of the large investment made by the defendant in his business and the serious consequences which would ensue as a result of possible conviction, the certificate of removal should be granted. See 

People v. Marinelli, 37 N.Y.S. 2d 321, where one of the bases for the granting of the certificate was the loss of livelihood and the welfare of the defendant's family. 

Another ground upon which the certificate has been granted is the instance where the decision is far-reaching in effect and will regulate a matter of general interest. 

One of the considerations in the granting of a certificate to a chiropractor arrested for illegally practicing medicine was the widespread interest that such a determination would have (In re Johnerson, 45 N.Y.S. 2d 538; People v. Ryan, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 806. See, similarly, People v. Faber, Misc. 29, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 374; Application of Pospichal, 180 

Misc. 168, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 486).

The court will grant a certificate on the ground that the accused cannot obtain a fair trial in the lower court. However, the judges are loath so to do, and assume that the defendant will obtain a fair trial and just verdict in the sessions court (People v. Gerra, 14 Misc. 2d 1051, 180 

N.Y.S. 2d 1001). Removal on this ground was granted in 

People v. Benzlesky, 206 Misc. 276, 132 N.Y.S. 2d 536, where the defendant's affidavit recited that the judge, in a prior case involving the accused, had stated that he had no use for the defendant and if he appeared before him again he would "throw the book" at him (People v. Ryan, 38 

N.Y.S. 2d 806; People v. Killorin, 123 N.Y.S. 2d 612).

The court will grant the certificate if the case is not of the type that ordinarily comes up for trial in the Court of 747

§  

Special Sessions, such as conspiracy to obstruct justice (People v. Ryan, supra; People v. Schulman, 175 Misc. 157, 22 N.Y.S. 2d 429). A factor in the granting of the certificate is whether the trial will take a considerable time and interfere with the business of the Special Sessions Court (People v. Shattls, 53 N.Y.S. 2d 186; People v. Schumann, 146 Misc. 395, 262 N.Y.S. 486).

The certificate should issue where the defendant will have to subpoena witnesses from outside of the State of New York, since the right to subpoena out-of-State witnesses emanates only from a court of record (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 618-a, subd. 2). In People v. Sheldon, 190 

Misc. 156, 74 N.Y.S. 2d 36, the certificate was granted where the only eyewitness was a resident of Pennsylvania, whom the defendant was compelled to examine on commission out of the State (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 636) to assure a fair trial.

Sec. 459. Effect of Grand Jury's Direction to File an Infor mation. It has been held that the direction of the Grand 

Jury that a matter be prosecuted by information is not binding upon the court and the matter may be sent back to the Grand Jury (Dodge v. Supreme Court, 276 N.Y. 

444). Although not bound by the Grand Jury's determination, the court should assume that the Grand Jury and the court had valid reasons for transferring the case to Special 

Sessions (People v. Wittekind, 161 Misc. 411, 292 N.Y.S. 

824). 

Sec. 460. Procedure after Grant or Denial of Certificate. 

If the application is granted, a certificate is signed by the judge that it is reasonable that the charge be prosecuted by indictment, and bail is fixed pending the presentment of the matter to the Grand Jury. This certificate is filed with the magistrate and upon execution of the undertaking in the sum required in the certificate, all proceedings before the magistrate are stayed. The magistrate, within five days thereafter, must make a return to the District At- 748

§ torney of the county of all proceedings had before him on the charge, the certificate and the undertaking given by the defendant. The District Attorney then has the duty of presenting the charge to the Grand Jury (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 57). 

In the Court of Special Sessions of the City of New York, the proceedings are stayed upon the filing of the certificate with the clerk of the part of the court where the charge is triable, and the chief clerk within five days makes or causes to be made a return of all the proceedings, the certificate and the undertaking to the District Attorney who must forthwith present the charge to the 

Grand Jury (N.Y.C. Cr. Cts. Act Sec. 31 (1), c). 

Section 58 of the Code provides that if on or before the adjourned day, the certificate is not filed with the magistrate or bail is not given as prescribed by the certificate, the magistrate, outside the City of New York, shall proceed with the trial. In the absence of the filing of the required certificate and bail in the courts within the City of New York, the Magistrate likewise proceeds with the trial. 

The grant or refusal of the certificate is an intermediate order and not appealable. Section 517 of the Code provides that an appeal may be taken only from a judgment of conviction (People v. Mascola, 174 App. Div. 360, 160 N.Y.S. 

940. See People v. Sanger, 168 App. Div. 835, 154 N.Y.S. 414). 749

Sec. 461. Definitions. "There is considerable difference between probation and parole; the former dealing with matters before judgment is imposed, while the latter concerns the suspension of the whole or a part of the judgment previously pronounced. *** the rights of the parties in such cases are quite different. In all such cases of parole violations before the Parole Commission, the legally constituted authorities should be allowed a wide discretion in the recalling of their earlier decisions. *** but, in probation cases, I should think the rule affording the accused the benefit of counsel at all stages of the proceedings might be successfully invoked." (City of New York v. 

Kriegel, 124 Misc. 67, 207 N.Y.S. 646.) Thus, parole may be defined as the release of the defendant, usually by the trial court, after his conviction, without imprisonment, and is a judicial act of the court as distinguished from 750

§ parole, which is the release of the defendant after he has been imprisoned and has served a portion of his sentence; the release being an administrative act of the executive. 

A similar distinction should be drawn between probation and the suspension of sentence ordered by the court under its inherent common law power. See discussion in chapter on "Sentence." It has been held, and it seems to be the more accurate usage, that where the word "probation" is used in the statute it refers to the "general scheme of probation established and authorized by statute, where the probationer is expressly made subject to the control, direction and discipline of the court, through probation officers or otherwise as prescribed in the statute law", and not to one who has had the execution of his sentence suspended, "under the common law power possessed by the court." (People v. Kaiser, 95 Misc. 681, 159 N.Y.S. 322.)

Thus, when probation is hereinafter referred to, it is intended that the above-quoted definition be applied. 

Sec. 462. Procedure in Ordering Probation. Under Code of 

Criminal Procedure, sec. 483, after a plea or verdict of guilty the court is empowered within its discretion to order the defendant placed on probation, and to subject him to the procedures established in Sections 927 et seq., of the Code, after ordering the suspension of imposition or execution of sentence. As in the case of a common law suspension of sentence, the court may, with the consent of the defendant, require the restitution or reparation of damages as a condition to the probation or, without the consent of the defendant, the court may require him to comply with any support orders concerning his dependents. If the suspension has been ordered by the Supreme 

Court, it may transfer jurisdiction over the matter, with the consent of the defendant, to the County Court of the county wherein the conviction occurred. The judgment roll, or a certified copy thereof, shall thereupon also be transferred to that court and the County Court then acquires all the powers over the defendant it would have 751

§ 

had if the probation were originally ordered in that court (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 483, subd. 3).

Once a judgment ordering the defendant placed on probation has been entered, the defendant must "forthwith" be placed under the care and supervision of the probation officers of the court sentencing him until the expiration of the period of probation (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 487). 

Sec. 463. Probation of Wayward Minors. Provision is made, in Section 913-c of the Code, for placing on probation persons adjudged wayward minors under Sections 913-a and 913-b. Wayward minors are, "so far as practicable", to be placed on probation for a period of not more than two years, before their commitment to an institution is ordered as a last resort. Where, because of previous delinquency or otherwise, it is deemed impracticable for the probation to be ordered a commitment may be ordered by the court.

Sec. 464. Procedure After Probation Ordered. Title 9 of 

Part 6 of the Code (Sections 928 through 938), together with the applicable portions of Correction Law, sections 14 through 14-f, regulate the administration of the probation system. The Correction Law sections relate, for the most part, to the internal administration of the system and provide for the establishment of a Director and Division of Probation, together with a Bureau and Commission of Probation within the Department of Correction, and for the allocation of State funds to county probation services, etc. In general, counsel will not have to deal with these provisions.

The Code sections regulating probation provide for the appointment by any court of criminal jurisdiction of probation officers, for their compensation and regulation (Sections 928 through 930), and for the investigation by such officers of the "circumstances of the offense, criminal record and social history of a defendant," whenever they are directed to do so by the court. The report of this in- 752

§ vestigation is to be submitted to the court prior to sentence or judgment, and copies forwarded to the person in charge of any institution to which the defendant may be committed for a period of more than three months (Code of 

Crim. Proc., sec. 931). Section 931 further provides: "Whenever desirable, and facilities exist therefor," a physical, mental, and psychiatric examination of the defendant shall be conducted. The court's consideration of this report, even if facts therein may be considered derogatory to the defendant, is not a denial of any constitutional right of the defendant (People v. Johnson, 252 N.Y. 

387). Nor will a failure to investigate invalidate a commitment where the court did not direct that a report be furnished (Anon. v. Anon., 195 Misc. 809, 91 N.Y.S. 2d 121).

Sec. 465. Conditions of Probation. Section 932 empowers the court to impose conditions upon probation. That section includes a list of some of the conditions that may be imposed, but that list is not exclusive, and other conditions may also be imposed by the court. In People ex rel. Schumaker v. Brophy, 147 Misc. 254, 263 N.Y.S. 571, affirmed 

240 App. Div. 802, 266 N.Y.S. 994, a defendant, convicted of sodomy, was placed on probation on condition he refrain from "associating with young boys in any manner." Some of the conditions listed in the section are the avoidance of injurious or vicious habits; avoidance of places or persons of disreputable or harmful character, abstention from intoxicating liquor; restitution of aggrieved parties; payment of a fine; support of dependents; attendance at a school; and undergoing treatment for narcotic addiction. 

However, it should be noted, as in the case of a suspended sentence, the court may not be completely unlimited in its choice of conditions. See chapter on "Sentence." Compare 

1923, Op. Atty. Gen. 177, indicating that the condition that a probationer leave the state permanently is valid, apparently contrary to the opinion concerning a defendant given a conditional pardon (1931, Op. Atty. Gen. 129). 

Who May Impose Condition. The Code provides that the 753

$465

"court" may impose the conditions upon the parole; the word court including a Justice of the Peace, in a case wherein he has jurisdiction (People v. Hill, 164 Misc. 370, 200 N.Y.S. 532), but not including a probation officer, who may not add to or change the conditions imposed by the court (People ex rel. Benacquista v. Blanchard, 267 App. 

Div. 663, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 22), although the officer may, of course, fix the times for the probationer to report to him, etc.

Notice of Condition. Notice of the conditions imposed must, of course, be given to the defendant before his probation may be revoked for a violation thereof. 

Period of Probation. The period of probation may extend up to the maximum term for which the defendant could have been sentenced (People ex rel. Meadowcraft v. Ashworth, 185 Misc. 384, 56 N.Y.S. 2d 756), and where no period has been fixed by the court in the probation order it will be presumed that the court intended to impose the maximum period (People v. Foote, 144 Misc. 134, 258 N.Y. 

S. 210). Section 933 regulates the period and provides that in cases involving minors, the probationary period may not extend beyond the child's minority; that for conviction of less than a felony the maximum period is three years, and that where the offense is abandonment, the probationary period may extend up to the seventeenth birthday of the defendant's youngest child. However, the provisions of Section 933 are limited, in cases involving disorderly conduct charges, by Penal Law, section 723, which provides that the maximum probation period in such cases is two years.

Where the defendant has been convicted of more than one crime in one proceeding, as upon more than one count of a multi-count indictment, he may be placed on probation for one crime, and imprisoned for another, although the periods may not be concurrent (1940, Op. Atty. Gen. 

366). If the probationer becomes a fugitive during the period of probation, that period will be extended for the amount of time the defendant retains that status (People 754

§ ex rel. Garlington v. Lawes, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 575). Violation of the conditions of probation, alone, will not extend the period although fleeing the jurisdiction, or remaining hidden, or being imprisoned for another crime, will (People v. Valle, 7 Misc. 2d 125, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 67).

Sec. 466. Discharge from Probation. At the end of the probationary period, or on a directed discharge at an earlier date, the probationer, unless good cause appears to the contrary, shall appear before the court "to be admonished or commended according to whether his conduct has improved or not." (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 

934.) This section also gives the court the power, at any time, to discharge the probationer from further supervision.

Sec. 467. Revocation, Modification or Continuation of 

Probation. Section 935 empowers the court to issue warrants for the arrest of any probationer who has violated the conditions of his probation, to commit him with or without bail, and to arraign him at a hearing upon the alleged violation, after which the court may "revoke, continue, or modify his probation." Any continuance so ordered may not extend beyond the maximum term for which the probationer could have been sentenced originally (1911, Op. Atty. Gen., vol. 2, p. 162). If the court orders the probation revoked, it may impose any sentence it might have originally imposed. The decision of the court that the probationer has breached the conditions of his probation is usually said to be non-reviewable (People ex rel. Garlington v. Lawes, 11 N.Y.S. 2d 575). People ex rel. Palladino v. Warden, 6 Misc. 2d 691, 167 N.Y.S. 2d 327, held that a writ of habeas corpus did lie to review a determination of a special sessions court that a condition of the petitioners' probation had been violated. However, the holding of that case can more accurately be stated to be that a writ of habeas corpus will lie to secure the review customary upon such a writ; that is, to determine if the 755

$ 

court revoking the probation had jurisdiction to do so, or if the defendant had been deprived of any of his fundamental rights by the manner in which the court ordered the revocation (People ex rel. Benacquista v. Blanchard, 286 App. Div. 663, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 22).

While the probationer is granted the right to be heard upon the revocation (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 935), no formal procedures are established in the Code to regulate that hearing. In the Benacquista case, one of the problems considered by the court on the habeas corpus application was whether this right to be heard had been sufficiently protected. The Court of Appeals has stated that the guarantee of the right to be heard "contemplates notice to the probationer of the violation charged, with an opportunity to attack or deny the charge." (People v. Oskroba, 305 N.Y. 

113.) In People v. Valle, 7 Misc. 2d 125, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 67, the court noted that deprivation of the right to counsel at such hearing might be a violation of due process, although it appears that the court is not required to inform the probationer of his right to counsel (People v. Roland, 6 Misc. 2d 686, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 521; People v. St. Louis, 3 

App. Div. 2d 883, 161 N.Y.S. 2d 170). Contrary to the view of the Valle case stands Nunz v. Monroe County Court, 5 Misc. 2d 592, 150 N.Y.S. 2d 698. It also appears that the probationer must be given an opportunity to testify, as held in People v. Hill, 164 Misc. 370, 300 N.Y.S. 532, involving the revocation of a suspended sentence, but the same principle would apply, a fortiori, in a probation revocation and the probationer should be given an opportunity to cross-examine adverse witnesses (People v. Oskroba, 305 N.Y. 113).

In People ex rel. Benacquista v. Blanchard, 267 App. Div. 

663, 48 N.Y.S. 2d 22, the court indicated that failure to comply with the requirements may be waived by the probationer, or the deficiency may not be considered error if it could not have changed the result of the hearing. In the 

Oskroba case, supra, the court noted that the decision of the court upon a revocation of probation lay within the 756

§ court's discretion; however, the court also indicated that the decision would be subject to review, to determine whether the court had abused its discretion. 

At the hearing, while it is deemed to be of the nature of a "summary proceeding" rather than a "criminal prosecution", a motion to dismiss the charge of violation may be made, and if granted such action deprives the court of authority to render a new judgment upon the matter (People v. Eames, 204 Misc. 798, 124 N.Y.S. 2d 622). After expiration of the probation period originally imposed, the court may not resentence the probationer for a violation committed during that period unless a warrant for the probationer's arrest had been issued before its expiration (People v. Valle, 7 Misc. 2d 125, 164 N.Y.S. 2d 67). However, if no attempt was made to arrest the probationer during the period after issuance of the warrant, and if there is no evidence that the probationer is evading arrest or hiding, the revocation and resentencing after the period may be held improper (Fishbein v. State, 204 Misc. 151, 120 

N.Y.S. 2d 92, aff'd. 282 App. Div. 600, 25 N.Y.S. 2d 845).

Code of Criminal Procedure, sec. 470-a, empowers the court to resentence the probationer after the expiration of the original probation period, if he has committed a crime during the period. No formal order revoking the probation is necessary; the imposition of a sentence will be considered sufficient (People ex rel. Wilson v. Additon, 40 N.Y.S. 2d 669). Compare People ex rel. Goldberg v. 

Sheriff, 206 Misc. 820, 137 N.Y.S. 2d 498, where the court stated: "There should be an express revocation and in addition a re-pronouncement of the sentence." 

Sec. 468. Parole. Parole, as above noted, differs from probation in that it is an executive act which occurs after imprisonment has commenced, and consists of allowing the prisoner to serve a portion of his term of imprisonment outside the walls of the prison. Therefore the Code refers to parole only so far as it affects other matters, such as the arrest and extradition of parole violators. See Code 757

§ 

of Criminal Procedure, secs. 842, 853, and 854, all sections of the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act discussed in chapter on "Extradition." See also Sections 154, designating parole officers as peace officers, and 937, permitting the use of probation officers as parole officers. The statutes concerning parole are found, primarily, in Correction. 

Law, secs. 210 through 224, and Executive Law, secs. 

115 and 116, which establish a Board of Parole as part of the Division of Parole, within the Executive Department. 

The powers and duties of that Board are found in Correction Law, sec. 210. 

Sec. 469. Time for Parole. Under Correction Law, sec. 210, the Board of Parole is charged with the duty of determining which prisoners, serving indeterminate sentences in State prisons, may be released, the time of their release, and the conditions thereof. Parole should be distinguished from the discretionary reduction of sentence which may be afforded by the executive pursuant to Correction Law, secs. 230 et seq., and which is discussed in the chapter on "Pardon"; such reduction is commonly known as "time off for good behavior."

An indeterminate sentence is one "having minimum and maximum limits fixed by the court or Governor," and differs from a definite sentence which is for a "definite fixed period of time." (Correction Law, sec. 230.) After a prisoner has been sentenced upon an indeterminate sentence, all records concerning that prisoner, and copies of all reports of investigations concerning him are to be filed with the Division of Parole (Correction Law. sec. 211). 

These records are not public and will not, ordinarily, be released (Jordan v. Loos, 204 Misc. 814, 125 N.Y.S. 2d 447, aff'd. 283 App. Div. 983, 130 N.Y.S. 2d 904).

Correction Law, sec. 212, provides that all prisoners sentenced for indeterminate terms are subject to the jurisdiction of the Board of Parole after they have been imprisoned for the minimum period of their sentence. 

From that point on, provided the prisoner has served at 758

§ least one year, the time of the prisoner's release upon parole lies within the discretion of the Parole Board, and their decisions, so long as they are not contrary to any positive statutory requirement, are absolute and nonreviewable (Hines v. State Board of Parole, 293 N.Y. 254; 

Razukas v. N. Y. State Board of Correction, 186 Misc. 429, 62 N.Y.S. 2d 914, affirmed 270 App. Div. 1074, 63 N.Y.S. 2d 

842). The one-year minimum sentence requirement does not apply to persons who have been sentenced for one day to life. Nor does it apply to persons committed under a sentence having no minimum or maximum time fixed, which persons are eligible for parole at any time (1946, Op. 

Atty. Gen. 207).

Persons sentenced upon consecutive sentences are not eligible for parole until all the minimum sentences imposed have, consecutively, been served (Simmons v. Prison 

Board, 3 App. Div. 2d 636, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 154, app. denied 

3 App. Div. 2d 688, 159 N.Y.S. 2d 944, app. denied 2 N.Y. 

2d 935, 162 N.Y.S. 2d 31). Discretionary allowances of time off for good behavior under Correction Law, sec. 230, are to be deducted from the minimum terms, not the maximums; thus the earliest time that parole may be allowed is the minimum term imposed less these allowances (People ex rel. Mason v. Brophy, 235 App. Div. 432, 257 N.Y.S. 

165). The Governor's commutation of the minimum sentence does not, of itself, affect the maximum term to be served, and the Parole Board, after such action by the Governor, has the power within the new period to determine whether to release the prisoner on parole or not (People ex rel. Van Moser v. N.Y. State Board of Parole, 179 Misc. 397, 39 N.Y.S. 2d 200, affirmed 266 App. Div. 896, 42 N.Y.S. 2d 728).

Sec. 470. Grounds for Parole. Correction Law, sec. 213, establishes, in a general manner, the conditions for the release of a prisoner on parole. "No prisoner shall be released on parole merely as a reward for good conduct or efficient performance of duties performed in prison, but 759

§ 

only if the Board of Parole is of the opinion that there is reasonable probability that, if such prisoner is released, he will live and remain at liberty without violating the law, and that his release is not incompatible with the welfare of society." When released, the parolee remains "in the legal custody of the warden of the prison from which he is paroled" until the expiration of the maximum term of his sentence (Correction Law, sec. 213). Another condition prerequisite to parole is contained in Correction Law, sec. 214, subd. 4, which provides that no prisoner shall be paroled unless the Board is satisfied that he will be suitably employed after release.

Sec. 471. Procedure Upon Release. Applications for release are not entertained by the Parole Board, which has the duty of examining all the records referred to in Correction Law, sec. 211, until one month prior to the expiration of the minimum term for each prisoner sentenced to an indeterminate term. In the case of prisoners sentenced to one day to life, a review of the records shall be conducted within six months after conviction, and at least once every two years thereafter. In that review, mental, physical and psychiatric reports concerning the prisoner, prepared within two months of the date of the review, are to be considered by the Board. The prisoner will also usually be examined by the Board (Correction Law, sec. 214).

Sec. 472. Review of Parole Board Decisions. Correction 

Law, sec. 212, provides that the determination by the 

Parole Board of the time of a prisoner's release upon parole "shall be deemed a judicial function and shall not be reviewable if done according to law." As stated by the 

Court of Appeals in Hines v. State Board of Parole, 293 

N.Y. 254: "so long as the Board violates no positive statutory requirement, its discretion is absolute and beyond review in the courts. *** The statutory scheme is such that no judicial review of the merits in any case is possible. 

The ***Board depends upon information in regard to the 760

§ personal traits and characteristics of the individual convicted and upon unanimous concurrence of the individual members of the Board. * * * The Board is to consider the prisoner's attitude towards society *** and the judge who sentenced him, *** the District Attorney who convicted him *** the policeman who arrested him *** the crime for which he is imprisoned and his previous criminal career. *** There are no statutory limitations upon the power of the Board upon due consideration of such matters. *** Furthermore no action need, nor can it be taken except upon the initiative of the Board itself. *** Matters of discretion affecting parole *** have not been confided to the courts." See, also, People ex rel. Kammerman v. 

Snyder, 73 N.Y.S. 2d 893; Razukas v. Department of Correction, 186 Misc. 429, 62 N.Y.S. 2d 914, affirmed without opinion 270 App. Div. 1074, 63 N.Y.S. 2d 842 (holding that the court will not mandamus the Board into releasing a prisoner or certifying him as eligible for parole).

Sec. 473. Conditions of Parole and Breach Thereof. The 

Code sections concerning probation refer to the Correction Law procedures established for parole cases, and adopt those procedures in determination of whether a breach of parole has occurred. Correction Law, sec. 215, describes some of the conditions that may be imposed upon a parolee (concerning the parolee's leaving the State, his place of residence within the State, etc.), and Section 216 prescribes the procedure to be followed in the determination of whether these conditions have been breached. Provision is made for the retaking of the parolee under a warrant that may be issued by any member of the Board of Parole becoming aware of the possibility of a breach of parole (Correction Law, secs. 216, 217); and for the parolee's imprisonment until a hearing before the Parole Board, at which hearing the prisoner alone shall be given an opportunity to be heard (Correction Law, sec. 218). It has been held that the determination by the Board lies 761

§ 

within its discretion and is not reviewable by the court where the applicable positive statutory provisions have been complied with (People ex rel. West v. Morhous, 179 

Misc. 238, 38 N.Y.S. 2d 321; People ex rel. Schuyler v. 

Brophy, 256 App. Div. 1045, 10 N.Y.S. 2d 754.

The question of whether a judicial determination or review of the Parole Board's decision is required by the Constitution has not been finally settled. In People ex rel. 

Madden v. Barr, 143 Misc. 716, 257 N.Y.S. 395, reversed 

236 App. Div. 319, 258 N.Y. 581, the court indicated its belief that, prior to the amendment of Section 696 of the Code in 1930, parolees were entitled to jury trials upon the issue of the breach. With the amendment of Section 696 and Correction Law, sec. 218, the court recognized that "since section 218*** provides for a parole court it thus furnishes the needful protection against arbitrariness." 

See, also, People ex rel. Kurzynski v. Hunt, 25 F. Supp, 647, to the same effect.

After the breach has been determined, the parolee is usually returned to prison to serve the unexpired portion of his sentence, excluding therefrom the time spent on parole prior to his delinquency (Ex parte Spitale, 276 

App. Div. 632, 97 N.Y.S. 2d 201, affirmed without opinion 

302 N.Y. 616). If the parolee has been a fugitive from justice for any part of that period, such time will not be credited towards his sentence. (See People ex rel. Sormberger v. Martin, 179 Misc. 524, 42 N.Y.S. 2d 197.) 

Commission of Felony. Under Correction Law, sec. 219, if a parolee is convicted of felony, prior to the commencement of his term of imprisonment for such felony he shall be required to serve the balance of the maximum term of his previous sentence. This section is applicable only to parolees from a State prison, not to parolees from reforma tories (People ex rel. Zakowicki v. Morhous, 285 App. Div. 

311, 136 N.Y.S. 2d 353, appeal denied, 305 N.Y. 1052). It is thus different in application from Section 218. The provisions of Section 219 apply if the parolee is convicted without the State for a crime that would be a felony if 762

§ committed within New York. A suspended sentence is considered a conviction within the scope of Section 219 (N.Y. 

State Board of Correction v. Satterfield, 3 App. Div. 2d 

629, 158 N.Y.S. 2d 109).

The interplay between Sections 218 and 219 has given rise to some interesting discussions. Section 218 provides that when the Parole Board acquires knowledge that there is reasonable cause to believe that a parolee has violated his parole, it may "declare such prisoner to be delinquent and time owed shall date from such delinquency," (not the date of the declaration as in Ex parte Spitale, supra). 

However, this action "does not terminate the parole so as to render inapplicable the provisions of Section 219 * * * [The prisoner] *** remains under the Board's jurisdiction and control until he is returned to prison." (People ex rel. Watkins v. Murphy, 3 N.Y. 2d 163.) Under Section 

219, which requires that a parolee convicted of a felony while on parole serve the full maximum sentence which was unexpired at the time he was released on parole, a problem arose concerning a parolee who had been previously declared delinquent, then committed a felony. The question posed was whether such a parolee was on parole, for the purposes of Section 219, at the time he committed the felony. The Watkins case held that the declaration of the prisoner as a delinquent parolee, prior to his committing the felony, did not terminate his parole as of the time of the declaration, so as to exclude the defendant from the application of the more severe terms, concerning time to be served, of Section 219.

Sec. 473(a). Interstate Parole Compact. Correction Law, sections 224 through 225, makes provision for out-of-State parole supervision, incarceration, and the deputization of out-of-State officers. In general, these sections provide for parolees to be allowed to reside out of the convicting State under certain circumstances (such as better opportunity for employment there, relatives residing there, etc.), and 763

§ 

they also allow the other State to supervise the parolee, and imprison him when necessary, subject to his return to the convicting State for imprisonment for the balance of the time owed if the parolee has breached the parole. 764

CHAPTER 41 PARDON, REPRIEVE AND COMMUTATION Sec. 474. Definitions OF SENTENCE Sec. 475. Statutory Regulation Sec. 476. Reprieves Sec. 477. Commutation of Sentence Sec. 478. Pardons Sec. 479. Conditional Pardons 

Sec. 480. Treason

Sec. 481. Determination of Whether Condition has been Breached Sec. 474. Definitions. The New York State Constitution 

(Art. IV, sec. 4) grants to the Governor "the power to grant reprieves, commutations and pardons after conviction, for all offenses except treason and cases of impeachment, upon such conditions and with such restrictions and limitations, as he may think proper," subject to any statutory regulation of the procedures to be followed in applying for a pardon that may be established. The Governor is required, by that section, to report all such actions to the 

Legislature annually.

A reprieve is "the withdrawing of a sentence for an interval of time whereby the execution is suspended." (In re Buchanan, 146 N.Y. 264, quoting 4 Blackstone Comm. 

394.) A reprieve, thus, merely "postpones the day of execution." (Ibid.) 

A pardon is "an act of grace, proceeding from the [executive] which exempts the individual, on whom it is bestowed, from the punishment the law inflicts. * * * It is the private, though official act of the executive magistrate. *** A pardon exempts a person who has received 765

§ 

and accepted it from further punishment for the crime of which he has been convicted, regardless of whether or not [it] *** wipes out the judicial finding of guilt." (People ex rel. Prisament v. Brophy, 287 N.Y. 432.)

A commutation is, like a pardon, an act of grace (People ex rel. Atkins v. Jennings, 248 N.Y. 446). It is "The change of a punishment to which a person has been condemned to a less severe one *** an affirmance of the sentence leaving it in effect in a modified form [and] relates only to the punishment." (People v. Larkman, 137 

Misc. 466, 244 N.Y.S. 431.) The power to commute is merely a part of the power to pardon, but instead of forgiving all punishment only a portion thereof is forgiven. 

Sec. 475. Statutory Regulation. Chapter XIII of Title 12, Part 4, of the Code (Sections 692 through 697) and Sec tions 261 through 266 of the Correction Law regulate the procedures upon reprieves, pardons and commutations of sentence.

Sections 692 through 694 of the Code merely restate the constitutional provision referred to; Section 696 provides that any person violating the provisions of a conditional pardon or commutation, or violating his parole regulations, shall be remanded to the place of his former imprisonment to be imprisoned for the unexpired portion of the original term of his sentence. The section then refers to the Correction Law for the procedures to be had in the determination of whether a violation of conditions has occurred.

Section 697 of the Code, a comparatively new section. added in 1946, provides that those pardoned upon the ground that their innocence has been established by evidence discovered after their conviction (and after the time within which a motion for a new trial could be made) may move, in the convicting court, for the setting aside of the judgment of conviction. The section provides that upon such a motion, the judgment of conviction "must be set aside," and that such action will place the defendant "in 766

PARDON, REPRIEVE AND COMMUTATION 

§ 476 the same position as if the indictment, information or complaint had been dismissed at the conclusion of the trial by the court because of the failure to establish the defendant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt."

The Correction Law sections above cited grant the Governor, or his appointed representative, the power in proceedings arising out of applications for executive clemency to subpoena persons or books and records (Correction Law, sec. 261); to appoint a person to hear the application, take testimony and forward his report thereof to the Governor (id., sec. 262); to administer oaths during such hearings (id., sec. 263); to pay witness fees required (id., sec. 266); to impose penalties upon defaulting witnesses of the same nature as those that may be imposed by a court for disobedience of a subpoena (id., sec. 265), and 

Section 264 provides the form of the subpoena that may be served. Applications for forms to be used in applying for clemency, and the rules established by the Governor which in general govern his actions, may be obtained from the Governor's office. Most of the applications made seek relief from one of the disabilities imposed upon felons, such as loss of right to obtain a license, vote, etc.

Sec. 476. Reprieves. As above noted, a reprieve merely suspends the execution of a sentence for a specified period of time, usually for the purpose of hearing an application for executive clemency in the form of a pardon or commutation, or to allow an appeal or some other action to be taken. One case held that if a reprieve is granted in a capital case until a certain date, on the expiration of the period of the reprieve the warden without further action should execute the sentence (In re Buchanan, 146 

N.Y. 264). See Section 503 of the Code, effective after the

Buchanan case, which requires the fixing of a new date by the court. Other than a stay pending an appeal under 

Section 528 of the Code, only a reprieve will suspend the execution of a sentence after it has been imposed by the court. The courts will not grant suspensions for purposes 767

§ 

such as the allowance of time to a defendant to testify in an application for a new trial (People v. Von Den Corputt, 177 App. Div. 682, 164 N.Y.S. 987). It has been held that the consent of the defendant is not required for a reprieve to become effective (Sterling v. Drake, 29 Ohio St. 457). 

Sec. 477. Commutations of Sentence. A commutation, as above noted, in effect remits or releases some of the punishment and does not affect the finding of guilt (People v. 

Frost, 133 App. Div. 179, 117 N.Y.S. 524). Acceptance of the commutation by the prisoner is not required (People v. Larkman, 137 Misc. 466, 244 N.Y.S. 431). But when conditions are imposed upon a commutation, the conditions remain in effect regardless of the prisoner's acceptance or rejection of them (People v. Larkman, supra; People ex rel. Smith v. Hunt, 177 Misc. 288, 29 N.Y.S. 2d 920).

The Governor may commute the sentence of a fourth offender (People ex rel. Smith v. Hunt, supra). All commutations lie within the discretion of the Governor, and the courts will not review these decisions nor will mandamus lie to compel such a decision (People v. Jennings, 234 

N.Y.S. 489, affirmed 227 App. Div. 763, 236 N.Y.S. 876;

People v. Larkman, supra). Determination of whether a person has violated any of the conditions imposed upon a commutation, as in the case of conditional paroles, will be had in the manner prescribed by the Correction Law (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 676). However, the Board, while determining whether a condition has been violated, cannot impose additional conditions upon the commutation (United States v. Hunt, 15 F. Supp. 608).

Sec. 478. Pardons. Acceptance. It is commonly stated that a pardon must be accepted by the prisoner to become effective, unlike commutations or reprieves (People v. Frost, 133 App. Div. 179, 117 N.Y.S. 524; Burdick v. United 

States, 236 U.S. 79). The acceptance need not be personal; a warden's acceptance is, prima facie, equivalent to a personal acceptance (Ex parte Powell, 73 Ala. 517), as is 768

PARDON, REPRIEVE AND COMMUTATION 

§ 478 delivery to a prisoner's counsel (In re Williams, 149 N.C. 

436). Acceptance is also implied if the prisoner relies upon the pardon (State v. Garrett, 135 Tenn. 617).

Review. Courts do not have the power to go behind the granting of a pardon, on a subsequent writ of habeas corpus, even though it is alleged that the pardon was fraudulently obtained (In re Edgmoin, 8 How. Pr. 478). "The Governor's power to grant reprieves, commutations and pardons upon such conditions, and with such restrictions and limitations, as he thinks proper, is unlimited, and cannot be limited either by statute or court decision." (People v. Larkman, 187 Misc. 135, 64 N.Y.S. 2d 277.)

Effect. Prior to the enactment of Section 696 of the Code, in 1946, it was commonly held that a pardon did not prevent consideration of defendant's conviction as a prior offense, within the purview of the statute providing for second offender punishment (People ex rel. Prisament v. 

Brophy, 287 N.Y. 132; People v. Carlisi, 208 N.Y. 547).

However, such holdings would appear no longer valid in cases wherein the pardon was founded upon the defendant's innocence (Code of Crim. Proc., sec. 697). It should be noted that that section applies only to a Governor's pardon, not that of the President, and that if the pardon does not indicate that it is founded upon the ground of defendant's innocence, the section is not applicable (People v. Larkman, supra). 

Other effects of pardons are: 1. Relief from a judgment of habitual criminality. However, a pardon will not prevent the defendant's subsequent adjudication as a habitual criminal after a subsequent prosecution (Penal Law, sec. 1022); 2. Restoration of the right to practice medicine (Education Law, sec. 1251); real estate brokerage (Real 

Prop. Law, sec. 299, subd. 5); the selling of liquor (Alcoholic Beverage Control Law, sec. 102, subd. 2); or the right to practice as a private detective (General Business 

Law, sec. 74, subd. 2). 

Compare Domestic Relations Law, sec. 58, under which a person sentenced to life loses certain marital rights, 769

§ 

which are not restored by a pardon. An incidental effect of a pardon, on the ground of innocence, is its possible use as a basis for a claim against the State under the Court of Claims Act, sec. 9 subd. 3-a. All such restorations of rights are applicable only when the pardon is founded upon the ground of the defendant's innocence, or if the pardon has been granted specifically to have the effect of removing such disqualification (1949, Op. Atty. Gen. 95). The pardon of a principal does not bar the subsequent prosecution of an accessory to a felony (Penal Law, secs. 1934, 571). 

Sec. 479. Conditional Pardons. Pardons may be conditional (People v. Burns, 143 N.Y. 665) and, on violation of an imposed condition, the violator may be imprisoned for the balance of the original sentence (People v. Potter, 1 Parker 

Cr. 47; People ex rel. Mark v. Lawes, 131 Misc. 426, 226 N.Y.

S. 196). The Attorney General has indicated that imposition of a condition that the prisoner remain outside the state would be unconstitutional (1931, Op. Atty. Gen. 129). 

This opinion is evidently contrary to the weight of authority in other jurisdictions. (See cases collected in 60 A.L.R. 

1415, 1416.) However, it is in accord with the generallyrecognized principle that the conditions imposed may not, in effect, act as an increase of the original sentence by remaining effective for a longer period of time than the original sentence (See State ex rel. Davis v. Hunter, 100 

N.W. 510 [Iowa]; In re Prout, 86 Pac. 275 [Idaho]).

The determination of whether a condition has been broken is discussed in the chapter on "Probation." However, once the fact of the breach has been determined, as above noted, the prisoner may be remanded for the balance of the term originally imposed. It has been held that, in the absence of a breach of condition, a conditional pardon may not be revoked (Ex parte Frazier, 239 S.W. 972 [Tex.]).

Sec. 480. Treason. Section 693 of the Code grants to the 

Governor the power to order the suspension of the execu- 770

PARDON, REPRIEVE AND COMMUTATION § 481 

tion of a sentence or judgment upon a conviction of treason. The suspension may be made effective until the 

Legislature considers the case and either pardons the defendant, or commutes the sentence, or grants a further reprieve, or orders execution of the original sentence.

Sec. 481. Determination of Whether Condition has been 

Breached. As above noted, Section 696 refers to the Correction Law for the procedures to be followed in the determination of whether a condition imposed upon a pardon or commutation of sentence has been breached by the defendant. Under the prior law, where questions of fact were presented concerning the alleged breach, a right to a trial by jury upon those fact issues existed. An information had to be laid before a magistrate charging the violation, and the issue was tried (See People ex rel. Atkins v. Jennings, 248 N.Y. 446). In 1930, the statute was amended to its present form whereby the procedures set forth in the 

Correction Law for determination of whether a parole has been violated, are adopted. In general, these sections provide for the reporting of violations by the parole officer having the parolee in charge; if no parole officer is in charge, it appears that any peace officer may make the report.

The report is made to the Board of Parole, or to any designated officer of the Division of Parole, which officer or Board shall thereupon cause a warrant to be issued for the retaking of the defendant and his imprisonment pending the further action of the Board (Correction Law, sec. 

216). At the next meeting of the Board, which is to be promptly notified of the return of any such defendant, the case of the defendant will be considered, and the prisoner must be given an opportunity to be heard to rebut the charges. However, the defendant is not permitted to have counsel represent him at the hearing (Correction Law, sec. 

218). The decision by the Board is not subject to review in a habeas corpus proceeding, so long as the Board has not acted contrary to law (People ex rel. Mahon v. Warden, 1 771

§ 

Misc. 2d 267, 144 N.Y.S. 2d 837), nor in an Article 78 proceeding (Mummiami v. N.Y. State Board of Parole, 5 App. 

Div. 2d 923, 171 N.Y.S. 2d 1018). See chapter on "Probation and Parole" for a further discussion of these procedures; and for the method of computing the time remaining upon a re-committed defendant's sentence, see chapter on "Sentence." Note should be made that where the condition imposed upon the release provides that upon violation thereof the prisoner shall be re-committed for the remaining period of his original sentence, no credit will be given for the time during which the prisoner was released (People ex rel. Mark v. Lawes, 131 Misc. 426, 226 N.Y.S. 196; People ex rel. Baum v. Morhous, 45 N.Y.S. 2d 772).

A failure of the Board to take action after violation of the conditions does not constitute a waiver of the right to thereafter enforce them (People ex rel. Mullins v. Jackson, 286 App. Div. 938, 142 N.Y.S. 2d 569). But, in Fishbein v. 

State, 204 Misc. 151, 120 N.Y.S. 2d 92, affirmed 282 App. 

Div. 600, 125 N.Y.S. 2d 845, it was indicated that if no attempt is made to retake the violator, and no effort was made by the violator to evade arrest, the Board may thereby lose its right to revoke after expiration of the parole period, even if a warrant for the arrest of the parolee had been issued prior to the expiration of that period.

One granted a release from imprisonment after he has been convicted is not entitled to a hearing, on any constitutional basis, on the determination of whether he has violated the conditions imposed upon his release (In re Kuney, 168 Misc. 285, 55 N.Y.S. 2d 644, aff'd. without opinion 256 

App. Div. 802, 95 N.Y.S. 2d 403, aff'd. without opinion 280

N.Y. 794; accord, Escoe v. Zerbst, 295 U.S. 490; contra, Fleenor v. Hammond, 116 F.2d 982). 772

Form No. 18: Affidavit in Support of Above Motion COURT COUNTY OF The People of the State of New York, against Plaintiff, Defendant.

STATE OF NEW YORK, COUNTY OF 

SS.: 

Ernest Pleader, being duly sworn, deposes and says: I am the attorney for the defendant above named, who, on the .... day of .... 19.., was indicted by the Grand Jury of

County, for the crimes of manslaughter in the first degree and abortion. The defendant was arraigned on the day of ...... 19.., at which time he pleaded not guilty. A copy of the indictment aforesaid is annexed hereto, marked "Exhibit A" and hereby made part of this affidavit. 

The first count of the said indictment charges the defendant with having committed the crime of .... (Here go into an analysis, giving the substance of each of the counts, dates alleged, etc. This summary should be worded to indicate the differences in the circumstances and the lack of connection as between the counts sought to be severed and the others) 

The indictment contains no allegation or intimation that the acts charged in the counts numbered 4, 5 and 6 are in any way connected with the act or transaction upon which the first three counts are based. Nor does it allege that the acts or transactions joined in the indictment constitute parts of a common scheme or plan. Consequently, the defendant's right to a fair and impartial trial, and a proper determination of his guilt or innocence of each of the crimes charged, requires that the first three counts, dealing with the same act or transaction and alleging that death resulted from the alleged acts of the defendant, be tried separately and apart from the distinct and independent charges of the remaining three counts. 

The evidence of death resulting from the abortion alleged in the first three counts would, perforce, have a strong influence upon the determination of the defendant's guilt or innocence of the abortions charged in the remaining counts. Conversely, evidence of the other abortions would distract the jury's mind from the proper consideration of the evidence of the specific charges involved in the first three counts. 

It is respectfully submitted, therefore, that in the light of the seriousness of the first three counts, including a charge of homicide, and the separateness and distinctness of the charges of the first three counts and those of the succeeding counts, with which they are not alleged to have been part of a common plan or scheme, the ends of justice urgently demand a severance of the first three counts, so that they may be tried separately. 

Wherefore, your deponent respectfully requests that such severance, for which no previous application has been made, be granted.

19..

Ernest Pleader, being duly sworn, deposes and says: I am the attorney for the defendant above named, and make this affidavit in support of a motion for an order directing the District Attorney to serve and file a bill of particulars of the items set forth in the notice of motion hereto annexed. 

On the .... day of

County indicted the defendant for the crime of murder in the first degree, it being therein charged that the defendant "on or about the .... day of 

19.., in the County of thought, killed 

19.., the Grand Jury of .. 

wilfully, feloniously and of malice afore by stabbing him with an ice pick and by strangling him." A copy of the said indictment is annexed hereto and made part hereof.

The defendant was duly arraigned on the .... day of ...... 19.. and pleaded not guilty. Thereafter, I conferred with the defendant at the County 

Jail of this county, where he is presently detained, in an effort to obtain information necessary for the preparation and presentation of the defense. 

The defendant asserted and insisted upon his innocence and was firm in his insistence that he knows absolutely nothing concerning the crime charged. 

My further inquiry has revealed that there was no preliminary hearing, inasmuch as the charge against the defendant originated with the Grand Jury. Hence, the defendant and his counsel have no means of obtaining precise information as to the claims that will be made by the District Attorney, other than the general allegations which are set forth in the indictment. 

These, while sufficient to comply with formal requirements, are inadequate for proper preparation for trial, unless amplified by a bill of particulars, as set forth in the notice of motion served herewith. 

The District Attorney's demand for a bill of particulars, which was served on me on the.... day of 

.., pursuant to the provisions of Section 

19.., 788

FORMS 

295-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, makes the relief now sought especially necessary. That demand, a copy of which is annexed hereto and made part hereof, requires the defendant, if he intends to offer testimony which may tend to establish his presence elsewhere than at the scene of the crime at the time of its commission, to serve and file a bill of particulars setting forth the place or places where he claims to have been, together with names, addresses, residences and places of employment of the witnesses on whom he intends to rely to establish the same. Failure to comply with this demand would subject the defendant to the possible exclusion at the trial of testimony of independent witnesses who may be in a position to support a defense of alibi. 

Inasmuch as the indictment merely charges that the crime was committed “on or about" the date stated, and states as the place of its commission only that it was "in the County of ", it is utterly and obviously impossible for him to prepare a defense of alibi, or to comply with the District Attorney's demand. It is therefore respectfully submitted that, unless the 

District Attorney is directed to serve the bill of particulars now sought, the defendant will be deprived of the opportunity to prepare to defend himself and be deprived of due process of law if, as a result, he is precluded from preparing a proper defense and presenting it. 

Wherefore it is respectfully requested that an order be granted for the relief prayed for in the annexed notice of motion. (Signed)

Form No. 45: Order Granting Above Motion 

(No form is provided for an order removing the action from the County Court to the Supreme Court in another county. Since 1953, it has been required by subdivision 2 of Section 346, Code of Criminal Procedure, that this application be made to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the Department in which the indictment is pending. Since the Appellate 

Divisions, unlike the Special and Trial Terms of the Supreme Court and the County Courts, do not require counsel to submit orders for signature but prepare their own, no such form is required for use by the practitioner. As to disposition of the application, see People v. Nicoll, 3 App. Div. 2d 813, 160 N.Y.S. 2d 319.)

I thereupon talked to the judge and respectfully requested that he disqualify himself from trying this case, because he had actively participated in bringing about the indictment, and had made statements in open court, generally construed by his auditors as indicating preconceived bias and prejudice on his part. The County Judge rejected my request and stated he would not tolerate any defendant's "shopping around" for a judge.

My request, and my contemplated application for removal, have no basis in any intention to "shop around", as the judge put it. I have been informed by John Smith, Esq., and several other attorneys who were present in the court room at the time, of the said County Judge's acts and words in this matter. In postponing the imposition of sentence on a prisoner found guilty 807

in his court, the County Judge openly stated that he was informed that the said prisoner had knowledge which would "solve" other crimes committed by the prisoner's "gang"; and that he would give the prisoner, before sentencing him, an opportunity to "come clean" and "help the District Attorney rid society of the members of this vicious gang." He further added that unless the prisoner cooperated, he would be sentenced for the maximum term permitted under the law. I am informed that the prisoner was then immediately taken before the Grand Jury, which was in session at the time, and that his testimony resulted in the indictment of the present defendant. 

In these circumstances, because of the unusual and unseemly haste in which the case has been noticed for trial before the same County Judge, I have not yet been able to prepare and obtain the affidavits and exhibits necessary for the application I intend to make, under Section 344, subd. 1, and Section 346, subd. 1, to remove this matter to the Supreme Court in the same county. a Judge of that Court, and a jury, such trial resulting in a verdict of guilty as charged. 

The uncontradicted evidence presented at the trial indicated that on the date on which the crime is alleged to have been committed the defendant resided, and was domiciled, in the County of ........; that his subsequent absence from the State of New York, as alleged in the indictment, was solely as a result of and in connection with his induction into the United States Army, and during all of such period he was under the orders of his military superiors, under which he was sent to the European theatre of operations. 

During all of this period, the defendant established no residence or domicile elsewhere than in the State of New York, and he consequently remained a resident and domiciliary of the State. Accordingly, a motion was made at the close of the case for a directed verdict of acquittal by reason of the expiration of the limitation period prior to the finding of the indictment, and that his absence under the orders of his military superiors was not such absence as affected his residence in the State or extended the running of the statutory limitation period. The motion, however, was denied. It is respectfully submitted that this denial was erroneous and that, because the bar of the Statute of Limitations is jurisdictional, the Court now lacks power to impose sentence.

Wherefore your deponent prays that an order be made arresting the judgment, setting aside the verdict of the jury and dismissing the indictment. (Signed)

I was arrested by a police officer during the month of and charged with having committed the crime of .... one John Smith. I was arraigned the next day before Robert Jones, Justice of the Peace of the Town of ..., County of 

Before my arraignment, the arresting officer told me that John Smith had signed a confession implicating me as a partner in the commission of the crime, that as 841

19... a result I would surely be convicted, and that the best thing for me to do was to plead guilty, as otherwise the District Attorney might insist on my being imprisoned for the maximum term. I cannot add anything to the facts stated in the annexed moving affidavit of the defendant, not having represented him or known of the matter at the time of the original proceedings. However, since my retainer in this matter some two weeks ago, I have examined the court records pertaining to the arraignment of the defendant, both with regard to the proceedings before Robert Jones, Esq., Justice of the Peace of the Town of 

County of and those in this court. These records, I respectfully point out to the court, and submit, corroborate and bear out the sworn statements of the defendant included in his said affidavit. 

Annexed hereto, made part hereof and marked "Exhibit A” is the certified photostatic copy of the record of the defendant's arraignment before the said Justice of the Peace. As is customary in Justice's Court in these matters, the only record made is by filling in the printed form on the back of the information form. This indicates that the information signed by Officer 

Town Police was read to the defendant, that he either demanded or waived examination, one or the other to be stricken out. A line is drawn through the word "demanded", leaving open the word "waived". No reference, whatever, is made on the form, or anywhere, to the defendant's being advised of his right to counsel. And where the form states: "Appearance for the defendant", it is followed by an unfilled blank. of the...

Annexed hereto, made part hereof, and marked "Exhibit B" are certified transcripts of the minutes of the arraignment and minutes of the sentence of the defendant in this court. Here, the record shows that the defendant was represented by no counsel at any stage of the proceeding, and there is no indication whatever that he was advised of his right to the aid of counsel, or, on the arraignment, that he could have counsel assigned to defend him if he so desired.

It is respectfully submitted that the record alone clearly substantiates the defendant's constitutional rights to being advised that he could be aided by counsel, and it would be flying in the face of the record for the District Attorney to contend otherwise. However, if any issue should be sought to be raised, I further respectfully submit that an order should be made directing the defendant's production in court at a hearing, at which he should be given the opportunity to testify and to present witnesses. 

Wherefore, it is prayed that the relief sought in the notice of motion and the defendant's moving affidavit, for which no previous application has been made, be granted.
